areas_of_operation.title: Area of Operation I. Preflight Preparation

tasks.title: Task A. Pilot Qualifications

questions.question: What certificate and ratings are required to act as pilot-in-command of a helicopter on an instrument flight rules flight plan in controlled airspace?
questions.answer: The pilot must hold at least a private pilot certificate with a helicopter category rating and an instrument rating for rotorcraft (or helicopter). For commercial operations, a commercial pilot certificate with the appropriate ratings is required. The pilot must also carry the certificate and a valid government-issued photo ID while exercising the privileges of that certificate.

questions.question: What are the instrument currency requirements a helicopter pilot must meet before acting as PIC under IFR or in IMC?
questions.answer: Within the preceding 6 calendar months, the pilot must have performed and logged at least 6 instrument approaches, holding procedures and tasks, and intercepting and tracking courses through the use of navigational electronic systems. These requirements must be accomplished in a helicopter or an approved helicopter simulator/FTD. If currency lapses, the pilot must pass an Instrument Proficiency Check (IPC) with an authorized instructor or examiner before acting as PIC under IFR.

questions.question: What recordkeeping is required after you complete instrument approaches for the purpose of maintaining instrument currency?
questions.answer: The pilot must log the instrument approaches in their logbook or other acceptable personal flight record. Each entry should include the date, location, type of approach, and the aircraft or simulator used. If an approved simulator or FTD is used, a logbook endorsement from a CFII or authorized instructor is required to credit those approaches toward instrument currency.

questions.question: You completed your last six instrument approaches in a fixed-wing airplane because your helicopter was down for maintenance. It has now been four months since those approaches. Can you legally serve as PIC of a helicopter on an IFR flight plan today?
questions.answer: No. Instrument currency for rotorcraft must be accomplished in a helicopter or a helicopter simulator/FTD approved for that purpose. Approaches flown in a fixed-wing airplane do not satisfy instrument currency requirements for acting as PIC of a helicopter under IFR. Since your last qualifying helicopter instrument approaches were more than 6 calendar months ago, you are no longer current and must complete an Instrument Proficiency Check (IPC) in a helicopter or approved helicopter FTD/simulator before acting as PIC under IFR.

questions.question: A commercial helicopter pilot with an instrument-helicopter rating wants to fly passengers on an IFR charter flight. Assuming this operation requires Part 135 certification, what other certification-related requirements must be met before the flight departs?
questions.answer: The pilot must: (1) hold a valid First Class or Second Class medical certificate (BasicMed is NOT acceptable for Part 135 commercial operations); (2) be authorized under the operator's Part 135 certificate and applicable operations specification; (3) meet all 14 CFR Part 135 pilot qualification requirements including recent flight time, PIC experience thresholds, and any required company check rides or training; (4) ensure the certificate, ratings, and medical are current and on their person; and (5) have completed any required ground or flight training for the specific helicopter make and model if required by Part 135 ops specs. [Note: If the flight were conducted under Part 91 by a private pilot without compensation, fewer requirements would apply, but accepting compensation for carrying passengers typically requires Part 135 certification or falls under 14 CFR 61.113 limitations.]
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.3, 14 CFR 61.23, 14 CFR Part 135 Subpart E

questions.question: A helicopter pilot's instrument rating expired more than 12 calendar months ago. What is the process they must complete before acting as PIC under IFR, and who is authorized to administer it?
questions.answer: Once more than 12 calendar months have passed since the pilot last met instrument currency requirements, they are no longer eligible to log approaches with a safety pilot — they must complete an Instrument Proficiency Check (IPC). The IPC must be given by an authorized check airman (for Part 121/135) or a CFII (certificated flight instructor with instrument rating) authorized to conduct it in the rotorcraft category. The IPC must be conducted in a helicopter or an approved helicopter FTD/simulator and must cover the elements specified in the Instrument Rating ACS or Practical Test Standards applicable to rotorcraft. After the IPC, the pilot must log it and can then resume acting as PIC under IFR.

questions.question: A private helicopter pilot holds a BasicMed authorization instead of a traditional FAA medical certificate. They want to fly a 5-passenger helicopter IFR cross-country at 12,000 feet MSL entirely within the United States. Walk me through every BasicMed limitation that applies to this scenario and whether the flight is legal.
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR Part 68 and 14 CFR 61.113(i), BasicMed allows a pilot to act as PIC without a traditional FAA medical certificate provided: (1) the aircraft has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than 12,500 lbs — must verify; (2) no more than 6 occupants (pilot + 5 passengers) — this scenario has 5 passengers plus the pilot, which equals 6 total, exactly at the limit; (3) the flight remains within the United States — satisfied; (4) altitude must not exceed 18,000 ft MSL — 12,000 ft satisfies this; (5) airspeed must not exceed 250 KIAS — must verify aircraft capability; (6) the flight cannot be for compensation or hire; (7) the pilot must have held a valid FAA medical at some point after July 14, 2006; (8) the pilot must have completed a BasicMed medical education course within the preceding 24 calendar months; (9) the pilot must have received a physical exam from a state-licensed physician within the preceding 48 calendar months. If all conditions are met, the flight as described is legal under BasicMed, including IFR operations, provided the pilot also holds an instrument rating for rotorcraft.
questions.follow_up: The helicopter in this scenario has a certificated max takeoff weight of 13,000 pounds. Can the pilot still use BasicMed?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. BasicMed is limited to aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of 12,500 pounds or less. At 13,000 lbs MTOW, the aircraft exceeds that limit and the pilot cannot exercise BasicMed privileges. They would need to hold a valid FAA-issued medical certificate appropriate for the operation — at minimum a third-class medical for private operations — before acting as PIC.

questions.question: During preflight, you realize your logbook is not on board the helicopter. Your last IFR flight with six approaches was logged 5 months ago. ATC calls and asks if you are IFR capable for a pop-up clearance. Are you legally current, and what are your obligations regarding logbook access and documentation?
questions.answer: You are likely still within currency if the six approaches, holding, and tracking/intercepting were performed within the last 6 calendar months, but the burden of proof is on you. Pilots are not required to carry their logbook while flying — there is no regulation requiring the logbook to be on board the aircraft. However, 14 CFR 61.51 requires pilots to present their logbook for inspection upon request by the FAA, an NTSB representative, or any federal, state, or local law enforcement officer. If you accept the IFR clearance and are later questioned about your currency, you must be able to produce evidence from your logbook. If you are uncertain whether you logged the required approaches within the 6-month window, the conservative and correct decision is to decline the IFR clearance and not act as PIC under IFR until you can confirm your currency from your records — consistent with sound ADM and SRM principles. Accepting the clearance while unsure of your currency would be a violation of 14 CFR 61.57(c).
questions.follow_up: What happens if it turns out your last qualifying approaches were exactly 6 calendar months and 2 days ago? Are you still current?
questions.follow_up_answer: No, you are not current. The 6 calendar month window means you must have completed the required tasks within the 6 calendar months preceding the month of the flight. Calendar months run from the first to the last day of the month regardless of the day of the original event. So if the approaches were performed more than 6 calendar months ago, currency has lapsed and you may not act as PIC under IFR until you complete an Instrument Proficiency Check (IPC) with an authorized CFII or check airman in a helicopter or approved helicopter FTD/simulator.

questions.question: As a certificated private pilot helicopter, what are your basic flight privileges under 14 CFR Part 61?
questions.answer: A private pilot helicopter certificate allows you to act as pilot-in-command of a helicopter for personal transportation, carry passengers, and fly for your own purposes. You may not act as PIC for compensation or hire, except in limited circumstances such as being reimbursed for pro-rata share of operating expenses when the flight is incidental to a business, or in certain search and rescue situations when authorized. You may also tow a glider or unpowered ultralight if you hold a category rating for that type.

questions.question: What does it mean when a pilot's certificate carries the limitation 'helicopter' under the aircraft category and class? Does a helicopter rating allow you to also fly powered-lift aircraft?
questions.answer: A 'helicopter' rating under the rotorcraft category means the pilot is authorized to fly helicopters only. It does not allow operation of powered-lift aircraft, gyroplanes, or any other category or class. Each category and class rating is independent. To fly a gyroplane, for example, the pilot would need a separate rotorcraft-gyroplane rating.

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 61.113, a private pilot may carry passengers for compensation or hire only in very specific limited situations. Name one of those authorized exceptions.
questions.answer: One authorized exception under 14 CFR 61.113(b) is that a private pilot may share the operating expenses of a flight with passengers, provided the expenses are shared equally among all occupants including the pilot. Another exception is that a private pilot who is a business owner may demonstrate an aircraft to a prospective buyer if the pilot is not employed to fly. Additional exceptions include certain charitable, volunteer, or community service operations authorized under 14 CFR 61.113(c), (d), (e), (f), and (g).

questions.question: You hold a private pilot certificate with a helicopter rating and a valid third-class medical. A friend asks if you can fly him to a business meeting — he offers to pay all the fuel costs in advance. Can you legally do this, and why or why not?
questions.answer: No, this is not legal. Although 14 CFR 61.113(b) allows a private pilot to share operating expenses with passengers, the key requirement is that expenses must be shared — meaning all occupants including the pilot each pay their pro-rata portion. If your passenger pays ALL the fuel costs, you are not sharing — you are being compensated. This crosses into 'compensation or hire,' which private pilots are prohibited from under 14 CFR 61.113(a). Additionally, the flight must not be for the purpose of serving the passenger's business travel as a charter; it must be incidental to your own legitimate purpose.

questions.question: You are a private pilot helicopter with an instrument rating. You've completed the BasicMed process. Your friend wants to fly with you tonight on a VFR cross-country in a light helicopter. What specific BasicMed limitations apply to this flight?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR Part 68 and 61.113(i), BasicMed authorizes flight when the aircraft has a maximum certificated takeoff weight no greater than 12,500 lbs, carries no more than 6 occupants (pilot + 5 passengers), does not exceed 18,000 ft MSL, does not exceed 250 KIAS, and remains within the United States. The flight cannot be for compensation or hire. The pilot must have held a valid FAA medical certificate at some point after July 14, 2006, completed the medical education course within the past 24 months, and had a physical exam from a state-licensed physician within the past 48 months. For a VFR night flight, none of these BasicMed parameters are violated as long as the helicopter and conditions meet those limits.

questions.question: You just earned your private pilot helicopter certificate, but you've never flown a turbine-powered helicopter. Your employer, who runs a sightseeing tour company, wants you to fly a turbine helicopter to pick up parts — not passengers. What limitations apply before you can legally act as PIC?
questions.answer: Multiple limitations apply here. First, under 14 CFR 61.31(a), you must hold the appropriate category and class rating, which you do (rotorcraft-helicopter). However, under 14 CFR 61.31(b), if the turbine helicopter requires a type rating, you must hold that type rating before acting as PIC. Additionally, acting as PIC for an employer — even without passengers — may constitute acting for compensation or hire depending on the employment relationship, which private pilots are prohibited from under 14 CFR 61.113(a). This flight would likely require at least a commercial pilot certificate. You should also review whether the specific turbine helicopter requires a type rating under 14 CFR 61.31(a).

questions.question: A private pilot helicopter holds both an airplane single-engine land rating and a helicopter rating. During a flight review in an airplane, the CFI endorses the pilot's logbook as satisfying 14 CFR 61.56. Does this flight review also satisfy the biennial flight review requirement for helicopter operations, or does the pilot need a separate helicopter flight review?
questions.answer: A flight review completed in any aircraft for which the pilot holds a rating satisfies the 14 CFR 61.56 requirement for all ratings that pilot holds. 14 CFR 61.56 does not require a separate review for each rating held — it requires a review with a flight in an aircraft for which the pilot is rated, one hour of flight training, and one hour of ground training. A review conducted in the airplane satisfies the overall flight review requirement. However, it is important to note that the flight review itself must include a review of current Federal Aviation Regulations and a flight assessment of the pilot's skills, and must be conducted by an authorized instructor. While legally current for helicopter privileges, a prudent pilot would benefit from a category-specific review in a helicopter if not recently flown.
questions.follow_up: What if the pilot completes the flight review in the airplane but has not flown a helicopter in 18 months — are they still current to carry helicopter passengers at night?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot's biennial flight review currency is satisfied by the airplane flight review under 14 CFR 61.56. However, to carry passengers at night in a helicopter, the pilot also needs night currency under 14 CFR 61.57(b) — three takeoffs and three landings to a full stop during the period beginning 1 hour after sunset and ending 1 hour before sunrise, in the same category and class of aircraft. 'Category and class' for currency purposes means rotorcraft-helicopter, so night landings in the airplane do NOT satisfy night currency for helicopter passenger-carrying flights. The pilot is legally current from a flight review standpoint but NOT night current in the helicopter.

questions.question: A commercial helicopter pilot whose medical certificate has expired decides to use BasicMed to continue flying. They plan to fly a 12-passenger tour helicopter at an FAA-authorized air tour operation. What privilege limitations make this scenario problematic, and what would need to change for legal operations?
questions.answer: This scenario has two fundamental problems. First, BasicMed under 14 CFR 61.113(i) and 14 CFR Part 68 explicitly prohibits flight for compensation or hire — commercial air tour operations involve compensation, so BasicMed does not authorize this activity regardless of the aircraft's weight. Second, air tour operations under Part 135 or Part 119 require an appropriate medical certificate (first- or second-class for required crewmembers), not BasicMed. To legally conduct commercial air tour flights, the pilot must hold a valid FAA medical certificate appropriate to the operation — typically a second-class medical for commercial operations. The pilot would need to obtain an AME-issued medical certificate and ensure it is current for the class required by the operation.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.113(i), 14 CFR Part 68, 14 CFR 61.23, 14 CFR Part 135
questions.follow_up: If this same commercial pilot loses their medical and uses BasicMed to fly a privately-owned helicopter recreationally, but the helicopter is certificated for 14 passengers and weighs 15,000 lbs MTOW, does BasicMed still authorize the flight?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. BasicMed under 14 CFR Part 68 and 61.113(i) limits operations to aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of 12,500 lbs or less. At 15,000 lbs MTOW, this helicopter exceeds the BasicMed weight limit regardless of how many seats are occupied or the non-commercial nature of the flight. The pilot would require a valid FAA-issued medical certificate to act as PIC of that aircraft.

questions.question: What are the three classes of FAA medical certificates, and what certificate class is required to exercise commercial helicopter pilot privileges?
questions.answer: The three classes are First Class, Second Class, and Third Class. To exercise commercial pilot privileges, a pilot must hold at least a Second Class medical certificate. A First Class is required for ATP privileges. Third Class is sufficient for private pilot privileges only.

questions.question: How long is a Second Class medical certificate valid for a pilot who is 38 years old and holds a commercial helicopter certificate?
questions.answer: For a pilot under age 40, a Second Class medical certificate is valid for 12 calendar months for commercial pilot privileges. After that 12-month period, it downgrades to Third Class privileges for an additional 48 calendar months (until the end of the 60th month after issuance for pilots under 40). Since this pilot is 38, the Second Class privileges last 12 months from the month of issuance.

questions.question: Name at least three conditions that can cause a temporary disqualification from acting as pilot-in-command, even if your medical certificate is still current.
questions.answer: Conditions causing temporary disqualification include: (1) use of any medication that affects faculties contrary to safety — such as over-the-counter antihistamines or sedatives; (2) any illness or injury that would interfere with safe performance, such as a head cold affecting equilibrium or sinus pressure; (3) impairment from alcohol consumption within 8 hours of flight or while having a blood alcohol content of 0.04% or greater; (4) scuba diving within the prescribed time limits before flight (generally 12–24 hours depending on dive profile); (5) fatigue or lack of sleep sufficient to impair judgment and safe control. Per 14 CFR 61.53, a pilot cannot act as PIC if unable to meet the medical standards for their certificate due to illness, medication effects, or any condition impairing faculties or safe performance of duties.

questions.question: You are a 45-year-old commercial helicopter pilot. Your Second Class medical was issued on March 15th of last year. It is now April 1st of this year. Can you legally fly a Part 135 charter flight today, and why or why not?
questions.answer: No, you cannot legally fly the Part 135 charter flight. For a pilot age 40 or older, Second Class medical privileges are valid for 12 calendar months from the month of issuance. The medical was issued in March of last year, so Second Class privileges expired at the end of March of this year. As of April 1st, the certificate has downgraded to Third Class privileges only, which do not authorize commercial pilot operations under Part 135. You would need to obtain a new medical examination before conducting the charter flight.

questions.question: A private helicopter pilot is prescribed a short course of antibiotics by their doctor for a sinus infection. The doctor says they are cleared to fly. Can this pilot legally act as PIC?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Under 14 CFR 61.53, a pilot must not act as PIC when they know of any medical condition that would make them unable to meet the requirements of their medical certificate. The pilot must make two independent assessments: (1) whether the underlying condition — the sinus infection — itself impairs safe flight (sinus congestion can cause sinus squeeze, equilibrium issues, and pain during altitude changes); and (2) whether the medication itself has side effects that could impair performance, such as drowsiness. The doctor's clearance is advisory; the legal determination rests with the pilot. If either the illness or the medication affects faculties contrary to safety, the pilot is self-disqualified regardless of the doctor's opinion.

questions.question: You receive a BasicMed physical from your family physician and complete the online medical education course. What helicopter operations are you authorized to conduct under BasicMed, and what are the key limitations you must observe?
questions.answer: Under BasicMed (14 CFR Part 68 and 14 CFR 61.113(i)), you may act as PIC of a helicopter with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of up to 12,500 lbs, carrying no more than 5 passengers (6 total occupants including pilot), at altitudes up to 18,000 ft MSL, at airspeeds up to 250 KIAS, and only within the United States. You cannot fly for compensation or hire. The online medical education course must be completed every 24 calendar months, and the physical examination with a state-licensed physician must be completed every 48 calendar months. You must also have held a valid FAA medical certificate at some point after July 14, 2006.

questions.question: A commercial helicopter pilot discovers during preflight that they were unknowingly exposed to carbon monoxide during a maintenance shop visit the previous day and feels slightly fatigued and has a mild headache. Their First Class medical is current and valid. What is their legal and practical obligation before flight, and what regulatory framework governs this situation?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.53, a pilot must not act as PIC or required flight crewmember when they have a known medical deficiency that would make them unable to meet the standards for their medical certificate. Carbon monoxide poisoning — even subclinical — impairs cognitive function, judgment, and coordination, all of which are required for safe PIC operations. Fatigue and headache after CO exposure are recognized symptoms of carboxyhemoglobin elevation. Regardless of the validity of the First Class medical, the pilot is self-disqualified and must not fly until asymptomatic and medically evaluated. The pilot should also report the suspected CO exposure to maintenance and document the event. The currency of the medical certificate is irrelevant — 61.53 creates an independent, ongoing duty of self-assessment that applies between medical exams.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot flies anyway and an accident occurs, what additional regulatory violation beyond 61.53 could the FAA pursue?
questions.follow_up_answer: The FAA could pursue a violation of 14 CFR 91.13 (careless or reckless operation), which is one of the broadest enforcement tools in the FARs. Acting as PIC while knowingly symptomatic from CO poisoning — with documented impairment indicators — would likely constitute careless or reckless operation endangering persons or property. This violation carries potential certificate suspension or revocation and is separate from any 61.53 self-disqualification finding.

questions.question: As a commercial helicopter pilot preparing for a revenue flight, what documents must you personally have on your person or in the aircraft to legally exercise your commercial pilot privileges?
questions.answer: The pilot must have: (1) a valid commercial pilot certificate (or higher) with appropriate category and class ratings, (2) a valid medical certificate (at least a third-class, but second-class is required to exercise commercial privileges without BasicMed), (3) a government-issued photo ID such as a driver's license or passport, and (4) a current logbook endorsement or other evidence of a flight review completed within the preceding 24 calendar months per 14 CFR 61.56. The aircraft must also have its required documents onboard (AROW), but those are separate from the pilot's personal documents.

questions.question: What class of medical certificate is required to exercise commercial pilot privileges, and how long is it valid for a pilot who is 29 years old?
questions.answer: A second-class medical certificate is required to exercise commercial pilot privileges. For a pilot under 40 years of age, a second-class medical certificate is valid for 12 calendar months for commercial pilot privileges. After 12 months it downgrades to third-class privileges only. Note: BasicMed cannot be used to exercise commercial pilot privileges — it is prohibited for compensation or hire operations.

questions.question: Does a commercial helicopter pilot need a separate helicopter type rating on their certificate to fly a Robinson R44 for hire, and what rating is required on the certificate?
questions.answer: No separate type rating is required for the R44 because it does not require a type rating — type ratings are only required for aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight over 12,500 lbs or turbojet-powered aircraft. For a commercial helicopter pilot to fly the R44 for hire, their commercial pilot certificate must show the rotorcraft category and helicopter class rating. No type rating is needed.

questions.question: You hold a commercial pilot certificate with a helicopter rating and your second-class medical expired 13 months ago. A friend offers to pay you to fly him to a hunting camp in a private helicopter. Can you legally make this flight, and what documents would you need?
questions.answer: No, you cannot make this flight as a commercial operation with an expired second-class medical. A second-class medical is valid for commercial privileges for 12 calendar months. After 13 months, the second-class has downgraded to third-class privileges for private operations only. Additionally, BasicMed cannot be used for operations conducted for compensation or hire. To legally accept payment, you would need a current second-class medical certificate. If the flight were conducted purely as a private operation (no compensation, not for hire), you could potentially use a current third-class medical or BasicMed, but you could not legally accept payment in that case under your commercial certificate's privilege without meeting the medical requirement.

questions.question: You are a commercial helicopter pilot hired to fly a Part 135 air taxi operation. You left your pilot certificate at home but have a digital photo of it on your phone. You have your physical medical certificate and government-issued ID. Can you legally conduct this flight, and what are your options?
questions.answer: No, you cannot legally conduct this flight. 14 CFR 61.3(a) requires the pilot certificate to be in the pilot's personal possession or readily accessible in the aircraft. A digital photo does not satisfy this requirement. Acceptable alternatives include a temporary certificate issued under 14 CFR 61.17 or airman verification from the FAA. Part 135 operators may have stricter OpSpec requirements. The compliant option is to retrieve the physical certificate or obtain a temporary certificate before flight.

questions.question: You recently completed your commercial helicopter checkride and the examiner issued you a temporary certificate. Your permanent certificate hasn't arrived yet. A charter company wants to hire you to fly immediately. Is your temporary certificate sufficient to exercise commercial privileges, and does it have any limitations compared to a permanent certificate?
questions.answer: Yes, a temporary airman certificate issued under 14 CFR 61.17 is valid for up to 120 days and has the same privileges as the permanent certificate it represents. You may exercise full commercial pilot privileges with the temporary certificate while awaiting your permanent certificate. The temporary certificate must be in your physical possession during flight, just as the permanent certificate would be. The only limitation is its expiration — if the permanent certificate does not arrive within 120 days, you would need to contact the FAA Airmen Certification Branch to resolve the issue.

questions.question: A commercial helicopter pilot holds an instrument rating and is flying a Part 91 compensation flight in IMC. The pilot's instrument currency has lapsed — they have not completed the required instrument experience in the past 6 months. What documents and currency requirements are now at issue, and what specific privileges has this pilot lost?
questions.answer: Two distinct issues are at play. First, instrument currency under 14 CFR 61.57(c) requires, within the preceding 6 calendar months, 6 instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting/tracking of courses using navigation systems. A pilot who has not met this requirement is not instrument current and cannot legally act as PIC under IFR or in IMC — regardless of their commercial certificate or medical certificate status. The documents required are still the same (commercial certificate with instrument rating, second-class medical, government ID), but the privilege of IFR flight as PIC is suspended until currency is restored. To restore currency, the pilot must either complete the required instrument experience with a safety pilot or complete an IPC with an authorized instructor under 14 CFR 61.57(d). Flying in IMC without instrument currency is a violation regardless of whether the certificate and medical are physically present.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot wanted to regain instrument currency today, what is the minimum they must do, and can they do it in actual IMC with a safety pilot?
questions.follow_up_answer: To restore instrument currency, the pilot must log at least 6 instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting/tracking of courses within a 6-month period. This can be accomplished in actual IMC, simulated IMC under a view-limiting device, or in a qualified flight simulator/FTD. If done in actual IMC with a safety pilot, the safety pilot must be a rated pilot who meets the requirements of 14 CFR 61.3 for the conditions of flight (i.e., instrument rated and current themselves if serving as PIC). However, if the pilot is more than 12 months past their last instrument experience, they cannot restore currency with a safety pilot alone — they must complete an Instrument Proficiency Check (IPC) with an authorized instructor. The 6-to-12 month window allows self-restoration; beyond 12 months requires an IPC.

questions.question: A commercial helicopter pilot wants to operate under BasicMed instead of a second-class medical to reduce the cost and frequency of FAA medical exams. They plan to use BasicMed while flying passengers for compensation in a privately-owned helicopter under Part 91. Is this legally permissible, and what are the relevant document requirements under BasicMed for this scenario?
questions.answer: No, this is not legally permissible. 14 CFR Part 68 (BasicMed) explicitly prohibits its use for operations conducted for compensation or hire. Even if all other BasicMed requirements are met — including the state-licensed physician exam every 48 months, the online medical education course every 24 months, the aircraft's maximum certificated takeoff weight being under 12,500 lbs, and operating within the United States below 18,000 ft MSL at or below 250 KIAS with no more than 6 occupants — the prohibition on compensation and hire operations is absolute. The pilot must hold a valid second-class medical certificate to legally accept compensation for this flight. Under BasicMed, the pilot must carry the completed FAA medical examination checklist signed by the state-licensed physician and evidence of completing the online medical education course, in addition to their pilot certificate and government-issued photo ID.
questions.follow_up: If this same pilot flies the identical passenger on the identical route but accepts no compensation and takes no passengers for hire, can they now use BasicMed, and does the fact that they hold a commercial certificate change anything?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, if no compensation is involved and the flight is purely private in nature (Part 91, no hire), a commercial certificate holder may use BasicMed to exercise private pilot privileges. Holding a commercial certificate does not disqualify a pilot from using BasicMed — it simply means they are operating at private pilot privilege levels during that flight. The commercial certificate itself is still a valid document and must be carried. BasicMed does not change the required documents on the pilot's person; it only replaces the requirement for an FAA-issued medical certificate. The pilot must still carry their pilot certificate, government-issued photo ID, the physician examination checklist, and proof of completing the medical education course. The key point is that the flight must not involve any compensation, hire, or Part 135/119 operations.

questions.question: Under BasicMed, what is the maximum certificated takeoff weight of an aircraft you are allowed to fly?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR Part 68 (BasicMed), the maximum certificated takeoff weight is 12,500 pounds. This applies to helicopters as well as fixed-wing aircraft.

questions.question: How often must a BasicMed pilot complete the required medical education course and the physical examination from a state-licensed physician?
questions.answer: The medical education course must be completed every 24 months, and the physical examination by a state-licensed physician must be completed every 48 months. Both must remain current for BasicMed privileges to be valid.

questions.question: Can a pilot operating under BasicMed fly for compensation or hire?
questions.answer: No. BasicMed explicitly prohibits operations conducted for compensation or hire. It is limited to private pilot privileges only. If a pilot intends to fly for compensation or hire in any capacity, a valid FAA medical certificate issued under 14 CFR Part 67 is required.

questions.question: You hold a commercial helicopter certificate and want to use BasicMed for a personal cross-country flight in a turbine-powered helicopter with a max gross weight of 10,000 pounds, carrying four passengers. Does BasicMed cover this operation? Walk me through your analysis.
questions.answer: Yes, this operation is covered under BasicMed, provided all other requirements are met. The helicopter's max gross weight of 10,000 lbs is below the 12,500 lb limit. Four passengers plus the pilot equals five occupants, which is within the six-occupant maximum (pilot + 5 passengers). BasicMed does not restrict turbine-powered aircraft. The flight is not for compensation or hire. The pilot must have a current medical education course (within 24 months) and a physician exam (within 48 months), and must have held a valid FAA medical at some point after July 14, 2006. As long as those requirements are satisfied, the operation is legal under BasicMed.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot using BasicMed wants to fly a photo mission where a media company is paying the aircraft owner — not the pilot directly — for use of the helicopter. The pilot receives no payment. Is this permissible under BasicMed?
questions.answer: No, this operation is NOT permissible under BasicMed. When an aircraft is operated in furtherance of a business for which compensation is received—even if paid to the owner rather than the pilot—the operation is considered 'for compensation or hire' under 14 CFR 61.113(i). BasicMed authorizes only operations that are not 'for compensation or hire.' The pilot must hold a valid Part 67 medical certificate and operate under commercial privileges for this photo mission.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.113(i); 14 CFR Part 68; FAA Legal Interpretation on compensation or hire

questions.question: A pilot's third-class FAA medical certificate expired two years ago. They have never completed a BasicMed medical education course. Can they legally fly using BasicMed today? What do they need to do first?
questions.answer: No, they cannot fly under BasicMed today. To use BasicMed, the pilot must have held a valid FAA medical certificate issued after July 14, 2006 — that historical requirement is met if they previously held any class of medical. However, they must also complete the medical education course (valid 24 months) and have a physical examination completed by a state-licensed physician (valid 48 months) before exercising BasicMed privileges. Since neither has been done, they must complete both steps before they can legally fly under BasicMed.

questions.question: A pilot operating under BasicMed is flying a helicopter at 17,500 feet MSL on a cross-country when ATC offers a climb to FL190 to avoid turbulence. Can the pilot accept? What if the helicopter's service ceiling is FL200?
questions.answer: No, the pilot cannot accept the climb to FL190 (19,000 feet MSL). BasicMed imposes a hard altitude ceiling of 18,000 feet MSL. Regardless of the aircraft's performance capability or ATC's offer, operating above 18,000 feet MSL is prohibited under BasicMed. The aircraft's service ceiling of FL200 is irrelevant to the BasicMed altitude restriction — the regulatory limit is 18,000 feet MSL, not the aircraft's performance ceiling. The pilot should decline the clearance and advise ATC of the altitude restriction.
questions.follow_up: The pilot accepts the FL190 clearance anyway, arguing the turbulence was severe and it was a safety-of-flight decision. Is that a valid defense, and what are the potential consequences?
questions.follow_up_answer: While the FAA recognizes that pilots have emergency authority under 14 CFR 91.3 to deviate from regulations to the extent necessary to meet an emergency, routinely exceeding a BasicMed altitude limit because turbulence was 'severe' would likely not meet the threshold of a true emergency justifying deviation. The pilot would need to demonstrate the deviation was absolutely necessary for safety. Even if accepted as an emergency deviation, the pilot would be required to submit a written report to the FAA if requested under 14 CFR 91.3(b). Potential consequences include certificate action, civil penalty, and invalidation of BasicMed privileges if the FAA determines the deviation was not justified. The better course of action would have been to request a deviation around the turbulence at or below 18,000 feet MSL.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot using BasicMed discovers mid-flight that their medical education course expired three days ago. They are currently 30 miles from their destination with no weather issues. What are their obligations, and what should they do?
questions.answer: At the moment the medical education course expires, the pilot no longer meets the currency requirements to exercise BasicMed privileges. Technically, continuing the flight constitutes operating as pilot in command without a valid medical authorization. The pilot faces a difficult situation: landing immediately at the nearest suitable area may itself constitute a continued violation. The most defensible course of action is to land at the nearest suitable airport or helipad as soon as practicable to minimize the unauthorized operation. Upon landing, the pilot should not fly again until the medical education course is renewed. The pilot should document the situation. Note that a previously held FAA medical certificate would not automatically cover this flight either, as it is expired. This highlights the critical importance of tracking BasicMed currency dates just as carefully as flight review and currency requirements.
questions.follow_up: Could the pilot invoke 14 CFR 91.3 emergency authority to justify completing the flight to their intended destination rather than diverting?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. 14 CFR 91.3 emergency authority applies to situations involving threats to safety of flight — not to situations where the pilot discovers an administrative currency lapse. There is no mechanical emergency, weather emergency, or other safety-of-flight threat in this scenario. Using 91.3 to justify completing a flight simply because diverting is inconvenient would be an improper application of the emergency authority provision and would not be accepted by the FAA as a valid defense. The pilot must divert as soon as practicable. This situation could also potentially be mitigated through NASA ASRS reporting, which provides limited protection from certificate action but does not shield against willful violations.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 68; 14 CFR 68.9; 14 CFR 61.113(i); 14 CFR 91.3; NASA ASRS Advisory Circular AC 00-46

questions.question: What is the difference between currency and proficiency as they apply to a helicopter pilot?
questions.answer: Currency means meeting the minimum regulatory requirements to legally act as pilot-in-command — for example, the 3 takeoffs and landings within 90 days required by 14 CFR 61.57. Proficiency is a higher standard: the actual skill level needed to safely handle the full range of conditions you may encounter in flight, including emergencies. A pilot can be legally current but dangerously unproficient.

questions.question: What are the minimum recent flight experience requirements for a helicopter pilot to act as PIC carrying passengers under day VFR?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.57(a), a pilot must have made at least 3 takeoffs and 3 landings within the preceding 90 days in the same category and class of aircraft — in this case, a helicopter. These must be actual takeoffs and landings, not simulated. There is no minimum hour requirement for recency; only the three-takeoff-and-landing rule applies for day VFR passenger-carrying.

questions.question: According to FAA research, at what point do helicopter accident rates show a significant decrease related to time in a specific aircraft model?
questions.answer: According to FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13, accident rates decrease significantly after approximately 100 hours in a specific helicopter type or model. This reinforces the concept that total flight hours alone are not an accurate measure of proficiency — pilots transitioning to a new aircraft type are at elevated risk even if they have thousands of total hours.

questions.question: You completed your instrument currency requirements last week — you logged the required approaches and holds. Tonight you're planning an IFR flight in IMC to a mountain destination with a complex non-precision approach. What risk factors related to proficiency versus currency should you evaluate before accepting this flight?
questions.answer: Meeting the minimum IFR currency requirements under 14 CFR 61.57(c) only means you are legally permitted to fly IFR. True proficiency for this specific flight requires evaluating: (1) whether your recent instrument practice included similar approach types in actual IMC versus simulator or VMC conditions, (2) your experience with terrain/mountainous environments and non-precision approach techniques, (3) your actual scan and workload management ability under pressure, and (4) whether you have sufficient hours in this specific helicopter model to handle a demanding approach. Currency alone does not equal readiness for a high-risk, complex IFR flight.

questions.question: A pilot returns from a 6-week vacation and has not flown since. Their medical and flight review are both current. They are legal to fly solo but plan to immediately take three passengers on a cross-country flight. What personal minimums framework should this pilot apply before making that decision?
questions.answer: While the pilot may be legally current for day VFR passenger-carrying after completing 3 takeoffs and 3 landings within the preceding 90 days, a 6-week break creates a meaningful proficiency gap. The pilot should: (1) complete solo currency flights or a dual refresher before carrying passengers, (2) apply a personal minimums checklist that includes higher weather minimums and simpler routes until proficiency is restored, (3) recognize that ADM and workload management skills degrade with inactivity, and (4) consider that approximately 80% of accidents involve human factors — returning from a break is a recognized elevated-risk period. Flying legal does not mean flying safe.

questions.question: You are transitioning from a piston helicopter with a manual throttle to a turbine helicopter with a FADEC system. Your logbook shows 2,000 total helicopter hours but only 8 hours in the new type. How does this scenario specifically illustrate the proficiency versus currency risk?
questions.answer: This scenario is a textbook example of the currency-proficiency gap. The pilot is legally current based on their overall recent flight experience, but their type-specific proficiency is extremely low. Research cited in FAA-H-8083-21B shows accident rates are highest in the early hours on a new type and decrease sharply after 100 hours in that specific model. The automation, power management, emergency procedures, and handling characteristics of a FADEC turbine are fundamentally different from a piston platform. High total hours can create overconfidence — a pilot must treat low time in type as a high-risk condition and use dual instruction, conservative flight profiles, and personal minimums until type-specific proficiency is established.

questions.question: A certificated flight instructor with a commercial helicopter certificate is preparing to conduct a flight review for a student who is legally current but hasn't flown in 5 months. The CFI's own last flight was 3 months ago. Walk me through how the proficiency versus currency risk applies simultaneously to both pilots on this flight.
questions.answer: Both pilots face proficiency gaps despite being legally current. The student hasn't flown in 5 months — their currency under 61.57 may still be valid if they completed 3 landings within 90 days before that gap, but their proficiency in aircraft control, emergency response, and situational awareness has degraded. The CFI, whose last flight was 3 months ago, may also have reduced proficiency, which is particularly dangerous in a dual-instruction context where the CFI may need to intervene quickly during a student error or emergency. The CFI should complete a personal proficiency refresher before conducting dual instruction involving a low-proficiency student. The error chain risk is compounded when two pilots with degraded proficiency share the same aircraft — each assumes the other can compensate.
questions.follow_up: If during this flight review the helicopter has an engine failure at low altitude, and both the student and CFI hesitate for one second before reacting due to their proficiency gaps, what specific emergency procedure is most affected by that one-second delay in a helicopter?
questions.follow_up_answer: Autorotation entry is critically time-sensitive. In a helicopter — especially one with a low-inertia rotor system — a one-second delay in lowering the collective following an engine failure can result in rotor RPM decay below the recoverable range. The FAA-H-8083-21B emphasizes that 'rotor stall in helicopters is not recoverable' and that 'low inertia rotors decay rapidly.' The immediate response — lowering collective simultaneously with aft cyclic and rudder input — must be an instinctive, proficiency-based reflex, not a thought-out procedural response. This is exactly why proficiency, not just currency, is a life-safety standard in helicopter operations.

questions.question: A night helicopter EMS pilot is legally current for night flight, IFR, and in type. However, the past 60 days of their logbook shows only daytime VMC flights due to scheduling. Tonight's mission involves a night approach to an unlit LZ with degraded visibility. What compounding proficiency risks exist, and how should this pilot evaluate the go/no-go decision?
questions.answer: Multiple proficiency gaps compound here: (1) Night currency may be technically met under 61.57(b), but actual night flying proficiency — dark adaptation management, use of visual illusions mitigation techniques, cockpit lighting management, and LZ assessment at night — degrades with 60 days of day-only flying. (2) IFR currency does not equal IFR proficiency if approaches have only been logged in VMC or simulator recently. (3) The unlit LZ removes normal night visual references, increasing CFIT risk substantially. The FAA-H-8083-21B notes that windscreens acceptable for day may not be for night, and that oil/fluid leaks are harder to detect at night during preflight — increasing equipment risk as well. The pilot should apply the 'probably' test from ADM guidance: if success will only 'probably' occur, choose a known-safe alternative. Options include delaying until conditions improve, requesting a lighted LZ, or passing the mission to a pilot with recent relevant night experience.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot decides to accept the flight and subsequently encounters inadvertent IMC during the approach, what is the single most important immediate action, and why is that action especially difficult for a pilot with degraded instrument proficiency?
questions.follow_up_answer: The single most important immediate action is to execute a go-around or missed approach procedure immediately — climbing and transitioning to IFR flight on instruments. However, this is extremely difficult for a pilot with degraded instrument proficiency because spatial disorientation onset is rapid in IMC, the vestibular system will produce false sensations that contradict the instruments, and the pilot must override strong physical instincts to trust the instruments. FAA-H-8083-21B and the IFH both emphasize that a pilot who has not recently maintained instrument proficiency will have slower scan cross-check speed, increased susceptibility to fixation errors, and reduced automation management capability — all of which are life-threatening in inadvertent IMC at low altitude during a night approach.

questions.question: According to the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook, how do accident statistics relate to time in a specific aircraft model, and why is this significant when flying an unfamiliar helicopter?
questions.answer: Accident rates correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft model than with total flight hours. Accidents decrease significantly after 100 hours in type. This means a highly experienced pilot with thousands of total hours is still at elevated risk when transitioning to an unfamiliar helicopter model, because type-specific proficiency — not just overall experience — is what primarily drives safety outcomes.

questions.question: What does it mean when we say a rotor system is 'semirigid' versus 'articulated,' and why does understanding this distinction matter before flying an unfamiliar helicopter?
questions.answer: A semirigid rotor allows blade pitch change (feathering) and flapping, but not lead/lag movement. An articulated rotor allows all three: feathering, flapping, and lead/lag. A rigid rotor allows only feathering. These differences affect how the helicopter responds to control inputs, its susceptibility to mast bumping or Coriolis effects, and the handling characteristics in maneuvers. A pilot unfamiliar with the rotor type may apply incorrect control inputs or misjudge the helicopter's response, creating a safety hazard.

questions.question: What is the risk associated with the word 'probably' when transitioning to an unfamiliar helicopter or avionics system, as discussed in the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook's ADM guidance?
questions.answer: The Helicopter Flying Handbook specifically warns pilots to avoid using the word 'probably' in decision-making. If an action will only 'probably' work — for example, assuming you can probably figure out an unfamiliar flight display system in flight — you should instead choose a course of action known to work. Applied to unfamiliar aircraft: if you are only 'probably' familiar enough with the avionics or systems to safely conduct a flight, that is a warning sign to obtain proper training or briefing before flight, not to press on and hope for the best.

questions.question: You are a commercial pilot with 2,000 hours in piston helicopters, but you have been offered a positioning flight in a turbine helicopter you have never flown before. The owner gives you a 20-minute walkaround and says 'it flies just like a piston, you'll be fine.' What specific risks must you identify before accepting this flight?
questions.answer: Several distinct risks exist here: (1) Low-inertia rotor systems common in turbines decay RPM rapidly in autorotation — without type-specific training, autorotation entry timing and technique may be dangerously unfamiliar. (2) Turbine power response is different from piston; throttle management and governor behavior require familiarization. (3) Unfamiliar avionics or glass cockpit displays increase workload and the chance of critical misinterpretation. (4) Emergency procedures — including antitorque failure, engine failure, and hydraulic failure — are aircraft-specific and must be known, not guessed. (5) Weight and balance, performance charts, and V-speeds differ from what the pilot knows. (6) Statistically, accident risk is highest in the early hours on a new type. A 20-minute walkaround does not satisfy the need for proper transition training, and accepting this flight would represent unacceptable risk.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapters 11 and 13; 14 CFR 61.31 (type rating and endorsement requirements)

questions.question: You are conducting a night VFR flight in a rental helicopter equipped with a glass cockpit EFIS system you have never used before. En route, the primary flight display begins showing what you think might be erroneous attitude information. How does your unfamiliarity with the avionics system elevate your risk, and what should you have done before the flight to mitigate this?
questions.answer: Unfamiliarity with the EFIS system means you may not know how to cross-check displays, switch to backup instruments, or interpret system failure annunciations — all critical in this scenario. At night, with potential spatial disorientation risk already elevated, the inability to quickly and confidently assess instrument status compounds the hazard significantly. The blocked static system and pitot-static failure modes relevant to IFR instruments also apply: misreading a glass cockpit failure message under pressure is a plausible error chain link. Before the flight, the pilot should have: (1) obtained a thorough ground briefing on the avionics from a qualified instructor or knowledgeable person; (2) reviewed the EFIS pilot's operating handbook or quick reference guide; (3) practiced in VMC or a simulator before flying at night; (4) understood the backup/reversionary mode and how to activate it. Failing to do so represents a self-imposed risk that violates sound SRM principles.

questions.question: A pilot transitioning from a semirigid rotor helicopter to one with a fully articulated rotor system notes that the new aircraft 'feels different' during low-speed maneuvering. Why is this sensation significant from a risk management perspective, and what specific aerodynamic hazards might be different between the two rotor systems?
questions.answer: The 'feels different' sensation is a critical red flag — it indicates the pilot's internalized mental model of how the helicopter responds does not match reality, which is a known precursor to loss of control. Specific hazard differences include: (1) Articulated rotors have lead/lag hinge movement that allows blade flapping and lead/lag in separate planes. This introduces different inertial coupling effects (Coriolis and gyroscopic coupling) compared to semirigid systems, affecting rotor response during aggressive inputs and during recovery from unusual attitudes. (2) Semirigid systems have mast bumping risk under low-G unloaded conditions; articulated rotors have different structural concerns. (3) Vortex ring state entry and recovery cues may feel different. (4) Control harmonics and required input forces differ. The pilot should stop, seek type-specific training, and not rationalize the difference away — using the 'error chain' concept, this discomfort is a link in a chain that could lead to an accident if ignored.

questions.question: A pilot has 5,000 total hours and adds a new helicopter model to their logbook after only a brief manufacturer demonstration flight, citing their extensive experience as justification. As an examiner, how do you evaluate whether this pilot's self-assessed currency represents an acceptable risk level for a checkride conducted in that helicopter, and what FAA ADM framework supports your evaluation?
questions.answer: The Helicopter Flying Handbook directly refutes the assumption that high total hours equals low risk in a new type — accidents correlate more strongly with hours in model than total hours, and risk is highest in the first hours on type. The pilot's self-assessment is a classic example of 'invulnerability' hazardous attitude: assuming their experience protects them from type-specific risks it does not address. As an examiner, I would evaluate: (1) Whether the pilot can demonstrate confident, accurate knowledge of the specific helicopter's systems, emergency procedures, and performance data — not just general helicopter knowledge; (2) Whether the pilot's unfamiliarity with avionics or displays is evident during preflight and oral examination; (3) Whether the error chain concept has been applied — has the pilot identified their own knowledge gaps honestly? (4) Whether the ADM framework of SRM — situational awareness, workload management, and risk management — is applied to their own self-assessment. A pilot who cannot articulate what they do NOT yet know about the aircraft presents an elevated checkride risk.
questions.follow_up: If during the checkride the pilot appears to fumble with an unfamiliar avionics mode during a simulated emergency, what action do you take as an examiner, and what FAA guidance supports that decision?
questions.follow_up_answer: If I observe that unfamiliarity with the avionics is creating an unsafe condition — for example, the pilot cannot locate the emergency procedure checklist on the display, or incorrectly interprets instrument data under simulated stress — I have authority under 14 CFR 61.43 to discontinue the practical test. The FAA's ADM guidance reinforces that a single degraded link — such as avionics unfamiliarity — can initiate an error chain. My responsibility is to the safety of flight, and the checkride must be discontinued before any unsafe condition develops into an actual hazard. The applicant would be issued a Notice of Disapproval, with the option to retest after demonstrating adequate familiarity through documented training.

questions.question: You are flying an unfamiliar helicopter with an integrated glass cockpit when you notice a tripped circuit breaker on preflight. You're unsure whether that breaker controls a primary avionics function or something non-essential — and you've never seen this panel layout before. Walk me through the risk management decision you should make, and what FAA guidance is directly applicable.
questions.answer: The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook explicitly states that tripped circuit breakers should be left for maintenance and not reset by the pilot before flight. The risk here is compounded by two factors: (1) the unfamiliar panel layout means the pilot cannot quickly determine whether the tripped breaker affects airworthiness-critical systems, and (2) resetting an unknown breaker could introduce an electrical fault into a system that was protected by the trip. The correct decision chain is: (a) Do not reset the breaker; (b) Consult the aircraft's Pilot's Operating Handbook or Rotorcraft Flight Manual to identify what the breaker controls — this is essential knowledge that should have been reviewed during preflight planning; (c) If the system controlled is required for the intended flight (e.g., a primary flight display or navigation system required for IFR), the aircraft is not airworthy for that operation; (d) If the system is not required, document the inoperative equipment and apply the MEL/POH inoperative equipment procedures before departing. Flying an unfamiliar helicopter without being able to interpret the circuit breaker panel is itself a risk factor that should have been identified and mitigated before reaching the aircraft.
questions.follow_up: If the POH for this unfamiliar helicopter is not aboard the aircraft and you cannot identify the circuit breaker function, what is your regulatory and safety obligation before flight?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.9 and 91.7, the pilot in command is responsible for determining that the aircraft is airworthy before flight. Under 14 CFR 91.203, required aircraft documents — including the FAA-approved Rotorcraft Flight Manual — must be aboard the aircraft. If the RFM is not present, the aircraft is not legally airworthy and the flight cannot be conducted. Beyond the regulatory requirement, operating an unfamiliar aircraft with an unidentified tripped circuit breaker and no documentation to reference is a clear risk management failure. The flight should not depart. This situation also illustrates why thorough preflight preparation — including reviewing the aircraft's documents and systems before arriving at the aircraft — is essential when flying any unfamiliar helicopter.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 12 (Night Preflight); 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 91.9; 14 CFR 91.203

questions.question: You hold a private pilot certificate with a helicopter rating. What documents must you have on your person before acting as PIC of a helicopter on a local VFR flight?
questions.answer: You must have: (1) a valid pilot certificate (private or higher with appropriate category/class rating), (2) a valid government-issued photo ID, and (3) a valid medical certificate — either a current FAA medical (3rd class or higher) or a valid BasicMed authorization if operating under 14 CFR 61.113(i). All three must be in your physical possession during the flight.

questions.question: You just passed your private helicopter checkride six months ago. What is the minimum flight review requirement you must meet before acting as PIC again after your privileges lapse?
questions.answer: A flight review is required every 24 calendar months. The review must include at least 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training with a CFI. The CFI must endorse your logbook upon satisfactory completion. Until this is completed, you cannot act as PIC. Note: successfully passing a checkride counts as a flight review, so after your private checkride, your 24-month clock restarts from that date.

questions.question: What currency requirement applies specifically to a helicopter pilot who wants to carry passengers on a VFR day flight?
questions.answer: To carry passengers, a pilot must have made at least three takeoffs and three landings within the preceding 90 days in an aircraft of the same category and class — in this case, a helicopter. For day passenger operations, these may be normal takeoffs and landings. The pilot must have been the sole manipulator of the controls for these currency flights.

questions.question: You are a private pilot with a helicopter rating and a current 3rd-class medical. A friend asks you to fly him and two other passengers from a private helipad to a mountain resort — he offers to split the fuel cost equally four ways. Is this operation legal, and what are your PIC obligations before accepting this flight?
questions.answer: Yes, this can be legal under the 'pro rata share' rule. A private pilot may accept payment for operating expenses on a flight if the flight is not for compensation or hire, the pilot pays their pro rata share (in this case 1/4), and the pilot holds appropriate certificates and currency for the flight. Before accepting, you must verify: (1) current pilot certificate with helicopter rating, (2) current 3rd-class medical or valid BasicMed, (3) current flight review within 24 months, (4) passenger-carrying currency — 3 takeoffs and landings in a helicopter within the past 90 days, and (5) the aircraft is airworthy with all required documents (ARROW) on board.

questions.question: You hold a commercial helicopter certificate and a current 2nd-class medical issued 13 months ago. A company wants to hire you for VFR aerial photography work — no passengers, just you and a camera system. Are you legally current to act as PIC for compensation, and what medical class do you actually need for this operation?
questions.answer: This depends on the operation. For compensation or hire operations, you need at least a commercial pilot certificate, which you have. Regarding medical currency: a 2nd-class medical is valid for commercial operations for 12 calendar months from the date of examination. After 12 months, a 2nd-class medical downgrades to 3rd-class privileges for private operations. Since 13 months have passed, your 2nd-class privileges have expired. However, a 3rd-class medical is valid for 60 months (under age 40) or 24 months (age 40 and over). If you are under age 40 and your medical was issued less than 60 months ago, it may still be valid as a 3rd class — but a 3rd-class medical does NOT authorize compensation or hire operations. You need a current 2nd-class (or 1st-class) medical to act as PIC for compensation. You are not current for paid PIC duties without obtaining a new 2nd-class medical.

questions.question: You are preparing to fly a Robinson R44 on a VFR cross-country. When you check your logbook, your last flight review was exactly 24 calendar months ago today. Are you legal to act as PIC, and how would you determine this?
questions.answer: The flight review must be completed within the preceding 24 calendar months. '24 calendar months' means the logbook endorsement must be dated no earlier than the same calendar month, 24 months prior. If the endorsement is dated exactly 24 calendar months ago (e.g., June 2023 and today is June 2025), the review is still current — it expires at the end of that calendar month. If today is the last day of that month, you are still legal. However, tomorrow (first day of the next month) you would no longer be current. You should verify the specific date on the endorsement and confirm you are within the calendar month window before acting as PIC.

questions.question: You are a private helicopter pilot who has not flown in 18 months. You have a valid medical, but your flight review is expired. A friend offers to let you take the controls of his helicopter for a solo practice session to get current. What are your options, and what is the correct legal path to regain PIC privileges?
questions.answer: You cannot act as PIC with an expired flight review — period. Your options are: (1) Schedule a flight review with a CFI who holds at least a commercial certificate with a helicopter rating and a flight instructor certificate. The review must include at least 1 hour of ground and 1 hour of flight instruction. The CFI acts as PIC during the review since you cannot act as PIC until it is completed and endorsed. (2) Alternatively, you could take a practical test (checkride) for an additional certificate or rating, which would also satisfy the flight review requirement. You should also assess your actual proficiency after 18 months of inactivity. Though not legally required, additional dual instruction before the review is strongly advisable given the gap and the accident data showing elevated risk for pilots returning after extended breaks — particularly those with fewer than 100 hours in type.
questions.follow_up: During the flight review, the CFI determines you're not yet proficient and declines to endorse you. Can the CFI log that flight time, and what are your options going forward?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, the CFI can log the flight time as dual instruction given — the flight review does not have to be completed in a single session, and an unsuccessful review does not have to be reported to the FAA. The CFI simply does not provide the logbook endorsement. You are not penalized for an unsatisfactory flight review; you simply remain not current as PIC. Your options are to continue training with that CFI or another CFI until proficiency is demonstrated, at which point the endorsement is given. The CFI has no obligation to report the unsatisfactory outcome, and it does not affect your certificate. This is distinct from a checkride failure, which does require reporting.

questions.question: An ATP-certificated helicopter pilot's First Class medical expires mid-trip while conducting a multi-day Part 135 operation. At what point exactly does the certificate expire, and what can and cannot the pilot do for the remainder of the trip?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.23(d)(1), a First Class medical certificate expires at the end of the last day of the 6th calendar month after the month of examination for pilots age 40 or older, and at the end of the last day of the 12th calendar month for pilots under age 40. Once First Class privileges expire, the certificate does not immediately become worthless — it downgrades and continues to confer lower-class privileges per 61.23(d)(2). For a pilot under age 40, the certificate functions as a Third Class after the 12-month First Class window closes (there is no intervening Second Class window). For a pilot age 40 or older, after the 6-month First Class window closes, the certificate functions as a Second Class for the next 12 months (through the end of the 12th calendar month), then downgrades to Third Class through the end of the 24th calendar month. Regarding Part 135 operations: Part 135 PIC operations require at least a Second Class medical. If the pilot is under 40 and the 12-month First Class window has expired, no Second Class window exists, and the pilot cannot act as PIC in Part 135 operations. If the pilot is 40 or older and is within the 6–12 month downgrade window, Second Class privileges remain valid and the pilot may continue as PIC in Part 135 operations, provided all other certificate and currency requirements are met. Once all commercial-level medical validity has expired, the pilot must ground themselves for Part 135 PIC duties, arrange for a qualified replacement, or obtain a new medical examination before continuing commercial operations.
questions.rewrite_note: Corrected the First Class validity duration to properly distinguish between pilots under 40 (12 calendar months) and pilots age 40 or older (6 calendar months), and clarified the downgrade mechanics per 14 CFR 61.23(d)(2), including the absence of a Second Class window for pilots under 40 and the 6-to-12 month Second Class window for pilots 40 or older.

tasks.title: Task B. Airworthiness Requirements

questions.question: What documents are required to be on board a helicopter before you can legally fly it, and where should each one be located?
questions.answer: The required documents are remembered with the acronym ARROW: Airworthiness Certificate (must be displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance or in a prominent place easily accessible to passengers per 14 CFR 91.9), Registration Certificate (on board), Radio Station License if equipped with certain radios and operating internationally (on board, FCC requirement), Operating Limitations/RFM (on board and specific to that aircraft's serial number), and Weight and Balance data (on board). The Airworthiness Certificate remains valid indefinitely as long as the helicopter is maintained in airworthy condition and no major repairs or alterations void it.

questions.question: A helicopter's airworthiness certificate has no expiration date printed on it. What can cause that certificate to become invalid, even though it shows no expiration?
questions.answer: An Airworthiness Certificate remains valid indefinitely as long as the helicopter is maintained in accordance with applicable FAA regulations, required inspections are completed, and no unapproved major repairs or alterations are made. It becomes invalid if: the aircraft is not maintained per its approved maintenance program, required inspections (annual, 100-hour, etc.) lapse, an Airworthiness Directive is not complied with within the required time, or a major alteration is performed without proper FAA approval. The certificate is aircraft-specific and does not transfer if the helicopter is re-registered.

questions.question: What is an Airworthiness Directive, and as the pilot in command, what is your responsibility regarding ADs on the helicopter you're about to fly?
questions.answer: An Airworthiness Directive (AD) is a legally enforceable regulation issued by the FAA under 14 CFR Part 39 to correct an unsafe condition found in an aircraft, engine, propeller, or appliance. ADs are mandatory — operating an aircraft that does not comply with an applicable AD is illegal. As PIC, you are responsible for ensuring the helicopter is airworthy before flight, which includes verifying that all applicable ADs have been complied with by reviewing the aircraft's maintenance records and logbooks. ADs come in two forms: one-time compliance and recurring compliance (which require re-inspection at specified intervals). The FAA also issues Special Airworthiness Information Bulletins (SAIBs), which are not mandatory but provide safety recommendations.

questions.question: You're preparing for a cross-country flight and discover during preflight that the helicopter's annual inspection expired three days ago. The owner says 'it's fine, it was just inspected last month for a 100-hour.' Can you legally make the flight? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: No, you cannot legally make the flight under normal circumstances. Under 14 CFR 91.409, aircraft operated under Part 91 must have an annual inspection every 12 calendar months. A 100-hour inspection does not substitute for an annual inspection — they serve different purposes. The 100-hour is required for aircraft used for hire or flight instruction, while the annual is required for all Part 91 operations. The annual can only be performed by an A&P mechanic with Inspection Authorization (IA), while a 100-hour can be done by an A&P without IA. With an expired annual, the helicopter is not airworthy and cannot be flown except under a special flight permit (ferry permit) issued under 14 CFR 21.197 to fly it to a maintenance facility for the inspection.

questions.question: While reviewing the maintenance logbook before a flight, you find an entry from six months ago noting an AD compliance for a recurring inspection — but you can't find any subsequent entry showing the follow-up inspection was done at the required interval. What do you do, and what are the implications if you fly?
questions.answer: You should not fly the helicopter until you resolve the discrepancy. First, contact the aircraft owner and/or the maintenance facility that performed the original AD compliance to determine if the follow-up inspection was completed but not logged, or if it was missed. If the follow-up was completed, the logbook entry must be made before the aircraft is airworthy. If the inspection was genuinely missed, the aircraft is not in compliance with an AD, making it unairworthy under 14 CFR 91.403 and 14 CFR Part 39. Flying an aircraft out of AD compliance exposes you to certificate action and civil penalties, and any accident would likely void insurance coverage. As PIC, you bear responsibility for airworthiness under 91.403, even if the maintenance lapse was not your fault.

questions.question: Your helicopter was involved in a minor hard landing last week. No structural damage was visible, and the aircraft was flown afterward without incident. What inspections or documentation actions, if any, are required before you can legally fly it again today?
questions.answer: A hard landing typically triggers the need for an inspection per the RFM/maintenance manual, as most helicopter manufacturers specify hard landing inspection criteria (G-load thresholds or procedural triggers). As PIC, you must determine whether: (1) the RFM specifies a hard landing inspection and whether that threshold was met, (2) any damage or deformation is present that would require an inspection by an A&P. If the manufacturer's maintenance manual requires a hard landing inspection and one has not been completed and documented in the logbook, the helicopter is not airworthy. Additionally, if the previous flight was made without the required inspection, that flight was conducted in an unairworthy aircraft. Any required inspection must be performed and logged by an appropriately certificated maintenance person before the next flight.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.403, 91.409, 91.417; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8; applicable RFM/Maintenance Manual

questions.question: A helicopter is grounded at a remote airstrip after a maintenance issue is discovered. The annual inspection is current, but a non-critical component has failed and no maintenance is available on-site. The owner wants to ferry it back to the home base for repair. Walk me through exactly how a special flight permit works and what limitations it imposes.
questions.answer: A special flight permit (ferry permit) is issued under 14 CFR 21.197 when an aircraft doesn't currently meet airworthiness requirements but is capable of safe flight for a specific purpose. To obtain one: (1) The applicant contacts the local FSDO or, in some cases, a Designated Airworthiness Representative (DAR). (2) A description of the discrepancy, the proposed flight route, and evidence that the aircraft can be safely flown must be provided. (3) The FSDO issues the permit with specific operating limitations — typically including the specific route, conditions (day/VFR), crew required, and any restrictions related to the known discrepancy. (4) The permit is valid only for the specific flight(s) described — it does not restore general airworthiness.
