The flight must be conducted exactly as authorized; deviating from the permit's conditions would make the flight illegal. Passengers may or may not be permitted depending on the permit's terms. The permit does not substitute for an annual inspection renewal.
questions.follow_up: If the FSDO is closed and the situation is urgent, is there any other way to obtain a special flight permit, and who else has authority to issue one?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 21.197(c), a special flight permit may be issued by an FAA Flight Standards District Office, a Manufacturing Inspection District Office, or a Designated Airworthiness Representative (DAR) who holds authority for that function. In practice, if the FSDO is closed, you can contact the nearest available FSDO (they maintain after-hours emergency contact information through the FAA), or work through a DAR with the appropriate authority. The key point is that someone with FAA-delegated authority must issue the permit — the pilot or owner cannot self-authorize flight in an unairworthy aircraft simply because they intend to fly to maintenance.

questions.question: You're examining the aircraft logbooks and find a major repair entry from two years ago where an A&P signed it off — but there is no FAA Form 337 in the aircraft records, and the repair appears to have involved the main rotor system. What are the implications of this, and how does it affect the helicopter's airworthiness today?
questions.answer: An FAA Form 337 (Major Repair and Alteration) is required by 14 CFR 43.9 and 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix B whenever a major repair or major alteration is performed on an aircraft. For the main rotor system, virtually any structural repair would qualify as a major repair. Without the Form 337: (1) There is no record that the repair was approved and performed to acceptable data, meaning there is no assurance the repair meets FAA standards. (2) The aircraft's airworthiness is legally in question — it may be considered unairworthy. (3) The A&P who signed off the logbook without completing the 337 violated 14 CFR 43.9 and could face certificate action. To resolve this, you should contact the FSDO. They may require the repair to be re-inspected by an A&P/IA or the aircraft manufacturer to determine if acceptable repair data was used. If the repair cannot be approved retroactively, the helicopter may require additional maintenance to bring it into conformity. Flying it in this condition exposes the PIC to legal liability under 91.403.
questions.follow_up: What is the difference between a major repair and a minor repair, and who determines which category a specific repair falls into for a helicopter's rotor system?
questions.follow_up_answer: The definitions are found in 14 CFR Part 1 and the criteria in 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix A. A major repair is one that might appreciably affect structural strength, flight characteristics, or other airworthiness qualities of the aircraft if not done properly. A minor repair is one that is not a major repair. For the rotor system specifically, Appendix A to Part 43 lists rotor blade repairs, hub repairs, and control system repairs as major repairs if they involve the primary structure or could affect airworthiness. The A&P performing the work makes the initial determination, but must use FAA-approved data and complete the 337 for major work. When in doubt, the manufacturer's maintenance manual, FAA Advisory Circulars (particularly AC 43.13), and consultation with the FSDO provide guidance. For certificated repair stations, a Return to Service document substitutes for the 337 in some cases.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 43.9, Part 43 Appendix A and B, 91.403, 14 CFR Part 1 definitions

questions.question: As a certificated pilot, are you legally allowed to perform maintenance on your helicopter? If so, what regulation governs this, and what is the general limitation?
questions.answer: Yes. Under 14 CFR 43.3(g), a certificated pilot who is the registered owner of an aircraft — or who operates it for their own use — may perform preventive maintenance on that aircraft, as long as it is not used under Part 121, 129, or 135. The work is limited to the specific tasks listed in 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A(c), which defines preventive maintenance. The pilot cannot perform work beyond that defined list.

questions.question: Name at least four specific tasks that are considered 'preventive maintenance' under 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A(c) that a pilot may legally perform.
questions.answer: 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A(c) lists preventive maintenance tasks including: (1) changing engine oil and filter; (2) servicing landing gear wheel bearings (e.g., cleaning and greasing); (3) replacing safety wiring and cotter pins; (4) replacing bulbs, reflectors, and lenses of position and landing lights; (5) replenishing hydraulic fluid; (6) replacing prefabricated fuel lines; (7) cleaning or replacing fuel and oil strainers; (8) replacing or cleaning spark plugs; (9) replacing batteries; (10) servicing, checking, and replacing tires. The list is exhaustive — if a task is not on the list, it is not preventive maintenance.

questions.question: After you perform an approved preventive maintenance task on your helicopter, what record-keeping is required before you return the aircraft to service?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 43.9, any person who performs maintenance must make an entry in the aircraft maintenance records. The entry must include: (1) a description of the work performed; (2) the date the work was completed; (3) the name of the person performing the work; and (4) the certificate type and number of the person approving the return to service — which in the case of preventive maintenance is the pilot themselves. The pilot must sign off their own work and make this logbook entry before flying the aircraft.

questions.question: You operate your helicopter under a Part 135 on-demand charter certificate. After a flight, you notice the tail rotor pitch change bearing needs grease — a task listed in Appendix A(c) as preventive maintenance. Can you perform this yourself and return the aircraft to service?
questions.answer: No. 14 CFR 43.3(g) explicitly prohibits pilot-performed preventive maintenance on aircraft used in operations conducted under Part 121, 129, or 135. Since this helicopter is operated under Part 135, only a certificated aviation maintenance technician (AMT) holding an appropriate rating — or someone authorized under Part 43 — may perform that work. The fact that the task appears on the Appendix A(c) list is irrelevant once the aircraft is under Part 135 operations. The pilot must ground the helicopter until properly certificated maintenance personnel complete and sign off the work.

questions.question: You changed the oil in your privately operated piston helicopter and made the required logbook entry. The next morning your A&P mechanic tells you the oil filter you installed is the wrong part number — but the correct filter for a different model. What is the airworthiness status of your helicopter, and what should have been done differently?
questions.answer: The helicopter is not airworthy. Installing an incorrect part number — even during a task that is otherwise permissible preventive maintenance — means the work was not performed to manufacturer specifications and constitutes an improper maintenance action. Preventive maintenance must be performed in accordance with the manufacturer's maintenance manual or instructions for continued airworthiness (ICA). Under 14 CFR 43.13(a), all maintenance must be done using the appropriate current manufacturer data. The incorrect filter must be removed and the correct part installed by someone authorized to do so. The aircraft cannot be flown until properly returned to service with the correct part and a corrected logbook entry.

questions.question: During your preflight of your privately owned Robinson R44, you discover a position light lens is cracked and non-functional. You have the correct replacement lens in your flight bag. Walk me through the steps you must complete before you can legally depart.
questions.answer: Replacing a position light lens is listed as preventive maintenance under 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A(c). As the certificated pilot-owner operating under Part 91, you are authorized to perform this task. Steps: (1) Obtain and verify the replacement lens is the correct manufacturer-approved part for the R44. (2) Perform the replacement using the manufacturer's maintenance manual guidance per 14 CFR 43.13(a). (3) Inspect the completed work to ensure it is correctly installed and functional. (4) Make a logbook entry per 14 CFR 43.9 that includes the description of work, date, your name, and your certificate type and number as the person approving return to service. (5) Conduct your normal preflight to verify airworthiness before departure.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 43.3(g); 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A(c); 14 CFR 43.9; 14 CFR 43.13(a)

questions.question: A student pilot who recently soloed their helicopter tells you they changed their own spark plugs last weekend because they read it on the Appendix A(c) list and thought that meant any pilot can do preventive maintenance. Are they correct, and what are the exact regulatory requirements for who may perform preventive maintenance?
questions.answer: The student pilot is incorrect. 14 CFR 43.3(g) specifies that only a certificated pilot holder — meaning someone who holds at least a private, commercial, or ATP certificate — may perform preventive maintenance. A student pilot certificate does not qualify. Additionally, the pilot must be the registered owner of the aircraft or must operate it for their own use — they cannot perform preventive maintenance on someone else's aircraft. Furthermore, the aircraft must not be used in Part 121, 129, or 135 operations. If the student pilot performed the spark plug replacement, the maintenance was unauthorized and the aircraft is not in an airworthy condition. A certificated AMT must inspect the work, correct any discrepancies, and properly return the aircraft to service with appropriate logbook entries before it can be flown.
questions.follow_up: If the student pilot performed this unauthorized maintenance and then flew the helicopter, what regulatory violations would have occurred and who could face enforcement action?
questions.follow_up_answer: Multiple violations would apply. The student pilot may have violated 14 CFR 43.3(g) by performing maintenance they were not authorized to perform, and 91.7(a) by operating an aircraft they knew or should have known was not airworthy. The flight instructor who authorized the solo and possibly the registered owner could also face scrutiny if they knew or should have known of the unauthorized maintenance. Operating an unairworthy aircraft is a violation of 14 CFR 91.7. Falsifying or improperly making a maintenance record entry — if the student made any — would violate 14 CFR 43.12. The FAA could pursue certificate action against any certificate holder involved, including suspension or revocation.

questions.question: You perform an approved preventive maintenance task — replacing a battery — on your helicopter and make a proper logbook entry. Two weeks later, during an annual inspection, the A&P/IA discovers the battery you installed was not properly secured and has been rubbing against a nearby hydraulic line, causing chafing. Who bears responsibility for this, and what are the airworthiness implications?
questions.answer: You, the pilot who performed the preventive maintenance, bear responsibility. Under 14 CFR 43.13(b), all maintenance must be done so that the work does not adversely affect the airworthiness of the aircraft. By improperly securing the battery, you performed the maintenance task incorrectly regardless of whether the task was otherwise authorized. The aircraft has been operating in an unairworthy condition since the battery was improperly installed. The chafed hydraulic line must now be inspected and likely replaced by a certificated AMT before flight. Your logbook entry for the battery replacement is misleading because it implies a proper return to service that did not actually occur. The FAA could pursue certificate action against you for operating an unairworthy aircraft under 14 CFR 91.7 and for improper maintenance under 14 CFR 43.13.
questions.follow_up: If the chafed hydraulic line had caused a hydraulic failure in flight, and it was later determined the improper battery installation was the cause, could the PIC of that subsequent flight — a different pilot who was unaware of the improper maintenance — face FAA enforcement action?
questions.follow_up_answer: Potentially yes, but to a more limited extent. The PIC of any flight is responsible under 14 CFR 91.7(b) to determine the airworthiness of the aircraft before flight. If a thorough preflight inspection would have reasonably revealed the improperly secured battery or the chafed line, the subsequent PIC could share responsibility for operating an unairworthy aircraft. However, if the defect was truly hidden from reasonable preflight inspection — for example, concealed behind a panel — enforcement against the subsequent PIC becomes much harder to sustain. Primary enforcement would focus on the pilot who performed the improper maintenance and approved the return to service. This illustrates why thorough, systematic preflight inspections are a PIC responsibility, not merely a formality.

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), what four conditions must be met before you can legally depart with an inoperative piece of equipment that is not covered by an approved MEL?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), the four conditions are: (1) The equipment is not required by the VFR day/night equipment lists in 14 CFR 91.205, or by an Airworthiness Directive, or by the Type Certificate/Airworthiness Certificate; (2) The equipment is either removed from the aircraft or deactivated and placarded INOPERATIVE; (3) If deactivation or removal constitutes maintenance, it must be performed by a certificated maintenance person; and (4) The pilot in command determines the inoperative equipment does not constitute a hazard to the flight.

questions.question: Name at least four instruments or equipment items required by 14 CFR 91.205 specifically for night VFR flight that are NOT required for day VFR flight.
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.205(c) requires the following for night VFR in addition to day VFR equipment: (1) Approved position lights (navigation lights); (2) Approved aviation red or aviation white anti-collision light system; (3) If operated for hire, one electric landing light; (4) Adequate source of electrical energy for all installed electrical and radio equipment; and (5) One spare set of fuses, or three spare fuses of each kind required, accessible to the pilot in flight.

questions.question: During your preflight on a Robinson R44, you discover the rotor tachometer is inoperative. Your operator does not have an approved MEL. Walk me through whether you can defer this item under 14 CFR 91.213(d) and depart legally.
questions.answer: You cannot defer the rotor tachometer under 91.213(d) because it is listed as required equipment in the R44 Rotorcraft Flight Manual and its Type Certificate Data Sheet. Under 91.213(d), equipment required by the aircraft's type certificate or the RFM cannot be deferred — those items are not eligible for the 91.213(d) deferral process at all. Additionally, the Helicopter Flying Handbook specifically calls out the rotor tachometer as an example of a component that requires repair before departure because it is not deferrable. The flight cannot legally depart until the tachometer is repaired.

questions.question: Your helicopter has an FAA-approved MEL. During flight, your hydraulic caution light illuminates and the system fails. Can you use your MEL to defer the hydraulic system and continue to your destination? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: No. The MEL deferral process under 14 CFR 91.213(a) applies to equipment found inoperative before departure, not to in-flight discrepancies. When equipment fails in flight, the MEL does not apply — you must follow the emergency or abnormal procedures in your RFM/POH for that specific malfunction. The Helicopter Flying Handbook explicitly states that maintenance deferrals under 91.213(d) are not used for in-flight discrepancies. After landing, once the aircraft is on the ground, you would then evaluate whether the hydraulic system failure could be deferred under the MEL before the next departure.

questions.question: Explain what a Kinds of Operations Equipment List (KOEL) is, where you find it, and how it differs from an MEL.
questions.answer: A KOEL is a list found in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (or Pilot's Operating Handbook) that identifies which equipment must be operative for specific kinds of operations — for example, day VFR, night VFR, IFR, or flight into known icing. Unlike an MEL, which is an FAA-approved document that allows you to operate with specifically listed equipment inoperative under defined conditions, the KOEL tells you what must be working for each type of operation your aircraft is approved for. The KOEL is part of the aircraft's FAA-approved flight manual and therefore carries the weight of the RFM limitations. If a KOEL item required for your intended operation is inoperative, you cannot conduct that kind of operation regardless of whether you have an MEL.

questions.question: You defer an inoperative radio under your helicopter's approved MEL. Describe every required record-keeping and placard action that must be completed before you can legally depart, and who is authorized to perform each step.
questions.answer: When deferring equipment under an approved MEL: (1) The inoperative equipment must be placarded 'INOPERATIVE' in a location visible to the pilot — this alerts the crew and any subsequent pilots to the discrepancy. (2) A maintenance discrepancy record or 'write-up' must be made in the aircraft maintenance records or a separate discrepancy log as required by the MEL's associated procedures document (typically called the MEL Master Minimum Equipment List or M-MEL procedures). (3) If deactivation of the equipment constitutes maintenance — such as pulling and collaring a circuit breaker per the MEL procedure, or physically removing the unit — that action must be performed by a certificated mechanic (A&P) or the work documented appropriately. (4) The MEL itself specifies (O) Operations procedures and (M) Maintenance procedures for each deferred item; the pilot may perform (O) procedures, but (M) procedures require a certificated maintenance person. The aircraft logbook or discrepancy record must reflect the deferral, what was done, and who performed any maintenance actions.
questions.follow_up: If you placard the radio INOPERATIVE and fly the trip, then a different pilot picks up the helicopter the next day — what is that pilot's responsibility regarding your deferred MEL item?
questions.follow_up_answer: The subsequent pilot in command must review the discrepancy record or MEL log before flight and is equally responsible for determining that the deferral is still valid and that the inoperative equipment does not constitute a hazard for their intended flight. The PIC cannot simply assume a prior deferral is acceptable — they must independently confirm the placard is in place, the discrepancy is properly documented, and the MEL category interval (A, B, C, or D — specifying how many days the item may remain inoperative) has not expired. If the deferral interval has lapsed, the equipment must be repaired before the aircraft can be flown.

questions.question: A student tells you: 'The fuel quantity gauge doesn't have to be accurate, so if it's broken I can just defer it under 91.213(d) and fly.' Evaluate whether this statement is correct and explain the full legal analysis.
questions.answer: The student is partially correct but reaches the wrong conclusion. It is true that 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1) only requires fuel quantity gauges to be accurate when reading empty — they are not required to be accurate across the full range. However, deferring an inoperative fuel quantity gauge under 91.213(d) still requires meeting all four conditions of that regulation. Critically, the PIC must determine the inoperative equipment does not constitute a hazard to the flight. An inoperative fuel gauge — even though not required to be accurate except at empty — could absolutely constitute a hazard depending on the flight: distance, fuel load, availability of fuel en route, and whether quantity can be verified by other means (fuel tabs, manual dipping). If the PIC cannot reliably determine fuel state throughout the flight, departing with an inoperative gauge may not satisfy the 'no hazard' determination. The student is conflating 'not required to be accurate' with 'not required to function at all' — the legal deferral analysis still applies and the PIC carries the burden of the hazard determination.
questions.follow_up: If you dip the tanks and confirm full fuel before departure, and your flight is only 45 minutes in a helicopter with a 3-hour endurance, does that change your hazard analysis for the inoperative fuel gauge?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, it substantially strengthens the argument that the inoperative gauge does not constitute a hazard for that specific flight. With confirmed full tanks, a 45-minute flight against a 3-hour endurance, and presumably no extended IFR or off-airport routing, the PIC has an objective basis to determine no hazard exists. However, the PIC must still formally make and document that determination, ensure the gauge is placarded INOPERATIVE, and ensure any required deactivation maintenance is performed by an authorized person. The analysis is flight-specific — that same deferral might not be appropriate for a 2.5-hour flight or one over remote terrain.

questions.question: What is a special airworthiness certificate, and how does it differ from a standard airworthiness certificate for a helicopter?
questions.answer: A standard airworthiness certificate is issued to helicopters that meet all FAA type design requirements and are in condition for safe operation under 14 CFR Part 21. A special airworthiness certificate is issued to aircraft in categories such as experimental, restricted, limited, light-sport, or provisional, when the aircraft does not meet — or is not required to meet — all the requirements for a standard certificate. Helicopters operating under a special airworthiness certificate carry specific operating limitations that restrict how, where, and for what purposes they may be flown, and these limitations are legally binding on the pilot-in-command.

questions.question: Where would you find the specific operating limitations for a helicopter operating under a special airworthiness certificate, and are those limitations required to be on board the aircraft?
questions.answer: The operating limitations for a special airworthiness certificate are issued by the FAA along with the certificate itself and must be carried in the aircraft at all times. They are typically a separate document accompanying the certificate and may restrict items such as geographic area of operation, altitude, airspeed, passenger carriage, flight over populated areas, and the specific purpose for which the aircraft may be flown. Under 14 CFR 91.9, the pilot must comply with the operating limitations prescribed for the aircraft.

questions.question: Name at least three categories of special airworthiness certificates under which a helicopter might operate and give one example of an operating limitation unique to one of those categories.
questions.answer: Categories of special airworthiness certificates applicable to helicopters include: (1) Experimental — issued for purposes such as research and development, crew training, or amateur-built aircraft; a common limitation is that the helicopter may not be operated over densely populated areas or in congested airways. (2) Restricted — issued for special-purpose operations such as aerial survey, agriculture, or external load work; limitations often restrict operations to the specific purpose stated on the certificate. (3) Limited — issued to former military surplus aircraft; limitations may restrict modifications and define specific operational boundaries. (4) Light-Sport Aircraft (LSA) — limitations include maximum gross weight, airspeed (120 KTAS), and VFR day operations only. Each category carries FAA-issued operating limitations that are as binding as the RFM for a standard certificated aircraft.

questions.question: You are offered a flight in an experimentally certificated helicopter. The owner tells you it's perfectly safe and that the operating limitations are 'basically the same as any other helicopter.' What is your responsibility as PIC before accepting this flight, and what specific items in the operating limitations would you look for?
questions.answer: As PIC, you are personally responsible for determining that the helicopter is airworthy and that you are legally authorized to act as pilot under its specific operating limitations — regardless of what the owner tells you. Under 14 CFR 91.9 and 91.203, you must have the operating limitations on board and comply with them. Key items to verify include: (1) Whether the flight purpose is permitted (e.g., experimental operating limitations may prohibit carrying passengers for hire, or restrict flights to specific purposes like crew training or R&D); (2) Geographic or airspace restrictions (e.g., no flight over populated areas); (3) Pilot experience requirements — some experimental aircraft limitations require a specific number of hours in type or a sign-off from the builder; (4) Airspeed and altitude restrictions that may differ from a standard RFM; (5) Any requirement for a flight test area or proximity to an airport during initial operating periods. Blindly accepting an owner's verbal assurance is not a substitute for reading the actual limitations document.

questions.question: A restricted-category helicopter is certificated for aerial survey operations. The operator asks you to use that same helicopter to carry a paying client on a sightseeing flight. Can you legally do this? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: No, this would not be legal. A restricted-category airworthiness certificate is issued for specific special-purpose operations enumerated under 14 CFR 21.185, such as aerial survey, agriculture, patrolling, or external load work. The operating limitations issued with the certificate define the exact purposes for which the helicopter may be flown. Carrying a paying sightseeing passenger is not an approved special purpose under the restricted certificate, and doing so would violate both the operating limitations and 14 CFR 91.313, which specifically prohibits carrying persons or property for compensation or hire in a restricted-category aircraft and also prohibits operations over densely populated areas or congested airways except under an FAA waiver. The helicopter would need a standard airworthiness certificate — and the operator would need the appropriate Part 119/135 certification — to conduct that type of commercial flight.

questions.question: During preflight, you discover that the operating limitations document for this experimental helicopter states it must remain within 25 nautical miles of the departure airport during all operations. The planned flight is 40 miles away. How does this limitation affect your go/no-go decision, and can you request a deviation from the FAA for this flight?
questions.answer: This limitation is a hard legal restriction issued as part of the special airworthiness certificate under 14 CFR 21.181. You cannot legally conduct the planned flight without violating the operating limitations. Operating limitations issued with a special airworthiness certificate are not suggestions — they have the same regulatory force as any FAA regulation, and the PIC is required to comply with them under 14 CFR 91.9. A geographic restriction of this type is common during initial operating periods for experimental aircraft to contain risk near an airport. To extend the operational area, the aircraft owner/operator would need to apply to the FAA FSDO to amend the operating limitations — typically after demonstrating satisfactory flight test results. You cannot obtain a one-time deviation for this; the limitation must be formally amended before the flight can legally occur. The correct decision is not to conduct the flight as planned.

questions.question: You're flying a restricted-category helicopter on an approved aerial survey mission when you experience a partial engine failure. The nearest suitable landing area is an open field in a densely populated suburban neighborhood. Your operating limitations prohibit flight over densely populated areas. What authority do you have to operate in apparent violation of those limitations, and what are your obligations after landing?
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.3(b) gives the PIC the authority to deviate from any FAA rule — including operating limitations — to the extent necessary to meet an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action. This is the foundation of PIC emergency authority and it supersedes the restrictions in the special airworthiness certificate operating limitations during the emergency. You are legally justified in landing in that suburban field if it is genuinely the best available option given the partial power emergency. However, this authority is narrow: 'to the extent necessary' means you use the minimum deviation from the operating limitations required to safely resolve the emergency. Post-flight, under 14 CFR 91.3(b), you must submit a written report to the FAA Administrator upon request. Additionally, operating a restricted-category helicopter over populated areas is addressed in 14 CFR 91.313(b), which does allow waivers — but in an emergency you cannot obtain a waiver in real time, so emergency authority is your only legal basis. After landing, you should notify your FSDO, document the emergency deviation, and be prepared to explain that the deviation was necessary and proportionate to the emergency.
questions.follow_up: After you land safely in that suburban field, can you then fly the helicopter out under the restricted certificate, or does the aircraft need to be transported out another way?
questions.follow_up_answer: After an emergency landing, the PIC's emergency deviation authority under 14 CFR 91.3(b) applied only to the emergency itself. Once on the ground in a location that violates your operating limitations — a densely populated area — you cannot invoke emergency authority again simply to reposition the aircraft, because there is no longer an immediate safety emergency requiring immediate action. To legally fly the helicopter out, you would need either: (1) a specific authorization or waiver from the FAA FSDO for that repositioning flight; (2) a determination that the operating limitations can be complied with for the departure (e.g., departing immediately to an unpopulated route), which may be possible depending on the layout of the area; or (3) in some cases, the aircraft may need to be disassembled and transported by ground. The practical answer is to contact the FSDO and explain the situation — they have authority to issue a special flight permit under 14 CFR 21.197 to allow the aircraft to be flown to a maintenance base or storage facility, which would cover the repositioning flight legally.

questions.question: You do your preflight and find that the rotor tachometer is inoperative. Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), what is the first thing you must determine before even considering whether to defer this item?
questions.answer: You must first determine whether the item is listed as required equipment on that specific aircraft's Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS) and whether it appears on any approved Minimum Equipment List (MEL). For most standard-category helicopters, rotor RPM indication is a required instrument for VFR operations. However, the requirement is aircraft-specific. If the rotor tachometer is required on your aircraft and is not listed as deferrable on the MEL, the helicopter is not airworthy for flight and must be repaired before departure. Do not assume the requirement applies universally — always check your TCDS and MEL first.

questions.question: What does the FAA consider an approved MEL to be from a regulatory standpoint, and why does that matter when you discover inoperative equipment before flight?
questions.answer: The FAA treats an approved MEL as a Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) for that specific aircraft. This matters because the MEL legally authorizes the operator to fly with specific equipment inoperative, overriding the standard airworthiness requirements — but only for the items explicitly listed in the MEL. If a piece of equipment is not listed in the MEL as deferrable, the MEL provides no authorization to fly with it inoperative, and the aircraft is unairworthy.

questions.question: If you discover an inoperative piece of equipment during preflight and decide to defer it under 14 CFR 91.213(d), what must physically happen to that equipment before you can legally depart?
questions.answer: The inoperative equipment must be either removed from the aircraft or deactivated, and it must be placarded 'INOPERATIVE' in a location visible to the pilot. If deactivation or removal requires maintenance actions — including pulling a circuit breaker and collaring it or physically removing the component — a certificated maintenance person must perform that work. The pilot cannot simply ignore the item; a proper placard and deactivation step are mandatory.

questions.question: During your preflight on a Part 91 helicopter with no approved MEL, you notice the cyclic trim system is not functioning. Your passenger is waiting, the weather is perfect, and the flight is only 20 minutes. Walk me through your risk management decision-making process.
questions.answer: First, I must check my aircraft's Type Certificate Data Sheet and any approved MEL to determine whether cyclic trim is required equipment for VFR day operations. For standard-category helicopters, cyclic trim control is typically a required system. Assuming it is required on this aircraft and does not appear as deferrable on the MEL, the aircraft is unairworthy and cannot depart. Regardless of favorable weather, short flight distance, or passenger pressure, I cannot legally or safely fly an aircraft with inoperative required equipment. This scenario is a classic test of recognizing hazardous attitudes — the 'it'll probably be fine' and 'get-there-itis' mindset — and my correct decision is to ground the aircraft, notify maintenance, and inform my passenger of the delay.

questions.question: Your helicopter has an FAA-approved MEL. During preflight, you find the outside air temperature (OAT) gauge is inoperative. The MEL lists OAT as a Category C deferral, meaning you have 10 days to repair it. What additional steps must you take beyond just logging the deferral, and what risk does this create if you need performance data?
questions.answer: Beyond logging the deferral in the aircraft maintenance records, I must ensure the item is properly placarded 'INOPERATIVE' and that any required deactivation steps listed in the MEL procedures section are completed by qualified maintenance personnel. The risk created is significant for performance planning: OAT is used to determine density altitude and calculate hover performance, power required, and maximum gross weight. Without a functional OAT gauge, I must obtain temperature data from an external source (ATIS, AWOS, METARs) and apply a conservative margin, since an unverified assumption about temperature can lead to operating outside safe performance limits — particularly critical during high-altitude or high-temperature operations where hover margin is already reduced.

questions.question: A fellow pilot tells you: 'I found an inop position light during my preflight, but I'm only flying in the daytime so I just ignored it and flew.' What regulatory and safety errors did that pilot make?
questions.answer: That pilot made at least two errors. First, they did not follow the required process under 14 CFR 91.213(d) — even for a daytime VFR flight, the pilot cannot simply 'ignore' inoperative equipment. They must determine whether the item is required, and if it is not required for the intended operation (VFR day), they must still formally deactivate it and placard it 'INOPERATIVE.' Simply not using the item and not placarding it is not compliant. Second, if the item required maintenance action to deactivate, a certificated maintenance person must perform that step — the pilot cannot do it themselves unless they also hold the appropriate maintenance certificate. This also reflects poor ADM: normalizing non-compliance because 'it worked out' erodes safety culture and sets a precedent for increasingly risky decisions.

questions.question: During preflight on your Part 91 helicopter with no approved MEL, you find the fuel quantity gauge is reading empty but the helicopter was just fueled and you visually confirmed full tanks. The gauge is clearly malfunctioning. Can you legally fly, and what is the regulatory basis for your answer?
questions.answer: Yes, you can likely fly, and here is the regulatory basis: 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1) — incorporated by reference into operating limitations — requires fuel quantity gauges to be accurate only when reading empty. A gauge that reads incorrectly when tanks are full but you have visually confirmed fuel quantity through direct inspection is not required to be accurate at that reading. Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), you would evaluate whether this gauge is required equipment for the intended operation. Since you have confirmed fuel quantity by direct sight and the gauge is only required to be accurate at empty, you could defer it following the 91.213(d) process: confirm it is not required in a way that grounds the flight, deactivate or placard it INOPERATIVE, log the discrepancy, and ensure any required maintenance action is performed by a qualified person. You must still ensure you have an alternate means of monitoring fuel state in flight.
questions.follow_up: If that same malfunctioning fuel gauge were discovered in flight rather than on the ground, would you apply 91.213(d) to defer it?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. The 91.213(d) deferral process applies to equipment found inoperative prior to flight — it is a ground-based, pre-departure decision tool. If the malfunction is discovered in flight, 91.213(d) does not apply. Instead, the pilot must refer to the RFM/POH emergency and abnormal procedures for guidance on how to handle the in-flight discrepancy and determine whether continued flight is safe or whether a precautionary landing is required. The FAA explicitly states that maintenance deferrals are not used for in-flight discrepancies.

questions.question: You are the PIC for a Part 91 flight and your certificated A&P mechanic friend deactivated an inoperative transponder and placarded it before the flight. ATC subsequently advises you that your transponder appears to be transmitting incorrectly. Putting aside the ATC issue, was the pre-departure deferral process legal, and what specific risk does the 'error chain' concept suggest about how you got to this point?
questions.answer: The deferral process was potentially legal if all steps were followed: the A&P determined the transponder was not required for the intended operation (e.g., VFR flight outside Class B, C, and the Mode C veil), deactivated it properly, and placarded it INOPERATIVE. However, the error chain here is worth examining — the fact that ATC says the transponder is transmitting incorrectly suggests the deactivation was incomplete or ineffective. The A&P may have thought the unit was off but it was still squawking. This represents multiple links in an error chain: an inoperative item not fully understood, an incomplete deactivation procedure, and a departure into controlled airspace or near it without confirming the transponder was truly silent. Each decision along the way seemed acceptable in isolation, but together they created a regulatory and safety problem. Breaking any one link — thorough deactivation verification, checking NOTAM for airspace, confirming with ATC before entering — would have prevented the outcome.
questions.follow_up: If the transponder was required for the airspace you were flying in and you departed anyway after the 'deferral,' what is your legal exposure as PIC?
questions.follow_up_answer: As PIC, I am fully responsible for the airworthiness of the aircraft before flight under 14 CFR 91.7. If the transponder was required equipment for the airspace (e.g., Class B, Class C, or within the Mode C veil per 14 CFR 91.215), and I departed knowing it was inoperative, I operated an unairworthy aircraft in violation of 91.7 and likely 91.215. The fact that my A&P friend performed the deactivation does not transfer my PIC responsibility. I could face certificate action. The A&P could also face certificate action for improper maintenance sign-off. This is why the PIC must independently verify that the deferral is legal for the intended operation — not just that a maintenance person performed a deactivation step.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 91.213(d); 14 CFR 91.215; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapters 8 and 13

questions.question: Show me where the airworthiness certificate is located in this helicopter and tell me what information is on it.
questions.answer: The airworthiness certificate must be displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance where it is legible to passengers and crew (14 CFR 91.203(b)). It shows the aircraft registration number, manufacturer, model designation, serial number, category (e.g., Normal), and the certifying FAA office signature and date. Unlike the registration, the airworthiness certificate has no expiration date — it remains valid as long as the aircraft is maintained in an airworthy condition.

questions.question: Pull out the aircraft registration for this helicopter and tell me when it expires and what information it contains.
questions.answer: The aircraft registration certificate must be on board and available for inspection (14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)). It shows the aircraft nationality and registration mark (N-number), make, model, serial number, registered owner's name and address, and the issuing FAA Airmen Registry office. Under 14 CFR 47.40, aircraft registrations must be renewed every three years. The certificate may be paper or an FAA-issued electronic equivalent.

questions.question: Point to where the Rotorcraft Flight Manual is for this helicopter and tell me how you know it's the correct manual for this specific aircraft.
questions.answer: The RFM must be kept on board the aircraft and is required by 14 CFR 91.9. To confirm it is the correct manual for this specific aircraft, I check the title page — the FAA-approved RFM must show the specific make, model, and serial number of the aircraft it was issued for, matching the serial number on the airworthiness certificate and the aircraft data plate. The registration number may also appear on the title page. A generic or mismatched RFM is not considered the approved document for that aircraft.

questions.question: During your preflight you discover the rotor tachometer is inoperative. Walk me through how you would determine whether this helicopter is airworthy to fly today.
questions.answer: First, I check the aircraft's equipment list and the RFM/POH to determine if the rotor tachometer is required equipment for the intended flight. Next, I check whether this aircraft has an FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List (MEL). If an MEL exists, I check whether the rotor tachometer is listed as deferrable — if it is, I follow the MEL's O and M procedures and placard the instrument INOPERATIVE. If no MEL exists, I apply the 14 CFR 91.213(d) deferral process: the item must not be required by the VFM or type certificate, must not be required by an airworthiness directive, must not affect airworthiness, and must be placarded INOPERATIVE. For most Part 91 helicopters operating VFR, the rotor tachometer is listed as required equipment in the aircraft's type certificate and cannot be legally deferred. However, deferability is determined by the specific aircraft's approved equipment list, not a blanket rule. I would confirm with the RFM and maintenance that it is deferrable for this specific helicopter before attempting to defer it — which is unlikely.

questions.question: You're doing a preflight and notice an inoperative piece of equipment that your mechanic says can be deferred under 91.213(d). He removes the component entirely and hands it to you. Is the helicopter now airworthy to depart?
questions.answer: Not necessarily, and there's a critical procedural issue here. Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), deactivating or removing inoperative equipment that requires maintenance — including physical removal — must be performed by a certificated maintenance person. If the mechanic is certificated and performed the removal, that part is acceptable. However, the mechanic must make an appropriate logbook entry, and the equipment must be placarded INOPERATIVE. If the item is not required by the VFR Day equipment list, not required by an AD, and does not affect airworthiness, then the aircraft may be legal to depart. The PIC must still make the final airworthiness determination. If the mechanic is not certificated, the removal itself was not authorized and the aircraft is not airworthy.

questions.question: You're preflighting a rental helicopter and find that the airworthiness certificate on display shows a different N-number than the one painted on the fuselage. What does this mean and what do you do?
questions.answer: This is a serious airworthiness concern. The airworthiness certificate is issued to a specific aircraft identified by its registration (N-number) and serial number. If the displayed certificate doesn't match the aircraft's registered N-number, either the certificate belongs to a different aircraft, or the aircraft was re-registered and the certificate wasn't updated/replaced. In either case, the aircraft cannot be legally operated under 14 CFR 91.203, which requires the airworthiness certificate to be the one issued for that specific aircraft. I would not fly this helicopter. I would notify the operator and defer to a certificated maintenance person or the FSDO to resolve the discrepancy.

questions.question: You pull out the RFM during preflight and the fuel quantity gauges section states they are only required to be accurate at the empty indication. You're looking at gauges showing roughly half tanks, but you're not sure you trust them. What is the regulatory basis for this limitation, and how does it affect your airworthiness determination and flight planning?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1), fuel quantity gauges in normal category rotorcraft are only required to be accurate when they read empty — there is no accuracy requirement for intermediate readings. This is also reflected in FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 5. This does NOT mean the gauges are broken or that the aircraft is unairworthy — it means the design standard permits inaccuracy at partial readings. For the airworthiness determination, as long as the gauges function (they move, they read empty correctly), they meet their certification standard. For flight planning, however, the PIC must physically verify usable fuel by visually checking fuel levels, using a calibrated dipstick, or draining a measured sample. I cannot rely solely on gauges at partial readings for fuel planning — this is a pilot judgment and risk management issue, not an airworthiness grounding item.
questions.follow_up: If you visually check the tanks and confirm the fuel level matches what the gauge shows, are you now confident in the fuel quantity?
questions.follow_up_answer: Reasonably so, but I still need to account for fuel that may not be visually verifiable — such as unusable fuel, fuel trapped in lines, or the geometry of the tank (sloped tanks can be hard to visually assess accurately). I should cross-check the visual inspection with the aircraft's fuel capacity from the RFM, calculate expected consumption for the flight, and add appropriate reserves per 14 CFR 91.151 (VFR) or 91.167 (IFR). The visual check is the most reliable method when gauges are uncertain, but it must be done carefully and with knowledge of the aircraft's specific fuel system geometry.

questions.question: During preflight you find a placard on the instrument panel near the VNE indicator that shows a lower VNE than what's printed in the RFM limitations section. Which one controls, and why does this matter specifically in a helicopter versus a fixed-wing aircraft?
questions.answer: The more restrictive limitation always controls, and in this case the cockpit placard would govern operational decisions. Per 14 CFR 91.9 and 91.7, the pilot must comply with all operating limitations, including placards. In a helicopter, VNE is not a single fixed number as it often is in fixed-wing aircraft — per FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 5, helicopter VNE varies with altitude and gross weight. The placard in the cockpit is designed to reflect the current, condition-specific VNE applicable to that aircraft's configuration and operating envelope. The RFM limitations section may show a theoretical maximum or include charts that define VNE across all conditions. If a placard shows a lower value, it may reflect a specific maintenance finding, an operational limitation imposed via an AD or STC, or a configuration-specific restriction. I would not depart until I understand why the placard and RFM differ, because exceeding VNE in a helicopter risks blade stall, mast bumping, or structural failure — all potentially non-survivable.
questions.follow_up: What if the placard appears to be old, faded, and possibly incorrect — how do you resolve a conflict between a questionable placard and the printed RFM?
questions.follow_up_answer: A placard cannot simply be ignored because it looks old. Under 14 CFR 91.9, operating limitations include placards, and they carry regulatory weight. If I believe the placard is incorrect, outdated, or was placed in error, I cannot make that determination myself — a certificated mechanic or the operator must investigate. They would check the maintenance logbooks for any AD, STC, or maintenance action that required the placard, and if the placard was placed in error, a certificated person would need to remove it and make a logbook entry. I would not fly the aircraft until the discrepancy is resolved through proper maintenance channels.

questions.question: Before you even open a checklist, what four documents must you physically verify are on board to consider the helicopter airworthy for today's flight?
questions.answer: The acronym AROW covers it: Airworthiness certificate, Registration, Operating limitations (RFM/POH, which must include the specific serial number and registration of this helicopter on the title page), and Weight and balance data. All four must be on board and current. The airworthiness certificate must be displayed where it is visible to passengers.

questions.question: You are about to defer an inoperative piece of equipment under 14 CFR 91.213(d). What must physically happen to that equipment before you can legally depart?
questions.answer: The inoperative equipment must be deactivated or removed, and it must be placarded INOPERATIVE. If the deactivation or removal requires maintenance — including any act that would constitute maintenance under the FARs — a certificated maintenance person must perform that work. The pilot cannot simply ignore or tape over the equipment; the placard and deactivation steps are required.

questions.question: I'm giving you this scenario: You complete your preflight and find a logbook entry showing a 100-hour inspection was performed, but it was signed off by an A&P mechanic without an Inspection Authorization. The next 100-hour is now due in 8 hours of flight time. Is the helicopter airworthy? How do you make that determination?
questions.answer: A 100-hour inspection under 14 CFR 91.409 must be performed by an appropriately rated mechanic or certificated repair station, but signing off an annual inspection requires an IA. However, a 100-hour inspection does NOT require an IA — an A&P alone can perform and sign off a 100-hour inspection. The sign-off by an A&P is therefore legally sufficient for a 100-hour. You would verify the inspection was performed within the required interval, check that the return-to-service entry is properly completed, confirm no discrepancies were noted or that noted discrepancies were corrected, and verify no ADs are outstanding. If all of that checks out, the helicopter is airworthy.

questions.question: Scenario: During runup you notice the fuel quantity gauge reads half full, but you know you only added 20 gallons to a 60-gallon tank that was previously empty. The gauge disagrees with your fuel records. Can you legally depart, and what is your airworthiness determination process?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1), fuel quantity gauges are only required to be accurate when they read empty — they are not required to be accurate at intermediate readings. So a discrepant fuel quantity gauge is not automatically an airworthiness issue. However, as PIC you must ensure adequate fuel for the flight plus reserves under 14 CFR 91.151. Your airworthiness determination: confirm the gauge reads empty correctly, then rely on your own fuel records (amount added, starting quantity verified visually via dipstick or sump), and calculate fuel load independently. If you can positively account for the 20 gallons on board and it meets reserve requirements for the planned flight, you may depart. Document the discrepancy.

questions.question: Scenario: You are the pilot for a Part 91 flight. Your helicopter has an approved MEL, and the cyclic trim system is inoperative. Maintenance says it's listed as deferrable. You check the MEL and don't see cyclic trim listed at all. What is your airworthiness call, and why?
questions.answer: If cyclic trim is not listed in the MEL, it cannot be deferred under the MEL — the MEL only authorizes deferral of equipment specifically listed within it. Per 14 CFR 91.213(d), components not listed in the MEL as deferrable must be either required by the type certificate, airworthiness directives, or essential for safe operation. Cyclic trim is a primary flight control necessary for safe helicopter operation and is almost certainly required by the type certificate. The helicopter is not airworthy for flight with the cyclic trim inoperative when it is absent from the MEL's deferral list. Repair or replacement is required before departure.

questions.question: Scenario: During your preflight you find a small but fresh hydraulic fluid leak at the tail rotor servo. There is no write-up in the discrepancy log, no previous maintenance entry referencing this area, and the helicopter's RFM is silent on acceptable leak rates. The previous pilot says 'it's always done that.' Walk me through your complete airworthiness determination and the go/no-go decision framework.
questions.answer: As PIC, you are responsible for ensuring the helicopter is airworthy before flight under 14 CFR 91.7. The absence of a logbook write-up means the discrepancy has not been assessed by a certificated maintenance person — it is unresolved and undocumented. Your steps: (1) Check the RFM for any guidance on hydraulic system limitations or acceptable leak criteria. (2) Consult the maintenance manual if available — most specify acceptable seepage versus leakage. (3) Since you cannot make an airworthiness determination on a hydraulic leak at a flight-critical component (tail rotor servo) without maintenance expertise, you must ground the aircraft and have a certificated A&P assess it. The tail rotor hydraulic system is flight-critical; failure could result in loss of directional control. 'It's always done that' is not an acceptable justification — undocumented and unassessed fluid leaks on primary flight control servos constitute an unknown airworthiness status. The helicopter does not depart until an A&P inspects and signs off the discrepancy or repairs it.
questions.follow_up: Suppose the A&P looks at it, says it's within limits per the maintenance manual, and makes a logbook entry. But you personally feel uncomfortable with the leak — you've never seen one this fresh. Do you have any authority to refuse the flight even after the A&P signs it off?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, absolutely. Under 14 CFR 91.7, the PIC has final authority and responsibility for the safe operation of the aircraft. A maintenance sign-off establishes that the discrepancy is within mechanical limits, but it does not override your aeronautical decision-making authority. You are never required to fly an aircraft you believe is unsafe. The A&P's sign-off addresses airworthiness from a regulatory maintenance standpoint, but the PIC always retains the right — and the duty — to refuse flight if they have a genuine safety concern. Document your reasoning, contact the operator or maintenance facility for further clarification, and do not fly until you are satisfied.

questions.question: Scenario: You pick up a helicopter at a remote location. The maintenance records show the annual inspection was completed 11 months ago, no 100-hour has been conducted, and the Hobbs shows 112 hours since annual. The owner says '100-hours only apply to for-hire operations.' Is the helicopter airworthy for your Part 91 flight? How do you verify this, and what are the limits of your authority as PIC in this situation?
questions.answer: The owner is correct that the 100-hour inspection requirement under 14 CFR 91.409(b) applies specifically to aircraft used for hire — for compensation or hire, carrying passengers or cargo. For a pure Part 91 private flight, only the annual inspection is required, and it must be completed within the preceding 12 calendar months. At 11 months since annual, the annual is still current. You must verify: (1) The annual inspection logbook entry is properly completed with date, aircraft TT, and IA signature. (2) No ADs are overdue — check the AD compliance record. (3) All required equipment is installed and functional per 91.205 and the RFM. (4) All required documents (AROW) are aboard. If all checks pass, the helicopter is airworthy for a Part 91 non-commercial flight, even though no 100-hour has been done. Your authority as PIC: you may accept the aircraft as airworthy once you've verified all regulatory requirements — but you may not substitute your judgment for an IA's regarding whether maintenance items are 'within limits.' If discrepancies exist, they must be addressed by certificated maintenance.
questions.follow_up: What if this same flight is being conducted for compensation — say, you are a CFI and you are charging your student for helicopter dual instruction? Does the 100-hour rule now apply, and what does that mean for the airworthiness status of this helicopter?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, the 100-hour rule applies. Under 14 CFR 91.409(b), aircraft used to carry passengers for hire, or used by a flight school for flight instruction for hire, must have a 100-hour inspection within the preceding 100 hours of time in service. Since the Hobbs shows 112 hours since the last inspection (which in this case served as the annual), the aircraft has exceeded the 100-hour limit by 12 hours. The only exception is if the aircraft was en route to a repair station or maintenance facility when the 100-hour expired — the aircraft may exceed the limit by up to 10 hours to reach the maintenance facility, but those extra hours count against the next 100-hour interval. At 12 hours over, even that exception does not apply. The helicopter is not airworthy for paid dual instruction until a 100-hour inspection is performed.

questions.question: During preflight, you discover an inoperative piece of equipment on your helicopter. Walk me through the two primary methods available under part 91 for determining whether you can legally defer that equipment and fly.
questions.answer: Under part 91, there are two methods: First, use an FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List (MEL) specific to that aircraft — if the MEL lists the item as deferrable and the deferral conditions are met, you may fly. Second, use the 14 CFR 91.213(d) deferral provision, which allows flight without an MEL if the inoperative equipment is not required by the type certificate data sheet, not required by an airworthiness directive, not required for the specific operation being conducted (e.g., VFR vs. IFR), and is either removed or deactivated and placarded INOPERATIVE. Both methods require PIC judgment and documentation of the discrepancy.

questions.question: You find an inoperative piece of equipment and determine it can be deferred under 91.213(d). What must physically happen to that equipment before you depart?
questions.answer: The inoperative equipment must be deactivated or removed, and it must be placarded as INOPERATIVE. If deactivating or removing the equipment requires maintenance action — including physical removal — a certificated maintenance person must perform that work. The pilot cannot simply ignore the item; a visible INOPERATIVE placard is required so that any crew member or subsequent pilot is aware of the discrepancy.

questions.question: Your helicopter has an FAA-approved MEL. During preflight you find the rotor tachometer is inoperative. You look it up and it is not listed in the MEL as a deferrable item. What does that mean for your flight?
questions.answer: If an item is not listed in the MEL as deferrable, it cannot be deferred under the MEL. The helicopter is not airworthy with that item inoperative, and the aircraft must be repaired before departure. The MEL only authorizes flight with items specifically listed as deferrable under the conditions stated. Non-listed items default to being required equipment, meaning the aircraft cannot legally fly until that equipment is restored to an operative condition.

questions.question: You're about to depart on a VFR cross-country in your part 91 helicopter when you notice the fuel quantity gauge is stuck and reads incorrectly. The aircraft does not have an MEL. Using the 91.213(d) process, walk me step by step through how you evaluate whether this flight can legally proceed.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Check the type certificate data sheet (TCDS) and airworthiness directives: determine whether the fuel quantity gauge is required equipment for the aircraft. Step 2 — Check 14 CFR 91 equipment requirements for the specific operation (VFR day/night, IFR, etc.) to see if a fuel quantity gauge is mandated. Note that 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1) requires fuel quantity gauges but only mandates accuracy at the empty reading, so gauge function matters. Step 3 — If the gauge is required by the TCDS or FARs, it cannot be deferred under 91.213(d) and the aircraft is not airworthy. Step 4 — If it is not listed as required, ensure it can be deactivated or removed, placard it INOPERATIVE, and confirm the PIC can safely determine fuel state by other means. Step 5 — The PIC makes the final airworthiness determination and logs the discrepancy. In practice, fuel quantity gauges are typically required instruments and this flight should not proceed until the gauge is repaired.

questions.question: You're conducting an IFR flight in a Part 91 helicopter equipped with an MEL. Thirty minutes after departure, you lose your number two communication radio. The MEL allows deferral of one comm radio for VFR operations only. How do you handle this in flight?
questions.answer: Because the MEL allows deferral of one comm radio for VFR only, and you are conducting an IFR operation, the MEL deferral does not apply to your current flight condition. However, 14 CFR 91.213 deferral provisions under (d) are specifically not used for in-flight discrepancies — the RFM/POH emergency procedures govern in-flight equipment failures. You must now use your single remaining comm radio to communicate with ATC, declare the situation if needed, and work with ATC to continue the flight safely. The MEL and 91.213(d) process applies to pre-departure decisions, not in-flight failures. Upon landing, the aircraft may not depart on another IFR flight until the radio is repaired or the MEL conditions for the applicable operation are met.

questions.question: During preflight you discover the cyclic trim system is inoperative on your helicopter. The aircraft has no MEL. A passenger is waiting and you're behind schedule. How do you apply the 91.213(d) process here, and what are the human factors risks in this scenario?
questions.answer: The cyclic trim system is an example of equipment the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook notes is not deferrable under standard provisions — it must be repaired before flight because it affects the pilot's ability to safely control the aircraft. Under 91.213(d), the PIC must confirm the item is not required by the TCDS, ADs, or applicable FARs. Cyclic trim directly affects flight control workload and safety; if it is listed as required by the TCDS or impacts airworthiness, the flight cannot legally proceed. The human factors risk here is significant: schedule pressure and a waiting passenger create 'get-there-itis' and external pressure bias, which are classic hazardous attitudes. The pilot must apply ADM, recognize these pressures, and ground the aircraft if the equipment is required — accepting a delay is always preferable to an unsafe departure. The PIC is the final authority on airworthiness.

questions.question: You're a Part 91 pilot with an MEL for your helicopter. The MEL states that the anti-collision light system may be deferred for daytime VFR operations only, with a placard required. You comply, placard the light INOPERATIVE, and depart on a daytime VFR flight. En route, the flight extends unexpectedly into night conditions. What are your obligations now, and what should you have considered before departure?
questions.answer: Once the flight transitions to night conditions, you are no longer operating within the MEL deferral conditions, which allowed the inoperative anti-collision light only for daytime VFR. 14 CFR 91.205(c) requires anti-collision lights for night VFR operations. Operating at night without them violates both the MEL conditions and the FARs. You should land at the nearest suitable airport and have the light repaired before continuing. The pre-departure consideration that should have occurred: always evaluate not just the current conditions at departure, but the full planned operation including potential contingencies. If there was any possibility the flight could extend into night, the aircraft should not have departed with the light deferred. This is a critical ADM failure — not anticipating how changing conditions interact with MEL limitations.
questions.follow_up: Let's say you land and call maintenance — they tell you the anti-collision light bulb is burned out and they can fix it in 20 minutes. While waiting, you review the MEL and notice it says 'repair within 3 days.' Does that 3-day window apply to your situation, and does it change anything about your decision to land?
questions.follow_up_answer: The 3-day repair interval in the MEL applies to the deferral period — it tells you how long you may legally operate with the item deferred under the MEL's authorized conditions. It does not mean you can continue operating outside those authorized conditions for 3 days. Since night operations are outside the MEL deferral authorization for this item, you cannot fly at night regardless of how much time remains in the repair interval. Your decision to land was correct and legally required. The repair interval clock applies only while operating within the MEL's approved deferral parameters.

questions.question: You're preparing for an IFR flight and discover two items are inoperative: the ELT and one VOR receiver. Your helicopter has an MEL. You check the MEL and both items are listed as individually deferrable for IFR operations. Can you legally defer both at the same time, and what broader airworthiness principle governs your decision?
questions.answer: The fact that two items are individually deferrable under the MEL does not automatically mean both may be deferred simultaneously. Many MELs contain provisos limiting concurrent deferrals, particularly for redundant systems or safety-critical equipment. You must read each MEL entry carefully for any language restricting simultaneous deferral with other inoperative items. Beyond the specific MEL language, the broader principle is the PIC's responsibility under 14 CFR 91.7 to determine the aircraft is airworthy before flight — this is a judgment call that goes beyond simply checking boxes. Even if both deferrals are technically permitted by the MEL, the PIC must evaluate the cumulative effect on safety. Flying IFR without an ELT and with only one VOR reduces your safety margins significantly; a conservative PIC might decline to fly until at least one item is repaired, even if the MEL technically permits the combination.
questions.follow_up: The MEL is silent on simultaneous deferral restrictions for these two items. You decide to defer both and depart. During the flight you encounter an emergency and must divert — you declare an emergency on 121.5. After landing, the FAA asks you to explain your airworthiness determination. What documentation and reasoning must you be able to show?
questions.follow_up_answer: You must be able to demonstrate: (1) The MEL entries for both items, showing they are listed as deferrable for IFR operations with no prohibition on concurrent deferral. (2) That both items were properly deactivated or placarded INOPERATIVE prior to departure, and if maintenance action was required for deactivation, it was performed by a certificated maintenance person. (3) A record of the discrepancies in the aircraft maintenance logbook or equivalent record. (4) Your PIC airworthiness determination under 14 CFR 91.7, documented through your preflight decision-making process. (5) That the MEL itself is an FAA-approved document (treated as an STC) specific to that aircraft's serial number. If your documentation is complete and the MEL permitted both deferrals, your decision was legally defensible — but the FAA may still examine whether your overall airworthiness judgment was sound given the cumulative reduction in safety systems.

questions.question: The FAA considers an approved MEL to be what kind of FAA approval document, and what does that mean practically for your helicopter?
questions.answer: The FAA considers an approved MEL to be a kind of operations specification or operational approval document — it is a FAA-approved document that, once accepted, allows an operator to legally fly an aircraft with certain inoperative equipment that would otherwise ground the aircraft. Practically, this means the MEL is specific to the aircraft type and the particular operator's approval. An operator must have an FAA-approved MEL for their specific aircraft type and configuration; they cannot simply borrow or use another operator's MEL without proper FAA acceptance. The MEL supplements the aircraft's airworthiness by defining which items may be inoperative, under what conditions, and what placarding or procedures are required — effectively creating a legal basis for continued operation that would not otherwise exist under 14 CFR 91.213.
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the incorrect characterization of an MEL as an STC and corrected the overly restrictive claim that MELs are tail-number-specific, instead accurately describing MELs as operator and type-specific operational approval documents under 14 CFR 91.213.

questions.question: A certificated flight instructor wants to give dual instruction in an amateur-built experimental helicopter to a student working toward a private pilot certificate. The operating limitations state 'no compensation or hire.' Is giving paid flight instruction in this aircraft legal? Walk me through your analysis.
questions.answer: This is a genuinely complex regulatory question without a simple yes/no answer from the FARs alone. Here is the framework for analysis: Under 14 CFR 91.319(a), an aircraft with an experimental certificate may not be operated for compensation or hire. The operating limitation 'no compensation or hire' directly mirrors this regulatory restriction. The FAA has addressed similar questions through legal interpretations, and the conservative, defensible position — consistent with FAA enforcement history — is that if any compensation is received in connection with flight in an experimental aircraft, it risks violating 91.319(a) and the operating limitations. The FAA does not clearly carve out an exception for 'instruction-only' fees when the flight itself occurs in an experimentally certificated aircraft subject to this limitation. There is no provision in 14 CFR Part 61 or Part 91 that explicitly authorizes paid instruction in an aircraft whose operating limitations prohibit compensation or hire. The distinction sometimes suggested — that a CFI is being paid for instruction rather than for aircraft use — has not been definitively codified in FAA regulations or a publicly available legal interpretation that resolves the ambiguity in favor of the CFI. Accordingly, the safest and most legally defensible course of action is to treat the prohibition as applying to the entire flight operation, meaning paid instruction in this aircraft should not proceed without first obtaining written guidance from the responsible FSDO. Operating contrary to experimental operating limitations can result in certificate action under 14 CFR 91.319 and potential enforcement under 49 U.S.C. 44709.
questions.rewrite_note: Removed unsupported hedged claims about a 'payment for instruction vs. aircraft use' distinction, acknowledged that no specific FAA legal interpretation definitively resolves the ambiguity in the CFI's favor, and grounded the analysis in the plain language of 14 CFR 91.319(a) and the operating limitations while directing the operator to FSDO for written guidance.

questions.question: During preflight, you discover the rotor tachometer is inoperative. Walk me through how you decide whether you can legally depart.
questions.answer: First, check whether the helicopter has an FAA-approved MEL. If it does, look up the rotor tachometer — if it is listed as deferrable, follow the MEL procedure and placard it INOPERATIVE. If it is not listed as deferrable in the MEL, or if no MEL exists, apply the 14 CFR 91.213(d) four-part test: determine whether the item is required by the type certificate data sheet, an airworthiness directive, the RFM/POH equipment list, or 14 CFR Part 91. The rotor tachometer is required for safe flight operations — it is essential for monitoring rotor RPM during all phases of flight, and the RFM/POH for virtually every certificated helicopter lists it as required equipment. If the RFM/POH or type certificate requires it and no MEL deferral exists, the helicopter is not airworthy and you may not depart until it is repaired.
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the unsupported claim that the Helicopter Flying Handbook specifically identifies the rotor tachometer as non-deferrable, and instead grounded the inoperability determination in the 14 CFR 91.213(d) framework and the RFM/POH required equipment list, which is the proper FAA-supported authority.

tasks.title: Task C. Weather Information

questions.question: What is the nationwide phone number you can call to reach Flight Service for a standard weather briefing before a helicopter flight?
questions.answer: 1-800-WX-BRIEF (1-800-992-7433). Flight Service (FSS) can be reached at this number from anywhere in the contiguous United States to obtain preflight weather briefings, file flight plans, receive NOTAMs, and get weather advisories.

questions.question: Name three sources of weather data you could use when planning a helicopter flight.
questions.answer: Acceptable sources include: (1) Flight Service Station (FSS) via 1-800-WX-BRIEF or online through 1800wxbrief.com; (2) National Weather Service (NWS) at weather.gov, which provides METARs, TAFs, PIREPs, AIRMETs, SIGMETs, and forecast products; (3) Aviation weather products through aviationweather.gov; (4) Automated Surface Observing Systems (ASOS/AWOS) for real-time surface observations; (5) ForeFlight or other FAA-approved electronic flight bag applications that pull NWS and FAA data. The key requirement is that the source must provide aviation-quality weather data appropriate for flight planning.

questions.question: What is the difference between a METAR and a TAF, and which government agency produces them?
questions.answer: A METAR (Meteorological Aerodrome Report) is a current surface weather observation that reports existing conditions at a specific airport at a specific time — it is a snapshot of what is happening right now. A TAF (Terminal Aerodrome Forecast) is a forecast of expected weather conditions at a specific airport, typically covering a 24- or 30-hour period. Both are produced by the National Weather Service (NWS), which is part of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Pilots use METARs to assess current conditions and TAFs to anticipate what conditions will be at the destination or alternate.

questions.question: You're planning a cross-country helicopter flight in an area with no airport at your intended landing zone. The nearest official reporting station is 40 miles away. How would you piece together an accurate weather picture for your specific route and destination?
questions.answer: Since no METAR or TAF exists for the landing zone, you would build a composite weather picture using multiple sources: (1) Obtain a standard briefing from FSS (1-800-WX-BRIEF) — the briefer can correlate nearby METARs and area forecasts for your route; (2) Review the Area Forecast (FA) or Graphical Forecasts for Aviation (GFA) at aviationweather.gov, which provide weather over large geographic regions, not just airports; (3) Check AIRMETs and SIGMETs for any advisories covering your route; (4) Review PIREPs (Pilot Reports) from pilots who have recently flown in the area — these are especially valuable for mountain or remote terrain; (5) Check ASOS/AWOS at the nearest reporting station and apply judgment about how those conditions translate to your off-airport site given terrain; (6) Consider wind forecasts (RAOBs, model data) to understand how local topography might affect conditions. This multi-source approach is required under 14 CFR 91.103, which requires pilots to become familiar with all available information.

questions.question: You receive an AIRMET Sierra for your route of flight while planning a low-altitude helicopter mission through mountainous terrain. What does that mean, and where would you have found that information during preflight?
