Reference: 14 CFR 61.53; 14 CFR 91.17; FAA Advisory Circular AC 67-2D 'Medical Facts for Pilots.'
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.53; 14 CFR 91.17; FAA-AM-400-01/02 Medications and Flying

questions.question: Research shows that accident rates decrease significantly after a pilot reaches 100 hours in a specific helicopter model. How should a low-time-in-type pilot factor this into their self-assessment before flying a model they recently transitioned into?
questions.answer: The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that accidents correlate more closely with hours in a specific aircraft type than with total flight hours. A pilot with 2,000 total hours transitioning into a new helicopter model carries higher risk during early hours in type because the automation, power management habits, center of gravity behavior, tail rotor authority margins, and emergency procedures are not yet second nature. During self-assessment, this pilot should honestly evaluate: currency in the specific model, familiarity with that aircraft's emergency checklists, comfort with its power margins (especially for confined area or high-density altitude operations), and whether their recent sim or dual instruction is adequate for the planned mission. They should apply conservative personal minimums — lower winds, higher fuel reserves, more familiar terrain — until reaching greater proficiency in type. This is a legitimate self-assessment factor that goes beyond the IMSAFE checklist into situational awareness and workload management.

questions.question: A pilot accurately completes the IMSAFE checklist, determines they are fit to fly, but mid-flight begins experiencing subtle spatial disorientation during a cloud encounter. At what point does self-assessment become a real-time, ongoing process rather than just a preflight activity, and how does this connect to Single-Pilot Resource Management?
questions.answer: Self-assessment does not end at the preflight — it is a continuous process throughout the flight. SRM explicitly includes situational awareness and workload management as ongoing pilot responsibilities. In IMC, spatial disorientation is an insidious threat because a pilot may feel fine during preflight but become incapacitated mid-flight by vestibular illusions. Real-time self-assessment means the pilot must continuously ask: 'Am I making good decisions? Are my instrument scan and control inputs accurate? Am I experiencing unusual sensations that don't match the instruments?' When disorientation is suspected, the correct SRM action is to immediately trust instruments over sensory input, reduce workload by shedding non-essential tasks, and if necessary, declare an emergency and request ATC assistance. The preflight IMSAFE assessment cannot predict all in-flight physiological changes — hypoxia, hyperventilation, CO poisoning, and dehydration can all develop in flight and require the pilot to recognize impairment and respond appropriately.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot becomes aware mid-flight that they are experiencing a medical episode — say, chest pain — what are their specific legal obligations and what resources are available to them?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.3, the PIC has final authority and responsibility for safe operation. If the pilot experiences a medical emergency mid-flight, they should immediately declare an emergency with ATC (7700 on transponder, MAYDAY on radio) to receive priority handling. ATC can coordinate with airport emergency services and provide vectors to the nearest suitable landing area. There is no FAR that prevents a pilot from landing at an uncontrolled or controlled airport without prior coordination in a genuine emergency — 14 CFR 91.3(b) explicitly allows deviation from any rule to meet an emergency. After landing, the pilot must file a written report with the FAA if requested under 14 CFR 91.3(c). Regarding the medical certificate: if the medical episode constitutes a new diagnosis that would affect medical standards, the pilot must not resume flight until cleared by an AME per 14 CFR 61.53.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 61.53; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 1

questions.question: During this checkride, I want you to demonstrate self-assessment right now — tell me how you evaluated your fitness to fly today and what personal minimums or concerns, if any, factored into that assessment.
questions.answer: This question evaluates whether the applicant can authentically apply self-assessment skills rather than just recite the IMSAFE acronym. A competent applicant should: (1) Walk through IMSAFE specifically — did they get adequate sleep? Any illness, medication, or emotional stressors? Alcohol at least 8+ hours prior and BAC under 0.04%? Had food and water? (2) Discuss currency — recent experience in this specific helicopter model, last night flight if applicable, recent instrument experience if the flight will involve any IMC. (3) Acknowledge the checkride-specific stressor: anxiety and pressure are normal but should be acknowledged and managed — this is itself an emotional factor. A strong applicant will note that checkride stress is real and describe how they've prepared to manage workload accordingly (briefings, personal minimums, knowing the aircraft cold). (4) Be honest — if they had poor sleep or are nervous, saying so and explaining mitigation is a stronger answer than claiming perfection. Examiners are looking for genuine self-awareness, not a scripted 'I'm perfectly fine' response.
questions.follow_up: Let's say you told me right now that you only slept four hours last night but feel fine — as the examiner, can I legally refuse to conduct this checkride, and what options do we both have?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, an examiner can decline to conduct a checkride if they have legitimate safety concerns about the applicant's fitness. The examiner is also acting as PIC or has responsibility for safe conduct of the evaluation. Under 14 CFR 61.43, an examiner has the authority to discontinue a practical test for safety reasons at any point. If the examiner believes fatigue poses a risk — even if the applicant insists they feel fine — the examiner can postpone the test. There is no regulatory penalty for postponing due to fitness concerns. The applicant may request a different date, and no failure is logged if the test is discontinued before the oral or practical begins. Conversely, if the examiner proceeds and the applicant causes an unsafe event due to fatigue, the examiner shares responsibility. This is also a teaching moment: 'I feel fine' is not a reliable self-assessment — it is the honest evaluation of objective fitness indicators that matters.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'continuously assess the environment for safe flight' during preflight, and why is this especially important for helicopter operations?
questions.answer: Continuously assessing the environment means actively monitoring all factors that could affect flight safety — weather, terrain, aircraft condition, personnel, and operational context — not just during the preflight walkaround but throughout the entire flight sequence. For helicopters specifically, this matters because helicopters often operate in confined areas, low altitudes, and dynamic environments (EMS pads, offshore platforms, mountain pinnacles) where conditions can change rapidly. A single-snapshot assessment at the start of preflight is insufficient; pilots must keep updating their situational awareness as conditions evolve.

questions.question: Name at least four environmental factors a helicopter pilot should continuously assess before and during preflight operations.
questions.answer: Environmental factors to continuously assess include: (1) weather conditions and trends — wind speed and direction, visibility, ceiling, precipitation, and forecasted changes; (2) surface and terrain conditions — slope, obstacles, surface type (dust, snow, loose debris that could cause brownout/whiteout); (3) airspace status — NOTAMs, TFRs, nearby traffic; (4) aircraft landing/takeoff area suitability — obstructions, power lines, wire hazards, bystander proximity; (5) density altitude — temperature, elevation, and humidity affecting performance; (6) bird or wildlife activity near the rotor arc. The environment is not static and must be re-evaluated continuously.

questions.question: How does the concept of the 'error chain' relate to continuously assessing the environment for safe flight?
questions.answer: The error chain describes how most accidents result not from a single catastrophic mistake but from a sequence of smaller poor decisions or unrecognized hazards that compound over time. Continuously assessing the environment allows a pilot to detect warning signs early — a deteriorating ceiling, an unexpected obstacle, a bystander moving near the tail rotor — before those hazards link together into an accident. Breaking even one link in that chain can change the outcome. Ongoing environmental assessment is the mechanism by which pilots catch developing error chains before they become irreversible.

questions.question: You arrive at your helicopter for a scheduled VFR flight. During preflight walkaround, the weather looks acceptable — 2,500 ft ceiling and 5 miles visibility. By the time you finish the cockpit checks 20 minutes later, you notice the ceiling has dropped and fog is forming on the ridgeline ahead. How should your ongoing environmental assessment change your decision-making at this point?
questions.answer: This scenario illustrates exactly why environmental assessment must be continuous rather than a one-time check. The initial VFR conditions appeared adequate but have deteriorated within the preflight window itself. At this point, the pilot should: (1) obtain an updated weather briefing — call FSS or check ASOS/AWOS for the route and destination; (2) reassess the filed route against the new conditions, particularly if the route crosses the ridgeline where fog is forming; (3) apply the SRM framework — is this a 'probably' situation? If the route will 'probably' be clear, that is insufficient — choose the option known to work; (4) consider delaying departure, rerouting, or canceling based on updated data. The evolving conditions during preflight itself are a strong caution flag that should not be rationalized away.

questions.question: You are conducting a preflight at a remote mountain landing zone at 7,500 ft MSL on a hot afternoon. The aircraft performance charts show you are very close to the OGE hover limit with your planned load. During the preflight, the wind — which was 10 knots on your nose when you landed — has shifted and is now a 5-knot tailwind. How does this environmental change affect your assessment and what should you do?
questions.answer: This is a significant environmental change that directly affects your ability to depart safely. The 10-knot headwind was likely contributing to translational lift during arrival and may have been partially compensating for the high-density-altitude performance limitation. A shift to a 5-knot tailwind changes the effective wind component by 15 knots and removes that aerodynamic advantage. Actions to take: (1) Recalculate performance with the tailwind — tailwinds reduce effective translational lift and increase power required for transition; (2) Reassess whether OGE hover power is achievable with the current load at this density altitude without the headwind benefit; (3) Consider off-loading fuel or cargo; (4) Wait for wind to shift back — wind at mountain LZs can be cyclical; (5) Reposition the helicopter if possible to take advantage of any available headwind component. Never depart on a 'probably' — if OGE hover isn't confirmed achievable, the option known to work is to reduce weight or wait.

questions.question: During preflight at an unfamiliar helipad, you notice ground crew moving equipment in the area behind your tail rotor, a fuel truck parked at the edge of your intended hover path, and a light aircraft taxiing nearby. How do you incorporate these simultaneous environmental threats into your preflight assessment before engine start?
questions.answer: This is a multi-threat environment requiring immediate active management before engine start. Steps to take: (1) Do not start the engine until the area is clear — the tail rotor zone is the highest-priority hazard; brief or gesture to ground crew to stay clear of the tail rotor arc, which is invisible when spinning; (2) Assess the fuel truck position — determine if it blocks your hover path and whether it will be moved before departure; if not, identify an alternate hover route before committing to engine start; (3) Monitor the taxiing light aircraft — confirm it will not conflict with your hover path or takeoff corridor; coordinate with ATC or ground personnel if at a towered facility; (4) Brief any passengers on the environmental hazards before boarding; (5) Delay engine start until all three threats are resolved or mitigated. Continuously re-evaluate as each factor changes. The principle of SRM applies — workload management means sequencing these threats rather than accepting all of them simultaneously.

questions.question: A pilot completes a thorough preflight and determines the environment is safe for flight. Fifteen minutes into the flight, new environmental threats emerge — unexpected IMC ahead and a low-fuel warning due to a fuel cap left off during preflight. At what point did the 'continuous' environmental assessment fail, and what structural habits could have caught both threats earlier?
questions.answer: The failure of continuous environmental assessment occurred at two distinct points: (1) The fuel cap issue represents a preflight failure — either the cap was not checked or not verified as secured after fueling. However, the continuous assessment failure occurred in flight when the pilot did not notice fuel state trending abnormally early enough. A habit of regular instrument cross-checks — including fuel quantity — at defined intervals would have caught the abnormal fuel burn rate before the warning light activated; (2) The unexpected IMC represents either a weather assessment failure at preflight (inadequate briefing or ignoring marginal trends) or a failure to monitor weather evolution during flight. Continuous assessment requires periodic in-flight weather updates via ATIS, AWOS, or ATC — not assuming the preflight briefing remains valid for the entire flight duration. Structural habits to build: (a) Use a defined cockpit scan interval — every 5-10 minutes, actively re-evaluate fuel, weather, terrain, and aircraft systems; (b) Set personal fuel minimums as hard limits, not guidelines; (c) Obtain en route weather updates proactively rather than reactively; (d) Apply the SRM 'PAVE' checklist (Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures) not just at preflight but at waypoints during flight.
questions.follow_up: With IMC now ahead and a fuel emergency developing simultaneously, what is the correct priority order for handling these two emergencies, and why is that order significant from an ADM standpoint?
questions.follow_up_answer: The correct priority is: (1) Aviate — maintain aircraft control and avoid inadvertent IMC entry, which is the more immediately lethal threat. Continued VFR flight into IMC is a leading cause of fatal helicopter accidents. Turn away from the IMC immediately, even if that means turning away from the nearest fuel source; (2) Navigate — once clear of the IMC threat, determine the nearest suitable landing area where fuel is available or where a precautionary landing can be made before fuel exhaustion; (3) Communicate — declare an emergency if needed; ATC can vector you to fuel and issue traffic advisories. From an ADM standpoint, the significance is that pilots under stress tend to fixate on the first threat they identified — in this case, possibly the fuel warning light — while continuing into IMC because 'it will only be a few more minutes.' This is classic get-there-itis and tunnel vision. The examiner lesson: emergencies rarely occur one at a time, and ADM training must prepare pilots to correctly triage simultaneous threats rather than serialize them in the wrong order.

questions.question: You are 100 hours into your first 200 hours on a new turbine helicopter type after transitioning from pistons. You preflight the aircraft and note that several systems feel 'different' from what you remember from your training but nothing appears definitively broken. How does pilot familiarity with the aircraft represent a risk category during preflight assessment, and what risk management principles apply?
questions.answer: Pilot familiarity with the specific aircraft model is a recognized risk factor that belongs in the preflight risk assessment even though it is technically a pilot risk — it directly shapes how accurately the pilot can detect aircraft anomalies during the preflight. If systems feel 'different' and the pilot lacks the experience baseline to know whether that difference is normal variation or a genuine discrepancy, the risk is elevated. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-21B) and the FAA's aeronautical decision-making guidance consistently identify pilot experience in type as a significant variable in accident risk, noting that pilots transitioning to new aircraft types are more vulnerable to misidentifying or overlooking anomalies due to unfamiliarity with normal system behavior and appearance. This pilot, relatively early in type experience on a complex turbine platform, should treat any 'feels different' observation as an unresolved discrepancy rather than normal variation until it can be confirmed otherwise. The appropriate risk management actions include: (1) consult the RFM system descriptions to verify whether what was observed is within normal parameters; (2) request a review from a more experienced pilot or mechanic familiar with that specific airframe; (3) lower the personal risk threshold for other variables on this flight — if the aircraft condition is uncertain, compensate by ensuring weather, routing, and workload are as benign as possible; (4) never dismiss 'it feels different' as mere pilot inexperience without first investigating the aircraft system. FAA ADM doctrine supports choosing a course of action known to be safe over one that is only assumed to be acceptable.
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the unsupported specific claim that FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 cites accident rate data correlated to hours in type and the reference to '100 hours as the boundary of the highest-risk transition period,' replacing these with accurately attributed, general FAA ADM and HFH principles about pilot familiarity as a risk factor.

questions.question: During a preflight assessment, how would you use the PAVE risk identification checklist to identify external pressure as a risk element, and what category does it fall under?
questions.answer: The FAA risk identification framework uses the PAVE checklist, which stands for Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, and External pressures. As presented in FAA training materials, external pressures form their own category within PAVE rather than being a subcategory of environment, though pilots should be aware that different editions or training materials may group these elements slightly differently. During preflight, the pilot should consciously ask whether schedule demands, passenger expectations, financial consequences, or personal commitments are influencing the decision to fly. If external pressures are identified, the pilot should factor them into the overall risk picture and apply mitigations such as establishing firm go/no-go criteria before the flight, communicating honestly with stakeholders about weather or maintenance holds, and reaffirming PIC authority and responsibility for the final go/no-go decision. The act of explicitly naming external pressure during a structured preflight risk assessment is itself a risk mitigation, because it moves the influence from subconscious to conscious evaluation where it can be properly weighed.
questions.rewrite_note: Clarified that the PAVE framework presents external pressures as their own category while acknowledging that some FAA materials may present the categories with slight variations, removing the overly definitive claim about the exact acronym structure.

questions.question: Research shows that helicopter accidents correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft model than with total flight hours. How should this fact inform how a pilot continuously assesses the environment when transitioning to a new helicopter type, even if they have thousands of total hours?
questions.answer: The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that experience in a specific aircraft type is a critical safety factor, and that total flight hours alone do not confer automatic proficiency in a new aircraft. A high-time pilot transitioning to a new type should recognize that their environmental assessment capability is temporarily degraded because: (1) Cockpit scanning patterns must be rebuilt for a new instrument layout — what took a fraction of a second in the old aircraft now requires conscious effort, consuming attentional resources needed for environmental awareness; (2) Performance limitations, power margins, and handling characteristics differ between types — the pilot may misjudge what the new aircraft can handle in a given environment; (3) Automation or avionics differences (such as transitioning to a glass cockpit) add workload during normal operations, leaving less mental capacity for environmental monitoring. Practical application: during the transition period, the pilot should apply more conservative environmental criteria — wider weather margins, more familiar operating environments, and simpler mission profiles — and actively counteract the tendency to assume that high total hours means full situational awareness in the new aircraft. Recognizing and managing this gap is a core element of SRM and ADM as outlined in FAA-H-8083-21B.
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the unsupported specific '100 hours in type' threshold and replaced it with the general principle that type-specific experience is a critical safety factor, which is supportable from FAA-H-8083-21B without citing an unverified numeric milestone.

tasks.title: Task B. Flight Deck Management

areas_of_operation.title: Area of Operation II. Preflight Procedures

tasks.title: Task B. Passenger Briefing and Preflight (partial)

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 91.107, when are passengers required to have their safety belts fastened during helicopter operations, and what are the child restraint requirements?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.107(a), all persons on board must have a safety belt fastened during flight operations. The PIC must ensure all occupants are briefed on how to fasten and unfasten their safety belts before the flight. For children, a child restraint system (approved under FAA TSO or labeled for use in aircraft) must be used for children under 2 years of age. Children 2 years of age or older must occupy a seat and be restrained by either an approved child restraint system or a safety belt.

questions.question: According to the Helicopter Flying Handbook, from which direction should passengers approach or depart a helicopter, and what should they always do while in the rotor arc?
questions.answer: Passengers should always approach and depart a helicopter from the side — specifically from the front quadrant where the pilot can see them. They should never approach from the rear due to the tail rotor hazard. Passengers should always crouch or duck-walk while under the rotor arc to stay clear of the main rotor blade tips. If a hat or other item blows away, passengers must never chase it — they should notify the pilot instead.

questions.question: What are the minimum elements a PIC must include in a passenger briefing before a part 91 helicopter flight?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.107, the PIC must brief passengers before flight on: (1) how to fasten and unfasten the safety belt and shoulder harness if installed; and (2) when safety belts must be fastened during the flight. Beyond regulatory minimums, best practices per FAA-H-8083-21B (Helicopter Flying Handbook) include rotor hazard awareness, emergency exits, emergency procedures, and prohibition on touching flight controls. Note: 14 CFR 91.519 applies to large transport-category aircraft and does not govern typical part 91 helicopter passenger briefings.

questions.question: During your passenger briefing before a flight to an off-airport site, one of your passengers asks if they can open the door in flight to get a better photo. What rotor-related safety issues must you address, and how does this relate to the passenger briefing requirements?
questions.answer: The passenger briefing must include specific helicopter hazards that don't exist in fixed-wing aircraft. Opening doors in flight can create aerodynamic disturbances, and if a door or loose item were to contact the main rotor, it could be catastrophic. The PIC should clearly instruct passengers: (1) do not open doors in flight without explicit permission; (2) secure all loose items such as scarves, hats, cameras, and bags before boarding and during flight; (3) never extend any body part outside the aircraft. This is part of the broader PIC responsibility to conduct a thorough safety briefing tailored to the helicopter environment, including rotor hazards unique to rotorcraft operations.

questions.question: You are conducting a passenger briefing and your helicopter has an inoperative shoulder harness on one seat that has been properly deferred under 91.213(d) and placarded INOPERATIVE. How does this affect your briefing requirement for that passenger?
questions.answer: The passenger must still be briefed on the available restraint — in this case the lap belt only — and must be shown how to fasten and unfasten it. The PIC must still comply with 91.107 for the operable restraint system. The PIC should also inform the passenger of the inoperative shoulder harness so they understand what restraint is available. Additionally, the PIC should consider whether the deferred equipment affects the safety of the intended flight and whether the operation is appropriate with that seat configuration. The placard serves as a reminder, but it does not eliminate the PIC's briefing obligation for the functioning components.

questions.question: A pilot argues that passenger briefings are just a formality and that experienced helicopter passengers don't need to hear it every flight. As an examiner, how would you evaluate this attitude, and what does the FAA say about the relationship between complacency and accident causation in helicopter operations?
questions.answer: This attitude reflects the hazardous thought pattern of complacency — one of the five antidotes described in ADM training. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that approximately 80% of aviation accidents are attributable to human factors and pilot error. The 'error chain' concept emphasizes that accidents rarely result from a single failure but from a series of small poor decisions — skipping a proper passenger briefing because a passenger seems experienced is exactly the kind of link that can contribute to that chain. The passenger briefing requirement under 91.107 is not discretionary; it is a regulatory mandate every flight, regardless of passenger experience. Even experienced passengers may be unfamiliar with a specific helicopter type's door latches, emergency exits, or restraint system differences. The correct ADM approach is to give a complete, consistent briefing every flight.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot is flying under BasicMed, does that change any of the passenger briefing requirements or the pilot's PIC responsibilities?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. BasicMed (14 CFR Part 68 / 61.113(i)) only addresses the medical certification requirements for the pilot — it does not alter, reduce, or modify any PIC responsibilities, operational rules, or passenger briefing requirements under 14 CFR 91.107. The pilot operating under BasicMed must comply with all the same 14 CFR Part 91 operating rules as a pilot holding a traditional medical certificate, including complete passenger briefings every flight.

questions.question: During hot refueling with passengers on board, what are the PIC's specific responsibilities, and how do those responsibilities interact with the requirement to brief passengers before and during this ground operation?
questions.answer: The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that during hot refueling — refueling with the engine running — the pilot must remain at the flight controls and be ready to immediately shut down and egress if a fire or emergency develops. Because the pilot cannot leave the controls, the passenger briefing for hot refueling must be completed before the operation begins. Passengers must be briefed on: (1) remaining seated with seatbelts fastened or exiting the aircraft completely and moving to a safe distance — the specific procedure depends on operator policy and the RFM; (2) no smoking within the refueling area; (3) the emergency egress path if immediate exit is required. The PIC cannot abandon the controls to re-brief a passenger during hot refueling — this underscores the critical importance of a thorough briefing before the operation begins.
questions.follow_up: If a passenger ignores your briefing and begins to exit the helicopter on the fuel cap side during hot refueling, what is your immediate priority and what does this scenario illustrate about ADM?
questions.follow_up_answer: The PIC's immediate priority is to secure the aircraft controls and verbally direct the passenger to stop — using the intercom or voice. If the passenger is in danger near the fueling area or tail rotor, the PIC may need to shut down immediately. This scenario illustrates the ADM principle of situational awareness and workload management under stress. It also illustrates why the pre-refueling briefing must be unambiguous and confirmed understood — not just delivered. The 'probably' trap applies here: if you only 'probably' think the passenger understood the briefing, that is insufficient. Confirmation of understanding should be part of the briefing process, consistent with the Trescott Tip from the HFH.

questions.question: Why does the FAA require the use of a checklist during helicopter preflight inspection rather than relying on memory alone?
questions.answer: The FAA emphasizes checklist use during preflight because it ensures no item is overlooked. Human memory is fallible, especially under stress, fatigue, or distraction. A checklist provides a systematic, repeatable process that guards against complacency and incomplete inspections. The PIC is responsible for ensuring the helicopter is in an airworthy condition before flight, and the checklist is the primary tool for fulfilling that responsibility.

questions.question: What is the difference between using a 'do-list' checklist and a 'check-list' (verify) checklist, and which approach does the FAA recommend for complex procedures like engine start?
questions.answer: A 'do-list' checklist is read item by item and each action is performed as you go, used for complex or unfamiliar procedures. A 'check-list' or verify checklist is used after completing a procedure from memory to confirm all items were accomplished. The FAA recommends using a step-by-step do-list approach for procedures like engine start to prevent omitting critical steps, while the verify checklist can be used for some normal flows. The helicopter's RFM/POH specifies which method to use for each phase of operation.

questions.question: Before starting the engine, the helicopter checklist calls for positioning the rotor blades perpendicular to the fuselage. Why is this step important?
questions.answer: Rotor blades must be positioned perpendicular to the fuselage before engine start to establish a balanced, stable rotor configuration and ensure adequate clearance for blade movement during rotor engagement and startup acceleration. This positioning prevents dynamic imbalance and enables smooth rotor ramp-up. Verification that blade tie-downs are removed is a separate but related preflight walkaround item performed to prevent catastrophic damage if rotation is attempted with restraints in place.

questions.question: You're hot refueling a turbine helicopter and a passenger asks you to run through the passenger briefing checklist while fuel is being added. What is the correct procedure, and why does the checklist sequence matter here?
questions.answer: During hot refueling, the pilot must remain at the flight controls and be ready to immediately shut down and egress — those are the priority requirements. Conducting the passenger briefing checklist at that moment is inappropriate because it diverts attention from fuel and engine monitoring duties. The correct sequence is to complete the passenger briefing checklist before refueling begins, or after it is completed and the aircraft is secured. Checklist sequencing matters because performing items out of order can create compounding hazards — in this case, divided attention during a high-risk ground operation.

questions.question: During your preflight, you discover an instrument that is not listed in the helicopter's MEL as deferrable — the rotor tachometer is inoperative. A co-pilot suggests you just placard it and fly. What does the checklist and regulatory framework require you to do?
questions.answer: If a component is not listed in the MEL as deferrable, it cannot be deferred — it must be repaired before the aircraft can be flown. The MEL only authorizes deferral for items specifically listed within it. An inoperative rotor tachometer would fall into this category since it is a critical flight instrument. Simply placarding it INOPERATIVE is not sufficient unless the MEL specifically permits that deferral. The preflight checklist process should identify the discrepancy, and the PIC must ground the aircraft until the item is repaired. Flying with a non-deferrable inoperative item renders the aircraft unairworthy.

questions.question: You're conducting a preflight at an unfamiliar off-airport site in low light conditions. You complete the walkaround from memory because your tablet with the checklist is dead and you didn't bring a printed backup. What risk does this scenario illustrate, and how should it have been handled?
questions.answer: This scenario illustrates how relying solely on memory for a checklist — especially under adverse conditions like low light and an unfamiliar environment — significantly increases the risk of missing critical airworthiness items. Human memory degrades under stress, fatigue, and environmental pressure. The FAA's guidance is that a checklist should always be used during preflight. The pilot should have had a printed backup checklist as standard equipment, or delayed the preflight until a usable checklist was available. This is a foreseeable situation that proper preflight planning should address — a missing checklist is a risk management item itself.

questions.question: A highly experienced helicopter pilot tells you that after 5,000 hours in type, checklists are just a formality — he knows every item by heart and the checklist slows him down. How would you evaluate this reasoning from both a human factors and regulatory standpoint?
questions.answer: This reasoning is flawed on both counts. From a human factors standpoint, the FAA's own data shows that approximately 80% of aviation accidents are caused by pilot error, and complacency is a well-documented hazard associated with high experience levels. High familiarity with an aircraft can actually increase susceptibility to complacency — experienced pilots may skip steps precisely because they 'know' the aircraft so well. The error chain often involves multiple seemingly minor decisions, and skipping checklist items is exactly how links get added. From a regulatory standpoint, 14 CFR 91.7 makes the PIC responsible for airworthiness, and the FAA's guidance in FAA-H-8083-21B explicitly states a checklist should always be used during preflight. Experienced pilots should use checklists as a discipline, not a crutch.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot then argues that the accident statistics you cited involve low-time pilots, not veterans with 5,000 hours, how do you respond?
questions.follow_up_answer: The FAA's research actually shows that accident rates correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft model than with total hours — and importantly, accidents decrease significantly after 100 hours in type, but they never reach zero. Beyond 100 hours in type, complacency and normalization of deviance become the dominant risk factors, not inexperience. Even at 5,000 hours in type, external pressures, fatigue, distraction, and breaking the habit of checklist discipline remain real threats. The FAA's ADM framework specifically identifies complacency as an unsafe attitude (the 'invulnerability' hazardous attitude), and the antidote is recognizing that it can happen to anyone, regardless of experience level.

questions.question: Your helicopter's RFM includes a normal checklist and a limitations section that prohibits certain operations. During preflight, the checklist does not explicitly reference all the limitations. If you complete the checklist without separately reviewing the limitations section, have you fulfilled your preflight responsibility? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No, completing the normal checklist alone does not fully satisfy the preflight responsibility. The checklist is an action-oriented tool, but it does not substitute for the pilot's knowledge of the RFM limitations section. The limitations section contains mandatory regulatory limits — such as airspeed, weight, CG range, operating temperature ranges, and prohibited maneuvers — that are part of the aircraft's airworthiness certificate and are binding under 14 CFR 91.9 and 91.7. The PIC is required to be knowledgeable about the aircraft's operating limitations and must ensure the flight is conducted within them. A proper preflight preparation includes reviewing the limitations section as part of a holistic airworthiness determination, not just running through a checklist of actions.
questions.follow_up: Let's say you discover during preflight that an ambient temperature is forecast to exceed a limitation listed only in the RFM limitations section — not flagged anywhere in the normal checklist. What is your obligation, and what are your options?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot's obligation is to not conduct the flight under conditions that would violate the RFM limitations, regardless of whether the checklist flags it. Operating outside RFM limitations renders the aircraft unairworthy under 14 CFR 91.7 and may constitute careless or reckless operation under 14 CFR 91.13. The options are: delay the flight until conditions are within limits, identify an alternative operational profile that stays within limits (e.g., reduced weight to address high-density altitude performance limits), or consult the manufacturer or a CFII/DPE if there is ambiguity about interpretation. The RFM limitations are not advisory — they are mandatory, and the PIC bears responsibility for knowing and complying with them.

questions.question: How often are electronic navigation databases — such as those used in GPS and FMS units — updated, and who is responsible for ensuring the database is current before an IFR flight?
questions.answer: Electronic navigation databases are updated every 28 days on an AIRAC cycle. The PIC is responsible for ensuring the database is current before flight. An out-of-date database may not reflect current procedures, waypoints, or airspace, and using one for IFR navigation could render the aircraft not airworthy for that purpose.

questions.question: What is the difference between the update cycle for en route and terminal procedure paper charts versus electronic navigation databases?
questions.answer: En route and terminal procedure charts (paper or PDF) are revised every 56 days. Electronic navigation databases are updated more frequently — every 28 days. This means a database could be updated twice within a single paper chart cycle, and pilots must verify currency for both independently.

questions.question: What does MEA stand for, and what two things does it guarantee that MOCA does not fully provide?
questions.answer: MEA stands for Minimum En Route Altitude. It guarantees two things: (1) obstacle clearance along the entire route segment, and (2) acceptable navigation signal reception from ground-based NAVAIDs along the entire segment. MOCA also guarantees obstacle clearance, but navigation signal reception is only guaranteed within 22 nautical miles of the defining NAVAID — not along the full segment.

questions.question: You're flying a Part 91 IFR helicopter flight and your GPS navigator's database expired 10 days ago. The unit still functions and the moving map looks correct. Can you legally use this unit for IFR navigation, and what options do you have?
questions.answer: Using an expired database for IFR approaches or primary navigation is generally not authorized because the database currency is a condition of the equipment's approval for that use. For IFR operations, the TSO and AFM/RFMS supplement typically require a current database. However, for situational awareness or cross-checking with current paper charts, the unit may be used with caution. The correct action is to update the database before the flight if IFR navigation reliance is intended, or to use current paper charts verified against NOTAMs and cross-check with other approved navigation sources. The PIC bears responsibility for airworthiness and must determine whether navigation data is appropriate for the intended operation.

questions.question: You are planning an IFR helicopter flight along a Victor airway segment. The chart in your EFB was last updated 45 days ago, but the paper chart cycle ended 3 days ago and a new one is now in effect. A NOTAM was issued 2 days ago changing the MEA on your route by 500 feet. Which source takes legal precedence, and how should you account for this in your planning?
questions.answer: NOTAMs take immediate effect and supersede published chart information for the conditions they describe. Even if the old chart is still technically within its 56-day cycle for general use, a NOTAM that amends an MEA must be applied. The pilot must check NOTAMs as part of preflight planning under 14 CFR 91.103 and fly the NOTAM-amended MEA, not the charted one. The EFB chart, now past its 56-day cycle, should also be treated as potentially outdated and cross-checked against the most current published information. Appropriate navigation data means current AND applicable to the route — both requirements must be met.

questions.question: Your helicopter's IFR GPS is approved for en route and terminal operations but NOT for approach operations. The database is current. You're shooting an RNAV (GPS) approach into a mountain heliport. What navigation data requirement are you missing, and what are the implications?
questions.answer: Even with a current database, the equipment must be approved and certified for the specific type of operation. If the GPS is only approved for en route and terminal use — not approach — it cannot be used as the primary means of navigation for an instrument approach, regardless of database currency. The relevant AFM supplement or AFMS will define the operational approval level. Using it for an approach would be a violation of the aircraft's operating limitations. The pilot would need either an approved approach-certified GPS or conventional approach aids (VOR, ILS, NDB if applicable) to legally fly the approach. Navigation data being 'current' is necessary but not sufficient — the data must also be 'appropriate' for the intended operation.

questions.question: A pilot argues that because their GPS receiver shows a RAIM alert has not activated and the moving map matches their paper chart, the navigation data must be both current and appropriate. As an examiner, why would you push back on that reasoning, and what's the more rigorous standard?
questions.answer: RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) monitors GPS satellite geometry and signal integrity — it does NOT verify that the waypoints, procedures, or altitudes stored in the database are current or correct. A database with outdated procedures could still pass all RAIM checks because the satellites are fine; it's the stored navigation data that's wrong. Additionally, a moving map that matches an old paper chart only confirms the old data is self-consistent, not that either source is current. The rigorous standard is: (1) verify the database update date against the current AIRAC cycle, (2) cross-check the procedure against the currently effective chart, (3) review applicable NOTAMs for the route and destination, and (4) confirm the equipment is approved for the intended phase of flight. Currency and appropriateness are distinct requirements — both must be independently verified.
questions.follow_up: If RAIM can't verify database currency, what ground-based check can a pilot perform before an IFR flight to confirm a waypoint or procedure in their GPS database is still valid?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot should cross-reference the specific waypoint coordinates, course, distance, and altitude constraints against the current published instrument procedure chart (either official paper or a current EFB chart still within its effective date). They should also pull NOTAMs for the departure airport, destination, and en route NAVAIDs to check for any amendments, procedure changes, or NAVAID outages. For GPS approaches specifically, the pilot can verify the approach via the FAA's NASR (National Airspace System Resources) database or the FAA's digital-TPP (terminal procedures publication), which are updated every 28 days in sync with the electronic database cycle.

questions.question: You're conducting an IFR helicopter flight in a remote area where your only navigation source is a GPS with a database that expired 3 days ago. An in-flight emergency forces a divert to an unfamiliar airport. The GPS shows the RNAV approach, but the database is expired. Walk me through your decision-making process regarding use of that navigation data.
questions.answer: In a true emergency (loss of life, serious injury, or substantial property damage imminent), 14 CFR 91.3(b) grants the PIC authority to deviate from regulations to the extent necessary to meet the emergency. This permits use of the expired GPS database as one navigational aid. However, you must understand that displayed procedures may not reflect current conditions (changed altitudes, closed waypoints, runway closures) and you must cross-check against all available information: ATC vectors, published approach procedures from memory or plates if available, ATIS, and verbal ATC guidance. Declare the emergency to ATC, request radar vectors or assistance, and use the expired data critically for situational awareness, not blind compliance. Under 14 CFR 91.3(c), the FAA may subsequently request a written report of any regulatory deviation.
questions.follow_up: After landing safely from that emergency divert, what are your obligations regarding the deviation from regulations, and what documentation might be required?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.3(c), the pilot in command who deviates from a regulation under emergency authority must, upon request of the FAA, send a written report of the deviation. The FAA may request this report, but the pilot is not required to submit one proactively unless requested. The pilot should also document the emergency in the aircraft maintenance records if any abnormal operations occurred, notify the operator (if applicable), and review the experience for ADM lessons. Using the expired database itself is the deviation from 14 CFR 91 equipment and airworthiness standards, but because it was justified under 91.3(b), it is legally defensible provided the pilot exercised sound judgment and did not take undue risks.

questions.question: Why is it especially important to secure loose items inside a helicopter cabin before flight compared to a fixed-wing aircraft?
questions.answer: Helicopters produce significant rotor wash, vibration, and frequently operate with doors removed or open. Loose items can shift during aggressive maneuvering, low-G flight conditions, or autorotation entries, potentially jamming flight controls — particularly the cyclic, collective, or tail rotor pedals. In a fixed-wing aircraft, controls are less exposed and flight envelopes are generally less dynamic. The PIC is responsible under 14 CFR 91.7 for aircraft airworthiness and under 91.9 for operating within limitations, both of which are compromised if an unsecured item interferes with controls.

questions.question: What regulation places the responsibility on the pilot in command to ensure that cargo and baggage are properly secured before flight?
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.7 makes the PIC responsible for the airworthiness of the aircraft during flight, and 14 CFR 91.9 prohibits operating an aircraft in a manner that exceeds its limitations — both apply when improperly secured cargo could affect flight control freedom or shift the center of gravity outside approved limits. Additionally, 14 CFR 91.527 addresses cargo in transport operations, but for Part 91 operations the PIC's general airworthiness responsibility under 91.7 is the primary authority.

questions.question: What are the two primary hazards created by improperly secured cargo or loose items aboard a helicopter?
questions.answer: The two primary hazards are: (1) Flight control interference — a loose item that migrates under or around the cyclic, collective, or tail rotor pedals can restrict or jam control inputs, potentially making the helicopter uncontrollable; and (2) Center of gravity (CG) shift — cargo that shifts during flight can move the CG outside the approved envelope, affecting helicopter stability, control authority, and in extreme cases making recovery impossible. Both hazards are addressed in FAA-H-8083-21B and the helicopter's Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM).
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8; RFM/POH weight and balance section

questions.question: You're doing a utility flight carrying two toolboxes and a bag of equipment in the back seat area of your R44. The bags are zipped but the toolboxes are not latched. How do you evaluate whether this load is acceptable for departure?
questions.answer: You must address three things before departure: (1) Weight and balance — calculate the actual loaded weight and CG using the RFM weight and balance data to confirm both are within limits for the loaded condition and anticipated fuel burn; (2) Physical securement — unlatched toolboxes are not secured. During turbulence, a rapid collective reduction, or an autorotation entry, they can slide, tip, or spill contents. They must be latched, strapped, or otherwise positively restrained so they cannot shift or open in flight; (3) Control clearance — verify that no cargo is positioned where it could contact or restrict the cyclic, collective, or interfere with any control travel. Departure is not appropriate until all three criteria are met. The PIC's responsibility under 14 CFR 91.7 requires that the aircraft be airworthy, which includes cargo securement.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8; RFM weight and balance section

questions.question: A passenger insists on keeping a large backpack on their lap rather than stowing it in the cargo area. What concerns do you have, and how do you handle this?
questions.answer: A backpack on a passenger's lap creates multiple risks: (1) Emergency egress — a bulky item on the lap can prevent rapid egress, particularly in a post-crash fire or water ditching scenario; (2) In-flight hazard — if the passenger shifts or the pack falls, it could strike the cyclic or other controls, especially in a two-seat helicopter where the cyclic is between or in front of occupants; (3) Injury during hard landing — the pack can become a projectile or crush the passenger's torso in a sudden stop. As PIC, you have the authority and responsibility under 14 CFR 91.7 to require the item be properly stowed. Brief the passenger on why this is required, not just that it is. If the passenger refuses, they do not fly.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8 (passenger briefing and safety)

questions.question: You're conducting a flight with doors removed. How does this change your approach to securing items and cargo compared to a normal enclosed-cabin flight?
questions.answer: With doors removed, any item that is not positively secured is a potential projectile that could exit the aircraft and strike the tail rotor, main rotor, or people on the ground — with potentially catastrophic results. The approach must be significantly more conservative: (1) All loose items must be secured with restraints rated for the anticipated aerodynamic loads, not just resting in place; (2) Passengers must be briefed that nothing — clothing, maps, headsets, bags — can be held loosely or placed where airflow can reach it; (3) Consider whether any cargo is appropriate for an open-door configuration at all. The rotor wash and slipstream at cruise speed create substantial aerodynamic forces. Hats, paper charts, and unzipped bags that would be harmless in a closed cabin become serious hazards. The PIC must account for this added risk as part of preflight planning under 14 CFR 91.7.

questions.question: During your preflight, you discover that the previous crew stowed a heavy camera case in the aft baggage compartment that is not mentioned in the aircraft weight and balance record. The item appears to weigh about 25 pounds. Walk me through exactly how you determine whether you can legally and safely depart with it.
questions.answer: This requires a complete weight and balance recalculation, not an estimate. Steps: (1) Weigh or obtain an accurate weight for the item — assumed weights are not acceptable for weight and balance purposes; (2) Identify the arm (moment arm location) for the aft baggage compartment from the RFM/POH; (3) Add the item's weight and calculated moment to the current loaded weight and balance; (4) Verify the new gross weight does not exceed the maximum certificated takeoff weight; (5) Verify the resulting CG falls within the approved envelope for the anticipated flight profile and fuel burn range — including the most forward and most aft CG conditions as fuel burns off; (6) If the new CG or weight is out of limits, the item must be repositioned or removed before departure. Additionally, the aircraft weight and balance record should be updated to reflect the actual loaded condition. Departing without completing this process would be a violation of 14 CFR 91.7 (airworthiness) and potentially 91.9 (operating limitations). The PIC cannot simply accept a prior crew's configuration without independent verification.
questions.follow_up: You run the numbers and the CG is technically within limits at takeoff, but you calculate it will move aft of limits as fuel burns to about half tanks. Can you legally depart?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. A weight and balance analysis must confirm the CG remains within limits throughout the entire flight envelope, including the most critical condition during fuel burn. If the CG will move aft of limits at a predictable point during the flight, departure is not legal. Options include: removing or repositioning the cargo to a more forward station, reducing fuel load so the critical burn point is avoided, or not accepting the flight. Simply landing before reaching half tanks is not a reliable mitigation — fuel burn rates vary, and an off-airport precautionary landing or extended hover could force you into the out-of-limits condition. The RFM envelope must be respected continuously, not just at takeoff.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 91.9; RFM/POH weight and balance section; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8

questions.question: Your helicopter's RFM states that cargo in the baggage compartment must be secured to the tie-down rings using restraints with a minimum load rating. You have appropriate tie-down straps but notice one of the tie-down rings has a crack at its base. How does this affect your go/no-go decision, and how does the MEL factor in?
questions.answer: A cracked tie-down ring is a structural component with an airworthiness implication. The analysis proceeds as follows: (1) A tie-down ring that is cracked cannot be considered airworthy — if the RFM requires cargo to be secured to these rings and one is unserviceable, the aircraft's ability to safely carry cargo per the RFM is compromised; (2) Consult the MEL if the aircraft has one — tie-down rings are not typically listed as deferrable items in an MEL because they are structural attachment points, not avionics or systems components. If not listed as deferrable, the defect must be repaired before flight under 14 CFR 91.213; (3) If no MEL exists, apply 14 CFR 91.213(d) — determine whether the item is required by the RFM, airworthiness directives, or type certificate. If the RFM requires cargo to be secured and the means of securement is compromised, the aircraft is not airworthy for cargo-carrying operations with that compartment; (4) If no cargo will be carried, the analysis changes — but the cracked ring still represents a structural defect that must be evaluated and logged. The PIC cannot simply ignore structural damage under 14 CFR 91.7. The correct action is to ground the aircraft for maintenance inspection and repair of the ring before further cargo operations.
questions.follow_up: If you decide to fly without any cargo in that compartment — leaving it empty — have you resolved the airworthiness issue with the cracked tie-down ring?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not necessarily. While removing cargo eliminates the immediate load-bearing function of the ring, the cracked ring is still a structural defect that must be evaluated by a certificated mechanic. A crack at the base of a tie-down ring could indicate fatigue in the surrounding airframe structure, not just the ring itself. Under 14 CFR 91.7, the PIC is responsible for airworthiness, and any known structural defect must be assessed before flight. The correct action is to have a certificated A&P mechanic inspect the ring and surrounding structure, make a maintenance logbook entry describing the finding, and either repair it or determine whether continued flight is permissible under the applicable maintenance data. The PIC cannot unilaterally determine that a structural crack is acceptable simply by removing the load on it.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 91.213; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8 (MEL and airworthiness); RFM cargo restraint requirements

questions.question: Before flight, you notice a piece of equipment on the helicopter is inoperative. What two methods does 14 CFR Part 91 provide for legally deferring that equipment and still flying?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.213, there are two primary methods: (1) Use an FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List (MEL) specific to that aircraft, which acts as a supplemental type certificate authorizing flight with the inoperative item under defined conditions; or (2) Use the deferral provision under 14 CFR 91.213(d), which allows flight without an MEL if the equipment is not required by the type certificate, airworthiness directives, VFR/IFR rules, or any other regulation — provided it is deactivated, placarded INOPERATIVE, and a preflight determination is made that it does not create a hazard.

questions.question: Your helicopter has an approved MEL. During preflight you find the rotor tachometer is inoperative. The MEL does not list the rotor tachometer as a deferrable item. What does that mean for your flight?
questions.answer: If the rotor tachometer is not listed in the MEL as a deferrable item, it cannot be deferred. The aircraft is not airworthy and must not be flown until the rotor tachometer is repaired and returned to service. The MEL only authorizes operations with equipment that is specifically listed as deferrable under defined conditions. Unlisted items require repair before departure.

questions.question: A passenger wants to use their personal tablet with a GPS moving map app during your flight. What is your primary risk management concern as PIC regarding that portable electronic device?
questions.answer: The primary concerns are: (1) potential electromagnetic interference with aircraft avionics and navigation equipment; (2) distraction to the pilot or crew during critical phases of flight; and (3) whether the device is being used as a substitute for required navigation equipment without appropriate authorization. Under 14 CFR 91.21, the PIC must ensure portable electronic devices do not cause interference with aircraft systems. Additionally, a passenger focused on a personal device may miss emergency briefing cues and could become a distraction hazard.

questions.question: You are conducting a hot refueling operation — rotors turning, engine running — when your EFB (Electronic Flight Bag) mounted to the cyclic loses power and reboots. Walk me through your risk priorities at that moment and how you manage the automation loss.
questions.answer: During hot refueling, the pilot must remain at the flight controls and be ready to immediately shut down and egress if a fire or emergency develops — that is the top priority. The EFB losing power is a secondary concern and should not divert attention away from fuel flow, aircraft security, and fire watch. After refueling is complete and it is safe to do so, troubleshoot the EFB. Do not attempt to restart or reconfigure the EFB while managing the aircraft during hot refueling. This scenario illustrates automation loss occurring at the worst possible time — the risk is compounded because your attention is already divided. The correct response is to maintain control priorities and defer the automation issue.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8 (hot refueling); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (workload management, SRM)

questions.question: During your preflight briefing, a passenger tells you they have a medical device implanted — a pacemaker — and asks if the helicopter's avionics or radio transmissions could affect it. How do you address this from a risk management standpoint?
questions.answer: This requires a conservative approach. While modern pacemakers are generally shielded, high-power RF transmissions (like VHF comm radios and transponders) in close proximity can theoretically interfere with implanted cardiac devices. As PIC, you should advise the passenger to consult their cardiologist before the flight, ensure they are seated away from high-power antenna locations if possible, and brief them on what to do if they feel any symptoms. You are not a medical authority, but you have a duty to make a reasonable risk assessment under your PIC responsibility. If there is any doubt about the passenger's fitness or safety, the flight should not proceed with that passenger.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3 (PIC authority); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8 (passenger briefing and safety)

questions.question: You are flying VFR and your autopilot unexpectedly engages in an attitude it did not command, pushing the nose down slightly. You are currently at 500 feet AGL. Describe your risk management response using the SRM framework.
questions.answer: This is a time-critical situation requiring immediate pilot action. Using SRM: (1) Situational Awareness — recognize immediately that automation is not behaving as expected and you are at low altitude with limited recovery margin; (2) Task Management — immediately take manual control by disengaging the autopilot (typically via dedicated disconnect switch or override), since at 500 feet AGL there is no altitude to troubleshoot; (3) Risk Management — do not attempt to re-engage or reprogram the autopilot at low altitude; climb to a safe altitude before diagnosing the issue; (4) ADM — declare the autopilot inoperative for the remainder of the flight and make an appropriate maintenance entry after landing. The autopilot should not be used again until inspected. This scenario illustrates why pilots must remain manually proficient and never be over-reliant on automation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (SRM, automation management, ADM); 14 CFR 91.7 (airworthy condition)

questions.question: You discover during preflight that a system listed in the MEL as deferrable was deactivated by someone other than a certificated maintenance person — the previous pilot simply pulled the circuit breaker and placarded it. The MEL condition states that deactivation must be performed by certificated maintenance. Is this aircraft airworthy, and what is your liability exposure as PIC if you accept it?
questions.answer: The aircraft is NOT airworthy in this condition. The MEL is an FAA-approved document that functions as an STC, and its deferral conditions are legally binding. If the MEL requires that deactivation be performed by certificated maintenance and that was not done, the deferral is invalid and the aircraft does not meet its airworthiness requirements. As PIC, accepting this aircraft and flying it makes you directly liable under 14 CFR 91.7 for operating an unairworthy aircraft. The fact that someone else performed the improper deactivation does not relieve you of PIC responsibility. The correct action is to refuse the aircraft and contact maintenance to properly perform the deactivation before flight.
questions.follow_up: What if the circuit breaker was pulled and the MEL specifically says 'deactivate by pulling and collaring the circuit breaker' — does that change whether a certificated maintenance person is required?
questions.follow_up_answer: It depends entirely on what the MEL states. If the MEL's deferral procedure specifies 'pull and collar circuit breaker' as the deactivation method AND does NOT require a certificated maintenance person to perform that action, then the previous pilot's action may have been acceptable — pulling a CB is not considered maintenance in that context. However, if the MEL language requires maintenance personnel involvement regardless of the deactivation method, the situation is unchanged and the aircraft remains unairworthy. The key is to read the MEL deferral conditions precisely — the document controls what is and is not authorized.

questions.question: A pilot tells you they use a tablet-based EFB running a third-party moving map application as their sole means of navigation for all flights. From a risk management and regulatory standpoint, what concerns would you raise — particularly regarding the FAA's position on EFBs and the potential for over-reliance on automation?
questions.answer: Several concerns arise: (1) Regulatory — an EFB app is not certified avionics; its database currency, accuracy, and reliability are the pilot's responsibility. Under 14 CFR 91.103, the PIC must have all available information before flight, but using uncertified software does not automatically satisfy navigation requirements for all operations. For IFR flight, approved navigation equipment is required; (2) Automation over-reliance — FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 emphasizes that accidents correlate with over-reliance on automation and loss of manual situational awareness; (3) Single point of failure — using a tablet as the sole navigation source creates a single point of failure. Device battery failure, software crash, or loss of GPS signal leaves the pilot with no navigation backup; (4) Database currency — third-party apps may not use the same 28-day AIRAC cycle or may not update automatically; an out-of-date moving map can show incorrect airspace, obstacle, and procedure data; (5) The FAA encourages EFBs as a supplement to, not replacement for, required navigation systems and pilot navigation skills.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot is flying under Part 91 VFR in uncontrolled airspace, is there any specific regulation they are violating by using only the EFB tablet for navigation?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under Part 91 VFR in uncontrolled airspace, there is no specific regulation requiring certified navigation equipment — 14 CFR Part 91 does not mandate a GPS or VOR for VFR flight. So technically, a pilot using only a tablet EFB for VFR navigation in Class G airspace may not be violating a specific equipment regulation. However, 14 CFR 91.7 requires the aircraft to be airworthy (not directly applicable to a portable device), and 14 CFR 91.103 requires preflight familiarity with all available information. The real exposure is operational: if the tablet fails and the pilot becomes lost or violates airspace, they could face enforcement action under 14 CFR 91.13 (careless or reckless operation) if they had no backup means of navigation. The risk management failure is the absence of any redundancy.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 91.103; 14 CFR 91.13; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 1

questions.question: You find an inoperative piece of equipment during preflight. Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), what four conditions must all be met before you can legally defer that equipment and depart?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), all four of these must be satisfied: (1) The equipment is not required by the VFR-day type certificate instruments and equipment list, (2) it is not required by an airworthiness directive, (3) it is not required for the specific flight being conducted (e.g., not required for IFR if you're flying IFR), and (4) the equipment is either removed from the aircraft or deactivated and placarded INOPERATIVE. If deactivation or removal constitutes maintenance, a certificated maintenance person must perform it.

questions.question: Your helicopter has an FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List. What legal standing does an approved MEL have on your specific aircraft, and who is responsible for ensuring the helicopter is in an airworthy condition before flight?
questions.answer: The FAA considers an approved MEL to be a supplemental type certificate (STC) for that specific aircraft — it effectively amends the aircraft's type certificate to allow flight with certain equipment inoperative under defined conditions. The pilot-in-command is always responsible for ensuring the helicopter is in an airworthy condition before flight, regardless of maintenance status or MEL provisions.

questions.question: You notice the rotor tachometer is inoperative during preflight. Can you defer this item under 91.213(d) and depart? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No. The rotor tachometer is a component that is not listed in an MEL as deferrable and is required for safe helicopter operations. Components such as the rotor tachometer, engine tachometer, and cyclic trim are examples of items that require repair before departure because they are either required by the type certificate data, a required instrument for the flight conditions, or essential to safe rotorcraft operation. The aircraft is not airworthy with this item inoperative.

questions.question: You are dispatched on a VFR cross-country in a helicopter with an approved MEL. The MEL allows deferral of the autopilot, but the weather is forecast to be marginal VMC with potential for inadvertent IMC entry. Walk me through your risk management decision about departing with the autopilot deferred.
questions.answer: Even though the MEL legally permits deferral of the autopilot, the PIC must evaluate whether the actual risk is acceptable for the specific flight. Risk factors include: (1) marginal VMC increases workload and the probability of inadvertent IMC, (2) without autopilot, pilot workload in degraded visibility is significantly higher, increasing susceptibility to spatial disorientation, (3) the MEL gives legal authority to fly but does not obligate you to — the PIC retains go/no-go authority. A sound ADM process using tools like IMSAFE and a risk matrix would likely produce a no-go or go-with-delay decision. The word 'probably' should be avoided — if the weather will only 'probably' remain VMC, choose the option known to work, which may mean waiting for improved conditions.

questions.question: During your preflight, you discover the helicopter's alternator warning light is inoperative — the light itself doesn't illuminate during the bulb check. You have no MEL. Under 91.213(d), describe step-by-step what you must do before you could legally depart, and what risk does this inoperative item create in flight?
questions.answer: Step-by-step under 91.213(d): (1) Verify the warning light is not required by the VFR-day type certificate equipment list, airworthiness directive, or the specific flight rules being conducted. (2) If it qualifies for deferral, determine whether deactivation or removal is needed — since a burned-out bulb may simply be replaced by the pilot if the RFM permits, or must be addressed by a certificated maintenance person if it constitutes maintenance. (3) Placard the item INOPERATIVE in a location visible to the pilot. (4) Log the discrepancy in the aircraft records appropriately. The risk in flight: without a functioning alternator warning light, you lose an early visual cue for electrical system failure. This means you must compensate with more frequent monitoring of electrical gauges (voltmeter, ammeter) to detect failures that the warning light would otherwise announce, increasing cockpit workload.

questions.question: You are flying part 91 and notice an equipment malfunction in flight — your fuel quantity gauge for one tank is reading erratically. Can you use the 91.213(d) deferral provision to continue the flight? What should guide your decision-making?
questions.answer: No — the 91.213(d) deferral provision applies to known inoperative equipment identified before departure, not to in-flight discrepancies. For equipment that fails in flight, the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) or Pilot's Operating Handbook emergency and abnormal procedures take precedence. For the erratic fuel gauge specifically, the risk is significant: without accurate fuel quantity information, fuel exhaustion or imbalance becomes a real hazard. The pilot should use all available means to assess fuel state — fuel burn calculations, time since last fuel check, known fuel load at departure — and land at the nearest suitable airport to have the gauge inspected before continuing. ADM and risk management, not a regulatory deferral, govern in-flight equipment failures.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.213; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8 (in-flight discrepancies); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: A certificated A&P mechanic deactivates an inoperative navigation light on your helicopter and placards it INOPERATIVE per 91.213(d). Two weeks later, you show up for a flight and notice no one entered the discrepancy or the deferral in the aircraft maintenance records. Is the aircraft legally airworthy to fly? What are the implications for you as PIC?
questions.answer: This is a gray area with real risk. The placard requirement and deactivation under 91.213(d) are met, but 14 CFR 91.417 requires that maintenance records be kept, and an A&P performing maintenance (including deactivation) should document the work per 43.9. The absence of a maintenance record entry for a deactivation that constitutes maintenance means the maintenance action itself is undocumented — this calls into question whether it was performed correctly and whether the aircraft records are complete. As PIC, you are responsible for airworthiness under 91.7. Flying with an undocumented maintenance action creates legal exposure: if an incident or accident occurs, you could face enforcement action for knowingly operating a non-airworthy aircraft. The prudent decision is to ground the helicopter until the maintenance record is properly completed.
questions.follow_up: What specific regulation requires the A&P to make a maintenance record entry, and what information must that entry contain?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 43.9 requires that a person performing maintenance make an entry in the maintenance record of the aircraft that includes: (1) a description of the work performed, (2) the date the work was completed, (3) the name of the person performing the work (if different from the person signing), (4) the signature, certificate number, and kind of certificate held by the person approving the aircraft for return to service. Without this entry, the maintenance action is not properly documented, and the return-to-service is incomplete.

questions.question: Your helicopter's MEL allows deferral of the radar altimeter for VFR day operations with no restrictions. You accept this deferral and depart on what starts as a VFR cross-country, but you then encounter deteriorating conditions and consider filing IFR en route. What are the compounding risk factors created by the deferred radar altimeter if you proceed IFR, and how does the MEL affect your options?
questions.answer: The MEL deferral was authorized specifically for VFR day operations—transitioning to IFR flight with a deferred radar altimeter violates 14 CFR 91.213(d) and renders the aircraft not airworthy for that operation. Risk factors compound significantly: (1) radar altimeter is required for many helicopter instrument approaches, Category II/III approaches, and low-visibility operations; (2) approach authorization may be restricted or denied by the MEL condition; (3) the aircraft is now in a legally non-airworthy configuration for the intended operation. The proper action is to divert immediately to a VFR-legal destination or land at the nearest suitable airport in VFR conditions before deterioration continues. Do not transition to IFR. If already on the ground unable to depart, remain at location until weather permits VFR departure or file for a special flight permit (14 CFR 21.197) to ferry to maintenance—but this is not a routine option and requires FAA approval.
questions.follow_up: If you land at an uncontrolled airport with this MEL deferral and a mechanic is not available, can you fly the helicopter to a maintenance facility to get the radar altimeter repaired, even though the MEL deferral was VFR-only and you are now in IFR conditions at the destination?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not legally without additional authorization. A ferry permit (special flight permit) under 14 CFR 21.197 may be required to fly the aircraft to a maintenance facility if it doesn't meet airworthiness requirements for the intended flight. The special flight permit allows flight to a location where repairs can be made, but must be issued by the FAA. Operating outside the MEL's authorized conditions means the aircraft is not airworthy for that operation. The PIC cannot simply decide to fly IFR because the weather dictates it — the regulatory and airworthiness framework must be followed.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.213; 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 21.197; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13
