questions.question: You are taxiing into position for a rolling takeoff and realize you skipped an item on your before-takeoff checklist. You are already lined up on the runway centerline and ATC has issued your takeoff clearance. What do you do, and why?
questions.answer: You hold your position, advise ATC you need a brief delay, and complete the missed checklist item before initiating the takeoff roll. No ATC clearance or schedule pressure justifies taking off with an incomplete checklist. The rolling takeoff requires the helicopter to accelerate to ETL before becoming airborne — any undetected configuration issue (e.g., an improperly set hydraulic system, a control binding, or abnormal engine instrument) could become critical at the most vulnerable phase of flight. ADM principles clearly identify 'press-on-itis' and external pressure as hazardous attitudes. The correct action is to prioritize safety over convenience.

questions.question: During your before-takeoff checklist for a rolling takeoff, you discover your hydraulic system has an amber caution light illuminated. Walk me through your decision-making process.
questions.answer: First, cross-check the indication against other instruments and confirm whether the light is a genuine system fault or a possible sensor/electrical issue. Refer to the RFM emergency or abnormal procedures checklist for the specific hydraulic caution indication — this is a non-normal checklist item and must be handled per the manufacturer's published procedures. Do not proceed with the rolling takeoff until the condition is resolved or cleared per the RFM. If the RFM directs you to land or not fly, comply. Contact maintenance if needed. The rolling takeoff places the helicopter in a configuration where hydraulic failure during the ground roll or just after liftoff (low altitude, accelerating) could result in very high control forces and potential loss of control. The correct decision is to not depart until the system is confirmed airworthy.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7 (airworthiness requirement); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 11; Aircraft RFM Abnormal/Emergency Procedures

questions.question: Your checklist calls for confirming the helicopter cannot hover OGE before attempting a rolling takeoff. How does completing this checklist item influence your decision to use a rolling takeoff versus a normal hovering takeoff?
questions.answer: Per the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook, a rolling takeoff should only be used when the helicopter cannot hover OGE — meaning available power is insufficient to sustain an OGE hover. If the before-takeoff checklist or performance planning confirms OGE hover is not achievable (due to high density altitude, heavy gross weight, or high temperature), then a rolling takeoff is the appropriate technique because it uses ground effect and translational lift to become airborne with less power than an OGE hover requires. Critically, the handbook also states that a rolling takeoff should NOT be attempted if the helicopter cannot even momentarily hover at least slightly — confirming at least a brief hover capability is a key checklist/go decision item. This confirms the aircraft has minimum controllability before committing to the roll.

questions.question: As an examiner, I want to see you demonstrate checklist usage during the rolling takeoff, but you complete the entire before-takeoff checklist from memory without referencing the actual printed or electronic checklist. Is that an acceptable technique, and would it meet the ACS standard?
questions.answer: No — completing a checklist entirely from memory is not the same as completing the checklist itself, and it would not fully meet the intent of the ACS skill standard. The ACS requires the applicant to 'complete the appropriate checklist(s),' which means actually using the published checklist as the reference — not reciting items from recall. Doing it from memory is called a 'do-list,' not a checklist, and it defeats the purpose of having a standardized, verified procedure. FAA guidance emphasizes that checklists are safeguards against the limitations of human memory. An applicant who performs checklist items by memory alone without referencing the document is demonstrating a substandard habit that, while possibly accurate on a simple flight, is not an acceptable professional standard and introduces risk on unfamiliar aircraft or after configuration changes.
questions.follow_up: What if the applicant argues their flight school trained them to use memory checklists and the RFM doesn't mandate using a written checklist explicitly?
questions.follow_up_answer: The argument doesn't hold. 14 CFR 91.7 requires the pilot to ensure the aircraft is in airworthy condition, and using published checklists is the industry-standard method for doing so. More directly, the ACS language 'complete the appropriate checklist(s)' references the manufacturer's or operator's published checklists — not a memorized sequence. Additionally, FAA-H-8083-21B and AC 91-79 both reinforce the use of written/electronic checklists as a standard operating procedure. A flight school that trains purely memory-based checklists is training below the FAA's published standards. On a checkride, the examiner can discontinue the practical test if the applicant demonstrates unsafe habits, and consistently bypassing published checklists in favor of memory is a risk management deficiency.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; ACS CH.V.E.S1; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; AC 91-79

questions.question: You are conducting a rolling takeoff from an unimproved grass surface at a remote site with no published procedures. There is no company SOP and the aircraft RFM has a standard before-takeoff checklist but no specific rolling takeoff checklist. How do you determine which checklist(s) to complete, and are you still meeting the ACS standard?
questions.answer: You complete the RFM's standard before-takeoff checklist in full, and you supplement it with any operationally appropriate items specific to the rolling takeoff from that surface — such as confirming the surface is free of obstructions, verifying wheel brake function, confirming the ground roll direction is into the wind or best available heading, and verifying the abort point. The ACS standard requires completing 'the appropriate checklist(s),' which means using whatever checklists exist in the applicable RFM or operator documentation. When no rolling-takeoff-specific checklist exists, the standard before-takeoff checklist is the appropriate one to use; the pilot must exercise judgment to add operationally relevant considerations. This is consistent with SRM principles — the pilot integrates available resources (RFM, training, situational awareness) to fill gaps. Yes, you are meeting the ACS standard by completing the published RFM before-takeoff checklist and applying sound aeronautical judgment for the non-standard environment.
questions.follow_up: If you add items to a checklist not in the RFM — such as a surface condition check — and something goes wrong on the takeoff roll, could that improvised item create any liability or operational concern?
questions.follow_up_answer: Adding operationally prudent items beyond what the RFM lists does not create liability — in fact, it demonstrates sound risk management. Pilots operating under 14 CFR Part 91 are the final authority on the airworthiness and safety of the flight (91.3), and exercising PIC authority to add a surface condition scan before a rolling takeoff from an unimproved surface is exactly what a competent, safety-focused pilot should do. What creates liability is skipping published checklist items or departing when known hazards exist. From an examiner's standpoint, an applicant who proactively identifies that a grass surface rolling takeoff introduces surface condition risk — and builds that into their flow — demonstrates a higher level of aeronautical decision-making than one who mechanically completes only the printed items without contextual awareness.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3 (PIC authority/responsibility); 14 CFR 91.7; ACS CH.V.E.S1; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and Chapter 13

questions.question: At a non-towered airport, what radio call would you make before beginning your rolling takeoff from the runway?
questions.answer: At a non-towered airport, you should make a self-announce call on the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF). A standard call includes: your aircraft type and registration, airport name, your position on the airport (e.g., 'runway 27'), your intentions (e.g., 'rolling takeoff, departing to the northwest'), and the airport name again at the end. Example: 'Riverside traffic, Helicopter N123AB, runway 27, rolling takeoff departing northwest, Riverside.'

questions.question: At a towered airport, what ATC clearance must you receive before beginning your rolling takeoff, and what does a typical clearance sound like?
questions.answer: At a towered airport, you must receive an explicit takeoff clearance from ground control or tower before entering the runway and departing. Tower will clear you with something like: 'Helicopter N123AB, runway 27, cleared for takeoff.' You should read back the runway designation and clearance: 'Runway 27, cleared for takeoff, Helicopter N123AB.' You cannot begin the rolling takeoff roll until this clearance is received and acknowledged.

questions.question: What is the purpose of making position and intention radio calls during a rolling takeoff, and when should the call be made relative to the maneuver?
questions.answer: The purpose of radio calls is to alert other traffic — both airborne and ground — of your position and intentions so conflicts can be avoided. At a non-towered airport, the call should be made before you begin the rolling takeoff, ideally while still stationary or taxiing into position on the runway. This gives other pilots time to adjust their traffic pattern or hold short. At a towered airport, the call is replaced by the ATC clearance and readback prior to movement.

questions.question: You are departing a non-towered airport via rolling takeoff on runway 18. While you are partway through your takeoff roll and transitioning through effective translational lift, another pilot announces they are on final for runway 18. What radio call do you make, and how does it affect your execution of the maneuver?
questions.answer: Once you are committed to the takeoff roll and have announced your intentions, if you hear conflicting traffic you should immediately broadcast your current position and status: 'Riverside traffic, Helicopter N123AB, rolling takeoff runway 18, approximately midfield, will be airborne shortly.' If the conflict is severe and you have sufficient runway remaining and performance to stop, you should abort and advise traffic accordingly. If airborne, continue climbing and turn clear of the approach path, then announce your turn: 'Riverside traffic, Helicopter N123AB, departing runway 18, turning left crosswind.' The key principle is that you must maintain situational awareness and communicate your actions to deconflict with inbound traffic.

questions.question: You are at a Class D airport and tower clears you to 'taxi into position and hold, runway 9.' What radio calls are required, and when do you finally receive authorization to begin your rolling takeoff?
questions.answer: When tower says 'taxi into position and hold,' you read back: 'Position and hold, runway 9, Helicopter N123AB.' You then taxi onto the runway and hold. You do NOT begin the rolling takeoff. You must wait for an explicit takeoff clearance, such as 'Helicopter N123AB, runway 9, cleared for takeoff.' At that point, you read back the runway and clearance — 'Runway 9, cleared for takeoff, N123AB' — and then begin your rolling takeoff. Note that 'position and hold' (now called 'hold short of runway' or 'line up and wait') only authorizes runway entry, not departure.

questions.question: You are performing a rolling takeoff at a non-towered airport and your radio fails after you've already made your departure call but before you've become airborne. What actions do you take, and what, if anything, substitutes for a radio call in this situation?
questions.answer: If the radio fails during the takeoff roll, you should assess whether you can safely continue the departure or abort. If you have already broadcast your intentions and the runway is clear, you may continue the rolling takeoff using visual scanning to ensure no conflicts. After becoming airborne, you should attempt to troubleshoot the radio. If the radio cannot be restored, you must continue to visually clear the traffic pattern, fly the standard traffic pattern, and be prepared to watch for light gun signals if entering Class D or C airspace. At non-towered airports, there is no regulatory requirement for radio communication, but you must use every means available to avoid collision — including visual clearing, standard traffic pattern altitudes, and making note of UNICOM/CTAF to attempt contact. Light gun signals are the substitute at towered airports.

questions.question: During a practical test, a candidate performing a rolling takeoff makes all required radio calls correctly in content, but the calls are made at the wrong times — specifically, the departure call is made while already accelerating down the runway rather than prior to beginning the roll. Does this meet the ACS standard, and how would you evaluate it as an examiner?
questions.answer: No, this does not fully meet the ACS standard. The intent of making radio calls 'as appropriate' includes not only content but also timing. A departure call made after the rolling takeoff has already begun provides no practical safety benefit to other traffic, who may already be turning onto final or beginning their own takeoff roll. The ACS standard requires that calls be appropriate in context, which includes being timely. As an examiner, I would note this as a deficiency — it demonstrates procedural awareness but lacks the situational judgment that defines 'appropriate.' If the candidate cannot explain why timing matters or repeats the error, it could rise to the level of an unsatisfactory performance. Proper procedure is to make the call before initiating the roll, while clear of the runway or holding in position, so other traffic can act on the information.
questions.follow_up: What if the candidate argues that at a non-towered airport, radio calls are not legally required at all, so any call — even a late one — satisfies the intent of the ACS?
questions.follow_up_answer: The candidate is technically correct that 14 CFR 91.126 does not mandate radio calls at non-towered airports. However, the ACS standard CH.V.E.S2 explicitly requires the applicant to 'make radio calls as appropriate,' which means the examiner is evaluating whether the applicant knows when, what, and how to communicate — not simply whether a legal minimum was met. The ACS represents best practice and professional airmanship, not just regulatory compliance. An applicant who understands radio calls are optional but chooses not to use them effectively, especially in a training context, is not demonstrating the level of aeronautical decision-making and situational awareness expected of a certificated pilot. The examiner's job is to evaluate judgment, and poor timing of a safety-critical call reflects poor judgment regardless of legality.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot conducting a rolling takeoff at a non-towered airport makes a position call on CTAF but omits mentioning that the departure will be a rolling takeoff versus a normal vertical departure. Why does this distinction matter, and what risk does it introduce to other traffic?
questions.answer: The distinction matters significantly because a rolling takeoff covers substantial runway distance before becoming airborne — potentially 500 to over 1,000 feet depending on conditions — and operates at low altitude and reduced maneuverability during the acceleration phase. If other traffic hears only 'departing runway 27' without knowing it is a rolling takeoff, a pilot entering on a short final or beginning a backtrack on the same runway may misjudge the time available to clear. They may assume the helicopter will lift off quickly and hover-taxi clear, which is the expected behavior of a helicopter. By specifying 'rolling takeoff,' you give other traffic accurate situational awareness, particularly important at airports where wheel-equipped helicopters are uncommon and other pilots may not anticipate extended ground roll. The omission represents a deficiency in ADM and communication completeness, even if the call was technically made.
questions.follow_up: If a fixed-wing pilot hears a helicopter call 'rolling takeoff, departing runway 27' and is on a 1-mile final to runway 27, what action should that pilot take, and what responsibility does the helicopter pilot have at that point?
questions.follow_up_answer: The fixed-wing pilot on a 1-mile final should execute a go-around or announce their position and intent clearly: 'N456, on one-mile final runway 27, going around.' The helicopter pilot has a responsibility under 14 CFR 91.113 to give way to aircraft on final approach — a landing aircraft has the right of way over a departing one. If the helicopter pilot has already heard the inbound call prior to beginning the roll, they should hold and allow the aircraft to land before initiating the rolling takeoff. If the call comes after the roll has begun, the helicopter pilot should continue the departure and exit the runway environment as quickly as possible, while broadcasting their position to maintain awareness. This scenario reinforces why radio calls must be made before initiating the maneuver and why monitoring CTAF traffic prior to departure is essential.

questions.question: You're at an unfamiliar off-airport site preparing for a rolling takeoff and there's no windsock. Name three environmental cues you can use right now to determine wind direction.
questions.answer: Without a windsock, you can determine wind direction by observing: (1) smoke from chimneys, fires, or industrial stacks — smoke drifts downwind; (2) flags, banners, or loose fabric on structures; (3) ripples or waves on water surfaces moving away from the wind; (4) grass, crops, or tall vegetation bending in the direction the wind is blowing; (5) dust or debris lofting and drifting downwind; (6) the feel of wind on your face during a pre-takeoff walk-around. For a rolling takeoff specifically, you want to identify the upwind direction so you can align the helicopter into the wind to maximize translational lift benefit during the ground roll.

questions.question: What does a standard windsock tell you about wind direction, and how do you read it correctly from the cockpit?
questions.answer: A windsock indicates wind direction by the position of its open end. The open end faces INTO the wind. Wind direction is FROM the direction the open end points. For example: if the open end points east, wind is FROM the east (flowing westward). Pilots should position themselves so they can clearly see the windsock before initiating any takeoff. The degree of extension also indicates relative wind speed — a fully extended windsock indicates winds of approximately 15 knots or greater; a limp sock indicates calm or very light winds.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9, Basic Flight Maneuvers; FAA-H-8083-25B Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge Chapter 12

questions.question: Why is determining accurate wind direction especially critical before initiating a rolling takeoff compared to a vertical takeoff?
questions.answer: A rolling takeoff is used when the helicopter cannot hover out of ground effect — meaning power is marginal and the pilot is relying on gaining translational lift during the ground roll to become airborne. If the helicopter is not aligned into the wind, or worse, is departing with a tailwind or crosswind component, translational lift is delayed or reduced, the ground roll distance increases, and the helicopter may reach obstacles before achieving safe climb performance. An accurate wind determination ensures the takeoff path maximizes effective translational lift onset, minimizes ground roll distance, and provides the best climb gradient over obstacles. In marginal power situations, a tailwind component during a rolling takeoff can make the difference between a successful departure and an accident.

questions.question: You're about to perform a rolling takeoff from a grass strip. The nearest windsock is at the far end of the runway and appears to indicate a quartering tailwind from your current position. However, grass near your helicopter appears to be bending in a different direction. How do you reconcile these conflicting cues, and what do you do before starting the takeoff roll?
questions.answer: Conflicting wind cues are common due to local terrain effects, buildings, or trees creating eddies that cause surface winds to vary significantly over short distances. The correct approach is: (1) Do not assume either indicator is definitively correct; (2) Use multiple cues — look at any additional vegetation movement, dust, or other indicators near your position; (3) Taxi or hover-taxi slowly to assess the wind feel on the helicopter and observe directional tendency; (4) If possible, taxi closer to the windsock to get a direct reading at that location; (5) Consider doing a brief hover check to directly feel the wind. If you cannot confidently determine wind direction, reposition the helicopter to an area with a clear, unambiguous wind reading. A rolling takeoff with a tailwind component in marginal power conditions is a serious safety risk — do not proceed until wind direction is confirmed.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Rolling/Running Takeoff; Chapter 13, ADM and risk management

questions.question: You're at a remote site at dusk performing a rolling takeoff. There are no visible wind indicators and the terrain is flat tundra with no vegetation. Describe your systematic process for determining wind direction before committing to the takeoff.
questions.answer: With no visual environmental cues available, use these methods in combination: (1) Check the METAR or AWOS for the nearest reporting station as a baseline — understand that surface winds can differ from reported winds at a distant station; (2) Look at any available PIREP or winds-aloft data; (3) Perform a slow 360-degree hover or ground taxi — the helicopter will naturally want to weathervane into the wind; note the heading where the least pedal input is required to maintain heading and where the nose tends to point; (4) Wet your finger and hold it up — the cooler side faces the wind; (5) Hover momentarily at minimum altitude and feel the aircraft drift — upwind drift requires you to push cyclic into the wind to hold position; (6) Observe any dust or disturbance from your own rotor wash to see how it drifts. Once wind direction is established, align for the into-wind departure before initiating the ground roll.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Rolling/Running Takeoff; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13, Situational Awareness

questions.question: During a rolling takeoff, you initiated your ground roll into what you believed was the headwind. Midway through the roll, you notice the helicopter is not accelerating as expected and translational lift onset is delayed. What does this tell you about your wind determination, and what are your options at this point?
questions.answer: Delayed translational lift onset and slower-than-expected acceleration during a rolling takeoff suggests you may have a tailwind component rather than a headwind — or at minimum, the wind is less favorable than assessed. It could also indicate higher density altitude or a mechanical performance issue. Options at this point depend on remaining runway/ground distance: (1) If sufficient distance remains and an abort can be safely executed, reduce collective, apply aft cyclic as needed, and bring the helicopter to a stop to reassess wind direction and performance; (2) If the helicopter is approaching translational lift and has enough remaining ground to safely continue, you may elect to complete the takeoff and climb away, then reassess from altitude; (3) Never continue a rolling takeoff in marginal performance conditions simply because you are committed — the FAA expects pilots to abort when the situation is not developing as planned. The abort decision must be made early. This situation highlights why accurate pre-takeoff wind determination is a safety-critical skill, not just a procedural checkbox.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Running/Rolling Takeoff and Abort Planning

questions.question: A pilot argues that because ATIS reported winds calm, there's no need to determine wind direction before a rolling takeoff — they'll just pick the longest available surface. As an examiner, how do you evaluate this reasoning, and what specific failure mode does this create for a rolling takeoff in a wheel-equipped helicopter?
questions.answer: This reasoning is flawed on two levels. First, ATIS/ASOS surface wind reports are measured at a specific point (typically the tower sensor) and may not accurately reflect conditions at the departure end of an unfamiliar runway or off-airport site — local terrain, structures, and time lag can all cause discrepancies. 'Calm winds' reported at 10-15 minutes ago may not reflect current conditions. Second, even in genuinely calm conditions, the pilot should still determine wind direction as a habit — conditions can change rapidly, and calm does not mean no wind preference exists. The specific failure mode created: during a rolling takeoff, if a light and variable wind happens to favor a tailwind component at the moment of liftoff, the helicopter's effective translational lift is achieved at a higher groundspeed than expected, ground roll is extended, and obstacle clearance is reduced. In marginal power situations, this can result in the helicopter becoming airborne too close to obstacles or not at all. Choosing the longest surface rather than the into-wind surface introduces unnecessary risk that is entirely avoidable with proper wind assessment.
questions.follow_up: The pilot says, 'But the helicopter has plenty of excess power — why does wind direction matter if I'm not power-limited?' How do you respond?
questions.follow_up_answer: Even with excess power, wind direction still matters for a rolling takeoff because: (1) The rolling takeoff procedure exists precisely because the helicopter cannot hover OGE — by definition, power is marginal even if the pilot believes otherwise; if the pilot had true excess power, a vertical departure would be used instead; (2) A tailwind increases groundspeed at liftoff, increasing landing gear stress and extending the ground roll — on unprepared surfaces with wheel-type gear, this increases the risk of a gear-related incident; (3) Crosswind components create asymmetric lift during the ground roll, requiring corrective cyclic inputs that can cause tip clearance issues and uneven liftoff; (4) Wind direction assessment is an ACS-required skill — if the applicant cannot demonstrate this skill because they deem it unnecessary, that alone is grounds for a task failure regardless of the power state of the helicopter.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Rolling/Running Takeoff; ACS CH.V.E.S3

questions.question: You're evaluating a commercial applicant who correctly identifies wind direction using a distant windsock before a rolling takeoff. However, between the windsock and the departure point, there is a large hangar that could be creating a mechanical turbulence or flow distortion effect. How should the applicant account for this, and at what point in the evaluation does their wind determination skill become relevant again after liftoff?
questions.answer: A well-prepared applicant should recognize that a large structure upwind of or adjacent to the takeoff path can create mechanical turbulence, accelerated flow around corners (venturi effect), or a local wind shadow on the lee side. The correct action is: (1) Approach the takeoff point and observe local cues — ground vegetation, any visible dust, or loose material near the actual departure point to see if they match the distant windsock; (2) During any hover check or taxi to the departure position, feel for wind direction changes relative to what the windsock indicated; (3) Factor possible turbulence into the takeoff — plan for a sudden airspeed change or rotor disturbance during initial climb when clearing the rotor-height of the hangar. Regarding post-liftoff relevance: wind determination remains critical throughout the climb-out. As the helicopter climbs above the obstruction, the local disturbed airflow transitions to the free-stream wind — the applicant must be ready for an airspeed increase or decrease and a heading change as the helicopter exits the mechanical turbulence zone. Failure to anticipate this transition has caused accidents when pilots were startled by sudden airspeed or attitude changes immediately after liftoff near large structures.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant simply said 'I'd trust the windsock and go,' what specific risk has not been mitigated, and how does this connect to the ADM error chain concept?
questions.follow_up_answer: Trusting a single, distant wind indicator without cross-checking local cues near the actual departure point is an example of plan continuation bias and over-reliance on a single data source — both recognized ADM hazardous attitudes and error chain contributors. The unmitigated risk is encountering unexpected mechanical turbulence or a wind gradient immediately after liftoff — precisely when the helicopter is at its most vulnerable (low altitude, transitioning through translational lift, power demand high). Per FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13, the error chain concept holds that accidents rarely result from a single failure but from multiple small poor decisions compounding. Trusting one indicator, not cross-checking, not briefing the turbulence potential, and not having an abort or recovery plan each represent individual links in that chain. Breaking any one of them — such as spending 30 seconds observing local wind cues near the hangar — can prevent the accident. This is exactly the type of systematic thinking the ACS expects a commercial applicant to demonstrate.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Rolling Takeoff; Chapter 13, ADM Error Chain; ACS CH.V.E.S3

questions.question: Before initiating a rolling takeoff, what does verifying the 'assigned takeoff path' mean in practical terms?
questions.answer: Verifying the assigned takeoff path means confirming the direction of departure matches what was assigned by ATC (or planned at an uncontrolled field), checking for obstacles along that path, ensuring the ground roll direction aligns with the available runway or surface, and confirming you are positioned correctly to roll in that direction. It includes confirming winds, obstacle clearance corridor, and any published departure procedures that apply.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; AIM 4-3-1 (Takeoff and Departure Clearances)

questions.question: At a towered airport, what must you do before beginning your rolling takeoff roll to confirm you are on the correct takeoff path?
questions.answer: You must read back your takeoff clearance to ATC, confirm the assigned runway and departure direction, visually verify you are aligned with that runway heading, check for any traffic on final or crossing the runway, and ensure your heading indicator and magnetic compass match the runway heading. You should also note any turn instructions issued with the clearance (e.g., 'left turn on course') before beginning the roll.

questions.question: During preflight planning for a rolling takeoff at an uncontrolled airport, how do you determine the correct takeoff path before you ever get in the helicopter?
questions.answer: During preflight planning you check the current ASOS/AWOS or ATIS for wind direction to identify the preferred runway, review the airport diagram for available runways and any displaced thresholds, check NOTAMs for closed runways or construction, review the Chart Supplement for any noise abatement or departure procedures, and identify obstacles in the departure corridor on the sectional or approach plates. The correct takeoff path is the one that provides a headwind component (or best compromise), obstacle clearance, and compliance with any published procedures.

questions.question: You are cleared for takeoff on Runway 27 at a towered airport. As you begin your rolling takeoff, you realize the wind sock is pointing strongly from the right, suggesting winds are actually favoring Runway 32. What should you do before continuing the roll?
questions.answer: Stop the takeoff roll immediately if you have not yet lifted off. Contact tower and advise them of your observation — something like 'Tower, N123AB, winds appear to favor Runway 32, requesting confirmation or change of runway.' Do not deviate from the assigned runway without a clearance. ATC may have operational reasons for assigning 27 (traffic sequencing, noise abatement, etc.) or they may approve Runway 32. If the crosswind component exceeds the aircraft's demonstrated or pilot's personal limits, it is your responsibility as PIC to request a more favorable runway under 14 CFR 91.3.

questions.question: You are planning a rolling takeoff from a private grass strip with no control tower. There is a clear path to the north but trees 50 feet high begin 400 feet from your starting point. To the south, the strip extends 800 feet with no obstacles. The wind is calm. Walk me through how you verify and select the correct takeoff path.
questions.answer: With calm winds, obstacle clearance becomes the primary factor. I would calculate whether the helicopter can clear the 50-foot trees to the north within 400 feet of ground roll using available performance data for current density altitude, gross weight, and temperature — specifically checking whether OGE hover power is available and what the climb gradient looks like. If performance data does not confirm obstacle clearance with an adequate margin, I select the southward departure path regardless of wind. I also check for obstructions in both corridors, confirm the surface condition of both directions, and mentally identify an abort point. The 'correct' takeoff path is the one that provides the safest departure with the highest probability of obstacle clearance.

questions.question: You receive a clearance that reads: 'Helicopter 456 Alpha, cleared for takeoff Runway 18, fly runway heading, expect vectors for the Bravo.' As you line up, another pilot on the radio says he was just told to make left traffic for Runway 18. How do you verify your takeoff path is correct and safe before rolling?
questions.answer: First, I confirm my clearance is specifically mine by call sign — my clearance was issued to 456 Alpha. I visually check the final approach to Runway 18 for any aircraft on final, and check the traffic pattern for the aircraft mentioned by the other pilot. I also verify my position on the runway is correct and I am not lined up on a parallel taxiway. I then cross-check my heading indicator with the runway heading (180°). If there is any doubt about conflicting traffic or my clearance, I hold position and query tower before beginning the roll. Rushing a rolling takeoff before verifying the departure path and traffic picture is a common cause of runway incursions and mid-air conflicts.

questions.question: During a rolling takeoff on Runway 09, you lift off and realize your heading indicator reads 270° — the opposite of what you expected. Describe every possible cause and your immediate actions.
questions.answer: A heading indicator reading 270° when departing Runway 09 indicates either: (1) the heading indicator was not properly set before departure — it was not aligned with the compass, (2) you are actually rolling in the wrong direction and lined up on Runway 27 rather than 09, or (3) the heading indicator has precessed significantly or failed. Immediate actions: if still on the ground, abort the takeoff. If airborne and still low, level off, assess situation. Check the magnetic compass as the primary backup — it is independent and will show the actual magnetic heading. If the compass shows 270°, you are flying westbound; do not climb into traffic for Runway 09 final. Contact tower immediately, declare the situation, request vectors and clarification. If the compass shows 090°, the heading indicator was simply not set — note the error, correct the HI, and continue with the departure. This scenario emphasizes why you verify heading against the runway centerline and compass before initiating any takeoff roll.
questions.follow_up: If you determine you did in fact take off on Runway 27 instead of Runway 09 without a clearance, what are your regulatory obligations after landing?
questions.follow_up_answer: Taking off on the wrong runway at a towered airport without a clearance is a runway incursion/deviation. Under 14 CFR 91.129, operating in Class D airspace requires ATC clearance. After landing, you must report the incident to ATC immediately — do not wait. Depending on severity, the FAA may initiate an investigation. Under 14 CFR 91.3, you are PIC and responsible for the error. You should also file a NASA ASRS report (Aviation Safety Reporting System) promptly, which provides limited immunity from certificate action under 14 CFR 91.25 for unintentional violations, provided the report is filed within 10 days and no accident occurred.

questions.question: You are conducting a rolling takeoff in a wheel-equipped helicopter at a busy uncontrolled airport. There is no published traffic pattern direction in the Chart Supplement, the windsock is limp, and two other aircraft are in the pattern — one on left downwind for Runway 14 and one on right downwind for Runway 32. How do you determine and verify the correct takeoff path, and what do you broadcast?
questions.answer: With calm winds and conflicting traffic patterns, I first try to determine which runway is more commonly favored at this airport — I check CTAF broadcasts already made by the other aircraft for clues. I assess which direction has fewer aircraft and which departure will create less conflict with existing traffic. In this scenario, I need to pick one runway and integrate into the flow — attempting to depart perpendicular to both patterns would be the most hazardous option. I should broadcast on CTAF: 'Airport traffic, Helicopter 789 Bravo, departing Runway [chosen runway], [direction] departure, [Airport name].' I verify the path is clear both on the ground and in the air before rolling, confirm no aircraft are on final for my chosen runway, and roll only after I am satisfied the path is clear. If I cannot determine a safe path, I hold and observe until the traffic situation clarifies. The key principle is that at an uncontrolled field, the pilot's see-and-avoid responsibility and good judgment determine the correct takeoff path — there is no substitute for verifying visually and aurally before every rolling takeoff.
questions.follow_up: If you choose Runway 14 and depart, but the pilot on left downwind for Runway 14 calls you out as a conflict and says you should have used Runway 32, do you have any regulatory obligation to use the runway they preferred?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. At an uncontrolled airport, there is no regulatory requirement to use any specific runway, and no other pilot has authority to direct your runway selection. Under 14 CFR 91.3, you are PIC and responsible for the safe operation of your aircraft. There is also no FAR that mandates using the most favored-wind runway. Best practice under the AIM recommends landing and taking off into the wind when practicable, but this is guidance, not a regulatory requirement. As long as you complied with right-of-way rules, made proper CTAF broadcasts, and operated safely, your runway choice was legally sound. However, this scenario illustrates why good airmanship includes assessing the traffic flow before departure — not just to comply with regulations, but to reduce conflict and increase safety.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.113; AIM 4-1-9 (Traffic Pattern Operations); AIM 4-1-10

questions.question: During a rolling takeoff, what instrument or indicator do you primarily monitor to confirm that Nr (rotor RPM) is remaining within normal limits as you accelerate and lift off?
questions.answer: The primary instrument is the tachometer — specifically the rotor RPM (Nr) needle, which may be a dual-needle tach showing both engine RPM (N2 or Nr) and rotor RPM together, or separate gauges depending on the aircraft. On turbine helicopters, torque and N1/N2 gauges are also monitored. During a rolling takeoff, the pilot must confirm Nr stays in the green arc throughout the ground roll and transition to flight. Any split between the engine and rotor needles on a dual-tach is an immediate warning of a drivetrain or governor issue.

questions.question: What is the pilot's primary collective input role in maintaining Nr within limits during the ground roll portion of a rolling takeoff before translational lift is achieved?
questions.answer: During the ground roll, the pilot holds the collective in a low position — typically just enough to reduce weight on the wheels without fully lifting off — allowing the helicopter to accelerate to translational lift speed. Raising collective too aggressively during the ground roll increases blade pitch and loads the rotor system, which can cause Nr to decay below normal limits, especially if the engine governor cannot compensate quickly enough. The collective is smoothly and progressively increased only as forward speed builds and translational lift assists in reducing the power required to maintain Nr.

questions.question: What is the significance of translational lift during a rolling takeoff in terms of maintaining Nr and powerplant limits?
questions.answer: Translational lift occurs as the helicopter accelerates through approximately 16–24 knots of effective translational lift (ETL). At this point, the rotor system transitions from operating in its own recirculating downwash to cleaner, undisturbed air, which significantly increases rotor efficiency. This means the rotor generates more lift for the same blade pitch and power, reducing the load on the engine and allowing Nr to stabilize or increase. During a rolling takeoff, the pilot times the collective increase to take advantage of translational lift, which reduces the risk of Nr decay and helps keep powerplant output within normal limits.

questions.question: You are executing a rolling takeoff on a hot, high-density altitude day. As you raise the collective through translational lift, you notice the torque is approaching the maximum continuous limit and Nr is beginning to sag below the green arc. Walk me through your control response and decision-making.
questions.answer: First, I would immediately reduce collective slightly to relieve the load on the rotor system and allow Nr to recover back into the green arc — Nr must take priority because a rotor stall is not recoverable. At the same time, I am monitoring torque to avoid exceeding limits on the engine side. If Nr cannot be maintained in the green arc with sufficient power to continue the takeoff safely, I must abort the takeoff — lower collective fully, use cyclic to maintain directional control, and come to a stop or return to the parking area. The key principle is that on a high-density-altitude day, OGE hover power may be marginal, and a rolling takeoff was likely chosen precisely because of that limitation. If even the rolling takeoff cannot sustain Nr in limits, conditions exceed the helicopter's performance capability and the flight should not proceed until conditions improve or weight is reduced.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; Chapter 11 (Low Rotor RPM/Stall); POH/RFM Performance Charts

questions.question: During a rolling takeoff, a student pilot raises the collective too rapidly just before reaching ETL. Describe what happens to Nr and how you would correct it as the instructor.
questions.answer: Raising collective too rapidly increases blade pitch angle before adequate airspeed has built up to provide translational lift benefits. This causes a sudden increase in induced drag on the rotor blades, which loads the engine beyond what the governor can immediately compensate for, and Nr begins to decay. If the student has not yet reached ETL, there is insufficient lift to fully support the weight, meaning the aircraft may settle back onto the wheels or skip. As the instructor, I would take the controls, reduce collective to a position that allows Nr to recover into the green arc, allow airspeed to build further toward and through ETL, then smoothly re-apply collective. I would verbally call out 'my controls' and explain after landing that collective must be increased gradually and in coordination with airspeed buildup to prevent rotor droop.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; Chapter 9 (Collective use in flight)

questions.question: On a helicopter with a free-wheeling unit (autorotation clutch), why is it critical to monitor the relationship between engine RPM and rotor RPM (Nr) specifically at the beginning of the ground roll during a rolling takeoff, and what does a split between the two indicate?
questions.answer: At the start of a rolling takeoff, the engine is engaged through the freewheeling unit to drive the rotor. If the engine RPM and Nr are in sync (needles married on a dual-tach), the drive system is functioning normally. A split where Nr drops below engine RPM could indicate a slipping or disengaged drive system — the engine is running but not fully transferring power to the rotor. This is extremely dangerous at the start of a takeoff because the rotor may lose RPM despite engine power appearing adequate. Conversely, if Nr exceeds engine RPM, the freewheeling unit has engaged because engine RPM dropped below rotor RPM — this is the autorotation condition. Either split at the initiation of a rolling takeoff requires the pilot to abort immediately and investigate before proceeding.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 5 (Main Rotor Systems); Chapter 11; POH/RFM

questions.question: An examiner-level scenario: You complete a rolling takeoff and the Nr is riding at the very top of the green arc — slightly high — throughout the acceleration. The engine gauges are all normal. What are the possible causes of a high Nr condition during a rolling takeoff, and what control action, if any, is appropriate?
questions.answer: A high Nr condition during a rolling takeoff with normal engine parameters could indicate: (1) The governor or correlator is over-speeding the rotor — the throttle/governor may be biased slightly high, which on a piston helicopter can be corrected by slightly rolling back the throttle or adjusting the governor trim if equipped. (2) The collective is too low for the phase of flight — insufficient blade pitch allows the rotor to spin faster than commanded because the load is very light, common early in the ground roll before meaningful pitch has been applied. (3) On a turbine helicopter, the FADEC or fuel control may be scheduling slightly more fuel than needed. If Nr is within the green arc (not in the yellow or red), no immediate action is required other than monitoring. If it approaches the yellow arc or red line, a slight increase in collective (adding pitch/load) or throttle reduction can bring it back to mid-green. The concern is that a sustained over-speed can cause rotor head stress and blade fatigue. An examiner wants to see the pilot recognize the trend early and take a precise, measured correction — not an overreaction.
questions.follow_up: If you increased collective to load the rotor and bring Nr back into mid-green, but doing so caused torque to exceed the maximum continuous limit, what is your priority — torque limit or Nr limit — and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: Nr takes priority over torque limit in the sense that a rotor stall is immediately catastrophic and unrecoverable, whereas a brief torque exceedance, while damaging to the engine and requiring a maintenance inspection, does not cause immediate loss of the aircraft. However, the correct answer in practice is that a pilot should not be in a situation where they must choose — a well-executed rolling takeoff should not require trading one limit for another. If the pilot cannot maintain both powerplant and Nr within limits simultaneously, the rolling takeoff should be aborted. The examiner is looking for the pilot to articulate that rotor RPM is the safety-of-flight parameter, torque limits protect the engine/drivetrain, and that 'picking one to exceed' signals a performance or technique problem requiring an abort, not a choice between two bad options.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; Chapter 11; POH/RFM Limitations Section

questions.question: During a rolling takeoff evaluation, I observe that the applicant allows Nr to briefly dip to the bottom of the green arc at the moment of liftoff before recovering. The aircraft lifts off safely and climb is established. Is this a passing performance, a discrepancy, or a task failure — and what standard applies?
questions.answer: Whether this is a passing performance or a discrepancy depends on the specific helicopter's POH/RFM normal operating range and the ACS standard, which requires maintaining Nr within normal limits throughout the task. 'Normal limits' means within the green arc at all times. A brief excursion to the very bottom of the green arc is technically still within limits, so it would not be an automatic task failure — but it is a discrepancy that indicates the applicant did not optimally time the collective increase relative to airspeed and ETL. It demonstrates marginal technique. However, if Nr dipped into the yellow caution arc or below the green arc entirely, even briefly, that is a task failure under CH.V.E.S5 because it means Nr was outside normal limits. An examiner would note the technique deficiency, could ask the applicant to explain what happened and how they would correct it, and would weigh it against overall performance in the task. Consistent, repeatable Nr management within the green arc is the standard.
questions.follow_up: The applicant tells you the Nr dip was intentional — they deliberately delayed the collective to let airspeed build further and were about to raise collective when Nr touched the bottom of the green and recovered on its own. Does this explanation change your evaluation, and what does it tell you about their understanding?
questions.follow_up_answer: This explanation actually demonstrates a misunderstanding of rotor RPM management. Nr should not be allowed to approach any limit as a technique choice — the pilot should be managing collective to keep Nr comfortably mid-green throughout. If the applicant deliberately allowed Nr to approach the low limit as a strategy, it shows they do not fully understand that Nr decay at low collective is unusual and may indicate a power or governor issue that should prompt a scan, not complacency. Additionally, 'recovering on its own' suggests the governor intervened, not the pilot — the applicant cannot take credit for a recovery they did not make. The explanation would lower the examiner's confidence in the applicant's understanding of powerplant and rotor RPM management, and the examiner would likely probe further with additional questions before making a final determination.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; ACS CH.V.E.S5; POH/RFM Limitations and Normal Procedures

questions.question: When initiating a rolling takeoff in a wheeled helicopter, what is the primary control input used to start the takeoff roll?
questions.answer: The cyclic is eased forward to begin rolling the helicopter forward on the ground. As forward movement begins, collective is simultaneously increased to load the rotor and begin to partially unload the landing gear, allowing the helicopter to roll forward with reducing ground friction. The inputs must be coordinated — forward cyclic alone without collective increase would produce little effective forward movement.

questions.question: What is the purpose of partially increasing collective during the initial takeoff roll of a rolling takeoff, even before the helicopter becomes airborne?
questions.answer: Increasing collective during the takeoff roll progressively unloads the landing gear by generating lift with the rotor system. This reduces rolling resistance (wheel friction) so the helicopter can accelerate along the ground more effectively. It also begins loading the rotor to ensure adequate rotor RPM and lift are available as translational lift is achieved and the helicopter transitions to flight.

questions.question: What pre-condition must exist before you attempt a rolling takeoff, according to the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook?
questions.answer: The helicopter must be capable of being hovered at least momentarily before a rolling or running takeoff is attempted. If the helicopter cannot hover, even briefly, a rolling takeoff should not be initiated. This confirms that sufficient rotor thrust exists for controlled flight, and the technique is being used to take advantage of translational lift rather than to compensate for a helicopter that is grossly underpowered.

questions.question: You are beginning a rolling takeoff on a paved surface. You apply forward cyclic and begin increasing collective, but the helicopter starts to weathervane to the left. What is happening and how do you correct it during the initiation of the takeoff roll?
questions.answer: As collective is increased, main rotor torque increases, causing the nose to yaw left (in a counterclockwise rotor system). Additionally, wind from the left could be contributing to the weathervaning tendency. The correction is to apply right pedal (right antitorque pedal) proportional to the collective increase to maintain directional alignment with the intended takeoff path. Pedal inputs during the ground roll serve the same antitorque function they do in flight — they must be coordinated with collective to keep the helicopter tracking straight.

questions.question: During the initiation of a rolling takeoff, a student applies an aggressive forward cyclic input to get the helicopter moving quickly. What hazard does this create and how should the control input be made instead?
questions.answer: An aggressive forward cyclic during the takeoff roll can cause the rotor disk to tilt sharply forward, increasing the risk of the rotor blades striking the tail boom or ground structures, and it can also cause the nose gear to dig in or the skid/wheel to catch if any unevenness exists on the surface. More critically, it could lead to a low-G condition if the collective is not increased simultaneously, reducing rotor thrust and lateral control authority. The correct technique is smooth, progressive forward cyclic coordinated with a gradual collective increase — allowing the helicopter to accelerate smoothly while maintaining rotor RPM and directional control.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; Chapter 11 (Low-G and Mast Bumping)

questions.question: You are conducting a rolling takeoff at a high-density altitude airport. Describe how the required control inputs to initiate the takeoff roll differ from a sea-level departure, and what you should be monitoring.
questions.answer: At high density altitude, the rotor operates in less dense air, generating less lift per blade pitch angle. To initiate the takeoff roll, the collective must be increased further to achieve the same partial gear unloading effect, meaning torque will be higher sooner — requiring more right pedal earlier in the roll. Forward cyclic inputs remain similar, but the helicopter will require a longer ground roll to reach effective translational lift (ETL) because aerodynamic forces build more slowly. The pilot should closely monitor rotor RPM for any decay as collective is applied, and must ensure torque and temperature limits are not exceeded. If the helicopter cannot hover even momentarily prior to the roll, the takeoff should be aborted.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; FAA-H-8083-25 Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (density altitude)

questions.question: During the initiation of a rolling takeoff, at what point in the control sequence should collective be increased relative to cyclic input, and what happens to rotor RPM and antitorque demand if collective is applied too aggressively before adequate forward airspeed is established?
questions.answer: Cyclic and collective should be applied nearly simultaneously — forward cyclic starts the roll while collective is increased progressively to unload the gear and load the rotor. If collective is applied too aggressively before forward airspeed is established, the helicopter is essentially demanding hover-level power while still on the ground without the benefit of translational lift. This can cause rotor RPM decay because the rotor is producing high drag without forward airflow to assist efficiency. Simultaneously, the high collective setting produces high torque, demanding maximum antitorque pedal — if pedal is not applied quickly enough, the aircraft yaws left on the ground, potentially causing a ground loop or runway excursion. In worst case, if RPM decays sufficiently and the pilot continues collective, rotor stall can occur — an unrecoverable condition.
questions.follow_up: If rotor RPM begins to decay during the ground roll before liftoff, what are the pilot's options and what is the correct immediate action?
questions.follow_up_answer: The correct immediate action is to immediately lower collective to reduce rotor drag and allow RPM to recover. If the takeoff roll has just started and airspeed is low, the pilot should abort the takeoff — reduce collective, apply aft cyclic to slow the ground roll, and bring the helicopter to a stop. Continuing to add collective while RPM is decaying will worsen the situation rapidly. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook is explicit: rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable, so early recognition and immediate corrective action (collective reduction) is imperative. Once stopped and RPM is stabilized, the pilot should assess why RPM decayed — over-pitching, high density altitude, mechanical issue — before attempting another departure.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Rolling Takeoff); Chapter 11 (Low Rotor RPM/Rotor Stall)

questions.question: During a rolling takeoff, which flight control is primarily used to maintain a straight ground track when a crosswind is present?
questions.answer: During a rolling takeoff in a crosswind, cyclic and antitorque pedals work together in a coordinated manner. Cyclic is applied into the wind to prevent lateral drift and maintain ground track alignment, while pedals maintain directional control (nose heading) and compensate for torque effect as collective is increased. Both controls must be used together throughout the takeoff roll to maintain a straight ground track.

questions.question: As the helicopter accelerates during a rolling takeoff with a crosswind from the left, what happens to the effectiveness of cyclic crosswind correction, and why?
questions.answer: As airspeed increases during the takeoff roll, translational lift develops and the rotor system becomes more aerodynamically efficient. The helicopter becomes more responsive to cyclic inputs, meaning smaller control displacements are needed to maintain the same ground track correction. The pilot must avoid over-controlling as ETL is approached and translational lift develops.

questions.question: During the ground roll phase of a rolling takeoff, before the helicopter becomes airborne, how should the pilot think about the desired ground track reference?
questions.answer: The pilot should select a distinct reference point at the far end of the takeoff path — such as a tree line, runway centerline marking, or distant landmark — and use it as a visual aiming point to maintain a straight ground track. Any drift caused by crosswind should be corrected with cyclic before it compounds, similar to tracking a centerline during a surface taxi.

questions.question: You're performing a rolling takeoff on a grass strip with a 15-knot direct crosswind from the right. As you accelerate through approximately 20 knots of airspeed, you notice the helicopter is drifting left of the intended ground track. What is your corrective action and what caused the drift?
questions.answer: The drift to the left is caused by the right crosswind pushing the fuselage and rotor disk laterally. The correction is to apply right cyclic to tilt the rotor disk into the wind and arrest the drift, realigning with the intended ground track. The pilot should apply the correction smoothly and early — waiting until the drift is significant makes correction harder, especially as the helicopter becomes light on the wheels. Pedals are simultaneously managed to keep the nose straight against torque, which may also be changing as collective is increased.

questions.question: During a rolling takeoff with a left crosswind, a student pilot is using left pedal to try to correct drift and maintain ground track. As the examiner, what would you tell them about this technique, and what is the correct method?
questions.answer: Using pedals to correct lateral drift during a rolling takeoff is incorrect. Pedals control yaw — the nose direction — not lateral ground track. Applying left pedal would yaw the nose left but would not stop the aircraft from drifting right with the crosswind. The correct technique is to use left cyclic to tilt the rotor disk into the wind, which creates a horizontal component of lift that counteracts the crosswind drift. Pedals should only be used to coordinate the turn and compensate for torque, not to steer laterally.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (Fundamentals of Flight) and Chapter 10

questions.question: You are departing from a narrow taxiway used as a temporary takeoff surface. There is a 10-knot crosswind from the right. Describe how you would manage crosswind correction from initiation of the rolling takeoff through liftoff to ensure you remain within the taxiway boundaries.
questions.answer: Prior to beginning the roll, pre-position the cyclic slightly into the wind (right) as an initial correction. As collective is smoothly increased and ground roll begins, continue monitoring lateral position relative to the taxiway edges. Apply right cyclic as needed to hold the ground track — the amount will vary as airspeed and ETL approach. Avoid large corrections; small early inputs are better than large late ones. As the helicopter becomes light on the wheels near liftoff speed, lateral controllability improves markedly. At liftoff, transition smoothly into a wings-level climb while maintaining the pre-planned ground track. Having a clear abort plan and identifying the point of no return before beginning the roll is essential on a confined surface.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Rolling/Running Takeoff; Chapter 11 (confined area concepts)

questions.question: During a rolling takeoff in a crosswind, a pilot pre-positions the cyclic into the wind correctly but fails to adjust cyclic pressure as airspeed builds through ETL. What specific hazard develops, and at what phase of the maneuver is it most dangerous?
questions.answer: If the pilot holds a fixed into-wind cyclic input and does not reduce it as airspeed builds and ETL develops, the increasing rotor efficiency amplifies the lateral tilt of the disk. This can cause the helicopter to bank into the wind rather than simply tracking into it, creating a lateral roll tendency at or just after liftoff — the most critical phase. The into-wind main wheel (or skid if applicable) could contact the ground during incipient liftoff, creating a dynamic rollover risk on wheel-type gear. The pilot must continuously modulate cyclic input throughout the acceleration, reducing crosswind correction pressure as the rotor becomes more responsive with increasing airspeed.
questions.follow_up: If you felt the helicopter begin to roll toward the into-wind side just as it lifted off during a crosswind rolling takeoff, and the wheel had not yet fully left the surface, what is the immediate correct response and what should you NOT do?
questions.follow_up_answer: The immediate correct response is to apply out-of-wind (downwind) cyclic to level the helicopter and arrest the roll before the critical rollover angle is exceeded — typically around 35 degrees for most helicopters. Do NOT lower collective rapidly or aggressively, as this can force the wheel back onto the ground and actually increase the pivot point contact, potentially worsening the dynamic rollover situation. If the roll cannot be arrested and the helicopter has not fully departed the surface, aborting the takeoff with a smooth collective reduction and re-establishing a stable ground attitude is preferable to continuing into a dynamic rollover.

questions.question: A pilot successfully maintains ground track during the ground roll of a rolling takeoff in a 20-knot crosswind, but immediately after liftoff, the helicopter begins tracking significantly to the downwind side despite continued cyclic correction into the wind. What are two possible reasons this is occurring, and how would you distinguish between them?
questions.answer: Two possible causes are: (1) The pilot relaxed cyclic crosswind correction at the moment of liftoff — a common instinctive reaction when transitioning attention from ground references to attitude — resulting in the rotor disk returning toward neutral and allowing the wind to push the helicopter downwind. (2) The collective was raised too aggressively at liftoff, causing an uncoordinated pitch/power interaction that momentarily disrupted rotor disk control authority while the pilot's attention was split between attitude and power. To distinguish: if the cyclic was simply released, the helicopter will drift smoothly in a predictable direction with normal control response restored when cyclic is re-applied. If it was a power-induced control disruption, there may also be yaw and RPM excursion symptoms simultaneously. In either case, the immediate action is to re-apply cyclic into the wind and stabilize the departure path before climbing. The pilot should also review whether OGE hover capability was confirmed before the takeoff — if not, the available control margin in the crosswind may be insufficient.
questions.follow_up: If this crosswind rolling takeoff was being conducted at a density altitude where the helicopter could only marginally achieve OGE hover, how does that affect the acceptable crosswind component for the maneuver, and is there a published crosswind limit for rolling takeoffs you can reference?
questions.follow_up_answer: At high density altitude with marginal OGE performance, the helicopter has less available power margin, which reduces the pilot's ability to add corrective collective without risking main rotor RPM decay. This directly limits the effective crosswind that can be safely managed — the pilot may not have enough power reserve to simultaneously fight wind effects and maintain rotor RPM during a crosswind correction. Regarding published limits: crosswind limits for rolling takeoffs are typically found in the specific helicopter's Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM), not in the FARs or FAA handbooks. There is no universal FAA-published crosswind limit for rolling takeoffs — it is aircraft-specific. The pilot is responsible for consulting the RFM for demonstrated crosswind component data and making a conservative go/no-go decision based on conditions, especially when performance margins are reduced.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Rolling Takeoff); RFM performance limitations section (aircraft-specific); 14 CFR 91.9 (operate within limitations)

questions.question: After a rolling takeoff, at what point should you begin transitioning to normal climb airspeed, and what control is primarily used to establish that airspeed?
questions.answer: Once the helicopter has lifted off and cleared any obstacles, you transition to normal climb airspeed using the cyclic to establish the appropriate climb attitude. The cyclic controls airspeed; once the target climb airspeed is set, collective is adjusted to set climb power. Normal climb airspeed is found in the helicopter's POH/RFM and varies by aircraft type.

questions.question: What does 'appropriate power' mean in the context of transitioning to normal climb after a rolling takeoff, and where do you find that value?
questions.answer: Appropriate power for a normal climb is the torque, manifold pressure, or engine power setting specified in the helicopter's POH/RFM for the normal climb configuration. It is typically less than maximum continuous power and is set after climb airspeed is established. The pilot references the POH performance charts and placards for the specific aircraft being flown.

questions.question: The ACS requires you to achieve normal climb airspeed within ±5 knots after a rolling takeoff. Why is it important not to let airspeed drop significantly below normal climb speed during this transition?
questions.answer: Allowing airspeed to drop significantly below normal climb speed during the transition reduces climb performance, may cause the helicopter to settle back toward obstacles or terrain, and could result in loss of effective translational lift (ETL). Additionally, operating at excessively low airspeed with high power increases torque and reduces single-engine margins in multi-engine aircraft. Maintaining airspeed within tolerance ensures optimal climb gradient and aircraft control.

questions.question: During a rolling takeoff on a hot day at a high-density altitude airport, you notice that after liftoff the helicopter accelerates very slowly toward normal climb airspeed. What adjustments should you make, and what is the risk if you prematurely pitch up to climb attitude before reaching that airspeed?
questions.answer: At high density altitude, excess power is reduced, so acceleration to climb airspeed takes longer. You should maintain a shallower pitch attitude and allow airspeed to build before transitioning to the normal climb attitude. If you prematurely pitch up before reaching normal climb airspeed, you risk decelerating back below ETL speed, reducing rotor efficiency, and potentially settling back onto the runway or into an area with insufficient power to climb. Patience and confirming airspeed before pitching to climb attitude is essential in high DA conditions.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; Helicopter POH/RFM performance charts

questions.question: You've completed the ground roll during a rolling takeoff and the helicopter is airborne. You set what you believe is climb power, but the VSI shows only a 100 FPM climb and airspeed is 5 knots above normal climb speed. What is the most likely cause and what corrective action do you take?
questions.answer: The most likely cause is that power (collective) is set too low or the cyclic pitch attitude is too shallow, allowing speed to increase above the target climb airspeed while climb performance suffers. The correction is to simultaneously increase collective slightly to add power toward the POH climb power setting and adjust cyclic to establish the proper climb attitude for normal climb airspeed. Confirm power instruments (torque/MP/RPM) are within POH limits for normal climb. Trim the aircraft to remove pedal pressure as power changes.

questions.question: After a rolling takeoff, as you increase collective to set climb power and pitch up for normal climb airspeed, the helicopter begins to yaw right. What is causing this and what is your immediate control input?
questions.answer: In a helicopter with a counterclockwise main rotor system (most American-made helicopters), increasing collective increases torque, which yaws the nose to the right. The immediate correction is left pedal input to maintain coordinated flight and keep the nose tracking straight ahead on the climb-out heading. The amount of left pedal required increases with power; during the rolling takeoff transition, the pilot must anticipate and apply left pedal as collective is raised to set climb power.

questions.question: A student consistently reaches normal climb airspeed after a rolling takeoff but overshoots by 8–10 knots before correcting, consistently exceeding the ±5 knot ACS tolerance. As their instructor, what specific visual or instrument scan error is most likely causing this, and how would you correct it in training?
questions.answer: The most likely cause is a delayed instrument scan — the student is waiting until they see the airspeed needle moving fast before reacting, rather than anticipating the transition point and beginning the pitch-up to climb attitude at the correct moment. Another contributing factor may be fixating on outside visual cues (obstacle clearance) while neglecting the airspeed indicator. The correction in training involves: (1) teaching the student to anticipate the transition airspeed and begin pitching to climb attitude proactively rather than reactively; (2) developing a cross-check between airspeed indicator and pitch attitude; (3) using a target attitude as a reference and then fine-tuning with airspeed. In a wheel-gear helicopter, the climb attitude reference should be established from ground training before the first flight so the student knows what the proper sight picture looks like.
questions.follow_up: If the student corrects the airspeed overshoot by aggressively pulling aft cyclic once they see the speed increasing, what new hazard are you now concerned about, and how does it relate to rotor system loading?
questions.follow_up_answer: Aggressive aft cyclic input at climbing airspeeds can create an abrupt pitch-up, rapidly increasing rotor disk angle of attack and load factor. In semi-rigid and rigid rotor systems, this can cause high blade loads and stress on the hub. More critically, if the nose pitches up aggressively while the pilot simultaneously adds collective to maintain altitude, RPM can droop momentarily. Additionally, a sharp aft cyclic combined with high power creates a high-torque, high-AOA situation that stresses the drivetrain. The student must be taught smooth, coordinated cyclic inputs — moderate rate of pitch change to reach the target attitude, not abrupt corrections. Reference: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 and rotor system chapters.

questions.question: During a practical test, a candidate completes a rolling takeoff and establishes normal climb airspeed within ±5 knots, but sets a power setting 15% above the POH-specified normal climb power. The airspeed is within standards. Would you grade this as a failure, and what are the specific safety implications of the excess power setting?
questions.answer: Yes, this would be grounds to fail this task element. The ACS standard explicitly requires setting 'appropriate power,' meaning the POH-specified normal climb power — not simply any power that achieves the airspeed. Operating at 15% excess power has several safety implications: (1) it may exceed engine or transmission torque limits, risking mechanical damage; (2) it increases fuel burn unnecessarily; (3) it reduces the available power margin for emergency maneuvers; (4) it may exceed transmission or rotor rpm operating limits if not monitored carefully; and (5) in a turbine helicopter, it could exceed temperature limits (TOT/TGT/ITT). Setting appropriate power requires the pilot to reference the POH/RFM and set the correct torque/manifold pressure/throttle position — not simply observe that the airspeed is acceptable.
questions.follow_up: The candidate argues that the extra power was intentional because there were trees at the departure end and they wanted extra climb performance. Is this a valid justification under the ACS, and what should the candidate have done instead?
questions.follow_up_answer: This is not a valid justification for exceeding POH-specified normal climb power without authorization. If the departure required extra obstacle clearance performance, the appropriate action would have been to plan a maximum performance takeoff using the appropriate power setting from the POH performance section, not improvise an excessive power setting during a standard rolling takeoff. The ACS task for rolling takeoff assumes a situation where a normal takeoff profile is appropriate; if obstacles required maximum performance, a different takeoff technique should have been selected and briefed during the pre-takeoff planning phase. The candidate demonstrated poor ADM and task planning rather than good performance management. Reference: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; ACS CH.V.E.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; Helicopter POH/RFM; ACS CH.V.E.S8

questions.question: After lifting off during a rolling takeoff, what control input do you use to maintain a straight ground track when there is a crosswind from the right?
questions.answer: After liftoff, you apply cyclic into the wind — in this case, left cyclic — to establish a crab angle or wind correction angle that keeps the helicopter tracking straight down the intended ground track. The amount of cyclic correction depends on the crosswind component. Pedals are used to maintain trim, not to correct for drift.

questions.question: What is the difference between a slip and a skid, and which condition are you most likely to create if you use pedals instead of cyclic to correct for a crosswind after liftoff?
questions.answer: A slip occurs when the rate of turn is too low for the bank angle — the horizontal component of lift exceeds inertia. A skid occurs when the rate of turn is too high — inertia exceeds the horizontal component of lift. If you use pedals to weathervane the nose into the wind instead of using cyclic to establish a crab, you are creating a skidding condition because you are yawing the fuselage without a corresponding bank. Pedals should only compensate for torque and maintain trim, not correct for crosswind drift.

questions.question: At what point during a rolling takeoff should you establish crosswind correction — before liftoff while still rolling, or immediately after the wheels leave the ground?
questions.answer: Crosswind correction should begin as the helicopter becomes airborne and leaves the surface. While still rolling on the ground, the wheels provide lateral ground contact that resists sideward drift. Once airborne, the helicopter is free to move laterally with the wind, so cyclic correction into the wind must be established immediately at or just after liftoff to prevent the helicopter from drifting downwind of the intended ground track.
