The key examiner point: radio calls at off-airport sites are entirely crew/pilot-initiated coordination tools. Their absence was the first breakdown here — pre-mission frequency coordination with all known site users is the correct ADM mitigation.

questions.question: During a shallow approach and running landing, what is the primary instrument or indicator you use to verify that Nr (rotor RPM) is staying within normal limits?
questions.answer: The tachometer — specifically the rotor RPM gauge (Nr), which on most helicopters is combined with the engine RPM (N2 or Ng) in a dual-needle or split-needle instrument. During a shallow approach, the pilot cross-checks the tachometer to confirm Nr remains in the green arc. If the needles are married (engine and rotor RPM synchronized), it also confirms the engine is driving the rotor normally through the freewheeling unit.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 9 — Basic Flight Maneuvers; Chapter 10 — Advanced Flight Maneuvers

questions.question: As you transition through effective translational lift (ETL) during a shallow approach, what tends to happen to rotor RPM if you do not adjust the collective, and why?
questions.answer: As the helicopter decelerates through ETL — approximately 16–24 knots — the rotor loses the efficiency gained from translational lift. The rotor system must now work harder to produce the same lift, which increases the load on the rotor and tends to cause Nr to decay (decrease) if the collective is not adjusted or engine power is not sufficient to compensate. The pilot must monitor Nr and make appropriate collective and throttle adjustments to keep Nr within the normal operating range.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 10 — Advanced Flight Maneuvers (Shallow Approach section); Chapter 2 — Aerodynamics of Flight (ETL)

questions.question: What does the term 'Nr within normal limits' specifically mean, and where do you find the acceptable range for your helicopter?
questions.answer: Nr within normal limits means the main rotor RPM is operating within the green arc on the rotor tachometer — the range approved by the manufacturer for normal flight operations. The specific RPM range is defined in the helicopter's Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) and displayed on the tachometer instrument face. Operating outside this range — either too high (overspeed) or too low (underspeed) — can lead to structural damage or rotor stall respectively, both of which are unacceptable during any phase of flight including a running landing.

questions.question: You are on a shallow approach in a piston-powered helicopter and notice the engine RPM and rotor RPM needles are beginning to split — engine is climbing while rotor is dropping. You are at 40 feet AGL at about 30 knots. What is happening and what do you do?
questions.answer: A split where engine RPM rises and Nr drops indicates a slippage or failure in the freewheeling unit or a disconnect in the drive system — the engine is no longer efficiently driving the rotor. This is an emergency. Immediately lower collective to reduce rotor load and attempt to maintain or recover Nr. If Nr cannot be recovered, treat this as an engine failure and execute an autorotation — in this case a running/roll-on autorotation is appropriate given the low altitude and airspeed already established. Announce the emergency, select the best available surface ahead, and complete the landing with minimum collective application at touchdown to preserve what Nr remains. Do not attempt to climb.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11 — Helicopter Emergencies (Autorotation, Drive System Failure); Chapter 10 — Running/Roll-On Landing

questions.question: You are performing a shallow approach and running landing on a hot day at a high-elevation airport. How does density altitude affect your ability to maintain Nr within normal limits during this maneuver, and what technique adjustments do you make?
questions.answer: At high density altitude, the engine produces less power and the rotor blades generate less lift per revolution due to thinner air. The reduced power available means the engine may struggle to maintain Nr under load, especially during the transition through ETL where power demand increases. The pilot must be more vigilant in monitoring Nr throughout the approach. Technique adjustments include: flying a shallower approach angle to extend the deceleration phase, accepting a slightly higher ground speed at touchdown to reduce power demand, avoiding abrupt collective inputs that could spike the load on the engine, and ensuring collective is reduced smoothly as translational lift is lost. If Nr begins to decay, reducing collective slightly and accepting more groundspeed is preferable to an Nr underspeed condition.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 10 — Running/Roll-On Landing; Chapter 4 — Helicopter Performance (Density Altitude)

questions.question: During the ground roll phase of a running landing, the helicopter touches down and you begin rolling to a stop. Should you be concerned about Nr at this point, and what collective position helps protect Nr during the roll-out?
questions.answer: Yes — Nr management does not end at touchdown. During the ground roll, the rotor is still turning and must remain in the normal RPM range. The collective should be kept low (near full down or at the minimum pitch position specified in the RFM) to minimize rotor load during the roll-out. Raising the collective during the ground roll can cause the skids or wheels to re-lift unevenly, creating a dynamic rollover risk, and can also load the rotor system in a way that stresses the drive components. The pilot should smoothly bring the helicopter to a complete stop, then follow the RFM shutdown sequence. On some helicopters, particularly piston types with a correlator, the throttle position also affects Nr during roll-out and should be monitored.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 10 — Running/Roll-On Landing; Chapter 11 — Dynamic Rollover

questions.question: An applicant executes a shallow approach and running landing with the Nr consistently at the top of the green arc — just below the red line — throughout the approach. The landing was otherwise smooth and controlled. Do you consider this acceptable performance, and what does this pattern of high Nr tell you about how the applicant is managing the maneuver?
questions.answer: While technically still within limits, Nr consistently near the top of the green arc throughout a shallow approach is a red flag indicating the applicant is likely carrying too much throttle or failing to anticipate power changes properly. During a powered shallow approach, Nr should be steady in the middle of the green arc with the needles married, reflecting balanced throttle and collective coordination. Nr trending high suggests the applicant may be over-throttling while simultaneously reducing collective, or is not using the correlator/governor effectively. In turbine helicopters, this pattern could indicate the applicant is not monitoring torque and N1/N2 relationships correctly. This is worth examining further — it reveals a lack of precision in power management even if the landing was smooth. I would ask the applicant to explain what they were doing with the throttle during the approach and have them repeat the maneuver with explicit attention to tachometer management.
questions.follow_up: If this same applicant then performs the maneuver with Nr slightly below the green arc on short final, what immediate action is required and what does the ACS say about the consequence of allowing Nr to drop out of the normal range?
questions.follow_up_answer: If Nr drops below the green arc on short final, the pilot must immediately reduce collective to unload the rotor and allow Nr to recover, while simultaneously assessing whether a go-around or continuation to a running landing is safer given the altitude and airspeed. Allowing Nr to continue decaying risks progressing toward rotor stall — which in a helicopter is not recoverable. The ACS standard for this task (CH.V.F.S3) explicitly requires maintaining Nr within normal limits throughout the maneuver; any exceedance — high or low — is a disqualifying performance error. The examiner must note this as a critical failure because operating outside normal rotor RPM limits in any flight condition is a direct threat to the airworthiness of the aircraft.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11 — Low Rotor RPM and Rotor Stall; ACS CH.V.F.S3; 14 CFR 91.9

questions.question: In a turbine helicopter with a full authority digital engine control (FADEC) or electronic engine control (EEC), the governor is automatically maintaining Nr. Does having an automatic governor eliminate the pilot's responsibility to monitor and maintain Nr within normal limits during a shallow approach and running landing? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No — the governor does not eliminate pilot responsibility. The ACS holds the pilot accountable for Nr regardless of the automation level. The governor is a tool, not a substitute for airmanship. During a shallow approach and running landing in a turbine helicopter, the pilot must still monitor Nr because: (1) governors can fail or reach their authority limits — if torque demand exceeds available power (e.g., high DA, high gross weight), the governor cannot create power that doesn't exist, and Nr will decay; (2) abrupt collective inputs can momentarily outpace the governor's response rate causing a transient Nr drop; (3) the pilot must recognize abnormal Nr trends early enough to intervene before limits are exceeded. The pilot should be cross-checking the Nr gauge, torque, turbine temperatures, and power available margin throughout the maneuver — not assuming the automation is handling it. Automation complacency is itself an ADM failure identified in FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13.
questions.follow_up: If the governor fails in-flight during the shallow approach and Nr begins to rise uncontrolled, what is your immediate action and what are the limits you are trying to protect against?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the governor fails and Nr rises uncontrolled, the pilot must immediately reduce throttle manually to bring Nr back within the normal range, treating it as a manual throttle operation for the remainder of the flight. The pilot is protecting against Nr overspeed, which can cause blade deformation, hub stress, and catastrophic rotor failure. The specific overspeed limits are in the RFM, typically marked as the red line on the tachometer. The approach should be continued as a manually controlled power approach, reducing collective smoothly to manage both Nr and rate of descent, with a priority on completing the running landing safely given the degraded control mode. Declaring an emergency (7700) is appropriate.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 13 — ADM/Automation Management; Chapter 11 — Engine and System Emergencies; ACS CH.V.F.S3; Helicopter RFM (aircraft-specific)

questions.question: What is the typical approach angle used for a shallow approach in a helicopter, and how does it differ from a normal approach angle?
questions.answer: A shallow approach uses an approach angle of approximately 5 degrees or less, compared to the normal approach angle of about 8-12 degrees. The shallower angle is used when obstacle clearance is not a concern and allows the helicopter to take advantage of translational lift longer into the approach, reducing the power required to complete the landing. This lower angle also results in a higher groundspeed throughout more of the approach.

questions.question: What does 'rate of closure' mean during a shallow approach, and what control inputs primarily regulate it?
questions.answer: Rate of closure refers to the rate at which the helicopter is approaching the intended touchdown point — essentially how quickly the helicopter is decelerating and descending toward the landing surface. It is primarily regulated by cyclic (controlling forward speed and pitch attitude) in combination with collective (controlling descent rate and power). A proper rate of closure means the helicopter is arriving at the touchdown zone at a manageable groundspeed consistent with a running or roll-on landing, not decelerating to a hover prematurely.

questions.question: What visual reference technique do you use to determine whether you are maintaining the correct approach angle during a shallow approach?
questions.answer: The pilot uses a point on the ground at or near the intended touchdown spot and monitors whether that reference point appears to move in the field of view. If the point rises in the windscreen, the approach angle is too shallow (undershooting). If the point descends in the windscreen, the approach is too steep (overshooting). The point should remain relatively stationary in the windscreen when the correct approach angle is maintained. Additionally, the pilot monitors airspeed, VSI, and altimeter to confirm a stabilized descent path.

questions.question: You're on a shallow approach and notice your rate of closure is too high — you're moving toward the touchdown point faster than intended. What is the correct corrective sequence, and what hazard do you need to avoid during the correction?
questions.answer: To reduce an excessive rate of closure, apply gentle aft cyclic to increase pitch attitude and reduce forward speed, while simultaneously monitoring collective to prevent an unwanted climb. The primary hazard to avoid is a low-G condition — if aft cyclic is applied abruptly or aggressively without sufficient power, especially in certain rotor systems, it can unload the rotor and lead to mast bumping or loss of directional control. Additionally, if too much collective is applied during the correction in a low-inertia rotor system, rotor RPM can decay. The correction should be smooth and coordinated. If speed and closure cannot be stabilized, a go-around should be initiated.

questions.question: During a shallow approach to a confined area, you recognize that you are drifting below the recommended approach angle at the midpoint of the approach. You still have ETL. What are your options, and how do you decide between a correction and a go-around?
questions.answer: If you are below the approach angle at the midpoint and still have ETL (above approximately 16-24 knots), you may be able to correct by adding collective and adjusting cyclic to steepen the approach angle and reestablish the glidepath. However, the key decision factor is whether you can correct while maintaining sufficient power margin and still clear any obstacles at the approach end. In a confined area, going below the intended glidepath increases the risk of striking obstacles. If the correction would require near-maximum power, if you cannot clearly see a safe path to the landing zone, or if the situation is developing faster than you can manage, a go-around is the correct choice. The go-around decision should be made early, while you still have airspeed and ETL to make it effective.

questions.question: How does a headwind versus a tailwind affect the rate of closure and your control inputs during a shallow approach, and which condition is more dangerous and why?
questions.answer: In a headwind, groundspeed is reduced for a given airspeed, so the rate of closure over the ground is slower. The pilot may need to use a slightly lower pitch attitude to maintain the same groundspeed arrival at the touchdown zone, and the approach will feel more stable. In a tailwind, groundspeed increases for the same airspeed, resulting in a faster rate of closure over the ground. The pilot must manage a higher approach speed, and the flare/deceleration phase requires more anticipation and distance. A tailwind is more dangerous because it compresses reaction time, reduces the effectiveness of translational lift benefits, and results in a higher groundspeed at touchdown — increasing rollout distance and the consequences of a misjudged approach. Shallow approaches with a tailwind component should be avoided when possible.

questions.question: A student pilot consistently establishes the correct approach angle initially but then allows the angle to steepen in the final third of the shallow approach, increasing the rate of closure. As an instructor, what are the most likely root causes of this error, and how does this steepening specifically compromise the running landing?
questions.answer: The most likely root causes are: (1) the student is fixating on the touchdown point and failing to divide attention between the approach path angle and the landing area, causing late recognition of the steepening; (2) the student is reducing collective too aggressively in anticipation of touchdown, increasing the descent rate and steepening the path; or (3) the student is allowing airspeed to decay below ETL too early without increasing collective to compensate for the loss of translational lift, causing an increasing sink rate. The steepening in the final third is particularly hazardous for a running landing because it results in a higher descent rate at touchdown — the helicopter contacts the ground with a vertical velocity component that the skids or wheels are not designed to absorb at that combination of forward and vertical speed. This can cause a hard landing, skid damage, or a dynamic rollover if the helicopter yaws or drifts laterally at touchdown.
questions.follow_up: If you observe this pattern across multiple approaches with the same student, what instructional technique would you use to correct the fixation and improve their approach angle management in the final segment?
questions.follow_up_answer: I would have the student verbally call out the approach angle indicator (whether visual glidepath reference point or VSI/airspeed cross-check) at regular intervals — every 100 feet of altitude, for example — to break fixation on the touchdown point and force distributed attention. I would also have them practice the approach with a pre-briefed 'checkpoint' at a defined altitude (e.g., 50 feet AGL) where they verbally confirm airspeed and VSI are within parameters before continuing. This introduces a structured scan habit at the critical phase of the approach. Additionally, practicing the approach at a higher altitude over a runway to allow recovery from errors without terrain consequences helps build the correct control feel without the consequence pressure.

questions.question: During a shallow approach at a remote site, you lose all forward visibility reference points due to brownout or whiteout just before touchdown. You believe your approach angle and rate of closure were correct at the point of visual degradation. What is the correct technique, and what are the risks of attempting to continue versus executing a go-around?
questions.answer: When visual reference is lost in brownout or whiteout, the correct technique is to immediately transition to instruments and execute a go-around by applying power and climbing away from the surface — do not attempt to continue the approach to touchdown. The risks of continuing are severe: without outside visual references, spatial disorientation can occur within seconds; the pilot cannot detect drift, settling, or terrain irregularities; and a small uncorrected lateral drift at touchdown speed can cause dynamic rollover. Even if the approach angle and rate of closure were correct at the moment of visual loss, the helicopter will continue to descend and decelerate, and any uncorrected deviation cannot be detected. A go-around, executed by applying collective smoothly, establishing a positive climb attitude with cyclic, and transitioning to instruments, is always the correct choice. Continuing to touchdown in zero-visibility IMC/degraded visual environment without proper training, equipment, and crew resource management is statistically fatal.
questions.follow_up: What pre-approach planning actions could have reduced the risk of encountering this brownout or whiteout scenario in the first place, and what does the FAA recommend regarding degraded visual environment operations?
questions.follow_up_answer: Pre-approach planning should include: a high reconnaissance to assess surface material (dust, sand, snow) and predict the likelihood of brownout or whiteout; pre-wetting the landing area if operationally feasible; selecting the slowest approach speed consistent with safety to reduce rotor downwash-induced particle suspension; and identifying abort decision points prior to entry. The FAA addresses Degraded Visual Environment (DVE) operations in advisory circulars and the Helicopter Flying Handbook, emphasizing that pilots should not enter conditions where visual meteorological conditions cannot be maintained unless properly trained and equipped for instrument flight. For military and offshore operations, formal DVE training protocols exist, but for civilian operations, the safest mitigation is avoidance. The pilot should also brief a specific go-around decision altitude before beginning the approach.

questions.question: During a shallow approach and running landing, what are the primary visual and cockpit cues you use to determine wind direction before beginning the approach?
questions.answer: Wind direction can be determined by several means: observing smoke, flags, or vegetation movement on the ground; checking the windsock or wind tee at the airport; noting surface water ripples; observing dust or debris movement; checking the ATIS or AWOS; and feeling the helicopter's tendency to weathervane during a hover. In flight, the difference between heading and ground track on GPS also indicates wind direction and magnitude.

questions.question: What flight control input do you use to correct for a crosswind and maintain your desired ground track during a shallow approach to a running landing?
questions.answer: Cyclic is used to correct for crosswind drift and maintain the desired ground track. The cyclic is displaced into the wind (upwind direction) to create a crab angle or to slip the helicopter, counteracting the crosswind component and keeping the helicopter tracking directly along the intended approach path. Pedals are used to keep the fuselage aligned as needed, and collective controls the descent rate.

questions.question: What is the difference between a crab correction and a sideslip correction when maintaining ground track during a crosswind approach in a helicopter, and which is more commonly used during a running/roll-on landing?
questions.answer: A crab correction involves pointing the helicopter's nose into the wind so the ground track remains aligned with the landing area, while the fuselage is angled to the runway centerline. A sideslip involves using cyclic into the wind and opposite pedal to align the fuselage with the ground track while drifting is arrested laterally. For a running/roll-on landing, the sideslip (or a combination transitioning to aligned at touchdown) is preferred because touching down in a significant crab angle places lateral stress on the landing gear and skids. The helicopter should ideally be aligned with the ground track at touchdown.

questions.question: You are on a shallow approach to a confined area for a running landing. Partway down the approach you notice your ground track is drifting right of the intended touchdown point. Wind conditions were calm on your reconnaissance, but now you can see treetops on the left side moving. What is your assessment and what corrections do you make?
questions.answer: The moving treetops indicate a left crosswind has developed or a valley/terrain-channeled wind is present. The rightward ground track drift confirms left-to-right crosswind pushing the helicopter off course. I would apply left cyclic to counteract the drift and reestablish the intended ground track. I would reassess whether the landing area still provides a safe, upwind-facing landing angle, consider whether a go-around is warranted to replan the approach into the wind if the crosswind is significant, and note any obstacles now potentially in the flight path due to the track deviation. Pedals are used to maintain trim throughout.

questions.question: During a shallow approach with a direct crosswind from the left, you are holding a crab angle to maintain ground track. As you approach ETL and begin to decelerate for the running landing, how does your crosswind correction technique change and why?
questions.answer: As ETL is lost during the deceleration, translational lift decreases and the helicopter requires more collective, which increases torque and affects yaw. Additionally, as airspeed decreases, the aerodynamic effectiveness of the cyclic crab diminishes relative to the rotor disc's response. At this stage, I transition from a pure crab to coordinating cyclic into the wind with appropriate pedal input to keep the fuselage aligned with the ground track, preventing a sideward touchdown. The goal is to arrive at touchdown with skids parallel to the direction of travel to avoid lateral ground contact stress. This requires anticipation and smooth, progressive control inputs as speed bleeds off.

questions.question: You are planning a shallow approach to a gravel bar alongside a river. On reconnaissance you notice the river surface shows ripples moving toward the near bank from across the river, and the tall grass at the near end of the gravel bar is bending away from you at approximately 45 degrees. How do you interpret this wind data and how does it affect your approach planning?
questions.answer: The river ripples moving toward the near bank indicate wind is blowing from across the river toward your side — confirming a crosswind component from that direction. The tall grass bending away from you at 45 degrees indicates the wind has a significant headwind component relative to your planned approach direction as well. Combined, I interpret this as a quartering headwind — wind coming from roughly a 45-degree angle off the nose on the upwind side. For the shallow approach, I will plan to crab into this quartering headwind to maintain my intended ground track down the gravel bar centerline, with cyclic displaced into the wind. I'll also note the headwind component will assist deceleration and provide better ETL performance, which is favorable for a marginal power situation.

questions.question: During a running/roll-on landing in a crosswind, the helicopter touches down with skids aligned to the ground track but there is still a crosswind pushing laterally. Walk me through the dynamic rollover risk in this scenario and how your control inputs immediately before and at touchdown mitigate it.
questions.answer: Dynamic rollover risk exists when a lateral force — such as a crosswind pushing the helicopter sideways — acts on the helicopter while one skid is on the ground and serves as a pivot point. If the downwind skid contacts first and the crosswind pushes the helicopter over the upwind skid pivot, the situation can escalate faster than the pilot can correct. To mitigate this: before touchdown I ensure the helicopter is tracking straight with no lateral drift — if there is any remaining lateral drift at touchdown, I am moving sideways on the ground which is the setup for dynamic rollover. I maintain cyclic into the wind (upwind cyclic) to counteract the crosswind lateral push. At touchdown with both skids simultaneously, I continue to hold upwind cyclic and smoothly lower collective to reduce lift and lock the helicopter onto the ground. Abrupt collective reduction with a lateral cyclic input could cause an overcorrection. If I detect the helicopter beginning to roll, the correct response is immediate collective reduction — not lateral cyclic — because attempting to correct roll with cyclic at low altitude and low RPM can accelerate the rollover.
questions.follow_up: If you are in a running landing and you feel one skid catch or dig in on the surface — for example on soft ground — and the helicopter begins to roll over that contact point, what is the single most important recovery action and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: The single most important action is to immediately and aggressively lower the collective to reduce lift and prevent the helicopter from pivoting over the snagged skid. Attempting to correct with cyclic across a fixed pivot point actually increases the rolling moment because the rotor thrust is now acting through a lever arm above the pivot. Lowering collective removes the energy driving the rollover. Once the rotor thrust is reduced, the helicopter will settle back onto both skids rather than continue rotating. This must be done immediately — dynamic rollover can exceed the cyclic's ability to stop it within fractions of a second above approximately 8-10 degrees of roll.

questions.question: You are executing a shallow approach with a direct 90-degree crosswind from the left. You are holding the crab angle well and your ground track looks good. As you cross the runway threshold at low altitude and airspeed, a sudden gust increases the crosswind significantly. Describe your complete decision-making process and control response in real time.
questions.answer: A sudden crosswind gust at low airspeed and low altitude is a high-risk scenario because I have minimal energy to correct and the margin above the surface is small. Immediately upon feeling the gust push the helicopter right and off ground track: First, I apply aggressive left cyclic to stop the lateral drift — my priority is ground track, not fuselage alignment. Second, I assess whether the drift can be arrested before reaching obstacles or the edge of the landing surface. If the landing area is wide enough and I can reestablish track quickly, I continue to touchdown with aligned skids. If I cannot confidently stop the drift before reaching a hazard or I am now tracking sideways with insufficient room, I initiate a go-around immediately — adding full power, aft cyclic as needed to arrest descent, and climbing out of the approach. At low altitude and low airspeed with a significant lateral gust, the go-around is almost always the right call. Attempting to salvage a compromised approach this close to the ground in a crosswind is exactly the scenario that leads to dynamic rollover or a hard lateral landing. After the go-around, I reassess wind conditions before attempting another approach, possibly repositioning the approach angle to reduce the crosswind component.
questions.follow_up: If you are committed to the landing — skids are about to touch — and this gust hits and you still have lateral drift, is there any technique to reduce lateral touchdown velocity beyond what you've already described?
questions.follow_up_answer: At the instant of touchdown with residual lateral drift, the pilot can use a brief, aggressive cyclic input directly into the drift direction to decelerate the lateral movement just before skid contact — essentially a last-moment 'bump' of upwind cyclic. This is a finesse technique and is only effective if the drift is minor. It must be done smoothly because an overcorrection with cyclic at touchdown could cause a hard lateral oscillation. More critically, the pilot must have downward collective pressure ready to immediately reduce lift at skid contact to prevent the helicopter from rebounding or pivoting. If the lateral velocity is significant — visible, felt drift — then the proper technique was the go-around before this point. There is no safe technique to fully arrest a large lateral drift velocity after skid contact; ground contact with sideward movement is what initiates the dynamic rollover sequence.

questions.question: What is effective translational lift (ETL) and at approximately what airspeed does a helicopter achieve it?
questions.answer: Effective translational lift (ETL) is the phenomenon in which rotor efficiency increases when the helicopter moves forward fast enough to exit its own induced downwash and operate in relatively undisturbed air. ETL typically occurs between approximately 16–24 knots, depending on helicopter type, weight, and atmospheric conditions; consult the aircraft POH for specific values. At ETL, pilots will notice increased rotor efficiency (producing more lift for the same power input), a distinct lightening or 'bump' in control feel, and reduced vibration as the rotor transitions from hover-induced turbulent air to cleaner forward-flight airflow.

questions.question: During a running or roll-on landing, why is it important to keep the landing gear parallel to the ground track rather than allowing the helicopter to drift sideways?
questions.answer: If the landing gear contacts the surface at an angle to the ground track rather than aligned with it, lateral forces are applied to the landing skids or wheels. This can cause the helicopter to tip, create dynamic rollover conditions, or damage the landing gear. In skid-equipped helicopters especially, any sideward motion on surface contact can produce a tripping effect on the skids, rapidly transferring momentum into a roll. Keeping the gear parallel to the ground track ensures all contact forces are longitudinal, which the airframe is designed to absorb.

questions.question: What is the primary reason a pilot would choose to perform a running or roll-on landing instead of a normal hover landing?
questions.answer: A running or roll-on landing is used when the helicopter cannot hover out of ground effect (OGE) due to high density altitude, heavy gross weight, or high-power-required conditions. By maintaining forward airspeed through touchdown, the helicopter benefits from translational lift, which reduces the power required compared to a hover. This technique allows the pilot to complete the landing safely when a hover would exceed the available power margin. The ACS specifies that a running takeoff should not be attempted unless the helicopter can be hovered at least momentarily, which parallels the logic for choosing this landing technique.

questions.question: You are on final for a running landing at a high-altitude mountain landing zone. As you approach the surface, you notice you are drifting approximately 5 degrees right of the runway centerline. You are already at minimum power available. Walk me through your exact control inputs to correct the drift and maintain gear alignment without going around.
questions.answer: With minimum power available, a go-around may not be feasible, but the correction must still be made carefully. First, use left cyclic to stop the drift and realign the nose with the intended ground track — cyclic controls both lateral movement and heading indirectly through coordinated flight. Use left pedal as needed to keep the nose pointed down the landing path (coordinated turn to align heading). Do not use pedals alone to weathervane the nose, as this will cause the tail to swing and skid the helicopter. The key is to bring the aircraft back to a coordinated, wings-level attitude with the longitudinal axis aligned with the ground track before or at surface contact. If the drift cannot be fully corrected before touchdown, a go-around must be initiated if power allows; otherwise a controlled touchdown with immediate recognition of rollover potential is required. Throughout all corrections, maintain the airspeed that keeps translational lift effective to preserve the reduced power requirement.

questions.question: During a running landing approach, you lose ETL just before touchdown because you reduced collective too aggressively. Describe what happens to the helicopter's behavior and what you should do to recover the landing.
questions.answer: When ETL is lost prematurely, the rotor re-enters its own induced downwash and loses efficiency. The helicopter will experience an increase in power required, a nose pitch attitude change, and increased vibration or roughness. The helicopter may begin to sink or settle more rapidly than expected, and if airspeed falls below approximately 16 knots without sufficient collective, the helicopter could contact the surface in a nose-high or tail-low attitude. To recover: smoothly increase collective to arrest the sink rate. If altitude permits, use forward cyclic to increase airspeed toward the speed at which translational lift becomes effective again (typically 16+ knots), while maintaining coordinated pedal inputs. However, if surface contact is imminent, prioritize collective and cyclic coordination for safe touchdown with proper gear alignment and nose attitude over attempting to reestablish ETL, as the primary goal is controlled contact rather than power recovery.

questions.question: You are performing a running landing on a short gravel strip with a slight crosswind from the left. How do you set up the approach so that your landing gear is parallel to the ground track at touchdown, not just the runway heading?
questions.answer: In a crosswind, the ground track and the aircraft heading will differ unless a crab or sideslip technique is used. To keep the landing gear parallel to the ground track — not the runway — you must align the helicopter's longitudinal axis with the actual direction of movement across the ground, which is the ground track. This means applying a slight right crab (into the wind) throughout the approach so the helicopter tracks straight down the strip. Just before and at touchdown, the aircraft's heading should be aligned with the ground track, not necessarily with the runway centerline. Use left cyclic and right pedal to maintain coordinated flight while crabbing. The gear, which is fixed to the airframe, will then be aligned with the direction of movement at contact, preventing lateral load on the skids or wheels. Do not attempt to kick out a crab with pedals at the last second as this introduces sideward velocity, which is exactly what must be avoided.

questions.question: A student pilot you are instructing consistently touches down during running landings with the helicopter yawed about 10 degrees right of the ground track, always on the left skid first. What specific aerodynamic or control habit is most likely causing this, and how would you diagnose and correct it?
questions.answer: This pattern — consistently yawed right with left skid contact — strongly suggests the student is over-applying right pedal during the approach. In a helicopter with a counterclockwise main rotor (standard U.S. configuration), as airspeed decreases during the approach, torque effect increases, requiring increasing left pedal input to maintain coordinated flight. A student who is not keeping pace with the increasing left pedal demand will fall behind on torque compensation, allowing the nose to yaw right. This puts the aircraft heading right of the ground track, and because the left skid is now leading (outboard in a right yaw relative to the track), it contacts first. To diagnose: observe the slip/skid ball — if it is consistently right of center during the approach, the student is under-applying left pedal. Correction includes: reinforcing pedal trim awareness as airspeed decreases, using the ball and outside visual cues simultaneously, and practicing coordinated deceleration exercises at altitude before returning to landing practice.
questions.follow_up: If this student is flying a helicopter with a clockwise main rotor (e.g., some Eurocopter models), would the pedal correction direction and yaw tendency be reversed?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes. In a helicopter with a clockwise-rotating main rotor (viewed from above), torque reaction pushes the fuselage to the left, requiring right pedal input to maintain directional trim. As airspeed decreases and power is applied, the torque effect increases, demanding increasing right pedal. A student lagging on this compensation would yaw left of the ground track, causing the right skid to lead and contact first — the exact mirror image of the counterclockwise rotor scenario. The diagnostic process is identical: monitor the ball and visual cues, identify the pedal deficit, and correct through awareness and practice. Knowing which direction the main rotor turns is essential when analyzing torque-related control problems.

questions.question: During a running landing at a remote site, you maintain ETL and touch down with the gear aligned to the ground track, but as the helicopter decelerates on the ground after touchdown you feel the left skid begin to dig in and the rotor disk tilting left. What is happening and what is your immediate control response?
questions.answer: This is the onset of dynamic rollover. Once ground contact is made, the left skid becomes a pivot point. If the rotor thrust vector tilts left — due to left cyclic input, wind, terrain slope, or an inadvertent control movement — the rolling moment about the grounded skid can exceed the restoring moment and the helicopter will roll over. This can develop extremely rapidly, within one to two seconds. Immediate response: apply right cyclic to move the thrust vector back over the aircraft centerline and reduce the rolling moment. Simultaneously, reduce collective to decrease rotor thrust and eliminate the lifting force that is enabling the roll. Do not apply left pedal or additional collective, as these will worsen the situation. If the roll has progressed beyond approximately 8–12 degrees of bank (varies by helicopter), recovery may not be possible and the pilot must shut down and exit. The critical lesson is that dynamic rollover prevention begins before touchdown — gear alignment, zero sideward velocity, and neutral cyclic at contact are the defenses; recovery after the fact is extremely limited.
questions.follow_up: Is dynamic rollover more likely to occur during a running landing or a normal hover landing, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: Dynamic rollover is actually more commonly associated with hover landings, particularly slope landings or landings where one skid contacts first, because those scenarios more often involve asymmetric ground contact and low-airspeed maneuvering where pilot attention is divided. However, running landings carry their own dynamic rollover risk specifically if sideward velocity or yaw misalignment exists at touchdown — the forward momentum combined with a lateral force at the skid can generate a rapid rolling moment. In a hover landing on flat ground with gear fully settled, the risk is lower because both skids contact simultaneously and cyclic corrections are straightforward. The running landing scenario is dangerous because the forward speed means any lateral skid snag or yaw misalignment is amplified by kinetic energy. Both scenarios demand the same prevention principle: ensure the rotor thrust vector is centered over the landing gear at and after contact.

questions.question: During a running/roll-on landing, once the skids make contact with the surface, what is the primary purpose of your cyclic inputs?
questions.answer: After skid contact, cyclic is used to maintain a wings-level, aligned attitude and prevent the helicopter from veering or rolling off the intended ground track. The cyclic should be held into any crosswind component to keep the skids tracking straight, and any tendency to drift or turn must be corrected with smooth, prompt cyclic inputs before the deviation becomes large.

questions.question: After surface contact in a roll-on landing, what happens to the collective and why?
questions.answer: After surface contact, the collective is progressively lowered to reduce lift and settle the helicopter firmly onto the surface. This prevents the helicopter from becoming airborne again or skipping, and it transfers weight to the skids, which improves directional stability and allows friction with the ground to help decelerate and track straight.

questions.question: What is the role of the antitorque pedals after skid contact during a running landing?
questions.answer: The antitorque pedals are used to maintain directional alignment — keeping the nose pointed straight down the intended landing path. As collective is reduced and torque decreases, pedal pressure requirements change, so the pilot must make smooth, coordinated pedal corrections to prevent the nose from yawing left or right while decelerating along the surface.

questions.question: You execute a roll-on landing with a slight crosswind from the left. At the moment of skid contact, the helicopter begins drifting right. Describe the specific control inputs you make and explain why late inputs are more dangerous than early ones.
questions.answer: At skid contact with a left crosswind, I should already have left cyclic applied to counter the drift. If the helicopter drifts right despite that, I increase left cyclic input promptly to stop the drift. Late inputs are more dangerous because at ground contact speed the helicopter has forward momentum combined with lateral drift — the longer the drift continues uncorrected, the more lateral load builds on the skids, increasing the risk of dynamic rollover or a skid digging in and causing the helicopter to pivot or tip. Early, smooth corrections keep forces manageable; late, abrupt corrections can over-correct and destabilize.

questions.question: During roll-on deceleration, a student pilot reacts to a slight right yaw by applying harsh, abrupt right pedal. What hazard does this create, and how should the correction have been made?
questions.answer: Abrupt right pedal input while decelerating on the ground can cause the nose to swing sharply right, creating asymmetric lateral loads on the skids and potentially inducing a ground loop or dynamic rollover tendency, especially if airspeed and some residual lift are still present. The correct technique is a smooth, progressive right pedal input — enough to stop the yaw trend without overcorrecting. The pilot should anticipate pedal changes as collective is reduced and torque diminishes, making corrections ahead of the deviation rather than reacting aggressively after it develops.

questions.question: You complete a running landing on a narrow unprepared strip. Just after skid contact, you notice the helicopter is tracking 10 degrees to the left of centerline and the strip edge is approaching. Walk me through your decision-making and control inputs to stay on the surface safely.
questions.answer: With limited strip width, I immediately assess whether correction is feasible or a go-around is safer. If I have sufficient distance and the deviation is developing slowly, I apply smooth right cyclic to bring the nose and track back toward centerline while holding directional heading with right pedal as needed. Simultaneously, I ensure collective is being lowered smoothly to keep weight on the skids for tracking stability. If the deviation is rapid, the edge is close, or I cannot confidently correct, I apply collective, establish a positive climb attitude, and execute a go-around — the strip edge or obstacles make continued landing a higher risk than a missed approach. The key principle is that aborting is always an option until the helicopter has stopped.

questions.question: A pilot performs a roll-on landing and, after skid contact, unconsciously holds aft cyclic to 'soften' the landing feel. Explain the aerodynamic consequence of sustained aft cyclic input after contact and what control problem this creates during the deceleration roll-out.
questions.answer: Sustained aft cyclic after skid contact tilts the rotor disk rearward, unloading the forward skids and loading the aft skid crossbars. This creates a nose-high attitude tendency on the ground that can cause the tail to drag or the aft skids to catch, and more critically, it pitches the rotor thrust vector aft — which combined with any residual translational lift can cause the helicopter to become airborne again unexpectedly or skip. During deceleration, aft cyclic also repositions the center of gravity relationship to the rotor mast, increasing the risk of mast bumping in semi-rigid rotor systems if the pilot then makes an abrupt correction. The correct technique after contact is to hold a neutral-to-slightly forward cyclic attitude, allowing the skids to settle flat and friction to decelerate the aircraft.
questions.follow_up: If this helicopter has a semi-rigid (teetering) rotor system and the pilot makes a large, abrupt aft-then-forward cyclic correction during the roll-out, what specific mechanical hazard does this introduce?
questions.follow_up_answer: In a semi-rigid (teetering) rotor system, large and abrupt cyclic reversals — especially in a low-G or unloaded condition — can cause mast bumping. When the rotor flaps beyond its normal range, the blade grips or hub can contact the rotor mast, potentially causing catastrophic structural failure. During a roll-out, if the pilot overcorrects from aft cyclic to aggressive forward cyclic, the rotor can flap to an extreme angle. This is why smooth, timely, and progressive cyclic inputs are not just a performance standard — they are a structural safety requirement in semi-rigid rotor systems.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapters 10 and 11; Helicopter Flying Handbook Glossary (semi-rigid rotor definition)

questions.question: During a checkride roll-on landing evaluation, the applicant maintains good directional control throughout the approach but, after skid contact, freezes on the controls — inputs become minimal and delayed while the helicopter slowly yaws left and drifts. The aircraft remains controllable and stops safely. Does this meet the standard, and what is the underlying human factors issue you are observing?
questions.answer: This does not meet the ACS standard for CH.V.F.S7, which specifically requires smooth, timely, AND correct control inputs after surface contact. 'Timely' is the failing element here — delayed inputs that allow a yaw and drift to develop are not timely even if eventual corrections are correct. The underlying human factors issue is task saturation or attentional narrowing: the applicant likely expended significant cognitive workload managing the approach and, upon touchdown confirmation, experienced a momentary cognitive unloading or fixation break that caused a delay in transitioning to ground control. This is a workload management failure within Single-Pilot Resource Management (SRM). The practical consequence is that small deviations become larger before correction, reducing the margin for confined or obstacle-laden landing areas.
questions.follow_up: What specific debrief technique would you use with this applicant to help them understand the transition from approach control to ground control as a continuous, uninterrupted task rather than two separate phases?
questions.follow_up_answer: I would use a mental model reframe: explain that surface contact is not a task completion cue — it is a phase transition cue. The applicant should be briefed to mentally 'stay in the seat' through the entire deceleration roll-out, treating the moment of skid contact as a signal to shift primary attention from approach path management to directional control on the surface, not as a signal to relax. A practical exercise is to have the applicant verbalize control inputs aloud after contact ('checking yaw — correcting with right pedal, lowering collective') to maintain active engagement and prevent attentional narrowing. This directly addresses the SRM workload management component identified in FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13.

questions.question: When conducting a running/roll-on landing at a towered airport, what is the minimum communication requirement before crossing any runway hold short line?
questions.answer: The pilot must receive explicit ATC clearance before crossing any runway hold short line. This includes hold short lines for active runways, intersecting taxiways that cross runways, and any runway incursion hot spots. The clearance must be read back verbatim, including the runway designation and instruction. Never assume a clearance — if in doubt, hold short and query ATC.

questions.question: What does a double solid yellow line and a double dashed yellow line painted on a taxiway surface indicate, and what does it mean for a helicopter rolling out after a running landing?
questions.answer: That marking is the runway holding position marking (hold short line). The solid lines face the direction from which aircraft must hold; the dashed lines face the side that may proceed. During a running landing rollout, if you cross the dashed side onto a taxiway, you have already exited the runway. However, if your rollout path approaches the solid-line side from the taxiway, you must stop and hold until ATC clears you across the runway. Awareness of orientation relative to these lines is critical during the rollout.

questions.question: During a shallow approach and running landing at an airport with runway incursion hot spots, where would you find those hot spot locations identified prior to flight?
questions.answer: Runway incursion hot spots are identified on the FAA airport diagram, which is published on instrument approach procedure charts and in the Chart Supplement (formerly Airport/Facility Directory). Hot spots are labeled as 'HS 1,' 'HS 2,' etc., with a brief description of the hazard. Pilots should review the airport diagram during preflight planning, note hot spot locations, and brief themselves on which taxiways or intersections require heightened awareness during the rollout and taxi.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Chart Supplement; FAA AC 150/5300-13B; FAA JO 7050.1B

questions.question: You are performing a running landing on Runway 27 at a controlled airport. During your rollout, ATC clears a departing aircraft for takeoff on Runway 27 behind you, and simultaneously instructs you to turn left on Taxiway Alpha. How do you prioritize these actions to avoid a runway incursion?
questions.answer: The immediate priority is to exit the active runway as efficiently as possible via the instructed taxiway turn. Acknowledge the taxi instruction with readback and clear the runway without delay — do not slow or hover-taxi on the runway surface unnecessarily. Once clear of the runway hold short line, contact ATC to confirm your position and receive further taxi instructions. The departing aircraft behind you creates urgency; however, do not rush in a way that causes directional control issues during rollout. If you are unable to exit at Taxiway Alpha due to speed or spacing, immediately advise ATC so they can hold the departing aircraft.

questions.question: You are operating at an uncontrolled airport and planning a running/roll-on landing on the active runway. Another pilot announces on CTAF that they are holding short of the same runway for departure. Describe how you would use runway incursion avoidance procedures throughout your approach and landing.
questions.answer: Prior to the approach, make a CTAF position call stating your aircraft type, position, intended runway, and that you are on final for a running landing. Listen carefully for the departing aircraft's response. During the approach, visually confirm the runway threshold and departure end — verify the holding aircraft has not moved onto the runway. After touchdown, make another CTAF call stating you are on the runway rolling out and will exit at a specific taxiway. Maintain awareness of the departure-end hold short area during rollout. After clearing the runway, announce clear of the runway on CTAF. At no point should you assume the other pilot heard you — visual verification is essential at uncontrolled fields.

questions.question: During your pre-landing briefing for a running/roll-on landing at an unfamiliar airport, what specific runway incursion avoidance items should you verbally cover before beginning the approach?
questions.answer: The briefing should include: (1) review of the airport diagram noting runway layout, crossing runways, and hot spots; (2) identification of the intended exit taxiway after rollout and a backup exit if speed is too high; (3) confirmation of which runways, if any, must be crossed to reach parking and whether clearances are required; (4) ATIS/AWOS review for active runways and any NOTAMs related to runway closures or construction; (5) LAHSO (Land and Hold Short Operations) awareness — know if any LAHSO clearances are in effect and whether you can comply given the running landing rollout distance; (6) a clear abort point if the approach becomes unstabilized. This briefing reduces task saturation during the rollout phase when incursion risk is highest.

questions.question: You are cleared for a running landing on Runway 18 with instructions to hold short of Runway 09/27 at Taxiway Bravo mid-field. During rollout, you realize your groundspeed is too high to stop before Runway 09/27. What are your options, and which do you choose?
questions.answer: Your immediate options are: (1) apply maximum aerodynamic and friction braking to stop before the hold short line — only choose this if stopping is truly achievable without loss of control; (2) execute a go-around/rejected landing — add power, transition back to flight, and advise ATC immediately; (3) if stopping is not possible and a go-around is not initiated in time, you must advise ATC of the incursion immediately and cross only if the crossing runway is clear — however, this must be the last resort and constitutes a runway incursion event requiring a report. The correct aeronautical decision is to reject the landing early once it becomes apparent the rollout distance is insufficient. This is why a pre-briefed abort point is essential before committing to a running landing. A go-around is always preferable to a runway incursion.
questions.follow_up: How does the unique characteristic of a running/roll-on landing — compared to a normal hover landing — specifically increase runway incursion risk, and what technique during the approach phase helps mitigate it?
questions.follow_up_answer: A running landing commits the pilot to a fixed rollout path and distance that cannot be easily altered once the skids or wheels touch down, unlike a hover landing where the pilot can stop or reposition while airborne. The higher groundspeed at touchdown means crossing runway hold short lines is possible before full deceleration. The mitigation technique is to identify the intended exit taxiway and a clear abort point during the approach — typically at a defined altitude or position — beyond which the approach is committed only if the runway environment is confirmed clear and the groundspeed at touchdown will allow a comfortable stop before any intersecting runway. If any doubt exists, the go-around is initiated before that abort point.

questions.question: At night, after completing a running landing at a towered airport, ATC clears you to taxi via Taxiway Charlie, cross Runway 14, then Taxiway Delta to the ramp. You read back the clearance incorrectly, omitting 'cross Runway 14,' and ATC does not catch the error. How should your runway incursion avoidance procedures catch this breakdown before it becomes an incident?
questions.answer: Sterile cockpit discipline and independent situational awareness are the final defense when ATC fails to catch a readback error. Before crossing any runway, regardless of a received clearance, you must: (1) positively identify the runway using signage, pavement markings, and airport diagram; (2) look left, look right, and scan final approach paths for traffic; (3) cross-check your taxi clearance against your airport diagram — if your written or mental model of the clearance does not include a runway crossing but you are approaching a runway, stop at the hold short line and query ATC for clarification. The principle is 'when in doubt, hold short.' Night operations amplify this risk because visual identification of runway markings and inbound traffic is harder. A printed or EFB-displayed airport diagram is essential during night taxi.
questions.follow_up: What FAA safety program or pilot behavior change was introduced specifically to address the scenario where ATC issues a taxi clearance and the pilot reads it back incorrectly without correction?
questions.follow_up_answer: The FAA's Runway Safety Program and AC 91-73B directly address this through the 'progressive taxi' option and the emphasis on 'taxi route readback with runway crossing explicit callout.' The FAA specifically trained controllers to require explicit readback of each runway crossing as a separate element, and pilots are trained under the Runway Safety Action Plan to treat any runway crossing as a discrete event requiring a positive clearance confirmation. Additionally, FAA's Runway Incursion Avoidance training emphasizes that a readback error not caught by ATC does not constitute a clearance — the pilot's independent verification and 'when in doubt, hold short' discipline is the final safeguard. This was reinforced following runway incursion accident investigations where readback/hearback errors were identified as causal factors.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA AC 91-73B; FAA JO 7110.65 (ATC Procedures); NTSB runway incursion accident studies; 14 CFR 91.123

tasks.title: Task G. Go-Around

questions.question: Name three situations during a helicopter approach that would require you to execute a go-around.
questions.answer: Any three of the following: (1) Loss of effective translational lift (ETL) occurs at a point where you cannot sustain a stable approach — especially critical on steep approaches where ETL is lost at a higher altitude than on normal approaches, requiring earlier power application. (2) Unexpected loss of power or settling with power (vortex ring state) developing during approach. (3) An obstacle or obstruction enters the intended landing area. (4) The landing surface is unsafe or unsuitable (soft ground, debris, unauthorized personnel). (5) Unstabilized approach — excessive sink rate, airspeed significantly deviating from target, or heading alignment lost. (6) Loss of visual reference, such as brownout, whiteout, or inadvertent IMC. (7) ATC instruction to go around. The fundamental principle is: if the approach is not proceeding safely and the pilot cannot correct it, a go-around must be initiated.

questions.question: What is vortex ring state, and why does it represent a situation on approach that demands an immediate go-around decision?
questions.answer: Vortex ring state (settling with power) occurs when the helicopter descends into its own rotor downwash, causing a recirculating vortex around the rotor system. This results in an uncommanded, rapid increase in sink rate that cannot be corrected by adding collective. It typically develops when the helicopter has: a descent rate greater than 300 FPM, airspeed below approximately 30 knots (including zero-airspeed approaches), and power applied (20–100% of available power). On approach, if a pilot adds collective to arrest a high sink rate at low airspeed and the sink rate continues or worsens, vortex ring state may be developing. Recovery requires moving the cyclic forward to gain airspeed and escape the vortex — essentially a go-around. Continuing the approach under these conditions risks ground contact with no means to arrest descent.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Helicopter Emergencies); Chapter 9 (Slow Flight, Vortex Ring State)

questions.question: On a steep approach to a confined area, why does loss of ETL occur at a higher altitude compared to a normal approach, and what consideration does this create for go-around planning?
questions.answer: On a steep approach, the helicopter's airspeed decelerates more rapidly and reaches the ETL threshold (approximately 16–24 knots) at a higher altitude above the landing zone compared to a shallower normal approach. Since ETL provides an aerodynamic efficiency benefit that reduces power required, losing ETL higher up means the pilot must apply additional collective earlier in the approach to compensate for the reduced rotor efficiency. If the pilot is unprepared for this increased power demand, or if the available power is insufficient (high density altitude, heavy gross weight), the sink rate may become uncontrollable before reaching the landing point. This narrows the window for a successful go-around — the pilot must make the go-around decision earlier, while still at an altitude and airspeed that allows safe escape from the landing zone.

questions.question: You are on final approach to a remote pinnacle landing site at 6,500 feet MSL on a hot afternoon. You detect a higher-than-normal sink rate at 50 feet AGL, add full collective, and the sink rate does not decrease. Walk me through the considerations that should have told you earlier in the approach that a go-around might be necessary.
questions.answer: Several earlier indicators should have prompted a go-around consideration: (1) Pre-approach power check: Before committing to the approach, the pilot should have verified whether OGE (out of ground effect) hover power was available at that altitude and temperature. High density altitude reduces available power significantly. If OGE power was marginal or unavailable, a vertical or steep approach to that pinnacle should have been reconsidered. (2) Approach profile: A high sink rate developing at 50 feet AGL suggests the approach was either too steep, airspeed was too slow (risking vortex ring state), or available power was insufficient. The stabilized approach check — verifiable well before 50 AGL — should have caught deviations in sink rate and airspeed. (3) ETL transition: As ETL was lost on the steep pinnacle approach, power demand increased. If the torque gauge was already near limits before ETL was lost, that was a clear go-around indicator. (4) Committed point: A go-around decision on a pinnacle approach must be made while there is still altitude and airspeed to accelerate away from the site — by 50 AGL with full collective applied and the sink rate not arresting, the go-around opportunity may already be critically compromised.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Pinnacle Operations, Maximum Performance Takeoff); Chapter 9 (Vortex Ring State)

questions.question: During an approach to a hospital helipad, you notice a ground crew member walk into your intended landing area at 100 feet AGL. You are stabilized and on profile. What considerations apply to your go-around decision, and what factors affect the execution?
questions.answer: The primary consideration is that the landing zone is no longer clear — continuing the approach would violate the basic safety requirement that the landing area be unobstructed. A go-around must be initiated immediately. Key considerations for execution: (1) Timing: At 100 feet AGL and stabilized, the pilot has adequate altitude and airspeed to initiate a safe go-around. Delaying the decision reduces options. (2) Obstacle clearance: Hospital helipads are often surrounded by structures, antennas, or rooftop equipment. The go-around flight path must be planned to avoid these obstacles — the pilot should have identified an abort/go-around route during the approach briefing and pre-approach reconnaissance. (3) Power availability: A go-around requires a rapid increase in collective and forward cyclic. At this point in the approach, airspeed may be relatively low and the helicopter may already be in or near the region of reversed command, meaning significant power must be available. (4) Communication: Notify ATC or the helipad operator of the go-around. (5) ADM: The situation is clear — continuing is unsafe. Hesitation or the 'get-there-itis' tendency to continue should be recognized and rejected. The go-around decision should be immediate and decisive.

questions.question: Describe how an unstabilized approach in a helicopter is defined, and explain why each deviation criterion represents a situation that should trigger a go-around consideration.
questions.answer: While specific criteria vary by operator and aircraft, a stabilized helicopter approach is generally defined as maintaining: (1) Target airspeed within ±5 knots — deviations indicate poor energy management; too fast increases landing roll and the risk of dynamic rollover or running into obstacles; too slow risks vortex ring state. (2) Target rate of descent — excessive sink rate (often cited as greater than 500–700 FPM below a certain altitude) increases the risk of hard landing, vortex ring state, or inability to arrest descent before touchdown. (3) Proper heading and alignment with the landing area — misalignment creates lateral drift at touchdown, increasing dynamic rollover risk and potential for tail rotor strikes. (4) Correct approach profile (angle) — too steep compresses the go-around window and increases ETL loss altitude; too shallow may cause obstacle clearance issues. The reason each deviation is a go-around trigger is cumulative risk: any single deviation increases workload and reduces safety margins, and multiple simultaneous deviations compound the risk. The helicopter's limited ability to add energy quickly (compared to a fixed-wing aircraft) means that allowing an unstabilized approach to continue dramatically reduces the margin for error.

questions.question: A student pilot tells you: 'I'll just go around if something goes wrong on approach — I can always do that.' What is wrong with this thinking, and how does helicopter aerodynamics and the approach environment specifically limit the go-around option in ways that differ from fixed-wing aircraft?
questions.answer: This thinking reflects a dangerous misunderstanding of helicopter go-around limitations. Key issues: (1) The go-around window closes rapidly. Unlike a fixed-wing aircraft that can add thrust and climb away from nearly any point in an approach, a helicopter must have sufficient airspeed, altitude, and available power to execute a successful go-around. At very low altitudes, very low airspeeds, or when power is already at or near limits, the go-around may be impossible or may result in a hard landing or crash. (2) Vortex ring state is a one-way door in a deteriorating situation. Once the helicopter has entered vortex ring state, adding collective makes it worse. Recovery requires forward cyclic — which needs altitude and distance ahead to be safe. At 20 feet AGL in a confined area, there may be neither. (3) Confined area and pinnacle approaches impose physical constraints. The go-around flight path may be blocked by terrain, trees, structures, or wires. The pre-approach reconnaissance must identify an escape route before committing — 'I'll figure it out' is not acceptable. (4) The region of reversed command: At low speeds on approach, the helicopter is operating where more power is required to fly slower. If power is already near limits, there may be nothing left for the go-around. (5) ADM failure mode: The 'I can always go around' attitude promotes continuation bias — the tendency to press on past safe limits because of a false sense of a safety net.
questions.follow_up: If the go-around option has been eliminated by a deteriorating approach — say, the helicopter is at 15 feet AGL, zero airspeed, high sink rate, full collective applied with no effect — what is the correct procedure and what does the RFM say about this scenario?
questions.follow_up_answer: If a true go-around is no longer possible and the helicopter is in an uncontrolled descent with full collective applied, the correct action is to execute an emergency landing using the best available technique for the surface and circumstances — this may mean accepting a firm landing while maintaining directional control with pedals and level attitude with cyclic to minimize rollover risk. The pilot should ensure the collective is full up to minimize rotor RPM decay and cushion the descent as much as possible. The RFM for each specific helicopter will contain emergency procedures for power failure at low altitude and low airspeed — these procedures are helicopter-specific and must be memorized. The Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that this scenario (low altitude, low airspeed, high sink rate) is why the approach must be planned and executed to preserve the go-around option at all times, and why power checks and abort point planning before entering the approach are non-negotiable safety steps.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Confined Area, Pinnacle Operations); Chapter 9 (Vortex Ring State); Chapter 13 (ADM); 14 CFR 91.13

questions.question: During a night approach to an unlit private helipad, you become uncertain whether your visual references are accurate — the pad looks closer than your instruments suggest, and you are unsure of your actual altitude and sink rate. What specific considerations make this situation a go-around trigger, and what does the Helicopter Flying Handbook say about night visual illusions on approach?
questions.answer: This scenario combines multiple go-around triggers: (1) Loss of reliable visual reference is itself a go-around/missed approach criterion. If the pilot cannot positively determine altitude, sink rate, or distance from the landing area, continuing the approach is unsafe. (2) Night visual illusions: The Helicopter Flying Handbook (Chapter 12) describes several illusions specific to night flight. A featureless or dark approach environment (black hole approach) removes the normal visual cues used to judge height above ground, angle of approach, and rate of closure. Pilots tend to fly lower and steeper than intended in black hole conditions because the visual references that normally indicate the correct profile are absent, potentially resulting in controlled flight into terrain (CFIT). (3) Unlit helipads remove the visual anchor points — perimeter lights, touchdown zone markers, and obstruction lights — that normally allow the pilot to judge approach angle. Without these, the pilot may misidentify the pad, misjudge the approach angle, or fail to see obstacles in the approach path. (4) A go-around should be initiated any time the pilot has doubt about the safety of continuing. The HFH states that night VFR seeing conditions are classified as high or low lighting based on moon illumination, cloud cover, and surface reflectivity — low lighting conditions dramatically reduce situational awareness on approach.
questions.follow_up: You decide to go around from the night approach. What are the specific lighting and instrument considerations for executing a safe go-around at night that differ from a daytime go-around?
questions.follow_up_answer: At night, the go-around execution requires greater instrument reliance because outside visual references are limited. Key considerations: (1) The pilot must transition to instruments immediately to verify attitude, airspeed, and rate of climb — outside cues for pitch attitude and bank may be unreliable or absent in dark conditions. (2) Panel lighting must be set appropriately — bright enough to read instruments but not so bright as to cause windshield glare or destroy dark adaptation. The HFH notes that panel lighting should be adjusted to match ambient light levels to prevent this issue. (3) Obstacle awareness is critical — the go-around flight path may pass near obstacles that were visible in daylight but are not lit at night. The pilot must rely on pre-briefed escape route knowledge. (4) Dark adaptation: if the pilot used white light during preflight or cockpit tasks, dark adaptation may be compromised, further reducing ability to see outside references. The HFH notes that dark adaptation takes approximately 30 minutes and can be partially destroyed by brief exposure to white light. (5) Position light interpretation: if flying near other traffic, the pilot must be able to correctly interpret position lights to maintain separation during the go-around.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 12 (Night Flight Operations); Chapter 13 (ADM, CFIT); 14 CFR 91.157 (if Special VFR applies)

questions.question: How does high density altitude affect the power available during a helicopter go-around?
questions.answer: High density altitude reduces air density, which decreases engine power output and rotor efficiency. During a go-around, the helicopter requires significant power to arrest the descent, accelerate, and climb. At high density altitude, the engine may not produce rated power, and the rotor blades generate less lift for the same collective pitch setting. This can result in the helicopter being unable to complete a go-around if power margins are insufficient — particularly critical if the helicopter is already near OGE hover limits.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 5 (RFM Performance Charts)

questions.question: How does outside air temperature affect helicopter engine performance during a go-around, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Higher outside air temperature reduces air density, which lowers engine power output (turbine engines are especially sensitive to hot temperatures) and reduces rotor blade efficiency. During a go-around, which demands maximum or near-maximum power, a high-temperature environment reduces the power margin available. Conversely, cold temperatures increase air density and generally improve engine performance, but can introduce other concerns like carburetor ice in piston-powered helicopters or reduced fuel efficiency. Pilots should check performance charts in the RFM, which account for temperature, to confirm go-around feasibility.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 5 (RFM Performance Charts); 14 CFR Part 91

questions.question: You're on short final in a helicopter when you decide to go around. The reported winds are calm, but you notice your groundspeed is much higher than expected. Temperatures are well above standard. What atmospheric factors could explain this and how should they affect your go-around decision?
questions.answer: Several atmospheric factors could be at play: first, calm-reported surface winds may not reflect winds at approach altitude — you may have an undetected tailwind component aloft. A tailwind increases true airspeed (which aids translational lift), but the increased groundspeed means the helicopter travels farther over the terrain, reducing obstacle clearance margins and go-around safety. Second, high temperatures increase density altitude, reducing rotor efficiency and available engine power. Combined, these factors mean climb performance will be degraded, power margins for the go-around may be reduced, and ground distance over obstacles increases significantly. The pilot should cross-check indicated airspeed versus groundspeed (if GPS is available), consult the RFM performance charts for the current density altitude, verify climb gradient capability over departure obstacles, and consider whether adequate power margin exists for a safe go-around. If power margin or obstacle clearance is marginal, a go-around may not be the safest option.

questions.question: During a go-around at a high-altitude mountain landing zone, you apply full collective but the helicopter barely climbs. What atmospheric condition is most likely responsible, and what are your immediate options?
questions.answer: The most likely cause is high density altitude — a combination of high field elevation, high temperature, and possibly low atmospheric pressure — which reduces both available engine power and rotor thrust. The helicopter may be operating at or beyond its OGE hover capability.
