Immediate options include: (1) transitioning to forward flight to gain ETL and improve lift efficiency; (2) using terrain slope or ground effect if available to assist the transition; (3) reducing gross weight (fuel, cargo, personnel) if time allows before the next attempt; and (4) aborting the go-around and landing immediately if the helicopter cannot maintain altitude. The pilot should reference RFM hover ceiling charts before committing to operations at high-altitude sites.

questions.question: How does a microburst or windshear encountered during a go-around differ in its effect on a helicopter compared to a normal wind shift, and why is it especially dangerous during that phase of flight?
questions.answer: A microburst produces a sudden headwind on the leading edge and a severe downdraft in the center, followed by a tailwind as the aircraft passes through it. During a go-around, the helicopter is at low altitude, slow speed, and high power demand — leaving almost no margin to recover from an unexpected performance loss. The initial headwind may cause a brief airspeed increase and false sense of improved performance, followed by a severe downdraft and tailwind that rapidly reduces lift and increases sink rate. Unlike a normal wind shift, which is gradual and predictable, a microburst can overwhelm the helicopter's power margins instantly. Helicopters are particularly vulnerable because they rely on precise power management and have limited climb rates at low airspeed.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM); Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM) Chapter 7-1-26

questions.question: A pilot conducts a go-around in high-humidity, standard-temperature conditions in a piston helicopter. The engine is producing normal power and the rotor RPM is in the green, yet climb performance is noticeably worse than expected. What atmospheric mechanism could explain this, and how should the pilot account for it in pre-approach planning?
questions.answer: High humidity reduces air density — water vapor (which is less dense than dry air) displaces oxygen molecules, effectively increasing density altitude beyond what temperature and pressure altitude alone would suggest. This is sometimes called 'humid air density altitude' and is not directly captured in standard density altitude calculations, which assume dry air. In a piston helicopter, this reduces both engine power output and rotor efficiency. During pre-approach planning, the pilot should: (1) use wet-bulb temperature or humidity-corrected density altitude calculations if available; (2) consult the RFM and apply a conservative power margin when humidity is high; (3) perform a high hover check prior to committing to a confined area approach to verify actual power margins; and (4) brief an abort point before beginning any approach where a go-around might be required.
questions.follow_up: If you complete a high hover check and determine you have 10% torque margin remaining, is that sufficient justification to commit to an approach requiring a potential go-around at a confined area site on a hot, humid day?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not necessarily. A 10% torque margin in hover does not directly translate to adequate go-around performance. During a go-around, the helicopter must transition from a decelerating, descending profile to a climbing profile — a transient condition that can momentarily demand power exceeding the hover requirement, especially when ETL is lost during deceleration. Additionally, on a hot, humid day, the margin can erode further with any deterioration in conditions (rising temperature, increasing humidity). Best practice is to check whether OGE hover is achievable with a comfortable margin (many operators use 15–20% as a rule of thumb), verify that the performance charts support the maneuver at the current density altitude and gross weight, and have a clearly defined abort point and abort procedure before beginning the approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 5; 14 CFR Part 91

questions.question: During a steep approach to a confined area, you lose effective translational lift and initiate a go-around. You're now in a low-airspeed, high-power demand state in turbulent conditions caused by mechanical turbulence from surrounding terrain. Walk me through the compounding atmospheric hazards you're facing and how each one affects your go-around execution.
questions.answer: In this scenario, multiple atmospheric hazards compound simultaneously: (1) Loss of ETL — the helicopter is in the region of reversed command, requiring more power for any given increase in airspeed. Any turbulence-induced speed fluctuation increases power demand unpredictably. (2) Mechanical turbulence from surrounding terrain — rotor wash from obstructions creates irregular airflow, causing uncommanded pitch, roll, and altitude excursions. At low airspeed and altitude, recovery options are extremely limited. (3) Potential vortex ring state risk — during the go-around transition, if the helicopter descends through its own rotor wash while at low airspeed with high power applied and a high rate of descent, it can enter vortex ring state. This is particularly dangerous because it reduces rotor efficiency exactly when maximum lift is needed. (4) Power settling and rotor RPM management — turbulent inflow can cause rotor RPM fluctuations; pilot must monitor RPM while simultaneously managing collective. The correct technique is to accelerate aggressively into forward flight to regain ETL as quickly as possible, use any available terrain slope or depression for ground effect if practical, and avoid further reduction in collective (which worsens the descent). Pre-approach planning must include recognition that a go-around from a steep approach in mechanically turbulent conditions may not be survivable — the better decision may be to not begin the approach unless landing is virtually assured.
questions.follow_up: What is the earliest recognizable warning sign that vortex ring state is developing during a go-around, and what is the immediate corrective action?
questions.follow_up_answer: The earliest warning signs of vortex ring state onset are: an abnormal increase in rate of descent that cannot be arrested by increasing collective; vibration and roughness through the controls; and loss of normal collective effectiveness. The rotor may feel 'soft' or unresponsive. Immediate corrective action is to apply forward cyclic to increase airspeed and fly the helicopter out of the settling vortex ring, simultaneously applying full power if not already done. Do not continue pulling collective, as this accelerates the vortex ring state by increasing recirculation. If altitude permits, an aggressive push forward on the cyclic to gain airspeed is the most reliable recovery. This is why altitude above the landing zone is critical — a go-around from a very low hover or near-zero altitude with VRS onset is unlikely to be recoverable.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Advanced Maneuvers); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Helicopter Emergencies — Vortex Ring State)

questions.question: What is a go-around in helicopter operations, and when is it initiated?
questions.answer: A go-around is a maneuver in which the pilot abandons a landing approach and transitions back to a climb or hover, either because the approach has become unstabilized, the landing area is unsafe or occupied, the aircraft is not in the correct position or attitude for a safe landing, or any other condition makes continuing the approach inadvisable. It should be initiated any time the pilot determines a safe landing cannot be completed, and the decision should be made as early as possible — before the helicopter enters a low, slow flight regime that limits options.

questions.question: What are the basic control inputs required to execute a go-around from a low approach in a helicopter?
questions.answer: To execute a go-around from a low approach, the pilot applies collective to arrest the descent and increase power, simultaneously applies forward cyclic to accelerate and transition toward translational lift, uses anti-torque pedals to maintain directional control as torque increases, and transitions to a normal climbing flight profile. The sequence must be coordinated to prevent excessive pitch up, loss of rotor RPM, or settling with power. The goal is to smoothly transition from an approach attitude to a positive climb attitude while maintaining control.

questions.question: Why is a timely go-around decision more critical in a helicopter than simply deciding at any point during the approach?
questions.answer: As the helicopter descends lower and slows on approach, the available energy and maneuvering options decrease significantly. At very low altitudes and airspeeds, the helicopter may enter the avoid region of the height-velocity (H-V) diagram, leaving insufficient altitude and rotor energy for an effective autorotation if power is lost, and insufficient airspeed to arrest a sink rate quickly. Additionally, ETL (effective translational lift) is lost during deceleration, meaning more power is required. A delayed go-around decision may place the helicopter in a flight regime where a safe go-around is no longer possible, making early recognition and action essential.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 9 and 11

questions.question: You are on a normal approach to a confined area and at approximately 50 feet AGL you notice the intended landing spot is occupied by personnel who walked in after your reconnaissance. Walk me through your go-around decision and execution from that point.
questions.answer: At 50 feet AGL on a confined area approach, the go-around decision must be made immediately — hesitation allows the helicopter to descend further into a position where a go-around may be impossible. First, assess whether sufficient power is available for a go-around versus an immediate autorotation if power were lost (check H-V diagram position). Initiate the go-around by smoothly but promptly increasing collective to arrest and then reverse the descent, simultaneously applying forward cyclic to begin accelerating and regaining translational lift. Use anti-torque pedals to maintain coordinated flight as torque changes. Climb along the safest exit path identified during reconnaissance — typically the same path used on approach or the planned abort route. Avoid abrupt aft cyclic which could cause the tail to strike terrain in a confined area. Communicate intentions on the appropriate frequency. The Trescott principle applies: if you are only 'probably' going to clear an obstacle, execute the go-around now — choose the option you know will work.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 9 and 10; 14 CFR 91.13

questions.question: How does the loss of effective translational lift (ETL) during a decelerating approach affect the urgency of a go-around decision, and what power consideration must you account for?
questions.answer: As the helicopter decelerates through approximately 16–24 knots during an approach, it transitions through ETL and loses the aerodynamic efficiency gained from translational lift. Below ETL, the rotor must work harder to generate the same lift, requiring significantly more power — approaching OGE (out of ground effect) hover power requirements. If the helicopter has already decelerated below ETL and is low to the ground with limited power margin, a go-around requires a rapid power application that may approach or exceed available engine torque. The pilot must assess whether sufficient power remains to safely climb away. If the helicopter is in a low-power-margin situation (high density altitude, heavy gross weight, high temperature), the go-around must be initiated before ETL is lost, while the helicopter still has airspeed advantage working in its favor. Waiting until below ETL narrows the power and energy window significantly.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 2 and 9

questions.question: A student pilot you are evaluating tells you they plan to decide whether to go around 'at the last second' to give themselves the most information possible before committing. How do you respond, and what is the safety risk in that philosophy?
questions.answer: This philosophy is dangerous and must be corrected. The 'more information' gained by waiting comes at the direct cost of energy, altitude, and maneuvering options — all of which are required to execute a safe go-around. The Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that go-around decisions should be made as early as possible. The error chain concept from ADM is directly applicable: waiting for 'the last second' is itself one link in an accident chain. In addition, the height-velocity (H-V) diagram defines regimes at low altitude and low airspeed where a safe go-around or autorotation may not be possible — a 'last second' decision may place the helicopter squarely in that avoid region. The correct philosophy is to establish personal minimums and stabilized approach criteria ahead of time, and execute the go-around the moment those criteria are not met — not when all options are nearly exhausted. Indecision and delayed action are more dangerous than a timely go-around on a good approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 9, 11, and 13

questions.question: You are executing a steep approach to a pinnacle at high density altitude, near maximum gross weight. You are 30 feet above the pinnacle at near-zero airspeed when you determine the surface is unsuitable for landing. You have marginal power available. Walk through your go-around options and decision hierarchy at that point.
questions.answer: This is one of the most critical go-around scenarios in helicopter operations. At 30 feet AGL, near-zero airspeed, high density altitude, and max gross weight, the options are extremely limited. First, assess immediately whether OGE hover power is available — without it, the helicopter cannot climb vertically and accelerating will require descending toward terrain. If sufficient power exists for at least a momentary hover, apply collective to stabilize, then transition with forward cyclic to gain airspeed while descending slightly along the departure path used on approach (the safest known obstacle-clear route). Do not attempt to climb vertically without confirmed power margin — this risks rotor RPM decay and loss of control. If power is insufficient to arrest descent and the surface is marginally acceptable, an immediate controlled landing may be safer than a failed go-around. The Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that OGE hover power is required for vertical operations at pinnacles — if that power was unavailable before the approach, a go-around in that condition was always going to be compromised. This underscores why the go-around decision must be made higher on the approach, before the helicopter is committed to the low-slow envelope over the pinnacle.
questions.follow_up: If you determined mid-approach — say at 200 feet AGL — that power was only marginally sufficient for landing, what should you have done at that point rather than continuing?
questions.follow_up_answer: At 200 feet AGL with only marginal power available, the correct action is to execute the go-around immediately while airspeed and altitude still provide energy for maneuvering. At that height, the helicopter still has translational lift working in its favor and sufficient altitude to transition to climbing flight along the departure corridor. The reconnaissance should have already identified an abort route. Continuing an approach to a pinnacle with marginal power violates the fundamental principle that you should only continue when success is assured — not merely probable. The Helicopter Flying Handbook specifically states that OGE hover power is required for pinnacle operations, and if that power is not available, the approach should not be continued. Recognizing the go-around need at 200 feet versus 30 feet is the difference between a routine rejected approach and a potential fatal accident.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 10 and 13; 14 CFR 91.13

questions.question: No change needed to question text.
questions.answer: A stabilized approach gate is a pre-defined point on the approach — typically at a specific height AGL — at which the pilot evaluates whether all approach parameters are within acceptable limits. If they are not, the go-around is executed automatically without further deliberation. For helicopter operations, a reasonable gate might be set at 100–200 feet AGL on a normal approach. At that gate, the pilot confirms: correct approach angle (on profile), appropriate airspeed for the approach type, stable descent rate, correct alignment with the landing area, obstacle clearance confirmed, and adequate power margin. If any single parameter is outside limits at the gate, the go-around is initiated — no re-evaluation, no 'maybe I can fix it.' This system leverages ADM principles by removing in-the-moment deliberation under pressure, replacing it with pre-planned, objective criteria. It directly combats get-there-itis, press-on-itis, and the tendency to rationalize continuing a deteriorating approach. The FAA's ADM material notes that accidents typically involve a chain of poor decisions rather than one catastrophic error — the stabilized approach gate is designed to break that chain early.
questions.follow_up: A student argues that using a stabilized approach gate is unnecessary because 'experienced pilots can judge it by feel.' How do you counter that argument using accident data or human factors principles?
questions.follow_up_answer: The argument fails on multiple human factors grounds. First, the Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that approximately 80% of aviation accidents involve pilot error, including errors made by experienced pilots. Experience does not eliminate the physiological and psychological factors that degrade judgment — startle response, task saturation, confirmation bias, and get-there-itis affect all pilots. Second, accident data shows that accidents correlate more closely with hours in a specific aircraft type than total flight hours, meaning even high-total-time pilots in unfamiliar aircraft are at elevated risk. Third, judgment 'by feel' is a subjective, variable standard that changes with fatigue, stress, and environmental conditions — a pre-defined gate is an objective, consistent standard. The stabilized approach gate is a formalized decision aid that removes ambiguity at a moment when cognitive load is high. It is not a substitute for skill; it is a system that ensures skill is applied at the right time.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 13; AC 90-117 (stabilized approach concepts)

areas_of_operation.title: Area of Operation V. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds

tasks.title: Task G. Go-Around (partial - risk management and skills only)

questions.question: What is a go-around, and in the context of a helicopter approach, when is it generally required?
questions.answer: A go-around is the decision to abandon an approach or landing attempt and return to flight. In a helicopter, a go-around is required any time the pilot determines the approach is unstabilized, the landing zone is unsafe, the aircraft is not in the correct position or configuration to land safely, or an unexpected hazard appears. The decision should be made early — the later the go-around is initiated, the more energy and altitude are required to execute it safely.

questions.question: Name at least four conditions during a helicopter approach that should trigger immediate recognition of the need for a go-around.
questions.answer: Conditions that should trigger a go-around include: (1) unstabilized approach — airspeed, rate of descent, or alignment not meeting criteria by a defined point; (2) landing zone obstruction or change in surface conditions discovered late in the approach; (3) unexpected loss of visual reference in deteriorating visibility; (4) loss of proper glide path or excessive sink rate that cannot be corrected without an aggressive control input; (5) conflicting traffic or ATC instruction; (6) mechanical anomaly or warning indication during approach; (7) inadvertent entry into vortex ring state conditions (high power, low airspeed, high sink rate). Any single condition is sufficient justification to go around.

questions.question: Why does the FAA emphasize that the go-around decision must be made early during a helicopter approach rather than at the last moment?
questions.answer: Helicopters operating at low airspeed and low altitude during an approach have limited energy reserves. Delaying the go-around decision reduces the time and altitude available to accelerate to a safe climb airspeed, increases the risk of entering the avoid region of the height-velocity (H-V) diagram, and may require aggressive collective inputs that risk exceeding rotor or engine limits. Early recognition preserves options; late recognition narrows them significantly and can place the aircraft in an unrecoverable situation.

questions.question: You are on a normal approach to a helipad. At 200 feet AGL and 40 knots, you notice your rate of descent is 800 FPM and increasing, power is already at 90%, and you feel slight pedal shudder. What are you recognizing and what is your immediate action?
questions.answer: This scenario describes early indicators of vortex ring state (VRS) onset — high sink rate, high power application, low forward airspeed, and the beginning of aerodynamic roughness. These are unambiguous signals that a go-around is required immediately. Continuing the approach risks progressing deeper into VRS, which can result in a catastrophic sink rate with no rotor thrust. The immediate action is to apply forward cyclic to gain airspeed and simultaneously adjust collective, transitioning to a climb configuration to escape the settling condition. Do not attempt to arrest the sink with collective alone — that will worsen VRS.

questions.question: A pilot on an approach to an off-airport landing zone tells himself, 'The LZ probably looks okay — I'll take a closer look before committing.' What risk does this mindset represent, and how does ADM address it?
questions.answer: The word 'probably' is a red flag in aeronautical decision-making. Per FAA ADM guidance in the Helicopter Flying Handbook, if the best outcome is only 'probably' acceptable, the pilot should choose a course of action known to work — in this case, executing a go-around and conducting a proper reconnaissance from a safe altitude. The mindset described reflects the 'press-on-itis' hazardous attitude combined with confirmation bias. The correct ADM response is to recognize that uncertainty about LZ suitability is itself sufficient reason to initiate a go-around and gather more information before committing to a landing.

questions.question: You are conducting a confined area approach. At the 'point of no return' — committed to the approach — you notice the wind has shifted and you now have a quartering tailwind. Describe the risk you must recognize and what factors determine whether a go-around is still possible.
questions.answer: A quartering tailwind in a confined area approach significantly increases the risk of loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE) and reduces effective translational lift, increasing power demand at a critical low-speed phase. The pilot must recognize that the original approach planning assumptions are no longer valid. Whether a go-around is still possible depends on: available power margin above current torque demand, obstacle clearance on the departure path, rotor RPM stability, current position relative to the H-V avoid region, and whether forward airspeed can be safely achieved. If any of these factors are marginal, the go-around must still be initiated — a compromised go-around is still preferable to a controlled-flight-into-terrain event in an unsuitable LZ.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapters 9 and 11 (LTE, confined area operations)

questions.question: A student pilot says: 'I didn't go around because I had already told the passenger we were landing and felt committed.' As an examiner, how do you evaluate this statement from a risk management standpoint, and what underlying cognitive trap does it represent?
questions.answer: This statement reflects the 'sunk cost' or 'plan continuation bias' cognitive trap — the pilot allowed prior communication and social pressure to override objective aeronautical judgment. Risk management requires that the decision to go around be based solely on the current state of the approach and the aircraft, not on prior statements, passenger expectations, or ego. The FAA's ADM framework specifically identifies 'self-imposed pressure' as a hazardous attitude that degrades decision quality. The correct standard is that recognition of an unsafe condition mandates a go-around regardless of any external commitment. As an examiner, this response would indicate inadequate risk management and require further evaluation of the applicant's ADM foundation.
questions.follow_up: If this same pilot had successfully landed despite the poor approach, how would you evaluate the outcome in terms of risk management quality?
questions.follow_up_answer: A successful outcome does not validate a poor decision. The FAA's ADM framework teaches that outcome-based thinking is a trap — a pilot who makes a poor risk management decision but 'gets away with it' has not demonstrated good judgment, only good luck. The quality of a risk management decision must be evaluated based on the information available at the time and whether proper standards were applied, not whether the aircraft was damaged. Repeated poor decisions that happen to succeed reinforce dangerous habits and will eventually result in an accident. This is the foundation of the 'error chain' concept — breaking one link matters regardless of how the chain ultimately resolves.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, hazardous attitudes, error chain)

questions.question: During a night approach to an unlighted private helipad, you lose visual reference with the surface at 150 feet AGL and 20 knots. You have GPS position and know the helipad is directly ahead. Walk me through the risk recognition process and your go-around decision logic.
questions.answer: Loss of visual reference during a low-speed, low-altitude helicopter approach is an immediate go-around trigger — full stop. At 150 feet AGL and 20 knots, the aircraft is deep within the H-V avoid region with minimal margin for a safe autorotation. Without a visual reference to the surface, spatial orientation and obstacle clearance cannot be maintained. GPS position confirms where the helipad is but provides no information about obstacle height, surface condition, or the precise 3D path needed for a safe landing. The correct recognition is: this is inadvertent IMC/NVFR conditions at a critical flight phase. The go-around must be initiated immediately using instrument references to establish a positive climb attitude, gain airspeed out of the H-V danger zone, and proceed to a suitable landing area with adequate visual or instrument references.
questions.follow_up: If you initiate the go-around and during the climb you become fully disoriented with no outside reference, what is your priority and what specific instrument becomes your primary pitch reference?
questions.follow_up_answer: The priority is maintaining controlled flight using instrument references — resist any urge to chase outside visual cues that do not exist. The attitude indicator (AI) becomes the primary instrument for both pitch and bank control, as it is the only instrument displaying direct aircraft attitude. Per the Instrument Flying Handbook, during attitude changes the AI is primary; once stabilized in the climb, the altimeter becomes the primary pitch instrument. The pilot should establish a known safe climb attitude on the AI, confirm a positive rate of climb on the VSI and altimeter, and navigate to VMC or declare an emergency for ATC assistance. This scenario underscores why all helicopter pilots should maintain instrument proficiency even if not instrument rated.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Inadvertent IMC); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on partial panel; H-V diagram guidance

questions.question: When initiating a go-around from a low approach in a helicopter, what is the primary risk associated with applying full power too abruptly?
questions.answer: Applying full power abruptly can cause a sudden yaw reaction due to increased torque from the main rotor. In a counterclockwise rotor system (most U.S. helicopters), rapid power application causes the nose to yaw right unless corrected with left pedal input. Additionally, abrupt collective application without coordinated cyclic can cause an uncontrolled pitch or roll attitude change, potentially placing the helicopter in a hazardous low-altitude situation during the transition to climb.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 9 (Basic Flight Maneuvers); Chapter 11 (Emergencies and Hazards)

questions.question: During a go-around, why is coordinated cyclic input just as important as collective input when applying power?
questions.answer: Collective controls power and lift, but cyclic controls attitude and airspeed. During a go-around, if the pilot raises collective to arrest descent without simultaneously applying aft cyclic to establish a climb attitude, the helicopter may continue in a nose-low pitch that drives it toward the ground even as power increases. All four flight controls must be coordinated — collective, cyclic, pedals, and throttle (if not correlated) — to transition safely from approach to climb flight.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 9 (Basic Flight Maneuvers — coordination of controls)

questions.question: What role do the antitorque pedals play during the power application phase of a helicopter go-around, and what happens if a pilot neglects them?
questions.answer: The antitorque pedals compensate for the increased torque produced when collective is raised during a go-around. In a helicopter with a counterclockwise main rotor, increased power requires left pedal to prevent the nose from yawing right. If the pilot neglects pedal input, the helicopter will begin a right yaw, causing the nose to swing off the intended flight path. At low altitude during a go-around, this uncoordinated condition can be especially hazardous, potentially leading to obstacle strike or loss of control.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 9 (pedals used to compensate for torque and maintain trim)

questions.question: You are on short final in a helicopter when you decide a go-around is necessary due to an obstacle appearing in your landing zone. You are at 50 feet AGL, low airspeed, and descending. Walk me through the specific sequence of flight control inputs and the risk each delayed input creates.
questions.answer: The priority sequence is: (1) Raise collective smoothly but firmly to arrest the descent and increase thrust — delay here risks ground contact before climb is established. (2) Simultaneously apply left pedal (counterclockwise rotor) to counteract increased torque — delay causes uncontrolled right yaw at low altitude. (3) Apply aft cyclic to transition from approach attitude to a climb attitude and prevent the nose from pitching forward into the obstacle — delay here risks accelerating toward the obstacle at low altitude. (4) Scan and adjust rotor RPM if throttle is not fully correlated. Each delayed input compounds the hazard because altitude and time margins are minimal at 50 feet AGL and low airspeed. The risk of vortex ring state is also present if power application is delayed while the helicopter remains in a descending, low-airspeed condition.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 9 (Basic Flight Maneuvers); Chapter 11 (Vortex Ring State)

questions.question: A student pilot tends to 'freeze' on the collective during a go-around — meaning they raise it quickly to maximum and stop making further adjustments. What risks does this create, and how would you coach them to manage power more effectively?
questions.answer: Raising collective to maximum and holding it there creates several risks: (1) Over-pitching the blades can cause rotor RPM to decay rapidly, particularly in a low-inertia rotor system. If RPM decays to critical levels, the blades enter a stalled condition and collective must be lowered to restore RPM. In certain high-pitch/low-RPM combinations during autorotation, recovery may not be possible. (2) Excess power without corresponding cyclic/pedal coordination causes an abrupt yaw and potential pitch-up or pitch-down excursion. (3) Structural limits or engine limits may be exceeded if torque/power limits are not respected during sustained maximum collective application. Coaching should emphasize smooth, progressive collective input to the power setting needed for climb (not necessarily maximum), simultaneous pedal and cyclic coordination, and continuous monitoring of rotor RPM throughout the maneuver. The goal is a controlled climb, not maximum power application.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 9 (coordination of controls); Chapter 11 (Rotor stalls not recoverable — early recognition of low RPM imperative)

questions.question: You are flying a right-hand traffic pattern and execute a go-around. During the initial climb after power application, you notice the helicopter is in a left skid. What does this tell you about your control inputs, and why is this particularly risky during a go-around?
questions.answer: A left skid in a helicopter with a counterclockwise rotor system indicates that the rate of turn is too high for the bank angle — meaning the helicopter's inertia is exceeding the horizontal component of lift. In the context of a go-around turning right (right-hand traffic), a left skid means the pilot may be applying excessive right pedal or allowing torque to push the tail left while attempting to turn. This is a risk because skidding flight during a low-altitude go-around reduces efficiency, creates asymmetric loading, and can lead to loss of tail rotor effectiveness or an uncontrolled yaw. Corrective action is to reduce turn rate with cyclic or reduce right pedal input to re-establish coordinated flight before continuing the turn.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 9 (skid definition — inertia exceeds HCL); Chapter 11 (Loss of Tail Rotor Effectiveness)

questions.question: A pilot consistently makes sound go-around decisions but repeatedly applies power and cyclic inputs in the correct sequence yet still finds the helicopter drifting laterally to the right after power-up. No mechanical anomaly is found during post-flight. What is the most likely root cause, and how does this relate to error chain theory and ADM?
questions.answer: The most likely root cause is insufficient left lateral cyclic correction during power application. When collective is raised, the increased rotor thrust vector is tilted slightly right in most helicopter designs due to the blade flapping response and translating tendency inherent to single-rotor systems. If the pilot is not applying left cyclic to counteract this translating tendency during the power application phase, the helicopter drifts right. From an ADM and error chain perspective: the pilot is making the correct decision to go around and applying the correct sequence, but an incomplete control input (inadequate lateral cyclic) is a subtle, repeating link in an error chain. If this drift goes uncorrected at low altitude, it could lead to obstacle contact or an off-runway excursion. The 'Trescott Tip' from the HFH is applicable — if the outcome is only 'probably' safe due to drift that usually stays within bounds, the pilot should identify and eliminate the deficient input rather than accept the risk.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot is flying a helicopter with a fully correlated throttle and an articulated rotor system, what additional control consideration during the go-around could also explain the rightward drift, and how would you differentiate it from translating tendency?
questions.follow_up_answer: In an articulated rotor system, Coriolis effect causes blade velocity changes as the blade's center of mass moves toward or away from the axis of rotation as collective is raised. This can produce transient blade lead/lag forces that create momentary attitude perturbations during rapid collective application. However, Coriolis-induced drift would typically be transient and self-correcting once rotor dynamics stabilize, whereas translating tendency drift is consistent and sustained throughout the power-up phase. To differentiate: if the rightward drift begins immediately at collective application and persists throughout the climb, translating tendency (requiring sustained left cyclic correction) is the cause. If drift is momentary and oscillatory, blade flap/lead-lag dynamics from the articulated system may be contributing. The examiner would verify by asking the pilot to deliberately hold left lateral cyclic during power application on the next attempt — if drift stops, translating tendency was the cause.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 9 (translating tendency); Glossary (articulated rotor, Coriolis effect); Chapter 13 (ADM, error chain, Trescott Tip)

questions.question: During a checkride, an applicant executes a go-around after a stabilized approach. They apply power correctly and establish a positive climb, but do so with noticeably abrupt, jerky control inputs rather than smooth ones. The outcome is safe. Should this be a passing performance, and what risk management principle makes this an examiner concern regardless of outcome?
questions.answer: While the immediate outcome was safe, abrupt and jerky control inputs during a go-around represent a significant risk management concern and may not meet the ACS standard requiring smooth, coordinated flight control application. From a risk management standpoint, abrupt inputs in a helicopter indicate a lack of anticipation and fine motor control — qualities that directly correlate to safety margins. Abrupt collective raises can cause rotor RPM decay; abrupt cyclic produces attitude excursions; abrupt pedal inputs can induce yaw oscillation or LTE conditions. The FAA's ADM framework (HFH Chapter 13) establishes that approximately 80% of accidents are caused by human factors — and degraded technique under pressure is a human factor. If the applicant's technique was abrupt on a planned go-around during a checkride (low-stress), the examiner must consider how those inputs would degrade further in a high-stress, unplanned actual emergency. An examiner's job is to evaluate not just binary pass/fail outcomes but the quality and safety margin of technique. This warrants additional discussion and potentially a refly of the task with emphasis on smooth, coordinated control inputs as required by the ACS skills standards.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant argues that the helicopter is certified for those control inputs and no limitations were exceeded, how do you as the examiner respond?
questions.follow_up_answer: The examiner responds that certification limits define what the aircraft can structurally tolerate, not what constitutes safe, proficient pilot technique. The ACS evaluates pilot skill and risk management, not merely structural survivability. A pilot who routinely operates at the edge of control input smoothness has no safety buffer when conditions degrade — wind gusts, turbulence, distraction, or fatigue will push those already-abrupt inputs into genuinely hazardous territory. The HFH explicitly emphasizes smooth, coordinated control inputs as the standard for all phases of flight, and the go-around is no exception. Operating legally is not the same as operating safely — the ACS requires demonstrated proficiency and sound risk management, both of which are undermined by consistently abrupt technique.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 9 (smooth inputs emphasized throughout); Chapter 13 (ADM, human factors account for ~80% of accidents); Helicopter ACS standards for go-around skills

questions.question: When executing a go-around in a helicopter, what are the primary collision hazard categories you must account for before initiating the maneuver?
questions.answer: The primary collision hazard categories during a helicopter go-around are: (1) traffic — other aircraft in the pattern or final approach corridor, including aircraft you may be overtaking or that are converging; (2) obstacles — towers, wires, trees, buildings, and terrain features in the climb-out path; and (3) wake turbulence — rotor wash or fixed-wing wake from preceding aircraft. The go-around requires an immediate transition from a descending, decelerating flight regime to a climbing, accelerating one, often at low altitude where reaction time to any of these hazards is minimal.

questions.question: Why are wire strikes a particularly serious collision hazard during a helicopter go-around compared to a normal climbout from a hover?
questions.answer: During a go-around, the pilot is transitioning from an approach configuration — often at low airspeed, low altitude, and already committed to a descent path — which means the helicopter may be below wire height or on a shallow angle that puts wires directly in the climb-out path. Unlike a normal hover takeoff where the pilot has situational awareness of the immediate environment, a go-around is often initiated abruptly, leaving less time to identify and avoid wires. Additionally, wires are difficult to see, especially in low-light conditions, against complex backgrounds, or when the pilot's attention is divided during the go-around transition.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Wire Strike Avoidance); FAA Safety Alert for Operators (SAFO)

questions.question: What is the see-and-avoid responsibility rule, and how does it apply to a helicopter pilot initiating a go-around in the traffic pattern?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.113(b), each pilot in command is responsible for vigilance in seeing and avoiding other aircraft. During a go-around, this means the pilot must scan for aircraft on final approach behind them, aircraft on base leg, aircraft in the pattern at pattern altitude, and any aircraft that may be departing from intersecting runways or helipads. A go-around that transitions to a climb puts the helicopter back into the traffic pattern flow, potentially conflicting with other aircraft. The pilot must announce intentions on CTAF (or coordinate with ATC at towered fields) and clear all quadrants visually before and during the maneuver.

questions.question: You are on short final at an uncontrolled helipad when a vehicle pulls onto the landing area. You initiate a go-around. Describe the specific collision threats present in the first 30 seconds of your go-around and how you would manage each one.
questions.answer: In the first 30 seconds: (1) The vehicle itself — as you apply collective and transition to climb, you must ensure lateral or vertical clearance from the vehicle; avoid climbing directly over it until sufficient altitude is gained to clear rotor wash injury risk and provide escape margin if a power issue occurs. (2) Obstacles in the immediate climbout path — wires, trees, or structures you identified during the approach briefing; execute the go-around along the planned escape route, not an improvised heading. (3) Traffic — announce 'going around' on CTAF immediately; scan for aircraft on base or final that may now be converging with your climb path. (4) Rotor wash/vortex near the ground — the go-around generates significant downwash; personnel near the pad are a collision/injury hazard. Prioritize flying the aircraft first, communicate second, and follow the pre-briefed go-around profile rather than improvising under pressure.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.113; AC 90-66B (non-towered airport operations)

questions.question: During a busy VFR day at a towered airport, ATC instructs you to go around and advises traffic on a 1-mile final behind you. You also notice a helicopter at your 10 o'clock at what appears to be pattern altitude. How do you prioritize and manage the collision hazards?
questions.answer: Immediate priorities: (1) Fly the aircraft — apply go-around power, establish a positive climb rate, and maintain aircraft control. (2) The 1-mile traffic behind you — ATC has called this traffic but has also sequenced them, so your obligation is to climb and clear the approach corridor promptly. Delay increases closure risk with that aircraft. (3) The helicopter at 10 o'clock — this is a visual acquisition that ATC may not have called; monitor its movement relative to your flight path. Under 14 CFR 91.113(a), when an ATC clearance is complied with, the pilot still retains see-and-avoid responsibility. If the conflict appears to be developing, immediately advise ATC. (4) Comply with ATC go-around instructions but do not sacrifice terrain/obstacle clearance to do so — the pilot retains final authority on aircraft safety. Maintain situational awareness by cross-checking visually, using ATC advisories, and using any traffic display (TIS-B/ADS-B) available.

questions.question: You are conducting approaches to a remote mountain helipad. The approach path crosses a ridgeline and there is no traffic in the area. During a go-around, what terrain and obstacle collision hazards demand the most attention, and how should your go-around profile be designed to mitigate them?
questions.answer: In a mountain environment, collision hazards during a go-around include: (1) Terrain — if the go-around heading is toward rising terrain, the helicopter's initial climb rate may be insufficient to clear the ridge, especially at high-density altitude where performance is degraded. (2) Wires and towers — mountain areas often have power lines crossing valleys and ridges that may not be charted. (3) Loss of visual reference — if the go-around is initiated during a confined-area approach, climbing into a box canyon with no escape route is a fatal collision hazard. Mitigation: Pre-brief a specific go-around heading toward the lowest terrain/best escape route before beginning any approach. Know the helicopter's out-of-ground-effect hover performance at that density altitude. Never go around toward rising terrain. Maintain VASI/PAPI-type profile awareness, and if the escape route is obscured, consider whether the approach should be initiated at all. This is a pre-approach risk decision, not a reactive one.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 and Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM); AC 90-95 (unanticipated right yaw)

questions.question: A student pilot you are evaluating initiates a go-around and immediately turns crosswind at low altitude — roughly 100 feet AGL — rather than continuing straight ahead to gain altitude first. Beyond the immediate collision hazard this creates, what systemic ADM failure does this behavior indicate, and how would you address it both in the debrief and in future training?
questions.answer: The immediate collision hazard is a conflict with any aircraft on base leg or lower final, as well as reduced obstacle clearance during the turn when climb performance is temporarily degraded. However, the deeper ADM failure is a 'plan continuation bias' or 'get-there-itis' variant — the student is pattern-following (getting back into the traffic pattern flow) rather than managing the primary risk of the go-around, which is terrain/obstacle clearance and traffic deconfliction from a position of altitude advantage. This indicates the student does not have a mental model where altitude = safety margin during a go-around. In the debrief, use the error chain concept from FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13: the premature turn is a symptom, not the root cause. Address: (1) lack of a pre-briefed go-around profile, (2) not prioritizing climb before turn, and (3) absence of traffic scan before turning. In future training, require the student to verbalize the go-around plan (heading, altitude before turn, traffic check) during the approach briefing, making it a deliberate decision rather than a reactive one.
questions.follow_up: If that same student argued that ATC had already cleared them for the pattern and therefore the early crosswind turn was authorized, how would you respond?
questions.follow_up_answer: ATC clearances do not override pilot-in-command responsibility for safety. Under 14 CFR 91.3(a), the PIC is directly responsible for and is the final authority as to the operation of the aircraft. An ATC clearance to fly the traffic pattern does not specify altitude during the go-around, nor does it relieve the pilot of the obligation under 14 CFR 91.113 to see and avoid other aircraft. Furthermore, 14 CFR 91.119 minimum safe altitude requirements still apply — the pilot cannot fly at an altitude that doesn't allow a safe emergency landing or that creates hazard to persons or property. The correct response to ATC is to continue the climb to a safe altitude before turning crosswind and, if necessary, advise ATC of the higher altitude for traffic sequencing.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3(a); 14 CFR 91.113; 14 CFR 91.119; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/Error Chain)

questions.question: You are examining a commercial helicopter applicant who is flying a turbine helicopter with an ADS-B Out/In system. During a go-around, they fixate on the traffic display showing a target at 3 miles and fail to clear visually for traffic at close range. What does this reveal about their risk management, and what is the regulatory limitation of ADS-B traffic displays that makes visual scanning irreplaceable?
questions.answer: This reveals a classic automation complacency failure — the applicant is treating the ADS-B traffic display as primary traffic awareness rather than as a supplementary tool. From an ADM standpoint per FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13, this is an SRM breakdown: over-reliance on automation without maintaining manual situational awareness. The regulatory limitation is critical: ADS-B traffic displays (TIS-B and ADS-B In) only show targets that are ADS-B Out equipped or are being tracked by radar and rebroadcast via TIS-B. Aircraft without ADS-B Out — including many helicopters operating under Part 91 at uncontrolled airports — are invisible to the display. Additionally, display update rates, processing latency, and ground station coverage gaps mean the picture may be seconds out of date. Under 14 CFR 91.113(b), the see-and-avoid requirement is absolute and is not satisfied by any electronic system. The applicant must understand that no traffic display substitutes for continuous visual scanning, and fixating on any single information source during a dynamic phase like a go-around is a high-risk behavior.
questions.follow_up: ADS-B Out is required under 14 CFR 91.225 in certain airspace. If the go-around is occurring at an uncontrolled helipad outside that airspace — such as a Class G environment below 10,000 feet MSL and not within 30 NM of a Class B airport — is ADS-B Out required, and does that change your analysis of the collision risk?
questions.follow_up_answer: No, ADS-B Out is not required in Class G airspace below the 14 CFR 91.225 trigger altitudes and distances. This actually increases the collision risk analysis because in that environment, the likelihood that other traffic is NOT ADS-B equipped is higher — meaning the ADS-B display is even less reliable as a complete traffic picture. Other helicopters, ultralights, agricultural aircraft, and gliders commonly operate in Class G without ADS-B Out. This reinforces that visual scanning is the only reliable traffic separation method in that environment. If anything, operating at an uncontrolled site in Class G should make the applicant more aggressive about visual clearing, not less. The absence of ATC separation services and the possibility of non-ADS-B traffic makes the human visual scan the last and only line of defense against a collision.

questions.question: During a go-around in a helicopter, what does 'task prioritization' mean, and what is the general order of priority a pilot should follow?
questions.answer: Task prioritization means deciding which cockpit tasks demand your attention first when multiple things compete for it simultaneously. The general priority order is: Aviate (fly the helicopter — power, attitude, flight path), Navigate (climb path, obstacles, traffic pattern), then Communicate (radio calls to tower or traffic). During a go-around, the pilot must first ensure a safe climb is established before dealing with ATC calls or cockpit management tasks.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; Aeronautical Decision-Making and SRM

questions.question: Define situational awareness as it applies to helicopter flight, and give one example of how it can be lost during a go-around.
questions.answer: Situational awareness (SA) is an accurate, real-time mental picture of your aircraft's position, flight path, environment, and the state of all systems relative to your intentions. It can be lost during a go-around when a pilot becomes fixated on a single task — for example, focusing entirely on an ATC radio call while allowing airspeed, altitude, or heading to deviate unnoticed. Other examples include failing to track nearby traffic or forgetting to reconfigure the aircraft (e.g., not adjusting collective or cyclic for the climb).

questions.question: What is spatial disorientation, and why are go-arounds a phase of flight where it can develop quickly in a helicopter?
questions.answer: Spatial disorientation is the inability to correctly perceive the helicopter's attitude, position, or motion relative to the earth, typically caused by conflicting or unreliable sensory inputs. Go-arounds are high-risk for disorientation because the maneuver involves rapid, simultaneous changes in power, pitch, bank, and direction — often at low altitude with high workload. If the pilot is task-saturated or distracted during these transitions, vestibular sensations can override visual cues and lead to incorrect control inputs. This risk increases significantly in reduced visibility or night conditions.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on Partial Panel Flight

questions.question: You are on short final in a Robinson R44 when the tower calls with a last-minute wind shear advisory and asks you to confirm your intentions. At the same time, you notice a deer on the runway. Walk me through how you manage task prioritization to execute a safe go-around.
questions.answer: First, aviate — immediately initiate the go-around: apply collective to arrest the descent, add appropriate right pedal to counteract torque increase, establish a positive climb attitude with cyclic, and verify rotor RPM is in the green. Do not try to respond to ATC until the aircraft is stabilized in a climb and clear of the runway environment. Once a safe climb is established and you have processing capacity, transmit a brief call — 'Going around' — so ATC knows your intentions. The deer on the runway is relevant to the go-around decision but is not a distraction requiring action once you've committed to the maneuver. Trying to respond to the tower while simultaneously reacting to the deer and reconfiguring the helicopter is exactly the kind of task stacking that leads to loss of SA or aircraft control. Aviate first, always.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; SRM and ADM; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (Basic Flight Maneuvers)

questions.question: During a practice approach to a confined area, your CFI introduces a simulated distraction — asking you a systems question — right as you decide to go around. How does accepting that distraction at that specific moment represent a risk, and what should you do?
questions.answer: The go-around initiation is a high-workload, time-critical moment requiring coordinated simultaneous control inputs — collective, cyclic, pedals — and immediate attention to climb attitude, obstacles, and rotor RPM. Accepting a cognitive task (answering a verbal question) at that exact moment divides attention during the highest-risk phase of the maneuver. This can cause delayed or incomplete control inputs, loss of situational awareness regarding obstacles or traffic, and potential for spatial disorientation if the aircraft attitude is not monitored. The correct response is to defer the question: state 'Stand by' or simply not respond until the helicopter is established in a stable climb. This is not rude — it is proper SRM. The error chain concept from FAA ADM literature warns that distraction is often one of the early links in an accident chain.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; ADM, error chain concept, SRM

questions.question: A student pilot describes the following: 'On my last solo go-around, I was so focused on getting the collective up and talking to the tower that I didn't realize I had turned 30 degrees off runway heading until I saw the control tower out my left window.' What human factors concepts explain what happened, and what corrective habit would you recommend?
questions.answer: This is a textbook example of task fixation leading to loss of situational awareness and potential disorientation. The student overloaded their attentional capacity by managing two high-demand tasks simultaneously — power management and radio communication — which consumed all cognitive resources and left no bandwidth to monitor heading. The 30-degree unnoticed deviation indicates the student's mental picture of aircraft position was no longer accurate (SA breakdown). Contributing factors from FAA ADM include channelized attention and task saturation. The recommended corrective habit is to use the 'Aviate, Navigate, Communicate' hierarchy strictly: do not key the mic until the aircraft is stabilized in the climb and on the correct heading. Additionally, using a visual reference point on the horizon during the go-around can help maintain heading without requiring instrument scan bandwidth.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; ADM, channelized attention, situational awareness

questions.question: You are conducting a night go-around at an unfamiliar airport. During the climb transition, you feel the aircraft is wings-level and climbing normally, but your attitude indicator shows a 15-degree left bank. What specific risk does this scenario represent, and what is the correct pilot action?
questions.answer: This scenario represents classic vestibular-visual conflict leading to spatial disorientation — specifically, the leans or somatogravic illusion may cause your body to perceive level flight while the instruments show a bank. At night with no outside visual references, vestibular sensations are unreliable and can be dangerously convincing. The risk is that if the pilot trusts physical sensation over instruments, they will fail to correct the bank, potentially entering a descending turn at low altitude during a go-around — a scenario with minimal recovery margin. The correct action is to trust the attitude indicator and apply positive corrective cyclic input to wings-level regardless of what your body tells you. This is instrument-based flight discipline even in VMC conditions. The pilot must resist the impulse to 'feel' the correction and instead fly by reference to instruments until visual orientation is reestablished.
questions.follow_up: If the attitude indicator in this helicopter is vacuum-driven and you suspect it may be tumbled or unreliable after an aggressive go-around maneuver, how do you cross-check its accuracy with partial panel references?
questions.follow_up_answer: Cross-check the attitude indicator against multiple other instruments: the turn coordinator (which uses a gyro on a different axis and shows rate/coordination), the airspeed indicator (if airspeed is increasing, nose may be low; decreasing, nose high), the VSI (rate of climb or descent), and the altimeter (trending). If the turn coordinator shows a left turn but the attitude indicator shows wings-level, the AI is likely unreliable. In a partial panel scenario at night during a go-around, the priority is to establish a shallow, controlled climb using the turn coordinator to maintain wings-level (needle centered), VSI to confirm a positive rate, and altimeter to confirm gain. Declare an emergency if needed and advise ATC of partial panel operations.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Partial Panel Flight chapter; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Hazards); 14 CFR 91.185 (IFR emergency procedures)

questions.question: The FAA states that approximately 80% of aviation accidents involve human factors. How does this statistic specifically apply to the go-around maneuver in helicopter operations, and what single habit most effectively reduces human-factors risk during this phase?
questions.answer: The 80% human factors figure from FAA ADM research means that the vast majority of accidents are not caused by mechanical failure but by pilot decisions, perceptions, and behaviors. In go-arounds specifically, human factors risks cluster around: (1) delayed decision-making — waiting too long to commit to the go-around; (2) task overload — attempting to fly, communicate, and troubleshoot simultaneously; (3) confirmation bias — continuing an unstabilized approach because 'it will probably work out'; and (4) loss of SA from distraction or fixation. The single most effective habit is developing and using a firm decision point — a defined altitude, airspeed, or visual cue — below which a go-around is automatically initiated without deliberation. This eliminates the most dangerous human factor (delayed decision) and converts a reactive maneuver into a trained, practiced response, reducing cognitive load precisely when it is highest.
questions.follow_up: The FAA ADM materials caution against the word 'probably' when evaluating a plan of action. How does this principle apply specifically to a pilot who is on short final thinking 'the approach is a little fast, but I can probably salvage it'?
questions.follow_up_answer: The Trescott Tip from FAA ADM guidance states: if the word 'probably' appears in your decision-making, you should choose the alternative that is known to work instead. 'I can probably salvage this approach' is the mental signature of a pilot who already knows the approach is not meeting standards but is allowing optimism bias and continuation bias to override sound judgment. The go-around is a known, reliable option — it always works if initiated with adequate altitude and energy. The salvaged approach 'probably' works, which means it sometimes doesn't. At low altitude with high workload and degraded energy margins, 'sometimes doesn't work' is unacceptable. The correct pilot response is to immediately transition the thought 'probably salvageable' into a committed go-around, because that is the option with a known outcome.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; ADM, Trescott Tip, continuation bias, human factors

questions.question: What is a runway incursion, and why is it particularly relevant to helicopter pilots operating at towered airports?
questions.answer: A runway incursion is any occurrence at an airport involving an aircraft, vehicle, person, or object on the ground that creates a collision hazard or results in a loss of required separation with an aircraft taking off, landing, or intending to land. Helicopter pilots face heightened exposure because helicopters frequently cross active runways to access helipads, hover-taxi along taxiways adjacent to runways, and may operate from non-standard movement areas — all of which require precise adherence to ATC clearances and situational awareness to avoid runway incursions.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA AC 150/5210-20A; 14 CFR 91.123 (ATC clearance compliance); FAA Runway Safety Program

questions.question: What are the four categories of runway incursion severity used by the FAA, and which category represents the most serious threat?
questions.answer: The FAA classifies runway incursions into four categories: Category A — a serious incident in which a collision was narrowly avoided; Category B — an incident with significant potential for collision requiring abrupt maneuver to avoid; Category C — an incident characterized by ample time and distance to avoid a collision; Category D — an incident that meets the definition of a runway incursion but with no immediate safety consequence. Category A represents the most serious threat, as a collision was only narrowly avoided.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Runway Incursion Severity Classification; FAA Order JO 7050.1B

questions.question: What does a hold short line look like on an airport surface, and what does it mean for a helicopter pilot hover-taxiing toward an active runway?
questions.answer: A hold short line consists of two solid yellow lines and two dashed yellow lines running perpendicular to the taxiway centerline. The solid lines face the direction from which you must hold — meaning a helicopter hover-taxiing toward an active runway must stop before the solid lines unless explicitly cleared by ATC to cross or enter the runway. Crossing the hold short line without a clearance constitutes a runway incursion and potentially a violation of 14 CFR 91.123.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.123; FAA AIM 2-3-5; AC 150/5340-1M (airport marking standards)

questions.question: You are on a go-around at a towered airport and ATC clears you to 'make left traffic, runway 27.' As you climb out and turn crosswind, the tower clears another aircraft to depart runway 32, which intersects runway 27. What runway incursion risk exists here and how do you manage it?
questions.answer: Runway 27 and Runway 32 share an intersection, creating a potential conflict between your go-around traffic pattern and the departing aircraft on Runway 32. The risk is that both aircraft could arrive at or near the intersection simultaneously — especially because helicopters in a go-around can vary significantly in airspeed and climb profile. To manage this risk: maintain the ATC-assigned pattern altitude and spacing; visually acquire the departing traffic immediately; be prepared to extend your downwind or widen your pattern if needed; and if there is any doubt about separation, immediately advise ATC and request clarification or amended instructions. Do not assume ATC has sequenced the traffic with adequate separation without confirming visually.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.113 (right-of-way rules); 14 CFR 91.123 (ATC clearance compliance); FAA AIM 4-3-15

questions.question: During a go-around at an unfamiliar airport, you are instructed by the tower to 'exit the runway, turn left, and hold short of runway 18.' You are in a helicopter and plan to hover-taxi to a nearby FBO. What specific actions reduce your runway incursion risk in this scenario?
questions.answer: To reduce runway incursion risk: (1) Write down or confirm the exact ATC instruction — 'hold short of runway 18' — before moving. (2) Pull up the airport diagram on your EFB or use the published taxi diagram to identify the physical location of runway 18's hold short line relative to your position. (3) Use progressive taxi instructions if unfamiliar with the airport layout. (4) During hover-taxi, maintain a slow, deliberate groundspeed that allows you to stop well before the hold short line. (5) Look both ways before approaching the hold short line and verbally confirm 'holding short runway 18' on the frequency. (6) Do not cross the hold short line until explicitly cleared. At an unfamiliar airport, 'heads-down' time with the avionics increases risk — brief taxi checks should be done while stopped, not while moving.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.123; FAA AIM 4-3-18; FAA Runway Safety — Hotspot awareness

questions.question: How does cockpit workload during a go-around specifically increase the risk of a runway incursion, and what can a helicopter pilot do to mitigate this during the transition from approach to go-around?
questions.answer: A go-around is one of the highest-workload phases of helicopter flight. The pilot must simultaneously increase collective, adjust cyclic for climb attitude, apply appropriate pedal input for torque, reconfigure the aircraft for departure, communicate with ATC, and mentally transition from an approach mindset to a departure mindset. This elevated workload degrades situational awareness — specifically, awareness of other aircraft and ground traffic on or near the runway. To mitigate runway incursion risk: (1) Immediately acknowledge go-around instructions and read back any runway or traffic information given by ATC. (2) Use a verbal or mental checklist priority: 'Aviate, Navigate, Communicate.' (3) Delay non-critical tasks (like frequency changes or FMS programming) until clear of the airport environment. (4) Maintain visual scan outside the cockpit — including the runway environment — throughout the maneuver. Tunnel vision on instruments during a go-around is a significant hazard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM/workload management); FAA AIM 4-3-15; 14 CFR 91.113

questions.question: A helicopter pilot executing a go-around at night receives an amended ATC clearance: 'Cleared to land runway 36, traffic runway 18 is a King Air on short final.' The pilot reads back the clearance correctly but then inadvertently turns toward runway 18 during the go-around climb. What chain of errors led to this runway incursion risk, and as an examiner, what corrective behaviors would you expect a commercial helicopter pilot to demonstrate?
questions.answer: This scenario illustrates the classic 'error chain' described in FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13. The contributing factors likely include: (1) Cognitive fixation — the mention of 'runway 18' in the clearance planted a mental image of that runway even though the clearance was for runway 36. (2) Night operations reduced visual cues needed to orient relative to runway layout. (3) High workload during go-around degraded cross-check of heading indicator against assigned runway heading. (4) The correct readback created false confidence that the instruction was fully internalized. A commercial helicopter pilot should demonstrate: immediate recognition of the heading deviation by cross-checking the heading indicator against the assigned runway (360°); prompt ATC notification of the error; willingness to declare a missed approach and request vectors if uncertain of position; and post-event self-critique identifying where the error chain began. The FAA handbook emphasizes that breaking even one link in the error chain — in this case, a heading cross-check before turning — could have prevented the incursion.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot had stated 'I'll probably be fine — the King Air is still on short final and I have room,' what does that tell you about their ADM, and what FAA guidance applies?
questions.follow_up_answer: The use of 'probably' is a direct red flag identified in FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 — the 'Trescott Tip' explicitly states that if an action will only 'probably' work out, the pilot should instead choose an option known to work. Rationalizing position uncertainty near an active runway with 'probably' indicates hazardous attitude (likely 'invulnerability' or 'anti-authority') and poor risk management. The correct ADM response is to immediately notify ATC, stop the conflicting movement, and obtain positive position confirmation before continuing — not to estimate safety margins in a dynamic traffic environment at night.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, error chain, Trescott Tip); 14 CFR 91.123; FAA AIM 4-3-15

questions.question: A helicopter conducting a go-around at a non-towered airport self-announces the go-around on CTAF but does not receive any acknowledgment. As the pilot climbs out, they observe a fixed-wing aircraft rolling for takeoff on the same runway. The helicopter pilot is positioned above and ahead of the fixed-wing. Does the helicopter pilot bear any right-of-way obligation, and what immediate actions should be taken to prevent a runway incursion or mid-air conflict?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.113, a helicopter does not have an inherent right-of-way over a fixed-wing aircraft in all situations. Specifically: 91.113(d) states that an aircraft in distress has right of way over all others; 91.113(f) gives right of way to a landing aircraft over those in flight or on the ground — but a departing aircraft is neither a landing aircraft nor on final approach and therefore does not receive this priority. The helicopter is in a go-around climb and is already airborne — both aircraft have conflicting flight paths. The helicopter pilot's immediate obligations are: (1) Under 91.113(b), see and avoid — regardless of right-of-way, both pilots share this duty. (2) Make an immediate CTAF broadcast identifying position and intentions to alert the departing aircraft. (3) Maneuver the helicopter laterally or vertically to increase separation — helicopters have superior maneuverability and can sidestep, climb rapidly, or decelerate in ways fixed-wing cannot. (4) Do not rely solely on the assumption the fixed-wing pilot will see and avoid the helicopter. At a non-towered airport with no ground control, runway incursion risk is highest when CTAF communication fails — the pilot must treat the situation as an active conflict and maneuver accordingly.
questions.follow_up: If the departing fixed-wing pilot later claims they had right-of-way because they were on the runway surface and the helicopter should have given way, is that claim legally correct under 14 CFR 91.113?
questions.follow_up_answer: No, that claim is not correct. 14 CFR 91.113(f) gives right-of-way to a landing aircraft over aircraft in flight or on the surface — but a departing aircraft is not a landing aircraft. 91.113(g) states that when two aircraft are approaching head-on, each shall alter course to the right. Neither provision gives a departing ground-roll aircraft blanket right-of-way over an airborne helicopter conducting a go-around. Both pilots share the see-and-avoid responsibility under 91.113(b). Practically, the pilot in the best position to maneuver — in this case the helicopter — has both the ability and the professional obligation to take evasive action regardless of legal right-of-way, because the right-of-way rules do not eliminate the collision risk.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.113 (right-of-way rules); 14 CFR 91.126 (non-towered airport operations); FAA AIM 4-1-9 (CTAF procedures)

questions.question: At what point during a helicopter approach should you initiate a go-around if you recognize the approach is unstabilized?
questions.answer: A go-around should be initiated as soon as you recognize the approach is not going to result in a safe landing — the earlier the better. This is a timely decision, meaning you should not delay hoping the approach will improve. If you are not stabilized on approach with the correct angle, airspeed, and rate of descent, or if obstacles, traffic, or landing zone conditions are unsuitable, initiate the go-around immediately. Delaying the decision reduces your options and increases risk.

questions.question: What are the basic control inputs required to execute a go-around from a normal approach in a helicopter?
questions.answer: To execute a go-around from a normal approach in a helicopter, you simultaneously apply collective to increase power and arrest the descent, adjust cyclic to transition to a climb attitude, apply appropriate pedal pressure to maintain trim and compensate for the torque increase from added power, and establish a positive climb attitude and airspeed. The transition must be smooth and coordinated to avoid exceeding power limits or losing rotor RPM. Maintain awareness of obstacles in the go-around flight path.

questions.question: If the evaluator verbally directs you to execute a go-around during an approach, what is the correct response?
questions.answer: You should immediately acknowledge the instruction and execute the go-around without hesitation. Promptly apply collective to arrest the descent and add power, transition cyclic to establish a climb attitude, apply pedal to maintain trim, and climb away from the landing area. Do not question the instruction or delay — during a checkride, the evaluator's direction to go around must be treated the same as any safety-critical decision you would make yourself. Communicate your actions as appropriate.

questions.question: You are on short final to a confined area landing zone. You notice the intended touchdown point is now partially obscured by a vehicle that just entered the LZ. You are at 50 feet AGL and 30 knots. Describe the decision process and execution of a go-around in this scenario.
questions.answer: This situation requires an immediate go-around decision — the landing zone is now obstructed and a safe landing cannot be completed. At 50 feet AGL and 30 knots you still have adequate energy and altitude to execute a safe go-around. Apply collective smoothly but firmly to arrest the descent and add climb power, transition cyclic forward slightly to maintain airspeed and establish a climb attitude, apply right pedal (in most helicopters) to counteract the increased torque, and climb away while clearing any obstacles on the departure path. Avoid the temptation to attempt repositioning at very low altitude — the correct decision is to climb to a safe altitude, assess the LZ, communicate with ground personnel if possible, and set up for another approach. Delaying this decision any further would compress your recovery options.

questions.question: During a practice approach to a pinnacle, you realize you have allowed airspeed to drop below the recommended approach speed and the rate of descent has become excessive. You are at 75 feet AGL. What factors affect your go-around decision at this point, and how do you execute it?
questions.answer: The combination of low airspeed and excessive rate of descent at 75 feet AGL places you in a potentially hazardous energy state. Before initiating a go-around you must assess whether sufficient power margin exists to arrest the descent and establish a climb — check engine torque/power available. Apply collective smoothly to arrest the descent; avoid an abrupt collective pull which could overpitch the blades and cause rotor RPM droop. Use cyclic to manage airspeed — bring it to at least translational lift speed to improve efficiency. Apply appropriate pedal for trim. Be aware that at very low airspeed near a pinnacle, obstacles on the upwind side may be a factor in the climb-out path. If power available is insufficient to arrest the descent, a modified run-on landing may be the only option.
