questions.question: Why is autorotation airspeed — not a faster or slower speed — the target airspeed for the power-off glide, and where do you find the published value for your specific helicopter?
questions.answer: Autorotation airspeed is the speed that produces the best balance of rotor RPM sustainability, glide distance, and descent rate for that specific helicopter design. Flying too slow increases induced drag and can cause rotor RPM decay; flying too fast increases parasite drag, steepens the descent angle, and reduces time available for a flare. The published autorotation airspeed (best glide or best rate of descent airspeed in autorotation) is found in the helicopter's Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) or Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) under the Emergency Procedures section and/or Performance section.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 2 and Chapter 11; 14 CFR 27.75 (normal category rotorcraft)

questions.question: You're flying cruise at 100 knots when the engine fails. You lower collective, apply aft cyclic, and after 5 seconds you look at the airspeed indicator — it reads 95 knots and is still decreasing. Your rotor RPM is at the bottom of the green arc. What do you do, and why?
questions.answer: The priority is rotor RPM — it is the energy source for the flare and cushion. With RPM at the bottom of the green arc, slightly forward cyclic will unload the rotor disk and allow RPM to recover. Once RPM is back into the normal operating range, re-establish aft cyclic to decelerate toward autorotation airspeed. Do not sacrifice rotor RPM to chase airspeed — a rotor stall is not recoverable, whereas being slightly fast in the glide is manageable. Monitor RPM continuously and prioritize it above airspeed until stabilized.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; rotor stall discussed as unrecoverable

questions.question: You enter autorotation on a hot day at a high-density altitude airport. Your RFM shows autorotation airspeed as 65 knots at sea level. Should you fly a different airspeed for the glide at high density altitude, and how does density altitude affect your rotor RPM management during the glide?
questions.answer: RFMs publish autorotation airspeed as indicated airspeed (IAS); fly the same IAS value regardless of density altitude. At high density altitude, engine power is reduced and the helicopter has less available power relative to its weight. This reduced power margin means the rotor is more vulnerable to RPM decay if you over-pitch or mismanage the collective. Maintain vigilant attention to rotor RPM and keep it in the green arc throughout the glide. Do not over-pitch the collective—additional pitch will bleed RPM faster when power margin is already reduced. If RPM trends downward, unload the rotor with forward cyclic to allow RPM recovery before re-establishing glide attitude.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation practice, your CFI reduces throttle to simulate engine failure while you are in a 30-degree bank turn. Walk me through how you establish a stabilized, trimmed power-off glide from that entry condition.
questions.answer: Upon power loss recognition, your priorities are: (1) Lower collective to full-down immediately to preserve rotor RPM—this is the top priority regardless of bank angle. (2) Simultaneously apply aft cyclic to establish autorotation pitch attitude and begin decelerating to autorotation airspeed. (3) Roll wings level with coordinated cyclic input while applying antitorque pedals to maintain trim throughout. A banked autorotation increases the vertical component of lift demand against gravity, increasing sink rate and steepening the descent angle, which reduces your available landing options and complicates flare management. Once wings are level, stabilize on autorotation airspeed ±5 knots, verify RPM is in the green arc, and confirm the slip/skid ball is centered before configuring the approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; ACS CH.VIII.B skills standard ±5 knots

questions.question: The ACS requires autorotation airspeed within ±5 knots. An applicant consistently flies 8 knots below autorotation airspeed throughout the glide — within the green arc for RPM and making smooth inputs otherwise. As an examiner, why is this a practical test failure even though the helicopter appears stable and under control?
questions.answer: Flying 8 knots below autorotation airspeed exceeds the ACS tolerance of ±5 knots, which is a standalone failure criterion. Beyond the standards issue, flying slow in autorotation has real safety consequences: induced drag is higher at lower airspeeds, meaning rotor RPM requires more careful management and is more susceptible to decay with any collective input. Additionally, glide distance is reduced, which shrinks the landing zone options. Most critically, arriving at the flare point with insufficient airspeed means the energy exchange in the flare is compromised — the aircraft cannot effectively trade airspeed for rotor RPM, resulting in a hard landing or inability to cushion the touchdown. The ±5-knot standard exists precisely because the autorotation energy budget is narrow.
questions.follow_up: If this applicant re-flies and is now consistently 4 knots slow — technically within standards — but the rotor RPM is consistently drifting toward the bottom of the green arc, what does that tell you as an examiner?
questions.follow_up_answer: RPM drifting toward the bottom of the green arc despite being within airspeed tolerances indicates the applicant is likely carrying more collective pitch than necessary during the glide — possibly 'riding' the collective rather than setting it fully down. It could also indicate the helicopter's weight or density altitude is requiring more rotor energy to maintain that airspeed, or the applicant is failing to manage the power-off descent profile correctly. As an examiner, I'm looking at whether the applicant understands the relationship between collective position, rotor RPM, and airspeed in autorotation. Allowing RPM to persistently ride near the bottom of the green arc demonstrates a lack of energy management awareness and could indicate the applicant would arrive at the flare with insufficient rotor inertia — a potentially fatal error in a real emergency.

questions.question: A pilot transitions from a piston helicopter to a turbine helicopter with a low-inertia rotor system. Both have the same published autorotation airspeed of 70 knots. The pilot says 'same airspeed, so the entry technique is identical.' What is wrong with that thinking, and how should the pilot adjust the power-off glide establishment technique?
questions.answer: The airspeed target may be the same, but rotor inertia fundamentally changes the urgency and technique of the entry. A low-inertia rotor system stores less kinetic energy and decays to an unrecoverable RPM range much faster than a high-inertia system — potentially in seconds versus many seconds. This means the pilot must lower collective even more immediately at engine failure recognition — any hesitation that might be tolerable in a high-inertia system could result in rotor stall in a low-inertia system before the pilot can recover. The pilot must also avoid any collective increase during the glide establishment phase that would be acceptable in a heavier-inertia aircraft. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook specifically notes that low-inertia rotors decay rapidly, making immediate collective reduction the most critical entry action. The pilot must train to this aircraft's specific RPM decay rate, not assume prior piston experience translates directly.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant has 500 hours in a high-inertia piston helicopter and 15 hours in this turbine, what does the accident data tell us about the relative risk during this transition, and what does that mean for the examiner's evaluation approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: FAA ADM research (FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13) indicates that accident rates correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft model than total hours — and that accidents are significantly elevated below 100 hours in type. A pilot with 500 total hours but only 15 in type is statistically in a higher-risk window than either a low-time pilot starting fresh or a high-time pilot in their primary aircraft. As an examiner, this means I should weight the evaluation toward verifying the applicant has genuinely internalized the low-inertia rotor's unique demands — not just reciting the correct airspeed — and that their hands-and-feet technique demonstrates appropriate urgency at entry. I would specifically look for any 'muscle memory' hesitation on the collective that reflects high-inertia habits, and probe deeply on RPM management and the consequences of delay in this aircraft.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (low-inertia rotors), Chapter 13 (ADM, hours in type)

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, what is the primary control used to maintain Nr within the normal operating range?
questions.answer: The collective pitch control is the primary tool for managing Nr during autorotation. Lowering collective reduces blade pitch and drag on the rotor system, allowing rotor RPM to increase or be maintained. Raising collective increases blade pitch and drag, which bleeds off RPM. The pilot must monitor the tachometer continuously and make small, smooth collective adjustments to keep Nr within the green arc throughout the descent.

questions.question: What does Nr stand for, and why is keeping it within the green arc critical during an autorotation?
questions.answer: Nr stands for rotor rotational speed, or rotor RPM. During autorotation, the engine is no longer driving the rotor, so the pilot must use aerodynamic forces — specifically upward airflow through the rotor disk — to maintain rotation. If Nr falls below the green arc (low RPM), rotor blade angle of attack may exceed the stall angle, leading to rotor stall which is not recoverable. If Nr exceeds the green arc (overspeed), structural damage to the rotor system can occur. Staying within limits ensures adequate stored energy for the flare and cushion during landing.

questions.question: At the moment of power loss entry into autorotation from cruise airspeed, what three simultaneous control inputs help preserve Nr?
questions.answer: The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook identifies three simultaneous inputs at autorotation entry from cruise airspeed: (1) lower the collective to reduce blade pitch and drag, allowing upward airflow to sustain rotor RPM; (2) apply aft cyclic to slow the aircraft and increase upward airflow through the rotor disk, which also contributes to rotor RPM; (3) apply appropriate pedal input (typically right pedal in counterclockwise-rotation helicopters) to compensate for the loss of torque and maintain trim. These coordinated inputs prevent Nr from decaying rapidly, which is especially critical in low-inertia rotor systems.

questions.question: You are established in a straight-in autorotation at the correct airspeed and glide angle when you notice Nr slowly creeping toward the top of the green arc. What is the most likely cause, and what correction do you make?
questions.answer: Nr creeping toward the upper limit of the green arc indicates that more energy is being extracted from the airflow than is needed to sustain a normal rotor speed — typically caused by a steeper-than-normal descent angle, higher-than-normal airspeed, or both. The correction is to raise the collective slightly to increase blade pitch and aerodynamic drag on the rotor, which will bleed off excess RPM. The pilot should also check airspeed and adjust cyclic if the aircraft is faster than the recommended autorotation airspeed for the specific helicopter. Smooth, small inputs are preferable to large corrections to avoid inducing an RPM oscillation.

questions.question: During the flare phase of a straight-in autorotation, how does the aft cyclic input affect Nr, and what is the pilot's responsibility at that moment regarding RPM management?
questions.answer: When aft cyclic is applied during the flare, the nose rises and the rotor disk tilts aft. This increases upward airflow through the disk, which drives rotor RPM upward — often noticeably. Simultaneously, the deceleration reduces both vertical and horizontal velocity, converting kinetic energy into rotor energy. The pilot must monitor Nr during the flare and be prepared to allow it to rise toward the upper portion of the green arc, as that stored RPM will be needed for the collective cushion. If Nr exceeds the green arc during the flare, a slight forward cyclic or small increase in collective can control it. The pilot should not allow RPM to go into the red, as overspeed can cause rotor component damage.

questions.question: A student pilot consistently allows Nr to decay toward the bottom of the green arc during the mid-descent phase of a straight-in autorotation. As their instructor, what are three possible root causes you would examine, and how would each be corrected?
questions.answer: Three likely root causes: (1) Insufficient collective reduction at entry — the student may not be fully lowering collective, leaving too much pitch on the blades, creating drag that bleeds RPM. Correction: ensure full or near-full down collective is applied promptly at entry. (2) Airspeed too slow — flying below the recommended autorotation airspeed reduces the relative wind and upward airflow through the rotor, providing less energy to sustain RPM. Correction: establish and hold the POH-specified autorotation airspeed using forward cyclic. (3) Delayed recognition and correction of RPM decay — the student may not be cross-checking the tachometer frequently enough. Correction: establish a disciplined instrument scan that includes the tachometer as a primary reference throughout the autorotation. In low-inertia rotor systems, RPM decay is rapid and recovery becomes difficult if not caught early.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation at altitude, you momentarily raise the collective to adjust your glide path to the landing zone, and Nr drops to the bottom of the green arc. You then lower collective again but Nr continues to decrease slowly below the green arc. Walk me through your assessment of what is happening and what options you have.
questions.answer: If Nr continues to decay below the green arc even after reducing collective, the rotor system is losing energy faster than the aerodynamic forces can replenish it. Possible contributing factors include very low airspeed (insufficient upward airflow through the disk), an extremely high altitude or density altitude environment reducing air density, or a rotor system with low inertia that cannot sustain RPM through a brief disturbance. The FAA is clear that rotor stall is not recoverable. Immediate actions: (1) Verify collective is fully lowered to minimize blade drag; (2) apply aft cyclic to pitch the nose up, increasing upward airflow through the disk — this is the most effective way to drive RPM back up during descent; (3) ensure airspeed is at or above the recommended autorotation speed. If RPM cannot be recovered and a power recovery is available (simulated emergency), execute it immediately. In an actual power-off situation with continuing RPM decay, the pilot must initiate the flare and collective cushion as soon as possible with whatever rotor energy remains, accepting a harder-than-normal touchdown rather than allowing a complete rotor stall.
questions.follow_up: The POH for your training helicopter specifies a minimum Nr for power recovery during practice autorotations. Why does that limitation exist, and what aerodynamic event are you trying to prevent if you recover too late?
questions.follow_up_answer: The minimum Nr for power recovery exists because reconnecting engine power when rotor RPM is very low causes a sudden, large increase in torque demand on an already slow-turning rotor system. If the rotor cannot absorb and transmit that torque, the engine may bog down or, worse, the rapid change in torque loading can cause blade stall or structural overstress. Additionally, when low RPM is combined with increased collective as power is applied, the blades may reach critical angle of attack and stall — which is unrecoverable. The manufacturer's minimum Nr for power recovery is designed to ensure the rotor has sufficient angular momentum to accept the sudden torque load and transition smoothly back to powered flight without aerodynamic or structural damage.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable rotorcraft flight manual/POH

questions.question: How does rotor system type — specifically articulated versus semi-rigid versus rigid — affect the pilot's urgency and technique when responding to Nr decay during an autorotation?
questions.answer: Rotor system type directly affects rotor inertia and the rate of RPM decay. Articulated rotor systems, which allow blade flapping and lead/lag movement, typically have higher rotor mass and greater polar moment of inertia — meaning they store more energy and decay more slowly when lift/drag balance is disrupted. Semi-rigid (teetering) rotors allow feathering and flapping but not lead/lag, and generally have less inertia than articulated systems. Rigid rotors allow only feathering and tend to have the lowest mass in their blade structure. The practical implication is that helicopters with low-inertia rotor systems (common in light piston-engine training helicopters with semi-rigid systems) have very short time-to-stall windows — the FAA specifically notes that 'low inertia rotors decay rapidly.' A pilot must respond within seconds of detecting RPM decay. High-inertia articulated systems (common in heavier turbine helicopters) provide more time for correction, but this should never breed complacency. Regardless of system type, technique remains the same — lower collective, aft cyclic to increase upward airflow — but the urgency and acceptable response time differ significantly based on the rotor type and its stored kinetic energy.
questions.follow_up: Given that rotor inertia is a factor, would it ever be appropriate to deliberately carry Nr slightly higher than the middle of the green arc during an autorotation descent as a safety buffer? What are the tradeoffs?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, there is a reasonable argument for managing Nr in the upper half of the green arc during autorotation, particularly in low-inertia rotor systems or during high-density altitude operations where rotor efficiency is reduced. Carrying higher Nr provides more stored kinetic energy available for the flare and collective cushion, and gives the pilot more margin before reaching the bottom of the green arc if a correction is delayed. The tradeoff is that higher Nr means the pilot must be attentive to not allowing RPM to exceed the upper limit (redline), particularly during the flare when aft cyclic naturally drives RPM upward. The pilot must also avoid overloading the rotor with aggressive collective inputs at a high RPM state. The POH is the authoritative reference — some manufacturers specify an exact target RPM for autorotation rather than a range, and that value reflects the optimal balance between stored energy, blade angle of attack efficiency, and structural limits. Pilots should follow POH guidance rather than improvising their own RPM target.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 2 (rotor system types); applicable POH

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, what effect does a direct headwind have on your glide to the landing area?
questions.answer: A headwind reduces your groundspeed while maintaining the same airspeed and rotor RPM, which means you cover less ground distance over the same time. This effectively steepens your approach angle relative to the ground and shortens your glide. In a headwind, you may need to manage your energy by adjusting your entry point, glide speed, or flare timing to avoid landing short of the intended touchdown area.

questions.question: What is the primary effect of a direct tailwind on a straight-in autorotation, and which direction does it push your landing point?
questions.answer: A tailwind increases your groundspeed while your airspeed and rotor RPM remain the same, which flattens your approach angle relative to the ground and extends your glide. This pushes your landing point farther down the intended landing area — increasing the risk of overshooting. The pilot must recognize this early and adjust by entering from a greater distance, flying a slower airspeed, or planning a steeper approach if the landing area allows.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, what are the two primary visual cues a pilot uses to determine whether they are going to undershoot or overshoot the selected landing area?
questions.answer: The two primary visual cues are: (1) Aim point movement on the windshield—if the aim point appears to move down and away from you on the windshield, you will overshoot; if it appears to move up and toward you, you will undershoot. (2) The apparent angle of the landing area relative to the horizon—if the landing area drops below your natural line of sight, you are overshooting; if it rises above your reference, you are undershooting. These cues allow the pilot to make early corrections using airspeed adjustments before the final flare.

questions.question: You are set up for a straight-in autorotation with a 15-knot crosswind from the left. As you descend, you notice you are drifting right of your selected landing area. How do you compensate, and what additional consideration must you address at the bottom of the flare?
questions.answer: To correct the drift, apply left cyclic to establish a crab angle into the wind, keeping the nose pointed down the intended flight path and the helicopter tracking toward the landing area. Throughout the descent, maintain a crab into the wind to compensate for drift. At the bottom of the flare, just before touchdown, apply left pedal to align the fuselage with the direction of travel to prevent a lateral groundspeed component at touchdown, which could cause a dynamic rollover or sideways landing. You must be on the ground with zero lateral drift to land safely. In strong crosswinds, consider whether the landing area allows a more favorable wind angle.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Autorotation; Chapter 9, Basic Flight Maneuvers

questions.question: You are mid-autorotation on final and recognize you are going to significantly overshoot due to an unexpected tailwind component you failed to account for. The landing area is confined and there is no room beyond it. What options do you have to increase your rate of descent and shorten your glide?
questions.answer: Options to steepen the descent and reduce glide distance include: (1) Reducing airspeed below the normal autorotation speed — flying slower increases induced drag and steepens the glide, though you must not let rotor RPM decay below limits. (2) If the helicopter is equipped with a governor, allow rotor RPM to increase toward the upper limit by lowering collective slightly (decreasing blade pitch) — higher RPM increases drag. (3) Beginning the flare earlier than normal — an early flare dramatically increases drag and bleeds off airspeed and altitude simultaneously, but this technique significantly reduces margin for recovery and is only used as a last resort in confined area landings. All techniques must preserve rotor RPM above the minimum required for the final collective application to arrest the descent.

questions.question: You are conducting a straight-in autorotation and the surface winds at the landing area appear calm, but at your entry altitude you had a 20-knot headwind. As you descend through 500 feet AGL, you notice you are going to undershoot. What is the most likely cause and how do you correct it?
questions.answer: The most likely cause is wind shear — the headwind that was extending your glide at altitude has decreased or disappeared at lower altitudes, reducing your actual glide distance. To correct an undershoot condition, lower collective (increase blade pitch angle) to increase airspeed and flatten the descent angle, extending your glide. If insufficient altitude remains to recover, execute the flare at the appropriate height to arrest the descent and use all available collective to cushion, accepting a landing point short of the intended area. Early recognition of wind conditions and their changes with altitude is critical to avoiding this situation.

questions.question: A student consistently overshoots during straight-in autorotations even when they correctly identify a headwind on the surface. As their instructor, you observe they are establishing their entry glide angle without accounting for the fact that the headwind is aloft — not at the surface. How do you explain the specific scanning and adjustment technique to correct this systematic error?
questions.answer: The error is that the student is using surface wind to predict a headwind benefit during the entire glide, when the wind at altitude may actually be a tailwind or quartering component that changes character as they descend. The correct technique is to continuously monitor the aim point throughout the descent — not just at entry. The student should establish an initial aim point on the near edge of the landing area at entry, then observe how the aim point moves relative to the helicopter's descent path during the first third of the glide. If the aim point drifts toward the far end of the landing area, they are getting less headwind assistance than expected and should fly a slightly faster airspeed or aim for a closer point. The key teaching point is that wind compensation is not a one-time calculation at entry — it is a continuous correction process throughout the autorotation. The student must also understand that aiming for the near edge of the landing area provides a safety margin: they can always extend, but they cannot pull back a shortfall in energy.
questions.follow_up: If this student then overcorrects and begins consistently undershooting, what is the single most important energy management principle you want them to internalize about the relationship between airspeed and glide distance in autorotation?
questions.follow_up_answer: The most important principle is that in autorotation, airspeed is the primary lever for controlling glide distance — not collective. Increasing airspeed extends the glide; decreasing airspeed shortens the glide and steepens the descent. The student must understand that the collective is largely reserved for the final cushion at the bottom and should not be used to modulate the glide path mid-autorotation, as raising collective bleeds off rotor RPM that cannot be recovered. The student should think of the autorotation as managing a fixed energy budget: rotor RPM is kinetic energy in the rotor system, and it must be preserved throughout the descent for a successful flare and cushion. Every unnecessary collective application during the glide is a withdrawal from that account they cannot afford.

questions.question: During a checkride, a private pilot applicant enters a straight-in autorotation with a direct crosswind that is gusting. On short final, the applicant aligns the fuselage with the landing direction using pedal but fails to hold the crab angle and drifts significantly downwind. The applicant lands safely but 150 feet from the intended point with notable lateral drift at touchdown. How do you evaluate this performance, and what are the risk management concerns you would discuss?
questions.answer: This performance would likely not meet ACS standards. The ACS requires the pilot to compensate for wind speed and direction to avoid undershooting or overshooting the selected landing area — a 150-foot lateral displacement from the intended point in gusty crosswind conditions indicates inadequate wind compensation throughout the descent. The applicant demonstrated an understanding of fuselage alignment at touchdown, which is correct, but failed to maintain the crab throughout the approach to track toward the intended area. The risk management concerns to discuss are: (1) Lateral drift at touchdown in a helicopter creates a rollover risk — dynamic rollover can occur at very small lateral tilt angles when the skid contacts the ground while lateral momentum exists. (2) In a real engine failure, the 150-foot displacement could mean landing in an unsuitable surface or obstacle. (3) Gusting crosswinds require the pilot to anticipate gusts and increase margins — flying to the windward side of the landing area accounts for gust-induced drift. (4) The decision to commit to this landing rather than adjusting mid-approach reflects a situational awareness breakdown that should be explored in the oral portion of the debrief. Depending on the totality of the checkride, this could be grounds for a discontinuance or a single unsatisfactory task.
questions.follow_up: The applicant argues that they maintained control and touched down safely, so the wind correction issue was minor. How do you respond, and what FAA standard do you apply to explain why proximity to the intended landing area is a safety-of-flight issue, not just a precision issue?
questions.follow_up_answer: The response is that in actual engine failure, the pilot does not get to choose a landing area 150 feet away — the terrain, obstacles, and surface conditions are fixed. The ability to precisely control the autorotation to a specific point is the entire safety margin. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that the pilot must select a suitable area and then fly to it — if they cannot consistently hit their selected point in training, they will not be able to do so in an actual emergency when the stakes are highest. Additionally, the ACS exists because the examiner must assess the applicant's ability to perform the task to a standard that demonstrates they can survive an actual emergency, not just land the helicopter somewhere. Safe outcomes in training with poor technique do not validate the technique — they simply mean the consequences were not realized this time. The examiner's job is to evaluate whether the applicant has the skill and judgment to handle the actual emergency, and tolerating 150 feet of wind-induced drift indicates they do not yet meet that standard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Autorotation; ACS CH.VIII.B; 14 CFR 61.43

questions.question: During the flare phase of a straight-in autorotation, what is the primary purpose of applying aft cyclic, and what does it do for tail boom clearance?
questions.answer: Aft cyclic during the flare pitches the nose up, which decelerates the helicopter and converts forward airspeed into rotor RPM. This nose-up attitude also raises the tail boom away from the surface, providing clearance. The flare must be initiated at the correct altitude — typically 40 to 100 feet AGL depending on airspeed and aircraft type — so that the tail does not contact the ground while the nose is still pitched up.

questions.question: At what point in a straight-in autorotation should you begin leveling the helicopter from the flare attitude, and why is timing critical for tail boom clearance?
questions.answer: The helicopter should be leveled from the flare attitude at a height that varies with airspeed and aircraft characteristics — typically 8 to 15 feet AGL for most training helicopters, but the specific height should be determined during practice under instructor supervision. Collective is applied simultaneously with or immediately following level-off to cushion the landing and arrest descent rate. The key is that the nose must be level (or nearly level) before the skids contact the ground to prevent tail boom strike. Collective must not be applied so aggressively that rotor RPM is depleted before touchdown, which would prevent proper cushioning.

questions.question: What happens to rotor RPM when you raise collective to cushion the landing during autorotation, and how does that affect how long you can use collective for deceleration?
questions.answer: Raising collective increases blade pitch, which increases drag on the rotor system and rapidly depletes rotor RPM. Once collective is raised, the rotor is consuming stored inertial energy that cannot be replaced without engine power. This means you have a limited and finite amount of collective available for cushioning. If collective is raised too early or too aggressively, RPM may fall to an unsafe level before the aircraft reaches the surface, resulting in a hard landing with no cushion remaining.

questions.question: You are conducting a straight-in autorotation and enter the flare 200 feet lower than your normal practice altitude due to a distraction. You recognize you are low. Walk me through how that compressed flare affects both deceleration and tail boom clearance risk.
questions.answer: A low flare entry means you have less altitude available to bleed off airspeed through aft cyclic application. The result is that you either under-flare — landing with excess forward speed that risks a dynamic rollover or nose-over — or you apply an aggressive, late flare very close to the ground with the nose pitched steeply up. A steep nose-up attitude at very low altitude dramatically increases the risk of tail boom strike because the tail is close to the ground while the nose is high. The correct response when recognizing a low entry is to apply a moderate, progressive flare immediately, use available collective earlier to help arrest descent rate, and accept a slightly faster than normal groundspeed landing while keeping the aircraft level to protect the tail boom.

questions.question: During autorotation practice, your instructor notices you are leveling the helicopter from the flare at 20 feet AGL and then raising collective at 5 feet. How does this sequencing affect tail boom clearance and energy management compared to the preferred technique of leveling around 8–15 feet and then raising collective shortly thereafter?
questions.answer: The flare phase (initiated at 40–75 feet AGL) uses aft cyclic to arrest descent rate and allows rotor RPM to recover while still in descent. Leveling at 20 feet and delaying collective raise until 5 feet creates a prolonged level-flight descent with high descent rate and decaying RPM—wasting the RPM cushion built during the earlier flare. By the time you raise collective at 5 feet, rotor RPM has fallen significantly, requiring a more aggressive collective pull that rapidly depletes remaining energy and tail boom clearance margins. The preferred technique is to level the fuselage around 8–15 feet (after the flare has done its work), then promptly raise collective to cushion the landing. This sequence preserves the RPM recovery achieved during the flare, applies the energy cushion at the right moment, and maintains better tail boom clearance and control authority throughout the final landing phase.

questions.question: You are autorotating into a short field with an obstacle at the threshold. You clear the obstacle at 50 feet AGL with significant forward airspeed remaining. How do you sequence deceleration and collective application to safely reach the surface without a tail boom strike?
questions.answer: After clearing the obstacle at 50 feet, immediately apply progressive aft cyclic to begin decelerating and flaring. The flare will raise the nose — and with it, the tail boom — providing clearance. As airspeed bleeds off and the helicopter descends to approximately 8 to 15 feet AGL, begin leveling the fuselage with forward cyclic to ensure the skids are level with the ground. As the nose comes level, simultaneously raise collective smoothly to cushion the landing and arrest descent rate. The key is not to rush the level-off while still too high, since that would drop the tail, and not to delay it so long that the nose is still raised at touchdown. The sequence is: flare — level — collective up — touchdown.

questions.question: A candidate consistently completes straight-in autorotations with good RPM but repeatedly lands with 10–15 knots of excess groundspeed, always touching down nose-low. What specific control sequence error most likely explains both findings simultaneously, and what does it mean for tail boom risk in a real emergency?
questions.answer: The most likely error is that the candidate is leveling the helicopter from the flare too early — before sufficient airspeed has been bled off — and simultaneously or prematurely lowering the nose through forward cyclic. Leveling early stops the aerodynamic deceleration of the flare, leaving excess forward speed. The nose-low touchdown suggests the candidate may also be applying forward cyclic to level the aircraft while still at altitude, which further accelerates the helicopter and pitches the nose down at contact. RPM remains good because the flare was at least partially executed, but without completing it, insufficient deceleration occurred. In a real emergency, this pattern is dangerous not because of tail boom strike — the nose-low attitude actually protects the tail — but because excess groundspeed on a confined or unprepared surface dramatically increases rollover and dynamic rollover risk upon contact, especially on uneven terrain.
questions.follow_up: If this same candidate were autorotating into a soft or upsloping surface, how would the nose-low touchdown attitude specifically increase the danger compared to landing on a prepared surface?
questions.follow_up_answer: On a soft or upsloping surface, a nose-low touchdown attitude causes the front of the skids to dig in or catch on terrain features before the aft portion contacts the ground. With residual forward speed, this can cause the nose to abruptly stop while the tail continues to rise — effectively pitching the helicopter over the front skids. This is sometimes called a nose-over or forward rollover, and it is catastrophic on an upslope because the main rotor blades may strike the upsloping terrain ahead of the helicopter. Additionally, soft ground can grab the forward skid toes, triggering dynamic rollover conditions even at relatively low groundspeeds. The combination of excess forward speed and nose-low attitude on anything other than a hard, flat, prepared surface is a recipe for rollover.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Autorotation and Dynamic Rollover

questions.question: During an actual engine failure at 500 feet AGL and 80 knots, a pilot correctly enters autorotation but then waits until 30 feet AGL to begin the flare, resulting in a hard landing. Explain the energy physics that made tail boom clearance and a safe cushion impossible from that flare initiation point, even with perfect control inputs.
questions.answer: Kinetic and potential energy available to the rotor system are both a function of altitude and airspeed at the time they are converted. At 30 feet AGL and 80 knots, there is minimal altitude remaining to convert to rotor RPM through flare aerodynamics, and the aft cyclic input to pitch the nose up requires distance above the ground to safely arrest. Pitching to a pronounced flare attitude at 30 feet would immediately place the tail boom extremely close to the surface — potentially causing a strike before any meaningful deceleration occurs. If the pilot softens the flare to protect the tail, they retain excess forward speed with very little altitude left to bleed it off, and there is insufficient rotor RPM stored to provide an adequate collective cushion. The physics are unforgiving: the potential energy (altitude) that would have powered the flare RPM recovery was dissipated as wasted descent during the delay. By 30 feet, the helicopter is moving fast downward and forward with a rotor system that has been windmilling at glide RPM — not the elevated RPM achieved by a timely flare — leaving no energy reserve for both deceleration and cushioning simultaneously.
questions.follow_up: Given that same scenario — 500 feet AGL engine failure — what is the minimum realistic flare initiation altitude for most training helicopters, and what handbook guidance informs that number?
questions.follow_up_answer: Most training helicopters require flare initiation between 40 and 75 feet AGL for a normal straight-in autorotation from cruise airspeed, though the specific altitude varies by aircraft weight, rotor inertia, and approach airspeed. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11) states that the flare should be initiated at approximately 40 to 75 feet AGL depending on the helicopter and conditions, and pilots should reference their specific Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for aircraft-specific guidance. High-inertia rotors (e.g., heavier helicopters) are more forgiving of late flares because they store more energy, while low-inertia rotor systems require earlier and more precise flare initiation. The RFM autorotation performance data and the height-velocity diagram together define the safe operational envelope for each specific aircraft.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Autorotation; Aircraft-specific RFM autorotation section

questions.question: At what point during a straight-in autorotation should you initiate the power recovery, and what is the first control input you make?
questions.answer: Power recovery is initiated at a low altitude—typically around 10 to 30 feet AGL in most training helicopters—after the flare (initiated at 40–75 feet) has slowed the descent rate and recovered rotor RPM. The first control input is a smooth, coordinated increase of collective pitch to cushion the landing and arrest the remaining descent while simultaneously increasing throttle (if not governor-equipped) to restore engine power and maintain rotor RPM. The flare and power recovery are separate sequential phases; the flare sets up RPM recovery, and power recovery applies that energy to decelerate and land.

questions.question: Why is rotor RPM so critical at the moment you initiate power recovery in an autorotation, and what is the consequence of recovering with RPM that is too low?
questions.answer: Rotor RPM must be within the green arc — at or above the normal operating range — when you initiate power recovery. If RPM is too low when you raise the collective, the blade pitch increase will demand more lift than the rotor can produce, causing RPM to decay further. This can lead to rotor stall, which is not recoverable. The FAA states that rotor stalls in helicopters are unrecoverable, so maintaining adequate RPM before initiating the recovery is imperative.

questions.question: During power recovery in a straight-in autorotation, what happens to torque as you raise the collective, and how do you compensate for it?
questions.answer: As collective is increased during power recovery, main rotor torque increases, which tends to yaw the helicopter to the right (in a counterclockwise-rotor helicopter). You compensate by applying left pedal to maintain heading and keep the helicopter in trim. The pedal input must be coordinated smoothly with the collective increase to prevent an uncoordinated yaw or skid.

questions.question: You are flying a straight-in autorotation and you flare too aggressively, causing ground speed to drop very quickly and the helicopter to balloon upward. How does this affect your power recovery timing and technique?
questions.answer: An aggressive flare that balloons the helicopter upward creates two problems for power recovery: it increases your height above the ground at the recovery point, and the rotor RPM may have peaked and begun to decay as the nose pitches back. You must level the helicopter sooner than normal to prevent a tail-low touchdown, and you need to monitor RPM carefully — if it has decayed significantly from the balloon, raising collective aggressively to arrest the re-descent could further drain RPM. The recovery must be executed with smooth, deliberate collective increase coordinated with forward cyclic to level the attitude, using whatever RPM remains effectively without inducing a rotor stall.

questions.question: You are demonstrating a practice autorotation and initiate the power recovery, but the engine is slow to respond and RPM begins to drop below the green arc. Walk me through your immediate actions.
questions.answer: If the engine is slow to respond and rotor RPM begins to decay below the green arc during power recovery, you must first and foremost avoid raising the collective further, which would accelerate RPM loss. Lower or hold collective to reduce blade pitch demand and allow any available airflow to sustain RPM. Simultaneously, verify throttle is fully open and check for any mechanical issue. If RPM continues to decay toward a stall, you are effectively in a deteriorating emergency — maintain the lowest collective position possible to preserve remaining RPM and execute the safest available landing. The key principle is that RPM preservation takes priority over cushioning the touchdown.

questions.question: How does the cyclic position change from the flare through the power recovery phase, and what is the purpose of each adjustment?
questions.answer: During the flare, aft cyclic is applied to increase rotor disk angle of attack, slow forward speed, and increase rotor RPM. As you approach the power recovery point and the aircraft is at the correct altitude, you progressively move cyclic forward to level the helicopter's attitude — this brings the fuselage to a near-level or slightly nose-high attitude for touchdown. This forward cyclic movement also reduces the tendency to balloon further. During the actual collective increase for cushioning, cyclic is held relatively neutral or slightly aft to maintain a controlled attitude. The coordinated transition from aft flare to level attitude is what separates a smooth power recovery from a hard landing or tail-strike.

questions.question: A student initiates power recovery correctly in terms of timing but applies collective too rapidly, causing the engine to bog and RPM to drop. The student then pushes the collective back down abruptly to recover RPM. What is the secondary hazard created by that abrupt collective reduction, and how would you coach the student to avoid this scenario entirely?
questions.answer: When the collective is pushed down abruptly after a RPM decay, the sudden unloading of the rotor can cause the fuselage to yaw rapidly to the left as torque is instantly reduced (in counterclockwise rotor systems), creating an uncoordinated, potentially violent yaw. Additionally, if the helicopter is already close to the ground with forward speed, the abrupt collective reduction increases the rate of descent, risking a hard landing. To avoid the scenario entirely, coach the student to raise collective slowly and smoothly — the rate of collective increase should match what the engine and rotor system can absorb without bogging. Practice the 'squeeze not yank' technique: steady pressure, not a pump. The student should also be trained to monitor the RPM gauge continuously throughout the recovery, not just at the initiation point.
questions.follow_up: If the student asks 'how slow is slow enough?' when raising collective during power recovery, what measurable or observable cue do you give them to gauge their rate of collective increase?
questions.follow_up_answer: Tell the student to watch the rotor RPM gauge continuously as they raise the collective. The RPM should remain steady or rise slightly as collective comes up — if it begins to drop, the rate of increase is too fast for the engine to keep up. A secondary cue is engine sound: a healthy engine response sounds like a smooth surge, while bogging produces a distinct audible decay. In turbine aircraft, torque and TOT gauges provide additional reference. The rule of thumb is: if RPM moves down as collective goes up, slow your collective rate immediately.

questions.question: You are evaluating a pilot on a straight-in autorotation to a power recovery. The pilot executes a textbook flare but initiates the power recovery about 20 feet higher than optimal, resulting in a hover at 15 feet AGL with nearly depleted rotor RPM. What are the compounding risks at this point, and what is the correct technique to salvage the situation?
questions.answer: At 15 feet AGL in a hover with depleted rotor RPM, the pilot faces compounding risks: first, insufficient RPM means any collective increase to maintain the hover will further drain the remaining energy, risking rotor stall; second, if the collective is reduced to arrest RPM decay, the helicopter will descend rapidly from 15 feet, likely resulting in a hard landing or dynamic rollover on touchdown; third, the hover altitude is too high for a safe cushioned landing but too low to build RPM through autorotative airflow. The correct technique is to accept a controlled but firm landing — reduce collective smoothly and progressively while maintaining attitude with cyclic to allow a descent to the surface. Do not attempt to sustain the hover or re-establish autorotation. Touch down with the available RPM while minimizing collective demand, absorbing the landing with legs, cyclic in neutral, and be prepared for a possible firm impact. Prevention is the lesson: power recovery altitude selection must account for the specific helicopter's inertia and RPM decay rate.
questions.follow_up: If this same scenario occurred in a high-inertia rotor helicopter versus a low-inertia rotor helicopter, would your technique or urgency differ, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, significantly. A low-inertia rotor system — common in lighter piston helicopters — decays RPM extremely rapidly once the energy is spent. At 15 feet with depleted RPM in a low-inertia system, you have very little time before the rotor stalls, so the descent to the surface must begin immediately with minimal hesitation. A high-inertia rotor system — common in larger turbine helicopters — stores more kinetic energy in the spinning blades and decays more slowly, giving the pilot slightly more time to manage the collective and descent rate. However, the fundamental principle is the same: do not try to hover or delay the landing. The FAA handbook notes that low-inertia rotors decay rapidly, which is why entry timing and rotor RPM management throughout the autorotation are especially critical in those aircraft.

questions.question: At what point during a straight-in autorotation should you begin applying collective to cushion the landing and transition to a stabilized hover?
questions.answer: Collective application begins during the flare as the helicopter decelerates and descends through approximately 8 to 15 feet AGL, depending on the aircraft. The pilot progressively increases collective to cushion the descent rate, simultaneously adjusting cyclic to level the aircraft and using pedals to maintain heading. The goal is to coordinate collective, cyclic, and pedals so that rotor RPM, altitude, and airspeed are all managed to arrive at a stabilized hover rather than a run-on landing.

questions.question: What does the ACS require regarding accuracy when terminating a straight-in autorotation to a hover at a designated point?
questions.answer: The ACS requires the pilot to terminate the autorotation to a stabilized hover within 100 feet of the designated point. This means the hover must be established with all four flight controls coordinated, rotor RPM in the normal operating range, and the aircraft positioned no more than 100 feet from the pre-selected touchdown or termination point.

issues: The 100-foot accuracy standard stated is reasonable for practical training, but the answer should clarify that this is an instructor/examiner benchmark rather than an explicit ACS requirement. The ACS (Airman Certification Standards) for helicopter private pilot uses qualitative language like 'within reasonable distance of a designated point' rather than a hard 100-foot standard. Verify against current ACS document to confirm exact wording.
verification.suggested_correction: Recommend reviewing the current ACS CH.VIII.B Terminate task to confirm whether a specific 100-foot tolerance is mandated or if language is more qualitative. Answer should align precisely with current ACS language.
verification.triage_note: The answer cites a 100-foot tolerance as an ACS requirement, but current ACS language for autorotation termination is qualitative ('within reasonable distance') rather than quantitative; the specific numerical standard requires verification against the current published ACS document to ensure regulatory accuracy.

questions.question: What does a 'stabilized hover' mean in the context of terminating an autorotation, and what control inputs confirm you've achieved it?
questions.answer: A stabilized hover means the helicopter is maintaining a constant position over a ground reference point at a consistent hover altitude — typically 2 to 5 feet skid height — with no significant drift in any direction. Confirmations include: rotor RPM in the normal operating arc, collective set to maintain altitude, cyclic centered with no translational movement, and pedals trimmed to prevent yaw. The aircraft should be in equilibrium requiring only minor corrections to remain stationary.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation you notice you are going to overshoot your designated point by approximately 150 feet. You are at 200 feet AGL with sufficient airspeed. What technique adjustments can you make to land closer to the point, and what are the limits of those adjustments?
questions.answer: From 200 feet AGL with adequate airspeed, the primary correction is to extend the flare (apply aft cyclic earlier) to bleed airspeed and reduce groundspeed, allowing the helicopter to settle closer to the desired landing point. This must be done carefully to avoid over-flaring, which depletes rotor RPM below the green arc and reduces the inertia available to cushion landing. Alternatively, a shallow S-turn can extend the descent path if the helicopter is aligned to turn toward the point. Forward cyclic should be avoided in this situation as it increases descent rate and reduces glide distance. The pilot must maintain rotor RPM in the green arc throughout all corrections and ensure sufficient energy (altitude and inertia) remains to complete the flare and landing.

questions.question: You are terminating a straight-in autorotation to a hover and realize at 20 feet AGL that your collective application has caused rotor RPM to decay into the low yellow arc. What do you do, and what is the risk if you continue to increase collective?
questions.answer: If rotor RPM decays into the low yellow arc at 20 feet AGL during termination, you must reduce collective slightly to allow rotor RPM to recover, accepting a harder touchdown if necessary. Continuing to increase collective when RPM is decaying further reduces the rotor's ability to generate lift — each degree of collective pitch increases drag on the blades, further slowing RPM in a self-reinforcing decay. The risk is rotor stall: if RPM decays below the minimum, the rotor blades lose the ability to generate sufficient lift and the helicopter descends rapidly with no recovery option. A firm landing on skids is always preferable to rotor stall at 20 feet.

questions.question: On a hot day at a high-density altitude airport, you are practicing straight-in autorotations. How does density altitude affect your ability to terminate to a stabilized hover within 100 feet of the designated point, and what technique adjustments should you anticipate?
questions.answer: High density altitude reduces air density, which has two significant effects on autorotation termination: First, the rotor must work at a higher pitch angle to generate the same lift, which increases induced drag and causes rotor RPM to decay more rapidly when collective is applied. Second, the tail rotor is less effective at high density altitude, requiring greater pedal input to maintain heading during the collective application phase. The pilot should expect to need more rotor RPM entering the flare to have sufficient inertia available for termination, apply collective more judiciously during cushion to avoid rapid RPM decay, and be prepared for the aircraft to require more forward cyclic to stop the groundspeed because translational lift is maintained longer in thinner air. The 100-foot accuracy standard remains the same, but energy management is tighter, and the pilot should brief these factors before the maneuver.

questions.question: During the termination phase of a straight-in autorotation at approximately 10 feet AGL, the aircraft begins to drift left with significant groundspeed remaining. You apply right cyclic to stop the drift but the aircraft continues moving. What sequence of control inputs do you prioritize, and at what point do you abandon the hover termination in favor of a run-on or slide-on landing?
questions.answer: At 10 feet AGL with a left drift and residual groundspeed, the priority sequence is: (1) Apply right cyclic firmly but smoothly to stop lateral movement — this is the primary correction. (2) If the aircraft is decelerating but not stopped, simultaneously increase collective slightly to extend the cushion and buy time for the drift to arrest. (3) Use right pedal as needed to prevent the nose from yawing with the power change. If the drift does not arrest and the aircraft is approaching terrain, obstacles, or the limits of rotor RPM, immediately transition to a controlled run-on or slide-on: level the aircraft fully with cyclic, reduce collective to near-bottom to maintain rotor RPM, and accept a sliding landing on the skids. The decision point is when there is insufficient altitude remaining to stop lateral movement before ground contact — typically when the aircraft is at 3 feet or below with uncorrected drift. A controlled slide is always preferable to a dynamic rollover, which can occur if the skids contact the ground while lateral movement continues.
questions.follow_up: You mentioned dynamic rollover — at what lateral bank angle does dynamic rollover typically become unrecoverable in a helicopter, and what control input is the primary recovery?
questions.follow_up_answer: Dynamic rollover becomes extremely difficult or impossible to recover from once the bank angle exceeds approximately 5 to 8 degrees with a skid on the ground, depending on the helicopter type and whether full opposite cyclic has been applied. The reason is that once the CG passes over the pivot point (the grounded skid), gravity accelerates the roll faster than the cyclic can generate a countering moment. The primary recovery input is immediate opposite cyclic — full if necessary — combined with reducing collective to decrease rotor thrust, which reduces the rolling moment. The FAA emphasizes that if lateral cyclic is already at the stop and the roll is continuing, reducing collective is the critical secondary input. Prevention is always more effective than recovery: the pilot should never allow lateral drift to persist when a skid is near or on the ground.

questions.question: A pilot consistently terminates straight-in autorotations to a hover 80 to 120 feet short of the designated point. As their examiner, what specific technique errors are you looking for as the root cause, and how would you differentiate between a flare timing issue versus a collective application rate issue?
questions.answer: Consistently landing short is typically caused by one or more of the following errors: (1) Initiating the flare too early — the nose rises before reaching the appropriate altitude, which decelerates the aircraft too far from the point. (2) An overly aggressive flare angle — more aft cyclic than necessary wastes groundspeed too early. (3) Applying collective too early during the cushion phase, bleeding rotor RPM and ending the glide prematurely. To differentiate between a flare timing issue and a collective rate issue: watch the aircraft's pitch attitude and altitude at which the flare begins — if the nose rises above approximately 10–15 degrees nose-up while still at 50+ feet AGL and well before the point, the problem is flare timing or angle. If the flare looks appropriate in timing and angle but the aircraft stops flying and descends steeply in the final 20 feet, the collective is being applied too rapidly, converting rotor inertia to lift before the aircraft has translated over the point. In a debrief, I would ask the pilot to describe what visual cues they used to initiate each phase — vague answers ('it felt right') indicate they are guessing rather than applying a repeatable technique tied to specific altitude and airspeed callouts.
questions.follow_up: If after three practice attempts the pilot still cannot consistently terminate within 100 feet, what options do you have as an examiner regarding the continuation of the practical test?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 61.43, if an applicant fails a task — including failing to meet the ACS performance standard of terminating within 100 feet of the designated point — the examiner may discontinue the test at any point and issue a Notice of Disapproval for the tasks not completed or not meeting standards. The examiner is not required to allow multiple attempts beyond what is reasonable to demonstrate the skill. If the task is failed, the applicant may apply for retesting after receiving the necessary additional training, endorsed by their instructor as required by 14 CFR 61.49. Importantly, a single poor attempt does not automatically mean failure — the examiner evaluates the overall demonstration of competency, but if the applicant cannot meet the 100-foot standard after reasonable attempts and demonstrates a clear pattern of the same error, discontinuation and disapproval is appropriate.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR 61.43; 14 CFR 61.49; ACS CH.VIII.B

questions.question: During a go-around following power recovery from a straight-in autorotation, your helicopter enters an unexpected low-G pushover condition as you apply forward cyclic to accelerate. What specific danger does this create that is unique to certain rotor systems, and how does it differ from a conventional low-G event?
questions.answer: A low-G (unloaded rotor) condition during a go-around is particularly dangerous on semi-rigid (teetering) rotor systems because unloading the rotor removes the restoring force that keeps the rotor disk properly oriented relative to the mast. When the rotor is unloaded and the fuselage tilts or yaws — from residual torque, wind, or pilot input — the mast can contact the rotor hub in a phenomenon known as mast bumping, which can sever the rotor from the airframe with catastrophic results. Semi-rigid rotors are especially vulnerable to this geometry because the hub teeter design relies on rotor loading to maintain proper blade-to-mast relationship. Fully articulated rotor systems use a different hub geometry and blade attachment design, so the mast bumping mechanism described for teetering rotors does not apply in the same way; however, articulated systems can experience their own forms of dynamic rotor-to-structure contact under extreme unloaded or unusual flight conditions — the hazards differ by design, and no rotor system is entirely free of risk from severe mast unloading. During a go-around from power recovery, the risk is amplified because: (1) power has just been restored, creating a torque yaw tendency; (2) the pilot may apply abrupt forward cyclic to accelerate, unloading the rotor; (3) low altitude leaves no margin for recovery. The correct response to inadvertent low-G is to apply smooth aft cyclic to reload the rotor disk — lateral cyclic or pedal inputs while the rotor is unloaded can worsen fuselage attitude and must be avoided.
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the overly broad claim that mast bumping risk 'does NOT exist' on articulated systems, replacing it with an accurate explanation that the teetering-rotor mast bumping mechanism differs from articulated rotor dynamics, while acknowledging that no rotor system is entirely free of risk from severe rotor unloading.

questions.question: Cold temperatures are often ignored by pilots during autorotation planning. How does a very cold day — say, minus 20°C — affect the autorotation compared to a standard day at sea level, and could the temperature actually work in your favor?
questions.answer: At very cold temperatures, air density increases above standard, which increases the mass flow through the rotor disk. This denser air produces more lift per unit of blade pitch angle, meaning the rotor generates more aerodynamic force for a given collective setting. As a result, the rotor will tend to run at higher RPM for a given collective position compared to a standard day — the increased aerodynamic damping of denser air acting on each blade keeps energy in the rotor system more efficiently. During the glide phase, the pilot may need to carry slightly less collective pitch than usual to keep RPM within the normal operating range and avoid an overspeed condition. During the flare and cushion, that same dense air means each degree of pitch change is more effective at arresting descent and decelerating the aircraft. Overall, cold dense air genuinely can work in the pilot's favor for autorotation efficiency compared to a hot or high-density-altitude environment — touchdown energy management is improved and the rotor system is more aerodynamically responsive. However, the pilot must remain alert to potential hazards associated with cold weather operations, including carburetor icing in applicable powerplants, rotor blade contamination from frost or ice, reduced lubricant performance, and degraded situational awareness from cold-weather environmental conditions.
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the contradictory claim that increased induced drag 'helps maintain rotor RPM,' and corrected the collective guidance so that it consistently advises carrying less collective (not more) to prevent overspeed when rotor RPM runs higher in cold dense air.

questions.question: What effect does high density altitude have on rotor RPM during an autorotation, and why?
questions.answer: At high density altitude, the air is less dense, meaning there are fewer air molecules per unit volume. With less air mass flowing through the rotor disk, the blades generate less aerodynamic drag per revolution. This reduced drag means there is less resistance to rotor rotation, so rotor RPM tends to build more readily and can run higher than at sea level conditions. The pilot must monitor rotor RPM carefully and may need to use collective adjustments to keep RPM within the proper operating range throughout the autorotative glide, flare, and cushion phases.
questions.rewrite_note: Corrected the fundamental error: high density altitude means less dense air (fewer air molecules), not more dense air, and clarified that reduced aerodynamic drag causes rotor RPM to trend higher rather than lower; also removed the tangential comment about engine restart capability.

tasks.title: Task C. Autorotation with Turns in a Single-Engine Helicopter

questions.question: How does high density altitude affect rotor RPM decay during the entry phase of an autorotation in a single-engine helicopter?
questions.answer: At high density altitude, the air is less dense, which reduces aerodynamic drag on the rotor blades. During the entry phase immediately after engine failure, this reduced drag means the rotor initially experiences slower RPM decay compared to standard density altitude. However, the reduced air density also means the rotor generates less lift at any given pitch angle. Consequently, the pilot must lower collective more aggressively and manage pitch more precisely because there is less margin for error. The net effect is a reduced RPM cushion throughout the autorotation and less tolerance for delayed collective application or aggressive pitch changes. While initial RPM decay may be slower, the overall usable RPM window is tighter, requiring disciplined energy management throughout the descent.

questions.question: All else being equal, how does operating at a higher gross weight affect the rate of descent during an autorotation?
questions.answer: A heavier helicopter descends faster during autorotation. Greater weight means more downward force, which requires a higher rate of descent to generate sufficient airflow up through the rotor disk to sustain rotor RPM and produce the lift needed to support that weight. The increased collective pitch required to maintain RPM at a heavier weight also increases induced drag on the blades, contributing to a steeper descent angle. This results in less time and altitude available to execute turns and reach a landing zone.

questions.question: You're planning a high-altitude mountain flight on a hot summer afternoon. Your helicopter is at max gross weight. During your preflight risk assessment, how would the combination of high density altitude and high gross weight compound the risks specifically during an autorotation with a turn to a landing zone?
questions.answer: This combination creates a compounded risk. High density altitude causes faster initial rotor RPM decay at engine failure and a higher descent rate during the glide. High gross weight independently increases descent rate and requires more collective pitch during the flare, reducing RPM margin further. When combined, the pilot has less time to establish autorotation, the glide ratio is steeper meaning fewer landing zone options, and turns during autorotation must be planned more conservatively because bank angle increases load factor — which at near-maximum gross weight further loads the rotor and can rapidly bleed RPM. The flare and collective pull at touchdown will require precise timing because the energy management window is narrowed on both ends.

questions.question: You experience an engine failure while flying downwind at 500 feet AGL with a 20-knot tailwind. You identify a suitable landing zone directly ahead — which means landing downwind. What are the aerodynamic trade-offs you must consider when deciding whether to turn into the wind or land straight ahead with the tailwind?
questions.answer: Landing straight ahead with a 20-knot tailwind means your groundspeed at touchdown will be significantly higher, increasing the risk of dynamic rollover, loss of directional control, or running off a suitable surface. However, executing a 180-degree turn at 500 feet AGL consumes both altitude and rotor RPM — especially problematic if density altitude is elevated or the helicopter is at higher gross weight. The pilot must assess whether sufficient altitude exists to complete the turn while maintaining rotor RPM within limits, whether the landing surface ahead is adequate for a higher-speed touchdown, and whether the wind is consistent. If the turn cannot be safely completed, landing downwind with a controlled deceleration using cyclic and collective may be preferable to an attempted turn that depletes RPM before reaching the flare point.

questions.question: During an autorotation practice at a high-elevation airport on a cold winter morning versus a hot summer afternoon, your instructor tells you the rotor RPM will behave differently during the flare at each. Why is that, and which condition requires more caution?
questions.answer: Cold air is denser than hot air, so on a cold morning the density altitude is lower. Denser air creates more aerodynamic force on the rotor blades for a given pitch and RPM, meaning the rotor is more responsive and easier to maintain within the green arc. During the flare, the increased aerodynamic braking on dense air helps sustain RPM as collective is raised. On a hot afternoon, density altitude is higher, air is less dense, the rotor produces less aerodynamic braking effect, and RPM decays more readily during the flare. The hot afternoon condition requires more caution — the pilot must be more precise with collective timing during the flare and touchdown, since the RPM buffer is smaller and recovery from an RPM excursion below minimum is more difficult.

questions.question: During an autorotation with a 180-degree turn, a student adds excessive bank angle in an attempt to tighten the turn and reach a landing zone. At a higher gross weight, why is this particularly dangerous, and at what point in the autorotation sequence is the consequence most severe?
questions.answer: Increasing bank angle in a turn increases load factor — at 60 degrees of bank, load factor doubles. In an autorotation, the rotor system is already managing a careful energy balance: rotor RPM is sustained by upward airflow through the disk, and the pilot is managing pitch to stay within the RPM green arc. When load factor increases due to steep bank, the rotor requires more lift to support the aircraft, which means either RPM increases (if pitch is held) or — more critically — if collective is held constant, rotor RPM can increase beyond the green arc. Conversely, if the pilot instinctively raises collective to control RPM or altitude, drag on the blades increases and RPM decays rapidly. At high gross weight, the rotor is already working harder to sustain lift, so RPM margins are smaller. The most dangerous point is the flare and collective application at the bottom of the autorotation — if RPM has been depleted during an aggressive steep turn, there is insufficient rotor energy stored to cushion the landing. Recovery from low RPM below minimum at that altitude is not possible.
questions.follow_up: If the student's rotor RPM goes above the red line during that steep turn, what is the immediate corrective action and what structural concern exists?
questions.follow_up_answer: The immediate corrective action is to raise the collective to increase blade pitch, which adds aerodynamic drag on the rotor and absorbs the excess RPM, bringing it back into the green arc. The pilot should also reduce bank angle to lower load factor. The structural concern is that excessive rotor RPM can cause centrifugal stress beyond design limits on the blade retention and hub components, and at extreme overspeed, blade flexing and tracking can become erratic. Additionally, in a steep banked turn with high RPM, retreating blade stall can be approached more quickly as the advancing blade sees higher relative airspeed. The manufacturer's RPM limits in the rotorcraft flight manual are absolute and must not be exceeded.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11; 14 CFR 27.309 (design load limits for normal category rotorcraft)

questions.question: A crosswind is present during an autorotation with a turn. The pilot is executing a 90-degree turn to align with a landing zone. How does the crosswind affect rotor RPM management and landing zone judgment during the turn, and what adjustment in technique is required?
questions.answer: A crosswind introduces asymmetric inflow across the rotor disk during the turn. As the helicopter rotates through the turn, one portion of the arc has the wind assisting airflow through the rotor, while another portion has the wind disrupting or reducing effective inflow. This means rotor RPM can fluctuate during the turn as the relative wind changes angle to the disk. Additionally, the pilot's groundspeed and drift will vary throughout the turn, making landing zone alignment less predictable. When turning into the wind, the groundspeed decreases but the rotor may see increased airflow; when the turn takes the helicopter temporarily downwind, groundspeed increases and rotor inflow may decrease slightly. The required adjustment is to anticipate these changes by being prepared for minor RPM fluctuations and compensating with small collective adjustments, use visual cues to track actual ground position rather than relying on airspeed alone for glide range calculation, and plan to roll out slightly into the wind to achieve a favorable final ground track. The pilot should also account for drift during the flare to avoid touching down in a sideward drift condition.
questions.follow_up: If the crosswind is directly from the left during the final approach phase of the autorotation, what specific rotor aerodynamic phenomenon becomes a concern and how does it relate to LTE risk at low altitude?
questions.follow_up_answer: A left crosswind during final approach at low airspeed creates a condition where the tail rotor may be operating in an unfavorable aerodynamic environment. As airspeed decreases through ETL during the approach, the helicopter becomes more susceptible to loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE). A wind from the left at approximately 270 degrees relative to the nose (left quartering tailwind relative to the nose) can cause weathervaning tendency and reduce tail rotor thrust effectiveness. In autorotation, the pilot has limited power options to counteract an uncommanded yaw — there is no engine power to increase tail rotor thrust by raising collective (since in autorotation collective is managed for RPM, not power). If LTE begins at low altitude during the final phase of an autorotation, recovery options are extremely limited. The pilot must anticipate this by maintaining airspeed slightly higher on final to preserve tail rotor authority, complete the turn to align with the wind before descending through ETL, and be prepared to immediately apply right pedal if yaw begins.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11 (LTE); Chapter 11 (Autorotation); FAA AC 90-95 (LTE awareness)

questions.question: What does Nr stand for, and what does it represent in helicopter operations?
questions.answer: Nr stands for rotor RPM, specifically the rotational speed of the main rotor system. It is a critical parameter that indicates how fast the main rotor blades are spinning, directly affecting the rotor's ability to generate lift. Maintaining Nr within the green arc (normal operating range) is essential for controlled flight, especially during autorotation when engine power is no longer driving the rotor.

questions.question: What is the primary control input used to manage Nr during an autorotation, and in what direction is it moved to prevent rotor RPM from decaying?
questions.answer: The collective is the primary control for managing Nr during autorotation. When rotor RPM begins to decay (Nr drops), the pilot should lower the collective to reduce the pitch angle of the rotor blades. This decreases drag on the rotor system and allows the upward airflow through the disk to accelerate the blades, restoring and maintaining Nr within limits. Raising the collective increases blade pitch and drag, which will cause Nr to decrease.

questions.question: Why is it critical to lower the collective immediately at the onset of engine failure in a helicopter?
questions.answer: When an engine fails, the torque driving the main rotor is lost and the load on the rotor (supporting the weight of the helicopter) will rapidly consume rotor energy, causing Nr to decay quickly. Lowering the collective immediately reduces the blade pitch angle, which reduces lift and drag on the rotor system. This allows the upward airflow through the decelerating rotor disk to sustain and then recover Nr.
