questions.answer: An aggressive flare with excessive aft cyclic in a two-bladed semi-rigid or teetering rotor system creates the risk of mast bumping, particularly if a low-G condition is momentarily encountered as the nose pitches up. Even in fully articulated systems, an extreme flare can cause the tail rotor to approach or contact the ground if altitude is insufficient. Additionally, an aggressive flare followed by rapid forward cyclic to level the aircraft before collective application risks a push-over into a low-G condition. The pilot must apply aft cyclic firmly but progressively, level the helicopter with coordinated forward cyclic before collective application, and avoid any unloading of the rotor system during the transition. Aircraft flight manual limitations on cyclic travel and rotor disk unloading must be respected.
questions.follow_up: If mast bumping occurred during the flare recovery of an autorotation, what is the post-incident requirement before the aircraft can fly again, and who has authority to make that determination?
questions.follow_up_answer: Mast bumping is considered a hard landing or abnormal stress event requiring an airworthiness inspection before further flight. The aircraft must be grounded and inspected by a certificated FAA-authorized mechanic (A&P) or, depending on the scope of inspection, an authorized inspector (IA) or the manufacturer's representative. The pilot in command has authority and legal obligation under 14 CFR 91.7 to ensure airworthiness before flight, but the actual mechanical determination of airworthiness must be made by an appropriately certificated maintenance professional. Mast bumping can cause internal damage to the mast, Jesus bolt, hub, and rotor head that may not be visually apparent, making a thorough inspection mandatory.

questions.question: During a power recovery from an autorotation, at what point should you begin increasing collective to arrest your descent rate before touchdown?
questions.answer: Power recovery should be initiated at a low enough altitude to complete the flare and arrest descent before touchdown, typically when the helicopter has decelerated through ETL and is at low airspeed and low altitude—commonly between 8 and 15 feet AGL depending on the aircraft. The collective is raised smoothly to arrest descent while cyclic is used to level the aircraft and control ground speed. The exact altitude depends on the specific aircraft's flight manual and available power.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for specific aircraft

questions.question: What is the definition of a go-around in the context of a helicopter autorotation with turns, and when is it appropriate to execute one?
questions.answer: A go-around is the decision to abandon a continued approach or power recovery and restore powered flight to climb away from the landing area. In the context of autorotation with turns, a go-around is appropriate when the selected landing area becomes unsuitable—due to obstacles, unfavorable winds, deteriorating surface conditions, or improper approach angle—and sufficient altitude and rotor RPM remain to restore power and climb safely. It must be initiated early enough that the engine and rotor system can spool up and provide adequate thrust before ground contact.

questions.question: During the power recovery phase of an autorotation, what happens to rotor RPM as you raise the collective, and why is this significant?
questions.answer: As collective is raised during power recovery, blade pitch increases, which increases drag on the rotor system and causes rotor RPM to decay. This is significant because the rotor must be within its normal operating RPM range before collective is applied—if RPM is too low when collective is raised, the rotor may not generate sufficient lift to arrest the descent, potentially leading to a hard landing or rotor stall. The pilot must monitor rotor RPM throughout the autorotation and ensure it is within limits before initiating the power recovery.

questions.question: You are practicing autorotation with turns in a confined area. During the final turn to align with the landing zone, you notice you are high and fast with limited distance remaining. Walk me through your risk assessment for proceeding with power recovery versus executing a go-around.
questions.answer: The key risk factors to assess are: (1) Available rotor RPM—is it within the normal operating range to support either a power recovery or go-around? (2) Altitude and airspeed—being high and fast means the descent rate may be difficult to arrest before reaching the landing zone boundary, increasing risk of overshooting or landing with excessive ground speed. (3) Available power—can the engine provide sufficient power for a go-around climb given density altitude and aircraft weight? (4) Obstacles on the go-around path—are there obstacles that would compromise a climb-out? If rotor RPM is good and sufficient engine power and altitude exist to safely climb away, the go-around is the lower-risk choice. Continuing a power recovery when high and fast risks running out of landing area or touching down with uncontrolled energy. The go-around decision must be made early—committing too late removes the option entirely.

questions.question: During autorotation with a 180-degree turn, you roll out on final and realize your rotor RPM has decayed to the low end of the green arc due to excessive collective application during the turn. How does this affect your power recovery options and what are the risks?
questions.answer: Low rotor RPM at the end of a turning autorotation is a serious hazard. With RPM at the low end of the green arc, the pilot has reduced margin before entering an unrecoverable rotor stall. Raising collective to arrest descent will further decay RPM, potentially driving it into the red or below. The pilot must first allow the rotor to recover RPM—using aft cyclic to increase upward airflow through the disk and ensuring collective is fully lowered—before attempting power recovery. The risk is a race between altitude loss and RPM recovery. If too low to allow RPM recovery before ground contact, a hard landing or dynamic rollover becomes likely. A go-around may not be viable if the engine cannot restore RPM fast enough or if altitude is insufficient. Early recognition of decaying RPM during the turn is critical to prevent this situation.

questions.question: You are performing a power recovery from autorotation and apply collective, but the engine response is sluggish and you sense the helicopter is not going to arrest its descent before the surface. What are your options and what risk factors drove you to this point?
questions.answer: If collective is raised and the engine is not providing adequate power to arrest descent in time, the pilot must immediately assess whether a run-on landing is feasible—using forward cyclic to convert descent energy into translational movement and reduce the vertical velocity component. If the surface allows, a run-on landing reduces impact energy significantly. The pilot should avoid an abrupt full-collective application as this can further decay rotor RPM and result in a harder impact. Risk factors that drove this scenario include: (1) engine deterioration or partial power loss not detected before initiating recovery; (2) density altitude or weight exceeding available power margin; (3) delayed power recovery initiation leaving insufficient altitude; (4) rotor RPM that was already at the low limit before collective was raised. Thorough pre-maneuver power checks and awareness of aircraft performance limits are the primary mitigations.

questions.question: A student executes the turning portion of the autorotation correctly but consistently initiates power recovery too late—at 5 feet AGL instead of the recommended altitude—arguing that a lower recovery gives a more realistic feel. As their instructor and as a risk management matter, what specific hazards does this habit create, and how would you address it with them before the checkride?
questions.answer: Initiating power recovery consistently at 5 feet AGL creates compounding risk factors: (1) There is minimal time and altitude to arrest descent rate before ground contact if collective response, engine spool-up, or rotor RPM is even slightly suboptimal—any variability in technique or aircraft performance becomes immediately consequential. (2) If rotor RPM has decayed even slightly during the maneuver, there is no altitude margin to allow recovery before touchdown, risking a hard landing. (3) At 5 feet, a go-around option is essentially eliminated—the pilot is committed regardless of what they observe on the approach. (4) In real emergencies, landing surfaces are rarely prepared; a late recovery over uneven terrain, obstacles, or soft ground significantly increases injury and damage risk. Addressing this with the student involves demonstrating the mathematical relationship between descent rate and altitude needed to arrest it, using the RFM data. The student must understand that the 'realistic feel' they seek is not aligned with risk management principles—the ACS evaluates judgment and consistency, not bravado. I would use scenario-based training showing consequences of late recovery with any single variable degraded.
questions.follow_up: If your student's aircraft has a low-inertia rotor system, how does that specifically change the altitude at which you'd recommend initiating power recovery, and what does the RFM typically say about this?
questions.follow_up_answer: Low-inertia rotor systems have less stored rotational energy than high-inertia systems, meaning rotor RPM decays significantly faster once collective is raised. This demands that power recovery be initiated at a higher altitude than aircraft with heavy rotor systems, because the pilot has less time between the onset of RPM decay and the point where the rotor can no longer generate sufficient lift. The RFM will specify the power recovery altitude range, minimum rotor RPM for collective application, and the autorotation RPM band unique to that aircraft. Some light turbine helicopters with low-inertia rotors require recovery to begin several feet higher than piston trainers. A student must study their specific RFM and understand why those numbers exist—not extrapolate from experience in a different aircraft type.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft-specific RFM; ACS CH.VIII.C

questions.question: During a checkride, an applicant completes the turning autorotation and executes a go-around, but during the go-around climb they fail to adjust pedals for the power change and enter a significant left yaw (counterclockwise rotor system). What risk does this specific control failure create in the go-around context, and what would you expect to see as a corrective sequence?
questions.answer: During a go-around from autorotation, engine power is increased rapidly, which dramatically increases main rotor torque reaction. On a counterclockwise rotor system, this torque reaction yaws the nose left. Failure to add right pedal to counteract this results in an uncontrolled left yaw. The risks include: (1) Loss of directional control during a critical low-altitude, low-airspeed phase of flight; (2) The uncontrolled yaw can cause the helicopter to weathervane away from the intended climb path, potentially placing it into obstacles; (3) At low airspeed, excessive yaw can lead to loss of translational lift on one side of the disk and aggravate dynamic instability; (4) In extreme cases, uncontrolled yaw with forward cyclic applied can cause a loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE) condition. The correct sequence is: as throttle and collective are advanced for go-around, simultaneously add right pedal proportional to the power increase to maintain heading—monitoring the slip/ball indicator or yaw cue—then establish a positive climb attitude with cyclic. The applicant's failure to coordinate the power addition with pedal input suggests a gap in understanding the relationship between power and torque management, which is an ACS deficiency in risk management.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant justifies the left yaw by saying 'I was going to correct it once I confirmed a positive rate of climb,' how do you evaluate that justification against the ACS standards?
questions.follow_up_answer: That justification is not acceptable under the ACS risk management standards. The go-around from a low-altitude autorotation does not afford the luxury of sequential corrections—the power application and pedal input must be simultaneous because the yaw begins the instant torque increases. Waiting until a positive rate of climb is confirmed means accepting several seconds of uncontrolled directional movement in the most vulnerable phase of the maneuver. The ACS expects the applicant to demonstrate proper coordination throughout the go-around, not recover from self-induced control failures. This reveals a reactive rather than anticipatory control philosophy, which is a deeper knowledge gap. As an examiner, I would note this as a deficiency and probe whether the applicant understands the cause-and-effect relationship between collective/throttle input and torque compensation—not just how to react to yaw after it occurs.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (torque effect), Chapter 11 (go-around); ACS CH.VIII.C Risk Management; 14 CFR 61.43

questions.question: During an autorotation, what is the single highest-priority task for the pilot immediately following engine failure, and why does everything else come second?
questions.answer: The immediate priority is lowering the collective to reduce blade pitch, preserve rotor RPM, and establish upward airflow through the rotor disk. Rotor RPM decay is rapid — especially in low-inertia rotor systems — and an unrecoverable rotor stall can result within seconds if this action is delayed. All other tasks (radio calls, troubleshooting, passenger advisories) are secondary because without adequate rotor RPM, no other action matters.

questions.question: What is situational awareness, and why is it particularly challenging to maintain during an autorotation that includes turns?
questions.answer: Situational awareness is the accurate, real-time perception of your position, altitude, airspeed, rotor RPM, and the environment around you, and the ability to project how those factors are changing. During a turning autorotation, the pilot must simultaneously manage rotor RPM via collective, control bank angle and heading with cyclic, maintain trim with pedals, monitor altitude loss, and plan a landing site. The high workload and rapid altitude loss compress the time available for each task, making it easy to fixate on one element — such as the turn — and lose awareness of others, like rotor RPM decay or proximity to obstacles.

questions.question: What is the definition of disorientation in a flight context, and name one scenario during a turning autorotation where spatial disorientation is most likely to occur?
questions.answer: Disorientation occurs when a pilot's sensory inputs — primarily from the vestibular system — conflict with actual aircraft attitude or position, leading to inaccurate perception of the helicopter's state. During a turning autorotation, spatial disorientation is most likely when the maneuver is initiated abruptly from cruise airspeed: the combination of rapid deceleration (aft cyclic), bank angle, and descent creates conflicting sensory cues. A pilot may perceive a pitch-up or a turn in the opposite direction, leading to incorrect control inputs at the worst possible moment.

questions.question: You are practicing autorotations at 700 feet AGL. Your passenger suddenly shouts that smoke is coming from the instrument panel. How do you prioritize tasks, and what is the risk if you divert attention away from flying the autorotation?
questions.answer: The priority sequence is: aviate, navigate, communicate — in that order. The autorotation demands full attention because you are already in a time-critical, altitude-limited emergency. You must maintain rotor RPM, control the flight path, and plan the landing. Turning to address the passenger or investigate the smoke could cause rotor RPM decay, a missed turn, or target fixation on the wrong landing zone. At 700 feet AGL, you have very little margin for error. The correct approach is to verbally acknowledge the passenger with a brief command ('hold on, hands off controls'), continue flying the autorotation to a safe landing, and address the secondary emergency after touchdown.

questions.question: During a practice autorotation with a 180-degree turn, a student becomes fixated on tracking the landing spot through the turn and stops cross-checking rotor RPM. At what point in the maneuver is this fixation most dangerous, and what are the consequences?
questions.answer: Fixation on the landing spot is most dangerous in the final phase of the turn when altitude is lowest and rotor RPM is most sensitive to collective position. If the student inadvertently raises collective while maneuvering — to correct altitude or bank — rotor RPM will decrease. With little altitude remaining, there is insufficient time and energy to recover RPM before touchdown. The consequence is a hard landing or rotor stall, both potentially fatal. The student must maintain a disciplined instrument scan that includes rotor RPM throughout the entire maneuver, not just during straight segments.

questions.question: How does a low-inertia rotor system specifically increase the risk of loss of situational awareness leading to rotor stall during a turning autorotation, compared to a high-inertia system?
questions.answer: Low-inertia rotor systems store less kinetic energy and therefore decay in RPM much faster when blade pitch is increased or autorotative flow is disrupted. During a turning autorotation, a pilot managing bank angle and heading may make small collective adjustments or allow inadvertent collective creep. In a high-inertia system, there is more time before RPM drops into the danger zone, giving the pilot a broader window to correct. In a low-inertia system, the same inputs can drive RPM into an unrecoverable stall within seconds. This compresses the time available for the pilot to recognize the problem, meaning a momentary lapse in situational awareness — such as fixating on the landing zone during the turn — can be fatal before the pilot realizes the RPM has bled off.

questions.question: A pilot transitioning from fixed-wing to helicopters has strong instrument scan habits but during turning autorotations consistently loses track of their position relative to the intended landing spot. What underlying cognitive mechanism explains this, and how would you address it in training?
questions.answer: The underlying mechanism is attentional tunneling combined with an instrument-scan habit that was optimized for a different task architecture. Fixed-wing pilots are trained to prioritize the attitude indicator and altitude — inside references — during instrument flight. In a turning autorotation, the critical references shift dynamically between the rotor tachometer (inside), the bank angle (inside), and the landing spot and obstacle clearance (outside), all on a compressed timeline. The pilot's ingrained scan pattern doesn't naturally include the outside spatial relationship to the landing area. The result is loss of situational awareness about position and turn completion. In training, this is addressed by first teaching the maneuver at altitude with power-on turns to build the visual-spatial habit of tracking the landing zone relative to aircraft position, then reintroducing the full autorotation with explicit callout checkpoints ('halfway through the turn,' 'rolling out on final') to externalize situational awareness until the scan becomes integrated.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot enters IMC inadvertently during a real autorotation following an engine failure at night, what is the highest-order risk and what is the recommended recovery philosophy?
questions.follow_up_answer: The highest-order risk is spatial disorientation leading to uncontrolled flight into terrain, because the pilot can no longer use visual references to manage the turn, altitude, or landing zone. The recommended philosophy is to prioritize aircraft control using instruments — attitude indicator for bank, rotor tachometer for RPM, VSI for descent rate — over attempting to locate or maneuver toward a specific landing spot. A controlled landing in an unknown area is survivable; spatial disorientation and rotor stall are not. The pilot should transition to instruments immediately, roll wings level, maintain best glide airspeed (per the RFM), and accept whatever terrain is below rather than attempting a turning maneuver to reach a specific zone without visual reference.

questions.question: During a checkride, a candidate is executing a 180-degree autorotation and at the completion of the turn you say, 'tell me your altitude, rotor RPM, and airspeed right now.' The candidate hesitates and cannot answer. What does this tell you as an examiner, and how does it reflect on the risk management standard for this task?
questions.answer: The inability to provide an immediate answer reveals that the candidate was not maintaining a continuous cross-check of critical flight parameters — they were managing control inputs reactively rather than flying with integrated situational awareness. From a risk management perspective, this is a direct failure to manage loss of situational awareness as required by this ACS element. In a real emergency, not knowing your altitude, rotor RPM, or airspeed during a turning autorotation means you cannot make informed decisions about when to complete the turn, whether to extend the glide, or when to begin the flare. This reflects a task prioritization problem: the candidate was prioritizing control manipulation over monitoring, when both must happen simultaneously. As an examiner, this warrants further evaluation and likely remedial training before certification.
questions.follow_up: If you ask the candidate to demonstrate the maneuver again and this time they correctly report all three values, but their rotor RPM is 5% below the bottom of the green arc, do they pass or fail, and what is the regulatory and safety basis for your decision?
questions.follow_up_answer: The candidate fails. Operating below the minimum rotor RPM specified in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual represents operation outside the approved flight envelope, which constitutes a safety of flight issue regardless of how well the candidate verbalized parameters. The FAA-H-8083-21B explicitly states that rotor stall in helicopters is not recoverable, and early recognition of low RPM is imperative. From a regulatory standpoint, the pilot in command is required under 14 CFR 91.9 to comply with aircraft operating limitations, which includes rotor RPM limits. Operating below the green arc even momentarily during an already-emergency condition (autorotation) demonstrates failure to maintain aircraft control within safe parameters, which is an independent basis for unsatisfactory performance on any ACS task.

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns, at what point in the maneuver are you expected to complete the engine-failure emergency checklist?
questions.answer: After establishing the autorotation and stabilizing the descent — once the aircraft is under control and you have a landing area selected. The priority sequence is aviate, navigate, communicate, then checklists. You do not attempt checklist items while still fighting for control of the aircraft.

questions.question: What is the purpose of completing a checklist during an autorotation, and why doesn't the checklist replace immediate corrective action?
questions.answer: Checklists confirm that all required actions have been accomplished in the correct sequence and that nothing is missed under stress. They do not replace immediate corrective action because the first priority upon engine failure is to lower collective and establish autorotation to preserve rotor RPM — a delay of even one second can result in rotor RPM decay that is unrecoverable. The checklist formalizes and verifies actions already taken.

questions.question: Name at least three items typically found on a helicopter engine-failure-in-flight emergency checklist that would apply during an autorotation.
questions.answer: Typical items include: (1) Collective — lower immediately to maintain rotor RPM; (2) Throttle — confirm engine failure, check for partial power; (3) Mayday call — declare emergency on current frequency; (4) Transponder — squawk 7700; (5) Fuel — confirm fuel shutoff valve open or closed per manufacturer's guidance; (6) Landing area — select suitable site. Specific items vary by aircraft make and model as published in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM).
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft-specific RFM Emergency Procedures

questions.question: You are practicing an autorotation with a 180-degree turn to a landing area. You complete the turn and stabilize on final at 500 feet AGL. At this point, your examiner asks you what checklist items remain. Walk me through how you would handle that without compromising aircraft control.
questions.answer: At 500 feet AGL on final, the workload is high and the landing is imminent — full checklist completion at this point is inappropriate. I would verbalize that the immediate-action items (collective down, rotor RPM confirmed in green, landing area selected) were completed at entry. If time and altitude permitted during the descent, I would have confirmed throttle position, declared Mayday, and set the transponder to 7700. Below approximately 500 feet, my focus is entirely on aircraft control, flare timing, and landing execution. Any remaining checklist items would be addressed after landing.

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns, you attempt to run through the engine-failure checklist but realize you skipped the transponder step. You are now at 800 feet AGL established on a straight-in glide. What do you do, and what does this tell you about checklist discipline?
questions.answer: At 800 feet AGL with the aircraft stabilized and a suitable landing area ahead, there is sufficient altitude to quickly set the transponder to 7700 without compromising aircraft control — I would do so now. This situation highlights the importance of memory items versus reference checklists: immediate-action memory items must be drilled to automaticity so nothing is missed under stress. A skipped step during a high-workload phase is a sign that checklist flows need more practice until they are habitual.

questions.question: Your training helicopter's RFM lists engine-failure checklist items in a specific sequence. During the checkride, you complete them in a different order because of workload during the turn. How would you justify or defend that deviation to an examiner?
questions.answer: The RFM sequence is designed for normal progression of the emergency, but aviate always comes first. I would explain that aviate-navigate-communicate-checklist is the universally accepted priority framework, and that during the turn — with changing airspeed, altitude, and rotor RPM to monitor — I deferred certain checklist steps until the aircraft was stabilized. I would then confirm that all required items were eventually completed before landing. A logical deviation driven by workload prioritization is acceptable; missing items entirely or completing them in a way that introduces new hazards is not.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft RFM Emergency Procedures section

questions.question: A student consistently completes the engine-failure checklist correctly during straight-in autorotations but forgets steps when a turn is added. What aerodynamic and physiological factors likely explain this, and how would you address it in training?
questions.answer: During a turning autorotation, the pilot's cognitive workload spikes because they must simultaneously manage rotor RPM, rate of turn, altitude, airspeed, and landing area geometry — all dynamically changing. Physiologically, working memory has limited capacity, and procedural memory (checklist recall) is the first task degraded under increased attentional demand. Aerodynamically, turns increase blade loading and can cause rotor RPM to fluctuate, demanding more active collective management which further competes for attention. The fix in training is to first drill checklist items to the level of automaticity through chair flying and repetition, then reintroduce turns at lower workload thresholds, progressively increasing complexity. The goal is to make the checklist a background task while primary aircraft control remains dominant.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot's rotor RPM decays during the turn while they are attempting to run the checklist, what does that tell you about their task prioritization, and what is the immediate correct action?
questions.follow_up_answer: It tells you the pilot has inverted their priorities — they are managing a piece of paper instead of the aircraft. Rotor RPM decay during autorotation is an immediate emergency within an emergency. The correct action is to immediately lower collective if not already at bottom, check that the turn rate is not excessive (steeper bank increases blade loading and can accelerate RPM decay), and if necessary, reduce the bank angle to reduce load on the rotor system. Checklist completion stops entirely until RPM is restored to the green arc. This is a potential unsatisfactory event on a checkride and a serious safety issue in actual flight.

questions.question: During a 180-degree autorotation turning to landing, you complete all memory items, call Mayday, and set 7700. On rollout, you realize you still have a checklist item that requires a switch action — one that the RFM says should be completed before touchdown. You are now at 300 feet AGL. What is your decision-making process?
questions.answer: At 300 feet AGL, the flare is imminent and the approach geometry is critical. I would assess whether the switch action is truly safety-critical before touchdown — for example, fuel shutoff or ignition — or administrative. If it is a safety-critical action (such as arming floats on a water landing or confirming fuel shutoff to prevent post-crash fire), I would complete it immediately with one hand while maintaining collective and cyclic with the other, accepting the brief degradation in control precision. If it is not immediately safety-critical, I would defer it until after landing and aircraft shutdown. In all cases, I would not allow the checklist item to distract me from the flare and collective pull at the correct altitude — a botched flare at 300 feet is fatal; a missed switch action may be manageable. After landing, the remaining checklist is completed before exiting the aircraft.
questions.follow_up: The RFM says to complete that checklist item before touchdown, but doing so at 300 feet creates a control risk. Who has final authority over that decision, and what regulation supports your answer?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot in command has final authority. Under 14 CFR 91.3(b), the PIC may deviate from any rule to the extent necessary to meet an emergency. If following the RFM checklist sequence to the letter creates a greater hazard than deferring an item, the PIC is both authorized and responsible for making that judgment call. The RFM establishes the manufacturer's recommended sequence under normal emergency conditions, but it cannot anticipate every scenario. The PIC's obligation is to exercise sound aeronautical decision-making to ensure the safest outcome.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3(b); Aircraft RFM Emergency Procedures; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: During a simulated autorotation with turns, what is the most critical radio call you should make, and to whom?
questions.answer: The most critical call is a MAYDAY or PAN-PAN distress/urgency call on the appropriate frequency — typically the controlling facility frequency you're already on, or 121.5 MHz if no other contact exists. You would identify your aircraft, state the emergency (engine failure), your position, altitude, and intentions. In a training environment, the call is coordinated with the instructor, but the applicant must demonstrate knowledge of what an actual emergency call would contain.

questions.question: What information should be included in a standard emergency radio call following an engine failure in a helicopter?
questions.answer: A complete emergency radio call should include: aircraft identification (call sign/tail number), nature of the emergency (engine failure), aircraft position (bearing and distance from a known fix, or GPS coordinates), altitude, number of persons on board, and your intentions (autorotating to a specific landing area). This follows the standard MAYDAY format: 'MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY, [call sign], engine failure, [position], [altitude], [POB], landing [location].'

questions.question: On what frequency should you broadcast a MAYDAY call if you have already lost communication with your controlling ATC facility during an autorotation?
questions.answer: You should transmit on 121.5 MHz, the international aeronautical emergency frequency, which is monitored by ATC facilities, most airliners, military aircraft, and emergency services. This is the guard frequency and represents the best chance of reaching someone who can render assistance when primary ATC contact is lost.

questions.question: You're conducting a practice autorotation at a non-towered airport in a traffic pattern with other aircraft. Your instructor initiates a simulated engine failure at 800 feet AGL while you are on downwind. Walk me through your radio communication priorities from that moment through touchdown.
questions.answer: Aviate is the first priority — immediately lower collective, establish best glide/autorotation attitude, and identify a landing area. Once the helicopter is stabilized, communicate: broadcast on CTAF (Common Traffic Advisory Frequency) something like '[Airport] traffic, [N-number], simulated emergency, autorotating to [runway/field], [airport].' This alerts pattern traffic to give way. During the turn phase, if you identify a conflict with other traffic, make an additional call. Near the bottom of the autorotation, no further radio work is needed — focus on the flare and collective management. In a real emergency, you would also squawk 7700 on the transponder as part of your workload, but radio calls and aircraft control take priority over transponder changes.

questions.question: You're operating at a towered airport and your instructor simulates an engine failure on the crosswind leg at 600 feet AGL. The tower has not cleared you to land. What radio action do you take, and does the tower's clearance affect your authority to land?
questions.answer: Immediately declare the emergency on the tower frequency: 'MAYDAY, [call sign], simulated — or actual — engine failure, autorotating runway [number].' However, in an actual emergency, 14 CFR 91.3 gives the pilot-in-command the authority to deviate from any regulation to the extent necessary to meet the emergency — including landing without a clearance. The tower's clearance is not required in an actual emergency. You land where and when the autorotation dictates. After landing, you may be required to submit a written report to ATC if you deviated from an ATC clearance. In a training scenario, the instructor should have coordinated with the tower before the maneuver, but the applicant should demonstrate awareness of this authority.

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns, your workload is extremely high — you're managing rotor RPM, selecting a landing zone, and executing a 180-degree turn. At what point in the maneuver should radio calls fit into your task prioritization, and why?
questions.answer: Radio calls fall into the 'communicate' phase of the aviate-navigate-communicate hierarchy. During the critical entry phase — first 5–10 seconds — your entire focus must be on lowering collective, maintaining rotor RPM, and establishing the autorotation attitude. Once the rotor is stabilized and a landing area is confirmed, a brief radio call is appropriate. During the turn itself, if you experience rotor RPM excursions or need corrective control inputs, radio communication is deferred again. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that rotor stall is not recoverable, so RPM management always takes absolute precedence. In a training environment, demonstrating the correct prioritization — controlling the aircraft first, communicating second — is what the examiner is evaluating.

questions.question: You are conducting an autorotation with turns and your transponder is already set to 1200. Walk me through whether and when you change it to 7700 during the emergency, and what the practical tradeoffs are in a low-altitude autorotation.
questions.answer: Squawking 7700 activates an automatic alert at ATC that immediately flags your aircraft as an emergency, enabling radar identification and priority handling. However, in a low-altitude autorotation — particularly one involving turns and RPM management — the time cost of reaching for the transponder and dialing in 7700 must be weighed against the short time available before touchdown. The FAA and AIM advise pilots to squawk 7700 when possible, but never at the expense of aircraft control. If you are below 500 feet AGL in an autorotation and fully occupied with rotor RPM, landing zone selection, and flare timing, the transponder change is deferred. If you have a moment of stable flight — for example, early in a high-altitude autorotation — squawking 7700 before or immediately after your radio call is appropriate. The priority remains: aviate, navigate, communicate, then transponder.
questions.follow_up: If ATC already has you on radar and you squawk 7700, what specific capabilities does that give them beyond knowing you're in an emergency?
questions.follow_up_answer: When a pilot squawks 7700, ATC receives an automatic alarm and the radar target is tagged with 'EMER' on the controller's display. This allows ATC to immediately identify your position without requiring radio contact, vector other traffic away from your location, coordinate with emergency services on the ground (alerting rescue/fire/crash teams at or near your intended landing area), and provide the pilot with any available assistance such as nearest airport or open area information. For a helicopter in autorotation, ATC can also relay your position to local law enforcement or EMS, which can significantly reduce rescue response time after landing.

questions.question: Your autorotation with turns is going well, but after landing you realize you deviated from your ATC clearance to reach your landing area. What are your post-landing radio and reporting obligations, and is there any protection for you under the FAA's Aviation Safety Reporting System?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.3(b), if the Administrator or ATC requests a written report of the emergency deviation, you must submit it. Separately, under 14 CFR 91.25 and FAA AC 00-46F, you may file a NASA Aviation Safety Report (ASRS) within 10 days of the incident; this provides immunity from civil penalty for inadvertent violations. ASRS immunity does not apply to deliberate violations, accidents, or certificate enforcement actions under 14 CFR 91.13 (careless/reckless operation). After landing, notify ATC immediately of your status and location. Filing an ASRS report proactively within 10 days provides a layer of protection and contributes to the safety database, but does not shield you from enforcement if the deviation resulted from your own carelessness or deliberate conduct.
questions.follow_up: Does filing an ASRS report protect you if the FAA determines the emergency was the result of your own careless or reckless operation — for example, you ran out of fuel?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. The ASRS immunity provision under 14 CFR 91.25 and FAA Advisory Circular 00-46F does not apply when the violation was deliberate, or when it is related to an accident. Additionally, while a fuel exhaustion situation may qualify for ASRS immunity for the deviation from ATC clearance itself, the FAA can still pursue certificate action under 14 CFR 91.13 (careless or reckless operation) separately from the ATC deviation. ASRS protects against civil penalties for inadvertent violations, not against all enforcement actions arising from the same event. A pilot who allowed fuel exhaustion to occur could still face certificate action on the grounds of poor preflight planning and reckless operation, even with an ASRS report filed.

questions.question: During an autorotation, what are the three primary factors you evaluate when selecting a landing area from altitude?
questions.answer: The three primary factors are: (1) Size and shape — the area must be large enough to complete the autorotation and landing roll-out without striking obstacles; (2) Surface condition — avoid water, tall vegetation, soft ground, or debris that could cause rollover or sudden deceleration; (3) Wind direction — landing into the wind reduces groundspeed at touchdown, shortening the landing roll and reducing impact forces. Obstacle clearance along the approach path is also a critical consideration.

questions.question: Why is wind direction important when selecting a landing area during an autorotation, and how does it affect your touchdown?
questions.answer: Landing into the wind reduces the helicopter's groundspeed at touchdown relative to the surface. Since rotor RPM and lift are related to airspeed, a headwind allows the rotor system to generate more lift at a lower groundspeed, resulting in a softer touchdown with a shorter ground roll. A tailwind landing increases groundspeed significantly, requiring more deceleration energy and increasing the risk of a hard landing or loss of directional control.

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns, at what point in the maneuver should you finalize your selection of a landing area, and why?
questions.answer: You should identify and commit to a landing area as early as possible after autorotation entry — ideally within the first few seconds. Early selection allows you to plan your pattern, manage energy, and position the helicopter for an optimal approach angle. Delaying the decision reduces your options and may leave insufficient altitude to maneuver into a good position. Turns should be used deliberately to align with the chosen area, not to continue searching for a better one at low altitude.

questions.question: You experience an engine failure at 1,500 feet AGL. You see two options: a paved road that is into the wind but has power lines on both sides, and a large grass field that requires a 180-degree turn and results in a slight downwind component. Which do you choose and how do you justify your decision?
questions.answer: The large grass field is likely the better choice, despite requiring a turn and a slight downwind. The power lines on the road present a severe, potentially fatal hazard — they are often difficult to see and can cause catastrophic structural damage. At 1,500 feet AGL, there is sufficient altitude to execute a 180-degree turn while maintaining rotor RPM within limits. The grass field's minor downwind component increases groundspeed at touchdown but is manageable with proper flare technique. The general priority is: avoid wires and fixed obstacles first, then optimize for surface, size, and wind direction in that order.

questions.question: You are executing an autorotation with turns and have selected a landing area that appears to be a clear field. As you descend through 300 feet AGL on final, you notice the field has tall corn stalks that were hidden by the sun angle. You still have just enough altitude to turn to a secondary area — a narrow gravel road with no obstructions. Walk me through your decision and the specific risks involved.
questions.answer: This is a genuine dilemma, but at 300 feet AGL you have very limited time and energy. Tall corn can cause significant rotor blade strike risk and deceleration forces that lead to dynamic rollover. The narrow gravel road, while not ideal for surface width, has known, predictable conditions. If the road is clear of wires, vehicles, and obstacles and is wide enough to land without striking skids on the edge, it is likely the safer choice. However, any turn at 300 feet AGL must be executed with extreme caution — steep banks increase load factor and can bleed rotor RPM rapidly. If the turn cannot be completed with adequate rotor RPM and airspeed for a safe flare, continuing to the corn field may be preferable. The key principle is: never sacrifice rotor RPM for landing area positioning at low altitude.

questions.question: How does the loss of effective translational lift (ETL) during an autorotation approach to a selected landing area affect your collective management, and how do you plan for it?
questions.answer: As the helicopter decelerates through approximately 16–24 knots during the autorotation approach, effective translational lift is progressively lost and rotor efficiency decreases. In a powered approach you would add collective to maintain rotor RPM; in autorotation, you must conserve collective pitch for the flare and landing cushion. The practical effect is that rotor RPM may trend higher or lower depending on descent rate and rotor disk angle. You plan for ETL loss by entering the flare at the airspeed and altitude specified in your aircraft's AFM—typically in the range of 40–60 knots and 50–100 feet AGL for most single-rotor helicopters—so that the flare arrests descent rate before ETL is fully lost and the final collective application uses rotor inertia to cushion touchdown. Recognize that in a steep approach, ETL is lost at a higher altitude; adjust your flare timing accordingly and verify all parameters in your specific aircraft's AFM.

questions.question: You are flying a low-inertia rotor system helicopter and experience an engine failure at 800 feet AGL over a dense forested area. The only suitable landing area requires a 270-degree turn to reach. Explain your thought process for evaluating whether that turn is survivable, and what rotor RPM considerations drive your decision.
questions.answer: Low-inertia rotor systems decay RPM much faster than high-inertia systems following engine failure, which means the immediate collective reduction is even more time-critical. For a 270-degree turn, you must evaluate whether sufficient rotor RPM can be maintained throughout the turn to preserve lift and control authority at the bottom. Bank angles in autorotation increase load factor, which in turn increases the pitch required to maintain disk position — this can bleed RPM further. If RPM cannot be maintained within the green arc through the turn, the turn should not be attempted. The decision framework is: (1) Is the RPM stable within limits after entry? (2) Can the bank angle needed for the turn be executed without exceeding RPM limits in the low end? (3) Is there sufficient altitude to complete the turn and still have an approach corridor? If any answer is uncertain, the survivable choice may be a forced landing in the trees using a run-on or vertical deceleration technique rather than risking rotor RPM decay mid-turn.
questions.follow_up: If you're in a low-inertia rotor system and your RPM is at the bottom of the green arc mid-turn during that 270-degree autorotation, what is the one control input that might recover RPM — and what is the trade-off?
questions.follow_up_answer: Reducing bank angle and allowing the helicopter to fly a wider arc will reduce load factor and the associated pitch demand on the rotor, potentially allowing RPM to recover. Alternatively, a slight forward cyclic can increase airflow upward through the disk, which also contributes to RPM recovery. The trade-off is that reducing bank angle means the turn radius widens — you may overshoot the intended landing area or require additional altitude to complete the maneuver. At low altitude, this trade-off may make reaching the selected area impossible, forcing you to reassess and accept a less desirable landing zone to preserve rotor integrity.

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns to a selected landing area, you are on final and realize you are going to overshoot the intended touchdown point significantly. What options do you have to correct, and which carry the greatest risk in a helicopter?
questions.answer: Options to address an overshoot in autorotation include: (1) S-turns — gentle left-right course deviations that bleed off distance without significantly affecting descent rate; (2) Slipping the helicopter — applying opposite cyclic and pedal to create a sideslip, which increases drag and steepens the approach; (3) Extending the flare — beginning the deceleration flare earlier to bleed more airspeed and reduce forward momentum before touchdown; (4) Accepting a landing further down the selected area if space permits. The greatest risk in a helicopter is an aggressive sideslip at low altitude, because it increases the probability of the tail rotor striking the ground and can induce a low-G condition on some rotor systems, particularly teetering rotors, risking mast bumping. S-turns are generally the preferred technique because they are more controllable and have less risk of creating asymmetric thrust or tail-low attitudes. Pilots must avoid the temptation to use cyclic aft aggressively at low altitude without monitoring collective, as a sudden RPM spike followed by collective application can result in a hard landing.
questions.follow_up: You mention slipping as a technique to steepen the approach in autorotation — under what specific rotor system configuration is a slip in autorotation most hazardous, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: A slip in autorotation is most hazardous in a teetering (semi-rigid, two-bladed) rotor system. During a slip, the helicopter is placed in a low-G or unloaded rotor condition, which reduces the centrifugal force that normally keeps the teetering rotor stable. In a low-G state, a teetering rotor can flap to an extreme angle, causing the rotor blade to contact the tail boom — a condition known as mast bumping or blade-to-tail strike. This is catastrophic and non-recoverable. In an articulated rotor system, the flapping hinges absorb these forces more safely. Therefore, slips in autorotation should be used with extreme caution in teetering-rotor helicopters and should generally be avoided in favor of S-turns as the primary distance-management technique.

questions.question: Before initiating an autorotation with turns, what does 'clear the area' mean, and why is it required?
questions.answer: Clearing the area means the pilot performs a systematic visual scan of the practice area — above, below, left, right, and behind — to ensure no other aircraft, obstacles, or hazards are present before beginning the maneuver. It is required because autorotations involve significant altitude loss and heading changes, which can create collision risks with other traffic that may not be visible during the maneuver itself.

questions.question: In what directions must you scan when clearing the area before an autorotation with turns, and is a single look in each direction sufficient?
questions.answer: You must scan above, below, left, right, ahead, and behind the helicopter. A single glance is not sufficient — you should complete at least one deliberate 360-degree clearing turn, or two 90-degree turns in opposite directions, to systematically check all quadrants. The goal is to visually confirm the area is free of conflicting traffic and obstacles before committing to the maneuver.

questions.question: At what point during the setup for an autorotation with turns is the area-clearing step performed — before, during, or after establishing the entry altitude and airspeed?
questions.answer: Clearing turns should be performed after achieving the appropriate entry altitude and airspeed and stabilizing the helicopter. Once at entry altitude and stabilized on airspeed, conduct a thorough 360-degree visual clearing scan to ensure the area is free of other aircraft and obstacles. Re-confirm the area is clear immediately before initiating the autorotation maneuver itself. This sequence ensures that the area is confirmed clear at the moment of actual maneuver entry, and that your clearing scan occurs from a stabilized platform without the distraction of establishing altitude or airspeed.

questions.question: You are at 1,500 feet AGL preparing to demonstrate an autorotation with turns. You complete a clearing turn to the left and spot a fixed-wing aircraft at your 9 o'clock, same altitude, converging. What should you do, and how does this affect your maneuver?
questions.answer: Do not initiate the autorotation. The clearing scan revealed a collision risk — a converging aircraft at the same altitude. You should maneuver as necessary to avoid the conflict (the fixed-wing aircraft on your left is the right-of-way aircraft if it is approaching head-on or from the right; however, safety takes priority). Delay the maneuver, communicate on CTAF or appropriate frequency if in the area, reposition, and re-clear the area before attempting the autorotation. The purpose of the clearing scan is exactly this — to catch such conflicts before committing to a high-workload maneuver.

questions.question: During a checkride, you clear the area and then spend about 90 seconds re-briefing yourself on the maneuver before initiating the autorotation. Should you re-clear the area before starting? Why or why not?
questions.answer: Yes, you should re-clear the area. Traffic situations are dynamic — an aircraft that was not present during your initial scan could have entered the area within 90 seconds. As a general rule of thumb, if more than approximately 30 seconds have elapsed since your clearing scan, or if you have been head-down or otherwise distracted, a new scan is warranted. On a checkride, demonstrating this habit shows sound aeronautical decision-making and situational awareness.

questions.question: You are practicing autorotations with turns at an uncontrolled airport near the traffic pattern. How does the proximity of the traffic pattern change how you clear the area before the maneuver?
questions.answer: Proximity to the traffic pattern significantly increases traffic density and the likelihood of conflict. You should monitor CTAF actively for position reports, announce your practice area location and intentions on CTAF, and perform a more thorough clearing scan that specifically targets pattern altitudes (typically 800–1,000 feet AGL) and common traffic flow directions. You may also need to reposition to a practice area further from the pattern to maintain safe separation and avoid disrupting normal traffic flow.

questions.question: On a checkride, a student performs a single, quick head swivel left and right and then immediately enters the autorotation, claiming the area is clear. As the examiner, what specific deficiencies would you identify, and what standard is actually required?
questions.answer: The deficiencies include: (1) failure to perform a systematic, deliberate clearing scan covering all quadrants including above and below; (2) no clearing turn was performed to check the blind spots behind and below the helicopter; (3) the scan was too brief to reliably identify traffic. The required standard is a methodical area-clearing procedure — typically one or two 90-degree turns in opposite directions or a full 360-degree clearing turn — combined with a visual scan that covers all six threat quadrants. The pilot must demonstrate they are actively looking for and identifying traffic, not just making a perfunctory head movement. This is an aeronautical decision-making deficiency that reflects unsafe habit patterns.
questions.follow_up: If the student argues that visibility was unrestricted and CTAF was quiet, so the quick scan was adequate, how would you respond?
questions.follow_up_answer: Visibility and radio silence do not substitute for a proper clearing procedure. CTAF is advisory only — non-radio aircraft, gliders, skydivers, and pilots not monitoring the frequency are never announced. Clear visibility simply means you can see further, not that a brief scan is sufficient; fast-moving traffic can enter your scan blind spot in seconds. The clearing turn serves to physically move the helicopter so that previously obscured areas come into view, which a head swivel cannot replicate. The procedural discipline of a thorough clearing scan must be consistent regardless of perceived conditions.

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns, after the turn is established and the pilot is committed to the descent, they notice an ultralight aircraft directly below on the intended flight path. What options exist at this point, and how does this situation reinforce the importance of the pre-maneuver clearing standard?
questions.answer: Once in autorotation, options are limited but not zero: the pilot can modify the turn rate or direction to alter the projected flight path and landing area, apply aft cyclic to stretch the glide if altitude permits, or in extremis re-engage the engine if power-on recovery is still safe per aircraft procedures. However, all of these options degrade the quality of the maneuver and introduce risk. The ultralight — likely operating under 14 CFR Part 103 — may have no radio and could be unaware of the helicopter. This scenario directly illustrates why the clearing scan must include the area below the helicopter and the full cone of the descent path, not just the immediate horizontal plane. A thorough pre-maneuver clearing scan is the only reliable opportunity to identify this hazard before it becomes a conflict.
questions.follow_up: What regulatory right-of-way considerations apply between your helicopter in autorotation and an ultralight in your descent path?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.113(b), when a rule of this section gives the right of way to one aircraft, the other aircraft shall give way and avoid passing over, under, or ahead of the other aircraft. Under 91.113(d), aircraft in distress have right of way over all other aircraft. While an autorotation is a practice emergency and not necessarily a declared emergency, the helicopter may have limited ability to maneuver. However, 91.113(b) also states each pilot has the responsibility to 'see and avoid.' Operationally, the safest resolution is to use whatever maneuverability remains to avoid the ultralight, regardless of technical right-of-way, because the consequence of a collision outweighs any procedural consideration.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.113; 14 CFR Part 103; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 and 11

questions.question: When setting up for an autorotation with turns practice maneuver, what is the general minimum entry altitude you should select, and why does that number matter?
questions.answer: The minimum entry altitude for a straight-in autorotation is approximately 500 feet AGL in favorable conditions, but turning autorotations are significantly more demanding and typically require 700–1000 feet AGL or higher, depending on aircraft rotor inertia, sink rate, and density altitude. Altitude matters because once you commit to autorotation entry, you have a fixed energy budget—insufficient altitude means insufficient time to complete the maneuver safely before ground contact. Always consult the specific aircraft POH/RFM and your training program minimums for exact entry altitudes.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; operator/POH minimums for specific aircraft

questions.question: What does 'appropriate entry altitude' mean in the context of a turning autorotation versus a straight-in autorotation?
questions.answer: A turning autorotation requires a higher entry altitude than a straight-in because turns consume altitude more rapidly. During a banked turn in autorotation, the rotor disk must support increased load factor to maintain the turn, which increases induced drag and accelerates altitude loss. Additionally, the pilot must reserve enough altitude to roll wings level and complete the flare and cushion before touchdown. The appropriate altitude must account for all these additional demands.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Chapter 9 (turns and load factor)

questions.question: Name two factors specific to the helicopter you are flying that directly influence what counts as an 'appropriate' entry altitude for an autorotation with turns.
questions.answer: 1) Rotor inertia (low-inertia rotor systems decay RPM much faster than high-inertia systems, requiring prompt collective reduction and more altitude margin for recovery). 2) Glide ratio / rate of descent in autorotation — an aircraft with a higher sink rate loses altitude faster, requiring a higher entry altitude to accomplish the same maneuver. Other valid factors include OGE hover ceiling, gross weight, and density altitude effects on rotor performance.

questions.question: You are flying at a high-density altitude airport on a hot afternoon. How does this condition affect the entry altitude you select for a practice autorotation with turns, and what specifically changes about your energy management?
questions.answer: High density altitude reduces air density, which increases the rate of descent in autorotation because the rotor must work harder to extract energy from thinner air — you need more disk area effect than the thinner air can support at equivalent RPM. This means altitude is consumed faster than at sea level standard conditions. You should select a higher entry altitude than you would under standard conditions. Additionally, the collective cushion at the bottom will be less effective because there is less air to compress, so more altitude is needed for the flare to arrest the sink rate before touchdown.

questions.question: During preflight planning for a training flight that includes autorotations with 180-degree turns, what information from the POH/RFM do you reference to determine an appropriate entry altitude, and how do you apply it?
questions.answer: You reference the autorotation performance data in the POH/RFM, which typically provides: (1) the steady-state rate of descent in autorotation at best glide airspeed, (2) rotor RPM operating range during autorotation, and (3) any published minimum entry altitudes for practice maneuvers. You apply this by calculating total altitude needed — altitude consumed during stabilization after entry, altitude lost during the 180-degree turn (which adds to the straight descent), altitude needed for the flare, and the cushion phase. You then add a safety margin and ensure the selected entry altitude provides all of this above any obstacles or the intended touchdown point.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; specific helicopter POH/RFM; 14 CFR 91.13

questions.question: You begin your autorotation practice at what you thought was an adequate entry altitude, but halfway through a 180-degree turn you recognize you are running low on altitude. What are your priority actions and what does this scenario tell you about how you selected your entry altitude?
questions.answer: Priority actions: (1) Roll out of the turn immediately to eliminate the excess load factor and stop accelerated altitude loss; (2) continue autorotation straight-in to the nearest suitable landing area; (3) execute flare and cushion normally. This scenario reveals the entry altitude was too low — either the rate of descent was higher than anticipated (perhaps due to density altitude or higher gross weight), the turn consumed more altitude than planned, or the entry was not established at the selected altitude. A proper entry altitude selection should include a deliberate buffer so that if the turn is completed at a higher altitude than the minimum required for flare and cushion, the pilot has options rather than being forced into a single outcome.

questions.question: A student consistently selects the same entry altitude for every autorotation practice — regardless of wind, density altitude, or degree of turn planned. As an instructor, how do you identify this as a systemic error in understanding 'appropriate' entry altitude, and what is the underlying aerodynamic concept the student is missing?
questions.answer: The systemic error is treating entry altitude as a fixed number rather than a dynamic calculation based on current conditions. The underlying concept the student is missing is the relationship between potential energy (altitude) and kinetic energy (rotor RPM and airspeed) in autorotation — it is fundamentally an energy management problem. Appropriate entry altitude must account for: (1) density altitude's effect on rotor efficiency and sink rate; (2) wind's effect on glide distance and approach angle; (3) degree of turn — a 360-degree turn requires significantly more altitude than a 90-degree turn; (4) aircraft gross weight affecting rotor inertia and sink rate; and (5) aircraft-specific rotor inertia. A student using a fixed number has memorized a procedure without understanding the energy trade-offs, which becomes dangerous when any variable changes from the training baseline.
questions.follow_up: If this student passes the checkride using a fixed entry altitude that happens to be safe for standard conditions, but then flies the same maneuver at a high-elevation mountain airport on a hot day — what specific failure point in the autorotation is most likely to catch them by surprise, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: The most likely failure point is during the flare and cushion phase. At high density altitude, the rotor generates less thrust per unit of collective input because the air is less dense. The student, accustomed to a specific flare initiation height and collective pull rate, will find that the same collective inputs produce less deceleration of sink rate. They will be lower than expected when rotor RPM begins to decay, with less altitude available to trade for additional cushion effect. They may contact the ground with excessive sink rate before recognizing the collective has been ineffective — this is compounded if rotor RPM was allowed to decay during the turn due to the same density altitude effect on autorotative RPM maintenance.

questions.question: During a checkride, the applicant selects an entry altitude that appears adequate on the surface but positions the helicopter directly over a residential neighborhood with no suitable forced landing area below during the early phase of the maneuver. How does this affect your evaluation of whether they selected an 'appropriate' entry altitude?
questions.answer: This is a significant deduction regardless of technical altitude adequacy. 'Appropriate' entry altitude is not solely about having enough feet above ground to complete the maneuver — it also encompasses selecting a position and altitude that keeps a suitable emergency landing area within reach throughout the entire maneuver. A truly appropriate setup positions the helicopter so that at every point during the autorotation, including during the turn, a landing area is accessible. Flying over an area with no landing option during the critical early stabilization phase violates the spirit of risk management and the ACS standard. Per 14 CFR 91.13, careless or reckless operations that endanger persons or property on the ground are prohibited. On the checkride, I would address this as an unsatisfactory risk management judgment even if the maneuver itself was mechanically executed correctly.
questions.follow_up: The applicant argues that the POH lists the minimum entry altitude as 700 feet AGL, they were at 800 feet AGL, and therefore their altitude was appropriate. How do you respond?
questions.follow_up_answer: The POH minimum entry altitude is a performance floor — it tells you the least altitude at which the maneuver can be mechanically completed under standard conditions. It says nothing about whether the position is operationally appropriate. Appropriate altitude selection integrates three factors: (1) mechanical sufficiency — enough altitude to complete the maneuver; (2) positional appropriateness — a suitable landing area within glide reach throughout; and (3) regulatory compliance — not creating hazards to third parties. Meeting (1) while failing (2) and (3) is not 'appropriate' — it is minimum survivable. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook and ACS standards require judgment that encompasses all three, not just meeting a published minimum.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.13; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; ACS CH.VIII.C risk management standards

questions.question: When practicing autorotation from cruise flight, at what point should you initiate the entry?
questions.answer: The entry should be initiated at the designated altitude, airspeed, and position specified for the maneuver — typically over a predetermined reference point or at a specific altitude called out by the examiner. The key is that the entry point allows sufficient altitude and time to complete a stabilized autorotation and flare to a simulated or actual landing area. The collective should be lowered immediately upon reaching the initiation point to prevent rotor RPM decay.

questions.question: What are the three simultaneous control inputs required when initiating an autorotation from cruise airspeed?
questions.answer: At autorotation entry from cruise airspeed, the pilot must simultaneously apply: (1) down collective to reduce blade pitch, decrease drag, and allow rotor RPM to increase via upward airflow; (2) aft cyclic to slow the aircraft to the best autorotation airspeed and increase upward airflow through the rotor disk; and (3) appropriate pedal input (typically right pedal in a counterclockwise rotor system) to compensate for the reduction in torque. These inputs must happen together — delay in any one can result in rotor RPM decay, especially in low-inertia rotor systems.

questions.question: Why is it critical that the entry into autorotation happens without delay once the initiation point is reached?
questions.answer: Because rotor RPM begins decaying immediately when engine power is lost or reduced. Low-inertia rotor systems can lose RPM very rapidly — within seconds — and if the collective is not lowered promptly, the rotor may stall. A rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that early recognition of low RPM is imperative, and the autorotation entry must be initiated without hesitation to maintain rotor RPM within the green arc.

questions.question: You are flying a traffic pattern for autorotation practice. As you roll out on final at 500 feet AGL, your examiner notes you initiated the autorotation 200 feet too high and too far from the landing point. How does an early initiation affect the rest of the autorotation, and how would you compensate?
questions.answer: Initiating too high and too far out means you will have excess altitude and distance to manage. This results in a shallower-than-normal glide angle and may require turns to use up altitude, or a more aggressive flare to manage excess energy. In an autorotation with turns, you could use coordinated 90-degree or 180-degree turns to bleed off altitude while maintaining rotor RPM. The risk is that poorly planned turns at lower altitudes can leave you in an unfavorable position — too high on short final with insufficient time to arrest the descent. The proper initiation point is chosen specifically to achieve a stabilized glide to the intended landing area without requiring extreme corrections.

questions.question: During a 180-degree autorotation from a simulated engine failure on the crosswind leg, at what point should you begin the turn to final, and what happens to rotor RPM during that turn?
questions.answer: The turn to final should be initiated early enough to roll out aligned with the intended landing area with sufficient altitude remaining for a proper flare—typically no lower than 100–150 feet AGL depending on the aircraft. During the turn, the pilot must increase collective to maintain adequate pitch control and arrest descent rate. If collective is raised too much, the rotor becomes over-pitched and rotor RPM may rise above the desired operating range. The pilot must carefully manage collective throughout the turn to maintain RPM within the green arc while maintaining adequate control authority for pitch and roll. Steep bank angles increase the control inputs required, so bank angle must be managed to avoid excessive RPM rise or arriving on final with RPM outside the normal range.

questions.question: You initiate an autorotation exactly at the briefed point, but you notice rotor RPM is already near the bottom of the green arc after your collective reduction. What went wrong, and what should you do?
questions.answer: If RPM is near the bottom of the green arc immediately after collective reduction, the most likely cause is that the aft cyclic input was delayed or insufficient — aft cyclic increases upward airflow through the rotor disk, which drives rotor RPM up. Another possible cause is that the collective was not lowered quickly enough, allowing the rotor to drag in powered pitch before transitioning to autorotative flow. The immediate correction is to apply more aft cyclic to increase relative airflow through the disk and allow the rotor to recover RPM. If the rotor is approaching a stall condition, recovery may not be possible — this is why proper simultaneous inputs at the correct initiation point are so critical.

questions.question: An examiner gives you a simulated engine failure at 800 feet AGL over terrain that requires a 270-degree turn to reach the only suitable landing area. How do you determine whether to initiate that turn immediately or delay it, and what factors could make initiating the turn immediately the wrong choice?
questions.answer: Determining when to initiate the turn requires a rapid mental calculation of available altitude, rotor energy, glide distance, and final approach requirements. Initiating a 270-degree turn immediately from 800 feet AGL may be feasible in some helicopters but risks arriving on final too low to complete a proper flare and landing. Factors that could make immediate initiation the wrong choice include: insufficient altitude to complete the turn and have meaningful altitude remaining for flare; a bank angle steep enough to cause excessive load factor and RPM fluctuation; wind that is unfavorable and will push you off the landing area during the turn; and a low-inertia rotor system that may not sustain RPM through a prolonged banked turn. The pilot should assess whether a closer but imperfect landing area is a better choice than a long turning autorotation to an ideal spot. The ACS requires the maneuver be initiated at the proper point — 'proper' means the point that gives the highest probability of a successful outcome, not simply the point that makes the desired landing area geometrically reachable.
questions.follow_up: If you commit to the 270-degree turn and midway through you realize you will not make the intended landing area, what are your options and what is the risk of each?
questions.follow_up_answer: Options include: (1) Steepen the bank to shorten the turning radius and reach the area — risk is increased load factor, potential RPM spike requiring collective management, and possible loss of control in a high-sink-rate, low-altitude turn; (2) Select an alternate landing area within the current ground track — risk is that terrain or obstacles may make it unsuitable; (3) Accept a controlled autorotative landing in the current area — risk depends on surface suitability. At low altitude, options narrow rapidly. The safest decision is made early — committing to a 270-degree turn from 800 feet AGL is a high-risk initiation choice to begin with, and this scenario illustrates why proper point selection is a safety-critical skill, not just a test standard.

questions.question: During a checkride debrief, you tell the examiner you initiated the autorotation at the correct point, but the examiner disagrees and says you were late. Walk me through how you would objectively evaluate your own initiation point — what references or cues were you using, and how do you know if they were accurate?
questions.answer: Objective evaluation of initiation point involves several cues: (1) Altitude — was the entry made at or above the briefed altitude? An altimeter cross-check at the moment of initiation provides a hard reference; (2) Airspeed — was the aircraft at the briefed cruise airspeed? Higher airspeed at entry shifts the energy envelope and affects glide; (3) Ground reference — was there a predetermined ground reference point used, or was the initiation based on a subjective judgment? If no defined reference was briefed, 'correct' becomes ambiguous; (4) Rotor RPM response — if RPM was already low at entry, a late or hesitant initiation is implied; (5) Outcome trajectory — did the glide path naturally point toward the landing area without requiring excessive maneuvering? If the pilot had to immediately make large corrections, the initiation point was likely off. The honest self-assessment must separate 'I felt I was at the right point' from 'my references confirmed I was at the right point.' Examiners note late initiations when they observe the pilot hesitate, check again, or when the resulting glide angle requires aggressive correction to reach the landing area.
questions.follow_up: If you and your examiner disagree on whether the initiation was timely, and you believe you were correct, how should you professionally handle that disagreement during the debrief?
questions.follow_up_answer: The appropriate response is to respectfully ask the examiner to walk through their specific observations — what did they see that indicated a late initiation? Reference concrete data: altitude at entry, airspeed, ground reference used, and resulting glide path. If the examiner identifies a valid reference point you were not using, acknowledge it and incorporate it. Arguing without data is unproductive and unprofessional. Ultimately, the examiner's determination on a checkride is final, but understanding the specific discrepancy is how you improve. Demonstrating the ability to objectively evaluate your own performance using concrete references — rather than defending a gut feeling — is itself a sign of pilot maturity and aeronautical decision-making.

questions.question: When you enter autorotation and establish the power-off glide, what is the primary control input used to set and maintain autorotation airspeed?
questions.answer: Cyclic pitch controls airspeed during the autorotation glide. Once collective is lowered to the full-down position to enter autorotation, the pilot uses aft or forward cyclic to adjust the nose attitude, which directly controls glide airspeed.
