Do not continue a GPS/RNAV approach without a valid GPS signal. Declare an emergency if situational awareness is compromised.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.225; 14 CFR 91.227; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 and Chapter 9; AIM 1-1-18

questions.question: During a low IFR helicopter EMS flight, you notice your Mode C altitude readout as shown on your ATC datablock is consistently 400 feet higher than your indicated altitude. ATC hasn't said anything. What are the possible causes, what obligation do you have to report or correct this, and what are the downstream risks if it goes unaddressed?
questions.answer: Mode C altitude encoding reports the aircraft's altitude as measured by the static pressure system and encoded by the altitude encoder—it is independent of the altimeter Kollsman setting. A 400-foot discrepancy most likely indicates: (1) the altitude encoder is miscalibrated or failing; (2) the static system has errors affecting the encoder differently than the altimeter; or (3) the encoder was installed or wired incorrectly. You must advise ATC of the discrepancy as soon as you notice it. Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), operating with a known inoperative or unreliable Mode C encoder in airspace where Mode C is required is not permitted. ATC may request Mode A only (no altitude squawk) or may vector you to suitable airspace for repairs. The downstream risks are serious: ATC may issue incorrect TCAS resolution advisories to nearby aircraft; separation assurance is compromised; in RVSM airspace, a 400-foot error would trigger an immediate ATC response; and terrain alerting in other aircraft may be incorrectly activated or suppressed. You should log this discrepancy and ensure the encoder is inspected before the next flight.
questions.follow_up: If ATC instructs you to 'stop altitude squawk,' what does that mean operationally, and does your obligation to maintain IFR altitude compliance change?
questions.follow_up_answer: Stopping altitude squawk means setting the transponder to reply in Mode A only — transmitting your squawk code but not encoding altitude. ATC will then track you positionally on radar but without an automated altitude readout; they will rely on pilot position reports for altitude verification. Your IFR altitude compliance obligations do not change at all — you must still maintain assigned altitudes, comply with all clearances, and make mandatory altitude reports. ATC will likely increase the frequency of altitude confirmation requests. You should also note this discrepancy in the aircraft maintenance log and ground the aircraft for inspection before the next flight if the encoder is confirmed faulty, as operating with a known inoperative required system violates 14 CFR 91.213 minimum equipment requirements if Mode C is required for that airspace.

questions.question: What does the term 'automation complacency' mean in the context of managing an autopilot or FMS during IFR helicopter flight?
questions.answer: Automation complacency occurs when a pilot over-trusts automated systems and reduces their active monitoring of the aircraft's flight path, systems status, and situational awareness. Because the autopilot or FMS is flying the helicopter, pilots may become passive observers rather than active pilots-in-command. This can lead to failing to catch system errors, mode mismatches, or navigation deviations until it is too late to correct safely. The pilot remains responsible for the outcome of the flight regardless of what the automation is doing.

questions.question: When using an FMS or GPS navigator in an IFR helicopter, what is the pilot's responsibility if the automation selects an unexpected route segment or executes an unanticipated turn?
questions.answer: The pilot-in-command is always responsible for the flight path of the aircraft, even when the automation is engaged. If the FMS or GPS executes an unexpected turn or selects an unintended route segment, the pilot must immediately take manual control or intervene to correct the deviation. The pilot should cross-check the automation's behavior against the cleared route, approach chart, or ATC clearance, and query ATC if there is any doubt. Allowing the automation to continue on an unknown or unapproved path is a serious risk management failure.

questions.question: What is 'mode confusion' in an automated flight system, and why is it a particular concern for IFR helicopter pilots?
questions.answer: Mode confusion occurs when a pilot believes the autopilot or FMS is operating in one mode, but the system has actually transitioned to a different mode — either automatically or due to an inadvertent input. For example, a pilot may believe the autopilot is holding altitude when it has transitioned to a vertical speed mode and is actually descending. In a helicopter, where margins can be tighter and flight dynamics are more sensitive than fixed-wing aircraft, an unrecognized mode change during an instrument approach or in IMC can quickly develop into a dangerous deviation. Pilots must continuously monitor and verify the active mode on the flight director or autopilot annunciator panel.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (Autopilots and FMS); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (SRM)

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter IFR in IMC with the autopilot coupled to the GPS approach. During the intermediate segment, ATC issues a radar vector that takes you off the published approach course. You re-engage the approach on the FMS, but the autopilot immediately begins a steep turn in an unexpected direction. What risk management steps should you take?
questions.answer: First, immediately disconnect the autopilot and assume manual control to stop the unexpected maneuver and prevent any further uncommanded flight path deviation. Second, maintain aircraft control — fly headings, altitudes, and airspeeds assigned by ATC while you troubleshoot. Third, advise ATC that you are discontinuing the approach and request vectors or a hold to allow time to sort out the FMS/autopilot issue. Fourth, identify the cause of the unexpected turn — likely the FMS sequenced to a waypoint that created an immediate course reversal because you re-intercepted the approach from an off-course position. Fifth, only re-engage the automation once you fully understand what it will do and have confirmed the correct active waypoint and course. If uncertain, fly the approach raw data manually. The key principle is: never let the automation fly a path you cannot explain or predict.

questions.question: You are hand-flying a helicopter IFR and notice your workload is becoming high during a complex reroute in IMC. You consider engaging the autopilot, but you know it has been intermittently dropping out of heading hold. How do you apply risk management principles to decide whether to use it?
questions.answer: This is a classic risk management tradeoff. An intermittently unreliable autopilot may actually increase risk rather than reduce it, because the pilot must monitor for unexpected disconnects on top of already managing high workload. Using the ADM framework, evaluate: (1) Can I manage current workload safely by hand — if yes, continue manually; (2) If autopilot is needed, can I safely respond to an unexpected disconnect — if not, avoid coupling it to critical functions like glideslope tracking; (3) Consider requesting reduced workload from ATC — ask for delay vectors or a hold to organize before proceeding. The principle is clear: if an automated system is unreliable, it becomes an additional task and distraction rather than a solution. Manual flight with a simplified clearance is the safer managed choice.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, SRM, Trescott Tip); 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: During an IFR helicopter flight, your FMS database has expired by three days. The unit is still functioning and displaying navigation data. What are the risk management and regulatory considerations before using it for an instrument approach?
questions.answer: Regulatory consideration: 14 CFR 91.223 requires that navigation databases used for IFR operations be current. An expired database may contain outdated procedure information — waypoints, altitudes, or frequencies could have changed, making the approach unsafe. From a risk management perspective, the pilot should not fly an instrument approach using an expired FMS database without cross-checking every waypoint, altitude, and course against the current published approach chart. Even then, the regulation requires the database to be current for IFR use. The practical risk management decision is: if the approach can be flown using raw data (VOR, ILS, or GPS with manual waypoint verification against a current chart), and regulatory compliance can be documented, that is the safer path. If full compliance is not possible, declare a non-emergency situation with ATC, request a visual approach if weather permits, or divert to an alternate. Flying an instrument approach with an expired database and unknown changes is not an acceptable risk.

questions.question: A newly rated IFR helicopter pilot tells you they prefer to keep the autopilot engaged at all times in IMC because 'it's more precise than hand-flying.' What are the hidden risks in this philosophy, and how would you counsel them from a risk management standpoint?
questions.answer: While autopilot precision is real, this philosophy creates several layered risks. First, skill degradation: a pilot who never hand-flies in IMC will gradually lose the manual instrument flying proficiency needed when the autopilot fails — which it can do without warning. Second, over-reliance means the pilot may not recognize when the autopilot is flying an incorrect path because they have stopped actively cross-checking flight instruments against expected values. Third, automation surprise: when the autopilot does disconnect — at the most critical moment, such as short final on an approach — a pilot who hasn't been actively flying becomes task-saturated at the worst time. From a risk management standpoint, proficient IFR helicopter pilots should regularly hand-fly approaches and en route segments in actual or simulated IMC to maintain skills. They should use automation as a tool that reduces workload during high-demand phases, not as a crutch that replaces fundamental skill. SRM requires that automation management be an active, conscious process — not a passive default.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot's autopilot fails on short final during an actual IMC approach in a helicopter, what immediate actions are required, and how does their prior automation dependency affect the outcome?
questions.follow_up_answer: When the autopilot disconnects on short final in IMC, the pilot must immediately assume manual control of all three axes — pitch, roll, and yaw/anti-torque — simultaneously, while continuing to fly the approach profile. In a helicopter this is more complex than fixed-wing because the helicopter requires continuous active inputs to maintain stability. A pilot who has been autopilot-dependent will experience a sudden, significant spike in workload at the exact moment when available altitude and time are most limited. If they have not maintained manual IMC proficiency, they are likely to experience spatial disorientation or loss of positional awareness during the transition. This scenario is a textbook example of why the error chain concept from ADM is critical — the decision to never hand-fly in IMC is an early link that makes a recoverable autopilot failure potentially catastrophic. Maintaining manual proficiency breaks that link.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, SRM, error chain); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (Autopilots); 14 CFR 61.57 (Instrument currency)

questions.question: You are flying an RNAV (GPS) approach to a remote heliport in IMC. The FMS shows 'LNAV only' guidance available — WAAS is not available for this approach at this time. Your GPS receiver shows RAIM is available. What risk management factors must you evaluate before continuing, and how does the loss of WAAS precision affect your approach minimums?
questions.answer: WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System) provides the vertical guidance needed for LPV or LNAV/VNAV approach minima, which offer lower decision altitudes similar to ILS precision approaches. If WAAS is unavailable, the approach must be flown to LNAV minimums, which are non-precision minimums with a higher MDA than LPV. Risk management factors to evaluate: (1) Is the MDA for LNAV minimums safely achievable given current weather — specifically, does your reported ceiling provide adequate margin above the MDA to visually acquire the heliport and transition to landing? (2) Is RAIM availability confirmed for the full approach, including missed approach? RAIM ensures GPS integrity for lateral navigation. (3) Is the heliport lighting and marking adequate for a higher-than-planned MDA breakout, especially at a remote site? (4) Do you have adequate fuel to fly the approach, execute a missed approach, and reach the alternate? If the ceiling is at or near LNAV MDA with little margin, or if you cannot positively identify the heliport environment in time to land safely, the risk management decision is to divert to the alternate while you still have fuel and options — not to continue hoping the weather improves at the MDA.
questions.follow_up: What is the specific difference in vertical accuracy between LPV and LNAV approach guidance, and why does that matter for a helicopter landing at a confined or elevated heliport?
questions.follow_up_answer: LPV (Localizer Performance with Vertical Guidance) uses WAAS to provide electronic vertical guidance with accuracy comparable to an ILS, typically allowing decision altitudes as low as 200 feet AGL with visibility minimums of 1/2 mile — similar to a Category I ILS. LNAV is a 2D non-precision approach; the pilot must level off at the MDA and fly level until the heliport is in sight, which is a fundamentally different and more demanding task. For a helicopter approaching an elevated or confined heliport in IMC, the difference is significant: an LPV provides a continuous stabilized descent to a much lower decision point, reducing the distance over which the pilot must visually acquire and transition. LNAV requires the pilot to arrest descent at a higher MDA, then fly level until visual, then re-establish descent — creating a more complex maneuver at low altitude in marginal conditions. At a confined heliport, missing visual acquisition at LNAV MDA leaves less room for maneuvering and higher terrain or obstacle clearance risk than at a conventional airport.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 97.3 (Instrument approach procedures); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (GPS, WAAS, RAIM, LPV vs LNAV); AIM 1-1-18 (GPS RAIM); AIM 5-4-18 (RNAV approach minima)

questions.question: When flying IFR in a helicopter and you receive an unexpected ATC reroute while simultaneously trying to reprogram your GPS, what is the single most important thing you must do first?
questions.answer: Aviate first — maintain aircraft control. In IMC or IFR conditions, the aviate-navigate-communicate hierarchy means you must keep the helicopter stable and on course before addressing any programming task or ATC communication. Cockpit distractions are a leading cause of spatial disorientation and loss of situational awareness. Acknowledge ATC with 'standby' if needed, stabilize the aircraft, then address the navigation change.

questions.question: What does the term 'error chain' mean in the context of aeronautical decision-making, and why is it relevant to managing distractions during IFR navigation?
questions.answer: The error chain refers to a sequence of multiple poor decisions or mistakes that together lead to an accident — no single event typically causes the crash alone. In IFR navigation, a distraction (e.g., radio call) can start the chain: pilot diverts attention, misses a heading change, loses situational awareness, then becomes disoriented. Breaking even one link — such as using automation, asking ATC for a short delay, or leveling off to regain awareness — can prevent the outcome. Approximately 80% of aviation accidents involve human factors as the root cause.

questions.question: When using an ADF/NDB while flying IFR in a helicopter, why is homing to the station considered a higher-risk technique than tracking, particularly when workload is high?
questions.answer: Homing involves continuously adjusting heading to keep the ADF needle at 0° relative bearing, which causes the aircraft to follow a curved, wind-influenced path. This technique requires frequent heading corrections and diverts pilot attention away from other tasks. Tracking, by contrast, establishes a wind correction angle and flies a straight course, requiring fewer heading adjustments. In high-workload IFR environments, homing increases distraction and reduces situational awareness — the pilot is reacting rather than planning ahead.

questions.question: You are a single-pilot IFR helicopter flying in IMC at 5,500 feet. ATC calls with a traffic alert, your transponder appears to have lost Mode C, and your VOR CDI is showing a full-scale deflection. How do you prioritize these three items without losing situational awareness?
questions.answer: Apply the aviate-navigate-communicate hierarchy. First, check aircraft control — if the VOR CDI is fully deflected, cross-check attitude and heading instruments immediately and correct course. Second, assess the traffic advisory from ATC — acknowledge and request traffic position relative to your helicopter; this is a safety-of-flight issue. Third, address the Mode C transponder issue — while important for ATC radar services, Mode C loss is the lowest immediate priority of the three. Note: Mode C altitude is encoded from your altimeter setting; if your Kollsman window is set incorrectly, both your indicated altitude and your Mode C transmission will be wrong. Confirm the correct altimeter setting with ATC and document the transponder anomaly.

questions.question: You are vectored by TRACON for an ILS approach in your helicopter. While descending on the glideslope, a passenger intercom call comes in, your TAWS issues a terrain warning, and ATC provides an amended altimeter setting. Walk me through how each of these items represents a distraction risk and what you do.
questions.answer: Each item represents a distraction layered on top of a high-workload phase of flight. (1) Passenger intercom — defer immediately; non-essential communication during an approach is a distraction that can break instrument scan. Tell the passenger to hold. (2) TAWS terrain warning — act on this immediately. TAWS is predictive (GPS + terrain database) and provides time-based warnings accounting for aircraft performance. A TAWS alert during an ILS approach may indicate deviation below the glideslope or an unstabilized approach — initiate a missed approach if in doubt. (3) Amended altimeter setting — set it promptly but systematically; each 1 Hg change equals 1,000 feet of indicated altitude error. Failing to update risks flying at the wrong altitude. The risk is cumulative distraction leading to loss of situational awareness on the approach — any one of these items alone is manageable; all three simultaneously require strict task shedding.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; Advanced Technology Systems section; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: A helicopter pilot with 1,200 total hours but only 40 hours in the specific IFR-equipped turbine model is conducting a GPS RNAV approach. Research shows accident rates correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft type than total hours. How should this fact influence how the pilot manages distractions during the approach?
questions.answer: With only 40 hours in type, the pilot has not yet developed the automation familiarity and cockpit resource habits specific to that aircraft — accident rates decrease significantly after 100 hours in type. This means the pilot should apply extra conservatism: brief the approach thoroughly before starting it to reduce in-flight workload, avoid accepting late clearance amendments that require GPS reprogramming in IMC, use all available automation (autopilot, FMS) as a workload management tool, and be more willing to request delays or declare 'unable' for complex clearances. The word 'probably' should be avoided — if the pilot is unsure whether they can manage a task safely, they should choose the known-safe option (go to the alternate, hold, or ask ATC for more time).

questions.question: During a high-workload IFR departure in your helicopter, you notice you've been fixated on reprogramming a waypoint for approximately 45 seconds while in IMC. You look up and realize you are uncertain of your heading and altitude. Describe the systematic recovery process and explain why spatial disorientation is particularly dangerous at this point.
questions.answer: Immediately cross-check the attitude indicator — this is the master instrument in IMC. Establish wings level and a known pitch attitude before doing anything else. Then scan: altimeter (check altitude and rate of change), heading indicator, airspeed. Do not rely on vestibular sensation — in IMC following a period of inattention, the vestibular system provides false cues and the leans or graveyard spiral illusions may already be developing. Advise ATC: 'Helicopter [N-number], temporarily uncertain of position, request immediate vectors.' ATC radar can provide headings and altitude verification. The danger at this moment is that spatial disorientation has a rapid onset after distraction in IMC — the pilot's body may be signaling a false 'wings level' while the helicopter is in a bank. Trust the instruments exclusively. The GPWS system, if installed, monitors descent rate and closure rate but is reactive; it cannot help you recover from a disoriented bank. Reassume the published departure procedure once situational awareness is restored.
questions.follow_up: What specific instrument indication would tell you that a graveyard spiral has already developed, and what makes recovery in a helicopter different from a fixed-wing aircraft?
questions.follow_up_answer: In a graveyard spiral, the altimeter is unwinding (descending), airspeed is increasing, and the VSI shows a sustained descent — but the attitude indicator shows a coordinated bank that the pilot's vestibular system interprets as straight and level. The turn coordinator will show a prolonged turn. Recovery requires rolling wings level using the attitude indicator, then gently pulling back to arrest the descent — pulling back while still banked tightens the spiral. In a helicopter, the collective adds an additional complexity: a pilot fixated on attitude may inadvertently lower collective while correcting pitch, accelerating the descent. The rotor RPM must also be monitored — in a steep spiral, airspeed increase can cause rotor overspeed in certain conditions. The helicopter's lower airspeed margins and different pitch/power coupling make graveyard spiral recovery more nuanced than in a fixed-wing aircraft.

questions.question: What is the primary limitation of a VOR signal at low altitudes and long distances from the station, and how does this affect IFR helicopter operations?
questions.answer: VOR uses VHF space waves, which are line-of-sight signals. At low altitudes or beyond a certain distance from the station, terrain, obstructions, and the curvature of the earth can block the signal, causing unreliable course guidance. The MEA guarantees both obstacle clearance AND reliable VOR signal reception along a victor airway, but the MOCA only guarantees obstacle clearance — VOR signal reception is only assured within 22 NM of the NAVAID at the MOCA. Helicopters operating at lower altitudes than fixed-wing aircraft are especially vulnerable to signal loss in mountainous or hilly terrain.

questions.question: When using an ADF/NDB for navigation, what is the primary reliability limitation of the NDB signal you need to be aware of as a helicopter IFR pilot?
questions.answer: NDB stations use ground waves for reliable short-range navigation, but they are highly susceptible to interference from several sources: thunderstorm static (precipitation static), nighttime sky wave interference (where HF signals refract off the ionosphere and corrupt the ground wave signal), coastal refraction near shorelines, and mountain effect near terrain. Because of these limitations, NDB approaches have higher weather minimums than ILS or GPS approaches, and the ADF is considered less precise and less reliable than VOR or GPS. Pilots should not rely on NDB/ADF guidance in or near thunderstorms.

questions.question: How sensitive is a localizer CDI compared to a VOR CDI, and why does that matter during a helicopter instrument approach?
questions.answer: A localizer CDI is approximately 4 to 5 times more sensitive than a VOR CDI. Full-scale deflection on a VOR CDI represents approximately 12 degrees off course, while full-scale deflection on a localizer represents only about 2.5 degrees off course. This means that small heading deviations produce large needle movements on a localizer. For helicopter pilots, this increased sensitivity requires very precise attitude and heading control during the approach — even minor input corrections must be made carefully to avoid over-controlling and chasing the needle.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter IFR en route at 2,500 feet MSL, navigating via a VOR on a route where the MEA is 4,000 feet MSL but you have been assigned 2,500 feet by ATC. The MOCA for this segment is 2,500 feet. What risk does this present regarding your navigation system, and how should you manage it?
questions.answer: At the MOCA, terrain clearance is guaranteed, but VOR signal reception is only assured within 22 NM of the NAVAID. If you are more than 22 NM from the VOR, your course guidance may be unreliable or lost entirely while operating at the MOCA. The risk is navigating with a degraded or intermittently valid VOR signal, which could lead to off-course deviations without your awareness. To manage this risk, you should: (1) verify the distance to the VOR using DME if available; (2) monitor signal quality indicators (CDI fluctuation, OFF flag); (3) use GPS as a backup if the aircraft is so equipped; (4) advise ATC immediately if navigation signal is lost. Being at or below the MEA on a Victor airway during en route IFR without a confirmed navigation signal is a serious situational awareness concern.

questions.question: During a helicopter IFR flight in mountainous terrain, your GPWS activates with a terrain warning. What is the critical limitation of GPWS that you must understand before relying on it as your primary terrain avoidance tool in this environment?
questions.answer: GPWS is a reactive system — it uses radio altimeter readings, barometric altitude, airspeed, gear and flap configuration, and ILS glideslope deviation to detect an imminent terrain conflict. Its critical limitation is that it cannot predict rising terrain ahead of the aircraft. It only warns you when you are already dangerously close to terrain based on current closure rate and altitude. In mountainous terrain, a rapidly rising ridgeline ahead may not trigger GPWS until it is too late to initiate an escape maneuver. TAWS, by contrast, is predictive because it uses GPS position combined with a terrain database and issues warnings based on projected flight path — giving earlier warning. Relying solely on GPWS in mountainous terrain without a TAWS or GPS terrain overlay is a documented contributor to CFIT accidents. (Reference: FAA-H-8083-15B, Advanced Technology Systems chapter; FAA-H-8083-21B; AC 25-11C or AC 27-1A for terrain awareness guidance)
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B, Advanced Technology Systems chapter; FAA AC 23-18

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter IFR approach using GPS with WAAS. Halfway down the approach, the avionics display drops from LPV to LNAV. What does this mean, and what is the risk management action you must take?
questions.answer: A downgrade from LPV (Localizer Performance with Vertical guidance) to LNAV (Lateral Navigation only) means the WAAS system has determined that GPS signal integrity is insufficient to support vertical guidance to LPV minimums. This could be due to satellite geometry, signal outage, or NOTAM'd GPS anomalies. The risk is significant: LPV minimums (often as low as 200 feet AGL) are now inapplicable — you must fly to published LNAV minimums, which are typically higher (often 300–400 feet AGL or more). You must immediately identify the LNAV MDA on the approach chart and ensure you are not below it when the aircraft is inside the final approach fix. If the downgrade occurs at a point where continuing safely to LNAV minimums is not possible, a missed approach is required. Always check NOTAMs for GPS outages before flight to anticipate this scenario.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot is conducting an NDB approach at night in IMC when a significant thunderstorm is developing approximately 15 miles northwest of the airport. The ADF needle is fluctuating slightly but appears generally stable. The pilot decides to continue because the needle is 'mostly pointing at the station.' What specific navigation system limitation is being underestimated here, and what decision-making principle from ADM directly applies?
questions.answer: The pilot is underestimating precipitation static and nighttime sky wave interference from the nearby thunderstorm. NDB signals are highly susceptible to electrical disturbance from lightning — even storms 15 or more miles away can cause the ADF to point toward the storm rather than the station, or produce erratic needle behavior. A 'mostly stable' needle is not reliable confirmation of accurate course guidance during thunderstorm activity. The specific limitation is that NDB/ADF provides no built-in integrity monitoring — it gives no warning flag when the needle is being influenced by extraneous signals. The ADM principle that directly applies is to select the safest course of action when options are uncertain: if an action will only 'probably' work — in this case, the needle is 'probably' correct — the pilot should select an option known to work (divert, hold, or use an alternate approach with GPS or ILS if available). Continuing on a probably-correct ADF needle in proximity to a thunderstorm represents overconfidence and failure to break the error chain. (Reference: FAA-H-8083-15B, Chapter 9; FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 13 for ADM/SRM principles)
questions.follow_up: If this same helicopter were equipped with an RMI that displays both ADF and VOR needle information simultaneously, and the VOR needle is also fluctuating erratically, what should the pilot conclude about the navigation environment?
questions.follow_up_answer: VOR uses VHF line-of-sight signals that are not susceptible to the same lightning-related interference that affects NDB. If the VOR needle is also fluctuating, the likely cause is something other than thunderstorm interference — possibilities include being below the MEA/MOCA with terrain blocking the signal, flying beyond the reliable service volume of the VOR, multipath signal interference, or a receiver/antenna malfunction. The fact that BOTH needles are unreliable at the same time strongly suggests either a receiver/electrical problem on the aircraft or that the pilot is below the altitude required for reliable signal reception in that area. The pilot should immediately advise ATC of navigation uncertainty, request radar vectors if available, and consider declaring an emergency if situational awareness cannot be restored.

questions.question: A helicopter IFR pilot is relying heavily on the moving map display from an EFB (tablet-based app) for situational awareness during a GPS approach. The certified IFR GPS in the panel shows the aircraft slightly right of course. The EFB shows the aircraft exactly on course. The pilot trusts the EFB because the display 'looks better.' What is the core risk management failure here, and what navigation system limitation underlies it?
questions.answer: The core risk management failure is substituting an uncertified, non-IFR-approved device for certified panel avionics during an instrument approach. EFB moving maps, regardless of their visual quality, use consumer-grade or uncertified GPS receivers that have no guaranteed integrity monitoring, no RAIM equivalent, and no FAA certification for IFR navigation. The certified panel GPS must be the primary navigation reference on an instrument approach because it meets TSO standards, provides integrity alerts, and has been tested for IFR use. A discrepancy between the two devices is a significant warning flag — it should trigger immediate cross-checking against raw data (CDI deflection, VOR if available), not a preference for whichever display 'looks right.' The pilot is also exhibiting an automation bias and confirmation bias — two ADM hazardous attitudes that contribute to accidents when pilots trust displays over certified instruments.
questions.follow_up: If the certified GPS and the EFB are showing different positions, and the pilot cannot determine which is correct, what is the appropriate IFR action, and is there any regulatory guidance about EFB use during instrument approaches?
questions.follow_up_answer: The appropriate IFR action is to immediately treat the navigation system as unreliable, advise ATC of the navigation discrepancy, and execute a missed approach. The pilot should not continue below MDA or the DA/DH with unresolved navigation uncertainty. Regarding EFB regulatory guidance: the FAA addressed EFB use in AC 91-78, which allows EFBs to replace paper charts but does not authorize them as primary IFR navigation systems. An EFB with non-certified GPS may be used for situational awareness only — it cannot serve as the basis for instrument approach decisions. 14 CFR 91.175 requires that instrument approaches be conducted using approved navigation systems and in accordance with the published procedure, not a consumer app.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; FAA AC 91-78; FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B, Chapter 5 (EFB/EFIS section)

questions.question: During IFR flight in a helicopter, your VOR CDI suddenly centers and the OFF flag appears. What does the OFF flag indicate, and what is your immediate responsibility?
questions.answer: The OFF flag on a VOR receiver indicates the signal is either too weak, the station is out of service, or there is a receiver failure — the displayed course information is unreliable and should not be used for navigation. Your immediate responsibility is to recognize the loss of navigation signal, notify ATC, and transition to an alternate navigation source such as GPS, another VOR, or ADF. Under IFR, you must maintain situational awareness and comply with your last ATC clearance until alternative guidance is established.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.187 (malfunction reports during IFR); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: What is the difference between a MOCA and an MEA, and why does this distinction matter specifically if you lose your VOR signal en route in a helicopter?
questions.answer: The MEA (Minimum En Route Altitude) guarantees both obstacle clearance AND navigation signal reception from the NAVAID along the entire airway segment. The MOCA (Minimum Obstruction Clearance Altitude) guarantees only obstacle clearance, and VOR navigation signal reception is guaranteed only within 22 NM of the NAVAID. If you lose your VOR signal while flying at the MOCA and you are more than 22 NM from the station, this is expected — you are below the altitude that guarantees signal. If you lose the VOR while at the MEA, this is an anomaly requiring immediate action and ATC notification. The distinction matters because your troubleshooting response differs based on which altitude you are flying.

questions.question: If your GPS navigator displays a RAIM failure or loss of integrity alert during an IFR helicopter flight, can you continue to use GPS for primary IFR navigation? What should you do?
questions.answer: No. A RAIM failure or loss of integrity means the GPS system cannot verify the accuracy of its position solution — the displayed position may be dangerously incorrect. You must not use GPS as a primary navigation source when RAIM is unavailable or integrity is flagged. You should immediately revert to an alternate navigation source (VOR, ADF, radar vectors from ATC), notify ATC of the navigation system degradation, and if conducting an approach, discontinue or divert unless an alternate means of navigation is available and authorized. RAIM prediction tools should be used during preflight to anticipate potential RAIM outages along the route.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter IFR on a cross-country in mountainous terrain at the MEA when both your VOR receivers simultaneously lose signal. You still have GPS with RAIM intact. ATC informs you radar contact has been lost. Walk me through your risk management process.
questions.answer: This scenario involves multiple simultaneous system degradations with elevated terrain — a classic error chain scenario. Risk management steps: First, maintain aircraft control and continue on the last assigned ATC clearance — do not deviate without a clearance or emergency. Second, confirm GPS is providing valid navigation with RAIM intact and use it as your primary navigation source. Third, attempt to re-establish ATC contact on the assigned frequency, then 121.5 MHz if unsuccessful — radar loss does not mean radio loss. Fourth, assess terrain: mountainous terrain increases the consequence of any altitude deviation, so verify you are at or above the MEA and consider requesting a higher altitude as a buffer. Fifth, evaluate whether the dual VOR failure suggests an electrical issue — check circuit breakers, avionics bus, and squawk 7600 if radio contact is also lost. Sixth, consider diverting to a lower-elevation alternate where terrain risk is reduced. The key ADM principle here is to avoid 'probably' thinking — confirm each system is working, not assume it probably is.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.185 (lost communications); 14 CFR 91.187; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: You are on an ILS approach to a helipad in IMC when the localizer CDI suddenly pegs full deflection and does not respond to aircraft movement. The glideslope is still functioning. What risks does this present, and how do you manage them?
questions.answer: A sudden full deflection of the localizer CDI without aircraft input indicates a loss of or corruption of the localizer signal — the display is unreliable. The risks include: (1) continuing the approach using a false or failed lateral guidance signal, which could result in controlled flight into terrain or obstacles; (2) glideslope alone is not sufficient for a complete ILS approach — you have lost the lateral component. Risk management: immediately execute a missed approach — do not attempt to salvage the approach using glideslope only unless specifically authorized and your operating minima allow for it. Localizer CDI is approximately 4-5 times more sensitive than a VOR CDI, meaning small signal errors produce large needle deflections; a pegged indication is a clear failure flag. Advise ATC of the navigation failure, request alternate approach clearance or radar vectors. Consider whether the localizer failure affects your alternate approach capability.

questions.question: During a helicopter IFR flight, you notice your ADF needle is spinning rather than pointing steadily at the NDB. Visibility is 1/4 mile in fog. What are the possible causes, and how does this affect your risk picture for the planned NDB approach ahead?
questions.answer: A spinning or erratic ADF needle can result from: (1) the helicopter passing directly over the station (cone of silence); (2) precipitation static — common in IMC, especially in low-altitude helicopter operations; (3) the NDB station being off the air; (4) an ADF receiver or antenna failure; (5) interference from other signals (thunderstorms can cause ADF deflection toward lightning). The risk picture for the planned NDB approach is significant: NDB approaches already have the highest minimums and greatest chance for error; losing reliable ADF needle guidance in 1/4-mile visibility with no valid needle indication removes your primary course guidance. Risk management: do not commence or continue the NDB approach without a reliably functioning ADF. Advise ATC, identify whether the NDB is NOTAMed out of service, check for precipitation static by noting if the identification code can be heard, and request an alternate approach or alternate airport. Attempting an NDB approach with a questionable needle in near-zero visibility is an unacceptable risk.

questions.question: A student tells you that during an IFR flight, they experienced a brief GPS outage but continued the approach because the signal came back within 30 seconds and 'everything was fine.' What human factors risk does this reasoning demonstrate, and how would you counsel them?
questions.answer: This reasoning demonstrates classic 'get-there-itis' combined with post-hoc rationalization — a significant human factors trap. The fact that it 'worked out' does not mean the decision was sound. The risks that were actually present during those 30 seconds include: flying without verified position integrity, being unable to detect a course deviation, and having no confirmed RAIM monitoring during a critical approach phase. The FAA-H-8083-21B identifies the error chain concept — a successful outcome does not break the chain, it merely means the chain did not reach its final link this time. The student should be counseled that IFR navigation standards require continuous, verified navigation signal — not intermittent. A 30-second outage during an approach could easily translate into a dangerous course deviation that only becomes apparent after it is too late. The correct action was to execute the missed approach the moment the signal was lost, regardless of whether it came back. The word 'probably' (it will probably come back) is exactly the mindset that the FAA warns against.
questions.follow_up: What specific regulation or guidance requires a pilot to report a navigation system malfunction experienced during IFR flight, and does that obligation extend to a self-correcting or brief outage?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 91.187 requires that 'the pilot in command of each aircraft operated in controlled airspace under IFR shall report as soon as practical to ATC any malfunctions of navigational, approach, or communication equipment occurring in flight.' The regulation uses the word 'malfunction' without limiting it to permanent failures — a GPS RAIM loss, even brief, is a malfunction of navigation equipment. The pilot should have reported it to ATC when it occurred. Failure to report a navigation malfunction during IFR flight is a regulatory violation, and it also deprives ATC of situational awareness needed to provide safe separation. In practice, even a transient GPS anomaly should be communicated to ATC.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter IFR using radar vectors to final. ATC suddenly goes silent for 4 minutes. You have no navigation receivers currently tuned — you were relying entirely on radar vectors. What are the risk factors unique to this situation, and walk through the exact lost communications procedure you would follow?
questions.answer: The risk factors here are compounded: (1) you have no independent navigation source currently providing guidance — you were entirely dependent on ATC; (2) loss of ATC communication means you also lose terrain and traffic separation service; (3) helicopters often operate in terminal environments close to terrain and obstacles, amplifying the risk of any deviation; (4) 4 minutes of silence suggests more than a transient radio issue. Risk management and lost comm procedure under 14 CFR 91.185: First, attempt to re-establish contact — try the last assigned frequency, try 121.5 MHz, try any visible FSS or ATIS frequency to verify your radio is transmitting. Squawk 7600. Second, if in VMC — continue VFR and land as soon as practicable. Third, if in IMC — comply with 91.185(c): route: fly the route assigned, vectored, expected, or filed (AVEF); altitude: fly the highest of the MEA, expected altitude, or assigned altitude for each route segment; leave the clearance limit at the expect further clearance time if given, or if not given, proceed to destination; commence descent and approach as close to the EFC time as possible, or if none, as close to the ETA as possible. The critical vulnerability here is that 'vectored' heading may not align with any published route — you must transition to a published fix or route as soon as possible to have a defined lost-comm track. Tune your navigation radios immediately to establish independent position awareness.
questions.follow_up: Under 91.185, when flying the AVEF route in lost communications, you receive a clearance via a different route just before departure that supersedes your filed flight plan. Which route do you fly in lost comm — the filed plan or the clearance you received on the ground?
questions.follow_up_answer: You fly the last ATC clearance received — in this case, the clearance issued before departure that superseded the filed flight plan. 14 CFR 91.185(c)(1) states the pilot shall fly the route assigned in the last ATC clearance received. The filed flight plan is only used if no clearance was received. A pre-departure clearance, even if it changed the route, is the 'last ATC clearance received' and governs lost comm routing. This is a common examiner trap because pilots sometimes revert to their filed flight plan thinking it is the 'official' route — it is not once a clearance has been issued.

questions.question: What is an Electronic Flight Bag (EFB), and what are the three classes of EFB hardware recognized by the FAA?
questions.answer: An EFB is an electronic display system that replaces traditional paper-based flight products in the cockpit. The FAA recognizes three hardware classes: Class 1 EFBs are portable, commercially available devices not mounted to the aircraft (e.g., tablets, laptops) with no aircraft power connection. Class 2 EFBs are also portable but may use aircraft power and a mounting device. Class 3 EFBs are installed aircraft equipment that meet TSO standards and are part of the certified avionics suite. Most helicopter pilots use Class 1 or Class 2 devices running applications such as ForeFlight or Garmin Pilot.

questions.question: What is the primary risk associated with relying on an EFB's moving map display for situational awareness during IFR flight in a helicopter?
questions.answer: The primary risk is over-reliance on the EFB as a sole source of navigation, which can create a false sense of situational awareness. EFB applications are typically not certified avionics — they run on commercial hardware and software that may not meet the reliability standards of installed avionics. Additionally, GPS signal loss, software crashes, battery failure, or screen glare can render the device unusable without warning. Pilots must maintain proficiency on backup navigation systems and not allow the EFB to become the primary instrument for IFR navigation unless it is a certified Class 3 installation.

questions.question: How often are aviation navigation databases in EFB applications typically updated, and why does currency of that database matter for IFR helicopter operations?
questions.answer: EFB navigation databases are updated on a 28-day AIRAC cycle. Using an expired database is a significant risk because approach procedures, airways, waypoints, frequencies, and airport data may have changed. Flying an IFR procedure with outdated database information could result in incorrect course guidance, missed procedure changes, or navigation to a decommissioned waypoint. Pilots must verify the database expiration date during preflight and ensure the EFB database is current before using it for any IFR navigation or approach.

questions.question: You are departing on an IFR helicopter tour flight and your EFB is your only moving map. Shortly after departure in IMC, your EFB freezes and becomes unresponsive. Walk me through how you manage this situation from a risk standpoint.
questions.answer: First, recognize the situation without panic — the EFB is a supplemental tool, not a certified navigation system. Immediately transfer primary navigation reference to the certified avionics in the helicopter (e.g., installed GPS, VOR, or ILS). Advise ATC of any workload issue and request radar vectors if needed to reduce navigation workload. Attempt a soft reset of the EFB if workload permits, but do not allow troubleshooting to distract from aircraft control and primary instrument scan. The broader risk lesson is that prior planning should always include: a fully charged backup device or paper approach plates, familiarity with the installed avionics as primary, and never departing IFR with EFB as the only navigation reference without a redundant plan.

questions.question: Your EFB is showing weather radar and traffic overlay while you are hand-flying a helicopter IFR approach. Describe the specific head-down time risk this creates and what mitigation strategy you should apply.
questions.answer: Monitoring an EFB during a critical phase of flight — especially an approach flown in IMC — significantly increases head-down time and reduces attention to the primary instrument scan. In a helicopter, where attitude changes are rapid and the margin for distraction is small, this is a high-risk scenario. The risk is compounded because EFB weather data (e.g., XM/SiriusXM or ADS-B weather) is not real-time — it typically has a 5–15 minute latency, which could lead to false confidence about weather conditions ahead. Mitigation: configure the EFB prior to the approach during a lower-workload phase, brief what you need to see from it, then minimize interaction during the approach. Use the installed avionics CDI/HSI as the primary navigation reference. If ADS-B traffic is available through certified avionics, use that instead of an EFB overlay.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA AC 120-76D; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: A helicopter pilot is planning an IFR flight and decides to use only an EFB tablet with a GPS app as the sole means of navigation because 'it's more accurate than the old VOR.' What risks does this attitude introduce, and what regulatory issue could arise?
questions.answer: This attitude introduces several compounding risks. First, most EFB applications running on commercial tablets are not TSO-certified navigation systems, meaning they cannot legally serve as a sole means of IFR navigation on routes or approaches requiring certified equipment. Second, the pilot is exhibiting overconfidence and complacency — a classic hazardous attitude. The tablet's GPS receiver is typically less robust than a certified IFR GPS receiver and may not meet RAIM requirements. Third, if the approach requires a certified GPS (e.g., RNAV (GPS) approach), the tablet does not meet that requirement. Regulatory issue: using a non-certified device as the sole IFR navigation source on an RNAV approach without approved equipment would violate 14 CFR 91.205 and applicable TERPS procedure requirements. The pilot must use installed, certificated avionics for IFR approaches.

questions.question: During an IFR helicopter flight, you notice a 0.3 NM discrepancy between your certified panel-mounted GPS and your EFB moving map. Both appear to have current databases. What is the highest-risk scenario this discrepancy could represent, and how do you resolve it as pilot-in-command?
questions.answer: The highest-risk scenario is that the EFB's GPS antenna (typically a built-in tablet chip or small Bluetooth puck) is receiving a degraded or spoofed GPS signal, or has a different datum or SBAS status than the certified panel GPS. A 0.3 NM discrepancy could place the helicopter on the wrong side of an obstacle or outside protected airspace, particularly critical during a GPS approach or in mountainous terrain. Resolution: always treat the certified panel-mounted GPS as authoritative for IFR navigation — it is held to TSO-C146 or TSO-C145 standards, includes RAIM integrity monitoring, and is connected to the aircraft's avionics bus. The EFB is supplemental only. Notify ATC if the discrepancy raises concern about position accuracy, cross-check with any available VOR or DME, and if in doubt, request radar identification to confirm position. Do not attempt to 'average' the two sources — use the certified system.
questions.follow_up: What is RAIM, and why does a certified IFR GPS have it while a typical EFB tablet does not?
questions.follow_up_answer: RAIM stands for Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring. It is a function built into certified GPS receivers that continuously checks the consistency of GPS satellite signals to detect faults that would degrade position accuracy below safe limits. If RAIM detects an integrity failure, it alerts the pilot and may flag the navigation as unreliable. TSO-C129, TSO-C145, and TSO-C146 certified GPS units are required to perform RAIM checks and predict RAIM availability. Commercial EFB tablets use mass-market GPS chipsets that do not perform RAIM — they have no way to tell the pilot that the GPS position has degraded, which is exactly why they cannot serve as the sole IFR navigation source.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.205; TSO-C145/C146; FAA AC 90-100B; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: A helicopter operator's operations manual requires pilots to use an EFB for all IFR flights, but the pilot finds the specific EFB mount blocks part of the instrument panel scan during a critical phase of flight. From a risk management and regulatory standpoint, what are the pilot's obligations and options?
questions.answer: The pilot-in-command has final authority and responsibility for the safe operation of the aircraft under 14 CFR 91.3. If the EFB mount physically obstructs the instrument panel to a degree that impairs the pilot's ability to see required instruments, this creates both a safety hazard and a potential regulatory violation — specifically, it could compromise compliance with 14 CFR 91.205 (required instruments must be operative and accessible). The pilot should document the obstruction concern, report it through the company's safety management system or hazard reporting program, and refuse to fly with the obstructed configuration. The company operations manual cannot override the FARs or the PIC's authority under 91.3. Options include: repositioning or removing the mount if it is a portable device (Class 1 or 2 EFB), requesting maintenance correction of an installed mount, or declining the flight and filing a safety report. Additionally, the pilot should evaluate whether the EFB installation was approved under the applicable STC or a field approval, and whether that approval addressed ergonomic and visibility requirements.
questions.follow_up: If a Class 2 EFB is mounted using an approved mounting device with an STC, does that STC approval guarantee the installation does not obstruct the pilot's view of required instruments?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. An STC approval verifies structural integrity, electrical compatibility, and airworthiness of the installation itself, but it does not guarantee that any specific pilot in any specific seat configuration will have an unobstructed view of all required instruments. Cockpit ergonomics vary by pilot size, seat position, and aircraft variant. The pilot's pre-flight responsibility under 14 CFR 91.3 and 91.7 (airworthy condition) includes ensuring the installation does not create a hazard to safe operation for that specific flight. If the STC-approved mount results in an obstruction for a given pilot, the pilot must report it and not fly — the STC does not transfer the PIC's safety responsibility to the certifying authority.

questions.question: You're flying IFR in a helicopter and tuned to a VOR. The CDI needle is deflected two dots to the right with a FROM flag showing. What does that tell you about your position relative to the selected radial?
questions.answer: A FROM flag means you are on the FROM side of the station. With the needle deflected two dots to the right, you are to the left of the selected radial — meaning you need to fly right (toward the needle) to intercept it. Each dot of CDI deflection represents approximately 6°, so two dots means you are roughly 12° off the selected radial. At full deflection (two dots), you are at or beyond the ±12° limit for a standard VOR CDI.

questions.question: When using an ADF/NDB for navigation in your helicopter, what does the ADF needle always point to, and how does that differ from a VOR RMI needle?
questions.answer: The ADF needle always points TO the NDB station, showing a relative bearing from the aircraft's nose. The VOR RMI needle displays the magnetic bearing to or from the VOR station depending on the FROM/TO selector setting. The key difference is that ADF requires manual conversion of relative bearing to magnetic bearing using the heading indicator, whereas the RMI automatically displays magnetic bearing by slaving to the heading system. In FROM mode, the RMI shows the magnetic bearing FROM the VOR station; in TO mode, it shows the bearing TO the station. (Reference: FAA-H-8083-15B, Chapter 9)

questions.question: During your IFR helicopter flight, you're asked by ATC if you have GPS RNAV capability. What does it mean practically for your navigation when you confirm GPS capability, and what database currency requirement must you meet to use it for IFR navigation?
questions.answer: Confirming GPS RNAV capability means you can fly GPS-based instrument procedures including en route, terminal, and approach segments using T-routes (low altitude) or Q-routes (high altitude) rather than being limited to ground-based NAVAIDs. To use GPS for IFR navigation, the onboard navigation database must be current — databases are updated on a 28-day cycle. Using an expired database for IFR flight is not authorized; it may be used for situational awareness only.

questions.question: You're flying your helicopter IFR on a VOR airway and notice your CDI is centered but then slowly drifts to full deflection over several minutes. You haven't changed heading. Walk me through how you would troubleshoot whether this is a navigation system error or an off-course situation.
questions.answer: First, I'd cross-check my heading indicator against the magnetic compass to confirm I'm actually maintaining the assigned heading — precession or gyro drift could cause me to drift off course while believing I'm on heading. Next, I'd check the VOR identifier by listening to the Morse code to confirm I'm tuned to the correct station and that the NAVAID is operational (some stations may have a test signal or NOTAM). I'd also verify the OBS setting matches the assigned airway course. If all those check out, I'd look for a DME readout to cross-check my along-track position. If another NAVAID is available, I'd cross-check position with it. If the indication appears erroneous and I cannot confirm position, I'd advise ATC that I'm experiencing a navigation discrepancy and request radar vectors while I troubleshoot.

questions.question: You're flying a helicopter IFR and decide to use ADF/NDB homing to navigate to an NDB station. ATC asks why you're tracking a curved path on their radar. Explain what's happening and what you should be doing instead.
questions.answer: Homing means I'm keeping the ADF needle pointed at 0° relative bearing — essentially always pointing the nose at the station. In a crosswind, this causes a constantly curving flight path as the wind pushes the aircraft downwind, requiring continuous heading corrections toward the station. On radar, this appears as a curved track rather than a straight course. The correct technique is NDB tracking — I should determine the wind correction angle needed by intentionally crabbing into the wind until the relative bearing stabilizes at a value equal to the wind correction angle (e.g., if the wind requires a 10° left correction, I track with the needle at 10° left of center and hold a heading that accounts for the crab). This produces a straight ground track to the station.

questions.question: You're flying an IFR helicopter flight using GPS as your primary navigation and ATC offers you radar flight following. Your GPS suddenly shows a loss of signal integrity (RAIM failure). Describe your immediate actions and how radar service changes your options.
questions.answer: A RAIM failure means the GPS can no longer guarantee position accuracy to the required standard — I must not use GPS as a primary navigation source for IFR. My immediate action is to notify ATC of the GPS navigation failure and request radar vectors or alternative routing. If I have a VOR receiver, I should identify and tune an appropriate VOR for backup navigation. Since ATC is already providing radar service, they can provide vectors to keep me on a safe route while I troubleshoot or transition to ground-based NAVAIDs. I would also check NOTAMs — RAIM outages are sometimes predicted and published. I'd declare the navigation equipment degradation to ATC under 14 CFR 91.187 (malfunction reports for IFR flight) so they can accommodate me.

questions.question: You're flying a helicopter IFR and your GPS approaches the destination showing normal operation, but when you shoot the GPS approach the CDI seems extremely sensitive compared to how it felt in the en route environment. Nothing is broken — what's actually happening, and how does this sensitivity change affect your flying technique on the approach?
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.171 requires a VOR accuracy check within the preceding 30 days before using VOR for IFR navigation, using one of the approved methods: VOT, certified checkpoint, dual VOR comparison, or airborne over a known fix. The ground check only confirms the receiver was within tolerance (+/- 4 degrees for ground checkpoint, +/- 6 degrees for airborne) at the time of the check. It does not guarantee the receiver continues to function correctly in flight. In-flight VOR failures can and do occur. If a suspicious in-flight indication cannot be reconciled through cross-checks and alternate navigation sources, you must immediately cease IFR reliance on that receiver and declare the equipment unairworthy, even if the ground check was recent. The ground check satisfies the pre-flight requirement, but does not authorize continued use of a receiver suspected of failure during flight.
questions.follow_up: If this GPS approach is an LPV procedure, how does the vertical guidance sensitivity compare to an ILS glideslope, and what minimum visibility and decision altitude can you expect relative to a traditional ILS?
questions.follow_up_answer: An LPV (Localizer Performance with Vertical guidance) approach uses WAAS-augmented GPS to provide angular vertical guidance very similar to an ILS glideslope in sensitivity. LPV decision altitudes can be as low as 200 feet HAT with visibility minimums as low as 1/2 SM — equivalent to a Category I ILS. In practice, LPV approaches may have slightly higher minimums than a collocated ILS depending on terrain, obstacles, and approach design, but they are the highest-performing GPS approach type currently available to GA pilots. Unlike an ILS, LPV does not require ground equipment at the runway, making it available at many more airports. However, LPV requires WAAS-capable GPS equipment; a standard GPS receiver without WAAS cannot fly LPV approaches.

questions.question: During an IFR helicopter flight, your transponder fails in Mode C. ATC informs you that they are no longer receiving altitude information. You're currently in Class B airspace. What are your obligations, and can you continue the flight?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.215, Mode C altitude-encoding transponder operation is required in Class B airspace and within 30 NM of a Class B primary airport. A Mode C failure in Class B is a significant issue. However, 14 CFR 91.215(d) provides that if the transponder fails after departure, ATC may authorize continued flight under their discretion. I must immediately notify ATC of the Mode C failure. ATC can elect to allow me to continue in Class B if they have primary radar and can maintain separation. I cannot enter Class B initially without an operating transponder unless ATC specifically authorizes it. If ATC cannot accommodate me, I may need to exit Class B and land at the nearest suitable airport to address the equipment failure. The key distinction is that a pre-departure failure prohibits entry, while an in-flight failure may be accommodated by ATC authorization.
questions.follow_up: The Mode C altitude reported to ATC does not change when you adjust your altimeter's Kollsman window. Why not, and what are the implications if your static system is blocked when you switch to alternate static?
questions.follow_up_answer: The transponder reports pressure altitude — the raw uncorrected altitude based on standard atmosphere (29.92 Hg) — directly from the encoder. Adjusting the Kollsman window only changes what the pilot reads on the altimeter face; it has no effect on the pressure altitude signal sent to ATC's computer, which applies its own correction to display true altitude to the controller. If the static system becomes blocked and I switch to alternate static (inside the cabin), the cabin is at slightly lower pressure than outside — this causes the altimeter to read slightly higher than actual, the VSI to momentarily show a climb, and the ASI to read slightly fast. The Mode C encoder, also connected to the static system, would similarly be affected if it uses the same static port — so ATC's altitude readout could also shift slightly when alternate static is selected, a factor worth noting if ATC questions your altitude.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.215; 14 CFR 91.215(d); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 2

questions.question: You're flying IFR in a helicopter with only a VOR receiver. The CDI is centered and the OBS is set to 090. The TO/FROM flag shows FROM. Where are you relative to the VOR station?
questions.answer: You are on the 090 radial FROM the VOR station, meaning the station is directly to your west (270 degrees magnetic from your position). A VOR radial is always measured FROM the station, so the 090 radial extends due east of the station. Your position is somewhere along that radial — the CDI only tells you you're on it, not how far out you are.

questions.question: Your helicopter is equipped with an ADF and you're tracking inbound to an NDB. The ADF needle is pointing to your 3 o'clock position — relative bearing 090. What does that tell you about the station's position?
questions.answer: The ADF needle always points TO the station. A relative bearing of 090 means the NDB station is 90 degrees to your right — directly off your right side. To determine the magnetic bearing to the station, you would add the relative bearing to your magnetic heading. For example, if you're heading 360, the magnetic bearing TO the station is 360 + 090 = 090 degrees magnetic.

questions.question: What is a VOR cross-radial fix, and why is it more useful for determining your helicopter's position than a single VOR radial alone?
questions.answer: A VOR cross-radial fix is your position determined by the intersection of two radials from two different VOR stations. A single radial only tells you you're somewhere along a line extending from the station — it gives you direction but not distance. When you tune a second VOR and identify which radial you're on from that station, the intersection of both radials gives you a precise geographic position. This is a fundamental IFR position-fixing technique when DME is not available.

questions.question: You're flying your helicopter IFR in a mountainous area at 9,500 feet MSL. Your GPS suddenly shows a RAIM failure alert. How do you determine your position, and what are the limitations of your backup navigation?
questions.answer: With RAIM failure, GPS-derived position can no longer be considered reliable for IFR navigation. You must revert to your backup navigation systems — typically VOR or NDB if equipped. Immediately identify the nearest VOR stations, tune them, and attempt to establish a cross-radial fix. Notify ATC of the GPS failure so they can provide radar identification and vectors if needed. Key limitation: at low altitudes in mountainous terrain, VOR signals may be unreliable below line-of-sight altitude, and the MOCA (Minimum Obstruction Clearance Altitude) only guarantees VOR signal reception within 22 NM of the NAVAID. ATC radar services and controller-provided position information become especially valuable in this scenario.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B, Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.187 (malfunction reports in IFR)

questions.question: You're flying an IFR helicopter approach and ATC asks you to report when established on the final approach fix. Your aircraft has a moving map GPS. How do you positively identify the FAF, and what's the risk of relying solely on the moving map depiction?
questions.answer: The FAF is positively identified using your approved navigation source — GPS CDI showing the waypoint is the active fix, with distance-to-waypoint showing you at or near that point. Cross-check with any available secondary references such as a crossing radial, NDB, or DME if published. The risk of relying solely on the moving map is that the map is a situational awareness tool — it may display the approach structure graphically, but the actual navigation guidance comes from the CDI and the active flight plan in the FMS/GPS. If the wrong approach is loaded, or the database is out of date, the map may look correct while the navigation is wrong. Always verify the active waypoint identifier matches the expected fix name.

questions.question: During an IFR cross-country in your helicopter, ATC provides a radar contact position that conflicts by 5 miles with what your GPS shows. Which do you trust, and how do you resolve the discrepancy?
questions.answer: Treat this as a potential navigation system anomaly and take it seriously. Begin by cross-checking all available navigation sources — GPS position, any available VOR radials, DME, or NDB. If your GPS has RAIM and is showing a valid position without integrity alerts, it is generally very accurate. However, ATC radar in modern facilities (ASR, ARSR) is also highly accurate. Inform ATC of the discrepancy immediately. Ask ATC to confirm their radar return and your squawk code to rule out false target or transponder issues. Request radar vectors if uncertain of position. Do not continue navigating on a potentially compromised system without reconciling the discrepancy — a 5-mile position error in mountainous terrain or during an approach could be life-threatening.

questions.question: You're flying a helicopter IFR in IMC along a Victor airway. Your VOR CDI is showing a steady full-scale deflection to the left, but you haven't changed heading and the OBS is still set correctly. Walk me through your complete systematic process to determine whether this is a navigation error, equipment failure, or actual off-course deviation.
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.171 requires a VOR accuracy check within the preceding 30 days before using VOR for IFR navigation, using one of the approved methods: VOT, certified checkpoint, dual VOR comparison, or airborne over a known fix. The ground check only confirms the receiver was within tolerance (+/- 4 degrees for ground checkpoint, +/- 6 degrees for airborne) at the time of the check. It does not guarantee the receiver continues to function correctly in flight. In-flight VOR failures can and do occur. If a suspicious in-flight indication cannot be reconciled through cross-checks and alternate navigation sources, you must immediately cease IFR reliance on that receiver and declare the equipment unairworthy, even if the ground check was recent. The ground check satisfies the pre-flight requirement, but does not authorize continued use of a receiver suspected of failure during flight.
questions.follow_up: What does 14 CFR 91.171 require you to do before using a VOR for IFR flight, and if you completed that check on the ground but the VOR is now showing a suspicious indication, does your ground check protect you in the air?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 91.171 requires a VOR accuracy check within the preceding 30 days before using VOR for IFR navigation, using one of the approved methods: VOT, certified checkpoint, dual VOR comparison, or airborne over a known fix. The ground check only confirms the receiver was within tolerance (+/- 4 degrees for ground checkpoint, +/- 6 degrees for airborne) at the time of the check. It does not guarantee the receiver continues to function correctly in flight. In-flight VOR failures can and do occur. A suspicious in-flight indication must be treated as a potential equipment failure regardless of the ground check. The ground check satisfies the regulatory requirement but is not a guarantee of continued airworthiness — you must evaluate the instrument's reliability based on current behavior and cross-checks.

questions.question: You're flying a helicopter IFR at night in IMC, and both your GPS and VOR are showing inconsistent position information. Your Mode C transponder is operating. Explain how ATC radar services can be used as a position-determining tool, and what are the limitations of using radar alone for IFR position awareness in a helicopter operating below MEA in mountainous terrain?
questions.answer: With navigation systems unreliable, ATC radar becomes a critical external position reference. Request immediate radar identification by squawking the assigned code and asking ATC to confirm radar contact and your current position. ATC can provide your position relative to a fix, distance and bearing from a NAVAID, or simply call out your location. They can also provide radar vectors to a safe altitude or approach. However, radar has significant limitations in mountainous terrain: terrain may mask your radar return at low altitudes, causing ATC to lose contact below certain elevations. ARTCC radar is en route radar and may have gaps at lower altitudes in mountainous areas; TRACON/approach control radar provides better low-altitude coverage in terminal areas. Additionally, if you are operating below the MEA, you may already be below the minimum safe obstacle clearance altitude — ATC radar cannot guarantee terrain separation, they can only work with your position. The MEA guarantees navigation signal reception and obstacle clearance; the MOCA only guarantees obstacle clearance. If below MEA in IMC without reliable navigation, you must climb immediately to MEA or MVA as directed by ATC, even before resolving the navigation discrepancy, because terrain is the immediate threat.
questions.follow_up: If ATC has you on radar and is providing vectors, are you relieved of responsibility for terrain and obstacle clearance, or does that responsibility remain with you as pilot in command?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot in command retains responsibility for terrain and obstacle clearance even when receiving ATC radar vectors. Per the AIM and FAA guidance, ATC is responsible for separating IFR traffic from other IFR traffic and providing obstruction clearance on assigned routes and altitudes — but the PIC remains responsible for the safe operation of the aircraft. If ATC issues a vector or altitude that you believe would take you into terrain or below safe altitude, you must advise ATC immediately and request an amended clearance. The phrase 'unable' is appropriate and important. This is especially critical in a helicopter IFR context where operations at lower altitudes in complex terrain are more common than fixed-wing IFR. Never blindly follow a radar vector without your own situational awareness of terrain.

questions.question: When you're given a VOR radial to track inbound, which direction does the needle deflect, and what does 'fly toward the needle' actually mean in terms of aircraft heading correction?
questions.answer: When tracking inbound on a VOR radial with the OBS set to the inbound course, a right needle deflection means you are left of course — you correct by turning right (toward the needle). The CDI deflection represents angular displacement from the selected radial. Each dot of deflection represents approximately 2° of angular error. Flying toward the needle means making a heading change in the direction of the deflection to re-intercept the course. Once re-established on course, you bracket the heading to correct for wind drift and maintain the radial.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'homing' to an NDB and 'tracking' to an NDB, and why is homing considered less precise?
questions.answer: Homing means adjusting heading continuously to keep the ADF needle pointed at 0° relative bearing — essentially always pointing the nose at the station. Tracking means establishing a specific magnetic course to the station and correcting for wind to maintain that course. Homing is less precise because in a crosswind, the aircraft follows a curved, arcing path to the station rather than a straight-line course. The pilot ends up drifting downwind and must constantly turn into the station. Tracking requires identifying wind correction angle, applying it, and bracketing to maintain a constant ground track.

questions.question: You're flying a helicopter inbound on a localizer and notice the CDI is showing a full-scale deflection. How does localizer sensitivity compare to a VOR, and what does full-scale deflection tell you about your position?
questions.answer: A localizer CDI reaches full-scale deflection at approximately 2.5° off centerline, while a VOR CDI reaches full-scale deflection at 12° or more off the selected radial. This makes the localizer approximately 4–5 times more sensitive than a VOR. A full-scale deflection on a localizer means you are at least 2.5° off the localizer centerline, which at typical intercept distances could be hundreds of feet laterally. Because of this sensitivity, corrections on the localizer must be small and timely — large heading corrections will cause the aircraft to overshoot the centerline.

questions.question: You're flying your helicopter eastbound at 090° and ATC tells you to intercept the 360 radial of a VOR located north of you and track it inbound. Walk me through your setup and intercept technique.
questions.answer: First, I identify the VOR and set the OBS to 180° (the inbound course on the 360 radial is 180°, flying south toward the station). Since the station is north of me and I'm east of the 360 radial, the CDI will deflect left indicating I need to turn toward the station. I would turn left to a heading that gives me an intercept angle — typically 30° to 45° off the inbound course, so a heading of approximately 135-150°.
