Additionally, if the fuel exhaustion was total and the engine quit — even if you land safely — this may meet the NTSB's definition of an incident (engine failure), which requires a report within 10 days to the NTSB under 49 CFR 830.15.

questions.question: A student pilot is flying solo cross-country in a helicopter and calls you on the radio saying they are lost, their GPS is showing an incorrect position, and they are not sure whether to trust their VOR indication. As their CFI flying a separate aircraft, how would you coach them to prioritize their available navigation resources, and at what point does the situation require them to contact ATC regardless of their comfort level?
questions.answer: Coach the student to immediately apply the 5 C's: Climb, Communicate, Confess, Comply, and Conserve. First, climb to improve radio and navigation signal reception — this is the single most impactful immediate action. Second, identify a known VOR by its Morse code identifier before trusting any CDI indication; a VOR showing the wrong identifier or no identifier should not be used. To cross-check the VOR against the GPS, tune the VOR manually, identify it, and see if the radial it shows is consistent with the GPS-indicated position — if the GPS shows you on the 090 radial from a station but the VOR CDI says you are on the 270 radial from the same station, one of them is wrong and you must not navigate on that data alone. Dead reckoning from the last confirmed fix is more reliable in that case. The point at which they must contact ATC is the moment they cannot confidently establish their position using available means within a reasonable time — this is not optional. A student pilot solo is not the time to let pride delay asking for help. Squawk 7700 if they cannot reach ATC on the working frequency, and transmit on 121.5. Remind them that accepting ATC assistance is not a failure — it is the correct aeronautical decision and the hallmark of sound ADM.
questions.follow_up: What specific failure mode could cause a GPS unit to show a plausible-looking but incorrect position, and how would a pilot detect that during flight?
questions.follow_up_answer: A GPS can show an incorrect but plausible position due to receiver autonomous integrity monitoring (RAIM) failure, where insufficient satellite geometry prevents the receiver from detecting a faulty signal. In that case, the GPS may show no RAIM alert but still compute an inaccurate position. Pilots detect this by: (1) watching for a RAIM or GPS integrity warning on the display — modern GPS units will annunciate RAIM unavailable or GPS not available when integrity cannot be assured; (2) cross-checking the GPS position against VOR radials, DME, or visual landmarks — if the GPS places you over flat farmland but you can clearly see a major city that should not be in that location, the GPS is suspect; (3) checking the satellite count — fewer than 4 satellites visible compromises 3D position accuracy. The takeaway is that no single navigation source should be trusted without cross-checking against at least one independent source, especially when disoriented.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9; AIM 1-1-17; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; AIM 6-2-6

areas_of_operation.title: Area of Operation VIII. Emergency Operations

tasks.title: Task A. Powerplant Failure in a Hover in a Single-Engine Helicopter

questions.question: When an engine fails during a hover, what is the immediate control input required to prevent rotor RPM decay, and why?
questions.answer: The immediate input is to lower the collective. When the engine fails, there is no longer power driving the rotor system. Lowering collective reduces blade pitch, which reduces the aerodynamic drag on the rotor blades, allowing the rotor to maintain RPM through autorotation. If collective is not lowered immediately, the rotor RPM will decay rapidly — potentially below the minimum RPM needed for a safe landing. Low inertia rotor systems decay especially fast, making this input time-critical.

questions.question: What energy sources are available to the pilot to cushion a landing after a powerplant failure in a hover?
questions.answer: The primary energy source is the kinetic energy stored in the rotating rotor system — this is rotor inertia. By increasing collective just before touchdown, the pilot converts that stored rotational energy into lift to cushion the landing. At a hover, there is little to no translational kinetic energy (forward speed) to work with, unlike an autorotation from altitude, so the pilot is almost entirely dependent on rotor inertia. The amount of energy available depends on rotor RPM at the time of failure and the inertia of the rotor system.

questions.question: During a hover autorotation, what happens to heading control after the engine fails?
questions.answer: Heading control is maintained with the antitorque pedals just as in normal flight. During autorotation, the tail rotor continues to be driven by the main rotor transmission, so it remains operational. The pilot must adjust pedal input because the torque demand from the engine is eliminated — requiring a change in pedal position to maintain the desired heading. The direction of the yaw tendency at power loss depends on the rotor system configuration (e.g., counterclockwise rotor systems will yaw right when power is lost).

questions.question: You are hovering at 8 feet AGL with a student on board when the engine quits. The rotor RPM is in the normal range at the time of failure. Walk me through your immediate actions and explain how hover height affects your ability to manage energy in this situation.
questions.answer: Immediately lower collective to maintain rotor RPM — this is the most critical first step. Simultaneously adjust pedals to counteract the change in torque and control heading. At 8 feet AGL, there is just enough height to allow the rotor RPM to stabilize and the helicopter to begin a controlled descent to the surface. As the skids are about to contact the ground, apply upward collective to use the stored rotor inertia for a cushioned touchdown. Hover height matters significantly: too low (under about 2-3 feet) and there may not be enough time to lower collective before ground contact; too high (over approximately 10-15 feet, depending on the aircraft) and rotor RPM may decay before the pilot can arrest the descent, leading to a hard landing. The ideal hover height for practice autorotations is typically specified in the RFM and is usually around 3-8 feet, where rotor inertia can be fully utilized.

questions.question: A pilot is hovering over a confined area with no suitable landing surface directly below when the engine fails. How does the lack of a clear landing zone affect energy management decisions, and what options does the pilot have?
questions.answer: In this scenario, the pilot cannot simply settle straight down, so energy management becomes more complex. If translational velocity can be established quickly — even a small amount of forward or lateral movement — the pilot gains additional translational lift and can extend the glide to a usable surface. However, at a hover, there is almost no stored translational kinetic energy, so any horizontal movement must come from cyclic inputs that bleed rotor inertia. The pilot must rapidly assess whether to: (1) attempt a shallow run-on landing at the edge of the confined area, (2) accept a hard landing on the unsuitable surface if no alternative exists, or (3) if altitude permits even slightly, use any available forward cyclic to reach better terrain. The core trade-off is that every cyclic input used to move laterally or forward draws on the same rotor energy reservoir that would otherwise be used to cushion the landing. Time is extremely short — typically 1-2 seconds before RPM decays to a dangerous level.

questions.question: How does gross weight affect the energy management problem following a powerplant failure in a hover? Specifically, what changes at heavier weights and why does it matter?
questions.answer: At heavier gross weights, the helicopter requires a higher collective pitch setting to hover, meaning the rotor blades are already working harder and producing more induced drag. When the engine fails, this higher pitch setting accelerates rotor RPM decay because the aerodynamic drag on the blades is greater. Additionally, more weight must be supported during the flare-to-landing phase, meaning the stored rotor energy (inertia) must do more work in less time to slow the rate of descent. Heavier helicopters also have greater momentum, which means the rate of descent at the time of touchdown may be higher if rotor RPM has decayed. In practical terms, pilots operating at or near maximum gross weight have a narrower margin for delayed collective reduction — the response must be faster and more precise.

questions.question: Some helicopter POH/RFMs specify a minimum rotor RPM for initiating the collective pull during a hover autorotation. What is the aerodynamic reason for this limitation, and what happens if the pilot pulls collective when rotor RPM is already below that minimum?
questions.answer: The minimum rotor RPM threshold for pulling collective exists because collective pitch increase only produces meaningful lift if the rotor is spinning fast enough to generate adequate centrifugal force and airflow over the blades. If RPM is too low, increasing collective increases blade AOA, but the blade velocity is insufficient to generate the lift required to support the aircraft's weight — the blades may stall instead. A rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable as in a fixed-wing aircraft; once the rotor stalls, there is no mechanism to re-energize it before ground contact. The result is a hard, uncontrolled landing with no cushioning. This is why the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable and early recognition of low RPM is imperative. Pilots must lower collective immediately upon power loss and monitor RPM to ensure it stabilizes in the green arc before attempting to use that energy for the cushioned landing.
questions.follow_up: If you are hovering and notice rotor RPM is already in the lower portion of the green arc before the engine fails — perhaps due to a high-density altitude or heavy gross weight — how does that change your technique and expected outcome?
questions.follow_up_answer: Starting with low RPM in the green arc means the energy reservoir is already diminished before the failure even occurs. The pilot still must immediately lower collective to stop further decay, but there is less stored inertia available for the flare and cushion. This compresses the timing window further — the collective pull for cushioning must happen at exactly the right moment and cannot be held as long as it would with full RPM. The landing may still be survivable, but the sink rate at touchdown will likely be higher. This scenario also reinforces the importance of pre-flight density altitude calculations and weight management — operating near the RPM floor during the hover means a single anomaly can put the pilot in an unrecoverable situation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft RFM (model-specific minimum RPM values)

questions.question: Explain the concept of the 'Height-Velocity (H-V) Diagram' (sometimes colloquially called 'dead man's curve') as it applies to a powerplant failure specifically at a low hover, and describe how this energy management concept was derived.
questions.answer: The 'Height-Velocity (H-V) Diagram' — the official term for this safety boundary in the POH/RFM — defines combinations of altitude and airspeed from which a safe autorotation cannot be completed following a sudden engine failure. The low-altitude portion of the H-V diagram (the lower left area, sometimes called the 'low-hover avoid region') identifies hover heights where there is insufficient altitude for rotor RPM to stabilize and for the pilot to complete a controlled landing. At very low hovers (typically under 2-3 feet AGL, model dependent), there is actually enough proximity to the ground that ground effect cushions the landing and the region is safe again. But at intermediate hover heights in the 'avoid' zone, there is too much altitude to simply 'drop in' safely and not enough altitude to complete a proper hover autorotation. The H-V diagram is derived from actual flight test data by the manufacturer and is aircraft-type and configuration-specific; the diagram must be obtained from the actual RFM being used. It represents a statistical boundary — not an absolute guarantee. Pilots should understand that operations within the avoid region are not prohibited by regulation but represent elevated risk, and that the envelope shrinks further with increased gross weight, density altitude, or degraded pilot response time.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot is conducting a pinnacle approach and must briefly hover within the avoid region of the H-V diagram to assess the landing area, what risk management principles apply, and what should the pilot do to minimize exposure?
questions.follow_up_answer: Hovering briefly in the avoid region of the H-V diagram is an accepted operational risk in helicopter work, but it should be minimized through deliberate risk management. The pilot should: (1) minimize time spent in the avoid region by keeping the assessment phase as brief as possible; (2) ensure rotor RPM is in the upper portion of the green arc before entering the region to maximize stored energy; (3) confirm gross weight and density altitude are within acceptable limits so the H-V envelope is not further degraded; (4) have a clear abort path identified before entering — know where the helicopter will go if power is lost during the hover; (5) apply ADM principles — if conditions are marginal (high DA, heavy, unfamiliar LZ), the risk of operating in the avoid region may not be acceptable and an alternative landing area should be sought. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that approximately 80% of aviation accidents involve human factors — deliberate, time-pressured exposure to the avoid region without a contingency plan is exactly the kind of error chain link that examiners and safety programs work to break.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Height-Velocity Diagram); Aircraft RFM H-V Diagram section; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/Risk Management)

questions.question: How does a higher density altitude affect your helicopter's ability to hover following a power failure?
questions.answer: At high density altitude, the air is less dense, which reduces rotor efficiency and lowers the available engine power. This means the rotor system produces less lift for a given RPM, and the stored rotor inertia may be reduced compared to sea-level conditions. Following a power failure in a hover at high density altitude, rotor RPM decays faster because there is less aerodynamic energy available to sustain it, leaving less time and energy for a controlled landing. The pilot must lower collective immediately and precisely to preserve what rotor RPM remains.

questions.question: What is the effect of a strong headwind on a hovering autorotation following engine failure?
questions.answer: A headwind during a hover power failure is beneficial. Even at hover relative to the ground, a headwind provides relative airflow through the rotor disk, which improves rotor efficiency and helps sustain rotor RPM longer than in calm conditions. As the helicopter descends with a headwind, it will move forward relative to the surface, effectively transitioning into a running landing rather than a pure vertical descent. This forward motion provides translational airflow through the rotor disk, improving lift generation and energy margin. The headwind also reduces the effective groundspeed at touchdown, decreasing the energy that must be absorbed on landing. The pilot must still execute prompt collective reduction, but the relative airspeed and forward drift provide significant margin for a successful autorotation.

questions.question: Why does gross weight matter when your engine fails during a hover?
questions.answer: Gross weight directly affects the rotor disk loading and the amount of lift required to support the helicopter. At higher gross weight, more collective pitch — and therefore more rotor drag — is needed just to hover. When the engine fails, that higher pitch setting causes rotor RPM to decay more rapidly. Additionally, heavier weight increases the energy that must be dissipated at ground contact. A heavy helicopter has a much smaller margin between power-on hover and the rotor RPM that can sustain a controlled settling, making precise and immediate collective reduction even more critical.

questions.question: You're planning a hover training demonstration in a mountain meadow at 7,500 feet MSL on a warm afternoon. How would the combination of high density altitude and elevated temperature change your engine-failure-in-hover recovery compared to doing the same exercise at sea level on a cool day?
questions.answer: At 7,500 feet MSL on a warm afternoon, density altitude could easily exceed 9,000–10,000 feet, significantly reducing both engine power output and rotor aerodynamic efficiency. The consequences for a hover power failure are compounded: (1) The rotor RPM decays faster because rotor blades generate less lift and drag per revolution in thin air, so the kinetic energy stored in the rotor system is depleted more quickly. (2) The collective must be lowered immediately and more aggressively to arrest RPM decay, yet the resulting rate of descent will be higher than at sea level because each collective reduction produces less cushioning effect. (3) The pilot has less margin for delay — the window between engine failure and an uncontrolled hard landing is shorter. Compared to a sea-level cool-day exercise, the same control inputs may not produce the same result; the pilot must be faster and expect a firmer touchdown.

questions.question: During an engine-failure-in-hover scenario, a tailwind is present. Walk me through specifically how that tailwind changes your hazard picture compared to hovering in calm wind.
questions.answer: A tailwind during a hover power failure creates several compounding hazards. First, a tailwind reduces the relative airflow entering the rotor disk from an optimal angle, increasing the induced power required to hover before the failure occurs—exactly the wrong time to have higher power demands. Second, upon engine failure and settling, a tailwind means the helicopter drifts backward relative to the ground. If forward cyclic is applied to arrest this drift or clear obstacles, groundspeed at touchdown increases, raising landing impact energy compared to a calm-wind scenario. Third, tail rotor authority may be degraded in tailwind conditions, increasing susceptibility to loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE), particularly in aircraft designs sensitive to quartering tailwind conditions. In summary, a tailwind compresses the already narrow time-and-energy margin of a hover autorotation while potentially complicating directional control.

questions.question: You are hovering at maximum gross weight on a hot day and your engine fails at 8 feet AGL. Compare this scenario to the same failure at 3 feet AGL on a cool day at light weight — which is more survivable and why?
questions.answer: The 3-foot AGL failure at light weight and cool temperature is significantly more survivable. At 3 feet AGL and light weight on a cool day: (1) The rotor system is at a lower collective pitch setting, so RPM decays more slowly upon engine failure. (2) The helicopter is close enough to the ground that it is within ground effect, which reduces induced power requirements and can cushion the descent. (3) Light weight means less energy to absorb at touchdown and less rotor drag to overcome. At 8 feet AGL at maximum gross weight and hot temperature: the rotor is working harder to hover (higher collective pitch), RPM decays faster, density altitude reduces available rotor energy, and the helicopter must descend farther before skids contact — burning through what little rotor inertia remains. Maximum gross weight also increases the impact energy at landing. The 8-foot/heavy/hot scenario demands near-perfect technique with almost no margin for error.

questions.question: A student argues that wind direction doesn't really matter for a hover power failure because the helicopter isn't moving anyway. How do you correct that misconception, and what specific wind condition most significantly degrades a hover autorotation?
questions.answer: The student's reasoning is flawed on two fronts. First, even at zero groundspeed, wind direction determines the aerodynamic environment the rotor disk operates in. A headwind reduces the induced power required to hover by improving the relative airflow into the rotor disk, while a tailwind increases induced power requirements—a critical penalty in a power-off condition. Second, wind direction affects tail rotor authority and the likelihood of loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE). For a helicopter with a counterclockwise main rotor, tailwind conditions (particularly left quartering tailwind) can degrade tail rotor effectiveness and increase the demand for right pedal authority—exactly the wrong combination during engine failure. The wind condition that most significantly degrades a hover autorotation is a tailwind combined with high gross weight and high density altitude, because it compounds reduced rotor efficiency, increases touchdown groundspeed, and may trigger LTE during the recovery. To mitigate: reposition into the wind before initiating the failure, reduce gross weight if possible, lower hover altitude to 2–3 feet AGL to minimize descent distance, and ensure directional control authority is verified before the maneuver.
questions.follow_up: If you're hovering and notice a tailwind condition just before you begin the engine-failure demonstration, what practical mitigation can you apply before initiating the failure?
questions.follow_up_answer: The practical mitigations are: (1) Reposition the helicopter into the wind before initiating the failure — even a few seconds of pedal turn to face the headwind changes the aerodynamic picture dramatically. (2) Reduce gross weight if possible (fuel burn, reduced load) to give more rotor inertia margin. (3) If repositioning is not possible, lower the hover altitude to 2–3 feet AGL to minimize descent distance before ground contact, maximizing the chance of a controlled landing before RPM is depleted. (4) Ensure the landing zone is clear in all directions since directional control may be compromised. The fundamental principle is to never accept a tailwind for a hover autorotation demonstration if you have the option to reposition.

questions.question: Density altitude is often described as a single factor, but it actually combines multiple variables. Break down the individual contributions of pressure altitude and temperature to the hover power failure problem, and explain why temperature has a disproportionate effect on turbine helicopter performance.
questions.answer: Density altitude = pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature. The two components affect hover power failure differently: Pressure altitude alone reduces air density (fewer air molecules per cubic foot), which reduces rotor aerodynamic efficiency and lowers the power ceiling at which the engine can operate. However, turbine engines are mass-flow devices — they ingest and process a mass of air, not a volume. Temperature compounds the pressure altitude effect because hot air is less dense for a given pressure, further reducing the mass flow the engine ingests. For turbine helicopters specifically, temperature has a disproportionate effect because most turbine engines are thermally limited (torque or turbine temperature limits) before they are aerodynamically limited. On a hot day, the engine reaches its temperature limit (TGT/TOT/ITT) at a lower power output, meaning the pilot may not have access to maximum rated power even though the rotor could theoretically absorb more. This 'double penalty' — reduced rotor efficiency AND reduced available power — makes the hover power failure at high temperature and altitude far more critical than either factor alone would suggest. The rotor RPM decay rate accelerates because available power is less while power required is more.
questions.follow_up: At what point does temperature stop being the limiting factor for a turbine engine and pressure altitude becomes dominant instead?
questions.follow_up_answer: At very high altitudes (above approximately 15,000–20,000 feet density altitude depending on the engine), the air becomes so thin that the engine can no longer reach its temperature limit — it is starved of mass flow entirely. Below that crossover point, temperature is typically the limiting factor (the engine hits TGT/TOT limits). Above that crossover, the engine is power-limited by air mass starvation regardless of temperature. For practical hover operations, this distinction matters at high mountain sites — the pilot at 12,000 feet MSL on a cold day may have relatively more usable power than at the same field on a hot day, but will still face dramatically reduced rotor efficiency from the pressure altitude alone. The Helicopter Flight Manual's hover ceiling charts account for this crossover, which is why OGE hover charts show steep performance loss curves at the intersection of high pressure altitude and high temperature.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 2; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-25 Rotorcraft Flight Manual performance charts

questions.question: What is meant by 'rotor inertia' in a helicopter, and what physical property most directly determines whether a rotor system is considered high or low inertia?
questions.answer: Rotor inertia refers to the rotor system's resistance to changes in rotational speed — its tendency to keep spinning once in motion. The primary physical property that determines high vs. low inertia is the mass of the rotor blades and how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation. Heavier blades with mass concentrated farther from the hub produce a high-inertia rotor system. Lighter blades, or those with mass closer to the hub, produce a low-inertia system. High-inertia rotors store more kinetic energy and resist RPM decay; low-inertia rotors lose RPM quickly when power is removed.

questions.question: During a hover autorotation following an engine failure, why does a low-inertia rotor system present a greater challenge to the pilot compared to a high-inertia system?
questions.answer: A low-inertia rotor system stores less kinetic energy in the spinning blades. When the engine fails, the rotor has very little energy reserve to sustain RPM while the pilot responds and lowers collective. The rotor RPM decays rapidly — sometimes in just 1 to 2 seconds — leaving a very small window for the pilot to take corrective action. If RPM decays below the minimum operating range before collective is lowered, the blades can stall and recovery is not possible. A high-inertia system decays more slowly, giving the pilot more time to react and execute the correct control inputs.

questions.question: What is the immediate control action required upon engine failure in a hover, and why is this action especially critical in a low-inertia rotor system?
questions.answer: Upon engine failure in a hover, the pilot must immediately lower the collective to reduce pitch angle on the rotor blades. This reduces the drag load on the rotor system, allowing aerodynamic forces — upward airflow through the disk — to maintain or slow the decay of rotor RPM. In a low-inertia rotor system, this action must occur almost instantaneously because the rotor has very little stored energy to sustain RPM against the drag created by blade pitch. Any delay allows RPM to drop below the usable range rapidly, and since rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable, early and immediate collective reduction is imperative.

questions.question: You are flying a light piston helicopter with composite blades — known to be a low-inertia design — and experience an engine failure at a hover over a confined area with obstacles on all sides. How does the low-inertia characteristic specifically affect your decision-making and technique during the landing?
questions.answer: The low-inertia characteristic means rotor RPM will decay very rapidly after engine failure, so the priority is immediate collective reduction to preserve whatever RPM remains. With limited stored energy, the pilot has almost no time to assess options before acting. The landing technique must be aggressive and decisive: lower collective immediately, allow the helicopter to settle vertically (hover autorotation), then use the remaining rotor energy to cushion the touchdown by slowly increasing collective just before ground contact. There is no time to reposition to a better landing spot in most cases — the helicopter will settle essentially straight down. The pilot should also be aware that the RPM window for a successful cushion is narrow; if collective is raised too early or too aggressively, RPM will bleed off before touchdown, resulting in a hard landing. Situational awareness and prior planning of the landing zone are therefore critical before entering a hover in a low-inertia aircraft.

questions.question: A high-inertia rotor system stores more energy and decays more slowly after engine failure. Does this mean a pilot flying a high-inertia helicopter can delay lowering the collective after an engine failure in a hover? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: No — even in a high-inertia helicopter, the pilot should lower collective immediately upon recognizing engine failure. While it is true that a high-inertia system gives the pilot a larger margin of time before RPM decays to a critical level, any deliberate delay is unsafe and unnecessary. The correct immediate action is the same regardless of rotor inertia: lower collective to unload the rotor and preserve RPM. The difference is that in a high-inertia aircraft, a momentary delay due to recognition time is less likely to be catastrophic, whereas in a low-inertia aircraft it can be immediately fatal. Training to always respond immediately builds the correct habit pattern for any helicopter flown. Additionally, the FAA notes that accidents decrease significantly with experience in a specific aircraft type — understanding your specific rotor system's inertia characteristics is part of that type-specific proficiency.

questions.question: How does the Coriolis effect relate to rotor inertia, and how could it affect RPM behavior during a hover autorotation following an engine failure?
questions.answer: The Coriolis effect in a rotor system describes the change in rotational velocity that occurs when the center of mass of a rotor blade moves toward or away from the axis of rotation. In an articulated rotor system, as blades flap up, their center of mass moves closer to the axis, which by conservation of angular momentum causes the blade to accelerate (speed up) in the plane of rotation. Conversely, when blades flap down, the center of mass moves outward and the blade decelerates. During a hover autorotation following engine failure, after collective is lowered, blades may flap and the Coriolis effect can contribute small changes to rotor RPM. In a high-inertia system these effects are smoothed out by the system's large energy storage. In a low-inertia system, the rotor is more sensitive to any RPM-affecting phenomena, including Coriolis-induced changes, making precise collective management even more critical.

questions.question: A student tells you: 'I fly a turbine helicopter with heavy metal blades, so I have plenty of time to react if the engine quits in a hover — I don't need to worry about rotor inertia as much.' As an examiner, how do you evaluate this statement, and what critical nuance about high-inertia systems is the student missing?
questions.answer: The student's reasoning is partially correct but dangerously incomplete. It is true that a high-inertia rotor system decays more slowly and provides a larger time margin for response. However, the student is missing several critical nuances: First, 'plenty of time' is relative — even high-inertia systems can decay below minimum RPM if the pilot is slow to react or hesitates. The correct response is always immediate collective reduction, not a relaxed one. Second, a high-inertia rotor stores more energy, which is useful for cushioning the landing, but that energy can only be used once — if it is wasted during a delayed response phase, less remains for the touchdown flare and cushion. Third, complacency born from believing you have 'plenty of time' is itself a human factors hazard; approximately 80% of aviation accidents involve pilot error, and overconfidence is a known ADM trap. Finally, even turbine helicopters with heavy blades have RPM limits, and operating near the lower end of the green arc at the time of failure reduces the effective margin. The student should understand that high inertia is an advantage, not a substitute for correct technique and immediate response.
questions.follow_up: If a high-inertia helicopter has more stored rotor energy available for the landing cushion, what technique error could still result in a hard landing even in that favorable helicopter?
questions.follow_up_answer: The most common technique error is raising collective too early during the cushion phase. If the pilot initiates the collective pull too high above the ground, the stored rotor energy is consumed prematurely — RPM bleeds off before the skids reach the ground. When the helicopter finally reaches touchdown altitude, there is insufficient rotor energy remaining to arrest the descent rate, resulting in a hard or even damaging landing. The collective should be raised smoothly and progressively at low altitude — typically just a few feet above the surface — to time the energy use with actual ground contact. This error is not inertia-dependent; it is a technique error that can occur in both high and low inertia systems, though the consequences manifest differently given the different RPM margins involved.

questions.question: During a hover autorotation evaluation, your applicant lowers collective immediately on cue but then holds full down collective all the way to touchdown, resulting in a hard landing. The applicant argues they did everything correctly because they 'lowered collective immediately like the book says.' How do you address this, and what does it reveal about the applicant's understanding of rotor inertia and energy management?
questions.answer: The applicant correctly identified and executed the first critical action — immediate collective reduction — but failed to understand the complete energy management picture. Lowering collective preserves rotor RPM by reducing drag load on the blades, allowing the rotor to maintain RPM through autorotative airflow. However, the stored kinetic energy in the rotor system is the resource used to cushion the landing. Holding full down collective to touchdown wastes that opportunity entirely — the helicopter hits the ground with no energy application to arrest descent rate. The correct technique is to lower collective immediately to preserve RPM, allow the helicopter to settle, then progressively raise collective just before touchdown to convert stored rotor kinetic energy into lift and arrest the descent. This is the energy conversion phase — the entire purpose of preserving RPM during the descent is to have it available for the cushion. The applicant's error reveals a memorized, fragmented understanding of the procedure without comprehension of the underlying rotor energy concept. In a low-inertia helicopter, this error would be catastrophic; in a high-inertia helicopter, it produces exactly what was observed — a hard landing. Understanding rotor inertia means understanding when and how to use the stored energy, not just how to preserve it.
questions.follow_up: How would your coaching approach differ if this same technique error occurred in a low-inertia helicopter versus the high-inertia helicopter in which it actually happened?
questions.follow_up_answer: In the high-inertia helicopter, the error produced a hard landing — significant but potentially repairable and survivable. The coaching focus would be on energy management timing: when to initiate the collective pull and how to gauge altitude above the ground for the cushion. In a low-inertia helicopter, holding full down collective to touchdown is likely to produce the same hard landing, but the margin for error during the entire sequence is far smaller — any hesitation or mistimed input can result in RPM falling below the stall threshold before touchdown, at which point the blades produce no lift regardless of collective position, and the result is an uncontrolled hard landing or rollover. The coaching approach for a low-inertia aircraft would emphasize recognition speed, the extremely tight RPM band available, and the absolute necessity of practicing this maneuver extensively to build muscle memory — because cognitive processing time alone may be too slow to save the aircraft. The FAA notes that accident rates drop significantly after 100 hours in a specific type, underscoring that type-specific practice in the actual aircraft is the mitigation for low-inertia system risks.

questions.question: When the engine fails during a hover, what immediately happens to rotor RPM if the pilot takes no corrective action?
questions.answer: Rotor RPM begins to decay immediately. Without engine power driving the rotor, the main rotor loses its energy source. The collective pitch setting at the time of failure creates drag on the blades, causing rapid RPM bleed-off. The rate of decay depends on rotor inertia — low-inertia rotor systems decay much faster than high-inertia systems, leaving the pilot very little time to respond.

questions.question: What is the purpose of immediately lowering the collective when the engine fails in a hover, and what aerodynamic effect does it produce?
questions.answer: Lowering the collective reduces the pitch angle of the rotor blades, which reduces blade drag and allows the rotor to maintain or recover RPM. It also reduces the lift being generated, which allows the helicopter to settle toward the ground in a controlled manner. The reduced angle of attack on the blades means less induced drag, which helps preserve what rotor energy remains. This is the single most critical immediate action in a hover autorotation.

questions.question: During a hover autorotation, does the tail rotor continue to function, and how does it affect heading control?
questions.answer: Yes. The tail rotor continues to function because it is mechanically driven by the main rotor transmission, not directly by the engine. As long as main rotor RPM exists, the tail rotor produces thrust. Antitorque pedals continue to control heading in the same manner as normal flight. However, as collective is lowered and torque decreases, less left pedal is required, so the pilot must adjust pedal inputs accordingly to maintain heading.

questions.question: You're hovering at 8 feet AGL when the engine fails. Explain the aerodynamic sequence of events from the moment of failure through touchdown if you execute a proper hover autorotation.
questions.answer: At failure, rotor RPM begins to decay due to blade drag with no driving force. The pilot immediately lowers collective, reducing blade pitch and drag, which arrests RPM decay and allows the helicopter to settle. As the helicopter descends, relative airflow begins moving upward through the rotor disk — but at hover height this airflow is minimal compared to a cruise autorotation. The stored kinetic energy in the rotor system is the primary resource. As the skids near the ground, the pilot applies collective to cushion the landing, converting rotor RPM (kinetic energy) into lift. Timing is critical — applying collective too early wastes rotor energy before ground contact; too late results in a hard landing. The helicopter touches down with whatever energy remains, ideally with minimal vertical velocity.

questions.question: A student says that a hover autorotation is easier than a power-off autorotation from cruise because you're already close to the ground. How would you correct this misunderstanding using aerodynamic principles?
questions.answer: This is a common and dangerous misconception. A hover autorotation is actually more aerodynamically challenging in several ways. At cruise altitude, forward airspeed converts to upward airflow through the rotor disk during entry, helping sustain rotor RPM. In a hover there is no forward airspeed to assist — the pilot is entirely dependent on stored rotor inertia. Additionally, the pilot has virtually no time to react and no altitude to trade for energy. The rotor RPM can decay to a critical level within one to two seconds. The collective cushion at the end must be perfectly timed because there is no ability to extend the glide or reposition. The aerodynamic margin for error is much smaller in a hover autorotation.

questions.question: How does hover height above the ground affect the aerodynamics and survivability of a powerplant failure in a hover?
questions.answer: Hover height is a critical factor. Very low hovers (under 3–5 feet) allow the pilot to simply lower collective and let the skids contact the ground before significant RPM decay occurs — the time window actually works in the pilot's favor. At moderate hover heights (8–20 feet), the pilot must carefully manage the descent rate and time the collective cushion; enough altitude exists to allow RPM decay before touchdown but not enough to recover significant RPM from airflow. At heights within the 'dead man's curve' or height-velocity diagram danger zones, the combination of insufficient altitude for an autorotative glide and insufficient time to react makes survival dependent almost entirely on rotor inertia and pilot reaction speed. Higher hovers may actually provide enough altitude for translational lift to develop during descent, improving the aerodynamic situation.

questions.question: During a powerplant failure in a hover, a pilot applies collective too aggressively to arrest the descent before touching down. Walk me through exactly what happens aerodynamically and what the likely outcome is.
questions.answer: Applying collective increases blade pitch angle, which increases induced drag on the rotor blades. This drag rapidly consumes rotor RPM — the kinetic energy stored in the rotating system. If collective is applied too aggressively or too early, the rotor RPM drops below the minimum required to sustain lift before the helicopter reaches the ground. At that point the rotor has no remaining energy to cushion the landing and the pilot has no corrective option. The helicopter enters a high-rate-of-descent condition with essentially no lift, resulting in a hard or catastrophic landing. This is sometimes called 'pulling pitch into a dying rotor.' The aerodynamic principle is that rotor RPM is the only energy reservoir in a hover autorotation, and that energy must be rationed and applied at precisely the right moment to convert it to lift for a cushioned touchdown.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot recognizes early that they've pulled too much collective and rotor RPM is decaying rapidly, is there any aerodynamic recovery option at this point?
questions.follow_up_answer: At very low altitude with decaying RPM, options are extremely limited. Lowering collective again would reduce drag on the blades and could slow the RPM decay, but it would also increase descent rate — and at hover height there may not be enough altitude to allow RPM to recover before ground contact. In most cases, the correct action is to immediately lower collective to stop the RPM bleed, accept a harder landing, and attempt to apply whatever collective remains when the skids are inches from the ground. The helicopter may still sustain significant airframe damage, but reducing the sink rate even slightly with remaining RPM can mean the difference between a repairable aircraft and a fatality. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that rotor stall in a helicopter is non-recoverable — early recognition and prevention is the only real defense.

questions.question: When a powerplant failure occurs during a hover, what should be your immediate orientation reference before executing any control inputs?
questions.answer: The pilot must instantly orient to three things: the helicopter's height above the ground (hover altitude), the wind direction relative to the helicopter's nose, and the surface condition and slope beneath and around the aircraft. These three factors directly dictate whether a hovering autorotation is survivable and which direction to settle the helicopter. At a normal hover height of 2–5 feet AGL with a level, clear surface below, the procedure is straightforward — lower collective to cushion touchdown. Without knowing these factors, control inputs may be incorrect and worsen the outcome.

questions.question: What does 'division of attention' mean specifically in the context of a powerplant failure at a hover, and what are the two competing demands on the pilot's attention?
questions.answer: Division of attention during a hover engine failure means simultaneously managing the aircraft's flight path and descent while also scanning and monitoring critical instruments and the environment outside. The two competing demands are: (1) executing precise and timely control inputs — lowering collective, maintaining heading with anti-torque pedals, and keeping cyclic centered to prevent drift — and (2) scanning outside for hazards such as obstacles, people on the ground, or an uneven surface while cross-checking cockpit instruments like rotor RPM. Fixating solely on one task — either the instruments or the view outside — can allow the other to deteriorate fatally.

questions.question: What does 'proper planning' mean before conducting a hover operation in a single-engine helicopter, specifically as it relates to surviving an engine failure?
questions.answer: Proper planning before hovering means mentally rehearsing the engine failure response before it happens. This includes: (1) selecting and confirming a suitable landing surface directly below or within immediate reach, (2) identifying the hover height — keeping it within the safe zone for a hovering autorotation (typically 0–5 feet AGL on a clear surface), (3) noting wind direction so you understand which pedal will be needed for heading control, (4) clearing the area of personnel and obstacles, and (5) briefing yourself on the immediate action — collective down, maintain heading, cushion landing. Planning eliminates hesitation; in a hover engine failure, the rotor RPM decay begins immediately and reaction time is measured in fractions of a second.

questions.question: You are hovering at 8 feet AGL over a paved ramp when the engine fails. You have a line of parked aircraft 30 feet to your left and an open taxiway directly ahead. How does your pre-failure orientation affect your control response?
questions.answer: At 8 feet AGL — above the typical safe hovering autorotation height — the pilot is in a more critical position because the collective must come down quickly to preserve rotor RPM, but there is not enough height to allow a significant drift before touchdown. Orientation to the parked aircraft on the left means left cyclic is NOT an option — lateral drift in that direction would cause a collision. The open taxiway ahead provides an escape path if a small forward cyclic input is used to drift slightly forward and away from the ramp hazards. The pilot should simultaneously lower collective immediately to arrest rotor RPM decay, apply forward cyclic minimally to clear toward the open taxiway, and use pedals to maintain heading. The key point is that pre-planned orientation to those obstacles determines which direction cyclic is applied within the first second — there is no time to evaluate this after the failure.

questions.question: During a training session, you are hovering in a confined area and your attention is fully on an air traffic control transmission when the engine fails. How does this lapse in division of attention change the difficulty of the recovery?
questions.answer: A lapse in attention at the moment of engine failure is extremely dangerous because the pilot's first cognitive task becomes recognition of the failure, not response to it. Rotor RPM begins decaying immediately upon engine failure — in a low-inertia rotor system, this can occur within 1–2 seconds. If the pilot is heads-down or distracted by ATC, recognition is delayed, the collective input is late, and RPM may have already decayed below the recoverable range. Additionally, the pilot loses situational awareness of aircraft position relative to obstacles, meaning the subsequent control inputs are made without knowing the best touchdown direction. This scenario illustrates why division of attention must be maintained continuously during hover operations — not just when convenient — and why ATC communications should be managed before entering a confined hover, not during.

questions.question: You are planning a hover over a sloped helipad. How does the slope affect your pre-failure orientation plan specifically regarding a hovering autorotation?
questions.answer: A sloped surface significantly affects the orientation plan for a hover engine failure. If the engine fails while hovering over a slope, settling straight down onto the slope risks dynamic rollover — particularly if one skid contacts the uphill side first while the rotor disk is still generating lift. Proper pre-failure orientation over a slope means: (1) identifying the slope direction and degree of angle, (2) mentally planning to direct the helicopter to touch down on the lowest side first or to drift laterally to a flat area if one exists nearby, (3) being prepared to apply cyclic toward the high side of the slope during touchdown to prevent the uphill skid from becoming a pivot point, and (4) accepting that a rapid descent straight down may not be the best option if a flat touchdown zone is reachable within the available rotor energy. Orientation to slope is a pre-hover planning item — it cannot be adequately assessed after rotor RPM is already decaying.

questions.question: A student pilot tells you that because the engine failure at a hover is so fast, there is no time to use orientation or planning — you simply have to react instinctively. How do you respond, and what does the research on accident causation say to support or refute this claim?
questions.answer: The student's claim confuses the execution phase with the preparation phase. The student is partially correct that the actual control response must be instinctive and immediate — there is no time during the failure to begin evaluating obstacles or surface conditions. However, that is precisely why orientation and planning must happen BEFORE the failure occurs. FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 notes that approximately 80% of aviation accidents are caused by human factors, and the error chain typically begins well before the accident event itself. In the hover engine failure context, the 'error' of not orienting to the landing zone and obstacles before the hover begins is the link in the error chain that causes the survivable engine failure to become a fatal accident. The instinctive reaction is only correct if it was pre-programmed through planning — a pilot who planned to land straight down onto a clear surface will instinctively lower collective and settle; a pilot who did not plan may hesitate, drift into an obstacle, or freeze. Pre-flight and pre-hover mental rehearsal is what makes the instinct correct.
questions.follow_up: If I told you that you had to hover over an unprepared surface at night with no lighting, what specific additional planning items would you add to your orientation checklist before beginning the hover?
questions.follow_up_answer: At night over an unprepared unlighted surface, the standard orientation items still apply but must be addressed using available lighting and pre-arrival reconnaissance. Additional planning items include: (1) Use landing light and/or night vision equipment to positively identify surface slope, texture, and any large obstacles before descending to hover height. (2) Establish a reference point — a fixed light source or marker — to detect any inadvertent drift during the hover, since visual ground cues are severely degraded at night. (3) Identify the touchdown direction before establishing the hover using that light reference, not trying to find it after failure. (4) Consider whether the operation is necessary at all — if surface conditions cannot be confirmed, crew resource management and aeronautical decision-making may dictate declining the operation or requesting additional lighting. (5) Set a personal minimum hover height lower than daytime (staying in ground effect with minimal cushion above the surface), since any drift at night over an unknown surface is more dangerous than in daytime. (6) Brief any crew or passengers that the engine failure procedure will be initiated without hesitation — no verbal confirmations required during the recovery.

questions.question: During a checkride hover task, your examiner asks: 'What single planning decision most directly affects whether you survive a hover engine failure — and what happens to that survival probability if your rotor system has low inertia compared to a high-inertia system?'
questions.answer: The RFM limitation carries regulatory weight under 14 CFR 91.9 when the manufacturer has established it as a certificated operating limitation. If the RFM explicitly states that hovering autorotations above a specific height are not certificated or are outside the aircraft's operating envelope, the PIC must treat this as an operational boundary under 91.9. If the statement is advisory (e.g., 'not recommended'), it is strong guidance but technically distinguishable from a hard limitation. In either case, prudent ADM treats an RFM caution about hovering autorotation survivability as an operational boundary. A deliberate decision to hover at a height where the manufacturer has documented that engine failure would be non-survivable — without mitigation (e.g., positioning over a clear, low-drag landing zone) — could constitute careless operation under 14 CFR 91.13 if an accident resulted, but the primary regulatory framework is 91.9 (adherence to operating limitations).
questions.follow_up: If your specific helicopter's RFM states that hovering autorotations are not recommended above a certain height AGL, are you prohibited from hovering higher than that — and what regulatory framework governs that limitation?
questions.follow_up_answer: The RFM limitation is not a regulatory prohibition in the same sense as a 14 CFR restriction, but it carries regulatory weight under 14 CFR 91.9, which prohibits operating an aircraft contrary to its operating limitations. If the RFM states that hovering autorotations above a specific height are not recommended or that the aircraft is not certificated for procedures above that height, the PIC is responsible under 91.9 for operating within those limitations. Hovering above that height is not automatically illegal if the hover itself is within the envelope — the limitation addresses the survivability of the autorotation, not the hover itself. However, a prudent pilot and good ADM should treat an RFM caution about hovering autorotation height as an operational boundary, not merely advisory. Additionally, the PIC bears responsibility under 14 CFR 91.13 (careless or reckless operation) if they deliberately hover at a height where a known, documented engine failure would result in a non-survivable situation without taking mitigation steps.

questions.question: When a powerplant failure occurs while hovering, what is the immediate control input priority and why?
questions.answer: The immediate priority is to lower the collective to minimum pitch. This reduces blade drag and allows the rotor system to maintain or recover RPM through autorotation. Delaying this input — even by a fraction of a second — allows rotor RPM to decay rapidly, especially in low-inertia rotor systems. Without adequate RPM, the pilot loses the stored energy needed to cushion the landing.

questions.question: Why is a powerplant failure during a hover considered one of the highest-risk phases of helicopter flight from a pilot response standpoint?
questions.answer: During a hover, the helicopter has little or no translational lift and minimal stored energy (airspeed). The rotor is doing all the work to support the aircraft's weight. Upon engine failure, rotor RPM decays almost immediately. There is virtually no time or altitude to recover, and the pilot must react with the correct control inputs — primarily immediate down collective — before RPM drops below a recoverable threshold. The consequence of hesitation is a hard landing or loss of control.

questions.question: How does hover altitude affect the risk and outcome of a powerplant failure in a single-engine helicopter?
questions.answer: Hover altitude is a critical risk factor. At very low hover heights (a few feet AGL — the normal operating hover), the pilot can perform a hovering autorotation with the collective already low and land in a relatively short distance. At higher hover altitudes (above approximately 10 feet depending on the aircraft), the pilot has more time for rotor RPM to decay but also needs more stored rotor energy to cushion the descent. Some hover altitudes fall within the height-velocity 'avoid' curve (deadman's curve), where a safe autorotation landing may not be achievable. Operating within the avoid curve significantly increases risk during engine failure.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Height-Velocity Diagram in RFM

questions.question: You are hovering at 8 feet AGL over a clear, flat, paved surface when the engine fails. What risk factors are most favorable here, and what could make this outcome worse?
questions.answer: Favorable factors: The surface is clear, flat, and paved — providing an unobstructed landing zone. At 8 feet AGL, the pilot has minimal altitude to lose and can lower collective immediately, allowing the rotor to drive down to the surface in a controlled hovering autorotation with limited vertical velocity if executed correctly. Unfavorable factors that could worsen the outcome: high gross weight (less rotor inertia margin), high density altitude (reduces rotor efficiency), low-inertia rotor system (faster RPM decay), wind from unfavorable direction, any delayed reaction to lowering collective, or landing gear configuration. Additionally, if the aircraft is loaded near max gross weight at high density altitude, the stored rotor energy may not be sufficient to arrest the descent adequately even with perfect technique.

questions.question: You are conducting an external load hover operation at 25 feet AGL when the engine fails. How does this scenario change your risk exposure compared to a standard 5-foot hover, and what options do you have?
questions.answer: At 25 feet AGL, you are likely within the high hover / low speed avoid area of the height-velocity diagram, which represents one of the highest-risk zones for powerplant failure. The primary risks are: (1) insufficient altitude to gain translational lift or airspeed for a normal autorotation, (2) insufficient rotor energy to fully arrest descent from 25 feet, and (3) the external load may complicate collective management and oscillate or pendulum upon touchdown. Options are limited — the pilot must immediately lower collective to preserve rotor RPM, apply aft cyclic to minimize forward movement, and attempt to reach the ground as controlled as possible. Jettisoning the external load (if equipped) should be considered to reduce weight and improve autorotation performance. Pre-planning landing zones directly below or within immediate reach is essential when operating at these altitudes.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Height-Velocity Diagram; 14 CFR 133.49 (external load jettison requirements)

questions.question: As a risk management decision, a pilot is asked to perform a confined area hover at 10 feet AGL surrounded by trees on all sides with no clear autorotation landing zone. What risk assessment should be made before accepting this hover position?
questions.answer: The pilot must evaluate this through the lens of the height-velocity diagram and available landing zones. Key risk considerations: (1) Is the hover altitude within the avoid area of the HV curve for this aircraft at the current gross weight and density altitude? (2) If the engine fails, is there any survivable landing option — or will the aircraft contact obstacles on the way down? (3) Can the pilot conduct a hovering autorotation within the confined area, or will obstacles prevent it? If there is no survivable forced landing option and the hover altitude falls within the avoid curve, the risk is extremely high and the mission should be declined or modified to reduce hover altitude (below 5 feet if the surface permits) or the pilot should plan an approach/departure path that minimizes time in the avoid zone. Risk management here is proactive — identify the hazard before entering the confined area.

questions.question: A pilot operating at a remote mountain site hovers at 6 feet AGL to load passengers at 8,500 feet MSL on a hot afternoon, with the helicopter at near-maximum gross weight. Walk me through the compounding risk factors for a powerplant failure in this hover and how you would mitigate them prior to the operation.
questions.answer: This scenario stacks multiple compounding risks: (1) High density altitude (8,500 ft MSL + high temperature) means the engine is producing near its limit of power just to hover — there is little to no power margin. Any fuel contamination, carburetor ice, or slight engine degradation could trigger failure. (2) Near-maximum gross weight reduces rotor inertia per unit weight and increases the descent rate during autorotation. (3) Mountain terrain likely means the confined area beneath and around the hover may not offer a clear autorotation landing zone. (4) At max gross weight / high DA, the pilot is likely hovering near or at the peak of the power required curve, with engines near a torque or temperature limit — a prolonged hover increases engine heat stress. Mitigations before the operation: (a) Calculate density altitude and confirm hover power available exceeds power required with margin per RFM charts. (b) Reduce gross weight if power margins are tight — carry fewer passengers or less fuel per leg. (c) Pre-identify landing zones: where will you go if the engine fails right now? (d) Minimize hover time — make a run-on or low-hover approach to reduce exposure time in the avoid zone. (e) Position aircraft so that in event of failure, the path of least resistance is clear of obstacles. (f) Ensure all passengers are briefed on emergency egress. (g) Consider the aircraft's HV curve at this gross weight and altitude and whether the hover is within or outside the avoid area.
questions.follow_up: You've done the math and find that at this density altitude and gross weight, you are right at the edge of OGE hover capability according to the performance charts. The mission is time-sensitive. What is the risk management principle that should govern your decision, and what practical alternatives do you offer?
questions.follow_up_answer: The governing principle is the 'avoid probably' concept from FAA ADM guidance — if the safe outcome of this operation will only 'probably' work, you should select an option known to work. Operating at the exact edge of OGE hover capability means any degradation — contaminated fuel, a slight power turbine efficiency loss, or a momentary gust — can exceed available power and cause power failure or uncontrolled descent. Practical alternatives: (1) Reduce payload — offload fuel or reduce passenger count to create a clear hover power margin per charts. (2) Coordinate a different landing site at lower elevation where power margins are confirmed. (3) Delay the flight until ambient temperature drops (early morning), increasing density of the air and improving engine and rotor performance. (4) Use a rolling or run-on landing approach to deliver passengers without sustained OGE hover. The time pressure is a known risk-inducing factor (hazardous attitude — 'get-there-itis') and should be recognized and actively resisted as part of ADM.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, 'Trescott Tip', Hazardous Attitudes); RFM Hover Performance Charts

questions.question: During a simulated engine failure at a hover, what is the correct immediate collective input and why is it critical?
questions.answer: The immediate response is to lower the collective to the full-down or near-full-down position. This action reduces the pitch angle on the main rotor blades, which decreases drag on the rotor system and allows the rotor RPM to be maintained as engine torque is lost. Failure to lower collective immediately will cause rotor RPM to decay rapidly, and in a low-inertia rotor system, RPM loss can become unrecoverable within seconds.

questions.question: When the engine fails in a hover, what happens to yaw tendency and which pedal input is required to correct it?
questions.answer: At the moment of engine failure, the loss of engine torque eliminates the main rotor's torque reaction on the fuselage. In a helicopter with a counterclockwise-rotating main rotor (standard US configuration), the nose will yaw left as tail rotor thrust is no longer being counteracted by engine torque. The pilot must apply left pedal to reduce tail rotor thrust and prevent the uncontrolled left yaw, then manage pedals throughout the maneuver to maintain directional control.

questions.question: What is the primary role of cyclic control input during a powerplant failure at a hover, and what is the goal of that input?
questions.answer: During an engine failure at a hover, the cyclic is used to control the helicopter's attitude and lateral position. The goal is to keep the helicopter level and prevent lateral drift so that when the helicopter settles to the ground, it contacts with little or no lateral movement. Lateral drift at touchdown can lead to dynamic rollover. Cyclic inputs should be smooth and coordinated to arrest any movement toward obstacles or hazardous terrain.

questions.question: You are hovering at 10 feet AGL over a confined area with obstacles on both sides. The engine fails. Walk me through your control inputs in sequence, and explain what risk each input is managing.
questions.answer: 1) Immediately lower collective to arrest rotor RPM decay — this manages the risk of rotor stall, which is unrecoverable. 2) Apply left pedal as needed to control yaw as engine torque disappears — this manages the risk of an uncontrolled spin on the way down. 3) Apply cyclic to level the aircraft and stop any lateral drift — this manages the risk of striking obstacles and the risk of dynamic rollover on touchdown. 4) As the helicopter descends and ground contact approaches, use any remaining rotor RPM and a slight collective cushion to soften the landing — this manages the risk of hard contact and structural damage. All inputs must be simultaneous and coordinated; prioritizing one while neglecting another can make the outcome worse.

questions.question: A student pilot instinctively pulls up on the collective when the engine fails at a hover during training. What is the risk created by that input, and how quickly can it become unrecoverable?
questions.answer: Pulling up on the collective increases blade pitch, which dramatically increases rotor drag. Without engine power to overcome that drag, the rotor RPM decays rapidly. In low-inertia rotor systems common to light training helicopters, the RPM can fall below the minimum effective range within one to two seconds. Once rotor RPM is lost to the point of blade stall, lift production collapses entirely and there is no recovery — the helicopter will fall with no means of controlled flight. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook specifically notes that rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable, making early and correct collective input the single most critical risk mitigation at engine failure.

questions.question: You experience an engine failure at a hover and during your descent you notice the helicopter drifting right toward a berm. You apply left cyclic to stop the drift, but you are slow to lower collective. What two compounding risks have you created with these combined inputs?
questions.answer: First, by being slow to lower collective, you are allowing rotor RPM to decay because increased blade pitch without engine power increases rotor drag — this creates the risk of rotor stall and loss of all lift. Second, by applying lateral cyclic while the rotor disk is tilted without adequate RPM, you are reducing lift efficiency further while simultaneously placing the helicopter in a lateral attitude. If the skids contact the ground during a right-to-left drift with a lateral tilt, you have created the conditions for dynamic rollover — where the rotor's lateral thrust will roll the helicopter past its critical rollover angle. These two risks together — rotor RPM decay and potential dynamic rollover — represent the primary causes of fatal hover autorotation accidents.

questions.question: During an engine failure at a high hover (out-of-ground-effect altitude, say 50 feet AGL), how does the required timing and magnitude of control inputs differ from a low hover failure at 3 feet AGL, and what unique risks emerge at the higher altitude?
questions.answer: At a low hover of 2–3 feet AGL, the pilot has minimal time but also minimal altitude to manage — the helicopter will contact the ground quickly, and the primary risk is a hard landing or dynamic rollover. The collective cushion technique with whatever remaining RPM is available is the primary tool. At a high hover of 50 feet AGL, the pilot has more time to manage inputs, but the risks are more complex: (1) There is enough altitude for the rotor RPM to decay significantly if collective is not lowered immediately — a longer time window does not mean a more forgiving window. (2) The pilot must decide whether to attempt a running landing if forward movement is possible, or execute a vertical autorotation to the surface. (3) At 50 feet AGL, the helicopter may actually be above the 'dead man's curve' (Height-Velocity diagram avoid region), meaning even a perfect autorotation may result in a hard landing because the altitude-to-airspeed energy exchange is insufficient for a cushioned touchdown. (4) Any lateral drift at this altitude will translate into significant horizontal velocity by touchdown, dramatically increasing dynamic rollover risk. The control inputs must be prioritized as: collective down immediately, heading control with pedals, attitude and drift control with cyclic, and then a decision on landing direction.
questions.follow_up: You mentioned the Height-Velocity diagram. If the pilot is operating in the 'avoid' region of that diagram and the engine fails, is there any control input sequence that guarantees a survivable outcome?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — by definition, the Height-Velocity diagram's 'avoid' region identifies combinations of altitude and airspeed from which a successful autorotation to a safe landing cannot be consistently executed even with perfect technique. This is why it is called an 'avoid' region, not a 'difficult' region. The specific boundary is established by the helicopter manufacturer through flight testing and is published in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual. If an engine failure occurs in this region, the pilot should still execute proper inputs — lower collective, control heading, level attitude — because even a partial mitigation may reduce the severity of the outcome. But the fundamental risk management lesson is that operating in the avoid region is itself the risk that must be managed before the flight, not during the emergency.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) Height-Velocity Diagram

questions.question: A pilot reports that during a practice hover autorotation, they felt they had 'good control' throughout but the skids contacted the ground with a hard thump and the helicopter rocked laterally before settling. What control input errors does this describe, and what could those errors have led to in an actual engine failure?
questions.answer: The 'hard thump' on contact indicates that the collective cushion — the slight upward collective pull near ground contact to use remaining rotor inertia to soften the touchdown — was either poorly timed, insufficient, or both. This means rotor RPM was not managed effectively throughout the descent, or the cushion was applied too early and RPM was depleted before contact. The lateral rock after contact indicates that there was residual lateral drift or lateral cyclic displacement at touchdown, meaning the pilot did not achieve a wings-level, zero-lateral-drift condition before ground contact. In an actual engine failure, the lateral rock is the precursor to dynamic rollover — if the skid catches on the surface during that lateral movement and the pilot reacts by pulling collective or applying opposite cyclic, the helicopter can roll inverted. The 'good control feeling' the pilot describes is a classic example of fixating on one axis (perhaps directional control) while neglecting others (collective RPM management and lateral drift). This ties directly to ADM and workload management — in a single-pilot emergency, the pilot must simultaneously manage all three axes and the energy state of the rotor without prioritizing one to the detriment of others.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot passed the maneuver during training with this technique, what responsibility does the instructor bear, and what standard should the maneuver be evaluated against?
questions.follow_up_answer: The instructor bears significant responsibility if they accepted a hard landing with lateral rock as a passing performance. The ACS specifies that the applicant must demonstrate correct control inputs — including a smooth collective cushion and a touchdown with minimal lateral movement. A hard landing indicates the pilot did not effectively use available rotor inertia, and lateral rock indicates failure to achieve directional and positional control. The instructor's role is not only to critique the outcome but to identify the specific control input errors causing it and require corrective practice before signing off the maneuver. Passing a student with marginally adequate results in an emergency procedure is a training risk management failure — the 'error chain' concept from ADM applies here, where an instructor's acceptance of poor technique becomes one link in a chain that could ultimately end in a fatal accident.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapters 11 and 13; ACS CH.X.A; 14 CFR Part 61

questions.question: When a powerplant failure occurs during a hover, what is the primary risk associated with uncontrolled helicopter movement in the first few seconds after engine failure?
questions.answer: The primary risk is that without immediate corrective control inputs, the helicopter will begin to drift, yaw, or settle in an uncontrolled manner. Without engine torque, the tail rotor thrust changes suddenly, causing an uncommanded yaw (typically to the right in helicopters with counterclockwise main rotor systems). Simultaneously, rotor RPM begins to decay and the helicopter starts to settle. Any uncontrolled movement during this critical phase can lead to dynamic rollover, main rotor contact with the ground or obstacles, or a hard landing with loss of directional control.

questions.question: Why does a helicopter tend to yaw in a specific direction immediately following a powerplant failure at a hover, and what control input addresses this movement?
questions.answer: In a helicopter with a counterclockwise-rotating main rotor system (most American helicopters), the engine drives the main rotor and tail rotor simultaneously. When the engine fails, the torque effect on the fuselage ceases abruptly, but the tail rotor continues to be driven by the main rotor through the transmission as long as rotor RPM is maintained. The tail rotor's continued thrust now tends to yaw the nose to the right (the tail pushes left). The pilot must reduce right pedal input, which had been holding the nose straight against engine torque, to prevent the uncommanded right yaw. Proper pedal coordination is critical to prevent uncontrolled directional movement during the failure.

questions.question: What is the significance of rotor RPM decay rate as a risk factor for uncontrolled helicopter movement during a hover engine failure, and how does rotor inertia affect the outcome?
questions.answer: When an engine fails at a hover, rotor RPM begins to decay immediately because the hovering rotor requires significant power and the energy source is gone. The rate of decay depends on rotor inertia — high-inertia rotor systems (heavier blades) decay more slowly, giving the pilot more time to react and lower the collective. Low-inertia rotor systems decay very rapidly, sometimes in just 1–2 seconds. As RPM decays, lift decreases and the helicopter settles. If the pilot does not immediately lower collective to reduce blade pitch and allow the remaining RPM to sustain the rotor, the rotor may reach a stall condition. A stalled rotor is not recoverable, meaning the helicopter will experience catastrophic uncontrolled movement — a hard, uncontrolled descent and contact with the ground.

questions.question: You are hovering a helicopter at 4 feet AGL in a confined area with obstacles on three sides. The engine fails. What specific movement risks are present in this environment that would not exist over an open field, and how does your response need to account for them?
questions.answer: In a confined area with obstacles on three sides, the risks of uncontrolled helicopter movement are significantly elevated compared to an open area. First, any lateral drift caused by wind, incorrect cyclic input, or the yaw-induced asymmetric rotor disk loading could bring the main rotor or tail rotor into contact with trees, buildings, or terrain walls. Second, the settling motion — which is unavoidable after engine failure — must be arrested quickly and precisely; an off-level surface or uneven settling could initiate dynamic rollover against a berm or obstacle. Third, the uncommanded yaw could swing the tail boom into an obstacle before the pilot can correct.
