Ensure the engine is delivering full available power to the transmission; if RPM is low because of throttle position or governor lag, correct this while the collective is reduced. (3) THIRD — Once RPM is back in the normal operating range, smoothly re-raise collective to re-establish hover altitude and position. Sequence matters because any delay in lowering collective while RPM is decaying reduces the recovery margin — RPM loss is exponential near stall, not linear. Attempting to 'hold altitude' with collective while RPM decays will guarantee a hard landing or rotor stall.
questions.follow_up: If you lower the collective all the way to the bottom stop and the RPM still does not recover, what does that tell you, and what is your next action?
questions.follow_up_answer: If full collective reduction (pitch flat) does not allow RPM to recover, this indicates either the engine has actually failed (not just simulated), the drive system is damaged, or there is a governor or throttle malfunction preventing power delivery. The rotor is now acting as a free-spinning disk with no meaningful lift production, and impact with the ground is imminent. At this point, the collective should remain at the bottom, cyclic should be used to keep the aircraft upright and minimize lateral drift, and the pilot must accept a hard, controlled landing. After touchdown, the pilot should immediately execute emergency shutdown procedures per the flight manual. This scenario underscores the importance of recognizing the difference between a simulated and actual engine failure during training, and ensuring adequate height/energy before beginning the recovery phase.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11 (Low Rotor RPM and Stall; Engine Failure at Hover); POH/RFM emergency procedures

questions.question: You've re-established power after a simulated hover engine failure and are attempting to establish the into-wind stationary hover, but you are operating at a high-altitude airport on a hot day with maximum gross weight on board. How does this density altitude environment specifically change the control feel and technique required to establish and hold the hover, and what limitations might prevent you from establishing the hover at all?
questions.answer: At high density altitude with maximum gross weight, rotor efficiency is significantly reduced because the air is less dense — the rotor must work harder (higher pitch angle / higher AOA) to generate the same lift. The control technique changes in the following ways: (1) Collective will be at or near the upper end of its range just to achieve hover — there is little remaining collective authority for maneuvering or correcting drift. (2) Power required may equal or exceed power available, meaning hover may not be achievable (hover ceiling exceeded). The pilot must check both IGE and OGE hover ceiling charts in the POH against current conditions before attempting. (3) Pedal authority is reduced — tail rotor thrust decreases in density altitude at the same pitch angle, requiring more pedal input to maintain heading; in extreme cases tail rotor may reach its pitch limit and directional control is lost (a form of LTE). (4) Control response is more sluggish — larger inputs may be needed but must still be smooth to avoid overshooting. Limitation: if required hover power exceeds available engine power for existing density altitude and gross weight, a stationary hover cannot be established. The pilot should either reduce weight, wait for cooler temperatures/lower pressure altitude, or transition directly to forward flight rather than attempting a sustained hover.
questions.follow_up: How do you determine before the flight whether you can hover at this location, and which specific performance chart do you reference?
questions.follow_up_answer: Before flight, the pilot references the Hover Ceiling vs. Gross Weight charts (or equivalent) in the helicopter's Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM/POH). There are typically two charts: one for Hover In Ground Effect (IGE) and one for Hover Out of Ground Effect (OGE). The pilot calculates current density altitude using pressure altitude and temperature, then finds the intersection of that density altitude with current gross weight on the chart. If the gross weight plotted falls to the right of or below the performance curve, a hover is not achievable under those conditions. Since the maneuver after an engine failure requires hovering, the pilot must confirm sufficient power margin exists prior to flight. 14 CFR 91.9 prohibits operating outside of weight and performance limits established in the aircraft's flight manual.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 9 (Hovering); 14 CFR 91.9; RFM/POH Hover Performance Charts; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Weight and Balance/Performance)

questions.question: When simulating a powerplant failure at a hover, what is the first and most critical control input you must make, and why?
questions.answer: The first and most critical input is to immediately lower the collective to the full-down or near full-down position. This reduces the pitch angle on the rotor blades, decreasing lift and drag, which allows the rotor system to maintain RPM through autorotative inflow. Without this immediate action, rotor RPM decays rapidly and may reach a stall condition that is not recoverable. In a real engine failure at a hover, the helicopter will settle; the pilot's goal is to preserve rotor RPM throughout the maneuver.

questions.question: During a simulated hover power failure, what happens to tail rotor effectiveness and how do you maintain directional control?
questions.answer: When the engine fails at a hover, engine torque is lost almost instantly. Since there is no longer engine-driven torque acting on the fuselage, the anti-torque input that was being held with the pedals will cause the nose to yaw. In a counterclockwise-rotating main rotor helicopter, the nose will yaw right when torque is lost if left pedal is not reduced. However, the tail rotor is still mechanically driven by the main rotor transmission as long as rotor RPM is maintained, so the pilot continues to use anti-torque pedals to control heading throughout the autorotative descent and landing. Smooth pedal adjustments maintain desired heading during the rapid descent to the surface.

questions.question: What is the typical altitude range considered a 'hover' for the purpose of practicing powerplant failure simulations, and what makes this altitude regime particularly demanding?
questions.answer: A hover powerplant failure is typically simulated at normal hovering altitude, generally 2 to 4 feet AGL (skid-equipped helicopters) or at the specific hovering height specified for the aircraft. This altitude regime is particularly demanding because there is very little time and almost no altitude margin to arrest the descent. The pilot cannot enter a glide to build rotor RPM as in a forward-flight autorotation — instead, the helicopter settles almost immediately. The pilot must cushion the landing using any residual rotor RPM stored in the rotor system by applying collective just before ground contact. Low-inertia rotor systems decay especially quickly, making timing critical.

questions.question: You are conducting a simulated hover power failure during a checkride. After lowering the collective, the helicopter begins settling rapidly and you notice the landing zone has a 6-inch rock directly below the left skid. Walk me through your decision-making and control inputs to avoid damage while still completing the maneuver safely.
questions.answer: First, recognize the hazard early — situational awareness prior to the maneuver requires pre-scanning the landing area. If the hazard is recognized during the maneuver, a small cyclic correction can be used to shift the touchdown point laterally, but cyclic inputs must be minimal and smooth to avoid disrupting rotor disk attitude during the rapid descent. If the obstacle cannot be avoided with minor cyclic correction, and if sufficient rotor RPM remains, a slight early collective cushion can be used to momentarily arrest the descent and allow repositioning, though this trades rotor RPM for altitude. The priority hierarchy is: (1) maintain rotor RPM, (2) achieve a controlled landing attitude, (3) avoid the obstacle. If the landing cannot be made safely, the simulated failure should be discontinued by the instructor before contact. In training, the instructor should have selected a clear landing area before initiating the simulation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM); ACS CH.X.A

questions.question: You are practicing hover power failure simulations and on your third repetition you notice the rotor RPM at the moment of touchdown is consistently in the yellow arc, not the green. What does this tell you about your technique, and what specific adjustment would you make?
questions.answer: Rotor RPM in the yellow arc at touchdown indicates the collective cushion is being applied too early in the descent. When collective is raised prematurely, blade pitch increases, load on the rotor disk increases, and rotor RPM is consumed before the helicopter reaches the ground — leaving insufficient RPM for an effective cushion at the critical last few inches. The correction is to delay the collective cushion until the helicopter is very close to the ground, typically within 1–2 feet, and then apply it smoothly but firmly to arrest the final rate of descent. Additionally, ensure the collective was fully lowered at the moment of simulated failure initiation; a partial reduction bleeds rotor RPM throughout the maneuver. Review the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for the specific aircraft's minimum rotor RPM limits and cushion timing guidance.

questions.question: How does hovering into the wind versus hovering with a tailwind change your technique and the outcome of a simulated hover power failure?
questions.answer: Hovering into the wind provides translational lift benefits even at low airspeeds if there is sufficient wind, which means the rotor is operating more efficiently with better inflow. During a power failure, an into-the-wind hover may allow slightly more time before RPM decay becomes critical, and the helicopter tends to settle more predictably. A tailwind hover is significantly more hazardous: the rotor may already be operating less efficiently, and if the helicopter has any rearward drift during the autorotative descent, the tail could contact the ground first, potentially causing a rollover or tail rotor strike. Technique adjustment for a tailwind hover failure includes using forward cyclic to ensure the helicopter remains in a slightly nose-low or neutral attitude during the descent, and being especially vigilant about any rearward movement. Operationally, simulated hover failures should ideally be conducted with the helicopter positioned into any prevailing wind.

questions.question: During a simulated hover powerplant failure on a checkride, the applicant lowers the collective but then simultaneously applies full aft cyclic, causing the tail to strike the ground first before the skids. As the examiner, what specific aerodynamic error occurred, and how would you explain the correct cyclic management during this maneuver to the applicant?
questions.answer: The applicant experienced what is essentially a tail-low attitude during the autorotative descent, likely caused by an instinctive or over-corrective aft cyclic input — possibly a trained response from fixed-wing flare technique, or an attempt to slow forward drift. During a hover power failure, the cyclic should remain essentially neutral or only minimally adjusted for drift correction. Aft cyclic tilts the rotor disk rearward, pitching the nose up and the tail down, which causes the tail boom or tail rotor to contact the ground before the skids. The correct technique is to maintain the helicopter in a level or very slightly nose-low attitude throughout the descent using minimal cyclic inputs, focused only on controlling lateral and longitudinal drift. The collective does all the energy management work; the cyclic manages attitude and position. Any significant aft cyclic during a hover autorotation dramatically increases the risk of tail strike and dynamic rollover.
questions.follow_up: You've corrected the applicant on cyclic technique. Now they ask: 'If I shouldn't use aft cyclic, how do I stop forward drift if the wind is pushing me toward a fence during the descent?' How do you answer?
questions.follow_up_answer: Forward drift during a hover autorotative descent should be stopped with very small, measured aft cyclic inputs — not a gross rearward pull. The key is anticipation: before initiating the simulated failure, ensure the helicopter is in a stable, drift-free hover with the wind factored in. If drift develops during the descent, a small corrective cyclic input is appropriate, but it must be balanced to avoid a tail-low attitude. If the drift toward the obstacle cannot be corrected without risking a tail strike, the simulation should be discontinued immediately by the instructor. The real lesson here is that pre-maneuver positioning and wind awareness are the primary defenses — the maneuver itself leaves almost no margin for large corrective inputs.

questions.question: An applicant with 250 total hours but only 15 hours in the specific make and model being tested consistently demonstrates delayed collective application during hover power failure simulations — rotor RPM decays 10–15% before they act. The RFM states minimum autorotative RPM is N1 equivalent to 90% NR. What does the research say about why this applicant may be struggling specifically in this aircraft, and what is the aerodynamic consequence if they delay this long in a real engine failure?
questions.answer: FAA research documented in the Helicopter Flying Handbook indicates that accident rates correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft type than total flight hours, and that proficiency improves dramatically after approximately 100 hours in type. At 15 hours in type, the applicant has not yet developed the automatic, conditioned response required for the hover power failure — a maneuver that allows less than one second for initial reaction. They may be reverting to muscle memory from a previous aircraft type with different rotor inertia, different collective position at hover, or different throttle correlation. Aerodynamically, if NR decays 10–15% before collective is lowered, the rotor is already operating with reduced RPM and reduced stored kinetic energy. When collective is then lowered, there is less RPM available to be maintained through the autorotative descent. In a low-inertia rotor system, a 10–15% RPM decay before initial response may approach or exceed the recoverable range — particularly if the simulated failure is initiated at a standard 3–4 foot hover AGL, leaving virtually no time to recover RPM before ground contact. The practical result is a hard landing with insufficient RPM remaining to cushion, potentially causing structural damage or occupant injury.
questions.follow_up: Given that this applicant is below the 100-hour type threshold and is demonstrating a safety-critical delayed response, would you pass, fail, or discontinue the practical test? What regulatory and safety framework guides your decision?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under the ACS standards for CH.X.A, the applicant must demonstrate the ability to simulate powerplant failure including correct initial control response. A consistent and repeated delayed collective application that results in RPM decay outside the normal operating range constitutes a failure to meet the skills standard — this is a disapproval item. The examiner should discontinue further attempts at the maneuver once the pattern of unsafe response is clearly established, document the specific deficiency in the Notice of Disapproval, and recommend the applicant receive additional dual instruction focused specifically on hover autorotation entry technique in this aircraft type. Under 14 CFR 61.43, the examiner has the authority and obligation to discontinue a practical test if a safety-of-flight issue arises. The applicant may re-test on this specific task (Area of Operation) after the deficiency is corrected, without needing to repeat the entire practical test.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; 14 CFR 61.43; ACS CH.X.A

questions.question: During a simulated engine failure at a hover, what does the ACS require you to maintain in terms of heading tolerance?
questions.answer: The ACS requires you to maintain heading within ±5° throughout the entire maneuver. This means from the moment of power loss through the settling to the surface, your heading must not deviate more than 5° in either direction from your initial hover heading.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS CH.X.A

issues: The answer states heading tolerance is ±5° but does not cite a specific ACS page or standard document where this tolerance is explicitly published. FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 covers hovering autorotation technique but the specific ±5° heading tolerance value should be verified against the current ACS document directly. This may be correct but needs confirmation from authoritative source.
verification.suggested_correction: Verify the ±5° heading tolerance requirement directly from the current ACS standards document for CH.X.A. If confirmed, add the specific ACS page reference. If this tolerance is not explicitly stated in the ACS, clarify what the actual heading control standard is for this maneuver.
verification.triage_note: The ±5° heading tolerance is stated as an ACS requirement but the verifier correctly notes that this specific numerical standard is not explicitly cited in available authoritative sources; confirmation against the current ACS document CH.X.A is needed before shipping.

questions.question: Which flight control is primarily responsible for maintaining heading during a hovering autorotation after an engine failure?
questions.answer: The antitorque pedals (tail rotor pedals) are primarily responsible for maintaining heading. When engine power is lost, torque effect disappears, so the pilot must adjust pedal input — typically reducing left pedal in a counterclockwise rotor system — to prevent the nose from yawing. Since the tail rotor continues to be driven by the main rotor transmission during autorotation, heading control via pedals is still available throughout the maneuver.

questions.question: When the engine fails at a hover, what immediate change in torque effect must you anticipate to keep the heading within the ±5° standard?
questions.answer: When the engine fails, the driving torque from the powerplant immediately ceases. In a helicopter with a counterclockwise-rotating main rotor (most American helicopters), the left anti-torque pedal input that was compensating for torque is no longer needed. If the pilot does not quickly reduce left pedal input, the nose will yaw left due to the now-excessive tail rotor thrust. The pilot must rapidly reduce left pedal — or apply right pedal — to neutralize the yaw and maintain heading within ±5°.

questions.question: You are hovering at 3 feet AGL facing north when your instructor pulls the throttle to simulate an engine failure. You immediately lower collective but notice the nose is drifting 8° to the right. What likely caused this, and how do you correct it before touching down?
questions.answer: An 8° rightward yaw in a counterclockwise-rotor helicopter suggests the pilot over-corrected by applying too much right pedal after losing torque, or failed to reduce left pedal quickly enough and then over-compensated. To correct: apply left pedal smoothly to arrest the yaw and return to the original heading. The correction must be immediate but not aggressive — over-controlling heading at low altitude with decaying rotor RPM adds risk. The goal is to stop the heading exceedance and stabilize within ±5° before ground contact, which in a hovering autorotation happens within 1–2 seconds of the failure.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS CH.X.A

questions.question: A student consistently loses heading control during simulated hovering engine failures and exceeds the ±5° standard. During debrief, they say they are focused entirely on lowering the collective. What training point would you emphasize, and how does task prioritization relate to this heading standard?
questions.answer: The student is demonstrating task fixation — prioritizing one control input (collective) while neglecting simultaneous pedal management. In a hovering autorotation, all critical inputs happen essentially at the same time: collective down to maintain rotor RPM, cyclic to hold position, and pedals to control heading. The heading standard of ±5° requires the pilot to manage pedal input concurrently with collective, not sequentially. Effective Single-Pilot Resource Management (SRM) and workload management require distributing attention across all controls. Training should include isolated pedal exercises and progressively building to combined inputs under simulated failure conditions.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 9 and 13; ACS CH.X.A

questions.question: You are performing a simulated hovering engine failure into a confined area with obstacles at your 2 and 10 o'clock positions. How does the ±5° heading standard take on added operational significance in this environment?
questions.answer: In open areas, a ±5° heading deviation is primarily a precision standard. In a confined area with obstacles nearby, that same 5° deviation could swing the tail rotor, skids, or main rotor disk toward structures or terrain. Maintaining tight heading control ensures the helicopter settles onto the intended landing point and that the rotor disk remains clear of obstacles. This is exactly why the ACS sets a firm ±5° standard — it reflects the real-world margin that separates a safe touchdown from a tail strike or main rotor contact in operational environments. The pilot must internalize heading control as a safety-critical skill, not just a testing requirement.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS CH.X.A

questions.question: During a hovering engine failure simulation, a pilot maintains heading perfectly within ±2° but allows rotor RPM to decay well below the green arc before touching down. As an examiner, how do you evaluate this performance — is the heading standard alone sufficient for a passing grade on this task?
questions.answer: No — maintaining heading within ±5° is one of several concurrent ACS skill standards for this task. The ACS also requires the pilot to recognize the failure promptly, lower collective immediately to preserve rotor RPM, and execute a safe touchdown. A pilot who holds heading beautifully but allows rotor RPM to decay below limits has demonstrated an unsafe technique that could result in rotor stall in a real emergency — an unrecoverable condition. As an examiner, I would note the precise heading control as a strength but evaluate the overall performance as unsatisfactory due to the RPM exceedance, because no single element can be performed safely in isolation from the others.
questions.follow_up: If that same pilot argues they were focused on heading because that is what you specifically asked them to demonstrate, how do you respond as an examiner?
questions.follow_up_answer: As an examiner, I clarify that the ACS tasks are evaluated holistically — I cannot isolate a single skill element and ignore concurrent safety-of-flight standards. The Practical Test Standards and ACS are designed so that each listed skill must be performed correctly simultaneously, not in sequence. Additionally, under 14 CFR 61.43, an applicant fails a checkride when they demonstrate a deficiency in any area that indicates they do not possess the skills required for the certificate or rating. Allowing rotor RPM to decay to an unsafe level is exactly that kind of deficiency, regardless of heading performance.

questions.question: On a calm day, a pilot consistently holds heading within ±5° during hovering engine failure simulations. On the day of the checkride, there is a 12-knot crosswind. The pilot exceeds the heading standard by 7°. What aerodynamic factor specific to this condition likely contributed, and what technique adjustment should have been anticipated?
questions.answer: In a crosswind, the tail rotor's effectiveness and the weathervaning tendency of the fuselage interact in ways that differ significantly from calm conditions. The crosswind creates a weathervaning force that pushes the nose into or away from the wind depending on wind direction relative to the fuselage, and the tail rotor must work against or with this tendency. When engine torque suddenly disappears in a crosswind hover, the balance point of pedal inputs shifts compared to a calm-day setting — the pilot's learned pedal reflexes from calm-day training may under- or over-compensate. The technique adjustment: prior to the maneuver, the pilot should note the current pedal trim position in the crosswind hover, mentally anticipate how that trim point will shift at power loss, and prepare to neutralize yaw more aggressively or conservatively depending on wind direction. Hovering in crosswinds before practicing engine failures is essential preparation.
questions.follow_up: What crosswind direction would require the most significant pedal adjustment in a counterclockwise-rotor helicopter at the moment of engine failure, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: A crosswind from the left (pilot's left, striking the left side of the fuselage) tends to push the tail to the right and the nose to the left — partially simulating the torque-induced left yaw. In a counterclockwise-rotor helicopter, the left pedal is already partially depressed to counter torque during normal hover. A left crosswind means the pilot is holding even more left pedal than a calm-day hover to keep the nose straight. At engine failure, torque stops AND the weathervane force may diminish or shift, requiring a rapid and larger reduction in left pedal — potentially a rapid right pedal input. This combined change is the most demanding pedal transition at power loss and most likely to cause a heading exceedance beyond ±5° if not anticipated.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 9 and 11; ACS CH.X.A

questions.question: During a hover autorotation, why is rearward movement at touchdown specifically prohibited, while the standard only requires 'minimum' sideward movement?
questions.answer: Rearward movement at touchdown creates a rollover risk because the helicopter's center of gravity is forward of the main rotor mast, and any rearward drift combined with skid contact can cause the tail to dig in or the helicopter to tip backward. Sideward movement, while also undesirable, is less likely to cause catastrophic rollover when kept to a minimum. Rearward movement also places the pilot in a position where visual reference to obstacles behind the aircraft is impossible, making it an absolute hazard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; ACS CH.X.A Touchdown standard

questions.question: What is the primary flight control input used to stop sideward drift just before touchdown during a hover autorotation?
questions.answer: Cyclic is the primary control used to arrest sideward drift. The pilot applies cyclic input opposite to the direction of drift to decelerate lateral movement and achieve a near-zero groundspeed touchdown. Collective management is also critical during this phase to control the rate of descent, and pedals are used to maintain heading alignment, but cyclic directly addresses sideward movement.

questions.question: At the moment of engine failure in a hover, what is the first critical collective input and why does it directly affect your ability to achieve a controlled touchdown?
questions.answer: The pilot must immediately lower the collective to reduce blade pitch and preserve rotor RPM. In a low hover autorotation, rotor RPM is the only energy source available to cushion the descent. If the collective is not lowered promptly, rotor RPM decays rapidly — especially on low-inertia rotor systems — and the pilot loses the ability to flare the descent rate with collective just before touchdown. Without adequate rotor RPM at touchdown, there is insufficient lift to cushion the landing, and the resulting hard landing makes controlling sideward or rearward movement nearly impossible.

questions.question: You are at a 3-foot hover over an uneven concrete ramp when the engine fails. The helicopter has a slight drift to the left at the moment of failure. Walk me through your control sequence from failure recognition through touchdown, specifically addressing how you eliminate that leftward drift before contact.
questions.answer: Immediately upon recognizing the engine failure, lower collective smoothly to preserve rotor RPM — this is non-negotiable and must be instinctive. Simultaneously apply right cyclic to arrest the leftward drift, and use pedals to maintain heading. As the helicopter settles, focus on achieving zero groundspeed before skid contact. Use the remaining rotor RPM to apply a small collective cushion in the last foot of descent to soften touchdown. The right cyclic input to stop lateral drift must be neutralized just before skids contact so you are not still pushing the helicopter sideways at the moment of touchdown — the goal is zero lateral movement at contact. Do not allow any rearward cyclic drift to develop; maintain a neutral-to-slightly-forward cyclic position throughout.

questions.question: Your training helicopter has a low-inertia rotor system. How does this characteristic specifically change the technique and timing required to achieve the touchdown standard of minimum sideward and no rearward movement compared to a high-inertia system?
questions.answer: A low-inertia rotor system decays RPM much faster after engine failure because there is less stored rotational energy. This means the pilot has a significantly shorter time window between failure recognition and RPM decay to an unusable level. The practical implication for the touchdown standard is that collective must be lowered even faster and the entire sequence — arresting drift, achieving zero groundspeed, and cushioning the touchdown — must be executed in a compressed timeframe. With high-inertia systems, a pilot may have a fraction of a second to assess drift and apply correction; with low-inertia systems, hesitation results in RPM decay that makes the cushion collective ineffective, producing a hard landing where lateral or rearward movement is then impossible to control. Pilots transitioning to low-inertia aircraft must develop faster instinctive response.

questions.question: During a hover autorotation practice, you notice the helicopter develops rearward movement just before touchdown. What specific error in cyclic control most likely caused this, and what is the hazard if you don't correct it before skid contact?
questions.answer: Rearward movement before touchdown is most commonly caused by excessive aft cyclic input — either as an instinctive reaction to the sudden descent or as an overcorrection attempt to slow the descent rate (which is a collective function, not cyclic). The pilot may also unconsciously tense up and pull back on the cyclic when startled by the engine failure. The hazard is significant: if the aft skid or tail contacts the ground first with any rearward momentum, the helicopter can tip backward rapidly. The tail rotor or tail boom may strike the ground, and the rotor disc can then contact the ground in what can become an unrecoverable dynamic situation. The touchdown standard explicitly prohibits rearward movement for this reason.

questions.question: A student consistently achieves good rotor RPM management during hover autorotations but repeatedly touches down with 2–3 feet of leftward drift because they are focused on the RPM gauge at the critical moment. As the instructor, how do you diagnose the root cause, and what specific training intervention corrects the fixation without degrading their RPM scan?
questions.answer: The root cause is improper scan priority and likely a lack of peripheral awareness — the student has correctly learned that RPM is critical but has over-indexed on the instrument at the expense of outside visual references. This is a classic fixation pattern. The correction involves teaching the student that during a hover autorotation, the outside visual scan for drift and ground reference is the primary input source, while rotor RPM awareness is maintained peripherally or through auditory cues (governor audio, rotor RPM audio alert if equipped, or the sound of rotor system). Training interventions: (1) Have the student verbalize 'RPM set, outside' as they lower collective to force an external scan transition. (2) Practice the maneuver with the student calling out drift corrections aloud to confirm external visual priority. (3) Brief the student on using tactile feedback — a smooth, firm collective cushion feel — rather than relying solely on the gauge in the final foot. (4) If available, use a view-limiting device scenario where the student must land on a reference line, reinforcing position awareness over instrument fixation.
questions.follow_up: If after these interventions the student still fixates on the RPM gauge, what underlying knowledge gap might be causing the behavior, and how would you address it before their next lesson?
questions.follow_up_answer: The underlying gap is likely that the student does not trust their motor memory for the collective input — they are checking the gauge because they are not confident that lowering collective the correct amount will produce the right RPM. This suggests insufficient practice of the initial collective movement to the point of muscle memory. The fix is ground-based chair flying: have the student rehearse the failure-to-collective sequence eyes closed, 20+ repetitions, until the input is automatic and they no longer need gauge confirmation to execute it. Only when the collective management is truly instinctive will they have cognitive capacity to maintain the external visual scan needed for drift correction and a proper touchdown.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, workload management)

questions.question: During a checkride, an applicant performs a hover autorotation that results in touchdown with approximately 1 foot of sideward movement but zero rearward movement. The applicant immediately corrects heading post-touchdown. Is this a passing performance, and what is your evaluation rationale under the ACS standard?
questions.answer: This is likely passing performance. The ACS standard requires 'minimum sideward movement and no rearward movement.' The word 'minimum' acknowledges that some sideward movement may occur — it does not require zero sideward movement. One foot of sideward movement at a low hover autorotation touchdown, while not ideal, is within the spirit of 'minimum' given the dynamic nature of the maneuver. The critical element — no rearward movement — was met absolutely. The examiner must evaluate the overall quality of the maneuver: was rotor RPM maintained, was the collective cushion effective, was the drift actively being arrested (even if not fully arrested at contact), and was there any safety-of-flight concern? If the answer to all of these favors the applicant, and the sideward movement was demonstrably controlled and decreasing at touchdown rather than unchecked, this meets the standard. A 3–4 foot sideward drift with no active correction would be a different evaluation.
questions.follow_up: The applicant argues that any sideward movement means they failed the standard. How do you explain the distinction between 'minimum sideward movement' and 'no sideward movement' as written in the ACS, and why is the language written this way?
questions.follow_up_answer: The ACS uses the word 'minimum' for sideward movement deliberately because, unlike rearward movement which is an absolute hazard, small sideward movements during a low hover autorotation are a recognized reality of the maneuver in real-world conditions — wind, rotor wash, surface irregularities, and reaction time all contribute. The FAA's intent is that the pilot actively manages and minimizes sideward movement, not that it be mathematically zero. Rearward movement has no acceptable minimum because the hazard — potential tail contact, tip-back, and rotor strike — is unacceptable at any magnitude. The distinction reflects the risk profile: sideward drift of a foot or two on a skid-equipped helicopter is manageable and unlikely to cause structural damage or rollover; any rearward movement during touchdown introduces immediate catastrophic risk potential, hence the absolute prohibition. This is why the two criteria use different language.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS CH.X.A Touchdown standard; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: When an engine fails during a hover and the helicopter begins to settle, what is the primary control input used to cushion the touchdown?
questions.answer: The collective is the primary control used to cushion the touchdown. As the helicopter settles toward the ground following a hover engine failure, the pilot applies a smooth upward collective input to increase rotor thrust and slow the rate of descent just before ground contact. This uses the remaining rotor RPM stored as inertia to arrest or reduce the sink rate at the moment of touchdown.

questions.question: Immediately after an engine failure in a hover, what happens to rotor RPM if you do not lower the collective, and why does that matter for cushioning the touchdown?
questions.answer: If you fail to lower the collective immediately after an engine failure in a hover, rotor RPM will decay rapidly because the blades continue to generate lift and drag but have no engine power to sustain rotation. As RPM decreases, you lose the stored rotational energy needed to cushion the touchdown. By the time the helicopter reaches the ground, there may be insufficient rotor RPM remaining to apply any effective collective cushion, resulting in a hard landing or loss of control.

questions.question: What role do the cyclic and antitorque pedals play when cushioning a touchdown after a hover engine failure?
questions.answer: The cyclic is used to keep the helicopter level and prevent it from drifting or tilting during the descent to touchdown — any lateral or longitudinal movement must be corrected to ensure the skids contact the ground evenly. The antitorque pedals are used to maintain heading and prevent unwanted yaw as torque changes with collective input. Both controls work together with collective to produce a controlled, level touchdown.

questions.question: You are hovering at 5 feet AGL when the engine fails. Walk me through your control sequence from the moment of failure to touchdown — specifically focusing on how and when you apply collective to cushion the landing.
questions.answer: At the moment of engine failure, immediately lower collective to the full-down position to reduce blade pitch, minimize drag on the rotor system, and preserve rotor RPM. Simultaneously use cyclic to correct any drift and pedals to maintain heading. As the helicopter descends and the skids approach within approximately 1–2 feet of the ground, apply a smooth, progressive upward collective to cushion the touchdown using the stored rotor inertia. The collective must be applied at the right moment — too early bleeds RPM before ground contact; too late results in a hard landing. The goal is to time the collective application so the upward thrust arrests the sink rate just as the skids contact the surface.

questions.question: You practice hover engine failure recoveries and notice that on every attempt you are landing hard — the collective cushion is not slowing the descent enough. What is the most likely cause, and how would you correct it?
questions.answer: The most likely cause is delayed initial lowering of the collective at the moment of engine failure, which allows rotor RPM to decay significantly before the descent even begins. By the time you try to cushion with collective at touchdown, there is insufficient rotor inertia left to generate meaningful thrust. The correction is to lower the collective more aggressively and immediately at the first indication of engine failure to preserve RPM, then apply the cushion earlier and more smoothly as the helicopter approaches the ground. A secondary cause could be applying the cushion too late — waiting until the skids are already at ground level rather than beginning the pull at 1–2 feet AGL.

questions.question: How does hovering at a higher height — say 10 feet AGL versus 3 feet AGL — change the way you manage the collective cushion during a hover engine failure?
questions.answer: At a greater hover height like 10 feet AGL, you have more time during the descent, but rotor RPM will decay more significantly, which means you must be even more disciplined about immediately lowering collective to preserve inertia. The additional altitude gives you slightly more time to stabilize the helicopter with cyclic before touchdown. The cushion application timing becomes more critical — you still want to begin the collective pull at approximately 1–2 feet AGL, but with lower available RPM at ground level, precision in collective application is essential. At 3 feet, there is very little time — the sequence is nearly immediate and leaves almost no margin for error.

questions.question: During a hover engine failure checkride task, a student applies the collective cushion correctly but the helicopter still contacts the ground with enough force to be considered a hard landing. As an examiner, what are the two most likely underlying control coordination failures you would look for beyond just collective timing?
questions.answer: First, I would look at cyclic control during the descent. If the student allowed the helicopter to drift laterally or tilt prior to touchdown, one skid contacts the ground before the other, concentrating all the impact force on a single point rather than distributing it across both skids simultaneously. Even a properly timed collective pull cannot fully compensate for an unlevel contact. Second, I would examine pedal inputs as the collective was raised. When collective is applied, torque demands change — in a counterclockwise rotor system, raising collective increases left yaw tendency. If the student did not anticipate and correct with right pedal, the nose may have yawed during the flare, causing the helicopter to land in a skewed attitude. Combined, these two failures — unleveled skids and yaw at touchdown — can produce a hard or dynamic landing regardless of collective timing.
questions.follow_up: If the student's helicopter has low-inertia rotor blades, how does that change your expectation for what a passing collective cushion performance looks like on this task?
questions.follow_up_answer: With a low-inertia rotor system, RPM decays much faster after engine failure than with a high-inertia system. This means the available energy for a collective cushion is significantly less, and the window for effective cushion application is extremely narrow. As an examiner, I would expect the student to demonstrate an even more aggressive and immediate collective-down input at the moment of failure, because any delay results in a near-total loss of usable rotor energy by the time the helicopter reaches the ground. A passing performance in a low-inertia aircraft may still result in a firmer touchdown than in a high-inertia helicopter — what I am evaluating is whether the student demonstrated correct and timely inputs throughout the sequence, not whether the landing felt perfectly smooth. The student must also demonstrate awareness of this characteristic during the oral, explaining why response timing is more critical in their specific aircraft.

questions.question: A pilot successfully cushions the touchdown after a hover engine failure, but the helicopter immediately begins to rock onto one skid after ground contact. What control input failure caused this, and what should the pilot do in the moment to prevent a dynamic rollover?
questions.answer: The rocking onto one skid after ground contact is most likely caused by a lateral cyclic input being held at or through the moment of touchdown — either the pilot was correcting a drift and held cyclic input as the skids contacted the surface, or there was an uncorrected translational drift that caused one skid to plant while the other was still off the ground. Once one skid is on the ground and the other is in the air, continuing to hold collective with a lateral cyclic input creates the classic dynamic rollover setup. In the moment, the pilot must immediately lower the collective fully to the floor to reduce lift and eliminate the rolling moment. Attempting to correct with opposite cyclic while the helicopter is on a single skid and still has collective applied can accelerate the rollover. The key instinct must be: skid on ground, collective down first.
questions.follow_up: At what critical rollover angle is recovery generally considered impossible in most helicopters, and how does that inform when the collective-down input must be made?
questions.follow_up_answer: Most helicopters reach a point of no-return at approximately 8 degrees of lateral roll once a skid is planted on the ground — beyond this angle, the lift vector has shifted far enough outside the contact point that the helicopter will continue to roll over regardless of control inputs. This means the collective-down response must happen within the first fraction of a second of sensing the lateral movement — before the roll angle develops. There is no time to assess and then act; the pilot must train the collective-down response as an instinctive reaction to any unexpected rolling tendency while on or near the ground. This is why ground resonance and dynamic rollover scenarios are practiced and discussed extensively in training — recognition and immediate response are the only defenses.

questions.question: After a hover engine failure and the skids touch down, what is the correct sequence of control inputs?
questions.answer: Immediately after touchdown, lower the collective to the full-down position to remove remaining lift and reduce blade pitch, then neutralize the cyclic and pedals. Lowering the collective prevents any residual lift from rocking or tipping the helicopter, and neutralizing the flight controls eliminates any tendency for the helicopter to skid, slide, or roll on the surface.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Powerplant Failure at a Hover

questions.question: Why is it important to lower the collective fully after the helicopter touches down following a hover power failure?
questions.answer: After touchdown, residual rotor RPM and blade pitch can still generate lift if the collective is not lowered. Failing to lower the collective can cause the helicopter to become partially airborne again, tip over, or skid across the surface. Lowering the collective removes blade pitch, eliminates lift production, and ensures the helicopter remains firmly on the ground.

questions.question: What does 'neutralize flight controls' mean in the context of a hover autorotation touchdown, and which controls are specifically included?
questions.answer: Neutralizing flight controls means returning the cyclic to a centered, level position so it is not displaced fore, aft, or laterally, and centering the anti-torque pedals so they are not commanding any yaw input. This prevents the helicopter from rocking, rolling, yawing, or sliding after ground contact. The collective should already be at the full-down position as part of the touchdown sequence.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Powerplant Failure at a Hover

questions.question: During your hover autorotation practice, the student touches down but keeps the collective at mid-position because they think rotor RPM is still high. What hazard does this create and how would you correct it?
questions.answer: Keeping the collective at mid-position after touchdown maintains blade pitch and allows the rotor to continue generating lift. This can cause the helicopter to become partially airborne, shift laterally, or tip onto one skid if the surface is uneven or if wind is present. The correction is to immediately lower the collective to the full-down position upon skid contact with the ground. The student should understand that once on the ground, the priority is to eliminate all lift — managing rotor RPM decay is no longer the concern.

questions.question: You've just touched down from a hover engine failure on a slight slope. How does the requirement to lower collective and neutralize controls interact with the slope, and what additional risk must you manage?
questions.answer: On a sloped surface, lowering the collective and neutralizing the cyclic is still the correct action, but the pilot must be alert to dynamic rollover tendency. As the collective is lowered and the downhill skid contacts the ground first, any lateral cyclic input or delay in control neutralization can allow the uphill skid to lift, creating a rollover pivot point. The pilot should lower collective smoothly and hold cyclic level or very slightly into the slope to keep both skids on the ground, while still fully reducing collective to prevent residual lift. The key is that control neutralization must be coordinated with the terrain contact sequence.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Dynamic Rollover; Hovering Autorotation

questions.question: A pilot completes a hover autorotation touchdown and immediately neutralizes the cyclic but forgets to lower the collective for about two seconds. The helicopter begins sliding sideways. Walk me through the aerodynamic reason this happened.
questions.answer: With the collective at mid-position after touchdown, the rotor blades still have positive pitch angle and the still-spinning rotor continues to generate lift — potentially enough to partially unload the skids. With reduced weight on the skids and a crosswind or slight ground slope, friction is insufficient to hold the helicopter in place. Additionally, if the cyclic was already neutralized but the TPP (tip-path plane) was not perfectly level at the moment of touchdown, the horizontal component of the partially-generated lift vector can push the helicopter laterally. Lowering the collective immediately removes blade pitch, collapses lift, fully loads the skids, and maximizes ground friction.

questions.question: During a checkride hover autorotation, the applicant touches down firmly, lowers collective immediately, but then instinctively applies left pedal aggressively while neutralizing controls. What problem can this cause, and why does it happen?
questions.answer: As the engine fails and rotor RPM begins to decay during a hover autorotation, torque effect diminishes rapidly. The pilot has been accustomed to holding right pedal pressure in a normal hover (in a counterclockwise rotor system) to counteract torque. When the engine fails, that torque disappears almost instantly, so the natural tendency is to apply left pedal to prevent the nose from yawing right. However, if the pilot applies aggressive left pedal after touchdown, the tail rotor — still turning with whatever residual RPM remains — can produce a yawing moment that spins the fuselage on the skids. This can lead to a ground handling accident or blade strike. The correct action is to neutralize pedals smoothly and symmetrically rather than applying aggressive inputs after ground contact.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot had instead frozen on right pedal throughout the touchdown, what would you expect to observe and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the pilot held excessive right pedal through touchdown, the tail rotor would continue commanding a left yaw (nose right) tendency from whatever rotor RPM remained. On the ground, this creates a yawing moment about the vertical axis, causing the helicopter to spin or pivot on the skids to the right. With weight partially unloaded (if collective wasn't fully lowered), the skids have less friction and the rotation can be pronounced. This reinforces why both collective lowering AND smooth control neutralization — including pedals — must occur simultaneously and deliberately at touchdown.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Powerplant Failure at a Hover; Chapter 5, Anti-Torque Pedals

questions.question: An applicant performs the hover autorotation perfectly — good entry, controlled descent, smooth touchdown — but after the skids contact the ground, they lower the collective slowly over about three seconds rather than immediately. As the examiner, would you consider this a failure point, and what is the actual risk window created by that delay?
questions.answer: Yes, a slow collective reduction after touchdown is a significant deviation from the standard and could be a failure point depending on the outcome and degree. The risk window created by a three-second delay is meaningful: during those three seconds, the rotor blades still have positive pitch and the system is still generating lift, even as RPM decays. The helicopter remains partially unloaded on the skids, creating vulnerability to lateral drift from wind, slope, or asymmetric skid contact. Additionally, if the touchdown was slightly off-level and the cyclic was not perfectly neutral, the partial lift can amplify a tipping tendency. The ACS standard requires the pilot to demonstrate proper technique — immediate collective reduction is the expected response. There is no explicit time tolerance stated in seconds in the handbook, but the standard implies immediacy as a safety-of-flight action. A slow reduction that results in no adverse consequence might be graded as 'got away with it' rather than 'executed correctly,' and an examiner should note it as a deficiency. If the delay caused any ground movement, skid rocking, or required a corrective input, it likely constitutes unsatisfactory performance under the task's risk management and skills elements.
questions.follow_up: What specific ACS performance standard governs the acceptability of this maneuver, and how would you document the deficiency if you chose not to fail the applicant?
questions.follow_up_answer: The ACS for Task CH.X.A specifies that after touchdown the applicant must lower the collective and neutralize the flight controls. There is no explicit time tolerance stated in seconds, but the standard implies immediacy — it is a safety-of-flight action. If the examiner determines the delay did not create a hazardous condition and the overall maneuver met standards, they may document it in the remarks section of the 8710 or in their personal notes, and verbally debrief the applicant on the deficiency. However, if the delay caused any ground movement, skid rocking, or required a corrective input, it likely constitutes unsatisfactory performance under the task's risk management and skills elements. The examiner has discretion but must evaluate whether the deviation reflected a lack of understanding of the correct procedure versus a minor timing lapse.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; ACS CH.X.A Skills Standard; 14 CFR 61.43 (Practical Test Failure)

questions.question: How does rotor system type — articulated versus semirigid versus rigid — affect the aerodynamic behavior and pilot response during an engine failure in a hover?
questions.answer: Rotor system type significantly influences how a helicopter responds to powerplant failure in a hover. Articulated rotor systems, which allow blade flapping and lead/lag movement, tend to have higher rotor inertia due to the mass of the articulated hub components and longer effective blade radius. This gives the pilot more time to react as RPM decays more slowly. Semirigid rotors (teetering systems) are typically lighter and may have lower rotor inertia, meaning RPM decays more quickly — demanding faster pilot response. Rigid rotor systems, which allow only feathering, also vary in inertia depending on design. The critical operational point is that low-inertia rotor systems require the pilot to lower collective almost instantly upon engine failure, while higher-inertia systems provide a slightly larger reaction window. Additionally, rotor system type affects how the helicopter behaves as collective is lowered — articulated blades can flap independently, which may create asymmetric lift transiently, while semirigid systems teeter as a unit. Pilots must know their specific aircraft's rotor characteristics, consult the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for any stated limitations or caution heights associated with hovering autorotations, and understand that operating contrary to RFM limitations constitutes a violation of 14 CFR 91.9. Practicing the hover autorotation to the standards appropriate for that rotor system, and within the conditions specified by the RFM, is essential for safe operation.
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the speculative 14 CFR 91.13 characterization and the ambiguous statement about hovering above RFM caution heights not being 'automatically illegal'; replaced with a straightforward reference to 14 CFR 91.9 and the obligation to operate within RFM limitations.

questions.question: A helicopter with a counterclockwise-rotating main rotor system (viewed from above) experiences a developing dynamic rollover to the left during liftoff from a level pad. Is a left roll easier or harder to arrest than a right roll, and what rotor system characteristic explains this asymmetry?
questions.answer: A left roll is generally harder to arrest with cyclic for a counterclockwise rotor system. The primary reason is that the retreating blade is on the left side of a counterclockwise rotor system, and the retreating blade inherently produces less lift due to reduced airspeed relative to the advancing blade. During a developing left roll, this asymmetry makes the left side more susceptible to further lift loss and rollover development. Additionally, in hover, the pilot must already hold left cyclic to compensate for translating tendency (tail rotor thrust pushes the helicopter right), reducing the available cyclic travel for left roll correction. These factors combine to make the left side the more critical direction for dynamic rollover risk in a counterclockwise rotor system, and FAA-H-8083-21B emphasizes that pilots must apply immediate, aggressive cyclic opposite to the roll direction and reduce collective if rollover appears imminent.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (Hazardous Attitudes, Hours-in-Type accident data, ADM); Chapter 11 (Hover Autorotation)
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the unsupported claim that articulated rotors are inherently higher-inertia than semirigid designs, replacing it with the accurate FAA-supported explanation that rotor inertia depends on blade mass and weight distribution specific to each aircraft design, not rotor type classification alone.

questions.question: A helicopter with a counterclockwise-rotating main rotor system (viewed from above) experiences a developing dynamic rollover to the left during liftoff from a level pad. Is a left roll easier or harder to arrest than a right roll, and what rotor system characteristic explains this asymmetry?
questions.answer: A left roll is generally harder to arrest with cyclic for a counterclockwise rotor system. The primary reason is that the retreating blade is on the left side of a counterclockwise rotor system, and the retreating blade inherently produces less lift due to reduced airspeed relative to the advancing blade. During a developing left roll, this asymmetry makes the left side more susceptible to further lift loss and rollover development. Additionally, in hover, the pilot must already hold left cyclic to compensate for translating tendency (tail rotor thrust pushes the helicopter right), reducing the available cyclic travel for left roll correction. These factors combine to make the left side the more critical direction for dynamic rollover risk in a counterclockwise rotor system, and FAA-H-8083-21B emphasizes that pilots must apply immediate, aggressive cyclic opposite to the roll direction and reduce collective if rollover appears imminent.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (Hazardous Attitudes, Hours-in-Type accident data, ADM); Chapter 11 (Hover Autorotation)
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the unsupported references to '100 hours in type' and accident rate correlation claims, which were irrelevant to this dynamic rollover question and not present in FAA-H-8083-21B; the answer now focuses solely on the rotor system characteristics (translating tendency and retreating blade side) that explain the rollover asymmetry, grounded in FAA-H-8083-21B.

questions.question: During a powerplant failure at hover training exercise, after re-establishing power, you attempt to transition from a touchdown back to a stationary hover into the wind and the aircraft begins to weathervane. How does weathervaning affect your ability to establish the required into-wind hover, and what technique do you use to manage it?
questions.answer: Weathervaning is the tendency of the helicopter's nose to align with the relative wind because the fuselage acts like a weather vane — the larger surface area of the tail section generates more aerodynamic drag, causing the nose to swing into the wind. This is a wind-driven directional behavior and is distinct from torque-induced yaw. On the ground or at very low altitude, as the helicopter lifts off and the skids lose contact with the surface, the fuselage becomes free to rotate, and a crosswind can cause the nose to swing unexpectedly toward the wind. If the wind is directly ahead, weathervaning can actually assist alignment; however, if the aircraft is not precisely aligned or the wind is gusty, the nose may overrotate past the desired heading, making it difficult to establish a stable into-wind hover. Technique: before lifting, visually identify a reference point on the horizon aligned with the wind direction to use as a heading cue. As collective is increased and the skids begin to lighten, anticipate the weathervaning tendency and use antitorque pedals to control the rate and direction of yaw — independently of torque compensation — to moderate the nose swing and stop the aircraft on the desired heading. Torque compensation pedal input (for a counterclockwise rotor system, right pedal) remains necessary to counteract rotor torque, but pedal inputs to manage weathervaning are made in response to the wind-driven yaw, not torque reaction. Combining these two separate pedal demands requires smooth coordination. (See FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 2.)
questions.rewrite_note: Separated and clarified the distinct concepts of weathervaning (wind-driven yaw) and torque-induced yaw, and corrected the erroneous statement that left pedal is used for torque compensation on a counterclockwise rotor system.

tasks.title: Task B. Powerplant Failure at Altitude in a Single-Engine Helicopter

questions.question: What is the very first control input a helicopter pilot must make the moment an engine fails at altitude, and why?
questions.answer: The pilot must immediately lower the collective to the full down or minimum pitch position. This action reduces the pitch angle on the rotor blades, which dramatically decreases drag on the rotor system. Without this input, the rotor RPM will decay rapidly as the blades continue to produce lift and drag but are no longer being driven by engine power. Maintaining rotor RPM within the green arc is the single most critical factor in a successful autorotation — if RPM decays too far, a rotor stall may occur and is not recoverable.

questions.question: During autorotation following an engine failure at altitude, what keeps the rotor blades turning since the engine is no longer providing power?
questions.answer: Once the collective is lowered and the helicopter begins descending, upward airflow through the rotor disk drives the blades like a windmill. This aerodynamic force — caused by the relative wind flowing upward through the disk as the helicopter descends — replaces the engine as the energy source maintaining rotor RPM. The aft cyclic input at entry also increases upward airflow through the disk, further contributing to RPM recovery. The rotor system essentially converts the helicopter's potential energy (altitude) into rotational kinetic energy.

questions.question: After an engine failure at altitude, what are the three simultaneous or near-simultaneous control inputs required at autorotation entry from cruise airspeed?
questions.answer: The three critical control inputs at autorotation entry from cruise airspeed are: (1) Down collective — immediately lower to reduce blade pitch and preserve rotor RPM; (2) Aft cyclic — to decelerate from cruise airspeed toward the best autorotation airspeed and to increase upward airflow through the disk, which helps recover or maintain rotor RPM; (3) Pedal trim — apply the appropriate pedal input (typically right pedal in most counterclockwise-rotor helicopters) to compensate for the torque change and maintain coordinated flight. The tail rotor continues to operate normally during autorotation because it is driven by the main rotor transmission, not directly by the engine.

questions.question: You are cruising at 2,500 feet AGL at 100 knots when the engine fails. You have a low-inertia rotor system. How does this rotor characteristic change the urgency of your initial collective response compared to a high-inertia system, and what is the consequence of even a 2-second delay?
questions.answer: A low-inertia rotor system has lighter blades that store less rotational kinetic energy than a high-inertia system. This means RPM decays very rapidly once engine power is lost — within seconds rather than the longer window a high-inertia system provides. A 2-second delay before lowering the collective in a low-inertia helicopter can result in rotor RPM decaying below the minimum operating limit or even into the rotor stall region. If rotor stall occurs, recovery is not possible. By contrast, a pilot flying a high-inertia system has a slightly larger buffer, though immediate collective reduction is still required. Pilots transitioning to low-inertia helicopters must have highly conditioned reflexes for this emergency.

questions.question: You experience a complete engine failure at 3,000 feet AGL over mountainous terrain with no suitable landing zones in glide range. Walk me through the decision-making framework and priority sequence you would use to manage this emergency.
questions.answer: Using the SRM and ADM framework: (1) Fly the aircraft first — immediately enter autorotation with down collective, aft cyclic, and pedal trim to stabilize rotor RPM and airspeed; (2) Troubleshoot if altitude permits — verify the failure (check throttle, fuel, mixture/condition lever as applicable) and attempt a restart per the POH emergency checklist; (3) Identify the best available landing area — even in mountains, scan for ridgelines, meadows, roads, or any relatively flat surface; prioritize the least-bad option over the 'perfect' zone that doesn't exist; (4) Transmit a MAYDAY on the current frequency or 121.5 MHz with position, nature of emergency, and souls on board; (5) Squawk 7700 if time permits; (6) Configure for the best autorotation glide (manufacturer's recommended airspeed) to maximize range and options. The error chain concept applies — avoid compounding the emergency with poor secondary decisions. 'Probably' is not acceptable; choose the option you know can work.

questions.question: During the descent in autorotation following an engine failure at altitude, your airspeed has stabilized at the manufacturer's recommended best glide airspeed. What physical relationship between induced drag and parasite drag exists at this airspeed, and why does the manufacturer recommend it for autorotation?
questions.answer: At the best autorotation glide airspeed, the helicopter is operating near its L/D maximum (best lift-to-drag ratio), which is the point where induced drag and parasite drag intersect on the total drag curve. Induced drag decreases as airspeed increases (because AOA is reduced), while parasite drag increases with the square of velocity. The crossover point represents the most aerodynamically efficient descent — the lowest rate of descent for the greatest horizontal distance traveled. This maximizes glide range, giving the pilot the most options for landing zone selection. Flying slower increases induced drag and sink rate; flying faster increases parasite drag and also increases sink rate. Either deviation from the recommended speed reduces your effective glide range.

questions.question: A student pilot tells you that during an engine failure at altitude, they would immediately begin troubleshooting the engine before entering autorotation because they want to attempt a restart. How do you evaluate this prioritization, and under what specific conditions — if any — might a brief troubleshoot be acceptable before fully committing to autorotation?
questions.answer: This prioritization is incorrect and potentially fatal. Aviate — especially rotor RPM control — must always precede navigate and communicate, and absolutely precedes troubleshooting. Rotor RPM is the most time-critical element of a powerplant failure; in a low-inertia helicopter, a delay of even 2-3 seconds attempting to troubleshoot before lowering the collective can result in RPM decaying into the unrecoverable stall range. The only condition under which a brief troubleshoot is acceptable is after autorotation is established — rotor RPM is in the green arc, airspeed is stabilized at the recommended autorotation speed, and sufficient altitude exists to allow time for a checklist review while still completing the autorotation. In practice, many manufacturers do include an engine restart checklist to be performed during autorotation descent if altitude permits. The student's statement reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of emergency priority hierarchy.
questions.follow_up: If you are established in autorotation at 2,500 feet AGL with a stabilized RPM and airspeed, and your POH restart checklist takes approximately 15 seconds, at what approximate rate of descent would you need to determine whether the restart attempt is viable before committing to the landing?
questions.follow_up_answer: At a typical helicopter autorotation rate of descent of approximately 1,500 to 2,000 feet per minute, a 15-second restart attempt would consume roughly 375 to 500 feet of altitude. Starting from 2,500 feet AGL, you would still have 2,000 to 2,125 feet remaining for the landing flare and cushion. In general, this is likely sufficient altitude to attempt a restart IF the aircraft is fully stabilized and the pilot is not distracted from the autorotation. However, this calculation must account for terrain, obstacles, available landing zones, and the specific helicopter's glide performance. Below approximately 500-1,000 feet AGL (varies by helicopter), most manufacturers advise abandoning restart attempts and focusing entirely on the autorotation landing. The pilot must know their specific POH limits and never allow troubleshooting to degrade control of the autorotation.

questions.question: Research shows that aviation accident rates are more strongly correlated with hours in a specific aircraft model than with total flight hours, and accidents decrease significantly after 100 hours in type. How does this data point shape the risk profile specifically for powerplant failure emergencies, and what practical implication does it have for a newly type-rated commercial helicopter pilot?
questions.answer: This data indicates that unfamiliarity with a specific aircraft's systems, limitations, and handling characteristics — not general inexperience — is the dominant risk factor in early operations. For powerplant failure emergencies, a pilot new to a type may not yet have internalized the specific RPM decay rate, the exact collective position for autorotation entry, the correct best autorotation airspeed, the restart checklist flow, or the sight picture for the landing flare. These gaps are dangerous because autorotation responses must be reflexive — there is no time to consult references. The practical implication for a newly type-rated commercial pilot is: (1) train to proficiency in powerplant failure procedures specifically in that aircraft type, not just in any helicopter; (2) know the POH emergency procedures to memory; (3) increase situational awareness about engine indications (EGT, RPM trends, fuel pressure) so that partial failures are caught early; (4) apply higher personal minimums (altitude, power margin, divert options) during the first 50-100 hours in type to reduce exposure. The ADM framework reinforces that risk acceptance should be conservative when operating within the highest-risk portion of the type-specific learning curve.
questions.follow_up: Given that 80% of accidents are caused by human factors, name two specific human factors traps that are most likely to degrade a pilot's response to an engine failure at altitude, and explain how each one affects the elements of autorotation entry.
questions.follow_up_answer: Two of the most relevant human factors traps are: (1) Startle/Surprise Effect — when an engine failure is unexpected (no prior indications), the startle response causes a momentary freeze or incorrect instinctive reaction. Many pilots instinctively pull up on the collective to arrest the sudden descent, which is exactly the wrong input and accelerates RPM decay toward rotor stall. This is why practiced, conditioned reflexes are essential — the correct response must override the instinct. (2) Fixation/Channeled Attention — a pilot may become fixated on attempting to diagnose or restart the engine, losing awareness of rotor RPM decay and airspeed exceedances. During autorotation entry, any attention diverted from rotor RPM, airspeed, and attitude can result in the pilot missing the narrow window to stabilize the descent. Both traps are addressable through recurrent training, scenario-based emergency exercises, and the SRM discipline of consciously scanning all critical parameters rather than fixating on a single instrument or problem.

questions.question: During an autorotation following engine failure, how does a headwind generally affect your glide distance compared to a calm-wind condition?
questions.answer: A headwind increases your glide distance over the ground because it reduces your groundspeed while your airspeed — and therefore rotor lift efficiency — remains relatively constant. This gives you more time and more ground coverage in front of you to reach a suitable landing area. Conversely, a tailwind decreases glide distance over the ground by increasing groundspeed relative to your descent profile.

questions.question: How does gross weight affect autorotation performance following an engine failure at altitude?
questions.answer: Higher gross weight increases the rate of descent during autorotation because the helicopter must generate more lift to support the greater weight, which requires a higher rotor inertia and collective setting at flare. A heavier helicopter descends faster and covers less distance for a given altitude, reducing your options for a landing site. However, a heavier helicopter also stores more kinetic energy in the rotor system if RPM is maintained, which can slightly improve flare effectiveness — but the faster descent rate and shorter glide are the dominant effects on autorotation performance.

questions.question: What is the effect of high density altitude on rotor RPM decay rate immediately following an engine failure, compared to sea-level conditions?
questions.answer: At high density altitude, the air is less dense, which means each rotor blade generates less aerodynamic drag per revolution. While this sounds beneficial, the reduced air density also means less lift per revolution, so more collective may be required to arrest the descent — drawing down rotor RPM faster. Additionally, since the engine was producing less power at high density altitude to begin with, the transition to autorotation may start from a lower power margin, potentially leaving less rotor inertia as a buffer. The net effect is that rotor RPM can decay more rapidly and the margin for error at autorotation entry is reduced.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 2

questions.question: You experience an engine failure at 3,000 feet AGL on a hot summer afternoon at a high-elevation mountain airport. Two landing areas are visible: one directly into the prevailing wind at moderate distance, and one closer but requiring you to autorotate with a tailwind. Walk me through how temperature and wind together factor into your decision about which landing area to select.
questions.answer: High temperature reduces air density (increases density altitude), which degrades autorotation performance in two key ways: increased rate of descent and reduced rotor efficiency. With a higher descent rate, you have less time and less glide distance available. Given these constraints, the wind direction becomes critical. Autorotating into the wind reduces groundspeed at touchdown, lowering kinetic energy and improving your ability to run on or land safely. A tailwind landing increases groundspeed at touchdown, raising the risk of a hard landing or rollover. Even though the tailwind site is closer, the combination of high density altitude (degraded performance) and a tailwind (higher touchdown groundspeed) makes the into-wind site safer, provided you have sufficient altitude and glide distance to reach it. You must assess whether your actual glide range — already shortened by the high density altitude — can realistically reach the into-wind area before committing.

questions.question: You're flying a fully loaded helicopter near max gross weight and lose the engine at altitude. How does the additional weight change the timing and execution of your flare and power recovery at the bottom of the autorotation compared to a lightly loaded aircraft?
questions.answer: At higher gross weight, the helicopter descends faster during autorotation, meaning you arrive at the flare point sooner and with more downward momentum to arrest. You need to initiate the flare slightly earlier to allow adequate time to convert airspeed to rotor RPM and reduce the descent rate. The flare itself must be more pronounced or timely because the greater inertia requires more work to decelerate. Additionally, more stored rotor energy is needed to cushion the landing — but this energy is more quickly consumed due to the higher collective required to support the greater weight.
