This can lead to a low-rotor-RPM condition or even rotor stall, which in a helicopter is not recoverable. The pilot must ensure RPM is in the green arc before applying significant collective.

questions.question: What does 'safe altitude' mean in the context of the evaluator directing a power recovery during an autorotation, and why does altitude matter?
questions.answer: A 'safe altitude' is a height above terrain that provides sufficient margin for the pilot to complete the power recovery, reestablish a normal climb or level flight attitude, and avoid ground contact if the recovery takes longer than expected. It is significant because recovering too low leaves no room to arrest a high descent rate if rotor RPM has decayed or if the engine is slow to respond, potentially resulting in a hard landing or accident.

questions.question: You are established in a practice autorotation at best glide airspeed descending through 500 feet AGL when the evaluator says 'power recovery.' Your rotor RPM is at the top of the green arc. Walk me through exactly what you do from that moment.
questions.answer: First, smoothly roll on throttle (or advance power lever on a turbine) to restore engine power while monitoring RPM gauges to ensure the engine is coupled and RPM stays in the green arc. As engine power comes in, begin smoothly raising the collective to arrest the descent, simultaneously applying aft cyclic to slow the descent rate and establish a level or climbing attitude. Use pedals throughout to maintain coordinated trim as torque changes. Monitor altitude and rate of descent — if RPM drops toward the lower caution range at any point, pause the collective rise until RPM recovers. Level off or transition to a climb once a positive rate of climb is confirmed and all gauges are in normal range.

questions.question: During a power recovery termination, you apply power and raise collective but notice rotor RPM is dropping out of the green arc. What do you do, and what caused this situation?
questions.answer: Immediately lower the collective to reduce blade pitch and rotor drag, allowing RPM to recover back into the green arc. The cause is likely that collective was raised faster than the engine could supply torque, or engine RPM lagged — creating a mismatch where the blades are demanding more power than is available. Once RPM is restored, slowly re-raise collective in coordination with available power. If altitude does not permit recovery, the pilot must be prepared to complete the landing in autorotation.

questions.question: How does your power recovery technique differ between a low-inertia rotor system and a high-inertia rotor system when the evaluator calls for termination at the same altitude?
questions.answer: With a low-inertia rotor system (lighter blades), stored rotor energy depletes much more rapidly during the descent, so RPM decays faster and you have less margin between receiving the command and needing to have power fully restored before raising collective. You must be quicker and more precise with throttle application before touching the collective. A high-inertia system stores more kinetic energy, giving slightly more time to get the engine spooled up before the collective is raised. In both cases the principle is the same — power must be available before demanding torque through collective — but the time window is significantly tighter with low-inertia systems.

questions.question: You're flying a turbine helicopter in a practice autorotation and the evaluator calls for a power recovery at 300 feet AGL. As you advance the power lever, you notice engine torque is rising but rotor RPM is still in the bottom third of the green arc and your descent rate is 1,200 FPM. Do you continue the power recovery or commit to a full autorotation landing? Defend your answer.
questions.answer: At 300 feet AGL with 1,200 FPM descent and rotor RPM at the bottom of the green arc, the decision is critical. If torque is rising, the engine is responding — the question is whether RPM will recover to mid-green fast enough to allow a safe collective rise before ground contact. At 300 feet with 1,200 FPM, you have approximately 15 seconds before touchdown. If RPM is trending back toward mid-green and the terrain/landing area is acceptable, you may continue the power recovery while holding collective steady until RPM normalizes. However, if RPM is not clearly recovering or the area below is unsuitable, the lower-risk decision is to complete the autorotation landing — accepting a firm but survivable landing — rather than risk an uncontrolled impact from rotor stall caused by premature collective application. The guiding principle from the HFH is that rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable; a controlled autorotation to the surface is the safer outcome.
questions.follow_up: If you decide to continue the power recovery and successfully level off, what must you check before returning to normal flight, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: After leveling off, the pilot must check: engine instruments (torque, turbine temperature, N1/N2) for any signs of over-temperature or damage from the rapid power demand; rotor RPM to confirm it has stabilized in the normal operating range; transmission oil pressure and temperature; and flight controls for any abnormal response. The rapid power application in a low-RPM state can stress drivetrain components and potentially over-temperature the turbine section. A maintenance inspection may be required before the next flight if limits were approached or exceeded.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft Flight Manual/POH for specific turbine limits

questions.question: The ACS requires you to terminate an approach with a power recovery 'at a safe altitude as directed by the evaluator.' What evaluator cues would make you override or delay responding to a power recovery command — in other words, when is it appropriate to deviate from the evaluator's direction?
questions.answer: An evaluator's command is not an absolute override of pilot-in-command authority. If by the time the evaluator calls for a power recovery the helicopter is already at an altitude where a safe recovery is not possible — for example, rotor RPM has already decayed significantly, the rate of descent is excessive, or the aircraft is below a meaningful decision height with unsuitable terrain ahead — the pilot should complete the autorotation to landing rather than attempt an unsafe power recovery. FAA guidance establishes that the pilot in command is responsible for the safe outcome of any maneuver. An evaluator-directed command during a checkride is still subject to real-world safety constraints. The correct professional response is to call out 'unable — committing to full autorotation' and execute the landing safely, then debrief the situation. Attempting an unsafe recovery simply because the evaluator said so is exactly the kind of error-chain behavior that ADM training exists to prevent.
questions.follow_up: Would a decision to override the evaluator's power recovery command and complete a full autorotation landing be grounds for a disapproval on the practical test?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — if the pilot's judgment that a full autorotation landing was the safer option was sound and well-executed, it demonstrates superior aeronautical decision-making and PIC responsibility, both of which are evaluated competencies on the ACS. The ACS evaluates risk management and ADM as standalone skills. A pilot who blindly follows an evaluator's command into an unsafe maneuver and causes an accident or nearly does so would face far more serious consequences. The evaluator's role is to assess judgment, and choosing the safe outcome over blind compliance is correct airmanship. The evaluator should have issued the command at an appropriate altitude to begin with; if they did not, that is a test administration issue, not a pilot failure.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3 (PIC authority and responsibility); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; ACS CH.X.B

questions.question: You are conducting a power-off autorotation and the winds aloft at your altitude are 25 knots on your nose, but at the surface the wind is calm. How does this wind gradient affect your perceived airspeed, actual groundspeed, rotor RPM behavior, and landing zone planning as you descend?
questions.answer: A significant headwind at altitude that diminishes to calm at the surface creates a challenging and deceptive environment. At altitude with a 25-knot headwind, if you are indicating 65 knots airspeed your groundspeed is only 40 knots — you are covering less ground per foot of altitude lost, so your actual glide distance to the ground is shorter than it appears. As you descend through the wind gradient, the headwind component reduces. To maintain the same indicated airspeed as the headwind decreases, the pilot must increase nose-up pitch attitude (pull back on cyclic), which changes the rotor's inflow angle. However, the primary risk of RPM decay stems from failure to maintain proper autorotation descent rate and airspeed as the wind gradient is encountered — if the pilot does not actively compensate for the diminishing headwind by adjusting pitch and descent rate, indicated airspeed will bleed off, breaking the power-off descent profile and degrading rotor RPM. The practical risk is that a pilot who fails to recognize and compensate for the diminishing headwind may allow indicated airspeed to decay near the flare point, at which time RPM recovery is difficult and there is little altitude remaining to recover. Additionally, the apparent glide path angle will steepen visually as groundspeed drops, potentially causing the pilot to overshoot a previously well-planned landing zone. Pilots must anticipate the airspeed change through the gradient, actively manage pitch attitude to maintain proper indicated airspeed and descent rate, monitor rotor RPM proactively, and plan a landing zone with a buffer for the steepening apparent descent angle. Reference: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Autorotation).
questions.rewrite_note: Corrected the aerodynamic explanation by clarifying that rotor RPM behavior in the gradient is driven by changes in indicated airspeed and the rotor's inflow angle of attack relationships rather than conflating groundspeed with inflow velocity.

questions.question: A student pilot tells you that in an engine failure, they always plan to land in the biggest open field they can find, regardless of position relative to wind or terrain slope. How would you address this mindset, and what are the specific dangers of applying a one-size-fits-all rule to landing area selection?
questions.answer: This mindset is a cognitive shortcut that bypasses the systematic evaluation required for safe autorotation landings. 'Biggest field' does not account for: (1) Slope — even a large flat-looking field can have a grade that causes dynamic rollover on landing; FAA-H-8083-21B discusses slope hazards and notes that dynamic rollover risk, particularly on downslope approaches, is the primary limiting factor for landing area selection, while upslope landings require careful attention to tail rotor clearance from rising terrain; (2) Surface condition — large fields may have irrigation ditches, furrows, boulders, or soft soil hidden from altitude; (3) Approach path obstructions — a large field surrounded by tall trees or wires on the upwind end is more dangerous than a smaller but obstruction-free surface; (4) Wind — landing downwind in a large field increases groundspeed significantly, elevating rollover risk. The correct approach is to evaluate all factors simultaneously: altitude, wind, terrain, and obstructions. The 'best' field is the one that, considering all factors, gives the highest probability of a controlled, survivable landing. Situational awareness must begin before the emergency — pilots should continuously scan terrain ahead and identify potential landing zones before they need them. Reference: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (Emergency Procedures).
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the unsupported specific degree threshold for slope hazard and replaced it with a reference to FAA-H-8083-21B's general slope guidance, while adding explicit clarification that tail rotor clearance from rising terrain is the primary geometric constraint on upslope landings.

tasks.title: Task C. Approach and Landing with One Engine Inoperative (OEI) (Simulated) (Multiengine Helicopter Only)

questions.question: During an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, what is the primary purpose of identifying the best single-engine rate of descent airspeed (or manufacturer-recommended OEI approach speed) before beginning the descent?
questions.answer: Flying the manufacturer-recommended OEI approach speed ensures the operating engine is working within its limits while providing the most favorable glide path and rotor RPM stability. At this speed, the helicopter achieves the best balance between lift, drag, and power required, giving the crew maximum time and options to manage the approach and landing with reduced power available.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) OEI procedures

questions.question: What does the term 'one engine inoperative (OEI) landing' mean in the context of a multiengine helicopter approach, and how does it differ from a standard autorotation?
questions.answer: An OEI landing means the helicopter is being flown with one engine failed or shut down while the remaining engine continues to produce power. Unlike a full autorotation where all engines are inoperative and the pilot relies entirely on stored rotor energy, an OEI approach uses the surviving engine to provide partial or full power as its limits allow, maintaining rotor RPM through engine drive rather than airflow alone. The pilot must manage the single engine's torque, temperature, and RPM limits throughout the approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM OEI section

questions.question: Name at least three cockpit indications a pilot would use to confirm that an engine has failed or become inoperative during an OEI approach.
questions.answer: Indications of an inoperative engine typically include: (1) a drop in torque or power on the affected engine's torque gauge, (2) a decrease or total loss of N1 or N2 (gas producer or power turbine) RPM on the failed engine, (3) a drop in turbine outlet or exhaust gas temperature (TOT/EGT/TGT) on the failed engine, (4) possible low rotor RPM warning (horn/light) if the operating engine cannot compensate, and (5) a yaw toward the failed engine side depending on helicopter design. The pilot cross-checks these to confirm which engine has failed before applying OEI procedures.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM engine failure indications

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter on approach at 500 feet AGL when one engine fails. The operating engine's torque immediately pegs at its maximum continuous limit. Walk me through your prioritized decision-making and control inputs for the next 30 seconds.
questions.answer: Immediately upon recognizing the engine failure: (1) Maintain rotor RPM — avoid pulling collective beyond what the single engine can support to prevent rotor droop. (2) Establish the OEI approach airspeed per the RFM, which typically requires lowering the nose slightly to trade altitude for airspeed and keep rotor RPM in the green arc. (3) Verify the failed engine by cross-checking torque, N1/N2, and temperature gauges — 'confirm, then secure' if required by checklist. (4) Declare emergency with ATC if workload permits; aviate first. (5) Select a suitable landing area — at 500 feet AGL with maximum single-engine power applied, a run-on or low-energy landing may be required rather than a hover. (6) Monitor the operating engine's torque and temperature to avoid exceeding 2½-minute or 30-second OEI ratings if applicable. Squawk 7700 when able.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM emergency procedures

questions.question: Your helicopter's RFM shows two OEI power ratings: a 30-second OEI limit and a 2½-minute OEI limit. During an OEI approach, when would you use each rating, and what is the risk of misusing them?
questions.answer: The 30-second OEI rating is the highest available power level and is intended only for the most critical phase — typically the decision point where the crew must either land immediately or execute a go-around/rejected landing. It should never be used as a sustained cruise or approach power setting. The 2½-minute OEI rating is a high but slightly lower power level used during the initial engine failure recognition, the approach, and the landing maneuver itself. Misusing these ratings — such as applying 30-second power during the entire approach — risks severe engine damage or failure of the remaining engine due to over-temperature or over-torque, leaving the crew with a dual-engine failure at low altitude. Time limits must be respected and the pilot must monitor gauges continuously.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM OEI power ratings section

questions.question: During an OEI approach to a confined landing zone, you realize the operating engine cannot sustain a hover out of ground effect (HOGE). How does this change your approach profile and landing technique compared to a normal two-engine approach?
questions.answer: If the helicopter cannot HOGE on one engine, the pilot must plan for a run-on landing or a hover-in-ground-effect (HIGE) landing only, accepting that a stationary hover out of ground effect is not available. The approach profile changes as follows: (1) Use a shallower approach angle to manage energy — a steep approach would require more power to arrest descent rate at the bottom. (2) Maintain a slightly higher airspeed into ground effect to preserve translational lift as long as possible. (3) Transition directly into ground effect rather than slowing to a hover OGE. (4) Be prepared for a run-on landing or very brief HIGE before touching down. (5) Do not attempt a go-around if it would require more power than the single engine can provide — commit to the landing. This requires precise landing site selection before beginning the approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; RFM OEI performance charts (HIGE/HOGE)

questions.question: During an OEI approach evaluation, an applicant correctly identifies the failed engine and establishes OEI airspeed, but then allows the operating engine's torque to exceed its 2½-minute limit for over 90 seconds before landing. The landing itself is safe. How do you address this from a standards standpoint, and what is the underlying aerodynamic or systems concept the applicant failed to demonstrate?
questions.answer: From an ACS standards standpoint, this represents a failure to manage powerplant limits, which is a critical item in multiengine emergency operations. Even though the landing outcome was safe, exceeding the 2½-minute OEI torque limit for 90 seconds beyond the allowed window constitutes an unsatisfactory performance in systems management. The underlying concept the applicant failed to demonstrate is understanding that OEI power ratings are based on engine metallurgical limits — turbine blades, hot-section components, and gearbox components are designed to tolerate extreme stress only for the rated duration. Exceeding these limits risks catastrophic failure of the remaining engine, turning a manageable OEI situation into a zero-power emergency at low altitude. The applicant must understand that managing the surviving engine's health is as critical as flying the approach profile.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant argues that the operating engine 'felt fine' and the gauges never went into the red, how do you respond?
questions.follow_up_answer: The response is that OEI time limits are not redline limits in the traditional sense — they are time-based metallurgical limits that do not show immediate gauge effects. Engine damage from exceeding OEI time limits is cumulative and internal; turbine blades experience creep, cracking, and fatigue at the cellular level that does not appear on any cockpit instrument in real time. The gauges staying below redline does not mean the engine is undamaged — it means the damage is not yet visible. Post-flight maintenance inspection and logbook entry of OEI exceedances are required per the RFM and manufacturer guidance. This is a fundamental reason why OEI time limits must be treated as absolute operational limits, not as soft advisory values.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM OEI limits; 14 CFR Part 27/29 airworthiness standards for powerplant installation

questions.question: A multiengine helicopter loses one engine at a density altitude where single-engine performance is marginal. The pilot establishes an OEI approach, but as airspeed decreases through translational lift, rotor RPM begins to decay. The pilot instinctively pulls more collective. Explain the aerodynamic error chain occurring here and what the correct response is.
questions.answer: The error chain is as follows: (1) As the helicopter slows through translational lift, induced power required increases significantly — the rotor must work harder to generate the same lift. (2) The single engine, already at or near its OEI limit, cannot supply the additional power demanded by the increased collective input. (3) Pulling more collective increases the pitch angle of the rotor blades, which increases drag on the rotor system, causing rotor RPM to decay further — this is a classic low-RPM death spiral. (4) With decaying rotor RPM, lift decreases, which may prompt the pilot to pull even more collective, accelerating the decay. The correct response is counterintuitive: lower the collective to reduce rotor drag and allow rotor RPM to recover, accept a higher descent rate, and maintain rotor RPM in the green arc above all else. The pilot should simultaneously attempt to maintain OEI airspeed with cyclic to preserve translational lift as long as possible. If rotor RPM cannot be maintained, the approach must be transitioned to an autorotation with whatever rotor energy remains. Rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable — preserving RPM takes absolute priority over maintaining altitude or approach profile.
questions.follow_up: At what rotor RPM percentage would you expect the low rotor RPM warning to activate in most turbine helicopters, and why does that warning represent a last-resort alert rather than an early caution?
questions.follow_up_answer: Most turbine helicopter low rotor RPM warnings activate at approximately 90–95% of normal operating RPM, depending on the specific aircraft (exact value is aircraft-specific and found in the RFM). This threshold represents a last-resort alert rather than an early caution because by the time the warning sounds, rotor RPM has already decayed to a point where blade lift is significantly degraded and the time available to recover is extremely short — sometimes only seconds. The warning is designed as an emergency alert, not a cautionary advisory. Pilots must develop awareness of rotor RPM trends through the tachometer and power instruments continuously, so that collective is reduced and corrective action is taken well before the horn activates. Waiting for the warning before reacting is operationally too late in many low-altitude OEI situations.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Low Rotor RPM/Rotor Stall section); applicable RFM rotor RPM limits and warning systems

questions.question: How does high density altitude affect your autorotation performance during a one-engine-inoperative approach in a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: High density altitude reduces air density, which decreases rotor efficiency and increases the power required to maintain rotor RPM. During an OEI approach, the remaining engine must work harder to compensate, and if autorotation becomes necessary, the reduced air density means less aerodynamic braking on the rotor blades, causing rotor RPM to decay more quickly. The helicopter will also have a higher true airspeed at any given indicated airspeed, resulting in a longer ground roll or slide distance on landing. Overall glide performance and rate of descent may be adversely affected.

questions.question: What effect does a strong headwind have on your glide distance during an OEI emergency approach?
questions.answer: A strong headwind reduces your ground speed relative to your descent rate, which shortens the over-ground distance you can cover during an OEI glide or autorotation. This means your effective glide range to a suitable landing area is reduced. However, a headwind also lowers your groundspeed at touchdown, which reduces landing roll or slide distance and can make the landing safer. Pilots must account for wind direction and speed when selecting a landing site and planning the approach profile.

questions.question: How does outside air temperature affect the power available from the remaining engine during an OEI approach?
questions.answer: Higher outside air temperatures reduce air density, which directly reduces the mass flow of air entering the engine. This lowers the engine's power output — the remaining engine produces less torque and shaft horsepower than it would in cooler conditions. As a result, at high temperatures, the operating engine may not be able to fully compensate for the failed engine, requiring a steeper approach angle, a faster descent rate, or a transition to autorotation. Cold temperatures have the opposite effect, generally improving engine performance and power availability.

questions.question: You are conducting a simulated OEI approach on a hot summer day at a mountain airport (field elevation 7,500 ft). Density altitude is calculated at 10,500 ft. How does this combination of conditions change your approach planning compared to a sea-level standard day?
questions.answer: At 10,500 ft density altitude, both rotor efficiency and remaining engine performance are significantly degraded. You should expect: (1) A higher true airspeed for any given indicated airspeed, requiring careful attention to landing zone selection since actual ground coverage is greater; (2) The remaining engine may be operating near or at its maximum continuous power limit just to maintain controlled flight, leaving little or no power margin for a go-around; (3) Rotor RPM will be harder to maintain during the approach, especially if power is reduced; (4) Rate of descent may be higher than at sea level, requiring a shallower approach angle or earlier flare; (5) Tail rotor effectiveness is also reduced, potentially complicating torque management. The pilot should select a longer, unobstructed landing area, plan for a no-hover or running landing, and avoid any maneuvers that demand sudden large power increases.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 7 and Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) OEI performance charts

questions.question: During an OEI approach in gusty wind conditions, you notice airspeed fluctuating ±10 knots. What specific risks does this create, and how do you manage them?
questions.answer: Gusty winds create airspeed fluctuations that directly affect rotor RPM and lift. During an OEI approach where power margin is already reduced, a sudden airspeed decrease (gust lull) can cause rotor RPM to decay and lift to drop unexpectedly, potentially placing the helicopter in a critical low-RPM situation. Conversely, a sudden gust can cause an airspeed spike, creating momentary balloon in altitude that distorts approach path judgment. Management strategies include: (1) Add a gust factor to approach airspeed (typically one-half the gust value, per RFM guidance); (2) Fly a slightly higher approach airspeed to provide a buffer against RPM decay; (3) Avoid steep approaches that increase rotor angle of attack sensitivity to airspeed changes; (4) Be prepared to convert to autorotation immediately if rotor RPM decays; (5) Plan for a no-hover running landing to reduce power demand at touchdown.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) emergency procedures

questions.question: You are flying an OEI approach when you encounter an unexpected area of rain and reduced visibility. How does precipitation affect your ability to complete a safe emergency approach and landing?
questions.answer: Precipitation during an OEI approach creates multiple compounding hazards: (1) Reduced visibility limits your ability to identify and maintain visual contact with the intended landing area, increasing CFIT risk; (2) Rain reduces rotor efficiency slightly by disrupting laminar airflow over the rotor blades; (3) Wet surfaces at the landing zone increase the risk of skidding or dynamic rollover on a running landing; (4) Rain on windshields degrades outside visual references, making altitude and terrain judgment harder; (5) If temperature is near freezing, icing of the rotor blades or engine inlets is a concern that could further reduce power and lift; (6) ADM becomes critical — if visibility drops below VFR minimums and the aircraft is not IFR certified/equipped, the pilot must prioritize an immediate landing rather than continuing to a distant suitable area.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; 14 CFR 91.155 (VFR weather minimums)

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter at gross weight in high density altitude conditions when one engine fails. Your flight manual shows you are outside the height-velocity (H-V) diagram avoid curve for the density altitude and weight combination. Explain the aerodynamic and atmospheric reasons why the H-V diagram shifts at high density altitude, and what this means for your emergency approach options.
questions.answer: The H-V diagram (also called the dead man's curve) defines combinations of height and airspeed from which a safe autorotation landing is not possible because rotor RPM cannot be recovered before ground contact. At high density altitude, the H-V diagram expands — the avoid areas become larger — for several reasons: (1) Lower air density means rotor blades generate less lift per unit of RPM, so a given rotor RPM translates into less actual lift than at sea level; (2) Rotor RPM decays faster at high density altitude because the thinner air provides less aerodynamic braking/torque to sustain RPM after collective is lowered; (3) The remaining engine (in a twin) may be producing less power, meaning it has already been working closer to its limit — leaving less ability to slow the descent or recover; (4) The helicopter's true airspeed is higher for a given indicated airspeed, meaning energy state is not proportionally better than it appears on the airspeed indicator. Practically, being outside the H-V avoid area at high density altitude means you have fewer safe emergency approach options — you may not be able to perform a successful autorotation to a full stop, and a running or sliding landing on a suitable area becomes the priority. The pilot should have pre-planned the approach to stay within the corrected H-V curve limits from the RFM performance section.
questions.follow_up: If the RFM only shows a standard day H-V diagram and not a density altitude-corrected one, how would you determine safe operational limits for today's conditions?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the RFM does not provide density altitude-corrected H-V curves, the pilot must apply conservative judgment and use the available data conservatively. Some manufacturers provide notes or guidance to expand the avoid areas by a percentage for elevated density altitudes or gross weights. In the absence of specific data, the pilot should: (1) Consult the manufacturer or approved POH/AFM supplements for any supplementary data; (2) Apply a conservative buffer by treating the published H-V curve as the minimum safe envelope and expanding it operationally; (3) Consider that at higher density altitudes, maintaining airspeed above the low-speed avoid region becomes increasingly critical; (4) Recognize that this is an ADM and risk management issue — if specific performance data is unavailable, the safest approach is to maintain airspeeds and altitudes that give the most time and distance for rotor RPM recovery. Ultimately, operations where certified performance data is unavailable for the existing conditions represent an elevated risk that should factor into go/no-go decisions.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Height-Velocity Diagram); Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) Section 5 (Performance); 14 CFR 91.9 (Operating limits)

questions.question: During an OEI approach on a cold winter day with a strong tailwind, you notice the aircraft is performing better than expected — the remaining engine has excess power and rotor RPM is stable. A student asks why cold temperatures help, but then suggests that since everything is going well, a tailwind shouldn't matter on final. How do you correct the student's understanding of tailwind risk during an OEI emergency approach?
questions.answer: The student is correct that cold temperatures improve engine performance by increasing air density, which boosts engine power output and rotor efficiency — this is a genuine performance benefit. However, their dismissal of tailwind risk reflects a significant misunderstanding. A tailwind during an OEI emergency approach is dangerous for several reasons: (1) Groundspeed is higher for any given airspeed — this dramatically increases the kinetic energy that must be dissipated at landing, requiring more stopping distance or a higher flare energy; (2) If the helicopter must transition to autorotation, the tailwind extends the ground distance covered during the descent, potentially placing the aircraft beyond the intended landing zone; (3) A tailwind reduces the effectiveness of the flare — the flare converts airspeed (relative to the air mass) into rotor RPM and lift, but the higher groundspeed means the touchdown still occurs at a much higher speed relative to the ground; (4) On a running or sliding landing — which is the likely outcome of an OEI approach — a tailwind dramatically increases the risk of loss of directional control, rollover, or overrunning the landing area; (5) From an ADM standpoint, the error chain here involves the student being lulled into complacency by one favorable condition (cold temp) while ignoring another hazard (tailwind). The examiner should reinforce that each atmospheric factor must be evaluated independently and cumulatively.
questions.follow_up: If the only available landing zone requires a tailwind landing, what technique adjustments would you make to minimize tailwind risk during an OEI running landing?
questions.follow_up_answer: If a tailwind landing is unavoidable, the pilot should: (1) Add extra airspeed on final to ensure adequate rotor RPM for the flare — do not fly a slow final because RPM decay risk is amplified; (2) Use the longest available run-on area and aim for the very beginning of it; (3) Establish a lower approach angle to reduce the rate of descent at touchdown, minimizing the vertical component of impact energy; (4) Time the flare precisely — flare too early and you lose airspeed too soon; flare too late and you contact the ground at high speed with insufficient lift; (5) After touchdown, maintain lateral cyclic to prevent dynamic rollover as the helicopter decelerates and skids; (6) Keep the tail rotor and collective inputs smooth — aggressive pedal or collective changes during ground run can cause the helicopter to pivot or roll; (7) Brief passengers on brace position if practical. Ultimately, if the zone is too short for a safe tailwind landing at the computed groundspeed, the pilot must weigh the risk of the landing against the risk of attempting to find a better area — a true ADM decision.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Emergency Landings, Running/Sliding Landings); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, Error Chain); Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) Emergency Procedures

questions.question: In the context of a one-engine-inoperative approach in a multiengine helicopter, what does the term 'stabilized approach' mean?
questions.answer: A stabilized approach means the helicopter is established on a consistent glidepath with a steady, controlled rate of descent, stable airspeed at or near the manufacturer's recommended OEI approach speed, coordinated flight, and no large or abrupt control corrections required to maintain the desired flight path. All variables — speed, rate of descent, and heading — should be relatively constant and within acceptable tolerances well before the landing point.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9, Chapter 11; Helicopter Flying Handbook

questions.question: Why is maintaining a stabilized approach especially critical when one engine is inoperative in a multiengine helicopter compared to a normal two-engine approach?
questions.answer: With one engine inoperative, the helicopter is operating at reduced power margin, meaning there is significantly less power available to correct deviations or arrest a high sink rate. If the approach becomes unstabilized — requiring large power corrections or aggressive cyclic inputs — the remaining engine may not be capable of providing the necessary thrust to recover, potentially leading to an uncontrolled hard landing or dynamic rollover. A stabilized approach minimizes the need for large power applications and keeps the energy state predictable.

questions.question: What are the key parameters a pilot monitors to confirm the approach is and remains stabilized during a simulated OEI approach?
questions.answer: The key parameters include: (1) airspeed — at or near the Rotorcraft Flight Manual's recommended OEI approach or best rate of descent speed; (2) rate of descent — steady and consistent, not increasing unexpectedly; (3) glidepath/descent angle — on profile and not deviating high or low; (4) heading/alignment — tracking toward the intended landing point with no significant drift; (5) rotor RPM — within the normal operating range; and (6) power setting — manageable without requiring abrupt or excessive collective changes.

questions.question: You are conducting a simulated OEI approach in a twin-engine helicopter. At 200 feet AGL your airspeed is 5 knots above the recommended approach speed and your rate of descent has increased to 600 FPM rather than the planned 400 FPM. Is this approach stabilized, and what should you do?
questions.answer: No, this approach is not stabilized. The airspeed deviation is minor, but the 50% increase in sink rate (from 400 to 600 FPM) is a significant deviation that indicates the approach is becoming unstabilized. With OEI power limitations, the pilot should immediately assess whether the remaining engine can support the power addition needed to arrest the sink rate and re-establish the glidepath. If the approach cannot be corrected promptly and smoothly, the pilot should execute a go-around using OEI go-around procedures per the RFM — provided sufficient altitude and power remain to do so safely. Continuing an unstabilized OEI approach risks a hard landing or loss of control during the landing flare.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM OEI procedures

questions.question: How does the concept of the 'error chain' from ADM relate to maintaining a stabilized OEI approach, and what early signs might indicate the chain is forming?
questions.answer: The error chain concept (from ADM) describes how accidents rarely result from one mistake but from multiple poor decisions accumulating. In an OEI approach, early links in the chain might include: arriving at the final approach fix too fast, flying the approach steep, waiting too long to configure the helicopter, poor wind assessment, or delayed recognition that the approach is drifting off profile. Each uncorrected deviation increases workload and narrows options. Recognizing any of these early signs — even a single parameter out of limits — and responding by adjusting or going around breaks the chain before it leads to an accident. The ADM principle that 'if it will only probably work out, choose an option known to work' directly applies: if the approach is only probably salvageable, a go-around is the known-safe option.

questions.question: A multiengine helicopter's RFM specifies an OEI approach speed of 70 KIAS. During training, your instructor tells you to fly the OEI approach at 60 KIAS to 'keep it slow.' What concerns does this raise regarding a stabilized approach?
questions.answer: Flying below the RFM-specified OEI approach speed creates several concerns. First, operating below the recommended speed may place the helicopter in or near the region of reversed command (back side of the power curve), where additional power — which is already limited OEI — is required to arrest any further deceleration. Second, the reduced airspeed could compromise the ability to maintain a controlled, stable glidepath and increase the risk of settling with power or dynamic rollover at touchdown. Third, the approach may not be stabilized per the standard because the airspeed is outside the RFM-prescribed parameters, meaning the aircraft's performance data for obstacle clearance and landing distance may not apply. The instructor's guidance conflicts with the RFM, and the RFM always takes precedence.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR 91.9 (operating limitations); applicable RFM

questions.question: During a simulated OEI approach, you are perfectly stabilized at the recommended speed and glidepath. At 50 feet AGL, a gust of wind increases your groundspeed significantly and pushes you 15 feet left of the intended landing point. The approach is now technically destabilized at low altitude OEI. Walk me through your decision-making process — do you continue or go around, and what factors drive that decision?
questions.answer: At 50 feet AGL with a remaining deviation of 15 feet lateral and unexpected windshear, the decision must be rapid and based on these factors: (1) Power availability — does the remaining single engine have enough torque margin to support a go-around from 50 feet? Many twin helicopters have limited OEI climb performance; a low-altitude OEI go-around may not be possible if the helicopter is near the height-velocity curve's shaded area. (2) Surface suitability — is 15 feet lateral displacement still over a safe, obstacle-free landing zone? If yes, a continuation may be safer than initiating a go-around at very low altitude with limited power. (3) Rate of deviation — is the aircraft still moving laterally or has it stabilized at the new position? (4) RFM guidance — the OEI height-velocity diagram and go-around minimums must be respected. In many cases, continuation with a smooth correction is the lower-risk option at 50 feet AGL compared to adding power for a climb with limited OEI performance. However, if a hard surface, obstacle, or people are in the new landing path, a go-around attempt — even with risk — may be necessary. The key principle: the decision must be deliberate, not reactive, and based on what is 'known to work' rather than what will 'probably' work.
questions.follow_up: You decide to continue. As you flare to land, you notice the collective is already near the top of its range and the rotor RPM is beginning to decay slightly. What does this tell you, and what immediate action do you take?
questions.follow_up_answer: This indicates the remaining engine is at or near its OEI torque/power limit and the rotor system is beginning to be overtorqued or under-driven. Rotor RPM decay at this stage — during the landing flare — means the rotor is absorbing more energy than the engine can supply. Immediate action: accept the landing without attempting to arrest the sink rate further with collective (which would accelerate RPM decay), maintain level skids with cyclic to prevent dynamic rollover, and get weight on the ground smoothly. Do NOT add more collective in an attempt to fully arrest the descent — doing so risks rotor stall, which the HFH states is not recoverable. A firm but controlled touchdown is the safest outcome.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (low rotor RPM, dynamic rollover, autorotation entry); OEI H-V diagram in applicable RFM

questions.question: Explain how the stabilized approach concept intersects with the height-velocity (H-V) diagram during an OEI approach, and describe a scenario where flying a perfectly stabilized approach could still result in an unsafe outcome if H-V diagram constraints are ignored.
questions.answer: The H-V diagram defines combinations of altitude and airspeed from which a safe autorotation or OEI landing cannot be guaranteed. A stabilized approach that tracks through the shaded (avoid) region of the H-V diagram — such as slowing to hover speed while still at 150 feet AGL during an OEI approach — is stabilized in the sense of consistent parameters, but is operating within an altitude-airspeed combination where, if the remaining engine fails, a survivable autorotation is not possible. For example: a helicopter on a 3° glidepath at 70 KIAS and 300 feet AGL may be perfectly stabilized and outside the H-V shaded area. But if the pilot slows prematurely to 40 KIAS at 200 feet AGL to 'set up for landing,' they may enter the H-V shaded region. If the second engine now fails, the pilot has insufficient altitude to establish autorotation and insufficient airspeed to flare effectively — a fatal combination. The lesson is that a stabilized approach must also be planned so that the entire final approach segment remains outside the H-V shaded area, and the pilot must understand that 'stabilized' is not just about smooth flight but also about operating in a survivable energy state throughout.
questions.follow_up: How does rotor system inertia affect the pilot's margin for error in this H-V scenario, and does it differ between helicopter models?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, rotor inertia varies significantly between helicopter models and directly affects how much time the pilot has to respond to a second engine failure inside the H-V shaded area. High-inertia rotor systems (typically found on larger, heavier helicopters with more blade mass) retain RPM longer after power loss, giving the pilot slightly more time to enter autorotation before RPM decays to an unsafe level. Low-inertia rotor systems (common in lighter turbine and piston helicopters) lose RPM very rapidly — sometimes in 1–2 seconds — leaving almost no margin for delay in lowering collective. The HFH specifically notes that simultaneous, immediate control inputs (down collective, aft cyclic, trim) are critical at autorotation entry, and that 'low inertia rotors decay rapidly.' This means a helicopter with a low-inertia rotor system has an even more unforgiving H-V shaded region, and the OEI approach must be planned more conservatively to ensure the aircraft is never placed in a position where a second failure inside that region could occur.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (autorotation, H-V diagram, rotor inertia); applicable RFM H-V diagram

questions.question: What is the primary difference between a normal two-engine approach profile and an OEI approach profile in a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: An OEI approach profile is typically shallower and flown at a higher airspeed than a normal two-engine approach. This keeps the helicopter in a favorable energy state and within the power margin of the remaining engine. The profile is designed to avoid low-speed, high-power demand regimes where the single remaining engine may be unable to arrest a descent or go-around. Most OEI profiles avoid a fully powered hover and instead terminate in a run-on or roll-on landing to minimize power demand at the most critical phase.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; specific aircraft RFM/POH OEI procedures

questions.question: What does the term 'aircraft configuration' mean in the context of an OEI approach, and what items are typically included?
questions.answer: Aircraft configuration for an OEI approach refers to the specific settings and conditions the helicopter should be in during the approach, as defined by the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM). This typically includes: identifying and confirming which engine is inoperative, verifying the operative engine is set to the appropriate power rating (such as OEI continuous or 30-minute power limit), confirming rotor RPM is within limits, landing gear position (if applicable), and any checklist items required by the RFM for single-engine operations. Some aircraft may also require specific bleed air, environmental, or electrical load shedding steps.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 27.1585 / 29.1585 (Rotorcraft Flight Manual requirements); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: Why is a run-on or roll-on landing commonly used as the preferred landing technique at the end of an OEI approach?
questions.answer: A run-on or roll-on landing is preferred during OEI operations because translating inertia into forward ground roll reduces the power demand at touchdown compared to a hover or vertical landing. During a hover, the remaining engine must provide all anti-torque and lift at a high power setting with no airspeed to assist rotor efficiency. A run-on landing allows the helicopter to touch down with forward speed, reducing required power, minimizing the risk of exceeding engine limits, and lowering the probability of settling or losing control if the remaining engine reaches its limit.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; specific aircraft RFM OEI landing procedures

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter and experience an engine failure during cruise at 2,000 feet AGL. After stabilizing on OEI power, you need to plan your approach to a nearby airport. Describe the key profile elements you would use and explain why you would not fly a standard 3° ILS glideslope approach.
questions.answer: After engine failure stabilization, I would plan an OEI approach using a shallower glidepath — typically the angle specified in the RFM — at or above the aircraft's OEI best rate of climb or minimum power required airspeed for that configuration. A standard 3° ILS glideslope may not be appropriate because: (1) at lower airspeeds near the threshold, the single engine may not have sufficient power margin for a go-around if needed; (2) the profile may not provide adequate energy for a safe flare and run-on landing; (3) the committed landing point philosophy means I must select an approach where, once I reach a decision point, I can successfully complete the landing with the power available. I would plan to arrive over the threshold with enough airspeed to transition smoothly into a run-on or roll-on landing, avoiding any need to hover. I would also confirm the operative engine is within its OEI power rating limits and monitor torque and engine temperatures throughout.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR 61.157 (multiengine rating training requirements); specific aircraft RFM

questions.question: During an OEI approach briefing, your student asks why the RFM specifies a higher approach airspeed than normal for the single-engine case. How do you explain the aerodynamic and performance reasons for this?
questions.answer: The higher approach airspeed in OEI operations is required for several reasons: (1) Translational lift — maintaining airspeed above effective translational lift (ETL) keeps rotor efficiency higher, meaning the remaining engine requires less power to maintain the glidepath; (2) Go-around margin — a higher approach airspeed provides more energy for acceleration and climb if a go-around becomes necessary, since the single engine may not have sufficient power to arrest a descent from a slow, high-drag condition; (3) Avoidance of the height-velocity (H-V) curve — some flight profiles at low airspeed and low altitude put the helicopter in an avoid area where a safe autorotation or powered recovery may not be possible; (4) Control margin — at higher airspeeds, the tail rotor is more effective, providing better yaw control authority in the asymmetric power condition. The tradeoff is a longer ground roll, which is why a suitable landing area must be selected.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapters 9 and 11; specific aircraft RFM performance charts

questions.question: You are on a simulated OEI approach and the examiner asks you to identify the 'committed point' or 'decision point' on the approach. What is this point, what factors determine where it occurs, and what are your options before and after reaching it?
questions.answer: The committed point (sometimes called the decision point or landing commitment point) is the point on the OEI approach beyond which a safe go-around or continued landing with the remaining engine is no longer guaranteed if a secondary failure or complication occurs — it is the point at which the pilot commits to landing. Factors that determine its location include: (1) aircraft altitude and airspeed at that point and whether a go-around is still achievable with OEI power available; (2) the height-velocity (H-V) avoid curve for the aircraft — if the aircraft enters the avoid area, options become very limited; (3) obstacle environment and available landing area. Before the committed point, the pilot retains the option to execute a go-around, divert, or abort the approach. After the committed point, the correct action is to complete the landing as planned with the existing power. The RFM and performance charts for the specific aircraft define these boundaries, and the approach profile must be designed so the committed point occurs at an altitude and speed consistent with completing a safe landing.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; specific aircraft RFM; 14 CFR 27.87 / 29.87 (H-V curve certification)

questions.question: A pilot argues that during an OEI approach simulation, since both engines are actually running, they should configure and fly the approach the same way regardless of wind conditions or density altitude because it is 'only simulated.' As an examiner, how do you respond, and what performance factors must the pilot account for in the actual OEI approach profile and configuration even during simulation?
questions.answer: This is a critical misunderstanding. Even during a simulated OEI approach, the pilot must plan and fly the approach as if the engine failure is real, using actual performance data from the RFM for the conditions that day. The reason is that the ACS evaluates whether the pilot can correctly apply OEI procedures, profiles, and configurations — not just go through the motions. Density altitude directly affects the power output of the remaining engine; at high DA, OEI power limits may be reached at a lower collective position, the approach airspeed may need to be higher to maintain ETL, and the landing distance may be significantly greater. Headwind or tailwind affects glidepath angle, approach airspeed over the ground, and landing distance. The pilot must use the RFM OEI power charts to determine whether a go-around is feasible at the planned approach airspeed and field elevation. Ignoring these factors means the pilot is not actually demonstrating OEI competency — they are only performing a choreographed exercise that could lead to a fatal error in a real emergency.
questions.follow_up: If the RFM states the helicopter is certified for Category A operations, how does Category A change the required approach profile and what additional protection does it provide compared to a Category B operation?
questions.follow_up_answer: Category A certification (14 CFR Part 29, Appendix C) means the rotorcraft is certified to a higher standard requiring a defined OEI takeoff flight path and, for approaches, a go-around capability from a specific point in the approach. Category A requires that the aircraft can safely continue the operation or abort from any point in the approach/landing using only one engine, based on published performance data. This means the RFM will contain specific Category A approach profiles — typically a steep, defined angle with a decision point — and the aircraft's engines are certified for OEI continued operation power ratings (2.5 minute, 30 minute, and continuous OEI ratings). Category B certification only requires demonstration of a safe landing after an engine failure; there is no requirement for a go-around capability from all points in the approach. The practical difference is that a Category A approach gives the crew a defined go-around option backed by certified performance data, while Category B operations require the crew to plan for a committed landing from a much earlier point in the approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 29.1 and Part 29 Appendix C (Category A); 14 CFR 27.1 (Category B); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; AC 29-2C

questions.question: During an OEI approach, at what point in the approach profile is the aircraft most vulnerable to exceeding the remaining engine's OEI power limits, and how should the pilot configure the aircraft and manage the approach geometry to prevent this?
questions.answer: The most vulnerable point is typically during the deceleration and flare phase just prior to touchdown — specifically when the helicopter transitions from forward flight below ETL to the lowest airspeed of the approach, requiring maximum collective to arrest the descent rate. At this point, induced power requirements spike because rotor efficiency is at its lowest (below ETL) while the aircraft still has significant inertia and descent rate to manage. To prevent exceeding engine limits: (1) Maintain airspeed above ETL as long as possible by flying the approach at the RFM-specified OEI approach speed; (2) Use a shallower glidepath to arrive at the threshold with less descent rate to arrest; (3) Plan a run-on or roll-on touchdown to transfer weight to the ground before full deceleration, reducing power demand; (4) Monitor engine torque, turbine temperature (TGT/TOT), and rotor RPM throughout — if engine temperature or torque is approaching limits during the flare, accept a firm landing rather than attempt to soften it with more collective; (5) Avoid going-around below the committed point, since the acceleration phase from a slow, low-altitude position demands the highest power and may exceed OEI limits. Configuration items include confirming OEI power mode is selected (if applicable to the aircraft), load shedding any non-essential electrical loads, and ensuring landing gear is in the correct position per the RFM.
questions.follow_up: If the remaining engine reaches its 30-minute OEI power limit during the approach and you still have runway ahead, what is the correct action and what are the consequences of ignoring that limit?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the 30-minute OEI power limit is reached or imminent, the correct action is to accept the landing immediately — even if it results in a firm or imperfect touchdown — rather than hold the collective up to soften the landing. The 30-minute OEI rating means the engine is certified to produce that power for a maximum of 30 continuous minutes; exceeding the time limit or the associated torque/temperature limits can cause hot section damage, compressor blade fatigue, or outright engine failure — leaving the aircraft with zero engines. A firm landing on a runway or prepared surface is survivable and the aircraft is repairable. A dual engine failure at 50 feet AGL during a poorly managed OEI approach is a catastrophic, likely unrecoverable event. Additionally, exceeding certificated engine limits constitutes a reportable maintenance event and may require engine removal and inspection before the next flight.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 33.7 (engine ratings and limits); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; specific aircraft RFM engine limitations section; 14 CFR 91.409 (maintenance requirements after limit exceedance)

questions.question: When you lose an engine in a multiengine helicopter and begin an OEI approach, why does your current altitude matter so much in terms of landing area options?
questions.answer: Altitude directly determines how much time and glide distance you have to assess and maneuver toward a suitable landing area. Greater altitude provides more options — you can cover more ground, perform a more deliberate approach profile, and select a better landing zone. At low altitude, your options collapse quickly and you may be committed to whatever is directly ahead. Altitude is effectively time and energy; losing an engine at 500 feet AGL leaves you far fewer choices than losing one at 2,000 feet AGL.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Helicopter Emergencies and Hazards

questions.question: What is the preferred wind orientation for an OEI approach and landing, and why?
questions.answer: An into-the-wind approach is preferred whenever possible. Landing into the wind reduces groundspeed at touchdown, shortens the ground roll or landing run, and provides better translational lift during the approach. It also improves the effectiveness of the remaining engine and rotor system. A tailwind OEI approach increases groundspeed and landing distance, reduces available performance margins, and can lead to dynamic rollover or loss of directional control during the landing roll.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Helicopter Emergencies and Hazards

questions.question: What characteristics define an acceptable emergency landing area for a multiengine helicopter conducting an OEI approach?
questions.answer: An acceptable landing area should be large enough to accommodate the helicopter's footprint with margin to spare, reasonably level to prevent rollover, free of obstacles in the approach and departure paths, have a firm and stable surface to support the helicopter's weight, and ideally allow an into-the-wind approach. The area should also be free of people or structures that could be harmed. Soft, sloped, or debris-covered surfaces significantly increase rollover and dynamic rollover risk on landing.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Helicopter Emergencies and Hazards

questions.question: You are flying a multiengine helicopter at 1,500 feet AGL over mountainous terrain when you lose one engine. The wind is 15 knots from the west, but the only available flat landing area is to the east, requiring a downwind approach. How do you weigh the terrain and wind factors in choosing your approach path?
questions.answer: This is a classic terrain-versus-wind tradeoff. First, assess whether remaining engine performance is sufficient to execute a controlled downwind approach — check your OEI performance charts and the current density altitude. A downwind approach increases approach speed and touchdown groundspeed, so verify the landing area is long enough to accommodate it. If the terrain to the west (upwind side) is rising or obstructed, attempting to circle to land into the wind may carry you over rising terrain and further reduce your altitude margins. In mountainous terrain, obstacle clearance and terrain separation may outweigh the wind advantage. Accept the downwind landing if the terrain threat is greater, but adjust your approach angle and anticipate a faster touchdown. Document the decision reasoning — this is exactly the kind of risk tradeoff the ACS expects you to articulate.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Helicopter Emergencies and Hazards; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 ADM

questions.question: During an OEI approach to a confined area, you notice power lines running across the final approach path that weren't visible from altitude. At this point you're at 200 feet AGL on short final. Walk me through your risk assessment and decision process.
questions.answer: At 200 feet AGL on short final with power lines crossing the approach path, the obstruction now becomes the most immediate threat. Your options narrow significantly. First, assess whether you have sufficient OEI power and altitude to execute a go-around or abort — at 200 feet AGL on one engine, a go-around requires significant power margin and clean execution. If a go-around is feasible with the remaining engine, execute it and reassess the landing area or select an alternate. If the power lines can be safely overflown — meaning you have clear identification of their height and sufficient rotor clearance — you might continue, but this is high-risk. If neither option is safe, look immediately for an alternate surface within glide range. The key principle is: an unseen obstruction on short final is a go-around trigger unless the go-around itself is demonstrably more hazardous. Continuing beneath or through power lines is not an acceptable option.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 ADM (error chain concept)

questions.question: You're flying a multiengine helicopter over flat agricultural terrain at 800 feet AGL when an engine fails. You see three possible landing areas: a harvested field directly ahead and slightly left, a paved road running perpendicular to your heading, and a small clearing in a tree line about a mile away. How do you prioritize these options and what factors drive your decision?
questions.answer: Prioritize the options using altitude, distance, obstacle content, and surface quality. The harvested field directly ahead is the highest-priority option — it's close, minimizing the time and energy required to reach it, it's likely flat, and agricultural fields generally have firm surfaces post-harvest. Verify there are no irrigation equipment, ditches, or fence lines crossing it. The paved road requires assessing traffic, power lines running alongside it, and the fact that it runs perpendicular to your heading, potentially forcing a crosswind landing. Roads also carry the risk of unexpected obstacles like vehicles or signs. The tree line clearing requires a full mile of OEI flight, consuming altitude and increasing exposure time — at 800 feet AGL with OEI, one mile may be achievable but leaves little margin. Generally, select the closest adequate area first. Distance is only justified if the closer area has a disqualifying hazard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Helicopter Emergencies and Hazards

questions.question: On an OEI approach, a pilot selects a landing area that appears adequate from altitude but commits to it without reassessing as they descend closer. The area turns out to have a significant downslope and tall grass concealing soft ground. What does this scenario illustrate about risk management during OEI operations, and at what point in the approach should reassessment occur?
questions.answer: This scenario illustrates the danger of fixation and premature commitment — sometimes called 'plan continuation bias.' The pilot allowed the initial decision to override new information that should have triggered a reassessment. In OEI operations, risk factors that are invisible or ambiguous from altitude often become clear during the approach. Reassessment should be continuous and structured at three key decision points: (1) at initial area selection from altitude, using available visual cues; (2) at mid-approach when the surface and slope become more discernible; and (3) on short final when surface texture, slope, and obstacles are clearly visible. At each point, if new disqualifying information emerges, a go-around must be considered — even late in the approach. The Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that breaking one link in the error chain changes the outcome. Fixation on an initial choice is a classic error chain component. Pilots must train themselves to treat each reassessment point as an independent go/no-go decision, not a confirmation of the original choice.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot is at 100 feet AGL on final when they recognize the slope problem, and the remaining engine is producing near-maximum continuous power, what specific factors determine whether a go-around is even possible at that point?
questions.follow_up_answer: At 100 feet AGL with the remaining engine near max continuous power, the go-around decision hinges on several factors: (1) whether the engine can produce additional power above current output — if already at MCP, there may be no additional thrust available without exceeding limits; (2) density altitude, as high DA reduces available power margin significantly; (3) rotor RPM state — if RPM has decayed during the approach, a power-demanding go-around may accelerate decay into low-RPM stall territory; (4) helicopter weight — heavier aircraft require more power to arrest sink rate and accelerate; (5) obstacles ahead and to the sides — a go-around at 100 feet over a sloped field may require flying through or over trees or terrain. If the engine cannot provide the power needed to arrest the descent rate, a go-around is not viable, and the pilot must instead select the best available surface within the existing approach path, adjust touchdown technique for slope (upslope skid first, minimal collective reduction), and accept the consequence. This is why pre-approach reconnaissance and early decision-making are critical — 100 feet AGL is not the right time to discover disqualifying hazards.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (error chain, ADM); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (dynamic rollover on slopes)

questions.question: A multiengine helicopter crew is flying at 3,000 feet AGL with a published OEI ceiling that's only 200 feet above current density altitude. One engine fails. The crew identifies a landing area two miles away into the wind, but the direct route passes over a populated residential neighborhood. Describe the risk management framework the crew should apply to balance the wind/terrain advantages against the overflight risk.
questions.answer: This scenario requires simultaneous assessment of four competing risk factors: performance margin, landing area quality, routing hazards, and third-party exposure. The OEI ceiling being only 200 feet above current density altitude means the helicopter is already operating near its performance limit — there is very little excess power. First, confirm the aircraft can maintain altitude or control its descent rate toward the landing area at all. If it cannot, the two-mile route is unachievable regardless of routing choice, and the crew must immediately select the nearest suitable area, even if not ideal. If the aircraft can reach the identified area, the crew must evaluate alternate routing: is there a path around the neighborhood that adds acceptable distance without exceeding glide capability? Even a modest deviation to avoid overflying populated areas is preferred when performance permits. If no deviation is possible, the routing directly over the neighborhood may be unavoidable — but the crew must fly the highest feasible altitude through that segment to maximize forced landing options away from structures if performance deteriorates further. ADM principles require that the crew actively communicate, divide tasks (one flies, one monitors engine instruments and identifies landing areas), and avoid the fixation trap. Under 14 CFR Part 91, there is no explicit prohibition against overflying populated areas in an emergency, and 14 CFR 91.3 grants the PIC authority to deviate from any regulation to the extent necessary to meet an emergency.
questions.follow_up: After landing safely in the identified area with no injuries, what are the crew's regulatory obligations regarding the emergency deviation and the engine failure itself?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.3(b), a pilot who deviates from an ATC clearance or FAR during an emergency must, upon ATC request, send a written report of the deviation to the Administrator. If no deviation from regulations occurred — for example, if no clearance was violated — no mandatory report is required under 91.3. However, the engine failure itself triggers separate reporting obligations. Under 14 CFR Part 830, the NTSB must be notified immediately of an aircraft accident or serious incident. An engine failure that required an off-airport landing would likely qualify as an accident or serious incident depending on damage and injury status. The operator must also report the mechanical failure under the operator's own safety management system procedures if operating under Part 135. Additionally, the crew should file an Aviation Safety Hotline or NASA ASRS report to document the event and preserve any operational safety lessons without enforcement risk, as ASRS filing provides limited immunity protection.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR Part 830 (NTSB notification); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 ADM; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: When planning an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, what is the primary consideration when selecting your landing area?
questions.answer: The landing area must be reachable with the power available from the operating engine, and it must be large enough and clear of obstacles to allow a safe landing. The pilot should select the nearest suitable area that can be reached without exceeding the operating engine's limitations, considering current altitude, airspeed, wind, and the helicopter's single-engine performance charts. Obstacle clearance along the entire flightpath must also be confirmed.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) OEI performance charts

questions.question: What does the term 'flightpath planning' mean in the context of an OEI approach, and why is it different from a normal approach?
questions.answer: Flightpath planning for an OEI approach means deliberately selecting and committing to a specific route from your current position to the landing area that accounts for reduced power margin, single-engine climb or glide capability, obstacle clearance, and wind. It differs from a normal approach because the pilot cannot rely on excess power to correct for poor planning — the margin for error is significantly reduced. Deviations from the planned path may result in obstacle strikes or inability to reach the landing area.

questions.question: What role does wind play when planning an OEI flightpath to a landing area in a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: Wind directly affects both the helicopter's ground track and its single-engine performance. A headwind on final approach reduces groundspeed and improves the ability to make a controlled landing, while a tailwind increases approach speed and extends the distance needed to touch down. Additionally, crosswinds increase workload on the remaining engine and complicate directional control. Pilots should plan the flightpath to take advantage of a headwind into the landing area whenever possible to maximize control and minimize landing distance.

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter at 3,000 feet AGL when one engine fails over mountainous terrain. There is a small paved parking lot 1.5 miles ahead and a larger open field 2.5 miles ahead. Your single-engine performance charts indicate you can maintain level flight but not climb. Which landing area do you choose, and how do you plan your flightpath?
questions.answer: Choose the parking lot 1.5 miles ahead. Since you cannot climb on one engine, altitude is a finite, non-renewable resource. The closer landing area reduces the time the operating engine must perform at high power settings and reduces exposure to further deterioration. Plan the flightpath to avoid terrain high points along the route, use a shallower approach angle to preserve energy and control rate of descent, and configure the helicopter per RFM OEI procedures as early as possible. The larger field 2.5 miles away introduces unacceptable risk of not making it over intervening terrain or running the remaining engine beyond its limits. Commit to the reachable option.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual OEI procedures

questions.question: During an OEI approach practice, your instructor tells you to abandon your planned flightpath and try a steeper angle to the same landing area. What risk does this introduce, and what should you consider before complying?
questions.answer: A steeper approach angle on one engine increases the rate of descent, which may require more power to arrest on short final — power that may not be available on one engine. This could result in a hard landing or loss of control near the ground. Before changing the flightpath, the pilot should assess whether the single-engine power available can arrest the increased rate of descent, confirm the approach is still within the Height-Velocity (H-V) diagram limitations, and verify no new obstacles have been introduced by the altered angle. In a real OEI scenario, deviating from a planned, calculated flightpath should only be done if clearly safer. The concept of 'avoid the word probably' from ADM principles applies — only change the plan if the new path is known to work, not just likely to work.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; Rotorcraft Flight Manual H-V diagram

questions.question: You are flying an OEI approach to a confined area landing zone. Halfway down the approach, you notice the flightpath will take you directly over a line of tall trees at the threshold. What is the risk management decision-making process you should use?
questions.answer: First, assess immediately whether the current altitude and remaining single-engine power allow you to clear the trees safely. If you are above the trees and can maintain clearance, adjust the flightpath angle to clear the obstacle while still being able to arrest descent before touchdown. If the trees cannot be safely cleared, execute an immediate go-around or divert to an alternate landing area — only if single-engine performance allows a go-around. The error chain concept from SRM tells us that pressing on with a known obstacle conflict is an accumulation of poor decisions. The preferred action is to have identified this obstacle during the initial planning phase before committing to the approach. If it was not identified, treat this as a link in the error chain and break it immediately by selecting an alternate course of action rather than hoping for the best.

questions.question: A multiengine helicopter pilot executing an OEI approach commits to a flightpath and landing area, but realizes at low altitude that the landing surface has a significant downslope that was not visible from altitude. What are the compounding risks, and how does late-stage flightpath replanning at low altitude over a confined area increase the danger compared to a normal two-engine approach?
questions.answer: At low altitude on one engine, the pilot has almost no margin for recovery from any error. A downsloping landing surface means the helicopter may touch down tail-low first, risking a tail rotor strike or dynamic rollover on uneven terrain.
