Replanning the flightpath at this stage is extremely dangerous because: (1) the helicopter is likely within or near the critical region of the H-V diagram, (2) a go-around requires the operating engine to rapidly accelerate the helicopter from a low-energy state, risking engine overtorque, (3) maneuvering at low altitude and low airspeed on one engine reduces the tail rotor's effectiveness against asymmetric torque, and (4) workload is at its highest precisely when decision time is shortest. In a two-engine approach, excess power allows replanning with manageable risk. On one engine, the only safe option may be to execute the landing with appropriate technique to compensate for terrain slope, such as landing slightly upslope or accepting a run-on landing to reduce rotor thrust requirements. This is why thorough pre-approach area reconnaissance is a non-negotiable risk management step.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot determines a go-around is necessary at this point, what specific single-engine performance limitations must be respected, and what is the greatest immediate danger during the go-around climb?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot must not exceed the operating engine's maximum continuous power (MCP) or 30-second/2-minute OEI power ratings as defined in the RFM, and must transition through the H-V diagram critical region as quickly as possible by accelerating to the best single-engine rate of climb speed (Vy OEI or VTOSS — Takeoff Safety Speed — as specified in the RFM). The greatest immediate danger during the go-around is entering an unrecoverable low rotor RPM condition or vortex ring state if aft cyclic is applied too aggressively without sufficient airspeed, combined with loss of directional control due to increased torque from the operating engine at high power setting — all while at low altitude with minimal reaction time.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual OEI performance; 14 CFR Part 27/29 rotorcraft airworthiness standards

questions.question: During a checkride, a candidate flying a simulated OEI approach plans and flies a flightpath that keeps the helicopter consistently on the high side of the planned glidepath. The examiner allows this to continue to touchdown. After landing, what specific risk management failure does this pattern reveal, and what are the downstream consequences of flying high on an OEI approach?
questions.answer: Flying consistently high on an OEI approach reveals a failure to plan and follow the flightpath — the candidate is not actually following their planned route, but rather allowing energy management to drift. The risk is that arriving high on final on one engine forces one of two bad options: (1) increasing the rate of descent steeply on short final, requiring power to arrest — power that may not exist — or (2) floating beyond the intended landing area into potential obstacles or unsuitable terrain at the far end of the zone. On a normal approach with two engines, excess power can mask a high final approach; on one engine, there is no such buffer. The correct risk management principle is to identify and correct glidepath deviation early, preferably above 200 feet AGL, while there is still altitude and time to adjust. Allowing a high approach to continue to short final on one engine represents a willingness to rely on 'probably' working out — exactly the ADM error the Helicopter Flying Handbook warns against.
questions.follow_up: If the candidate argues they intentionally stayed high to preserve options, how would you evaluate whether this was sound risk management or a rationalization of poor flightpath discipline?
questions.follow_up_answer: Sound risk management of flying slightly high early in the approach is legitimate if the pilot stated this intention during pre-approach planning, had a specific altitude gate at which they would commit to the glidepath, and actively managed the energy by reducing power or adjusting cyclic to arrive at that gate on profile. It becomes rationalization if the pilot drifted high without a defined plan, had no stated decision altitude for committing to the profile, and simply reacted to being high without a structured response. A real examiner distinguishes between deliberate energy management with identified checkpoints versus unplanned glidepath deviation explained away after the fact. The key question is: 'At what point in your approach did you plan to be on the correct glidepath, and how were you going to get there?' If the candidate cannot answer precisely, it was not planned — it was drifting.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM); ACS CH.X.C risk management standards

questions.question: During an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, why is collision with obstacles or terrain considered a primary hazard — more so than in a normal powered approach?
questions.answer: During an OEI approach, the pilot's attention is heavily divided between managing the failed engine, monitoring the operating engine, adjusting power, and flying the approach profile. This increased workload reduces situational awareness of the surrounding environment. Additionally, the helicopter may have a reduced ability to climb or go-around if an obstacle is encountered, meaning there is little or no margin to correct a collision course once one is identified. The combination of degraded performance and elevated cockpit workload makes terrain and obstacle collision a leading risk.

questions.question: What types of collision hazards should a pilot brief and account for before beginning an OEI approach to an unfamiliar landing area?
questions.answer: Before beginning an OEI approach, the pilot should identify and brief: terrain features (hills, ridgelines, rising ground along the approach path), man-made obstacles (towers, wires, antennas, buildings, trees near the landing zone), other air traffic in the pattern or vicinity, personnel and vehicles on or near the landing area, and any wires or fence lines that may be difficult to see. Since an OEI approach limits go-around capability, all of these must be positively identified and cleared before committing to the approach. A thorough reconnaissance pass, when performance permits, is strongly recommended.

questions.question: How does reduced go-around capability during an OEI approach increase the consequence of misjudging obstacle clearance on final?
questions.answer: In normal operations, if a pilot misjudges obstacle clearance on final they can apply full power and climb away. During an OEI approach, the available power is significantly reduced because only one engine is operating. Depending on the helicopter's single-engine performance, density altitude, and gross weight, the aircraft may be unable to climb at all or may only achieve a shallow climb rate. This means a misjudged approach that puts the helicopter on a collision course with an obstacle or terrain may be unrecoverable. The pilot must get the approach geometry correct the first time, which demands precise planning and heightened obstacle awareness throughout the entire approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual performance data

questions.question: You are conducting a simulated OEI approach to a confined area. On short final you notice a wire running across your intended flight path that you did not see during your reconnaissance. What is your immediate risk assessment and decision-making process?
questions.answer: This is a high-risk situation because you have a wire hazard directly in your path and your ability to climb over it or maneuver around it may be severely limited by single-engine performance. The immediate risk assessment must consider: (1) Can the helicopter climb over the wire with single-engine power available? Check RFM single-engine climb performance against current density altitude and gross weight. (2) Is there lateral maneuvering room to go around the wire while maintaining obstacle clearance on both sides? (3) Is there sufficient altitude and distance to reverse course and fly away? If none of these options are clearly achievable, the safest action may be to transition to a normal two-engine approach — in a simulated scenario, the examiner should be notified and the simulation discontinued. In a real emergency, the pilot should avoid committing to an approach where a collision hazard has been identified that cannot be cleared. The Trescott principle applies: if the outcome will only 'probably' be okay, choose the option known to work.

questions.question: During an OEI approach at night to an unprepared landing zone, how does the collision hazard environment change compared to a daytime OEI approach, and what mitigation strategies should you use?
questions.answer: At night, the collision hazard environment is significantly more dangerous because obstacles such as wires, trees, antennas, and terrain features are much harder or impossible to see without artificial lighting. The pilot's depth perception and ability to judge distance to obstacles is degraded. Mitigation strategies include: (1) Using all available lighting — landing light, search/spotlight if equipped — to illuminate the approach path and landing zone well ahead of the aircraft. (2) If time permits before the emergency, conducting a thorough daylight or lighted reconnaissance of the area. (3) Using NVGs if qualified, equipped, and authorized. (4) Selecting the highest-probability-of-success landing zone rather than the most convenient one — prioritizing obstacle-free approaches. (5) Flying a steeper approach angle if single-engine performance permits, to remain above wire strike height longer. (6) Accepting that under certain night conditions the safest outcome may be a precautionary landing in a less ideal but more hazard-free location.

questions.question: You are practicing a simulated OEI approach at a busy uncontrolled airport. Another helicopter is also in the pattern. How do you manage the collision hazard with the other aircraft while still managing the simulated emergency?
questions.answer: Managing traffic collision risk while simultaneously handling a simulated OEI emergency requires deliberate workload management. Before beginning the simulated approach: (1) Announce intentions clearly and specifically on CTAF — including that you are practicing an OEI approach, your location, and intended runway/landing area — so other pilots can anticipate your non-standard maneuvering and potentially reduced go-around capability. (2) Visually acquire the other helicopter and confirm a clear sequence before beginning the approach. (3) Assign the safety pilot or instructor responsibility for traffic scanning so your attention can remain on the simulated emergency procedures. (4) If the traffic conflict cannot be resolved prior to approach entry, delay the practice approach until the pattern is clear. (5) Be prepared to abandon the simulated emergency and revert to normal flight to avoid a mid-air collision — no training exercise justifies accepting a collision risk. Collision avoidance always takes priority over training fidelity.

questions.question: A pilot argues that because an OEI approach is flown at a lower approach angle than normal to preserve energy, it actually reduces the collision hazard with terrain and obstacles on final. Evaluate this argument — is it correct, and what does it miss?
questions.answer: This argument is partially correct but fundamentally incomplete and potentially dangerous. It is true that a shallower approach angle keeps the aircraft higher over the ground for a longer portion of the final approach, which may increase horizontal clearance above low obstacles like fences or low vegetation. However, the argument misses several critical points: (1) A shallower approach angle actually increases the risk of wire strikes and collision with obstacles at mid-height — like utility lines — because the aircraft spends more time and distance at wire-strike altitudes rather than descending steeply through them. (2) A shallower approach extends the final approach course, increasing the total distance over which obstacles must be cleared and over which an engine failure on the remaining engine would leave no recovery option. (3) The reduction in kinetic energy reserve that justifies the shallow approach also means less energy available to flare and avoid terrain at the bottom of the approach. (4) The shallow approach is designed for energy management at the landing, not primarily for obstacle clearance — conflating the two purposes creates a false sense of security. The pilot must conduct a full obstacle survey and not rely on approach angle alone to mitigate collision hazards.
questions.follow_up: If the shallow OEI approach angle actually increases wire-strike risk as you described, what technique can you use on final to improve wire awareness and detection?
questions.follow_up_answer: On final approach, the pilot should use the landing light proactively to scan across the intended flight path at wire-strike heights, not just straight ahead. Wires are most visible when the light is angled slightly downward and across the path, causing the wire to reflect. Additionally, looking for the support structures — poles, towers, anchor points on buildings or trees — is often more effective than trying to see the wires themselves, which may be invisible in certain lighting. If flying with a second crew member, that crewmember should be specifically tasked with low-level obstacle scanning. Slowing the approach if performance permits also gives more reaction time upon wire detection.

questions.question: During an actual OEI emergency requiring an immediate off-airport landing, how do you prioritize among multiple collision hazards — terrain, wires, vehicles, and personnel — when your decision time is extremely compressed?
questions.answer: In a compressed-time OEI emergency, collision hazard prioritization must be pre-planned through training and mental rehearsal rather than improvised in the moment. The general priority hierarchy is: (1) Terrain — catastrophic and unrecoverable; avoid CFIT at all costs; select a flight path that maintains the best achievable obstacle clearance above terrain until committed to the landing zone. (2) Wires — wires are nearly impossible to see at the last moment and a wire strike can be fatal; if a wire is seen and cannot be overflown or gone around, flare aggressively to reduce forward speed and attempt to pass under rather than through, or accept the controlled crash into terrain as preferable. (3) Immovable man-made structures — aim for the most open ground available; avoid solid structures. (4) Vehicles and personnel — these are mobile and may move; direct the landing to an area away from them, but do not compromise terrain or wire avoidance to do so. The overarching principle is to land the aircraft under control; a controlled landing into open terrain that damages only the aircraft is always preferable to an uncontrolled collision. Declare the emergency early on 121.5 or ATC frequency to alert rescue services and, where possible, use the radio to warn ground personnel.
questions.follow_up: After the OEI landing, if you landed in an area with potential ground personnel collision risk and they are now approaching the aircraft, what is your primary concern and what action do you take?
questions.follow_up_answer: The primary concern after landing is rotor strike — bystanders who are unfamiliar with helicopter operations frequently walk toward a helicopter from the tail, directly into the tail rotor arc, or approach from the side without watching the main rotor blade height, especially on sloped ground where a blade may be at head height. The pilot must keep the rotor turning only as long as operationally necessary, then shut down to eliminate the rotor hazard before allowing anyone to approach. If unable to shut down immediately, establish visual contact with approaching personnel and use hand signals or radio to direct them to remain clear until rotor stop. Ground personnel should always approach from the front in the pilot's field of view. This is a crew resource management issue and should be briefed to any passengers or ground crew before the flight.

questions.question: During an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, what does 'task prioritization' mean, and why is it critical at this phase of flight?
questions.answer: Task prioritization means consciously ranking tasks by importance and completing them in order of urgency. During an OEI approach, the pilot's workload is dramatically increased — managing a degraded power plant, monitoring remaining engine performance, flying a precise approach profile, and communicating with ATC all compete for attention simultaneously. Prioritization ensures that aviate (fly the aircraft) always comes first, navigate second, and communicate third. Failing to prioritize correctly can cause the pilot to devote attention to secondary tasks — such as checklists or radio calls — at the expense of controlling airspeed, rotor RPM, or glide path, all of which are life-critical on an OEI approach.

questions.question: Define 'situational awareness' as it applies to an OEI approach, and name two specific ways a pilot can lose it during that maneuver.
questions.answer: Situational awareness (SA) is the accurate, real-time perception of all elements affecting the flight — aircraft state, environment, and future outcome. During an OEI approach, SA means knowing where you are relative to the intended landing point, what the remaining engine is doing, rotor RPM status, and what comes next in the approach sequence. Two specific ways SA can be lost: (1) Fixation — the pilot focuses entirely on the inoperative engine instruments or an emergency checklist while losing track of aircraft altitude, airspeed, and glide path; (2) Task saturation — so many simultaneous demands (ATC calls, engine-out checklists, passenger communication, power management) overwhelm the pilot's mental capacity, causing critical cues such as decaying rotor RPM or a high sink rate to go unnoticed.

questions.question: What is spatial disorientation, and under what OEI approach conditions is a helicopter pilot most vulnerable to it?
questions.answer: Spatial disorientation is the inability to correctly perceive the aircraft's attitude, position, or motion relative to the earth, typically caused by reliance on false sensory cues when visual references are degraded. During an OEI approach, vulnerability is highest when: (1) the approach is conducted at night or in reduced visibility/IMC, where outside visual references are limited; (2) the pilot is task-saturated managing the failed engine, which forces increased reliance on vestibular (inner ear) cues that are inherently unreliable; and (3) an asymmetric power condition may produce unusual torque and vibration sensations that further confuse the pilot's perception of attitude. The combination of high workload and reduced visual cues creates an ideal environment for the leans or graveyard spiral.

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter on final approach when the left engine fails. ATC begins asking you a series of non-urgent questions about your intentions for taxi routing after landing. How do you manage this distraction without compromising safety?
questions.answer: Immediately apply the aviate-navigate-communicate hierarchy. The engine failure and the OEI approach demand 100% of available attention — ATC's taxi routing question is completely non-urgent and should be deferred. Transmit a brief, clear response: 'Unable, emergency, standby.' or declare an emergency with a single call — this shifts ATC from expecting dialogue to providing assistance. This also invokes emergency priority, which means ATC will not initiate further non-essential transmissions. Once stabilized on the OEI approach and workload permits, address ATC's questions. The FAA's SRM framework specifically identifies distraction management as a pilot responsibility — an 'error chain' often begins when a pilot allows secondary tasks to compete with primary aircraft control during a degraded flight condition.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3 (PIC authority); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM, error chain); 14 CFR 91.123

questions.question: During a simulated OEI approach training flight, your student becomes fixated on monitoring the 'failed' engine's gauges and allows airspeed to decay 15 knots below the target approach speed. As an instructor, what does this event illustrate about task prioritization, and what teaching point would you emphasize?
questions.answer: This scenario is a textbook example of fixation-induced task prioritization failure. The student correctly identified the inoperative engine as a concern but incorrectly elevated monitoring it above the higher-priority task of flying a stabilized approach. In an actual OEI approach, a failed engine cannot be restarted by staring at it — the primary threats are loss of rotor RPM, an unstable approach profile, and insufficient energy for the landing flare. The key teaching point is that gauges on a dead engine are informational, not actionable — the student should cross-check them once, confirm the failure, and redirect attention to airspeed, altitude, rotor RPM, and glide path. This also illustrates the 'error chain' concept: fixation led to airspeed decay, which could progress to rotor RPM loss and loss of control. Breaking the chain early — by expanding scan — is the correct intervention.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, error chain, SRM); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: You are conducting an OEI approach to a confined area at night with a passenger who is becoming increasingly vocal and agitated about the emergency. How does this scenario combine multiple risk factors from the ACS element of distractions, task prioritization, loss of SA, and disorientation — and what actions mitigate each?
questions.answer: This scenario stacks all four risk factors simultaneously: (1) Distraction — the agitated passenger creates an auditory and emotional distraction pulling pilot attention away from flight instruments and approach profile. Mitigation: Firmly but briefly tell the passenger to remain quiet and keep their seatbelt on; do not engage in extended conversation. (2) Task prioritization failure — the pilot may feel compelled to reassure the passenger, which is a lower-priority task than flying the approach. Mitigation: Strictly enforce aviate-navigate-communicate hierarchy; use automation (if available) to reduce workload. (3) Loss of situational awareness — night conditions reduce external visual cues, and passenger distraction compounds inattention to instrument cross-check, potentially allowing deviations in altitude or airspeed to go unnoticed. Mitigation: Maintain rigorous instrument scan; use any available moving map or GPS for position awareness. (4) Spatial disorientation — night flight with degraded outside references and high mental workload increases reliance on vestibular cues. Mitigation: Trust flight instruments exclusively; do not chase perceived sensations. Together, these mitigations break multiple links in the error chain before they compound.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (SRM, ADM, error chain); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: The FAA handbook states that the word 'probably' should be avoided in aeronautical decision-making — if something will only 'probably' work out, choose an option you know will work. How does this principle apply specifically to the decision-making a pilot faces when managing distractions during an OEI approach, and can you give a concrete example where ignoring this principle leads to an accident scenario?
questions.answer: The 'probably' principle means pilots should not rely on hoped-for outcomes when a definitive safe option exists. Applied to OEI approach distraction management: a pilot who thinks 'I can probably handle this ATC frequency change, update the FMS, and keep the approach stable simultaneously' is gambling on a positive outcome with no certainty. The correct application is to choose the option known to work — defer the FMS update, defer the frequency change, and maintain approach stability. Concrete accident scenario: A twin-engine helicopter crew on an OEI approach to an offshore platform is distracted by an ACAS/TCAS advisory and a simultaneous ATC frequency change request. The PF thinks they can probably maintain the approach profile while the PM handles both distractions. The PF's scan collapses — rotor RPM decays unnoticed as the remaining engine approaches its OEI power limit. By the time the PM recognizes the rotor RPM decay and calls it out, the helicopter is too low and slow to recover. The accident chain started with the PF's 'probably' decision — the correct choice was to immediately announce 'my controls, stop all distractions, declare emergency, stabilize approach first.' This mirrors real-world CFIT and controlled-flight-into-terrain accident profiles documented in NTSB reports where crew distraction during a degraded power state preceded impact.
questions.follow_up: After an OEI approach and landing, during the debrief, your co-pilot argues that handling the ATC frequency change mid-approach was the right call because 'it worked out fine.' How do you respond, and what ADM concept does their reasoning violate?
questions.follow_up_answer: This reasoning is outcome bias — evaluating the quality of a decision based on its result rather than on the quality of the decision-making process at the time it was made. The fact that it 'worked out' does not mean it was a sound decision; it means the crew got lucky. This is exactly the reasoning pattern the FAA handbook's 'probably' principle is designed to counter. A good decision is one that would be correct to repeat in the same circumstances — if handling a non-urgent ATC frequency change while managing an OEI approach creates unnecessary risk and adds workload at the most critical phase of flight, it was a poor decision regardless of outcome. I would use this debrief to reinforce that the standard is not 'did it work' but 'was it the safest available choice given what we knew at the time,' and I would require a re-fly of the scenario with the distraction injected again to demonstrate the correct prioritization response.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (Trescott Tip/'probably' principle; ADM; outcome bias); NTSB accident data (CFIT/distraction correlation)

questions.question: During an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, what does the term 'OEI limits' refer to, and where do you find them?
questions.answer: OEI limits are the maximum power, torque, turbine outlet temperature (TOT), and rotor RPM values that the operating engine is certified to produce continuously or for a specified time duration with one engine inoperative. These limits are found in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for the specific helicopter model, typically in the limitations section. OEI ratings are often broken into time-limited categories such as 2-minute OEI, 30-minute OEI, and continuous OEI, each with its own maximum torque and temperature values.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 27 or 29 (type certification basis); RFM Limitations Section

questions.question: What are the two most commonly monitored engine parameters a pilot must watch to ensure the operating engine stays within OEI limits during an approach?
questions.answer: The two most commonly monitored parameters are torque (expressed as a percentage or foot-pounds) and turbine outlet temperature (TOT) or turbine gas temperature (TGT), depending on the aircraft. These are the primary indicators of engine loading. Exceeding torque limits can cause gearbox or drivetrain damage, while exceeding temperature limits can cause turbine blade damage or engine failure. Rotor RPM (Nr) must also be monitored to prevent rotor droop or overspeed. Specific limits and their associated time durations are found in the RFM.

questions.question: What is the difference between a 2-minute OEI power rating and a continuous OEI power rating on a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: A 2-minute OEI rating is the maximum power the operating engine is certified to produce for up to 2 minutes following an engine failure — it is the highest OEI rating and is intended for use during the critical phase immediately after failure, such as preventing a crash or completing a maneuver. Continuous OEI is a lower power setting the engine can sustain indefinitely. Using the 2-minute rating beyond its time limit risks engine damage or failure. Pilots must transition to a lower power setting — typically 30-minute OEI — as soon as the situation permits. These ratings and time limits are specified in the RFM.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 29.1 (transport category certification); RFM Limitations Section; FAA-H-8083-21B

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter on an OEI approach to a confined area. During the approach, you notice the torque on the operating engine is creeping toward the 30-minute OEI limit but has not yet exceeded it. The landing zone is 200 feet ahead. What is your decision-making process?
questions.answer: First, assess whether you are within the time limit for the power rating being used. If torque is approaching but not exceeding the 30-minute OEI limit and you are 200 feet from touchdown, you should evaluate whether you can complete the landing before exceeding either the torque limit or the 30-minute time window. If the approach profile is stable and touchdown is imminent, it may be appropriate to continue. However, if there is any doubt — such as an unstabilized approach, excessive sink rate, or obstacle clearance concern — the correct decision is to execute a go-around using available OEI power, even if that means momentarily using the higher 2-minute OEI rating to arrest descent. After landing, record the exceedance data and report per the RFM. Risk management must prevail — do not sacrifice engine integrity to force a landing.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); RFM Limitations and Emergency Procedures

questions.question: During an OEI simulated approach at altitude, the examiner asks you to demonstrate how you would configure the helicopter to keep the operating engine within limits while maintaining a normal approach profile. Walk me through your power management technique.
questions.answer: To maintain the operating engine within OEI limits during an approach, I would: (1) Establish the OEI approach power setting per the RFM or Quick Reference Handbook, referencing the appropriate OEI chart for current density altitude, gross weight, and temperature. (2) Use smooth, coordinated collective inputs — abrupt collective pulls dramatically spike torque and TOT, risking a limit exceedance. (3) Monitor torque, TOT, and Nr continuously and cross-check with published OEI limits. (4) Fly the approach at the recommended OEI approach airspeed to minimize power demands while maintaining rotor RPM. (5) Plan the approach to require minimal power additions — a slightly steeper approach to a normal glide path may help avoid power surprises near the ground. (6) If any parameter approaches limits, either adjust the approach profile or execute a go-around before exceeding limits.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (approaches) and Chapter 11 (emergencies); RFM Normal and Emergency Procedures

questions.question: On a hot, high-density altitude day, you are practicing OEI approaches in a twin-engine helicopter. What specific challenge does high density altitude create for keeping the operating engine within OEI limits, and how do you compensate?
questions.answer: At high density altitude, the air is less dense, meaning the engine must work harder to produce the same amount of lift — the operating engine is under greater load and will reach OEI torque and temperature limits at a lower collective position than at sea level on a standard day. This significantly reduces the power margin available. To compensate: (1) Consult the OEI performance charts in the RFM to determine available OEI hover and climb performance for current conditions — you may find that a normal OEI approach and landing is not feasible. (2) Use a lower approach profile or choose a landing area that minimizes power requirements. (3) Accept a higher rate of descent on short final rather than pulling collective and risking a limit exceedance. (4) Consider a run-on landing to reduce hover power demands. (5) If OEI performance charts indicate insufficient power to safely complete the approach, the appropriate action is to land immediately on the best available surface or fly to a lower elevation. Per 14 CFR 91.3, the pilot-in-command is ultimately responsible for ensuring the aircraft is not operated beyond its mechanical limits, and no ACS tolerance supersedes aircraft limitations.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; RFM OEI Performance Charts; FAA-H-8083-25B Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (density altitude)

questions.question: During an OEI approach to a rooftop helipad, you inadvertently exceed the 2-minute OEI torque limit by 3% for approximately 15 seconds before catching it and reducing power. You complete the landing without further incident. What are your obligations after landing, and what is the consequence of not addressing this exceedance?
questions.answer: A torque exceedance — even a brief one — is a reportable event per the RFM and the engine manufacturer's maintenance manual. After landing, I am obligated to: (1) Record the exceedance in the aircraft maintenance logbook, including the parameter exceeded, the amount of exceedance, and the duration. (2) Notify the operator and maintenance personnel — the aircraft should be removed from service pending an engine inspection in accordance with the engine manufacturer's maintenance instructions. In many cases, even minor exceedances require a borescope inspection of the turbine section and gearbox. (3) Depending on the operator's SMS or maintenance program, file an internal safety report. Failing to report the exceedance constitutes operating an aircraft that may not be in an airworthy condition, which violates 14 CFR 91.7. It also creates liability for the pilot and can result in certificate action if the exceedance leads to an engine failure that injures someone and the unreported event is later discovered.
questions.follow_up: What if the exceedance occurred during a Part 135 revenue flight — does that change your reporting obligations?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes. Under Part 135, the pilot-in-command has additional obligations. Per 14 CFR 135.65, the PIC must make entries in the aircraft maintenance records for any mechanical irregularity or malfunction. Additionally, the certificate holder's General Operations Manual (GOM) and maintenance program will specify exceedance reporting procedures and required maintenance actions before return to service. If the exceedance caused or could have caused a mechanical malfunction, it may also need to be reported under 14 CFR Part 135's mechanical reliability reporting requirements. The operator must ensure the aircraft is returned to an airworthy condition before the next revenue flight — the PIC cannot simply defer the discrepancy.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7 (airworthiness); 14 CFR 135.65 (maintenance record entries); RFM Limitations and Abnormal Procedures; Engine Manufacturer's Maintenance Manual

questions.question: You are flying an OEI approach in a twin-engine helicopter and notice that as you reduce collective on final, the rotor RPM begins to climb above the upper limit while the operating engine is still within torque limits. What is happening aerodynamically, and how do you correct it without causing a different limit exceedance?
questions.answer: With one engine failed, the operating engine is driving the rotor through the transmission. If collective is reduced on final — as would happen in a normal approach — the rotor blade pitch decreases, reducing the load on the rotor system. With less drag on the rotor and the operating engine still contributing power, rotor RPM can overspeed. To correct this without over-torquing the operating engine: (1) Apply a small amount of collective to increase blade pitch and load the rotor — this will reduce Nr. However, adding collective increases the demand on the operating engine, so the torque must be monitored closely to avoid exceeding OEI limits. (2) The correction must be gradual — a rapid collective pull will spike torque and TOT simultaneously. (3) The underlying technique is to pre-plan the approach so that the power setting remains relatively stable, avoiding the need for large collective reductions that create this Nr overspeed scenario. This is why OEI approaches use a specific airspeed and approach angle designed to keep power demands in a manageable, stable range throughout the maneuver.
questions.follow_up: If you simultaneously have Nr approaching the upper limit AND torque approaching the OEI limit, what is your priority and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: Nr overspeed is the immediate priority because rotor overspeed can cause structural damage to the rotor system, blade separation, or transmission failure — consequences that are immediate and potentially catastrophic. Torque exceedances, while serious, typically have a slightly longer failure timeline and may allow time for correction. The correct technique is to reduce collective slightly to bring Nr down, accepting a brief moment closer to torque limits if necessary, while simultaneously adjusting the approach to reduce overall power demand — such as increasing airspeed slightly to reduce the angle of attack, or steepening the approach to reduce power requirements. The goal is to find a stable configuration that keeps both parameters within limits simultaneously. If that is not achievable in the current approach profile, a go-around is mandatory.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Helicopter Emergencies); RFM Limitations Section; 14 CFR Part 27/29 rotor system certification standards

questions.question: Before you begin the final approach segment on an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, what are the ACS tolerances you must maintain for altitude, airspeed, and heading?
questions.answer: The ACS requires you to maintain altitude within ±100 feet, airspeed within ±10 knots, and heading within ±5° of the recommended flight profile prior to beginning the final approach segment. You must also maintain the assigned or required track.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-17 Commercial Pilot for Helicopter ACS, Area X, Task C; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: Why is it critical to stabilize your altitude, airspeed, and heading BEFORE reaching the final approach segment fix during an OEI approach, rather than correcting on the way down?
questions.answer: During an OEI approach, the helicopter is already operating at reduced power margin with one engine inoperative. If you are chasing deviations on the final approach segment, you are simultaneously managing high workload, degraded performance, and precise flight path control. Becoming stabilized before the final approach segment gives you a known, controlled energy state so that any adjustments on final are small and manageable rather than large corrections that could destabilize the approach or exceed the operating engine's limits.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-S-ACS-17 Area X Task C

questions.question: What is the 'recommended flight profile' referenced in the OEI approach task, and where do you find that information for your specific helicopter?
questions.answer: The recommended flight profile for an OEI approach refers to the manufacturer-specified airspeed, altitude, and configuration profile for conducting an approach with one engine inoperative. This information is found in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) or Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) for the specific helicopter being flown — typically in the emergency procedures section or OEI operating procedures. It may specify items such as Vy, approach airspeed, single-engine service ceiling, and torque limits on the operating engine.

questions.question: You're flying a twin-engine helicopter conducting a simulated OEI instrument approach. On the downwind leg, you notice your airspeed is 12 knots above the recommended profile speed and you're 120 feet above the desired altitude. You're 3 miles from the final approach fix. What actions do you take, and what's the priority order?
questions.answer: With 3 miles to the FAF, you have adequate time to correct before the final approach segment — this is exactly when corrections should be made. Priority order: First, reduce collective slightly to address both the excess altitude and excess airspeed simultaneously, since lowering collective reduces both lift and drag-induced power, allowing the helicopter to descend and decelerate. Use cyclic to maintain the desired attitude as you reduce collective. Monitor the operating engine torque carefully since any collective change directly affects torque on the operating engine. Re-trim with pedals as power changes affect torque. Aim to be within ±100 feet and ±10 knots before reaching the FAF. Avoid large, abrupt inputs that could cause torque spikes on the operating engine or destabilize the helicopter.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (flight control coordination), Chapter 11 (OEI procedures); FAA-S-ACS-17 Area X Task C

questions.question: During a simulated OEI approach, you are maintaining the recommended profile airspeed and altitude, but your heading is 7° left of centerline and the localizer needle is beginning to deflect. You are 1 mile from the final approach fix. Describe how you correct heading while not busting the other tolerances.
questions.answer: A 7° heading deviation exceeds the ±5° ACS tolerance and must be corrected before the FAF. Apply a shallow bank cyclic input toward the right to turn back onto the assigned heading. In a twin helicopter with OEI, be cautious about the amount of bank because increasing bank angle increases the load factor and thus induced drag, which demands more power from the single operating engine. Use a coordinated turn with appropriate pedal input to prevent slip or skid. As you turn, monitor altitude — do not allow the turn to bleed altitude beyond the ±100 foot tolerance. Return to wings-level when approaching the correct heading, not when on it, to prevent overshooting. Simultaneously cross-check the localizer needle to ensure the track is being regained. If you cannot achieve stabilization before the FAF, a go-around/missed approach should be considered.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 (turns, coordination); FAA-S-ACS-17 Area X Task C; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 4

questions.question: On a hot, high-density altitude day, you are practicing OEI approaches in a twin-engine helicopter. What specific challenge does high density altitude create for keeping the operating engine within OEI limits, and how do you compensate?
questions.answer: At high density altitude, the air is less dense, meaning the engine must work harder to produce the same amount of lift — the operating engine is under greater load and will reach OEI torque and temperature limits at a lower collective position than at sea level on a standard day. This significantly reduces the power margin available. To compensate: (1) Consult the OEI performance charts in the RFM to determine available OEI hover and climb performance for current conditions — you may find that a normal OEI approach and landing is not feasible. (2) Use a lower approach profile or choose a landing area that minimizes power requirements. (3) Accept a higher rate of descent on short final rather than pulling collective and risking a limit exceedance. (4) Consider a run-on landing to reduce hover power demands. (5) If OEI performance charts indicate insufficient power to safely complete the approach, the appropriate action is to land immediately on the best available surface or fly to a lower elevation. Per 14 CFR 91.3, the pilot-in-command is ultimately responsible for ensuring the aircraft is not operated beyond its mechanical limits, and no ACS tolerance supersedes aircraft limitations.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (OEI operations, emergency procedures), Chapter 13 (ADM); 14 CFR 91.3 (pilot-in-command authority)

questions.question: A student on an OEI checkride consistently meets the ±100/±10/±5° tolerances in straight segments but allows deviations to accumulate at each turn in the pattern before correcting just prior to the FAF. Technically within tolerance at the FAF, but the pattern is ragged. As an examiner, would you be concerned, and why or why not?
questions.answer: To cancel the emergency, you transmit: '[ATC facility], [callsign], canceling MAYDAY, emergency is concluded, aircraft is airworthy, request normal ATC services.' ATC will acknowledge and may ask for a pilot report. Regulatory obligations: Under 14 CFR 91.3(c), if the FAA questions your emergency deviation from an FAR, you must submit a written report within 10 days upon request. Additionally, if the emergency resulted from an aircraft system failure that meets 49 CFR Part 830 reporting thresholds, you must report that to the NTSB. You are also encouraged to file a NASA ASRS report to document the event without punitive action. Failure to properly cancel the MAYDAY leaves emergency equipment on standby and may result in unnecessary resource expenditure.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant argues that they met the ACS tolerances at every required checkpoint, how do you respond as an examiner?
questions.follow_up_answer: The ACS tolerances define the minimum acceptable standard at critical measurement points, but the ACS also evaluates the overall quality and consistency of flight management. The word 'maintains' in the task description implies continuous control, not just snapshot compliance. FAA Order 8900.2 and examiner guidance make clear that the DPE evaluates not just whether standards are met at isolated checkpoints but whether the pilot demonstrates the skill, judgment, and discipline expected of a certificated pilot. A pilot who consistently recovers to standards at the last moment but flies a poor pattern in between does not demonstrate the level of proficiency the certificate demands — especially in an OEI emergency scenario where poor profile management could result in an accident before the FAF is even reached.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-17 Area X Task C; FAA Order 8900.2 (General Aviation Airman Designee Policy); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, SRM)

questions.question: During a simulated OEI approach in IMC conditions, you are exactly on profile — altitude, airspeed, and heading all within tolerance — but the 'simulated failed' engine's instruments show rising turbine temperature trending toward the red arc. The simulated failure is being conducted at flight idle, not actually failed. How does this scenario test your understanding of the OEI task, and what should you do?
questions.answer: This scenario highlights the distinction between a simulated OEI training exercise and a real emergency. In a simulation with the engine at flight idle, rising TIT/turbine temperature trending toward limits is abnormal and indicates a real aircraft malfunction developing, separate from the simulated failure. The correct action is to immediately abandon the simulation, restore the engine to normal operating power or shut it down per the emergency checklist as appropriate, and address the actual developing emergency. This is not a profile management question anymore — it is a priorities-of-flight question. Maintaining ACS tolerances is irrelevant when a real emergency is emerging. The skill being tested here is whether the pilot recognizes when a training scenario must be terminated because real aircraft safety is at risk. The examiner should also be alerted. This reflects the ADM principle: never let a training scenario prevent appropriate response to a real emergency.
questions.follow_up: Under what FAR authority can a pilot deviate from any clearance, procedure, or standard during an actual emergency, and does that apply in this scenario?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 91.3(b) states that in an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, the pilot-in-command may deviate from any rule to the extent necessary to meet the emergency. This absolutely applies to this scenario — if the aircraft is developing a real mechanical emergency, the PIC is authorized and obligated to deviate from the simulated OEI profile, ATC instructions, or any other procedure to the extent necessary to address the real emergency. After the emergency, the pilot must submit a written report to the ATC facility if a deviation from an ATC clearance occurred, upon request per 91.3(c).
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3 (PIC responsibility and authority in emergencies); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; FAA-S-ACS-17 Area X Task C

questions.question: When you declare an emergency on a simulated OEI approach during a checkride, what is the standard phraseology and which frequency do you use if you are not already in contact with ATC?
questions.answer: The standard phraseology is 'MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY' followed by your aircraft identification, nature of the emergency, position, altitude, intentions, and number of persons on board. If not already in contact with ATC, the universal emergency frequency is 121.5 MHz. In a real OEI situation, declaring an emergency gives you priority handling and obligates ATC to provide all possible assistance.

questions.question: During an OEI approach, at what point in the maneuver would you make your initial call to the tower or CTAF, and what minimum information must that call contain?
questions.answer: The initial call should be made as early as practical once the emergency or simulated OEI condition is recognized — ideally before beginning the approach. At minimum the call must include: aircraft identification, position relative to the airport or fix, altitude, nature of the emergency (engine failure), and your intentions (type of approach, which runway). This gives the facility time to clear traffic, position emergency equipment, and provide priority sequencing.

questions.question: What does the phrase 'souls on board' mean in the context of an OEI emergency radio call, and why is it required?
questions.answer: 'Souls on board' refers to the total number of people on the aircraft — both crew and passengers. It is reported during an emergency so that rescue and firefighting personnel know exactly how many individuals to account for during an accident or rescue response. This information is critical for search and rescue coordination if the aircraft goes down.

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter on an IFR flight plan at 4,500 feet MSL and experience an actual engine failure. You declare MAYDAY and ATC offers you the ILS to Runway 18 at the airport 12 miles ahead. Walk me through the sequence of radio calls you would make from the time of engine failure until you are on short final.
questions.answer: 1. Immediately after engine failure and completing time-critical checklist steps: 'MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, [callsign], engine failure, [position], [altitude], requesting immediate approach ILS Runway 18, [number] souls on board, [fuel remaining].' 2. When ATC clears you for the approach: readback the clearance fully — heading, altitude restrictions, approach clearance, and any frequency changes. 3. Switching to approach control if directed: re-state emergency status so the new controller is immediately aware. 4. On tower frequency: '[Callsign], [position] on ILS Runway 18, OEI, request emergency services standing by.' 5. Short final: standard position report confirming gear down (if applicable) and landing assured. Workload management is critical — aviate first, then navigate, then communicate.
questions.regulatory_ref: AIM 6-3-1; 14 CFR 91.183; Helicopter Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: You are practicing a simulated OEI approach at an uncontrolled airport using CTAF. Other traffic is in the pattern. How do you structure your radio calls to communicate urgency without causing unnecessary alarm to other pilots, and how does this differ from declaring a full MAYDAY?
questions.answer: On CTAF for a simulated OEI training scenario, you should make standard position calls but add clear, concise information: '[Airport] traffic, [callsign], simulated OEI approach, [position], [runway], request all traffic hold position or extend for priority.' You should NOT declare MAYDAY for a simulated emergency because it triggers real emergency responses including airport notifications and possible regulatory follow-up. If it were a real engine failure, you would declare MAYDAY and expect other traffic to yield. The key difference is that in training you communicate your intentions clearly for safety without activating emergency services. Situational awareness for both you and other traffic in the pattern is paramount.

questions.question: During an actual OEI approach, your workload is extremely high managing aircraft performance, checklists, and flying a stabilized approach. How do you prioritize your radio calls without compromising flight safety, and what is the correct ADM framework to apply?
questions.answer: The Aviate-Navigate-Communicate hierarchy applies directly: aircraft control and flying the approach come first. Radio calls, while important, are secondary to maintaining rotor RPM, airspeed at or above Vyse/VTOSS, and a stabilized approach path. Use the 'IMSAFE' and SRM framework — delegate communications to the other pilot if crew-assisted, use brief and precise calls rather than lengthy explanations, and batch communications during lower-workload windows (e.g., established on final rather than at the power failure point). The HFH notes that approximately 80% of accidents are caused by pilot error, often from poor workload prioritization. A partial or delayed radio call is always preferable to a botched approach due to distraction.

questions.question: You declared a MAYDAY for an OEI condition, landed safely, and the situation is resolved — the engine was restarted successfully and you confirm the aircraft is airworthy. What radio call do you make to cancel the emergency, and what are your regulatory obligations after the flight?
questions.answer: To cancel the emergency, you transmit: '[ATC facility], [callsign], canceling MAYDAY, emergency is concluded, aircraft is airworthy, request normal ATC services.' ATC will acknowledge and may ask for a pilot report. Regulatory obligations: Under 14 CFR 91.3(c), if the FAA questions your emergency deviation from an FAR, you must submit a written report within 10 days upon request. Additionally, if the emergency resulted from an aircraft system failure that meets 49 CFR Part 830 reporting thresholds, you must report that to the NTSB. You are also encouraged to file a NASA ASRS report to document the event without punitive action. Failure to properly cancel the MAYDAY leaves emergency equipment on standby and may result in unnecessary resource expenditure.
questions.follow_up: If an FAA inspector contacts you after the flight asking about the MAYDAY declaration, are you required to speak with them, and could your emergency declaration itself be used against you in an enforcement action?
questions.follow_up_answer: You are not legally required to make statements to an FAA inspector without counsel present. However, regarding the emergency declaration itself: under 14 CFR 91.3(b), a pilot in command may deviate from any rule to meet an emergency, and under 14 CFR 91.3(c), if deviation is questioned, the PIC shall send a written report to the FAA upon request. The FAA's general policy is that emergency declarations made in good faith are not used as a basis for certificate action — the FAA recognizes that pilots should not fear declaring emergencies. Filing a NASA ASRS report within 10 days provides additional protection from certificate action for unintentional FAR violations discovered during the event.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.183; 49 CFR Part 830; NASA ASRS Advisory Circular AC 00-46

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter IFR in IMC and experience an engine failure. ATC instructs you to 'squawk 7700 and ident.' You are in a high-workload phase of flight reconfiguring the aircraft for single-engine performance. What is the correct response to ATC's instruction, and how do you manage the competing demands of flying, checklist execution, and radio communication?
questions.answer: The correct immediate response is to squawk 7700 on the transponder — this is a single switch action that takes less than two seconds and immediately alerts all ATC facilities to your emergency. 'Ident' activates the identification feature which causes your return to blossom on radar. These actions should be accomplished as a paired action during a stable moment. Verbally acknowledge ATC with a brief: '[Callsign], 7700, ident.' Do not attempt a lengthy readback during a high-workload phase. Apply the SRM framework: if single pilot, batch the squawk change with any checklist item that requires hands on the avionics panel; aviate first, complete time-critical emergency checklist items, then communicate. The HFH emphasizes that the 'error chain' in accidents often includes task saturation leading to missed steps — deliberately pausing workload to make a structured radio call is preferable to a rushed incomplete call.
questions.follow_up: If squawking 7700 while in Class B airspace without an explicit ATC clearance to enter that airspace, are you in violation of 14 CFR 91.131?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. Under 14 CFR 91.3(b), a pilot in command may deviate from any FAR to the extent necessary to meet an emergency. This explicitly includes deviating from Class B airspace entry requirements. The squawk 7700 itself signals to ATC that an emergency exists, and controllers are trained to immediately provide separation and assistance. You are protected from enforcement action for the airspace deviation as long as it was necessitated by the emergency. Upon request, you must submit a written report to the FAA administrator describing the deviation under 14 CFR 91.3(c).

questions.question: When planning a flightpath to your selected landing area following an OEI situation in a multiengine helicopter, what four primary factors must you account for?
questions.answer: You must account for altitude (how much energy margin you have to maneuver), wind (direction and speed affect your approach path and landing rollout/hover), terrain (high ground or rising terrain that could cut off your approach), and obstructions (wires, trees, structures along or near the intended flightpath). These four factors work together to determine whether your planned path to the landing area is achievable with the performance available from the remaining engine.

questions.question: Why is wind direction particularly important when selecting and planning your flightpath to a landing area during a simulated OEI approach?
questions.answer: Wind direction is critical for two reasons. First, landing into the wind reduces your groundspeed at touchdown, shortening the landing distance and reducing the load on the remaining engine during deceleration to land. Second, a headwind improves your single-engine climb performance and extends glide/power margin, giving you more options during the approach. A tailwind approach degrades performance significantly and may exceed the remaining engine's capability, especially at higher weights or density altitudes.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Chapter 9 Basic Flight Maneuvers

questions.question: What does 'following a flightpath' to the selected landing area mean in practice during an OEI approach, as opposed to simply 'selecting' the landing area?
questions.answer: Selecting the landing area is the decision of where to land. Following a flightpath means actively managing the helicopter's position, altitude, and energy throughout the approach so you actually arrive at the landing area in a condition to complete the landing safely. This includes making course corrections, adjusting power on the remaining engine as needed, managing airspeed for best single-engine performance, and continuously reassessing whether the selected area remains achievable. If the path becomes unachievable, you must be prepared to go around or select an alternate area.

questions.question: You're flying a twin-engine helicopter at 3,000 feet AGL when you simulate an OEI failure. You identify a large open field 2 miles ahead, but there is a ridgeline between you and the field that tops out 500 feet below your current altitude. How do you plan your flightpath to that field while accounting for terrain and your single-engine performance?
questions.answer: First, immediately assess whether the remaining engine can maintain altitude or at minimum achieve a controlled descent rate that allows you to clear the ridgeline with margin. Check your single-engine performance charts or know your OEI ceiling for current weight and density altitude. If you have at least 300–500 feet of margin over the ridgeline with comfortable power settings, plan a direct or slightly offset path to cross the ridge with adequate clearance before beginning your final descent to the field. If single-engine performance is marginal for the ridge crossing, you must either select an alternate landing area on the near side of the ridge or fly around the terrain. Never commit to terrain you are not certain you can clear — terrain is unforgiving and the error chain compounds quickly in an emergency.

questions.question: During a simulated OEI approach to a confined area, you planned your flightpath and are established on final. You realize you are arriving high and fast with significant obstructions (tall trees) on the approach end. What are your options and how do you decide between them?
questions.answer: You have three main options: (1) Execute a go-around using the remaining engine if single-engine go-around performance is available — this is the safest option if power margin exists. (2) Modify your approach angle by adjusting airspeed and power to steepen the descent, but only if you can do so without risking dynamic rollover or LTE on the remaining engine. (3) Select an alternate landing area that does not require clearing the obstructions. The key decision factor is whether the remaining engine can support a go-around at your current weight and density altitude. Never continue an unstabilized approach into a confined area under OEI conditions hoping it will work out — that is exactly the kind of 'probably' thinking that leads to accidents. If in doubt, go around or choose an alternate.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 ADM; ACS CH.X.C

questions.question: You are simulating an OEI scenario at 1,500 feet AGL over flat terrain with a 15-knot crosswind. You've selected a suitable landing pad to your right. Describe how wind affects the flightpath you plan to that pad compared to a calm-wind scenario.
questions.answer: With a 15-knot crosswind, you must compensate with a crab angle or slip throughout the approach to maintain the desired track to the pad, which increases pilot workload on the remaining engine's controls. More importantly, you should plan the approach so you arrive aligned into the wind or at worst on a crosswind leg rather than downwind, to benefit from headwind performance. If a direct path to the pad means landing with a tailwind, a better plan is to offset your path — fly past the pad, turn into the wind, and conduct the final approach with the headwind component. This improves single-engine climb performance on the go-around option and reduces touchdown groundspeed. In calm wind, the direct path is usually optimal. Always factor that a crosswind increases the complexity of pedal management on the single operating engine during the landing flare.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9 and Chapter 11; ACS CH.X.C

questions.question: During a simulated OEI approach, you follow your planned flightpath, but at 200 feet AGL on final you encounter a power line crossing the approach path that you did not identify during your initial planning. How does this scenario reflect on your original flightpath planning, and what immediate action do you take?
questions.answer: This scenario reveals a failure in the obstruction survey phase of flightpath planning — power lines are notoriously difficult to see, especially at altitude, and must be actively sought out by looking for their support poles and expecting wires between them rather than looking for the wires themselves. At 200 feet AGL on final OEI, your immediate options are: if you have sufficient single-engine climb performance, execute a go-around immediately. If go-around performance is insufficient or the wires are too close to avoid by climbing, you may need to maneuver laterally to a gap in the wire span if one exists, or accept a forced landing short of the wires in the best available area. This situation illustrates exactly why the 'follow a flightpath' standard demands continuous re-evaluation — obstruction identification must happen throughout the approach, not just at planning. Fixation on the landing spot is a known error chain that leads to wire strikes. (Reference: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR Part 91; ACS CH.X.C)
questions.follow_up: If you successfully complete the go-around from 200 feet AGL with one engine inoperative, what performance data do you need to know before attempting another approach, and where do you find it?
questions.follow_up_answer: You need to know your OEI hover ceiling (out-of-ground-effect and in-ground-effect), OEI climb rate at your current weight and density altitude, and whether your helicopter is certified for Category A or Category B operations. For Category A, the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) contains specific OEI takeoff and landing profiles with climb gradients. For Category B, performance is less precisely defined. You find this data in the aircraft's FAA-approved Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM), specifically the performance section for OEI operations. Without knowing this data, you cannot reliably plan whether a second approach is safe or whether you need to fly to a more suitable landing area with better obstruction clearance.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR Part 29; ACS CH.X.C

questions.question: A student tells you: 'When I simulate OEI, I always just pick the biggest open field I can see and fly straight to it.' What is wrong with this flightpath planning philosophy, even if the field is large and clear?
questions.answer: Flying straight to the nearest large field ignores three of the four critical planning factors. First, altitude — a straight-line path may place you too high or too low on final, creating an energy management problem. Second, wind — a straight shot may result in a downwind or crosswind approach that degrades single-engine performance and increases landing distance. Third, terrain and obstructions — a straight-line path may cross terrain that is marginal with OEI climb performance, or pass over unseen obstructions. Effective OEI flightpath planning requires selecting an approach path that arrives at the field from a direction that is into the wind, clear of terrain and obstructions, and at an energy state that allows a controlled touchdown. A large field gives you margin in landing area, but poor path planning can still result in a high-speed, downwind landing with terrain exposure. ADM and SRM principles require systematic evaluation, not the first instinct answer.
questions.follow_up: If the straight-line path to that large field happens to pass over a populated residential area, does that change your flightpath decision even if all other factors are acceptable?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, it absolutely should. While there is no regulation that explicitly prohibits overflying residential areas at low altitude during an OEI emergency if the pilot in command determines it is necessary for safety under 14 CFR 91.3 (pilot-in-command authority and responsibility), good ADM and airmanship demand that you avoid routes that unnecessarily expose persons on the ground to risk if an alternative is available. If an alternate approach path to the same field or a comparable alternate landing area avoids the residential area without significantly compromising safety, that path should be chosen. In a true emergency, 91.3 gives PIC authority to deviate from regulations as necessary, but this authority does not remove the obligation to exercise sound judgment and minimize risk to others consistent with flight safety.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 ADM; ACS CH.X.C

questions.question: During a simulated OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter, when should you complete the engine failure checklist — before or after you have established a stabilized approach?
questions.answer: The priority sequence is: aviate first, then navigate, then complete checklists. Immediate memory items (such as maintaining rotor RPM and airspeed) are accomplished first. Once the helicopter is stabilized and the situation is under control, you complete the appropriate emergency checklist from the POH/RFM. Completing a checklist while the helicopter is not yet stabilized divides critical attention at the worst possible moment.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable POH/RFM emergency procedures

questions.question: What is the difference between a 'memory item' and a checklist item in the context of an OEI emergency in a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: Memory items are immediate action steps that must be performed from memory without reference to a checklist because any delay could be dangerous or fatal — for example, maintaining rotor RPM and airspeed following engine failure. Checklist items are subsequent steps that are verified by reading the printed checklist after the immediate threat is controlled. The POH/RFM designates which steps are memory items and which require checklist confirmation.

questions.question: After identifying a failed engine and completing the immediate memory items during an OEI approach, which checklist would you typically reference next according to standard multiengine helicopter procedures?
questions.answer: After immediate memory items are complete, you would reference the 'Engine Failure in Flight' or 'OEI Operations' checklist in the POH/RFM. This typically covers securing the failed engine (confirming fuel control position, ignition, engine bleed air if applicable), monitoring the operating engine parameters, and configuring the aircraft for a single-engine approach and landing. The exact title and sequence vary by aircraft model, so you must use the specific POH/RFM for the helicopter being flown.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable POH/RFM emergency and abnormal checklists

questions.question: You are flying an OEI approach to a confined area with a 12-knot crosswind from the left. As you transition through translational lift on short final, the helicopter suddenly yaws and the nose dips. Walk me through what just happened and how you correct it while maintaining your approach path.
questions.answer: As you transition through translational lift (ETL), two aerodynamic effects combine: (1) Loss of translational lift reduces tail rotor effectiveness as airspeed decays; (2) the asymmetric power condition from the single operating engine creates inherent torque imbalance. Together, these cause the nose to yaw left (in a counterclockwise rotor system). Simultaneously, reduced rotor efficiency and ETL loss can cause uncommanded settling. Corrective actions: (1) Apply right pedal promptly to counter the yaw and maintain heading — this is the primary control to fight the OEI torque imbalance as airspeed decreases through ETL. (2) Apply collective as needed to arrest settling while staying within the operative engine's power margin. (3) Maintain left cyclic to correct for the left crosswind and prevent rightward drift. (4) Use aft cyclic to control deceleration and avoid an excessively nose-low attitude. This phase requires the most active and coordinated control input in the OEI approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable POH/RFM; CRM/SRM principles

questions.question: You are conducting a simulated OEI approach solo in a multiengine helicopter. At what point in the approach profile is it safest to physically reference and work through the printed checklist, and how do you manage workload to accomplish this without compromising aircraft control?
questions.answer: The safest time to reference the printed checklist is after the immediate memory items are complete and the helicopter is stabilized in the approach — ideally at a point where altitude, airspeed, and power are set and you have a brief period of lower workload before the final approach fix or decision point. Workload management techniques include: trimming the aircraft to reduce control inputs, using automation if available (autopilot/SAS), pausing checklist reading at high-workload moments (such as turns or power adjustments), and using checklists in a 'challenge-response' format. Never attempt to complete checklist steps simultaneously with high-workload control tasks.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); applicable POH/RFM

questions.question: During an OEI approach, you complete the engine failure checklist and begin the landing checklist. On short final, you realize you skipped the 'Landing Gear — DOWN AND LOCKED' item on the landing checklist. What is the correct action, and what does this situation illustrate about checklist discipline?
questions.answer: Immediately confirm the landing gear position — visually verify the indicator lights and physically confirm gear is down and locked before touchdown. If not confirmed, go around if altitude and single-engine performance permit, or if already committed to landing, complete the gear extension and verify before touchdown. This situation illustrates why checklists must be completed methodically and not rushed — high stress and increased workload during OEI operations create conditions where critical steps are easily skipped. The 'read and do' or 'do and verify' method prevents such omissions. Rushing a checklist is as dangerous as not completing it at all.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable POH/RFM landing checklist

questions.question: You are on an OEI approach and your examiner asks you to verbalize your checklist usage. You complete the engine failure checklist correctly, but when you reach the approach checklist, you skip several items because you are 'already configured.' The examiner stops you. What fundamental flaw does this demonstrate, and how does it relate to accident causation in helicopter operations?
questions.answer: Skipping checklist items because you believe the aircraft is 'already configured' defeats the entire purpose of a checklist — which is to verify, not to remember. This is a classic example of complacency and task truncation. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that approximately 80% of aviation accidents are linked to human factors, and complacency-driven omissions are a well-documented contributing cause. The 'error chain' concept is directly relevant: assuming a step is done without verifying it is a single link that, combined with other small errors (distraction, workload, abnormal situation), can lead to an accident. Checklists must be completed in full on every flight, regardless of perceived redundancy, because conditions may have changed and assumptions are not verifications.
questions.follow_up: If completing the full checklist on short final creates an unsafe distraction, what is the correct solution — skip items or do something else?
questions.follow_up_answer: The correct solution is to adjust when the checklist is completed, not to skip items. The 'below 1,000 feet' sterile cockpit concept applies — complex checklist activity should be completed before reaching the critical phase of flight. If the checklist cannot be completed safely before short final, the pilot should consider going around to a higher altitude, stabilizing the aircraft, completing the checklist, and then commencing another approach. The checklist must never be abbreviated or skipped; the timing of completion is what should be adjusted.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); applicable POH/RFM

questions.question: During an OEI approach checkride, after completing all checklists correctly, you touch down and the examiner asks: 'What checklist do you complete after landing with one engine inoperative, and why does its sequence matter?' Walk me through your answer.
questions.answer: After an OEI landing, you complete the 'Engine Shutdown' or 'Post-Landing OEI' checklist as specified in the POH/RFM. Sequence matters critically because improperly securing a failed or shutdown engine — for example, leaving a fuel control in the wrong position, failing to close fuel shutoffs, or leaving ignition on — can create fire, fuel leak, or inadvertent restart hazards on the ground. Additionally, the operating engine must be properly monitored and shut down per normal procedures after clearing the landing area. Post-landing checklists also address rotor brake application timing, hydraulic system status, and documenting the engine event for maintenance. Rushing or reversing the order of these steps can convert a successful emergency landing into a post-landing incident.
questions.follow_up: If a fire warning activates on the failed engine just after touchdown during your OEI landing, do you continue with the post-landing OEI checklist or switch to a different checklist?
questions.follow_up_answer: You immediately transition to the 'Engine Fire on the Ground' or 'Post-Crash Fire' checklist — whichever is applicable per the POH/RFM — and execute those memory items first (which typically include shutting off fuel, activating fire suppression if equipped, and evacuating if the fire cannot be controlled). The post-landing OEI checklist is superseded by the more immediate threat. This illustrates the principle that checklists are hierarchical: a new, higher-priority emergency always takes precedence over a lower-priority procedure already in progress.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable POH/RFM post-landing and emergency checklists

questions.question: During an OEI approach in a multiengine helicopter with a counterclockwise main rotor, which pedal input is typically required to maintain directional control as you reduce power on final, and why?
