Each item affects either the damping of blade movement or the natural frequency of the fuselage-ground interface — the two factors that must align for resonance to develop.

questions.question: You are hovering taxi-ing across an uneven ramp and transition onto a patch of soft asphalt on a hot day. The helicopter begins to rock side to side with increasing amplitude. What is happening aerodynamically and mechanically, and what do you do?
questions.answer: What is happening: The soft asphalt is acting like an under-inflated surface, changing the effective stiffness of the landing gear-ground interface. As the skids or wheels sink unevenly into the soft surface, the helicopter's oscillation frequency shifts and may couple with the rotational frequency of any blade imbalance in the lead-lag plane. This creates the feedback loop that defines ground resonance — the fuselage rocks, which further disturbs blade spacing, which increases the imbalance force, which amplifies rocking. The increasing amplitude confirms resonance is developing rather than a one-time bump. My immediate action: Since I am in a hover taxi, rotor RPM should be in the normal range and I have collective in. I immediately apply collective to fly off the surface and transition to a stable hover over a firm area. Once airborne even a few feet, the resonance stops because the fuselage oscillation is no longer sustained by ground contact. I then land on a firm, level surface and have the rotor system and dampers inspected before further flight, because resonance onset can indicate a damper problem even if the episode is brief.

questions.question: A student tells you that during ground resonance, you should apply opposite cyclic to counteract the rocking motion, just like correcting a dynamic rollover. How do you correct this misconception, and what makes ground resonance fundamentally different from dynamic rollover in terms of pilot control response?
questions.answer: This is a dangerous misconception and I would correct it firmly. In dynamic rollover, the helicopter is rotating about a fixed pivot point — typically a caught skid — and cyclic input opposite to the roll direction applies a corrective moment that can arrest the rotation before it reaches the critical rollover angle. The pilot has meaningful control authority and time to apply a correction. Ground resonance is categorically different. The oscillation is a resonant mechanical phenomenon — a positive feedback loop between rotor imbalance and fuselage movement. Applying cyclic to counteract the rocking does nothing to address the source of the problem, which is the blade lead-lag imbalance. Worse, cyclic inputs during active resonance can couple with the oscillation and actually amplify it by changing the rotor disk orientation in a way that reinforces the imbalance. The only correct pilot responses are to remove one of the two required conditions: either fly off (remove ground contact) or shut down rapidly (remove rotor energy). Cyclic is not a tool for managing ground resonance — the pilot's only decision is which of those two actions is safer given the current RPM state.
questions.follow_up: What happens to the helicopter structurally if ground resonance is not corrected within the first few seconds, and why does it escalate so rapidly?
questions.follow_up_answer: Ground resonance is an exponentially growing oscillation — the amplitude does not increase linearly but accelerates. Each oscillation cycle reinforces and amplifies the next because the energy input from the rotor imbalance exceeds the damping capacity of the airframe and landing gear. Within seconds, the lateral G-forces on the fuselage can exceed structural design limits. The main rotor mast — which is not designed to absorb large lateral cyclic loads at the frequency of ground resonance — can flex, crack, or fail. If the mast fails or the rotor disk contacts the fuselage (rotor blade strike), the helicopter is destroyed. This is why every training resource emphasizes that the corrective decision must be instantaneous — there is no time to troubleshoot, analyze, or try intermediate measures. The physics of resonance mean that hesitation of even two to three seconds can move the oscillation beyond the point where shutdown will prevent structural damage.

questions.question: You are flying a fully articulated rotor helicopter and you experience what feels like ground resonance during a running landing on a firm surface with properly serviced landing gear and normal tire pressure. All maintenance is current. What are the possible explanations, and what is your post-incident responsibility?
questions.answer: If ground resonance occurs on a properly maintained helicopter with a firm surface, the most likely explanations are: (1) A failed or degraded lead-lag damper that was not detected during preflight — dampers can fail internally without visible external leaks, and their effectiveness degrades gradually. (2) An asymmetric landing that placed abnormal lateral load on one side of the gear momentarily, altering the effective contact stiffness enough to briefly couple with rotor imbalance — possible but less likely on firm level ground. (3) An undetected rotor track and balance issue that created lead-lag imbalance — the blades may be tracking normally visually but have a dynamic imbalance condition. (4) A landing gear component failure that occurred during the landing itself — cracked cross tube, failed oleo seal, or bearing failure. Post-incident responsibilities: Under 14 CFR 91.7, I am responsible for airworthiness, so the aircraft must be grounded until inspected by a certificated A&P mechanic. I should document the incident in the aircraft logbook and report the symptoms accurately. If the helicopter is operated under Part 135 or under an operator certificate, additional reporting requirements may apply. I should also consider whether the event meets NTSB 49 CFR Part 830 reporting criteria — ground resonance that causes structural damage would require immediate notification. The helicopter should not be returned to service until the dampers, landing gear, and rotor track and balance have been verified by maintenance.
questions.follow_up: If you shut the helicopter down during ground resonance and the blades struck the fuselage or tail boom, what are your regulatory notification obligations before you can move or disturb the aircraft?
questions.follow_up_answer: A rotor blade strike against the fuselage or tail boom during ground resonance constitutes an aircraft accident under NTSB definitions if it results in substantial damage — which a blade-fuselage strike almost certainly does. Under 49 CFR Part 830.5, the pilot in command must immediately notify the nearest NTSB field office. 49 CFR Part 830.10 requires that the aircraft, wreckage, mail, and cargo not be disturbed or moved from its accident site until the NTSB authorizes it — except to the extent necessary to remove persons injured or trapped, to protect the wreckage from further damage, or to protect the public from injury. The operator must also notify the FAA. If the helicopter is operated under 14 CFR Part 135, the operator's operations specifications likely impose additional notification timelines to the certificate-holding district office. The aircraft cannot be returned to service without an NTSB release and FAA-approved maintenance inspection confirming airworthiness.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR 91.7; 49 CFR Part 830.5; 49 CFR Part 830.10

tasks.title: Task J. Low Gravity (G) Recognition and Recovery

questions.question: What is the correct immediate recovery procedure if a pilot inadvertently enters a low-G condition in a helicopter with a teetering rotor system?
questions.answer: The correct recovery procedure is to smoothly and steadily apply aft cyclic only — do NOT apply any lateral cyclic input. Aft cyclic re-loads the rotor disk by increasing the angle of attack of the advancing and retreating blades, restoring positive G loading. Once positive G is re-established (the helicopter feels normal again), the pilot can return to level flight using coordinated control inputs. The critical rule is: no lateral cyclic until positive G is restored. Any lateral cyclic input during the unloaded condition can cause mast bumping and structural failure.

questions.question: Explain why a pilot flying a fully articulated rotor helicopter — such as a Bell 412 or Sikorsky S-76 — faces a different risk profile during a low-G event compared to a pilot flying a teetering rotor helicopter like a Robinson R22.
questions.answer: Fully articulated rotor systems have individual blade flapping, lead/lag, and feathering hinges for each blade, and they are attached to a rotor hub that sits firmly on the mast without a teetering pivot point. Because the blades can flap independently through their individual hinges, there is no single point at which the rotor disk as a whole can contact the mast or tail boom — the geometric constraint that causes mast bumping in teetering systems does not exist. However, a fully articulated helicopter is not immune to low-G hazards: loss of rotor thrust still creates a loss of control authority, the helicopter can pitch or roll uncontrollably, and excessive negative G can still cause structural problems. The recovery principle — apply aft cyclic to re-load the disk — is the same, but the catastrophic mast-strike risk specific to semirigid systems is significantly reduced.

questions.question: A student asks you: 'If I enter a low-G condition accidentally, can I just apply left pedal or left cyclic to stop the helicopter from rolling right?' How do you respond and why?
questions.answer: No — that response could be fatal in a teetering rotor helicopter. When the rotor is unloaded in a low-G condition, the rotor disk has flapped upward and the clearance between the rotor blades and the tail boom is critically reduced. Applying lateral cyclic — left or right — at that moment can cause the rotor disk to contact the mast or tail boom, resulting in mast bumping or a tail strike. The rotor is not in a position where lateral inputs will predictably stop the roll; instead, they may cause immediate structural failure. The only safe initial input is aft cyclic to re-load the rotor by increasing thrust and restoring positive G. Once you feel normal G loading return and the helicopter responds predictably, then you can make coordinated lateral and collective inputs to stabilize the flight path.

questions.question: During a checkride debrief, a candidate says: 'I would recognize a low-G condition because I'd feel weightless, so I'd know it right away and react in time.' As the examiner, how do you challenge this assumption, and what are the realistic recognition challenges that make low-G events so often fatal before recovery is attempted?
questions.answer: The candidate's assumption is dangerously overconfident. Low-G events in helicopters often occur in fractions of a second, particularly in turbulence or during a rapid push-over. The 'weightless feeling' may last less than a second before the subsequent roll begins — and that roll can reach catastrophic bank angles in another 1–2 seconds, leaving almost no time to recognize, correctly diagnose, and input the proper recovery before mast contact or terrain impact. Additionally, the sensations of turbulence, aircraft motion, and spatial disorientation can mask or confuse the low-G onset cue. Pilots often instinctively apply lateral cyclic to stop the roll — the wrong input — rather than aft cyclic. The startle factor and counter-intuitive nature of the correct response (don't stop the roll — reload the disk first) means that training and deeply ingrained procedural memory are the only reliable defenses. Passive reliance on 'feeling it in time' is insufficient.
questions.follow_up: What specific training strategy or habit can a pilot develop to reduce the likelihood of making the wrong input — lateral cyclic — when a low-G roll develops?
questions.follow_up_answer: The most effective strategy is repetitive, scenario-based ground training and simulator practice that specifically drills the 'aft cyclic only first' response until it becomes an automatic, overlearned reaction. Instructors should explain and reinforce the principle that in any unexpected roll at cruise speed, the first input is always aft cyclic to re-establish positive G before any roll correction is attempted. Some operators use memory aids or cockpit placards as reminders. Additionally, maintaining airspeed discipline — avoiding high-speed cruise in turbulent conditions when operating a teetering rotor helicopter — reduces exposure to the scenario. Pilots should also study accident reports involving low-G/mast bumping to internalize the real-world consequences and time scale involved.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); NTSB accident reports involving mast bumping

questions.question: A pilot argues that because their Robinson R66 is turbine-powered and certified to a higher gross weight than an R22, it must have a more robust rotor system and is therefore less susceptible to low-G/mast bumping. Evaluate this reasoning and explain whether rotor system vulnerability is determined by engine type or rotor design.
questions.answer: The pilot's reasoning is incorrect. Vulnerability to low-G and mast bumping is determined entirely by rotor system design — specifically whether the helicopter has a teetering (semirigid) rotor — not by engine type, horsepower, or gross weight. The Robinson R66, like the R22 and R44, uses a two-bladed teetering rotor system. Therefore, despite being turbine-powered and heavier, the R66 carries the same low-G/mast bumping risk as the piston-powered Robinson models. A heavier helicopter may actually develop a low-G condition more readily in certain turbulence scenarios due to greater inertia. Engine type (reciprocating vs. turbine) has no bearing on rotor hub geometry or the teetering pivot mechanics that create mast bumping vulnerability. The pilot should apply the same avoidance and recovery procedures as any other teetering rotor helicopter.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot transitions from a Robinson R66 to a Bell 206B — also a turbine helicopter — do the low-G procedures change, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, the risk profile changes significantly. The Bell 206B uses a two-bladed semi-rigid teetering rotor, so it shares the same fundamental mast bumping vulnerability as the Robinson models. However, the Bell 206 teetering system has different geometry, underslung rotor characteristics, and different blade inertia compared to the Robinson, so the specific envelope and sensitivity may differ. The recovery procedure — aft cyclic first, no lateral cyclic until positive G returns — remains the same. What changes in a true fully articulated or rigid rotor transition (e.g., to an AS350 or S-76) is that mast bumping risk is substantially reduced by design, though rotor unloading remains hazardous. The pilot should always know the specific rotor system type of any helicopter they fly and understand its unique low-G characteristics as described in the rotorcraft flight manual.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4 (Rotor Systems); Chapter 11 (Low-G/Mast Bumping); Robinson R66 POH

questions.question: During a low-G event, what happens to the lateral stability and control effectiveness of a helicopter equipped with a semirigid rotor system?
questions.answer: During a low-G event with a semirigid rotor, the rotor disk becomes unloaded and centrifugal force — which normally holds the blades taut and provides inherent lateral stability — is greatly reduced. This causes the rotor to lose its stabilizing stiffness. If the pilot applies lateral cyclic input while the rotor is unloaded, the control response becomes unpredictable and potentially violent. The rotor disk may tilt rapidly, and since the unloaded blades are not producing significant lift, the helicopter body may roll in an unexpected direction due to fuselage inertia. The danger is that pilots may instinctively apply lateral cyclic to correct a roll, which can worsen the mast bumping risk.

questions.question: How does a fully articulated rotor system respond differently than a semirigid rotor system during a low-G condition, and does this make it immune to low-G hazards?
questions.answer: A fully articulated rotor system allows each blade to flap, lead/lag, and feather independently through individual hinges. During a low-G condition, the blades can flap individually, which prevents the entire disk from unloading and tilting as a rigid unit the way a semirigid rotor does. This significantly reduces — but does not eliminate — the mast bumping risk. However, fully articulated systems are not immune to low-G hazards. They can still experience blade-to-fuselage contact under extreme unloading, reduced control effectiveness, and abrupt control response changes. The overall risk of catastrophic mast contact is lower, but pilots of all helicopter types should still avoid prolonged low-G flight and recover using smooth aft cyclic.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4 (Fully Articulated Rotor Systems) and Chapter 11

questions.question: Explain why low-G conditions are particularly dangerous in turbine-powered helicopters with semirigid rotor systems operating at high cruise speeds, and what environmental scenario most commonly produces this condition.
questions.answer: At high cruise speeds, rotor blade aerodynamic forces are high, and any sudden unloading — such as a sharp push-over input or a strong updraft immediately followed by a downdraft — can produce a rapid transition to near-zero G. The high kinetic energy of forward flight means the rotor disk can change orientation very quickly relative to the mast once unloaded, increasing mast bumping risk. Turbine engines produce greater power and allow higher cruise speeds, which amplifies the consequences. The most common environmental trigger is mountain wave turbulence or rotor wash, where a strong updraft abruptly gives way to a downdraft. Pilots focused on terrain or navigation may make sharp forward cyclic inputs to correct an inadvertent climb, creating the exact pushover scenario that unloads the rotor.

questions.question: A pilot reports that after encountering a brief low-G event, they heard a loud bang from the rotor mast area and noticed abnormal vibration, but the helicopter continued to fly. They decided to continue to the destination. Critically evaluate this decision from a structural and risk management standpoint.
questions.answer: This decision is extremely dangerous and represents a textbook failure of ADM and risk management. A loud bang from the rotor mast area following a low-G event is a strong indicator of mast bumping, which can cause internal cracking of the mast, damage to the rotor hub, or shearing of the mast itself — structural damage that may not be immediately apparent in handling but can result in catastrophic in-flight separation. Abnormal vibration following such an event may indicate blade track/balance changes, mast deformation, or bearing damage. The correct action is to execute a precautionary landing at the nearest suitable area immediately, consistent with 14 CFR 91.13 (avoiding careless or reckless operation). The pilot's error chain here involves: normalizing a dangerous symptom, failure to recognize the severity of mast bumping consequences, and continuation bias. Per the Helicopter Flying Handbook, mast bumping damage may not be externally visible and requires thorough maintenance inspection before any further flight.
questions.follow_up: If this same pilot told you 'the helicopter felt fine after the bang and the vibration went away after a minute, so I figured it sorted itself out' — how would you respond, and what does this reasoning tell you about their understanding of helicopter structural failure modes?
questions.follow_up_answer: This reasoning reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of fatigue crack propagation and structural failure modes. In helicopter mast and rotor hub components, a crack or internal deformation caused by mast contact does not 'sort itself out.' Vibration disappearing can actually indicate the damaged component has shifted to a temporarily stable but compromised state — the absence of vibration is not evidence of structural integrity. Rotor mast failures are typically catastrophic and sudden, not gradual. The pilot is essentially relying on survivorship bias — the helicopter continued to fly, therefore it must be okay — which is a dangerous cognitive trap. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook specifically warns that mast bumping damage is often internal and not detectable without maintenance inspection. This pilot needs significant ground training in structural failure modes, ADM, and the concept that continued safe flight after a potential structural event cannot be assumed.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR 91.13; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/Error Chain)

questions.question: Compare the blade flapping behavior of a rigid rotor system versus a semirigid rotor system during a low-G pushover, and explain why rigid rotor helicopters are considered safer in this regime but still carry low-G risks.
questions.answer: In a semirigid (teetering) rotor, both blades are connected at a single teetering hinge. When the rotor unloads in low G, the entire disk can tilt as a unit relative to the mast — there is no per-blade accommodation of asymmetric loading. This creates the classic mast bumping scenario where the hub contacts the mast. In a rigid rotor system, the blades are attached directly to the hub with no teetering hinge, and blade deflection is accommodated through blade material flexibility rather than mechanical hinges. Because the disk cannot tilt independently of the mast, the mast bumping mechanism is essentially eliminated. However, rigid rotor systems are not risk-free in low G: the absence of flapping freedom means that an abrupt low-G pushover can produce very high bending loads at the blade root and hub attachment points, potentially exceeding design limits. Additionally, low G still reduces rotor thrust to near zero, meaning the helicopter becomes ballistically uncontrolled momentarily. The pilot may also experience an unexpected roll due to translating tendency and fuselage pendulum effects, and if they respond with aggressive cyclic, they can impose extreme structural loads even on a rigid system.
questions.follow_up: Given that rigid rotor helicopters largely eliminate mast bumping risk, why does the FAA still require pilots of rigid rotor helicopters to be trained on low-G awareness and recovery?
questions.follow_up_answer: Even without mast bumping risk, low-G conditions in rigid rotor helicopters create several dangerous situations that require specific training. First, near-zero rotor thrust means loss of positive aircraft control — the pilot cannot generate meaningful lift or lateral control authority until G loading is restored. Second, extreme low-G can expose the rotor blades and hub to abnormal bending stress loads at the root, which can exceed certification envelope limits if abrupt cyclic inputs are made. Third, the pilot unfamiliar with low-G response may over-correct with large cyclic inputs when G is restored, causing an abrupt high-G recovery that could itself overstress the airframe or cause dynamic rollover tendencies near the ground. Fourth, if low G occurs near terrain or in instrument conditions, the loss of control effectiveness — even briefly — can be catastrophic. The FAA's position, consistent with the ACS and HFH Chapter 11, is that all helicopter pilots regardless of rotor type must recognize low-G conditions and respond with smooth aft cyclic to reload the rotor as the universal first response.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4 (Rigid Rotor Systems) and Chapter 11 (Low-G); ACS CH.X.J

questions.question: What is the correct recovery procedure when a helicopter pilot recognizes a low-G condition has developed?
questions.answer: The correct recovery from a low-G condition is to smoothly apply aft cyclic to reload the rotor disk and restore positive G-loading. The pilot must resist the urge to apply lateral cyclic while the rotor is unloaded. Once positive G is restored and the rotor is again loaded, normal coordinated control inputs can be used to return to level flight. Applying lateral cyclic during a low-G state is the dangerous pilot response — it can cause the rotor to contact the mast (mast bumping), which can be catastrophic.

questions.question: Why does applying lateral cyclic during a low-G condition significantly increase the risk of mast bumping compared to simply remaining in a low-G state?
questions.answer: In a low-G condition, the rotor system is unloaded and blade tension is greatly reduced. In a semirigid rotor system, the rotor can flap freely relative to the mast. When lateral cyclic is applied with the rotor unloaded, the cyclic tilts the rotor disk, but because the disk is not loaded against the mast with centrifugal force, one side of the rotor head can swing violently toward the mast. This asymmetric, unloaded flapping motion creates the contact geometry for mast bumping. In a normally loaded rotor, centrifugal force keeps the blades taut and the rotor disk stiff, so lateral cyclic tilts the disk predictably without the free flapping that causes mast contact.

questions.question: A student pilot describes the following sequence of events: 'I was descending at cruise speed, hit some smooth air after a ridge, the helicopter rolled right unexpectedly, so I pushed left cyclic to correct it.' What hazardous condition may have preceded that roll, and how should the student have responded instead?
questions.answer: The unexpected right roll after crossing a ridge is a classic symptom of a low-G condition induced by a downdraft or a pilot pushover during the descent. With the rotor unloaded, the helicopter can roll in response to small aerodynamic inputs or even gyroscopic precession. The student's response — pushing lateral cyclic to correct the roll while the rotor was still unloaded — is exactly the pilot input that causes mast bumping in a semirigid rotor system. The correct response was to first apply smooth aft cyclic to re-establish positive G-loading and rotor rigidity, and only then use coordinated cyclic and pedal inputs to correct the bank. Lateral cyclic must not be applied as the first response to a roll when a low-G condition is suspected.

questions.question: After a suspected low-G event with no obvious control or vibration anomalies, a pilot continues the flight and lands uneventfully. Was this the correct decision, and what should the pilot do after landing?
questions.answer: Continuing the flight after a suspected low-G event is not the correct decision. Even if no immediate vibration, control change, or visual anomaly was noticed, mast bumping can cause internal structural damage to the rotor head, mast, or teeter hinge that is not detectable by the pilot during flight. The correct action after any suspected low-G or mast bumping event is to land as soon as practicable and have the helicopter inspected by a certificated airframe and powerplant (A&P) mechanic or the manufacturer's representative before further flight. The mast, rotor head, teeter bolt, and associated hardware must be inspected for cracks, deformation, or fatigue damage. Continuing flight risks catastrophic rotor separation.
questions.follow_up: What regulatory obligation does a pilot or operator have to report a mast bumping event, and does it automatically ground the helicopter?
questions.follow_up_answer: There is no specific FAR requiring a pilot to file a report solely for a mast bumping event unless it results in an accident or serious incident as defined under 49 CFR Part 830 (NTSB regulations). However, if the event caused substantial damage to the aircraft or involved loss of control, it may meet the NTSB definition of an aircraft accident requiring immediate notification to the NTSB (49 CFR 830.5) and a written report within 10 days (49 CFR 830.15). Operationally, 14 CFR 91.7 requires a pilot in command to determine the aircraft is in airworthy condition before flight. If there is any doubt about airworthiness following a mast bumping event, the aircraft is effectively grounded until inspected and returned to airworthy status by an authorized mechanic.

questions.question: You are conducting a mountain flying course in a semirigid rotor helicopter. During a ridge crossing, the student inadvertently enters a low-G state and immediately applies right lateral cyclic to arrest a left roll. You hear a sharp bang. What has likely happened, what are your immediate priorities, and how does rotor system design physics explain why this outcome was almost certain?
questions.answer: The sharp bang almost certainly indicates a mast bumping event — the rotor head contacted the mast while the rotor was unloaded and lateral cyclic was applied. In a semirigid (teetering) rotor, the rotor hub pivots on a single teeter bolt above the mast. Centrifugal force normally keeps the blades taut and the rotor disk stiff, preventing extreme flapping. In a low-G state, centrifugal stiffness collapses and the rotor can flap freely. Applying lateral cyclic tilts the swash plate, which commands a differential pitch change across the disk. With no centrifugal stiffness to resist the resultant flapping moment, one blade flaps violently downward and the rotor head pivots into the mast. The outcome was nearly certain because the student applied the most dangerous input (lateral cyclic) at the worst moment (unloaded rotor). Immediate priorities: (1) take control smoothly — do not make abrupt inputs; (2) look for any change in vibration, controls, or sounds indicating progressive structural failure; (3) land immediately at the nearest safe area — do not attempt to fly back to the departure point; (4) shut down and inspect before any further flight. This event may constitute an aircraft accident requiring NTSB notification depending on resulting damage.
questions.follow_up: If the helicopter appears to fly normally after the bang with no vibration change, can you conclude the mast bump was minor and the aircraft is structurally sound?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. Normal flight characteristics after a mast bump cannot be used to infer structural integrity. The teeter bolt, mast, and rotor head can sustain cracks or plastic deformation that are not apparent from cockpit indications. Fatigue cracks may propagate rapidly under continued flight loads and cause sudden rotor separation with no warning. The absence of vibration does not clear the aircraft — vibration signatures from structural damage are sometimes absent at cruise power settings and only apparent at specific RPM or load conditions, if at all. The aircraft must be landed immediately and inspected by qualified maintenance personnel. The FAA and helicopter manufacturers universally state that any mast bumping event requires thorough inspection before further flight, regardless of apparent flight characteristics.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4; 14 CFR 91.7; 49 CFR 830.5

questions.question: What specific control input is most likely to produce a low-G condition in a helicopter?
questions.answer: Pushing forward on the cyclic abruptly, particularly from cruise flight, can rapidly unload the rotor disk and produce a low-G (reduced or near-zero gravity) condition. This reduces the centrifugal force acting on the rotor blades, which is critical for maintaining blade stiffness and rotor stability, especially on semirigid and teetering rotor systems.

questions.question: Which rotor system type is most vulnerable to mast bumping as a result of a low-G condition, and why?
questions.answer: Semirigid (teetering) rotor systems are most vulnerable to mast bumping during low-G conditions. In a low-G state, the rotor disk is unloaded and blades lose the centrifugal stiffness that normally keeps them in plane. Without that load, the rotor disk can tilt and contact the mast, which on a semirigid system has very limited tolerance for this movement. Fully articulated and rigid rotor systems have greater structural capacity to tolerate blade displacement.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4 (Rotor Systems) and Chapter 11 (Low-G/Mast Bumping)

questions.question: What does 'low-G' mean in the context of helicopter flight, and how does it differ from normal loaded rotor flight?
questions.answer: Low-G refers to a condition in which the rotor system is producing little to no positive lift, resulting in reduced or near-zero gravitational loading on the pilot and airframe. In normal flight, the rotor is positively loaded — it is generating lift equal to or greater than the weight of the helicopter. In a low-G state, the rotor thrust is significantly reduced, centrifugal blade stiffness decreases, and the rotor disk becomes susceptible to uncontrolled tilting. This is especially dangerous on teetering rotor systems where the rotor's lateral stability depends heavily on centrifugal loading.

questions.question: You're cruising at 100 knots in a Robinson R44 when you encounter unexpected turbulence and instinctively push forward on the cyclic to level the nose. What risk does this input create, and what is the correct immediate corrective action?
questions.answer: Pushing forward on the cyclic in a teetering rotor system like the R44 can rapidly unload the rotor, creating a low-G condition. In this state, the rotor blades lose centrifugal stiffness and the disk may tilt laterally. The fuselage, still subject to its own inertia, can roll toward the low side — if the pilot then instinctively applies lateral cyclic to stop the roll, this can cause mast bumping or blade-to-fuselage contact. The correct recovery is to smoothly apply aft cyclic to reload the rotor disk first — restoring positive G loading — before making any lateral corrections. Do not apply lateral cyclic while in a low-G state.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Low-G/Mast Bumping; Robinson R44 POH/RFM Safety Notices

questions.question: A student pilot tells you that during a steep diving turn, he felt momentarily weightless and then noticed a loud 'clunk' from above. What control sequence likely caused this, and what does the 'clunk' most likely indicate?
questions.answer: During a steep diving turn, if the pilot applied forward cyclic to increase the descent rate, this could have unloaded the rotor, creating a low-G state. The weightless sensation confirms rotor unloading occurred. The subsequent lateral roll of the fuselage (from the tilted disk) may have prompted a reflexive lateral cyclic input, further destabilizing the rotor relative to the mast. The 'clunk' most likely indicates mast bumping — physical contact between the rotor hub or teeter block and the main rotor mast. This is a serious structural event that requires immediate landing and a maintenance inspection before further flight. The helicopter must be grounded until cleared by a certificated mechanic.

questions.question: How does flying in turbulent conditions increase the risk of inadvertently inducing a low-G condition, and what SRM strategy can a pilot use to mitigate this risk?
questions.answer: Turbulence causes sudden, unexpected pitch and roll disturbances. A pilot's instinctive reaction to a sudden nose-up pitch excursion is often to push forward on the cyclic, which can rapidly unload the rotor and produce a low-G condition — especially dangerous in teetering rotor systems. From an SRM perspective, risk mitigation strategies include: (1) slowing to turbulence penetration speed to reduce the magnitude of control inputs needed; (2) maintaining a relaxed, smooth grip on the cyclic to avoid sharp inputs; (3) using situation awareness to anticipate turbulent areas (terrain, weather, rotor wash) and route around them when possible; and (4) briefing oneself ahead of time on the correct recovery technique so that the instinctive push-forward reflex is replaced by a trained aft-cyclic response. Per ADM principles, avoiding the situation entirely is the most reliable solution.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Low-G) and Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 4 (Aerodynamic Factors)

questions.question: A pilot reports that while transitioning from level cruise to a rapid nose-low descent on a teetering-rotor helicopter, the fuselage suddenly rolled right even though he made no lateral cyclic input. Explain the aerodynamic sequence of events that caused this roll, and why applying left cyclic at that moment would have been the worst possible response.
questions.answer: When the pilot pushed forward on the cyclic to initiate the rapid descent, the rotor disk unloaded, creating a low-G state. With centrifugal stiffness reduced, the rotor disk — still tilted slightly to the right from some pre-existing asymmetry (such as tail rotor thrust, wind, or torque) — was no longer constrained by blade stiffness and tilted further right relative to the mast. The fuselage, now essentially in free-fall, lagged behind the rotor disk and appeared to roll right. Applying left lateral cyclic at this point — while the rotor is unloaded — would have tilted the disk further relative to the mast on the opposite side, increasing the risk of mast bumping. On a teetering rotor, mast contact during a low-G condition can apply enormous bending loads to the mast in microseconds, potentially resulting in mast separation and catastrophic loss of the aircraft. The correct action is aft cyclic to reload the rotor first, restoring centrifugal blade stiffness and disk control, before addressing any lateral deviation.
questions.follow_up: If this same low-G induced roll occurred on a fully articulated rotor system, would the risk of mast bumping be the same? Why or why not, and are there other risks unique to fully articulated systems in low-G conditions?
questions.follow_up_answer: Fully articulated rotor systems are significantly less susceptible to mast bumping because each blade has a drag hinge, flapping hinge, and pitch change bearing — the blade can move independently in all three axes without transmitting large bending loads directly to the mast. The system is designed to accommodate a wide range of blade movement. However, low-G conditions in fully articulated systems are not risk-free: the reduced blade loading can cause flapping exceedances beyond design limits (droop stop pounding), and if the condition is severe enough, blade-to-fuselage or blade-to-tail boom contact remains a risk. Additionally, any rotor system operating in a low-G state has degraded cyclic control effectiveness since lateral and longitudinal disk tilting depends on aerodynamic forces that are reduced when the disk is unloaded.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4 (Rotor Systems — articulated vs. semirigid) and Chapter 11 (Low-G/Mast Bumping)

questions.question: From a risk management standpoint, why does the FAA consider the low-G/mast bumping accident sequence particularly insidious compared to other helicopter emergencies, and what specific training limitation makes it especially difficult to mitigate?
questions.answer: Low-G/mast bumping is particularly insidious for several reasons: (1) The initiating control input — forward cyclic — is an instinctive, natural pilot reaction to a nose-high pitch upset or turbulence. Unlike failures such as engine loss, which demand a trained response to an abnormal event, low-G is triggered by the pilot's own corrective instincts. (2) The sequence from low-G state to mast contact can occur in a fraction of a second, leaving virtually no time for recognition and recovery once the lateral roll begins. (3) The warning cues are subtle — the weightless sensation and lateral fuselage roll may not be immediately associated with rotor unloading. From a training limitation standpoint, the low-G condition and mast bumping sequence cannot be safely demonstrated in the actual aircraft — instructors cannot allow a student to experience the full event without catastrophic risk. This means pilots must rely entirely on ground-based learning, simulation (where available), and cognitive pre-programming of the correct response (aft cyclic first). Per ADM/SRM principles, this is a scenario where anticipatory risk management — knowing the hazard, avoiding the trigger inputs, and rehearsing the correct recovery mentally — is the only viable mitigation strategy, since in-flight experiential learning is not possible.
questions.follow_up: Given that low-G mast bumping cannot be demonstrated in flight, what specific evaluation methods can you as an examiner use on a practical test to assess whether an applicant truly understands and can manage this risk?
questions.follow_up_answer: On a practical test, I can assess low-G risk management through: (1) Oral questioning to verify the applicant understands which specific control inputs cause the condition (forward cyclic, especially abrupt pushover), why teetering rotor systems are most vulnerable, and what the correct recovery sequence is (aft cyclic to reload before any lateral input). (2) Scenario-based oral questions placing the applicant in a turbulence encounter or steep diving turn and asking them to verbalize decision-making. (3) Observing actual flight for control smoothness — an applicant who makes abrupt forward cyclic inputs during the practical test is demonstrating the exact behavior that creates low-G risk. (4) Assessing whether the applicant self-identifies low-G avoidance in their risk management discussion during preflight planning, particularly when the flight involves turbulent conditions or high-speed maneuvering. Per the ACS, the examiner is evaluating whether the applicant can identify and manage the risk — not demonstrate the emergency itself.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Low-G/Mast Bumping) and Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); ACS CH.X.J Risk Management

questions.question: Why are turbulence and gusty wind conditions considered a specific risk factor for low-G situations in helicopters?
questions.answer: Gusty or turbulent conditions amplify the risk of low-G situations, particularly when combined with pilot control inputs. A sudden gust may unload the rotor momentarily; if the pilot perceives this as a pitch or roll excursion and makes an instinctive control input (especially forward cyclic), rotor thrust can be further reduced, driving the helicopter into a low-G or near-zero-G state. Additionally, turbulence makes pilot inputs more reactive and less deliberate, increasing the likelihood of abrupt control movements that unload the rotor. In a low-G condition, especially on semirigid or teetering rotor systems, the rotor hub loses centrifugal force stabilization and mast bumping becomes a serious risk. Turbulence makes this hazard unpredictable and sudden.

questions.question: What type of rotor system is most vulnerable to mast bumping when rotor thrust is suddenly reduced by a gust, and why?
questions.answer: Semirigid (teetering) rotor systems are most vulnerable. In a semirigid design, the rotor blades are connected to the mast by a teetering hinge and are not individually articulated. When rotor thrust drops—as can happen in a gust-induced low-G condition—there is reduced centrifugal force holding the blades in their normal cone angle. This allows the rotor disk to tilt relative to the mast, and the blade grips or hub can strike the mast—a potentially catastrophic event. Fully articulated rotor systems are more resistant because individual blade flapping and drag hinges accommodate disk tilting without transmitting large bending loads to the mast. Rigid rotors are the most resistant but still require proper rotor loading to maintain stability.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4 (rotor system types); Chapter 11 (mast bumping)

questions.question: What flight regime or combination of conditions makes a helicopter most susceptible to a gust-induced low-G event?
questions.answer: A helicopter is most susceptible to gust-induced low-G in high-speed forward flight combined with turbulent or gusty conditions. At higher airspeeds, a sudden upward gust can rapidly reduce the rotor's angle of attack and unload the disk. Additionally, any flight condition where the pilot applies forward cyclic aggressively — such as in turbulence while trying to maintain altitude — can push the rotor into an unloaded state. Flying a teetering-rotor helicopter fast and low in gusty conditions is the highest-risk combination.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (low-G/mast bumping); Chapter 2 (aerodynamics of forward flight)

questions.question: You are flying a Robinson R44 at 100 knots on a cross-country route and your weather briefing mentioned isolated moderate turbulence along your route. What specific actions would you take before and during the flight to mitigate the risk of a low-G event?
questions.answer: Before flight: Review the POH for turbulence penetration speed (Va or manufacturer's recommended turbulence speed) and plan to fly at or below that speed through known turbulent areas. Robinson aircraft have specific warnings about low-G — review those limitations. Consider re-routing or delaying the flight if turbulence is forecast to be more than light. During flight: Slow to the recommended turbulence penetration airspeed before entering turbulent areas. Maintain a positive but gentle grip on the controls — avoid aggressive aft-cyclic inputs that could follow a gust-induced forward surge. If the helicopter experiences a low-G condition, immediately and smoothly apply aft cyclic to reload the rotor — do NOT use left lateral cyclic first, as this can induce mast bumping. Maintain situational awareness about escape routes to calmer air or lower altitudes where turbulence may be reduced.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Robinson R44 POH (manufacturer limitations); ADM principles Chapter 13

questions.question: A pilot argues that flying faster through a turbulent area is better because it reduces exposure time. How would you evaluate this reasoning from a low-G risk management perspective?
questions.answer: This reasoning is flawed and actually increases risk for helicopters with semirigid rotor systems. Higher airspeed in turbulence increases the severity of rotor unloading when a gust is encountered, making a low-G event more likely and more severe. At higher speeds, aerodynamic forces act more abruptly on the rotor disk, and the potential for mast bumping is significantly greater. The correct strategy is to reduce airspeed to the manufacturer's recommended turbulence penetration speed before entering turbulent air. This reduces the magnitude of gust-induced load changes on the rotor and gives the pilot more time to respond. 'Faster through turbulence' is a fixed-wing mindset that does not translate safely to semirigid-rotor helicopters.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (low-G/mast bumping); Chapter 13 (ADM, hazardous attitudes — anti-authority/invulnerability)

questions.question: You are planning a mountain cross-country in a teetering-rotor helicopter. Winds aloft are forecast at 25 knots with gusts to 35 knots near ridgelines. Walk me through your go/no-go decision-making process specifically related to low-G risk.
questions.answer: I would evaluate several factors: First, the mechanical turbulence near ridgelines with 25-35 knot winds is well-documented to produce severe rotary turbulence on the leeward side — this is high risk for any aircraft and especially dangerous for a teetering-rotor helicopter due to the low-G mast bumping threat. Second, I would check the manufacturer's guidance — many Robinson helicopters, for example, have specific warnings about operations in conditions where low-G is likely. Third, I would assess whether I can route around or over the ridgelines at an altitude where turbulence is reduced (typically well above ridge elevation). Fourth, I would evaluate my own recency and proficiency with low-G recognition and recovery. If I cannot avoid the turbulent areas at a safe altitude, and the winds are forecast to produce mechanical turbulence that could unload the rotor, the go/no-go decision should favor a no-go or significant re-route. The risk of mast bumping in a teetering-rotor helicopter in moderate to severe turbulence near terrain is potentially catastrophic and not acceptable.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM, SRM, risk management); Manufacturer POH limitations

questions.question: Some pilots believe that if they maintain a tight grip on the controls in turbulence, they can prevent a low-G event. Evaluate this belief from both a physiological and aerodynamic standpoint.
questions.answer: This belief is partially understandable but fundamentally incorrect and potentially dangerous. Aerodynamically, a low-G event is caused by an external gust reducing the rotor's angle of attack or thrust — this happens faster than most pilots can react, regardless of control grip. A gust that unloads the rotor acts on the entire disk simultaneously; no grip tightness prevents it. From a physiological standpoint, a tight grip actually introduces the risk of involuntary control input. In turbulence, if the pilot's body is jolted and they are gripping tightly, their hands can inadvertently push the cyclic forward — which is exactly the control input that worsens a low-G condition. The FAA and manufacturers recommend a firm but relaxed grip in turbulence, with body position stabilized by the seat and harness rather than through the controls. The risk management strategy is to reduce airspeed to turbulence penetration speed, brief yourself on low-G recognition cues (sudden lightness, reduced G sensation), and know the recovery procedure so it is executed immediately and correctly if triggered.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot is already in a low-G condition and they are being thrown around by turbulence, what is the practical challenge in executing the aft-cyclic recovery, and how should they train for it?
questions.follow_up_answer: The practical challenge is that in turbulence, the pilot may not be able to distinguish between a low-G event and normal turbulent jolting — the sensory cues are mixed and can be confusing. Additionally, the same turbulence that caused the low-G event may be physically moving the pilot's body and hands in ways that make a precise, smooth aft cyclic application difficult. If the pilot overcorrects with too-aggressive aft cyclic, they risk an abrupt rotor reload which could cause a structural overstress or initiate a dynamic stability problem. Training should include: simulator exposure to low-G recognition under turbulence conditions, chair-flying the recovery procedure until it is instinctive, briefing the recovery before every flight in gusty conditions, and ensuring the harness is tight so body movement does not translate into unintended control inputs. Some training programs also conduct actual low-G demonstrations at altitude in calm conditions so pilots know exactly what the sensation feels like before encountering it in turbulence.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (low-G recovery procedure); Chapter 13 (ADM, workload management, SRM); Chapter 4 (rotor systems)

questions.question: Why does a low-G pushover create the conditions for mast bumping even before any incorrect control input is applied?
questions.answer: During a low-G pushover, the pilot has applied forward cyclic aggressively — often in turbulence or during a dive — reducing the load on the rotor disk toward or below zero G. With the rotor unloaded, centrifugal force is the only force keeping the blades extended outward, and the rotor loses its gyroscopic stiffness. The disk is now free to flap more than normal limits allow. In this unloaded, destabilized state, the rotor hub is dangerously close to the mast, and any additional cyclic input — especially aft — can cause the hub to contact the mast immediately.

questions.question: A student pilot asks why turbulence-induced low-G is more dangerous in a helicopter than in a fixed-wing aircraft. How would you explain the mast bumping risk in terms of control inputs and rotor dynamics?
questions.answer: In a fixed-wing aircraft, a low-G upset reduces wing loading but the wing remains structurally attached — there is no rotating component that can physically strike the airframe from the inside. In a helicopter with a semirigid rotor, the rotor hub teeters on a hinge above the mast. When G-loading drops toward zero, the rotor loses gyroscopic rigidity and centrifugal force alone maintains blade extension. If the pilot then makes an aft cyclic input — a natural startle response to a nose-down pitch — the disk tilts and the hub swings toward the mast. This contact can sever the mast and cause complete loss of the helicopter. The fixed-wing pilot's instinctive recovery (pull back) is exactly the wrong input in a semirigid helicopter during low-G.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11 (Low-G/Mast Bumping); Chapter 4 (Semirigid Rotor Systems)

questions.question: During a steep descent at high speed following a missed approach, you push forward cyclic to accelerate for the go-around and momentarily experience very light seat pressure. You then notice your rotor RPM is still in the green. Does normal rotor RPM indicate the rotor is safely loaded, and what is your risk management concern here?
questions.answer: No — normal rotor RPM does not confirm the rotor is loaded. Rotor RPM reflects rotational speed, not the G-load on the disk. During a low-G pushover, the rotor can briefly continue spinning at normal RPM while being aerodynamically unloaded. The risk management concern is that the helicopter — especially if equipped with a semirigid rotor — is in a condition where the hub can contact the mast if aft cyclic is applied. The pilot should not interpret the green RPM arc as a safe signal. The correct action is to immediately and gently apply lateral cyclic to reload the rotor, confirm return of seat pressure (positive G), and then recover the flight attitude. Do not rely on gauges alone to assess rotor load state.

questions.question: A pilot reports that during a low-G event, they applied right lateral cyclic per their training, but the helicopter still exhibited a violent lateral roll before recovering. What control inputs or conditions could explain why the correct recovery technique still led to an aggressive aircraft response, and what does this tell you about the risk management of low-G situations?
questions.answer: Several factors could explain the violent roll despite correct lateral cyclic input. First, if the cyclic input was abrupt rather than smooth and progressive, the sudden lateral disk tilt on an unloaded rotor can itself cause an aggressive roll before the rotor reloads. Second, if the low-G condition had persisted long enough, the rotor flapping may have reached extreme values, meaning even a correct gentle input encounters a highly destabilized system. Third, if there was a simultaneous inadvertent aft cyclic component in the input (due to pilot startle or poor ergonomics), hub-to-mast proximity could have caused a structural impulse. The risk management lesson is profound: the best recovery from a low-G mast bumping event is to never enter one. Avoid aggressive pushovers, fly with smooth coordinated inputs in turbulence, and maintain situational awareness of airspeed and attitude to prevent the unloaded rotor condition in the first place. Prevention is the only reliable strategy — recovery technique must be smooth and cannot be guaranteed to prevent damage if the condition is severe.
questions.follow_up: If a semirigid rotor helicopter experienced an actual mast bump during flight and the pilot was able to land safely, what is required before the helicopter can fly again?
questions.follow_up_answer: The helicopter is grounded and must undergo a detailed maintenance inspection by a certificated airframe and powerplant (A&P) mechanic, and in many cases an FAA-certificated repair station, before any further flight. The mast, rotor hub, teeter hinge, rotor blades, blade bolts, and associated airframe attachment structure must all be inspected for deformation, cracking, or fatigue damage. This type of inspection is typically required by the manufacturer's maintenance manual and possibly an Airworthiness Directive (AD). Even if no visible damage is found, a mast bump event is considered a hard landing/unusual stress event and must be documented in the aircraft maintenance records per 14 CFR 43.9. In many cases, Robinson Helicopter Company, for example, requires the mast and hub to be returned to the factory or an authorized facility for inspection after a confirmed mast bump.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11 (Low-G/Mast Bumping); 14 CFR Part 43.9; Manufacturer's Maintenance Manual

questions.question: Some pilots believe that because they fly a helicopter with a fully rigid rotor system, they have no mast bumping risk and can apply aft cyclic freely during unusual attitude recovery. Is this belief accurate, and what residual risks from aggressive cyclic inputs still apply to rigid rotor helicopters during low-G events?
questions.answer: The belief is largely — but not entirely — accurate regarding mast bumping specifically. Rigid rotor helicopters, such as those with hingeless or bearingless rotor systems, do not have a teeter hinge, so the physical hub-to-mast contact that defines mast bumping in semirigid systems is not a risk. However, this does not mean aggressive cyclic inputs during low-G conditions are safe. Rigid rotor systems transmit large bending moments directly into the mast and airframe because there is no hinge to absorb flapping loads — this means that an aggressive cyclic input during an unloaded rotor condition can impose extreme structural loads on the mast attachment, airframe, and rotor blade roots, potentially exceeding design limits. Additionally, in any helicopter, a very aggressive aft cyclic input during a nose-low attitude can lead to dynamic rollover, blade strike of the fuselage, or tail rotor/empennage contact with the main rotor on some designs. Pilots of rigid rotor helicopters must still apply smooth, progressive control inputs during all unusual attitude recoveries.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot is transitioning from a Robinson R22 (semirigid rotor) to a military-derived rigid rotor helicopter, what specific low-G training emphasis would you require before solo flight in the new aircraft?
questions.follow_up_answer: I would require the transitioning pilot to demonstrate a thorough understanding that the absence of mast bumping risk does not eliminate the need for smooth, progressive cyclic inputs during unusual attitudes. Training emphasis would include: (1) understanding the structural load transfer characteristics of rigid rotor systems and how aggressive inputs still risk exceeding blade root and mast structural limits; (2) recognition that the instinctive aft cyclic pull habit from fixed-wing or semirigid training must be consciously replaced with smooth progressive recovery technique; (3) simulator or dual instruction in turbulence penetration technique; and (4) review of the specific aircraft POH/flight manual for any manufacturer guidance on unusual attitude recovery and low-G procedures. The pilot must not assume that eliminating one risk (mast bumping) means all low-G risks have been eliminated — the hazard profile changes, it does not disappear.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 4 (Rigid Rotor Systems) and Chapter 11 (Low-G/Mast Bumping); 14 CFR 61.31 (Type Rating and additional training requirements)

questions.question: During a mountain flight, you encounter a severe downdraft and instinctively push forward on the cyclic to maintain altitude. The helicopter develops a right roll and you feel reduced G-loading. Walk me through exactly what is happening aerodynamically and what your control inputs should be.
questions.answer: Pushing forward on the cyclic in response to the downdraft has reduced the angle of attack of the rotor disk, unloading it and creating a low-G condition. The rotor is now producing minimal lift and the fuselage is free to roll — in this case to the right. The danger is that applying right lateral cyclic to stop the roll while the rotor is unloaded could cause the rotor disk to flap violently toward the mast (mast bumping) on a semirigid system. The correct response is: resist the urge to apply lateral cyclic, immediately apply smooth aft cyclic to reload the rotor and restore lift, and then — once G-loading is felt returning — use gentle lateral cyclic to correct any bank. After recovery, reassess the mountain flying situation and consider a retreat from the downdraft area.

questions.question: A pilot reports that after flying through turbulence, they heard a loud 'bang' from the rotor mast area and landed immediately. Upon inspection, what damage would be consistent with a mast bumping event, and what should the pilot have done to prevent it?
questions.answer: Mast bumping leaves characteristic damage: a groove or ring cut into the mast itself where the rotor hub made contact, and potentially damage to the rotor hub and teeter stop. In severe cases, the mast can be completely severed. This is consistent with a low-G event in turbulence where the pilot likely applied lateral cyclic while the rotor was unloaded — perhaps trying to roll wings-level — causing the rotor hub to strike the mast. Prevention requires recognizing the low-G state (light sensation, reduced seat pressure, abrupt forward pitch), immediately applying aft cyclic to reload the rotor before making any lateral corrections, and never applying lateral cyclic while G-loading is absent. After any suspected mast bumping event, the helicopter is unairworthy and must be inspected before further flight.

questions.question: A fully articulated rotor system helicopter, such as a Bell 412, enters a low-G condition. Is the pilot at the same risk of mast bumping as a semirigid rotor aircraft? How does rotor system design change the hazard profile and the required pilot response?
questions.answer: A fully articulated rotor system significantly reduces — but does not eliminate — the mast bumping risk during a low-G event. Fully articulated rotors incorporate lead/lag, flapping, and feathering hinges, which allow each blade to move independently. This articulation means the rotor hub does not transmit the same extreme flapping forces to the mast during an unloaded condition as a semirigid teeter rotor does. However, a low-G condition is still hazardous in any helicopter because rotor control authority is reduced when the disk is unloaded — lateral and fore-aft cyclic inputs produce unpredictable or diminished responses. The pilot's response should still prioritize reloading the rotor with aft cyclic before attempting any lateral correction. The risk of controllability loss and structural damage to the rotor system remains, even if catastrophic mast severing is less likely than in a semirigid system.
questions.follow_up: If the low-G condition occurs during a high-speed cruise descent — say, 120 knots in a Bell 407 — how does forward airspeed affect the severity and recovery from the event?
questions.follow_up_answer: At higher forward airspeeds, a low-G condition is generally more hazardous because the rotor is operating with greater asymmetric lift between the advancing and retreating sides. When the rotor is unloaded at high speed, the advancing blade (which already produces more lift) may flap up aggressively while the retreating blade flaps down — creating a significant rolling moment. This asymmetric flapping can be violent and rapid. Additionally, at higher speeds, any roll that develops builds quickly, increasing the temptation to apply lateral cyclic prematurely. The recovery principle remains the same — smooth aft cyclic first to reload — but the time available before the situation worsens is shorter, and precise, unhurried inputs are critical. Pilots should also reduce airspeed after recovery to reduce future asymmetric lift risk.

questions.question: From a skills demonstration standpoint, how would you expect a candidate to physically demonstrate awareness and prevention of low-G during a checkride, and what specific control habits or errors would cause you to fail them on this task?
questions.answer: During a practical exam, I would evaluate low-G awareness through scenario-based discussion and observation of flight technique — particularly during high-speed cruise, cruise descents, and turbulence encounters. A candidate should demonstrate smooth, deliberate cyclic inputs without abrupt forward pushes, and articulate the recognition cues (reduced seat pressure, floating sensation, sudden nose-down pitch). In actual flight, I would note whether the candidate maintains proper cyclic discipline when transitioning from climbs to level flight or descents. Failure criteria include: (1) demonstrating or tolerating abrupt forward cyclic inputs without correction; (2) inability to verbalize the correct recovery sequence (aft cyclic before any lateral input); (3) stating they would apply lateral cyclic to stop a roll during unloaded rotor condition; or (4) inability to identify their specific aircraft's rotor system type and its relevance to low-G risk. A candidate who says 'I'd just push down on the collective to stop the descent' reveals a critical misunderstanding — collective reduction is appropriate for autorotation entry, not low-G recovery.
questions.follow_up: A candidate correctly states that aft cyclic reloads the rotor during a low-G recovery, but then says 'and then I'd immediately pull full aft collective to arrest the descent.' What's wrong with that answer?
questions.follow_up_answer: Pulling full aft collective immediately after reloading the rotor is dangerous for two reasons. First, a rapid, large collective increase dramatically increases the pitch angle of all rotor blades simultaneously, which can cause rotor RPM decay if the engine cannot respond fast enough — particularly in reciprocating engine helicopters where throttle correlation is required. Second, an aggressive collective pull after a low-G recovery could cause an abrupt pitch-up and balloon, potentially leading to a secondary loss of control. The correct action after reloading with aft cyclic is to assess the situation, apply smooth and measured collective as needed, and stabilize the flight attitude before making power corrections. The recovery should be deliberate, not reactive.

questions.question: A student pilot tells you that during a gusty-wind training flight, the helicopter 'felt light' for a moment and then rocked sideways unexpectedly before they added some right cyclic to correct it. What aerodynamic event likely occurred, and what was the danger in their instinctive correction?
questions.answer: What likely occurred was a gust-induced low-G condition — a momentary unloading of the rotor disk. The 'felt light' sensation is the classic cue of rotor thrust reduction. The subsequent sideward rocking was likely the rotor disk tilting relative to the mast due to loss of centrifugal loading on a semirigid teetering rotor system. The student's instinctive response of applying lateral cyclic — in any direction — to correct the roll is precisely the wrong and most dangerous input in this situation. On a semirigid teetering rotor, applying lateral cyclic during a low-G condition tilts the rotor disk further relative to the mast, which can drive the blade grips or hub into the mast — a condition known as mast bumping — which can cause mast separation and catastrophic loss of control. The correct recovery is to first apply gentle aft cyclic to re-load the rotor and restore positive G. Only after rotor thrust is restored should any roll correction be made. The key point to instill in the student is that during low-G, lateral cyclic inputs must be avoided; restoring rotor loading via aft cyclic is always the priority first step.
questions.rewrite_note: Clarified that lateral cyclic in any direction (not specifically right or left) is the dangerous input to avoid during low-G, eliminating the apparent contradiction between the opening and closing statements, and reinforced that aft cyclic to restore rotor loading is the correct first recovery action.

questions.question: What is the correct recovery procedure when you recognize you have entered a low-G condition in a semirigid rotor helicopter?
questions.answer: When a low-G (unloaded rotor) condition is recognized in a semirigid rotor helicopter, the correct recovery is to apply gentle, smooth lateral cyclic (typically right lateral cyclic) to reload the rotor disk. Do NOT apply aft cyclic as the primary recovery input, and do NOT apply lateral cyclic to correct a bank while the rotor remains unloaded, as either can lead to mast bumping. The lateral cyclic input reloads the rotor system, restoring normal thrust and control. Once the rotor is reloaded and normal rotor thrust is restored, the helicopter can be returned to coordinated flight. The danger of low-G flight in semirigid rotor helicopters is that the rotor disc is unloaded and cannot transmit corrective forces to the fuselage effectively, making instinctive control inputs — particularly aft cyclic or lateral cyclic to correct a roll — potentially catastrophic.
questions.rewrite_note: Corrected the primary recovery input from 'aft cyclic' to 'gentle lateral cyclic' (consistent with FAA-H-8083-21B guidance on low-G recovery in semirigid rotor helicopters) and clarified why aft cyclic is not the correct first response.

tasks.title: Task K. Emergency Equipment and Survival Gear

questions.question: On what frequencies does a 406 MHz ELT transmit, and why does it transmit on more than one frequency?
questions.answer: A 406 MHz ELT transmits on 406.028 MHz (the digital distress frequency monitored by COSPAS-SARSAT satellites) and simultaneously on 121.5 MHz (the international aeronautical emergency frequency monitored by rescue personnel and aircraft). The 406 MHz signal carries a digitally encoded identifier linked to the aircraft's registration, allowing SAR authorities to identify the aircraft before dispatching resources. The 121.5 MHz signal serves as a homing beacon that allows rescue personnel on scene to home in on the ELT's location using direction-finding equipment.

questions.question: What are the testing rules for an ELT — when can you test it, and how long can the test transmission last?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.207(g), ELT operational tests are authorized only during the first five minutes of any UTC hour. The test transmission must not exceed three audio sweeps. If the ELT is tested outside of that window, or the transmission lasts longer than three sweeps, it may be reported as an inadvertent activation and trigger a SAR response. Testing should be done with someone monitoring 121.5 MHz to confirm the signal, and any test should be coordinated with the nearest ATC facility if practical.

questions.question: How often must an ELT's battery be replaced or recharged, and what is the required battery life for the transmitter?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.207(c), an ELT battery must be replaced or recharged when: (1) the ELT has been in use for more than one cumulative hour, OR (2) when 50% of the battery's useful life (or 50% of the useful life of a rechargeable battery) has expired. The replacement or recharge date must be legibly marked on the outside of the transmitter. ELT batteries must be capable of powering the transmitter for a minimum of 48 hours of continuous operation at temperatures ranging from -20°C to +55°C.

questions.question: You land your helicopter following a hard autorotation touchdown that you don't consider a crash. During shutdown, you notice the ELT light is illuminated and 121.5 MHz is broadcasting a tone. What are your immediate actions, and what reporting obligations do you have?
questions.answer: Immediately switch the ELT to the OFF or ARM position to stop the transmission. Monitor 121.5 MHz to confirm the signal has stopped. Contact the nearest ATC facility or FSS immediately — on 121.5 MHz if necessary — to report the inadvertent activation, the duration of the transmission, your location, and that the signal has been terminated. This notification allows SAR authorities to stand down any response. Log the activation, duration, and all corrective actions taken. Have the ELT inspected before the next flight, because an activation from a hard landing may indicate the G-switch is triggered and the unit's structural integrity or mounting may be compromised. The ELT is required equipment under 14 CFR 91.207, so the helicopter is not airworthy until the ELT is confirmed serviceable.

questions.question: You are planning a remote mountain helicopter operation where cell phone coverage is unavailable. What are the key operational differences between a 406 MHz ELT and a personal locator beacon (PLB) that affect your survival gear decision?
questions.answer: A 406 MHz ELT is aircraft-mounted, activates automatically on impact via a G-switch, and is tied to the aircraft registration in the NOAA beacon registry. It transmits on both 406 MHz (satellite detection) and 121.5 MHz (homing). However, it is only useful if rescuers can reach the aircraft — in a remote mountain crash, the aircraft may be in a location inaccessible or invisible from the air. A PLB is a portable, person-worn device that also transmits on 406 MHz and 121.5 MHz, and many modern PLBs include integrated GPS that encodes your precise coordinates in the distress signal, dramatically reducing SAR response time. PLBs require manual activation. In a remote operation, carrying a GPS-equipped PLB on your person provides survival coverage even if you are separated from the aircraft. Neither device requires a subscription (unlike SPOT/InReach satellite messengers). The FAA requires a 406 MHz ELT on the aircraft under 14 CFR 91.207, but the PLB is additive crew/passenger survival gear, not a substitute.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.207; 47 CFR Part 95 Subpart F (PLB regulations); AIM 6-2-5

questions.question: During your preflight, you discover the ELT inoperative light is illuminated and the unit shows a fault. Under what conditions can you legally depart, and what must you do before flight?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.207(e), an aircraft may be operated without a functioning ELT only for the following: (1) ferrying a newly purchased aircraft from the manufacturer, (2) ferrying an aircraft with an inoperative ELT to a repair station, (3) aircraft engaged in training operations conducted entirely within 50 NM of the departure airport, (4) aircraft being ferried for installation of an ELT, or (5) aircraft operated in accordance with an approved MEL that specifically allows ELT deferral. For most routine helicopter operations, a malfunctioning ELT makes the aircraft unairworthy and you cannot depart. You must document the discrepancy in the aircraft maintenance records and have it repaired before flight. If you qualify for one of the ferry/training exceptions, you must log a notation in the aircraft records per 14 CFR 91.207(f). Do not simply switch the ELT to OFF and depart — that is not a legal solution.

questions.question: A pilot tells you: 'My ELT is in the ARM position, so if I crash it will go off automatically — I don't need to do anything else.' What is wrong with this reasoning, and what should a pilot actually understand about ELT activation limitations following a helicopter crash?
questions.answer: This reasoning is dangerously incomplete for several reasons specific to helicopter operations. First, the G-switch in an ELT is calibrated to activate under a specific impact deceleration force — typically around 5Gs in the crash axis. A helicopter crash involving a controlled autorotation with a hard touchdown, a wire strike, or a rollover may not generate sufficient linear deceleration in the correct axis to reliably trigger the G-switch. Water immersion, rolling terrain impacts, and dynamic rollover are all crash scenarios where ELT auto-activation cannot be guaranteed. Second, even if the ELT activates, it may be submerged, buried under wreckage, or its antenna may be damaged — all of which degrade or eliminate signal transmission. Third, the 406 MHz signal reaches satellites in low-Earth orbit, but GPS-equipped 406 ELTs dramatically reduce alert-to-location time; if the unit lacks GPS integration, SAR must triangulate position from multiple satellite passes, which can take 90 minutes or more. The pilot should know the ELT's manual activation procedure, know its physical location, and plan to manually activate it if conscious and able — never assume the G-switch handled it.
questions.follow_up: You mentioned the G-switch may not activate in some helicopter crashes. Is there anything about how helicopters typically crash that makes this a more significant concern than in fixed-wing accidents?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes — fixed-wing crashes frequently involve a high-energy forward deceleration on impact, which aligns well with the G-switch's design axis. Helicopter accidents are more kinematically varied: dynamic rollover produces lateral and rotational forces rather than axial deceleration; mast bumping and blade strike events can cause catastrophic structural failure without significant translational impact; settling with power or vortex ring state may produce a near-vertical descent with relatively low forward speed at impact. Additionally, helicopter main and tail rotor strikes during a crash often cause the airframe to rotate or tumble, meaning the peak deceleration vector may not align with the G-switch sensitive axis. This is precisely why helicopter pilots should be trained to manually activate the ELT immediately after any survivable accident if they are capable of doing so.

questions.question: What are the three main classes of fire extinguishing agents commonly found in helicopter emergency equipment, and what type of fire is each designed to combat?
questions.answer: The three common classes are: (1) CO2 (carbon dioxide) — effective on Class B (flammable liquid) and Class C (electrical) fires; suppresses oxygen but leaves no residue. (2) Dry chemical (e.g., monoammonium phosphate-based formulations or PKP) — effective on Class A (ordinary combustibles such as upholstery and insulation), Class B, and Class C fires; leaves residue that can damage avionics. (3) Halon 1211 or Halon replacement agents (e.g., Halotron I) — effective on Class B and C fires; leave no residue and are preferred for aircraft use due to minimal equipment damage. Class A fires can occur in helicopter cabins and involve materials like upholstery, insulation, and wiring jackets, making dry chemical agents valuable for cabin fire suppression.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10; NFPA fire classification standards
