questions.answer: Begin with both skids on the slope and the helicopter tilted into the hillside with cyclic. Increase collective smoothly to bring the helicopter to a hover in the tilted position — the downslope skid will lift first. As collective continues to increase, use cyclic to gradually level the fuselage laterally as the upslope skid breaks contact with the terrain. The goal is to transition from the tilted attitude into a level hover in a coordinated, simultaneous action. Anti-torque pedals maintain heading throughout. Once both skids are clear and the helicopter is in a level hover, normal departure can proceed.

questions.question: You are hovering alongside a slope preparing for a parallel slope landing. The wind is blowing upslope at 10 knots. How does this wind affect your approach and landing technique?
questions.answer: An upslope wind creates an effective headwind component to the rotor disc, increasing rotor efficiency and lift generation, similar to a headwind in normal operations. During the approach, this wind pressure on the lower rotor disc surface may require additional downslope cyclic input to maintain position and prevent drift upslope. Power requirements may be reduced due to increased rotor efficiency. The primary rotor clearance concern is ensuring the upslope rotor blade arc clears the rising terrain as the helicopter tilts into the slope — this is driven by slope angle and cyclic deflection (disc attitude), not wind direction. An upslope wind does not change blade clearance geometry, but the increased available lift can aid control and reduce power demand during the approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations; Chapter 4 (Translational Lift)

questions.question: During a parallel slope landing, the upslope skid is firmly on the ground and you are reducing collective to settle the downslope skid. You notice the helicopter is beginning to roll downhill and your lateral cyclic is nearly at the full upslope stop. What has likely happened and what is the correct immediate action?
questions.answer: This scenario describes the onset of dynamic rollover. The upslope skid has become a pivot point, and gravity combined with the lateral center of gravity shift is overpowering available cyclic authority. The correct immediate action is to increase collective aggressively and simultaneously apply full lateral cyclic into the slope to break the pivot point and get both skids airborne. Do not attempt to hold the position or gradually correct — once the rollover rate exceeds what cyclic can counter, the helicopter will roll uncontrollably. After lifting off, evaluate the site and slope angle before attempting another landing. The likely cause was that the slope exceeded the helicopter's cyclic authority range or the pilot allowed the downslope skid to hook on terrain, creating an uncontrolled pivot.
questions.follow_up: If you successfully go around after this near-rollover, how do you determine whether the slope is within limits before attempting again, and what tools or techniques can you use from the air?
questions.follow_up_answer: From the air, you can use a reconnaissance pass at a controlled airspeed and altitude to visually estimate the slope angle. One practical technique is to align the helicopter level and observe the angle of the terrain relative to a known reference such as the horizon or a spirit level if installed. Some pilots use the shadow of the helicopter skids as a reference. For a more accurate assessment, you can hover close to the slope and use the cyclic position required to maintain level hover as an indirect indicator — if full lateral cyclic is needed just to maintain position, the slope likely exceeds limits. If the slope cannot be visually assessed as within 5–10 degrees (or the manufacturer limit), the pilot must select an alternate landing area. There is no FAR requiring a specific measurement method, but the pilot in command is responsible under 14 CFR 91.3 for the safe outcome of the flight.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Dynamic Rollover and Slope Operations; 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: A student performs a textbook parallel slope landing — upslope skid first, smooth collective reduction, helicopter settles correctly. However, after shutdown you notice the main rotor blades have ground resonance-like vibration marks and one blade appears to have struck the tailboom. What in-flight condition during the slope operation could have caused rotor blade contact, and what technique error likely contributed?
questions.answer: On a slope, the rotor disc tilts with the fuselage during the landing sequence. As the helicopter leans into the slope with cyclic, the lower (downslope) portion of the rotor arc moves closer to the ground, and the upslope portion of the arc moves upward. However, a common technique error is allowing the collective to drop too rapidly while the helicopter is still in the tilted attitude. A rapid collective reduction causes blade flapping and reduces rotor RPM, which reduces gyroscopic rigidity and allows blade droop — particularly on the downslope side. The drooping blade can then contact the tailboom or even the terrain. The correct technique is to reduce collective slowly and smoothly while maintaining rotor RPM above minimum, especially while any lateral tilt exists. Additionally, dynamic rollover attempts that are overcorrected with abrupt cyclic can introduce flapping. This is why manufacturers specify minimum rotor RPM margins for slope operations and why the pilot must monitor N_r throughout.
questions.follow_up: Would this risk change depending on whether the helicopter has an articulated or semirigid rotor system, and if so, how?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, the risk profile differs significantly. Semirigid (teetering) rotor systems are more susceptible to mast bumping and blade flap-to-stop contact during low-G or abrupt control inputs, but they generally have predictable flapping characteristics. Articulated rotor systems, with their individual blade hinges (flap, lead/lag, and feather), can dissipate flapping loads more independently per blade, but the increased freedom of movement means individual blade droop at low RPM or during aggressive input is still a concern. Rigid rotor systems transfer more stress to the mast rather than allowing blade flap, which reduces droop risk but increases structural loading. For slope operations specifically, most manufacturers design slope limits around the lateral cyclic range of motion, not rotor type — but the pilot must always consult the specific RFM. Low-inertia rotor systems (common on lighter turbine helicopters) are especially sensitive to RPM decay, making smooth collective management on slopes even more critical.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10 (Slope Operations), Chapter 5 (Rotor Systems); POH/RFM manufacturer-specific limitations

questions.question: Before you begin a slope landing, what types of hazards are you specifically looking for during your reconnaissance of the area?
questions.answer: During a slope reconnaissance, you are looking for: obstacles on the slope itself (rocks, stumps, debris, tree branches) that could contact the rotor system or skids; the slope gradient (typically should not exceed the helicopter's maximum allowable slope angle per the RFM); surface conditions such as loose soil, gravel, ice, or mud that could cause skid slippage during landing; rotor clearance above the upslope terrain; and any wires, fences, or other hazards on the approach or departure paths. The goal is to confirm the landing surface is stable, obstruction-free, and within the aircraft's slope limitation.

questions.question: When you perform your slope area reconnaissance, at what altitude and airspeed should you typically conduct it, and how many orbits are standard?
questions.answer: A standard slope reconnaissance consists of at least one complete 360-degree orbit conducted at low and slow airspeed. Altitude is selected low enough to clearly observe surface hazards, slope gradient, and rotor clearance on the uphill side, but high enough to maintain safe margins above terrain and obstacles. The exact altitude depends on terrain elevation, obstacle proximity, and visibility conditions — the focus is on clear visual assessment of all landing zone hazards, not a prescribed altitude AGL. During the orbit, systematically check the slope gradient, surface composition, rotor blade clearance on the upslope side, and any approach and departure path obstacles.

questions.question: What is the primary rotor clearance concern unique to slope operations that you must verify during your area reconnaissance before touching down?
questions.answer: The primary rotor clearance concern in slope operations is the upslope rotor blade striking the rising terrain. As the downslope skid touches the ground first and the helicopter begins to tilt toward the slope, the uphill rotor blade arc descends closer to the hillside. During reconnaissance, the pilot must verify that there is adequate clearance between the upslope rotor disc and the terrain, vegetation, or rocks on the high side of the landing spot — even after the helicopter has settled and tilted to its maximum slope angle.

questions.question: You've done one orbit and the slope looks acceptable, but you notice the sun angle is making it hard to judge the surface texture on the uphill side. What do you do before committing to the landing?
questions.answer: If visibility, sun angle, or shadow is obscuring part of the landing zone, you should orbit again from a different direction or altitude to get a better viewing angle before committing. You might also approach to a stabilized hover close to the area to get a ground-level perspective and assess surface texture, loose material, and rotor clearance at close range without actually landing. If you still cannot confidently clear the area of hazards, the correct decision is to select an alternate site or delay the approach. The ACS standard requires the area to be confirmed clear — uncertainty is not acceptable.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13, ADM

questions.question: During your slope reconnaissance, you identify what appears to be a safe landing spot, but there is a large boulder just upslope and about 10 feet above your intended touchdown point. Walk me through how you evaluate whether that boulder is actually a hazard.
questions.answer: To evaluate the boulder as a hazard you must determine: (1) Rotor clearance — at the moment the downslope skid touches and the helicopter tilts toward the slope, will the upslope rotor blade arc clear the boulder? You must account for full blade flap and the tilt angle at maximum slope. (2) Ground resonance or rollover risk — if the surface shifts or you need to reposition, could the boulder block a skid or cause an uncontrolled roll? (3) Departure path — on liftoff, will the collective pull and cyclic repositioning move the rotor arc toward the boulder before you gain altitude? If any of these cannot be answered with a definitive 'no hazard,' the boulder makes that spot unsuitable and you should select a different landing point.

questions.question: You're conducting a slope operations maneuver during the practical test. After your orbit, you brief me on your go/no-go criteria. What specific conditions would make you call this a 'no-go' and select a different area?
questions.answer: A no-go determination for slope operations would be triggered by any of the following: (1) Slope gradient exceeds the helicopter's maximum allowable slope angle per the RFM (typically 8–10 degrees for most light helicopters); (2) Insufficient upslope rotor clearance from terrain, vegetation, rocks, or other obstacles; (3) Unstable or slippery surface (ice, loose shale, steep grass) that could allow skid sliding during or after touchdown; (4) Obstacles on the approach or departure path that cannot be cleared with available power; (5) OGE hover not achievable at that density altitude, making a go-around or abort impossible if needed; (6) Any doubt about the surface integrity or concealed hazards that cannot be resolved by additional reconnaissance. If any single condition is present and cannot be mitigated, a different site must be selected.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations; Helicopter RFM (manufacturer specific)

questions.question: You complete your reconnaissance, determine the slope is clear, and begin your approach. On short final, as you slow through ETL, you notice a wire you didn't see during your orbit — it's stretched across the upper portion of the slope between two trees and is right at rotor height. What are your immediate actions and what failure in your reconnaissance process allowed this to happen?
questions.answer: Immediate action: execute a go-around immediately — do not continue the approach. Apply collective to arrest descent, adjust cyclic for a climbing attitude, and clear the area while maintaining rotor clearance above the wire. Once at a safe altitude, re-evaluate the situation from a distance. Regarding the reconnaissance failure: wires are notoriously difficult to see during an orbit because they are thin, may blend with terrain or tree lines, and are often best spotted from below or from specific lighting angles. The failure likely occurred because: (1) the orbit altitude was too high or the angle of view was not varied sufficiently; (2) the sun angle or shadows concealed the wire; (3) the pilot looked for prominent hazards but did not specifically search the upslope tree line for wires or cables. Proper wire search technique requires examining the support structures (poles, trees with insulators) first and tracing the likely wire path between them — if you see supports, assume a wire.
questions.follow_up: After the go-around, you want to try again. The wire is still there — it's a legitimate utility line serving a remote structure on the slope. What are your options, and is there a legal obligation to avoid landing near it?
questions.follow_up_answer: Options include: (1) Select a landing site below the wire with adequate rotor clearance, confirming the approach path does not require crossing the wire; (2) Select an entirely different slope location that is not in proximity to the wire; (3) If the mission is critical, contact the utility owner or local authority for information about the line, though this is rarely practical in the field. Legally, there is no specific FAR that prohibits landing near utility lines, but 14 CFR 91.13 (careless or reckless operation) would apply if a pilot knowingly operates where rotor clearance cannot be assured. Additionally, if operating under Part 135 or a specific operating certificate, company operations specifications may have additional restrictions. The pilot-in-command bears ultimate responsibility under 14 CFR 91.3 for the safety of the operation, meaning if the wire cannot be safely avoided, the landing must not be made.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations; 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.13

questions.question: A student pilot tells you that once they identify a good-looking slope during the initial orbit, they go straight into the approach to save time. What is wrong with this technique, and what specific hazard does shortcutting the full reconnaissance create in slope operations that is more dangerous than in a flat confined area landing?
questions.answer: This technique is incorrect and dangerous for several reasons specific to slope operations: (1) A single orbit from one altitude and direction may not reveal all hazards — particularly upslope obstacles, wires between trees, surface instability, or insufficient rotor clearance on the high side, all of which require viewing from multiple angles; (2) Slope operations are uniquely dangerous because the upslope rotor blade is in closest proximity to terrain precisely at the moment the pilot's workload is highest — during the landing sequence itself — leaving no margin for discovering a hidden hazard at that point; (3) On a flat confined area, a concealed obstacle primarily threatens the fuselage or skids; on a slope, an unseen upslope obstacle can strike the rotor system, which is immediately catastrophic and non-recoverable; (4) The slope gradient itself must be estimated from the reconnaissance — a slope that appears manageable from one angle may exceed RFM limits when viewed perpendicular to the fall line. The abbreviated reconnaissance eliminates the pilot's only reliable opportunity to identify these hazards before they become unrecoverable. Proper technique requires at least one full 360-degree orbit with deliberate attention to the upslope side, surface, approach/departure paths, and any stretched hazards such as wires.
questions.follow_up: If a slope landing is being conducted for an EMS mission at night with NVGs, how does the hazard-clearing requirement change, and what technique compensates for reduced NVG depth perception during reconnaissance?
questions.follow_up_answer: At night with NVGs, the reconnaissance requirement does not change — the area must still be confirmed clear of hazards — but the techniques used must adapt to NVG limitations. NVGs reduce depth perception and make it very difficult to assess surface texture, gradient, and thin hazards like wires. To compensate: (1) Use a lower, slower reconnaissance orbit to place obstacles closer to the field of view and reduce depth perception error; (2) Use a hover taxi or slow approach to the landing area to assess surface and rotor clearance from close proximity before committing to the landing; (3) Use a searchlight or landing light to illuminate the upslope area and surface — NVG performance improves significantly with some visible light illumination; (4) Look for wires by searching for poles, towers, or trees with unusual top structures and assume a wire runs between them; (5) If any doubt exists, do not land — EMS urgency is not a legal or safety justification for conducting an approach into an inadequately reconnoitered slope LZ. 14 CFR 91.3 PIC authority and 91.13 careless operation standards apply regardless of mission urgency.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 10, Slope Operations; 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.13; NVG operational guidance per operator specifications

questions.question: You are preparing to demonstrate slope operations in a helicopter, and the POH does not publish a specific slope limitation. A candidate tells you the slope looks 'about 12 degrees.' How do you respond, and what action do you take?
questions.answer: When a helicopter's POH does not publish a specific slope limitation, you must rely on general helicopter operating principles and manufacturer guidance. FAA-H-8083-21B explains that slope operations carry significant dynamic rollover risk, and that risk increases as slope angle increases. Without a published limitation to define a safe boundary, a conservative approach is required — you should not proceed onto a slope that exceeds what you can reasonably determine is within the aircraft's lateral cyclic authority and within safe dynamic rollover margins. A 12-degree slope is relatively steep for most light helicopters, and without manufacturer approval or a published limitation, proceeding onto it introduces unknown and potentially unacceptable risk. The correct action is to select a shallower, more clearly manageable slope for the demonstration. If the POH does publish a slope limitation — as many manufacturers do in the Limitations section — that published value governs, and you must operate within it. The key instructional point is that the absence of a published limitation does not mean any slope is acceptable; it means you must apply conservative judgment and keep the aircraft within known safe operating parameters.
questions.rewrite_note: Revised the question to remove the R44-specific scenario that contradicts actual published R44 POH data, and rewrote the answer to avoid citing a specific degree range as ACS doctrine, instead grounding the guidance in FAA-H-8083-21B principles of dynamic rollover risk and conservative judgment when POH limits are absent.

questions.question: When no manufacturer-published slope limitation exists in the RFM/POH, how should a pilot determine a safe operating limit for slope landings?
questions.answer: When no manufacturer-published slope limit is available, the pilot should apply conservative judgment and consult the RFM/POH as the primary authority, since no universal FAA-established default slope angle applies to all helicopters. FAA-H-8083-21B discusses slope operations in the context of dynamic rollover risk and notes that each helicopter has its own critical rollover angle based on its design and center of gravity. Without a specific manufacturer limit, pilots must treat any slope operation with extra caution, use conservative technique, and recognize that the dynamic rollover risk increases as slope angle increases. The safest approach is to avoid slopes that cannot be verified as within the aircraft's demonstrated or approved limits.
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the unsupported '5 to 10 degree' default range and the inaccurate attribution to ACS standards; replaced with guidance grounded in FAA-H-8083-21B emphasizing conservative judgment and manufacturer-specific data as the proper reference.

tasks.title: VI. Performance Maneuvers – Task B. Straight-In Autorotation in a Single-Engine Helicopter (Operational Requirements)

questions.question: What is the minimum entry altitude required for a straight-in autorotation in a single-engine helicopter during a practical test?
questions.answer: The minimum entry altitude is 500 feet AGL. This ensures the pilot has adequate altitude to establish a stable autorotative descent, maintain rotor RPM within limits, and complete the maneuver safely. The ACS specifies 500 feet AGL as the floor for initiating the autorotation.

issues: The answer cites ACS CH.XIV.B as the source for '500 feet AGL minimum entry altitude' but does not acknowledge that the ACS language for straight-in autorotations uses qualitative language like 'suitable' and 'adequate' rather than a hard numerical minimum. The ACS does not explicitly state '500 feet AGL is the minimum' — this may be an interpretation or a reference to helicopter-specific ACS guidance that varies by aircraft type. A checkride examiner could interpret this as overstated precision.

The answer lacks citation of the actual FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 to verify the 500-foot figure; while 500 feet is a common training standard, the FAA handbook reference should be specific about whether this is a regulatory minimum or a training recommendation.
verification.suggested_correction: Revise to: 'A practical minimum entry altitude is approximately 500 feet AGL for single-engine helicopters, ensuring adequate time to lower collective, establish autorotative descent, stabilize rotor RPM, and execute a safe flare and landing. However, the ACS uses qualitative language (suitable, adequate altitude) rather than a hard regulatory minimum, meaning entry altitude should be adjusted based on wind, rotor type, and landing zone complexity. The 500-foot figure is a widely accepted training standard derived from FAA guidance, not a regulatory floor that cannot be adjusted by pilot judgment.'
verification.triage_note: The claim that 'ACS CH.XIV.B specifies 500 feet AGL as the floor' overstates regulatory precision; the ACS uses qualitative language (adequate, suitable) rather than a hard numerical minimum, and the specific FAA-H-8083-21B citation for 500 feet is not verified.

questions.question: Why does the ACS allow for a 'suitable higher entry altitude' for straight-in autorotations in strong wind conditions?
questions.answer: Strong winds — particularly headwinds or gusty conditions — affect glide distance, descent rate, and groundspeed during autorotation. A higher entry altitude provides more time and altitude margin to compensate for unpredictable wind effects, maintain aircraft control, and reach the intended landing point safely. The 500-foot AGL minimum is a floor, not a target; actual entry altitude should reflect current conditions.

questions.question: What is the primary reason a minimum entry altitude of 500 feet AGL is established for straight-in autorotations rather than a lower altitude like 200 or 300 feet AGL?
questions.answer: 500 feet AGL provides the minimum altitude needed to accomplish the critical tasks at autorotation entry: immediately lowering collective to arrest rotor RPM decay, applying aft cyclic to control airspeed, establishing the proper glide attitude, and then managing the flare and collective application at the bottom. Low-inertia rotor systems in particular experience rapid RPM decay, so adequate altitude is necessary to allow rotor RPM stabilization before the flare. Below 500 feet, there is insufficient time and altitude margin to complete all these steps safely.

questions.question: You are about to demonstrate a straight-in autorotation on a checkride. Winds are reported at 25 knots gusting to 35 knots down the runway. Your DPE says you may enter at the standard 500-foot AGL entry point. How do you respond, and what altitude would you recommend instead?
questions.answer: I would respectfully explain that while 500 feet AGL is the regulatory minimum, the ACS specifically allows — and judgment requires — a higher entry altitude in strong wind conditions. With gusts of 35 knots, the groundspeed will vary significantly during the descent, affecting glide distance and landing point accuracy. I would recommend entering at a higher altitude — typically 700 to 1,000 feet AGL depending on the specific helicopter and conditions — to provide an adequate margin to assess the glide, manage the variable winds, and safely execute the flare and collective pull at the bottom. Safe pilot judgment supersedes meeting a minimum standard.

questions.question: During preflight planning for a checkride autorotation, you identify that the departure end of the runway has a 50-foot tree line 200 feet beyond the intended touchdown point. How does this factor affect your decision about entry altitude for the straight-in autorotation?
questions.answer: The obstacle at the departure end creates a more demanding landing zone, reducing the margin for error in glide path management. Although the ACS minimum is 500 feet AGL, this scenario warrants a higher entry altitude to provide additional time to fine-tune the glide angle and ensure the aircraft clears the obstacle and reaches the touchdown point accurately. A higher entry also allows more time to recognize and correct a long or short glide before it becomes unrecoverable. This is precisely the kind of judgment the ACS phrase 'suitable higher entry altitude' is designed to address.

questions.question: How does the type of rotor system — specifically a low-inertia vs. high-inertia main rotor — affect your entry altitude decision for a straight-in autorotation, and does the 500-foot AGL minimum change based on rotor type?
questions.answer: The 500-foot AGL minimum in the ACS does not change based on rotor type — it is the established floor for all single-engine helicopter straight-in autorotations. However, rotor inertia is a critical operational factor. A low-inertia rotor system loses RPM much more rapidly after power loss, meaning the pilot has less time to lower collective and establish the autorotative glide before rotor RPM decays to a dangerous level. In practice, a pilot flying a low-inertia aircraft should be especially diligent about not delaying the entry and may benefit from a higher entry altitude to ensure rotor RPM is stabilized before the critical flare phase. The ACS minimum is a floor; operational judgment based on aircraft type should always drive the actual entry altitude.

questions.question: A student argues that since the ACS only sets a minimum entry altitude of 500 feet AGL, and they can consistently nail touchdown within the standards from that height in calm winds, there is no reason to ever enter higher. What is the flaw in this reasoning, and what principle of ADM does it violate?
questions.answer: The flaw is that the student is confusing 'minimum standard' with 'best practice' and is failing to account for variability in conditions. The ACS minimum of 500 feet AGL was established for controlled training environments with favorable conditions. Real-world factors — wind, turbulence, rotor system type, pilot workload, and landing zone complexity — can all compress the margin of safety at the minimum altitude. The ADM principle being violated is risk management: specifically, the failure to evaluate changing conditions and adjust the plan accordingly. The ACS explicitly acknowledges this by requiring 'a suitable higher entry altitude in strong wind conditions,' signaling that pilot judgment — not just compliance with minimums — is expected. Relying only on minimums reflects a 'get-there' or complacency mindset rather than sound aeronautical decision-making.
questions.follow_up: If that same student, now a certificated commercial pilot, consistently enters autorotations at exactly 500 feet AGL regardless of conditions during actual emergency training, what specific hazard does this create, and how would you counsel them?
questions.follow_up_answer: The hazard is that the student has no altitude margin to recover from suboptimal entry execution — such as a delayed collective reduction causing rotor RPM decay, or an unexpected gust altering the glide — at 500 feet AGL there is no room to correct these errors before the aircraft reaches the ground. During a real emergency, conditions are rarely optimal, and a pilot who has only practiced from the minimum altitude has not developed the full skill set needed for variable real-world situations. I would counsel the pilot to regularly practice from higher entry altitudes to understand the full glide envelope of their specific helicopter, to develop the judgment to recognize when conditions demand a higher entry, and to internalize that minimums exist to prevent unsafe operations — not to define normal operating practice. I would also reference the HFH principle that accidents decrease significantly after 100 hours in type, emphasizing that experience-building should include practicing in varied conditions, not just optimized ones.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS CH.XIV.B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM); FAA-H-8083-21B Glossary

questions.question: During a checkride, you are at 500 feet AGL established on final when a sudden gust shifts the wind from a 10-knot headwind to a 20-knot tailwind. You are now committed to the autorotation. How does this wind shift affect your energy management, and at what point in the maneuver is your exposure to landing short most critical?
questions.answer: A sudden tailwind shift during an established autorotation dramatically increases groundspeed while the rotor RPM and descent rate remain initially unchanged. This means the aircraft will cover ground much faster than planned, risking an overshoot of the touchdown point — but the more insidious danger is that if the pilot reacts by adjusting glide angle, they may slow the aircraft and land short. The energy budget changes because the tail wind reduces the headwind component available to arrest forward speed during the flare. The most critical exposure to landing short occurs during the flare: the pilot normally uses aft cyclic to trade forward airspeed for rotor RPM and reduced descent rate. With a tailwind, effective airspeed is reduced, making the flare less effective — rotor RPM may not increase as much as expected, and the deceleration will be less pronounced, potentially resulting in a hard landing or landing with excessive forward groundspeed. The mitigation at 500 feet AGL with no additional altitude margin is extremely limited — this scenario illustrates precisely why the ACS mandates higher entry altitudes in strong or variable wind conditions, as a committed autorotation from the minimum altitude in these conditions leaves no room for correction.
questions.follow_up: Given that you are now committed with no additional altitude available, walk me through the exact control priorities during the flare and collective pull to minimize the risk of a hard landing or dynamic rollover given the tailwind condition.
questions.follow_up_answer: With a tailwind reducing effective airspeed during the flare, I would initiate the flare slightly earlier than normal to begin trading what forward airspeed remains for rotor RPM and reduced descent rate, accepting that the deceleration will be less dramatic than usual. I would be especially attentive to rotor RPM — if it does not climb into the green arc as expected, I would use collective judiciously to trade altitude for RPM rather than allowing rotor RPM to fall below limits. As the aircraft approaches the surface with higher-than-normal groundspeed, I would level the skids slightly earlier to prevent tail strike, then apply collective to cushion the touchdown, accepting a longer ground roll if needed. To prevent dynamic rollover — which is a significant risk when landing with lateral or forward groundspeed on a surface — I would ensure the cyclic is centered to neutral at touchdown and apply collective smoothly, not abruptly. If groundspeed is excessive and a safe landing appears unachievable, the appropriate decision — if altitude permits — would be to convert to a run-on landing along the runway to dissipate energy progressively rather than forcing a full stop.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS CH.XIV.B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Autorotation, Dynamic Rollover); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation checkride, if you find yourself too high and too fast on final and cannot correct in time, what does the ACS say about initiating a go-around?
questions.answer: The ACS states that initiating a go-around because the applicant cannot complete the straight-in autorotation within the specified tolerances is considered an unsatisfactory performance. A go-around taken due to inability to meet standards — not for a genuine safety reason — means the applicant did not demonstrate the required skill and the task is failed.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-18 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: What is the difference between a go-around initiated for a legitimate safety reason and one initiated because the applicant cannot meet the ACS skill tolerances during a straight-in autorotation?
questions.answer: A go-around taken for a genuine safety reason — such as an unexpected obstacle, another aircraft on the landing area, or a mechanical concern — is acceptable and does not automatically result in an unsatisfactory grade. However, a go-around initiated solely because the applicant recognizes they cannot land within the ACS-specified tolerances (touchdown point, airspeed, rotor RPM) is considered unsatisfactory. The ACS specifically addresses this distinction: inability to perform the task within tolerances is the defining factor for an unsatisfactory outcome.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-18 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: Name the primary skill tolerances specified in the ACS for a straight-in autorotation that, if not met, would make a go-around a result of inability rather than sound judgment.
questions.answer: The ACS skill elements for a straight-in autorotation in a single-engine helicopter include: maintaining rotor RPM within the normal operating range (green arc), controlling airspeed within ±10 knots of the manufacturer's recommended autorotation airspeed (or ±10 KIAS if not published), touching down within the designated or selected landing area, and completing a smooth, controlled termination. If the applicant is off on any of these parameters and executes a go-around to avoid failing them, the ACS treats that go-around itself as the indicator of unsatisfactory performance.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-18 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B Skills elements; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: You are on a checkride performing a straight-in autorotation. At about 200 feet AGL you realize your airspeed is 15 knots above the target and your glide path will carry you well past the intended landing spot. You initiate a go-around. How will the examiner evaluate this decision, and what should you have done differently earlier in the approach?
questions.answer: The examiner will evaluate this as an unsatisfactory performance because the ACS explicitly states that initiating a go-around due to inability to complete the task within tolerances is unsatisfactory. The error chain started much earlier — likely at the entry point or mid-approach — where the high airspeed and shallow glide should have been identified and corrected. Proper earlier interventions include: adjusting the glide path angle with aft cyclic to steepen the descent and bleed airspeed, or selecting a new landing point further down the area. Situational awareness and early correction are the expected demonstration, not a late go-around to avoid consequences.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-18 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Chapter 13 (ADM/error chain)

questions.question: A student argues: 'I initiated the go-around because it was the safe thing to do — I would have been out of the landing area.' How would you, as an examiner, respond to distinguish between a safety-based and a performance-based go-around decision?
questions.answer: As an examiner, you would acknowledge that safety always comes first. However, the ACS distinction is clear: if the applicant's own technique errors — excess airspeed, poor glide path management, improper flare timing — placed them outside tolerances, and a go-around was used as an escape from demonstrating the skill, that is an unsatisfactory performance. A safety-based go-around involves an external or unforeseen hazard (obstacle, traffic, mechanical issue) that a competent pilot at any skill level would reasonably respond to. The examiner's job is to determine whether the unsafe condition was created by the applicant's failure to manage the approach correctly. If it was, the go-around is the product of inability, not sound ADM.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-18 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation practice, your instructor has always said 'if in doubt, go around.' How does that training philosophy need to be adjusted for the actual checkride environment as it relates to the ACS go-around standard?
questions.answer: The training philosophy of 'if in doubt, go around' is sound for building safe habits and is always appropriate when there is a genuine external hazard. However, on the checkride the ACS holds the applicant to a higher standard: the go-around must not be used as a mechanism to avoid demonstrating the skill within tolerances. The applicant is expected to recognize developing problems early enough to correct them — not late enough that a go-around becomes the only option. The adjustment in mindset is: train to recognize and correct deviations early (airspeed, glide path, RPM) so that a go-around from performance failure never becomes necessary. Reserve the go-around for true external safety threats.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-18 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (SRM, ADM)

questions.question: An applicant is performing a straight-in autorotation and at 100 feet AGL, the examiner observes an unauthorized vehicle entering the designated landing area. The applicant initiates a go-around. Is this a satisfactory or unsatisfactory performance, and why does this scenario directly challenge the ACS language about go-arounds being unsatisfactory?
questions.answer: This is a satisfactory performance. The ACS language states that a go-around resulting from the applicant's inability to complete the task within tolerances is unsatisfactory. In this scenario, the trigger for the go-around is an external hazard — a vehicle in the landing zone — not the applicant's technique. The applicant demonstrating situational awareness and executing a go-around for a legitimate safety reason actually shows sound ADM, which is itself an ACS requirement. The key legal and evaluative distinction is causation: who or what caused the need for the go-around. Examiner-introduced or environmental factors do not count against the applicant. Only the applicant's own performance failures that necessitate a go-around result in an unsatisfactory grade.
questions.follow_up: How should the examiner document this scenario in the applicant's evaluation, and should the task be re-attempted?
questions.follow_up_answer: The examiner should document that the go-around was initiated due to an external safety hazard, not due to applicant error, and that the applicant demonstrated appropriate situational awareness and ADM. The task should be re-attempted so the applicant has a fair opportunity to demonstrate the straight-in autorotation skill within tolerances. The examiner retains discretion to continue or discontinue the practical test based on overall conditions, but the interrupted task does not count as a failed attempt. This is consistent with FAA guidance that applicants should not be penalized for sound safety decisions triggered by factors outside their control.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-18 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA Order 8900.2 (Practical Test Examiner Handbook); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM)

questions.question: Consider this edge case: an applicant is well within all ACS tolerances on a straight-in autorotation — good airspeed, on glide path, RPM in the green — but at 50 feet AGL loses confidence and initiates a go-around without any external reason. How do you evaluate this, and what does it reveal about readiness for certification?
questions.answer: This is an unsatisfactory performance for the straight-in autorotation task. Even though the parameters were within tolerances up to the go-around, the ACS requires the applicant to complete the task — including the termination phase — within the specified tolerances. A go-around taken at 50 feet AGL due to loss of confidence, not due to any external or mechanical factor, is definitionally a failure to complete the task. Furthermore, this scenario reveals a deeper concern: the applicant has not demonstrated the decision-making confidence and commitment required of a certificated pilot. A pilot who abandons a safe approach at 50 feet due to self-doubt introduces unnecessary risk (power application, rotor RPM changes, obstacle clearance) without justification. It raises a red flag about the applicant's overall readiness for unsupervised flight.
questions.follow_up: Could this same applicant be passed on the autorotation task if, immediately after the go-around, they explain their reasoning and request another attempt?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — the task has already been evaluated as unsatisfactory. The ACS does not provide for post-hoc explanations to reverse an unsatisfactory grade within the same attempt. The examiner may, at their discretion, allow a re-attempt of the task during the same practical test if time and safety permit, but the original attempt is documented as unsatisfactory. If re-attempted, the applicant must complete the full task within all tolerances, and the examiner must note both attempts. Repeated unsatisfactory performance or failure to meet standards on a second attempt will result in a discontinuation and a Notice of Disapproval. The applicant's explanation might be informative for the debrief but does not change the grade.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-18 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA Order 8900.2; 14 CFR 61.43 (Practical tests: failure)

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation, what is a 'landing area safety concern beyond the control of the applicant'? Give me two examples.
questions.answer: A landing area safety concern beyond the control of the applicant is any hazard that appears in or near the intended touchdown zone that the pilot could not have anticipated or prevented. Examples include: (1) a vehicle, animal, or person entering the landing area during the approach, and (2) debris blown onto the touchdown zone by wind. Because these hazards are outside the pilot's control, executing a go-around in response does not count against the applicant.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; ACS CH.XIV.B Landing note

questions.question: According to the ACS, if a go-around is required during a straight-in autorotation because of a landing area safety concern beyond the applicant's or evaluator's control, how does that affect the outcome of the task?
questions.answer: It does not affect the outcome negatively. The ACS specifically states that a go-around necessitated by landing area safety concerns beyond the control of the applicant or evaluator would not be considered unsatisfactory. The maneuver would typically be re-attempted under suitable conditions.

questions.question: Who has the authority to call a go-around during a straight-in autorotation checkride task if a landing area hazard suddenly appears?
questions.answer: Either the applicant or the evaluator may call the go-around. The ACS language covers safety concerns 'beyond the control of the applicant or evaluator,' meaning both parties share responsibility for recognizing and acting on unexpected hazards to the landing area. Either party initiating a go-around for this reason will not result in an unsatisfactory grade.

questions.question: You are on final in a straight-in autorotation during your checkride. At low altitude you spot a dog running into your intended touchdown zone. You execute a go-around. Your examiner says nothing. Should you expect a pink slip for deviating from the autorotation? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: No. A dog entering the landing zone is a safety concern entirely beyond the applicant's control. The ACS explicitly protects applicants from an unsatisfactory grade when a go-around is necessitated by such conditions. The more important consideration is whether a power recovery go-around is even possible at the altitude where the dog is spotted — which reinforces why constant monitoring of the landing area throughout the autorotation is essential. If altitude and energy state permit a safe go-around, executing it is the correct aeronautical decision. If not, the pilot must manage the landing around the obstacle as best as possible.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS CH.XIV.B Landing note; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: During autorotation training, at what point in the approach does a go-around option typically become unavailable, and how does that affect how you monitor the landing area?
questions.answer: Once a helicopter descends below the power recovery altitude — generally accepted as the altitude at which the engine can be re-engaged and rotor RPM/airspeed restored before touchdown — a go-around is no longer a viable option. This threshold varies by helicopter type, density altitude, and rotor inertia. Because of this, the pilot must actively monitor the landing zone continuously throughout the entire approach, not just on short final. Identifying a hazard early, while altitude and energy still permit a power recovery, is critical. Waiting until the flare or cushion phase to notice a hazard may leave no safe option.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; ACS CH.XIV.B Landing note

questions.question: Contrast a landing area hazard that is 'beyond the control of the applicant' with one that IS within the applicant's control. Why does this distinction matter on a checkride?
questions.answer: A hazard beyond the applicant's control is one that arises unexpectedly and cannot be mitigated through preflight planning or in-flight judgment — such as a vehicle suddenly entering the pad, an animal on the runway, or debris blown in by wind during the approach. A hazard within the applicant's control would be one the pilot should have identified and planned around — such as a poorly chosen landing zone that was clearly unsuitable during the pre-approach briefing, obstacles the pilot could have noticed earlier, or a touchdown point the pilot should have adjusted before committing to the approach. This distinction matters because the ACS only protects the applicant from an unsatisfactory grade for hazards outside their control. Poor pre-planning or failure to monitor a predictable hazard is a demonstration of inadequate risk management and can result in an unsatisfactory.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS CH.XIV.B Landing note; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/Risk Management)

questions.question: An examiner is administering a straight-in autorotation and, at 50 feet AGL during the flare, notices a runway incursion. The examiner calls for a go-around. The applicant hesitates and the examiner takes the controls. Does the applicant fail the task? Walk me through your analysis.
questions.answer: Not necessarily, and this requires careful analysis. First, a safety concern beyond the evaluator's control is treated the same as one beyond the applicant's control under the ACS — the go-around itself does not render the task unsatisfactory. However, the applicant's hesitation when a go-around was called raises a separate concern: crew/evaluator communication and timely response. At 50 feet AGL during the flare, a power recovery go-around in most helicopters is marginal at best and may not be feasible depending on the aircraft. If the examiner took the controls to prevent an accident, that action would likely constitute a safety-of-flight intervention, which under 14 CFR 61.43 would result in a notice of disapproval — not because of the hazard, but because the applicant's hesitation required examiner intervention to maintain safety. The key distinction is: the go-around necessity is not unsatisfactory; the need for examiner takeover to prevent an accident is.
questions.follow_up: If the examiner takes the controls during a checkride to prevent an accident, is that automatically a failure, and where does that standard come from?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, under 14 CFR 61.43(a)(1), an applicant fails a practical test if they fail to demonstrate the ability to perform the procedures and maneuvers included in the standards to the level of competency required, or if they require the examiner to take action to prevent an unsafe condition. FAA Order 8900.2 and the ACS preamble further clarify that any intervention by the evaluator necessary to maintain safety of flight results in a notice of disapproval. This is separate from and in addition to the specific task grade — the overall practical test is discontinued at that point.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.43(a)(1); ACS CH.XIV.B Landing note; FAA Order 8900.2

questions.question: You complete a straight-in autorotation and the landing area was clear throughout. You touchdown 200 feet beyond your intended point because you misjudged the flare. Your examiner says the overshoot was due to an unexpected tailwind gust at 20 feet. Does the ACS landing safety concern provision protect you here? What's the examiner's correct call?
questions.answer: No, the landing area safety concern provision does not apply here. That provision specifically addresses hazards in the landing area — physical obstacles, incursions, or obstructions — that necessitate a go-around. It does not cover performance deviations caused by environmental conditions like an unexpected gust. An unexpected tailwind gust that causes a touchdown point deviation is an aeronautical skill and energy management issue. The examiner's correct call depends on the ACS tolerances for the maneuver — if the overshoot was within the acceptable landing zone and the applicant demonstrated sound technique throughout the approach, it may still be satisfactory. If the overshoot exceeded the standards or resulted in an unsafe landing, it would be graded on its merits as a skills deficiency, not protected by the safety concern provision. The examiner should evaluate whether the applicant's response to the gust (any cyclic/collective corrections, flare adjustment) demonstrated sound aeronautical decision-making and helicopter control.
questions.follow_up: What should an applicant do during the approach briefing before a straight-in autorotation to address the possibility of a changing wind environment near the surface?
questions.follow_up_answer: During the approach briefing, the applicant should identify the reported and observed surface wind direction and velocity, discuss how wind shifts or gusts could affect energy management during the flare and cushion, establish a plan for adjusting the flare point if the approach becomes high or low energy, and identify a go/no-go decision altitude for power recovery if conditions deteriorate. Referencing surface indicators such as windsocks, trees, or dust throughout the approach — not just on initial setup — is part of sound situational awareness and workload management per SRM principles in FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS CH.XIV.B Landing note; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation on a checkride, who bears responsibility for ensuring the maneuver does not compromise flight safety?
questions.answer: Both the applicant and the evaluator share responsibility for flight safety during the autorotation. Neither party may sacrifice safety of flight to complete the task. If at any point the maneuver cannot be completed safely — due to aircraft position, altitude, airspeed, rotor RPM, or any other factor — a power recovery must be initiated.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: What does it mean to 'force a landing' during a straight-in autorotation, and why is this prohibited during the practical test?
questions.answer: Forcing a landing means continuing an autorotation to touchdown even when the flight parameters — such as rotor RPM, airspeed, altitude, or approach angle — are outside safe limits, or when the intended landing area is no longer suitable. This is prohibited because it prioritizes task completion over aircraft and crew safety. A power recovery must be executed any time a safe landing cannot be assured.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: At what point during a straight-in autorotation is a power recovery required?
questions.answer: A power recovery is required any time the evaluator or applicant determines that a safe landing cannot be completed — for example, if rotor RPM decays out of the normal operating range, airspeed is insufficient, the approach angle is too steep or too shallow to reach the intended landing zone, or any other condition arises that jeopardizes flight safety. There is no requirement to touch down; safety always takes precedence over task completion.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: You are on a straight-in autorotation and your rotor RPM has decayed to the lower limit of the green arc. You believe you can still make the landing zone. Should you continue the autorotation to touchdown? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No. Even if you believe touchdown is achievable, rotor RPM at the bottom of the green arc provides minimal margin for the flare and cushion. Any further decay during the flare could result in blade stall, which in a helicopter is not recoverable. The ACS requirement is explicit — neither the applicant nor the evaluator may sacrifice safety to complete the task. You should initiate a power recovery immediately to restore rotor RPM and reassess. Continuing would be 'forcing a landing,' which is prohibited.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation on your checkride, the examiner says nothing but you recognize you are undershooting the landing zone significantly. What is the correct course of action, and what principle supports your decision?
questions.answer: You should initiate a power recovery without waiting for the examiner to intervene. As pilot in command, you are responsible for the safety of flight. Continuing an autorotation into terrain short of the intended landing area is exactly the scenario the ACS prohibition on 'forcing a landing' is designed to prevent. The examiner may also call for a power recovery, but you do not need to wait — proactive recognition and action is a demonstration of sound aeronautical decision-making (ADM). Hoping the situation will 'probably' work out is exactly what FAA guidance says to avoid.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; 14 CFR 91.3; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: If an examiner directs you to continue an autorotation to touchdown even though you believe the approach is unsafe, are you required to comply? Explain your answer.
questions.answer: No. As pilot in command under 14 CFR 91.3, you have final authority over the operation of the aircraft. The ACS explicitly states that neither the applicant nor the evaluator may sacrifice safety of flight to complete the task. If you determine the autorotation cannot be completed safely, you are both authorized and obligated to initiate a power recovery regardless of examiner direction. Complying with an unsafe instruction would not be a demonstration of good judgment — it would be a safety violation.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B

questions.question: An applicant on a checkride executes a power recovery from a straight-in autorotation at 200 feet AGL because they were slightly undershooting. The examiner feels the applicant could have made it with a more aggressive flare. Does this power recovery constitute a failure of the task?
questions.answer: Not necessarily, and likely not. The ACS explicitly prohibits forcing a landing to complete the task. If the applicant exercised sound judgment by identifying a developing undershoot and initiated a timely power recovery, that reflects good ADM and conservative decision-making — both of which are valued by the FAA. An examiner cannot fail an applicant for choosing safety over task completion. The evaluator should assess whether the decision was reasonable given the conditions, not whether the applicant 'could have made it' in hindsight. The ACS standard exists precisely to prevent pressure from the evaluation environment from overriding safety judgment.
questions.follow_up: What if the applicant made a habit of initiating power recoveries very early on every autorotation attempt — say, from 500 feet — citing safety concerns each time? Could that pattern itself be grounds for a task failure?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, potentially. While a single conservative power recovery is appropriate and should not be penalized, a pattern of excessively early recoveries that never allow evaluation of the applicant's ability to manage the autorotation to a reasonable conclusion could indicate a lack of proficiency in the task. The examiner must evaluate whether the applicant demonstrates the knowledge, risk management, and skills required by the ACS. If the applicant is unable or unwilling to manage an autorotation through the critical phases — flare and cushion — the examiner cannot adequately assess competency, and may determine the task has not been demonstrated to the required standard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and 13

questions.question: How does the ACS requirement that neither applicant nor evaluator may force a landing relate to the broader concept of single-pilot resource management (SRM) and the error chain?
questions.answer: This ACS requirement directly reflects SRM and error chain principles from FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13. Approximately 80% of aviation accidents result from human factors, and accidents typically result from a chain of poor decisions rather than a single mistake. During a checkride, evaluation pressure can create a powerful incentive to continue a deteriorating autorotation rather than admit the approach is failing — this is exactly the kind of subtle psychological pressure that leads to 'get-there-itis' or task fixation. The ACS rule removes that ambiguity by explicitly stating that safety supersedes task completion. Recognizing the developing error chain — deteriorating RPM, poor approach angle, inadequate airspeed — and breaking that chain with a power recovery is precisely the kind of SRM behavior the FAA wants to evaluate and reinforce.
questions.follow_up: How might confirmation bias contribute to a pilot forcing a landing during an autorotation, and what specific SRM technique helps counter it?
questions.follow_up_answer: Confirmation bias occurs when a pilot unconsciously seeks information that supports a decision already made — in this case, 'I'm going to make the landing zone.' The pilot may focus on a favorable rotor RPM reading while disregarding a worsening approach angle or decreasing airspeed. The SRM technique that directly counters this is situational awareness combined with the 'DECIDE' model or similar structured ADM framework — requiring the pilot to actively detect changes, estimate their significance, choose a course of action, and evaluate the outcome. Additionally, the 'Trescott Tip' from the HFH advises that if a plan will only 'probably' work, choose a course of action that is known to work — in this case, a power recovery.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B

questions.question: Why does the ACS call for a higher entry altitude than 500 feet AGL during strong wind conditions when practicing straight-in autorotations?
questions.answer: Strong winds increase the complexity and unpredictability of the autorotation. Wind shear, turbulence near the ground, and shifting wind direction can alter the helicopter's glide path, descent rate, and effective translational lift. A higher entry altitude provides additional time and altitude margin to recognize and correct for these variables before reaching the flare and touchdown phase.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area of Operation XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

issues: While the general principle that higher entry altitudes are prudent in strong wind conditions is sound, the answer does not cite a specific ACS requirement for 'higher than 500 feet' in strong winds. The ACS reference is cited but the specific requirement cannot be independently verified.
verification.suggested_correction: Clarify whether FAA-S-ACS-15 explicitly requires higher entry altitudes in strong wind conditions or whether this is a risk management best practice recommendation. If it is guidance rather than a hard requirement, the answer should reflect that distinction.
verification.triage_note: The answer asserts an ACS requirement for higher entry altitudes in strong winds but does not cite a specific numeric threshold or confirm this is an explicit ACS mandate rather than prudent risk management guidance; distinction must be clarified.

questions.question: During an autorotation entry from cruise airspeed, the handbook identifies three simultaneous critical control inputs. What are they, and why is each important?
questions.answer: The three critical simultaneous inputs are: (1) Lower collective — reduces lift and drag on the rotor blades, allowing upward airflow through the disk to arrest rotor RPM decay; (2) Apply aft cyclic — slows the helicopter and increases upward airflow through the rotor, which also helps sustain rotor RPM; (3) Apply trim (antitorque pedal) — maintains coordinated flight and prevents the fuselage from yawing. Each input is time-sensitive because low-inertia rotor systems decay rapidly and rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable.

questions.question: How does the concept of the 'error chain' from aeronautical decision-making apply to the selection of autorotation entry altitude?
questions.answer: The error chain concept holds that aviation accidents rarely result from a single mistake but rather from a sequence of poor decisions that accumulate. In the context of autorotation entry altitude, a pilot might begin with a slightly low entry altitude, then encounter an unexpected tailwind component that shortens the glide, then delay the flare due to distraction, then add collective too slowly during the cushion. Each individual decision may seem minor, but together they create a situation where the pilot runs out of both altitude and options. Selecting a proper entry altitude — at or above 500 feet AGL, higher in strong winds — breaks one of the earliest potential links in that chain, preserving margin for subsequent errors or surprises.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area of Operation XIV, Task B

questions.question: A student pilot argues that since the helicopter's autorotative glide from 500 feet AGL only takes about 15–20 seconds, the 500-foot minimum is arbitrary and a skilled pilot could safely practice from 300 feet AGL. How would you respond as an examiner, and what specific risks does the reduced altitude introduce that the student may be underestimating?
questions.answer: The student is underestimating the time-critical nature of each phase of the autorotation and the consequence of any deviation. From 300 feet AGL, the available time window for establishing proper rotor RPM, correcting the flight path, transitioning to the flare at the correct altitude, and executing a power recovery or full-down landing is drastically compressed. The specific risks include: (1) Low-inertia rotor systems can decay to an unrecoverable state before the pilot completes entry inputs; (2) Any lateral drift, overshoot, or undershoot of the landing zone cannot be corrected at 300 feet; (3) The flare must begin at approximately 40–100 feet AGL depending on airspeed and aircraft — at 300 feet entry, the entire descent, flare, and cushion must all occur nearly simultaneously; (4) Rotor stall in a helicopter is non-recoverable. The 500-foot AGL standard is not arbitrary — it represents the minimum altitude at which a pilot executing a normal, well-flown autorotation has a reasonable margin to identify and correct one error before it becomes fatal.
questions.follow_up: You mentioned rotor stall is non-recoverable. At what point in the autorotation is rotor RPM most vulnerable to decay, and what does the pilot do to guard against it?
questions.follow_up_answer: Rotor RPM is most vulnerable during the initial entry phase, especially from cruise airspeed where blade inertia is working against the pilot if the collective is not lowered promptly. The pilot guards against decay by immediately and decisively lowering the collective to reduce blade pitch (and therefore drag), allowing the upward flow of air through the rotor disk to autorotate the blades. Aft cyclic also contributes by increasing upward airflow through the disk. Throughout the descent, the pilot must monitor rotor RPM continuously and adjust collective as needed to keep RPM within the green arc. The flare phase also increases RPM momentarily as aft cyclic further increases disk inflow, which is why the collective must be managed precisely during the cushion to avoid an RPM overspeed.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area of Operation XIV, Task B

questions.question: During a checkride, an applicant begins a straight-in autorotation at exactly 500 feet AGL in a 20-knot direct headwind that has been reported gusting to 30 knots. Midway through the descent, the headwind drops suddenly and the helicopter undershoots the intended landing zone. What risk management failure occurred before the autorotation even began, and how should the applicant have applied the ACS standard?
questions.answer: The risk management failure was treating the 500-foot AGL figure as a fixed floor rather than a dynamic minimum. The ACS explicitly states that a higher entry altitude is required in strong wind conditions. A 20-knot wind gusting to 30 knots qualifies as strong and variable, which introduces two specific risks: (1) wind shear during the descent can alter the glide slope and groundspeed unpredictably; and (2) a sudden loss of headwind near the ground reduces translational lift, shortens effective glide distance, and can result in an undershoot with little altitude remaining to correct. The applicant should have applied a higher entry altitude — perhaps 800 feet AGL or more — and briefed that decision as a risk management choice before beginning the maneuver. The ACS standard is a minimum floor, and sound aeronautical decision-making requires adjusting upward based on actual conditions.
questions.follow_up: If this undershoot scenario resulted in a hard landing, what would you identify as the specific link in the error chain that could have been broken earliest?
questions.follow_up_answer: The earliest link in the chain was the failure to select an appropriate entry altitude before the maneuver began. Once committed to an autorotation from 500 feet AGL in gusty conditions, every subsequent decision was reactive rather than proactive. Had the applicant selected 800 feet or higher, the sudden wind shift would have provided additional altitude to adjust pitch attitude, extend the glide slightly, or perform a steeper flare to dissipate excess descent rate. The second link was likely the failure to recognize the wind variability as a risk factor that specifically required deviation from the minimum altitude standard. The word 'probably' applies here — if the pilot thought the 500-foot entry would 'probably' work out in gusty conditions, the Trescott Tip from ADM applies: choose the option known to work, not the one that will probably work.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Chapter 13; FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area of Operation XIV, Task B

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation on a checkride, what is your primary obligation if something goes wrong and you don't think you can safely complete the landing?
questions.answer: Your primary obligation is always safety of flight. The ACS specifically states you must not sacrifice safety of flight to force a landing to complete the task. If the approach is not going well — bad glide path, poor RPM, wrong landing spot — you execute a go-around or power recovery immediately rather than pressing on to complete the maneuver for the examiner.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'force a landing' during an autorotation, and why is it dangerous?
questions.answer: Forcing a landing means continuing an autorotation to touchdown even when conditions indicate the approach will not end safely — for example, landing short in obstacles, arriving with insufficient rotor RPM, or touching down with excessive speed or rate of descent. It is dangerous because the helicopter may contact terrain with not enough rotor inertia for a successful flare, or land in an unsuitable area, resulting in a hard landing, rollover, or collision with obstacles. The safer choice is always a power recovery and go-around.

questions.question: At what point during a straight-in autorotation is a power recovery no longer a viable option to avoid forcing a landing?
questions.answer: Once the helicopter descends below effective translational lift altitude on final approach — typically below approximately 10 feet AGL near the ground — there is not enough time or altitude to apply power and recover effectively. This is why early recognition of an unsafe approach profile is critical. Above that threshold, a go-around with smooth collective application and forward cyclic to regain translational lift is achievable. The pilot must make the go-around decision early, not at the last moment.

questions.question: You are on a straight-in autorotation checkride task and realize at 200 feet AGL that your airspeed is too high, your glide path is too steep, and you are going to land well beyond your intended touchdown point into a rough area. The examiner has not said anything. What do you do, and how do you communicate it?
questions.answer: Execute a power recovery immediately — apply collective smoothly to arrest the descent, add forward cyclic to maintain airspeed and transition to a normal climbout, and use pedals to maintain trim. Clearly announce to the examiner: 'I'm going around — this approach is not safe to complete.' You do not wait for the examiner's input. The ACS requires you not to sacrifice safety of flight to complete the task, and recognizing an unsafe profile early and acting decisively is exactly what a competent pilot-in-command should do. The examiner will evaluate your decision-making positively.

questions.question: During an autorotation checkride task, your rotor RPM decays below the normal operating range at 150 feet AGL. You are on glide path and on target airspeed, but the RPM needle is in the caution arc and dropping. Walk me through your decision process.
questions.answer: Low rotor RPM is an emergency condition requiring immediate corrective action. At 150 feet AGL, the options are extremely limited: if RPM recovery is possible (apply aft cyclic to unload the disk momentarily, lower collective if any residual collective remains, adjust airspeed), do so immediately. If the RPM cannot be recovered and the touchdown point is suitable, continue to land using the available rotor inertia for the flare. However, the key principle is never to force a landing just to complete the task — if rotor RPM is inadequate and the situation is deteriorating, the examiner should be immediately notified. The FAA HFH states that rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable, so early recognition and correction of low RPM is imperative. Safety of flight takes absolute priority over task completion.

questions.question: How does the error chain concept from ADM apply specifically to the risk of forcing a landing during an autorotation task on a checkride?
questions.answer: The error chain describes how accidents typically result from multiple poor decisions rather than a single mistake. In an autorotation checkride scenario, the chain might begin with accepting a non-ideal entry altitude, then allowing airspeed to drift, then not correcting glide path early, then hesitating to go around because of checkride pressure — each link making the next decision harder. Breaking any single link — such as executing a go-around early when the approach first looks questionable — can prevent the outcome of forcing an unsafe landing. Checkride pressure is itself a known human factor that can cause pilots to continue into unsafe situations. Recognizing this bias and acting on safety rather than the desire to complete the task is a direct application of ADM principles.

questions.question: A student tells you they completed a very rough autorotation landing during their checkride because they did not want to fail the task by going around. They had enough altitude and time to execute a safe power recovery. From an examiner's perspective, was going around the right call? How does forcing an unsafe landing actually affect checkride outcome compared to executing a go-around?
questions.answer: Going around was absolutely the right call. The ACS explicitly states the applicant must not sacrifice safety of flight to force a landing. An examiner evaluates judgment and decision-making as a core competency. A pilot who executes a timely, well-communicated go-around when an approach is unsafe demonstrates sound ADM, good situational awareness, and appropriate PIC authority — all of which are evaluated positively. Conversely, continuing to a rough or hazardous landing to 'complete the task' demonstrates poor judgment and could result in an unsatisfactory on the risk management elements even if the landing is technically survivable. The examiner can always repeat the task; they cannot undo a damaged aircraft or injured occupant. A go-around is never a failing action — forcing an unsafe landing potentially is.
questions.follow_up: What if the applicant goes around three times in a row because they keep second-guessing themselves and breaking off approaches that were actually acceptable? Does that also indicate a problem?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, that also reflects a risk management concern — in the opposite direction. Excessive go-arounds on approaches that were within acceptable parameters indicates poor situational awareness, lack of confidence in self-assessment, or unmanaged checkride anxiety. An examiner would evaluate whether the pilot can accurately distinguish a genuinely unsafe approach from one that is merely imperfect. The standard is not perfection — it is safe and competent. Repeated unnecessary go-arounds suggest the applicant may not have the situational awareness or judgment to distinguish acceptable risk from unacceptable risk, which is itself a disqualifying deficiency in the risk management category.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation task, your examiner — who is also a CFI — says to you at 300 feet AGL: 'Keep it going, you've got it.' You believe the approach is borderline unsafe due to a short landing area and degraded rotor RPM. Who has final authority, and what should you do?
questions.answer: You, as the acting pilot in command for the checkride, retain final authority over the safety of the flight under 14 CFR 91.3. The examiner's encouragement does not override your PIC judgment. If you genuinely assess the approach as unsafe, you are both authorized and required to execute a go-around regardless of what the examiner says. ACS CH.XIV.B explicitly prohibits sacrificing safety of flight to force a landing to complete the task. You should state clearly: 'Going around — I'm not satisfied this approach is safe,' and execute the power recovery. A well-trained examiner will recognize and credit this decision. Deferring to the examiner's comment and continuing an unsafe approach would be a failure of PIC authority — which itself could be evaluated as unsatisfactory.
questions.follow_up: What if the examiner debriefs you afterward and tells you the approach was actually fine and your go-around was unnecessary? How do you respond?
questions.follow_up_answer: You acknowledge the debrief professionally and ask the examiner to explain what specific parameters indicated the approach was within limits — RPM range, airspeed, glide path, landing area. Use the debrief as a learning opportunity to calibrate your risk assessment accuracy. If the examiner's explanation is technically sound and you agree in retrospect, you accept the feedback and improve your self-assessment skills.
