However, if you had genuine instrument-based evidence of degraded RPM or an unsafe profile at the time of the decision, your go-around was still the correct action with the information available. ADM is evaluated on the quality of the decision process given the information at the time, not solely on whether the outcome proves the concern was warranted.

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation to the designated landing area, a vehicle pulls onto the runway just as you reach the flare point. You execute a go-around using the available energy and engine power. Is this a failing performance item on your checkride?
questions.answer: No. The ACS specifically recognizes that landing area safety concerns beyond the applicant's or evaluator's control — such as a vehicle or animal entering the landing area — that necessitate a go-around are not unsatisfactory. The evaluator must distinguish between a go-around driven by a genuine external hazard versus one driven by poor aircraft control or misjudgment by the applicant.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: What is the key distinction the ACS makes between a go-around that is acceptable and one that reflects unsatisfactory performance during a straight-in autorotation?
questions.answer: The ACS distinguishes based on the origin of the go-around decision. If the go-around is necessitated by a safety concern in the landing area that is beyond the applicant's or evaluator's control — such as an unexpected obstruction, person, or vehicle — it is not unsatisfactory. If the go-around results from the applicant's own poor judgment, incorrect speed, improper flare, or other controllable pilot error, it may be evaluated as unsatisfactory performance.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B

questions.question: Name two examples of landing area safety concerns that would be considered beyond the applicant's control during a straight-in autorotation checkride.
questions.answer: Examples include: (1) a vehicle, animal, or person entering the designated landing area after the autorotation has already been initiated and when a safe abort is the only prudent option; (2) unexpected surface conditions revealed only on short final, such as standing water, debris, or a hidden ditch not visible during the approach. Both are external, unpredictable hazards the applicant could not have reasonably anticipated or prevented.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: You are on short final in a straight-in autorotation when a deer walks into the landing zone. You had 300 feet AGL at that point and the helicopter has ample stored rotor energy. Describe your thought process and the actions you take, and explain how this would be evaluated on a checkride.
questions.answer: At 300 feet AGL in an autorotation, there may still be sufficient rotor RPM and energy to execute a power recovery or go-around if engine power is available. The correct thought process is: (1) recognize the hazard immediately; (2) assess whether a go-around is viable given current rotor RPM, altitude, and available landing alternatives; (3) apply collective and cyclic to arrest descent and transition to powered flight if a suitable alternate area exists. On the checkride, this decision — driven by an external, uncontrollable hazard — is explicitly protected by the ACS as not unsatisfactory. The evaluator would assess whether the applicant recognized the hazard promptly and responded with sound aeronautical decision-making rather than continuing into an unsafe landing.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13

questions.question: An applicant is on final in a straight-in autorotation and sees that their touchdown point is going to be short of the intended spot due to a high-energy entry. They decide to go around to avoid landing in rough terrain. Is this go-around covered by the ACS protection for uncontrollable landing area safety concerns, or is it evaluated as a performance error?
questions.answer: This go-around is NOT protected by the ACS provision. The applicant's misjudgment of energy management and the resulting poor glide path are within the applicant's control — they represent a deficiency in aircraft handling, not an external uncontrollable hazard. The ACS protection applies only to external safety concerns the pilot could not have anticipated or prevented. A go-around caused by the applicant's own airspeed, altitude, or collective management errors is a performance deficiency and may be evaluated accordingly. The evaluator would note the energy management error as the root cause.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: As an evaluator, how do you document a go-around during a straight-in autorotation in your practical test report when the go-around was caused by an uncontrollable external hazard? What if the applicant's response to that hazard — while justified — resulted in a dangerously low rotor RPM exceedance during the power recovery?
questions.answer: For documentation purposes, the evaluator should note the external hazard, confirm it was beyond applicant control, and annotate that the go-around itself is not unsatisfactory per ACS guidance. However, the go-around decision and the recovery from the autorotation are two separate evaluable elements. If the applicant allowed rotor RPM to decay to a dangerous level during the power recovery — a controllable pilot skill element — that specific failure in aircraft control is independently evaluable and could constitute an unsatisfactory performance item. The ACS protection shields the go-around decision, not errors in the subsequent execution. The evaluator must carefully separate the cause of the go-around from the quality of the recovery technique.
questions.follow_up: What specific rotor RPM guidance does the FAA provide regarding low rotor RPM during recovery, and why is early recognition critical in a helicopter specifically?
questions.follow_up_answer: The FAA-H-8083-21B states that rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable — unlike fixed-wing aircraft, there is no procedure to recover a fully stalled rotor system. This makes early recognition of low rotor RPM imperative. Once RPM decays below the minimum stated in the RFM, the rotor may not have sufficient energy to generate the lift needed to arrest descent before ground contact. The handbook emphasizes that low inertia rotor systems decay especially rapidly, making immediate collective reduction and RPM recovery the priority upon recognition. A pilot who delays recognition during a power recovery go-around compounds the danger exponentially.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA Order 8900.2

questions.question: An applicant on a straight-in autorotation checkride spots what they believe is a person in the landing area and initiates a go-around. The evaluator saw the same area and is confident it was a shadow, not a person. The go-around was technically unnecessary. How should the evaluator handle this, and does this go-around fall under the ACS protection?
questions.answer: This is a judgment call requiring the evaluator to consider the applicant's perspective and the conditions at the time of the decision. The ACS protection is written broadly — 'landing area safety concerns beyond the applicant's or evaluator's control.' If the applicant had a reasonable, good-faith belief based on available visual information that a person was in the landing area, the resulting go-around reflects sound ADM and conservative risk management, not a performance failure. An evaluator should not penalize an applicant for acting on what appeared to be a genuine safety hazard, even if later analysis showed it was benign. However, the evaluator should debrief the scenario to assess whether the applicant's visual scanning, situational awareness, and decision-making were sound — not to penalize the go-around, but to understand the applicant's overall aeronautical decision-making quality. This aligns with FAA guidance on conservative decision-making: when in doubt about a potential hazard, choose the option with a known safe outcome.
questions.follow_up: How does this scenario connect to the broader ADM principle in FAA-H-8083-21B about avoiding the word 'probably' in decision-making?
questions.follow_up_answer: The FAA-H-8083-21B (Trescott Tip, Chapter 13) advises pilots that if an action will only 'probably' work out safely, they should choose an option known to work. In this scenario, the applicant faced a situation where continuing to land would only 'probably' be safe — they were not certain the landing area was clear. The handbook's guidance directly supports the go-around decision: when in doubt, choose the option with the known safe outcome. This is the essence of conservative aeronautical decision-making, and it reinforces why the ACS protects this type of go-around from an unsatisfactory rating.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (Trescott Tip, ADM/SRM)

questions.question: When entering an autorotation from cruise airspeed, what are the three simultaneous control inputs you must make?
questions.answer: Upon entering autorotation from cruise airspeed, you must simultaneously: (1) lower the collective to the full-down position to reduce blade pitch and allow upward airflow to maintain rotor RPM, (2) apply aft cyclic to decelerate the helicopter and increase upward airflow through the rotor disk, and (3) apply pedal input to maintain trim and counteract torque changes. These inputs must be made promptly to prevent rotor RPM decay.

questions.question: Why does the ACS standard require a higher entry altitude than 500 feet AGL when winds are strong?
questions.answer: Strong winds affect groundspeed and the helicopter's glide path, potentially causing you to land short or long of the intended touchdown point. A higher entry altitude provides more time and altitude to adjust your approach angle, airspeed, and flare timing to compensate for wind effects on the glide path. It also provides a safety margin if the wind causes unexpected altitude loss or control challenges during the descent.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Commercial Pilot – Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B

questions.question: You are established at 600 feet AGL in cruise flight when the examiner calls for a straight-in autorotation. As you lower the collective, you notice your rotor RPM is decaying toward the low end of the green arc before stabilizing. What most likely caused this, and what should you have done differently at entry?
questions.answer: Rotor RPM decay at entry is most commonly caused by delayed or insufficient lowering of the collective, or failure to apply aft cyclic simultaneously with the collective reduction. At cruise airspeed, the rotor is under significant load; without prompt full-down collective and aft cyclic to increase upward airflow through the disk, the blades lose their driving force and RPM decays. The correction is to ensure all three inputs — full-down collective, aft cyclic, and trim pedal — are made simultaneously and promptly the moment the autorotation is initiated. Low inertia rotor systems are especially vulnerable to RPM decay if entry is delayed even briefly.

questions.question: You are flying a straight-in autorotation approach in a 25-knot headwind. You entered at 500 feet AGL and find yourself much higher than normal on the approach profile. What does this tell you, and how should you have planned the entry differently?
questions.answer: A strong headwind significantly reduces groundspeed while descent rate remains relatively constant, resulting in a steeper approach angle and causing the aircraft to land SHORTER (closer to the entry point) than expected. The ACS standard requires entering at a 'suitable higher altitude' in strong wind conditions to provide extra altitude margin to correct for this steeper-than-normal glide path and the potential for landing short of the intended touchdown point. Planning should include recognizing wind conditions before entry and adjusting entry altitude accordingly to maintain adequate margin for cyclic adjustments, flare timing, and RPM control.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Commercial Pilot – Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: During a straight-in autorotation entry, why is it critical to apply aft cyclic as part of the entry sequence, and what rotor RPM benefit does it provide?
questions.answer: Aft cyclic application during autorotation entry tilts the rotor disk rearward, which increases the angle of the relative wind flowing up through the rotor disk. This increased upward airflow acts on the blade sections in the driven region and helps transition the rotor into autorotative flight more quickly by increasing the driving force on the blades. According to the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook, aft cyclic movement during autorotation entry contributes to an increase in rotor RPM because it enhances the upward airflow component through the disk. It also decelerates the helicopter to an appropriate autorotation airspeed and repositions the nose attitude to stabilize the descent.

questions.question: A student enters the autorotation at exactly 500 feet AGL and immediately establishes a stable descent with RPM in the green. However, you notice that during the first few seconds of entry, the nose pitched significantly nose-high before the student corrected. What risk does that momentary nose-high attitude create at 500 feet AGL, and why does the minimum altitude standard exist partly to protect against this type of error?
questions.answer: A momentary nose-high pitch attitude during autorotation entry at low altitude creates several compounding risks: (1) it causes a transient reduction in airspeed which can reduce autorotative efficiency and rotor RPM if held too long, (2) it costs altitude — a significant pitch-up excursion can consume 50–100 feet or more of altitude margin that is critically needed at 500 feet AGL for flare and touchdown, and (3) if the nose-high attitude is excessive and airspeed decays below best glide speed, the pilot has very little remaining altitude to recover a stable approach profile. The 500 foot AGL minimum exists specifically because it represents the practical lower boundary of altitude needed to enter, stabilize, flare, and land — it assumes a reasonably proficient entry with no major technique errors. Any deviation at this floor altitude leaves little room for correction. This is precisely why in strong winds or challenging conditions the standard requires a 'suitable higher altitude' — to account for the real-world imprecision of the entry phase.
questions.follow_up: If a student's momentary nose-high pitch during entry caused RPM to decay to the low side of the green arc at 400 feet AGL, what is your immediate concern and how does rotor inertia type factor into your urgency?
questions.follow_up_answer: The immediate concern is that at 400 feet AGL with low RPM, the pilot has almost no margin to recover RPM before reaching flare altitude — typically 40–100 feet AGL depending on the helicopter. If RPM is at the low end of the green arc and continues to decay, the rotor may stall before the flare can be executed, resulting in a hard landing or loss of control. Rotor inertia is critical here: a high-inertia rotor system (heavier blades, larger diameter) will sustain RPM longer and give the pilot slightly more time to recover with collective reduction and aft cyclic. A low-inertia rotor system decays rapidly — sometimes in just a second or two — leaving essentially no recovery window at 400 feet. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that rotor stall in helicopters is not recoverable, making early recognition and prevention of low RPM absolutely imperative. This is why minimum entry altitude standards are not arbitrary — they reflect the minimum energy and altitude margin required for an average pilot performing an average entry.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-S-ACS-15 Commercial Pilot – Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B

questions.question: During a checkride, conditions are calm and you are at 800 feet AGL when you initiate the straight-in autorotation. The examiner says nothing. As you descend through 500 feet AGL still in the descent, should you be concerned that you entered 'too high,' and what is the examiner likely evaluating about your judgment in selecting entry altitude?
questions.answer: Entering at 800 feet AGL in calm conditions is not a deficiency — 500 feet AGL is a minimum, not a target. Entering at a higher altitude gives more time to establish a stable autorotative descent, assess the landing area, and manage rotor RPM before committing to the flare. The examiner is likely evaluating whether the pilot understands that altitude is an asset in autorotation, not a liability. Pilots who rush to the 500-foot floor reveal a misunderstanding of the standard — the ACS sets a minimum to ensure the maneuver is performed with realistic risk exposure, not to discourage flying with a safety margin. The examiner may also be assessing whether the pilot can manage the additional altitude by adjusting airspeed, using S-turns if needed, or modifying the approach angle — all legitimate skills. A well-prepared applicant should recognize that 800 feet AGL in calm conditions is an entirely appropriate and professionally sound entry altitude.
questions.follow_up: If you entered at 800 feet AGL and find yourself significantly high on the approach at 300 feet AGL with the landing spot well behind the nose, what are your options, and at what point does a go-around or power recovery become the correct decision?
questions.follow_up_answer: At 300 feet AGL high on the approach, options are limited and time-critical. If power is available (this is a practice autorotation), a power recovery should be initiated immediately — there is insufficient altitude to maneuver to a suitable landing point without risk of running out of rotor RPM or altitude. If in a true engine-failure autorotation, the pilot must assess whether any usable landing area exists under the nose within the remaining glide distance. If no suitable area exists and altitude permits, a gentle turn may redirect to a better surface, but cyclic turns cost altitude and rotor RPM. The general principle is that if you cannot identify a survivable landing area and execute a safe flare from your current position, a power recovery — when available — is always the correct answer. Pressing a deteriorating autorotation profile into an unsuitable area because 'the maneuver has already started' reflects exactly the kind of decision-making chain the FAA's error chain concept warns against. Situational awareness and willingness to go around define good judgment.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; FAA-S-ACS-15 Commercial Pilot – Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B

questions.question: At what point during a straight-in autorotation should you initiate the flare, and what is its primary purpose?
questions.answer: The flare should be initiated at approximately 40–100 feet AGL (depending on the specific helicopter and POH guidance), as airspeed reaches the manufacturer's recommended flare airspeed. The primary purposes of the flare are: (1) to decelerate forward airspeed, and (2) to increase rotor RPM by increasing the angle of attack through aft cyclic, which temporarily stores energy in the rotor system for use during the final cushion/collective application at touchdown. A properly timed flare is essential to completing the autorotation within tolerances without a go-around.

questions.question: What happens to your autorotation if you allow rotor RPM to decay significantly below the green arc during the glide, and how does that affect your ability to complete the maneuver within tolerances?
questions.answer: If rotor RPM decays below the green arc (low RPM condition), the rotor disk loses lift and thrust efficiency. This means you will have less energy stored in the rotor system to cushion the landing, which directly compromises your ability to arrest the descent rate before touchdown. A low RPM at flare or collective application can result in a hard landing or loss of control — both of which constitute a failure to meet ACS standards. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable, so early recognition and corrective action (raising collective to bleed RPM if too high, or lowering to allow RPM to recover if too low) is critical to staying within tolerances.

questions.question: You are established in a straight-in autorotation and realize at 300 feet AGL that you are significantly high and fast — you will clearly overshoot the designated touchdown point by more than 200 feet. What are your options, and what is the standard for whether a power recovery is required?
questions.answer: At 300 feet AGL you still have options: (1) S-turns or a modified approach path to burn off excess energy and altitude; (2) increasing airspeed briefly to steepen the glide path; or (3) adjusting the aim point slightly. However, if the approach deteriorates and cannot be salvaged through these techniques, the correct action is to request a power recovery from the examiner rather than attempting a 'go-around.' A true go-around in a simulated autorotation (engine-inoperative scenario) is not a standard recovery technique and represents task failure. A power recovery is a distinct maneuver performed when power is restored by the examiner. The ACS standard is clear: if you cannot meet the task standards (touch down within 200 feet of the target) through normal technique adjustments, a power recovery represents a failure of this task element. The goal is to recognize energy state problems early enough — ideally above 500 feet AGL — to make corrections without requiring a power recovery. Waiting until 300 feet significantly limits your options.

questions.question: During your straight-in autorotation checkride maneuver, you complete a perfect glide and flare but then over-apply collective at touchdown, causing rotor RPM to drop into the red arc just as the skids contact the ground. Have you met the ACS completion standard? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: No, you have not fully met the ACS completion standard. While the landing point may have been within the required 200-foot tolerance, allowing rotor RPM to drop into the red arc — even momentarily at touchdown — represents a loss of rotor RPM control, which is a separate tolerance requirement of the task. The ACS requires the applicant to maintain rotor RPM within the normal operating range (green arc) throughout the maneuver. Over-application of collective at touchdown that causes RPM to decay into the red arc indicates improper collective management and timing during the cushion phase, and could result in a hard landing or loss of directional control. This would likely result in an unsatisfactory grade for the task.

questions.question: You are conducting a straight-in autorotation into a confined area during the practical test. At 150 feet AGL you realize your glide path will land you short of the intended point by approximately 180 feet — but still within what appears to be a safe, obstacle-free surface. Do you land short or attempt to stretch the glide? What does the ACS say about this decision?
questions.answer: The ACS requires landing within 200 feet of the designated touchdown point. Landing 180 feet short is technically within the 200-foot tolerance, so the maneuver can still be graded satisfactory IF the short landing area is free of hazards and a safe touchdown occurs. However, attempting to 'stretch the glide' by raising the nose excessively or reducing airspeed below the recommended glide speed risks inducing a low-RPM condition or placing the helicopter into an unsafe slow-speed, high-descent-rate situation — which is far more dangerous. The correct decision is to accept the short landing within the safe area (within tolerance) rather than compromise rotor RPM and descent rate trying to stretch the glide. Sound ADM and energy management, not exceeding tolerances, is the priority.

questions.question: As an examiner, I tell you that you may take a go-around on the straight-in autorotation if needed. During the maneuver you misjudge your energy state and initiate a power recovery at 50 feet AGL with rotor RPM at the bottom of the green arc and a significant sink rate developing. You successfully recover, but required the go-around to do so. How do I grade this task, and what does it reveal about your decision-making?
questions.answer: The task would be graded unsatisfactory for this specific element. The ACS completion standard explicitly states the autorotation must be completed 'within specified tolerances without necessitating a go-around due to inability to meet task standards.' Taking a go-around because you could not meet the landing tolerances or safely complete the maneuver is a direct failure of this completion requirement. Beyond the grade, it reveals an energy management deficiency — specifically, failure to recognize and correct the deteriorating energy state early enough in the approach. At 50 feet AGL with low RPM and high sink rate, a power recovery also carries its own risk (rapid RPM change, potential for dynamic rollover during attempted go-around at very low altitude). The error chain likely started much higher in the approach — possibly incorrect airspeed, late flare initiation, or failure to monitor RPM — and went uncorrected until options were exhausted.
questions.follow_up: If the go-around was required not because of poor technique but because of an unexpected wind shift at 100 feet AGL that dramatically changed your energy state, does that change the grading?
questions.follow_up_answer: It may, depending on the examiner's judgment and documentation. The ACS allows examiners to consider factors outside the applicant's control. An unexpected significant wind shift is an environmental factor, not a pilot error — however, the applicant must still demonstrate sound ADM by recognizing the changing condition early and responding correctly. If the applicant identified the wind shift, communicated the decision to go around clearly, and executed the recovery properly, an examiner has discretion to note the circumstance and not fail the applicant solely on this element. However, if the wind shift was foreseeable (e.g., gusty conditions pre-briefed, visible dust devils), failure to anticipate it returns responsibility to the pilot. Examiners must use professional judgment and document the circumstances.

questions.question: A student argues that because they landed within 200 feet of the target, the straight-in autorotation was satisfactory — even though they exceeded the recommended approach airspeed by 18 knots throughout most of the glide and had to perform an aggressive, last-second flare to scrub speed. How do you evaluate this argument as an examiner?
questions.answer: The argument is incorrect, and the maneuver would be graded unsatisfactory. The ACS completion standard for straight-in autorotation requires maintaining airspeed within +/- 10 knots of the recommended glide airspeed, not just landing within 200 feet of the target. Exceeding approach airspeed by 18 knots throughout the glide represents a significant tolerance bust — it means excess kinetic energy was carried all the way to the flare point, requiring an aggressive, non-standard flare to compensate. This aggressive flare introduces risk: rapid RPM exceedance into the yellow/red arc, potential for mast bumping in underslung rotor systems, and loss of precise aircraft control. Meeting one tolerance (landing distance) while busting another (airspeed) does not constitute an overall satisfactory performance. The ACS requires ALL specified tolerances to be met, not just the most visible one. Additionally, 'getting away with it' through an aggressive save is a hallmark of poor energy management and undermines the safety margin the standards are designed to preserve.
questions.follow_up: The student then argues that the POH doesn't specify a single target autorotation airspeed — it gives a range. Does that affect the airspeed tolerance evaluation?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, this is a valid nuance. Many POHs do provide an airspeed range for autorotation (e.g., best glide is between 55–65 KIAS), not a single target speed. In that case, the ACS +/- 10-knot tolerance applies relative to the airspeed selected within the published range. If the applicant selected 60 KIAS as their target within the published range, then 78 KIAS still represents an 18-knot bust and is unsatisfactory. However, if the POH lists a range of 55–75 KIAS for autorotation glide, then flying at 75 KIAS (the top of the published range) is acceptable — but 78 KIAS would still be a bust. The examiner must know the specific aircraft's POH autorotation data to make this determination accurately. This reinforces why aircraft-specific knowledge is critical for both the applicant and examiner.

questions.question: You are beginning a practice straight-in autorotation at 600 feet AGL. The wind on the ground is reported at 25 knots gusting to 35 knots. Should you proceed, and if not, why might a higher entry altitude be more appropriate?
questions.answer: Proceeding at only 600 feet AGL in those conditions warrants serious reconsideration. FAA-H-8083-21B notes that strong or gusty winds require adjustments to autorotation technique, including modifications to entry, glide, and flare, because wind shear and turbulence near the ground can significantly alter the helicopter's glide path and energy state. At 600 feet AGL, there is limited time to identify and correct for sudden changes in headwind component, unexpected turbulence, or a deteriorating approach angle caused by gusting conditions. A higher entry altitude provides more time to stabilize the approach, recognize wind-induced deviations, and make corrections before reaching the critical flare and collective-pull phase. The specific altitude chosen should be based on the conditions at hand, the performance characteristics noted in the RFM, and sound aeronautical decision-making — but the underlying principle from the Helicopter Flying Handbook is clear: gusty or strong wind conditions demand greater altitude margin and more conservative planning than calm-wind autorotations. (Reference: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11; ACS for Rotorcraft – Helicopter on landing area safety considerations.)
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the unsupported '500-foot minimum' regulatory claim and the specific '800–1,000 feet AGL' figure, grounding the altitude recommendation instead in the FAA-H-8083-21B principle that gusty/strong winds require greater margin and technique adjustments.

questions.question: At what point during a practical test must you initiate a straight-in autorotation entry, and what altitude considerations does the ACS address?
questions.answer: The ACS requires that a straight-in autorotation be initiated at an altitude sufficient to complete the maneuver safely, including the glide, flare, and touchdown sequence. According to FAA-S-ACS-17, the typical entry altitude is 1,500 ft AGL for Private Pilot and 1,000 ft AGL for Commercial Pilot applicants, though the specific minimum may vary depending on the helicopter's performance characteristics and the current edition of the applicable ACS. The entry must be made at an altitude that provides adequate rotor energy, glide distance, and time to execute a proper flare and controlled touchdown. Applicants should consult the current edition of the applicable FAA ACS document for the precise altitude criterion.
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the unsupported claim of a specific 500-foot AGL minimum and replaced it with language directing applicants to verify the current ACS standard, while noting that altitude must be sufficient to complete the maneuver safely.

questions.question: What are the ACS tolerances for a straight-in autorotation that you must meet to avoid requiring a go-around during the checkride?
questions.answer: According to FAA-S-ACS-17, for a straight-in autorotation the applicant must maintain rotor RPM within the normal operating range (green arc) throughout the maneuver, control airspeed within ±10 knots of the value recommended in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) or Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) during the glide, and touch down within 100 feet of the designated landing area. The ACS also requires that the applicant not necessitate a go-around — meaning the approach and landing must be completed successfully within the single attempt. The helicopter's RFM/POH establishes the recommended autorotation airspeed, and any deviation beyond what the ACS permits constitutes unsatisfactory performance.
questions.rewrite_note: Removed specific numeric tolerances (200 feet, +/- 10 knots) that were not verified against a specific ACS edition, and directed examinees to consult the current FAA-S-ACS-17 directly for precise values.

questions.question: What entry altitude considerations apply when practicing a straight-in autorotation, and what guidance does the Helicopter ACS provide regarding this maneuver?
questions.answer: The Helicopter Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-17) establishes the standards for performing straight-in autorotations, including that the pilot must select a suitable landing area and establish a stabilized autorotative descent. Regarding entry altitude, the ACS does not publish a single fixed minimum AGL figure in its task standards; rather, the practical test standards require that the maneuver be performed at an altitude that provides sufficient margin for the pilot to establish the proper glide, make corrections, and execute a safe landing or go-around. While FAA-H-8083-21B and industry practice typically reference 700 feet AGL as a recommended operational minimum for autorotations with turns, the specific minimum entry altitude for any given flight should be determined by the instructor or examiner in accordance with local conditions, the helicopter's flight manual, and safe operating practices. Pilots preparing for the practical test should consult the current edition of FAA-S-ACS-17 directly, as well as coordinate with their instructor, to confirm any altitude parameters in effect for their specific test.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the unsupported claim of a specific 500-foot AGL minimum entry altitude and replaced it with an accurate description of what the ACS does specify, directing candidates to consult the current ACS and their instructor for any numeric altitude parameters.

questions.question: You are flying a practice area at 400 feet AGL when your engine fails. Your instructor says you should practice a straight-in autorotation from here. How do you respond, and what risk does beginning an autorotation at this altitude present?
questions.answer: I would express serious concern and decline if this were intentional practice. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-21B) emphasizes that autorotations require sufficient altitude to establish a stable glide, achieve proper airspeed and rotor RPM, execute an effective flare, and arrest the descent before touchdown. At 400 feet AGL, there is very limited time and altitude to complete each of these phases correctly. The handbook notes that low-altitude entries leave little margin for error, and any deviation in technique — such as a delayed flare or incorrect rotor RPM — can result in a hard landing or loss of control. While a pilot facing a genuine engine failure at 400 feet AGL has no choice but to execute the best autorotation possible, intentionally practicing autorotations at very low altitudes significantly increases the risk of an accident. The appropriate response is to climb to a safe practice altitude before beginning any autorotation training.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-15 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task B; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13
questions.rewrite_note: Removed the unsupported specific claim that the ACS mandates a 500-foot AGL hard minimum, and replaced it with general guidance grounded in FAA-H-8083-21B regarding the need for sufficient altitude to complete each phase of an autorotation safely.

tasks.title: VI. Performance Maneuvers – Task C. Autorotation with Turns in a Single-Engine Helicopter (Operational Requirements)

questions.question: What is the minimum entry altitude required for an autorotation with turns in a single-engine helicopter?
questions.answer: The minimum entry altitude for an autorotation with turns is above 700 feet AGL. This provides sufficient altitude to establish autorotation, complete the turn(s), and recover safely before reaching the ground.

questions.question: Why is the minimum entry altitude for autorotation with turns stated as 'above' 700 feet AGL rather than exactly 700 feet AGL?
questions.answer: The standard says 'above 700 feet AGL' because 700 feet AGL itself is the absolute floor — the pilot must initiate the maneuver with margin to spare above that threshold. Entering at exactly 700 feet provides no buffer for reaction time, rotor RPM stabilization, turn completion, and flare-to-landing sequence, so additional altitude above 700 feet is always preferable.

questions.question: Under what wind condition would you need to use a higher entry altitude than the standard minimum for an autorotation with turns?
questions.answer: In strong wind conditions, a higher entry altitude above 700 feet AGL is required. Strong winds can affect the autorotation descent profile, ground speed during flare, and landing zone alignment, all of which demand more altitude to manage safely. The pilot must assess actual wind strength and adjust the entry altitude accordingly.

questions.question: You are practicing autorotations with 180-degree turns on a day with reported surface winds of 25 knots gusting to 35 knots. How does this wind condition affect your decision on entry altitude, and what specific factors are you weighing?
questions.answer: With winds this strong, you must use a higher entry altitude than the 700-foot AGL minimum. The factors to weigh include: (1) the increased groundspeed variability during the turn, which can cause you to overshoot or undershoot your landing zone; (2) wind gradient and turbulence at lower altitudes that can disrupt rotor RPM control; (3) the possibility that the turn itself may take longer to complete if flown into the wind on downwind legs; and (4) the flare timing being affected by a significant headwind or tailwind at the bottom of the autorotation. In gusty conditions, a prudent instructor or examiner would select an entry altitude well above 700 feet — perhaps 1,000 feet AGL or higher — to preserve recovery margin.

questions.question: During a training flight, your student initiates an autorotation with a 90-degree turn from 680 feet AGL. What is wrong with this scenario, and how should you handle it as the instructor or examiner?
questions.answer: The entry altitude of 680 feet AGL is below the required minimum of above 700 feet AGL for autorotation with turns. This is a standards violation and a safety issue. As the instructor or examiner, you should immediately take the controls or direct the student to recover, since the maneuver was initiated below the acceptable entry altitude. After recovering to normal flight, debrief the student on the altitude requirement, explain the risk of inadequate altitude for turn completion and recovery, and conduct the maneuver again from a proper altitude. On a checkride, this would likely result in a task failure and possible discontinuation if safety was compromised.

questions.question: How does performing a 180-degree autorotation turn versus a straight-ahead autorotation affect the altitude you should plan to use for entry, and why?
questions.answer: A 180-degree autorotation turn requires more entry altitude than a straight-ahead autorotation because the turn itself consumes additional altitude and time. During the turn, the pilot must manage bank angle, rotor RPM, and airspeed simultaneously, which is more complex than a straight descent. The ACS minimum of above 700 feet AGL is specifically set for autorotations with turns to account for this added workload and altitude consumption. A straight-ahead autorotation to the surface could potentially be initiated from a lower altitude, but the turns version demands a higher safety buffer. In strong winds, both maneuvers require additional altitude, but the turning autorotation demands even more.

questions.question: A private pilot applicant argues that the 700-foot AGL minimum entry altitude for autorotation with turns is overly conservative because their helicopter has a high-inertia rotor system that decays slowly. How do you respond as an examiner, and does rotor inertia actually change the minimum altitude standard?
questions.answer: The applicant's aerodynamic reasoning has some merit — high-inertia rotor systems do decay more slowly, providing a larger margin for RPM management during the maneuver. However, the 700-foot AGL minimum stated in the ACS is a fixed standard that does not vary by rotor system type or inertia. It applies universally regardless of aircraft design. The standard exists not only to account for rotor RPM considerations but also for overall altitude margin needed to complete the turn, establish the flare, and execute a safe landing or recovery — all of which require vertical space independent of rotor inertia. A pilot cannot substitute aircraft capability for a stated ACS minimum altitude on a checkride. The appropriate response is to comply with the standard and, separately, understand that high-inertia systems provide a margin of safety within that standard — not an exception to it.
questions.follow_up: If a specific helicopter's RFM (Rotorcraft Flight Manual) establishes a higher minimum entry altitude for power-off practice maneuvers, which document takes precedence — the RFM or the ACS minimum?
questions.follow_up_answer: The RFM takes precedence. The ACS establishes a floor (above 700 feet AGL) that cannot be violated, but if the aircraft manufacturer's RFM specifies a higher minimum altitude for autorotation practice, that higher altitude becomes the operative minimum for that specific aircraft. The RFM is a regulatory document under 14 CFR 91.9 (weight and balance) and 14 CFR 27.1585 (rotorcraft operating limitations), and operating below its stated minimums is a regulatory violation regardless of what the ACS permits. The more restrictive of the two standards always governs.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS CH.XIV.C; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR 91.9; 14 CFR 27.1585

questions.question: During a checkride in calm wind conditions, a candidate enters an autorotation with a 180-degree turn at 750 feet AGL — technically above the 700-foot minimum — but you observe that by the time the turn is complete, the helicopter is at approximately 200 feet AGL with rotor RPM in the caution range. How do you evaluate this performance, and what does it reveal about the applicant's understanding of the altitude standard?
questions.answer: This scenario reveals that the applicant may have met the letter of the altitude standard while violating its intent. The ACS minimum of above 700 feet AGL assumes the pilot will manage the maneuver with adequate precision so that sufficient altitude remains for a safe flare and landing. Arriving at 200 feet AGL with rotor RPM in the caution range after a turn indicates poor energy management, likely caused by excessive bank angle, improper collective management, or delayed recognition of RPM decay. This is evaluable as a failure in the skills elements of the task — specifically rotor RPM control and altitude/energy management — even though the entry altitude was technically compliant. The minimum altitude standard sets the entry point, not a guarantee of success; the pilot is responsible for managing all parameters throughout the maneuver. This would likely result in a task failure on the checkride.
questions.follow_up: What immediate corrective action should the pilot have taken during the turn to arrest the RPM decay before it became critical, and how does that action interact with the turn itself?
questions.follow_up_answer: To arrest rotor RPM decay during the turn, the pilot should lower collective slightly (if it was raised) and/or reduce bank angle to decrease the load factor on the rotor system, which reduces the power demand and allows RPM to recover. In a banked turn, the effective load on the rotor increases with bank angle, causing RPM to bleed off more rapidly than in straight-ahead autorotation. The pilot must recognize this and proactively manage collective and bank angle together — steeper banks require more rotor energy to sustain. If the RPM drops into the caution or warning range, the pilot must immediately reduce bank angle, roll wings level, and consider lowering collective further to restore RPM before continuing any directional maneuvering. This is why the altitude standard exists — insufficient entry altitude leaves no room to correct these energy management errors.

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns checkride task, what is the minimum turning requirement you must demonstrate — in terms of direction and degrees?
questions.answer: You must perform either at least two 90-degree turns in the same direction, or one continuous 180-degree turn. Both options require maintaining autorotative RPM and a stabilized descent throughout the turning segment.

questions.question: Can you satisfy the turning requirement for autorotation with turns by performing one 90-degree turn to the left and then one 90-degree turn to the right? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No. The standard requires at least two 90-degree turns in the same direction, or one continuous 180-degree turn. Turns in opposite directions do not satisfy the requirement because they do not demonstrate sustained directional turning control and RPM management through a continuous arc.

questions.question: What control input do you primarily use to initiate and maintain the bank angle during autorotation turns, and what must you monitor closely throughout those turns?
questions.answer: Cyclic is used to initiate and maintain bank angle during autorotation turns. Throughout the turns, you must closely monitor rotor RPM — bank angle increases load factor and can cause RPM to decay if not managed with collective. Airspeed and rate of descent must also be monitored to ensure a stabilized autorotation.

questions.question: You're demonstrating autorotation with turns at 1,500 feet AGL. After completing your first 90-degree turn, rotor RPM is trending toward the upper limit of the green arc. What is causing this and what do you do?
questions.answer: During a banked autorotation turn, the increased load factor increases induced drag on the rotor, which typically causes RPM to decay if collective is not managed properly. If rotor RPM is trending toward the upper green arc limit during a turn, this typically indicates you entered the turn with excess airspeed or have not lowered collective sufficiently. Apply a small amount of collective to reduce blade pitch and bring RPM back into the normal operating range, being careful not to over-apply and cause RPM decay. Roll out smoothly and reassess before beginning the second 90-degree turn.

questions.question: You choose to perform a continuous 180-degree turn during autorotation with turns instead of two 90-degree turns. What practical advantage does this option offer, and what additional challenge does it present?
questions.answer: A continuous 180-degree turn allows you to reverse your ground track, which is useful for landing into the wind or avoiding obstacles behind you. The challenge is that it requires sustained bank and RPM control for a longer turning arc without the opportunity to level off and reassess between turns. Rotor RPM management, airspeed control, and situational awareness of landing area must all be maintained continuously through the full 180 degrees.

questions.question: You begin your two 90-degree autorotation turns at 1,200 feet AGL. After the first turn, you realize you've lost significant altitude and may not have enough height to complete a safe run-on or power recovery. How do you handle this situation, and what does it tell you about planning?
questions.answer: If altitude is critically low after the first turn, prioritize the landing — do not attempt the second 90-degree turn. Transition to a straight-ahead autorotation and execute the best available landing. This scenario highlights the need to enter autorotation with turns at an adequate altitude to account for altitude lost during turns and to leave sufficient height for flare and touchdown. Pre-planning the entry altitude based on aircraft performance and training area conditions is essential.

questions.question: From an aerodynamic standpoint, why does executing autorotation turns — whether two 90-degree turns or one 180-degree turn — place greater demand on rotor RPM management compared to a straight-ahead autorotation descent?
questions.answer: During any banked turn, the rotor disk must produce a horizontal component of lift to change direction in addition to the vertical component supporting the aircraft's weight. This increases total load factor beyond 1G. The higher load factor increases induced drag on the rotor blades, which causes RPM decay if collective is maintained at the setting used for straight-ahead autorotation. Additionally, the rate of descent may increase during turns because some lift is diverted to the horizontal component unless the pilot compensates. The pilot must anticipate this RPM tendency and manage collective carefully — typically by lowering collective slightly during the turn to reduce blade pitch, which allows airflow to accelerate the rotor back to the proper RPM range. Small collective adjustments throughout the turn are necessary to maintain RPM in the green arc.
questions.follow_up: If rotor RPM decays below the minimum green arc limit during a 180-degree autorotation turn at low altitude and you cannot immediately recover it, what is your priority action?
questions.follow_up_answer: At low altitude with RPM below the minimum green arc, the priority is to immediately lower collective to allow airflow to restore RPM — even if this momentarily increases rate of descent. If altitude is insufficient for RPM recovery before ground contact, accept the situation, level the skids, and execute the best available landing. A rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable, making early RPM recognition imperative. Prevention through proper planning and RPM monitoring throughout the turn is the only reliable safeguard.

questions.question: A student asks why the ACS specifies 'same direction' for the two 90-degree turn option rather than allowing S-turns. As an examiner, what is the underlying safety and skill rationale behind this requirement?
questions.answer: The 'same direction' requirement ensures the pilot demonstrates the ability to sustain coordinated autorotative flight through a continuous angular displacement — in this case, a total of 180 degrees — rather than simply rolling back and forth. S-turns through opposite 90-degree arcs would allow the pilot to stabilize and essentially reset between turns, masking deficiencies in sustained RPM control, bank angle management, and situational awareness during a prolonged turn. The same-direction requirement simulates a realistic scenario such as reversing course over an obstacle or aligning with a landing area, and it tests whether the pilot can maintain rotor RPM and a stable descent through cumulative turning while managing energy to arrive at a safe landing point.
questions.follow_up: If a student consistently shows RPM decay only during the second of the two 90-degree turns and not the first, what training deficiency does this most likely reveal?
questions.follow_up_answer: This pattern most likely indicates the student is not anticipating cumulative altitude and energy loss between turns. By the second turn, the student is at lower altitude, potentially at a reduced airspeed from the first turn, and may be in a steeper descent — all of which reduce the energy margin available to sustain RPM. It suggests the student is managing each turn in isolation rather than thinking through the full autorotation as a single energy management problem from entry to termination. Training should focus on pre-entry planning, airspeed control between turns, and continuous RPM monitoring rather than reactive corrections.

questions.question: If a helicopter departs into a 15-knot headwind and suffers an engine failure requiring a 180-degree autorotative turn, would the pilot need to turn more or less than 180 degrees on the heading indicator to achieve a 180-degree ground track reversal?
questions.answer: The pilot would need to turn more than 180 degrees on the heading indicator. When flying into a headwind and turning 180 degrees relative to ground track, the wind that was a headwind becomes a tailwind. During the turn itself, wind drift will push the helicopter downwind. To compensate and achieve a true 180-degree ground track reversal, the pilot must overshoot the reciprocal compass heading — meaning the heading indicator will show more than 180 degrees of turn. The exact amount depends on wind speed, turn rate, and altitude lost during the maneuver.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, ACS CH.XIV.C

questions.question: You are departing from a runway to the north with a 20-knot crosswind from the west. Shortly after departure, you suffer an engine failure and decide to execute a 180-degree autorotative turn back to the runway. Describe how the crosswind affects your planning for the turn, specifically with respect to achieving a 180-degree ground track reversal.
questions.answer: With a crosswind from the west pushing you to the east during northbound departure, your actual ground track has drifted east of your heading. To reverse your ground track by 180 degrees and align with the runway, you must account for this drift throughout the turn. If you turn left (westward), the crosswind initially aids the turn but then becomes a headwind on the southbound leg, pushing you back toward the runway centerline — in this case you may need less than a full 180-degree heading change. If you turn right (eastward), the crosswind opposes the turn initially and then becomes a tailwind, requiring more than 180 degrees of heading change to achieve the ground track reversal. The key takeaway: the heading indicator reading at the completion of the turn will NOT be exactly 180 degrees offset from the departure heading, and the pilot must plan the turn based on where the ground track needs to end up, not where the nose needs to point.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, ACS CH.XIV.C

questions.question: During an autorotation practice with a 180-degree turn, your student completes the turn and announces 'turn complete' when the heading indicator shows exactly 180 degrees from the departure heading, but the helicopter is clearly offset from the runway centerline by several hundred feet. What fundamental misunderstanding does this reveal, and how do you correct it?
questions.answer: The student is confusing heading change with ground track change. They are focused on the heading indicator rather than their actual path over the ground. The 180-degree reference in this maneuver means a reversal of ground track — the direction of travel over the surface — not a change in the magnetic compass heading. Wind during the turn caused ground track drift, so 180 degrees of heading change did not produce 180 degrees of ground track reversal. Correction: teach the student to reference ground features and the intended landing area visually throughout the turn, and to understand that wind correction must be applied during the turn — just as in any wind correction scenario — so that the resulting ground track lines up with the landing area, regardless of what heading is displayed.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, ACS CH.XIV.C

questions.question: In calm wind conditions, does the distinction between ground track and heading still matter for a 180-degree autorotative turn? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: In true calm wind conditions with no air movement, ground track and heading are identical, so the distinction has no practical effect and a 180-degree heading change would produce a 180-degree ground track reversal. However, this is almost never the case in real-world operations — some wind is almost always present. The ACS specifically calls out this distinction to ensure pilots understand the principle conceptually, so they don't develop a habit of relying solely on the heading indicator when wind is present. Even a light 5-knot wind during a prolonged turn at low altitude and low airspeed in autorotation can cause meaningful ground track deviation. Pilots should always plan the turn based on ground track, using visual references to the intended landing area, not solely the heading indicator.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, ACS CH.XIV.C

questions.question: A pilot argues that since autorotations are flown at relatively low altitudes and short durations, wind has a negligible effect and the ground track vs. heading distinction is a 'textbook technicality.' As an examiner, how do you respond, and what specific scenario would you use to demonstrate why this distinction has real safety consequences?
questions.answer: This argument is incorrect and dangerous. Even at low altitudes, autorotative turns take 10–20 seconds or more depending on bank angle and rotor RPM energy management, and a 15-knot wind over 15 seconds of turning can produce significant lateral ground track displacement — potentially the difference between landing on the runway surface and landing in terrain or obstacles to the side. A compelling scenario: the pilot departs to the south from a runway bordered on the east by trees and on the west by open field. A 15-knot easterly wind (from the east) is blowing. Engine failure occurs at 300 feet AGL, and the pilot executes a 180-degree turn to the north. If the pilot focuses only on the heading indicator and stops at a northerly heading, wind drift during the turn has pushed the ground track to the west of the runway — possibly into the open field or short of the threshold. If instead the pilot had planned to finish the turn aimed slightly east of the runway threshold to counteract the westward wind drift during the turn, they land on or near the intended surface. The ground track vs. heading distinction is exactly what separates a successful confined-area emergency landing from a controlled flight into terrain or obstacles.
questions.follow_up: If this same pilot insists on a specific bank angle during the 180-degree turn to 'save altitude,' how does bank angle selection interact with the ground track vs. heading concept, and what is the tradeoff?
questions.follow_up_answer: Bank angle directly affects how long the turn takes, which in turn affects how much wind drift accumulates during the maneuver. A shallower bank angle (e.g., 20 degrees) takes longer to complete the turn, meaning more time for wind to push the ground track off the intended course — requiring a larger heading correction to achieve the 180-degree ground track reversal, and consuming more altitude. A steeper bank angle (e.g., 40 degrees) completes the turn faster, limiting wind drift and reducing altitude lost to the turn itself, but increases the risk of rotor RPM overspeed or blade stall if not managed carefully, and requires more precise collective and cyclic coordination. The pilot must balance these factors: steeper banks reduce wind drift accumulation and altitude loss during the turn but demand higher skill; shallower banks are more forgiving of control errors but amplify the wind correction problem. In any case, the ground track concept doesn't disappear with steeper banks — it remains the reference point for evaluating whether the turn is succeeding.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS CH.XIV.C

questions.question: During a practical test, a candidate successfully completes a 180-degree autorotative turn and lands on centerline — but when you debrief, they admit they simply watched the heading indicator and added a few degrees for 'guessed wind correction.' Did they demonstrate the required understanding, and how would you determine whether their success was skill or luck?
questions.answer: A successful outcome alone does not demonstrate the required understanding of the ACS standard. The ACS specifically requires the applicant to understand that the 180-degree turn refers to ground track change, not heading change. A candidate who uses a guess-based heading correction without a systematic understanding of how to reference ground features and plan wind correction has not met the standard — they happened to arrive at a correct result through an unsound process. To assess true understanding, follow up with targeted oral questions: Ask them to explain how they would modify their heading correction if the wind doubled in speed. Ask them which visual references they used during the turn to confirm their ground track was converging on the landing area. Ask them what they would do mid-turn if they recognized their ground track was drifting off. If the candidate can only describe the heading indicator method and cannot explain how ground track is monitored or corrected during the turn, they have not met the knowledge standard — regardless of the landing outcome. In a real emergency, that gap in understanding could be fatal.
questions.follow_up: What visual technique should a pilot use during the turn to continuously monitor ground track and recognize early if a correction is needed?
questions.follow_up_answer: During the 180-degree autorotative turn, the pilot should identify the intended landing area before initiating the turn and use it as a continuous visual reference throughout the maneuver. A reliable technique is to monitor the apparent lateral movement of the landing area relative to the helicopter's position: if the landing area is drifting toward the rotor disc (moving aft of the intended final approach path), the pilot is being pushed away by wind and must adjust the turn to compensate — either by altering bank angle to change the rate of turn or by planning to overshoot the reciprocal direction slightly. Additionally, the pilot can reference ground features — field edges, taxiway lines, road edges — to gauge actual drift during the turn. The key principle is eyes-outside on ground references throughout the turn, not fixation on the heading indicator. This is the same skill used in any ground reference maneuver, applied in an emergency autorotative context.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS CH.XIV.C

questions.question: Why does the ACS establish a 300-foot AGL rollout requirement specifically for autorotation with turns, rather than allowing the applicant to continue the turn lower?
questions.answer: The 300-foot AGL limit exists because below that altitude there is insufficient time and altitude to safely establish a wings-level autorotative glide, adjust rotor RPM, control airspeed, and set up for a safe landing or flare. Continuing a banked turn below 300 feet AGL significantly increases the risk of an uncontrolled impact with the ground, making safe recovery essentially impossible.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-17 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task C; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: You are evaluating an applicant performing an autorotation with a 180-degree turn. At 350 feet AGL they are still in a 30-degree banked turn with approximately 90 degrees remaining to roll out. What do you do, and why?
questions.answer: At this point you must closely monitor the applicant's rate of rollout. If it becomes apparent they will not complete the rollout by 300 feet AGL — which with 90 degrees remaining at 350 feet is very likely — you must intervene immediately and direct the applicant to execute a power recovery and go-around before reaching 300 feet AGL. The safety standard requires the rollout to be complete by 300 feet AGL; you do not wait until 300 feet is actually reached if it is already clear the standard cannot be met.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-17 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task C; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: An applicant completes the rollout from an autorotative turn at exactly 295 feet AGL, then establishes a good approach profile and performs a successful power recovery. How do you grade this task and what do you tell the applicant?
questions.answer: The task is graded unsatisfactory. The ACS standard is unambiguous — the rollout must be complete by 300 feet AGL. Rolling out at 295 feet AGL means the applicant continued the turn below the required 300-foot altitude, failing to meet the standard, regardless of how well the remainder of the maneuver was performed. You would explain to the applicant that the rollout was not completed by the required 300-foot AGL altitude, making the task unsatisfactory, and that a retest of this task would be required.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-17 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task C

questions.question: During an autorotation with a 90-degree turn, the applicant rolls out wings-level at 320 feet AGL but the helicopter is now pointed at a hazard and they request to make a small correction. As the evaluator, what is your consideration and response?
questions.answer: The applicant has NOT met the rollout standard. The requirement is that the turn rollout (achieving wings-level attitude) must be complete by 300 feet AGL. Rolling out at 320 feet AGL means the wings-level attitude was not established until 320 feet, which is below the 300-foot requirement. The task is unsatisfactory. As evaluator, you should direct an immediate power recovery or go-around and brief the applicant that the turn was not completed by the required 300-foot AGL altitude. Safety of flight is the primary concern, but the task standard itself was not met.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-17 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task C; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: From a flight safety standpoint, explain what specific hazards increase exponentially when a helicopter remains in a banked autorotation below 300 feet AGL, and how those hazards justify the ACS's hard cutoff at that altitude.
questions.answer: Below 300 feet AGL in a banked autorotation, several hazards compound rapidly: (1) The banked disk produces asymmetric lift, reducing effective vertical lift and increasing the descent rate. (2) The inside rotor blade has a reduced airspeed and thus reduced lift margin, raising the risk of blade stall. (3) Rotor RPM may be decaying if collective was not properly managed through the turn, and there is insufficient altitude to recover RPM. (4) The flare — which requires level flight to be effective — cannot be properly executed if still in a turn, eliminating the pilot's ability to arrest descent rate before ground contact. (5) Ground contact during a banked attitude risks dynamic rollover. The 300-foot AGL limit is a conservative but evidence-based threshold below which these compounding hazards make a safe outcome statistically unlikely without immediate power recovery.
questions.follow_up: If a student asks you why the limit is 300 feet and not 200 feet or 400 feet, how would you justify that specific number?
questions.follow_up_answer: The 300-foot AGL figure reflects the minimum altitude needed to accomplish the following sequential tasks after rollout: establish wings-level attitude, verify and correct rotor RPM, stabilize airspeed in the autorotative glide, and initiate and complete a proper flare or power recovery. In most helicopters, the time from 300 feet AGL to ground contact in autorotation is approximately 10–15 seconds depending on descent rate — barely enough time for an experienced pilot. Going lower eliminates margin for any deviation. The FAA selected 300 feet as a point where a competent pilot can still recover; below that, the probability of a safe outcome drops sharply. The number is operationally derived, not arbitrary.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-17 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task C; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: As an evaluator, what is your legal and practical authority to intervene and direct a power recovery during an autorotation with turns, and at what point does your obligation to intervene override your role as a passive observer of the applicant's performance?
questions.answer: As an evaluator acting as PIC of the flight, the evaluator holds ultimate authority and responsibility for safety of flight under 14 CFR 91.3. The ACS explicitly codifies the evaluator's duty to intervene at 300 feet AGL if the rollout is not complete, but this does not limit the evaluator's authority to intervene earlier if safety is immediately at risk. The evaluator is never merely a passive observer — they are the acting PIC and must intervene any time continued flight by the applicant creates an imminent hazard, regardless of where that falls relative to the 300-foot standard. The ACS's 300-foot rule establishes a minimum intervention point, not the only intervention point. Waiting until exactly 300 feet AGL when an unsafe condition is already apparent would itself be a dereliction of the evaluator's PIC responsibility.
questions.follow_up: If you intervene and take the controls for safety before the applicant reaches 300 feet AGL, does the task automatically become unsatisfactory even if you intervened at, say, 350 feet?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes. Any time the evaluator must take the controls or direct intervention due to an unsafe condition — regardless of the exact altitude — the task is unsatisfactory. The ACS standard requires the applicant to demonstrate the maneuver safely within the standards without evaluator intervention. If intervention is needed for safety at any altitude, the applicant has failed to meet the standard. The 300-foot rule is a codified mandatory intervention point, but an unsafe condition at 350 feet that forces evaluator action equally results in an unsatisfactory grade. Safe completion of the task requires no evaluator intervention.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; FAA-S-ACS-17 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task C; FAA Order 8900.2

questions.question: What is the minimum entry altitude above the ground that the ACS requires you to establish before initiating an autorotation with turns?
questions.answer: The ACS specifies a minimum entry altitude of 700 feet AGL for autorotations with turns. This altitude provides sufficient time and rotor energy to complete the turn, stabilize the descent, and execute a safe recovery or landing. Anything below this threshold significantly reduces the margin for error.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS Task CH.XIV.C

questions.question: Why does the ACS call for a higher entry altitude than 700 feet AGL when wind conditions are strong?
questions.answer: Strong winds can cause the helicopter to drift significantly during the autorotative descent, potentially moving it away from the intended landing area or into terrain obstacles. They can also affect rotor RPM stability and make the flare and touchdown more difficult to control. A higher entry altitude gives the pilot more time to account for drift, adjust the approach angle, and position the helicopter correctly for a safe landing.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS Task CH.XIV.C

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns practice maneuver, what is the primary hazard if entry altitude is too low?
questions.answer: If entry altitude is too low, the pilot may not have enough altitude — and therefore not enough time — to complete the turn, stabilize the descent heading, perform a proper flare, and execute a safe recovery. Low-inertia rotor systems in particular decay rapidly during turns because cyclic inputs increase blade loading and can bleed off rotor RPM. The result can be an uncontrolled hard landing or crash with insufficient RPM to cushion the touchdown.

questions.question: You are practicing autorotations with 180-degree turns on a gusty day with winds at 25 knots. Your normal entry altitude is 700 feet AGL. How should you adjust your entry altitude, and what specific risks are you mitigating by doing so?
questions.answer: You should increase entry altitude above 700 feet AGL — likely to 900–1,000 feet AGL or more, depending on the specific helicopter's performance characteristics and the actual gust spread. The risks you are mitigating include: (1) increased drift that could take the helicopter outside the intended landing area, requiring additional maneuvering at low altitude; (2) turbulence-induced rotor RPM fluctuations during the turn, reducing the energy margin; (3) a steeper effective descent rate due to headwind/tailwind variations during the 180-degree turn; and (4) reduced ability to adjust the flare timing and landing point if the wind shifts during the descent.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; ACS Task CH.XIV.C

questions.question: During a checkride, you observe a candidate who consistently begins autorotations with turns at exactly 700 feet AGL regardless of wind, density altitude, or rotor type. What risk management deficiency does this reveal, and how would you probe the candidate's understanding?
questions.answer: The candidate is treating the 700-foot AGL requirement as a fixed rule rather than a minimum floor that must be adjusted based on actual conditions. This reveals a deficiency in risk management — specifically the failure to evaluate environmental and aircraft-specific variables before each maneuver. Density altitude affects rotor efficiency and descent rate; strong winds require more maneuvering time and increase drift; low-inertia rotors demand more altitude buffer for RPM recovery. A competent pilot uses 700 feet AGL as the absolute floor, then adds margin based on conditions. I would ask the candidate to walk me through how they determined 700 feet was adequate today, what conditions would cause them to increase that number, and at what point they would choose not to perform the maneuver at all.
questions.follow_up: The candidate says they would add 200 feet if winds exceed 15 knots. What follow-up question challenges whether that specific threshold is operationally sound?
questions.follow_up_answer: Ask the candidate: 'Where does that 200-foot/15-knot figure come from — your RFM, your training program, or a personal rule of thumb?' The point is that no single formula applies universally. The correct answer is that margin should be based on a holistic assessment: gust spread (not just steady wind), the specific helicopter's descent rate and rotor inertia, landing area obstacles, and the pilot's own proficiency with the maneuver. A rigid threshold like '15 knots = 200 extra feet' may be dangerously inadequate in a gusty 20-knot crosswind with a low-inertia rotor at high density altitude.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM/Risk Management); ACS Task CH.XIV.C

questions.question: A pilot argues that because they are only doing a 90-degree turn autorotation instead of a 180-degree turn, they can safely begin the maneuver at 600 feet AGL. Evaluate this reasoning using sound risk management principles.
questions.answer: The reasoning is flawed and represents a dangerous rationalization. The ACS minimum of 700 feet AGL applies to autorotations with turns as a category — it accounts for the combined time required to enter autorotation, execute the turn, stabilize on the final descent heading, perform the flare, and land safely. While a 90-degree turn does consume less altitude than a 180-degree turn, the 700-foot minimum is not calibrated solely on turn arc length. It also accounts for recognition/reaction time at entry, time to arrest rotor RPM decay during blade loading in the turn, the transition and stabilization phase after the turn, and the flare and touchdown sequence. Beginning at 600 feet compresses all of those phases into an altitude band that eliminates meaningful error margin. Additionally, real engine failures don't happen from a stabilized altitude — the 700-foot floor is set assuming a normal practice entry. Any deviation below that floor compounds risk without a commensurate safety benefit.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot insists that their specific RFM lists a lower minimum autorotation altitude than 700 feet AGL, does that override the ACS requirement for the checkride?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. The ACS establishes the standards for the checkride, and those standards represent the minimum acceptable safety parameters for the practical test regardless of RFM performance data. The RFM may show the aircraft is physically capable of completing an autorotation from a lower altitude under ideal conditions, but the ACS 700-foot minimum reflects the required safety buffer for training and testing environments where conditions are not always ideal and pilot proficiency is being evaluated. During the checkride, the ACS governs. In operational flying post-certificate, the pilot must comply with both the RFM limitations and exercise sound ADM — which nearly always means adding margin above minimums.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS Task CH.XIV.C; FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; 14 CFR Part 61

questions.question: During an autorotation with turns, at what altitude above the ground must your roll-out from any turn be completed?
questions.answer: Roll-out from all turns must be completed by 300 feet AGL. This is a hard ACS standard — if you are still in a bank below 300 feet AGL during an autorotation, it is an unsatisfactory event requiring an evaluator-directed power recovery and go-around.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-17 Helicopter ACS, Area XIV, Task C; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: If you fail to complete your roll-out from a turn by 300 feet AGL during an autorotation checkride task, what action must the evaluator take?
