questions.question: What authority must approve a curriculum or training program before an FSTD can be used for practical test purposes?
questions.answer: The FAA must approve the curriculum or training program. This approval can be granted to certificated training centers operating under 14 CFR Part 142, to Part 135 or Part 121 operators whose training programs have received specific FAA approval, or to Part 61 flight schools that formally develop and submit their training curriculum for FAA review and authorization. An individual Part 61 flight school or independent instructor cannot automatically or unilaterally designate their own program as approved for FSTD practical test use without formal FAA authorization and demonstrated compliance with 14 CFR Part 60 FSTD qualification standards.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 142; 14 CFR Part 60; ACS Appendix 3

questions.question: A helicopter student trained exclusively under a Part 61 flight school wants to use an FTD for their private pilot practical test. The FTD is a qualified Level 5 FTD. Is this permissible, and what conditions must be met?
questions.answer: Not automatically. Even if the FTD is a properly qualified Level 5 device under Part 60, its use during a practical test is only permissible if the training program is part of an FAA-approved curriculum. A standard Part 61 operation does not automatically qualify. The student would need to have trained under a Part 142-approved curriculum or another FAA-approved program that specifically authorizes FSTD credit for the practical test. Without that program approval, the practical test tasks must be conducted in the actual helicopter.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 60; 14 CFR Part 142; 14 CFR 61.64; ACS Appendix 3

questions.question: During a checkride, an applicant insists that because their Part 142 school used an FSTD for all their instrument training, the entire instrument rating practical test can be done in the simulator. As the examiner, how do you evaluate this claim?
questions.answer: As examiner, I would verify two things: first, that the Part 142 school's approved training program specifically authorizes FSTD use for the instrument practical test, and second, that the specific FSTD being used is qualified at the appropriate level for each task being tested. I would review the school's FAA-approved training program documentation and confirm the FSTD's qualification under Part 60. If any required task is not covered under the approved FSTD authorization, that task must be conducted in the actual aircraft. Program approval and device qualification are both required — one alone is insufficient.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 60; 14 CFR Part 142; ACS Appendix 3

questions.question: How does the requirement for an 'approved curriculum or training program' protect the integrity of the practical test when an FSTD is used instead of an actual helicopter?
questions.answer: The approved curriculum requirement ensures that FSTD training has been structured, validated, and overseen by the FAA to produce competency equivalent to actual aircraft training. Without this safeguard, there would be no standardized assurance that the FSTD scenarios, fidelity levels, and training sequences adequately prepare the applicant for real-world operations. FAA approval of the program means the agency has reviewed the training syllabus, confirmed the FSTD's suitability for specific tasks, and determined that practical test standards can be meaningfully evaluated in that simulated environment.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 60; 14 CFR Part 142; ACS Appendix 3

questions.question: An applicant for an ATP helicopter certificate completed all training at a Part 142 training center using a Level D Full Flight Simulator. On the day of the checkride, the examiner discovers that the FFS qualification certificate has lapsed by two weeks due to an overdue evaluation. Can the checkride proceed in the simulator?
questions.answer: No. A lapsed FSTD qualification certificate means the device is no longer a qualified FSTD under 14 CFR Part 60. Regardless of the approved curriculum or training program, the device must be currently qualified at the appropriate level at the time of the practical test. An unqualified simulator — even one that was previously qualified and physically unchanged — cannot be used for practical test purposes. The practical test would need to be rescheduled either after the simulator's qualification is restored or conducted in the actual aircraft if permitted by the program.
questions.follow_up: What if the lapse was only a matter of hours — say, the qualification expired at midnight and the checkride was scheduled for 8 AM that morning — is there any regulatory flexibility or grace period?
questions.follow_up_answer: No regulatory grace period exists under 14 CFR Part 60 for an expired FSTD qualification. The device either holds a current, valid qualification or it does not. The FAA does not provide a grace window for lapsed simulator qualifications the way it does for certain pilot certificates or currency requirements. The appropriate action would be to contact the FSTD sponsor and the NSPM (National Simulator Program Manager) office to address the lapse before proceeding. Conducting the practical test on an unqualified device would invalidate the results.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 60, Subparts B and C; 14 CFR Part 142

questions.question: A Part 135 helicopter operator has FAA-approved training programs and uses a qualified FTD for checkrides. A pilot trained in one specific helicopter model completes the checkride in an FTD representing a different but similar model. The operator claims both models are covered in their approved program. What is the regulatory concern, and what must be verified?
questions.answer: The regulatory concern is whether the FAA-approved training program specifically authorizes the use of that FTD for the aircraft type or variant being certificated, and whether the FTD is qualified to represent the specific aircraft model on which the pilot will be rated. Under Part 60, an FSTD is qualified for a specific aircraft make, model, and series. Using an FTD configured for one variant to certificate a pilot in a different variant — even a similar one — is only permissible if the approved program explicitly addresses that substitution and the FAA has approved it. You must verify the program's aircraft-specific authorization, the FTD's qualification data sheet, and any FAA-issued deviation or equivalent level of safety finding that permits cross-model use.
questions.follow_up: What document would you look at to confirm which aircraft models and variants a specific FSTD is qualified to represent?
questions.follow_up_answer: The FSTD's Statement of Qualification (SOQ), issued by the FAA under 14 CFR Part 60, specifies the exact aircraft make, model, and series the device is qualified to represent, along with the qualification level and any limitations. The SOQ is the authoritative document. Additionally, the FSTD sponsor's approved training program documentation and any FAA-issued letters of authorization or deviation would clarify what cross-model use, if any, has been specifically approved.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 60, Subpart B; 14 CFR Part 135, Subpart H; Statement of Qualification (SOQ)

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 61.45, who is ultimately responsible for ensuring the aircraft used on a practical test meets the required equipment standards?
questions.answer: The applicant is responsible for providing an aircraft that meets the requirements of 14 CFR 61.45. The aircraft must be of the appropriate category and class (and type, if applicable), airworthy, and equipped with the systems and instruments required for the certificate or rating being tested.

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 61.45, what are the basic airworthiness requirements an aircraft must meet before it can be used on a checkride?
questions.answer: The aircraft must have a current airworthiness certificate, be in an airworthy condition, and have all required equipment installed and operative for the certificate or rating being sought. It must also be the appropriate category and class for the practical test being conducted.

questions.question: Does 14 CFR 61.45 allow an applicant to use a certificated aircraft that belongs to a flight school or another person for their checkride, or must the applicant own the aircraft?
questions.answer: The applicant does not need to own the aircraft. Under 14 CFR 61.45, the aircraft may be owned by any person or organization — including a flight school — as long as it meets all the applicable airworthiness, equipment, and category/class requirements for the practical test.

questions.question: You show up for your instrument helicopter checkride in a Robinson R44 that has a functioning autopilot installed but it is currently placarded inoperative. The aircraft is operated under 14 CFR Part 91 and no approved MEL is in place. Can this aircraft still be used for your IFR practical test, and what must you consider?
questions.answer: Potentially yes, but it depends on whether the autopilot is required equipment for the IFR operations being evaluated. Under 14 CFR 61.45(b), all instruments and equipment required for the certificate or rating being tested must be operative. For a Part 91 operator without an approved MEL, inoperative equipment is deferred under 14 CFR 91.213(d) (permissive list). The autopilot would generally be allowed inoperative if it is not required for the specific practical test task. However, verify that: (1) the inoperative autopilot is properly placarded per 91.213(d)(2); (2) the inoperative status is logged per 91.213(d)(2); and (3) the examiner confirms the practical test does not require the autopilot for any evaluated IFR tasks. Coordinate with the examiner beforehand to avoid delays on checkride day.

questions.question: A student wants to use an experimental helicopter for their private pilot checkride. Under 14 CFR 61.45, is this allowed, and what conditions would have to be met?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.45(b)(1), the aircraft used on a practical test must hold a standard airworthiness certificate, a primary category airworthiness certificate, or a special airworthiness certificate in the light-sport category. Experimental aircraft are generally not eligible because they do not hold a standard airworthiness certificate. However, 14 CFR 61.45(b) does allow certain aircraft with a special airworthiness certificate if approved by the FAA Administrator. In practice, an experimental helicopter would not be an acceptable checkride aircraft without specific FAA authorization.

questions.question: You are taking your instrument helicopter checkride and the examiner wants to evaluate a task that requires a view-limiting device. Under 14 CFR 61.45, who is responsible for making sure the view-limiting device is available, and what are the requirements for it?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.45(d), the applicant must provide a view-limiting device acceptable to the examiner when a task requires flight by reference to instruments. The device must prevent the applicant from having outside visual references while not preventing the safety pilot or examiner from seeing outside the aircraft. It must be installed and functional for the duration of tasks requiring its use.

questions.question: An applicant arrives for an instrument helicopter checkride and the aircraft's encoding altimeter has a current IFR certification from the avionics shop dated 23 months ago, but the static system check was done 26 months ago as a combined test. The VFR altimeter works fine. Can the test proceed, and how does 14 CFR 61.45 interact with 14 CFR 91.411 here?
questions.answer: No, the test cannot legally proceed for IFR operations. Under 14 CFR 91.411, the static pressure system, each altimeter, and the automatic pressure altitude reporting system must be tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months for IFR operations in controlled airspace. Even if the encoding altimeter cert is within 24 months, if the static system test is outside 24 calendar months, the aircraft is not legal for IFR flight. Under 14 CFR 61.45(b), the aircraft must be equipped with instruments and equipment required for the practical test and must be airworthy. Since the aircraft would not be legal for IFR flight per 91.411, it does not meet the 61.45 standard and the IFR checkride cannot proceed.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant discovers this discrepancy on the ramp just before the test, can they still complete the VFR portions of the checkride, or does the entire test get discontinued?
questions.follow_up_answer: The examiner has discretion here. Under 61.45, if the deficiency only affects the aircraft's eligibility for IFR portions, the examiner may conduct the VFR portions of the test if the aircraft is otherwise airworthy for VFR flight. However, for an instrument rating checkride, virtually all flight tasks require IFR-legal equipment. The examiner would likely discontinue the practical test rather than conduct only partial tasks, as completing meaningful evaluation of instrument competency requires a legally IFR-equipped aircraft. The applicant could reschedule once the 91.411 tests are completed.

questions.question: During a helicopter instrument checkride, the examiner notices that the aircraft's transponder was tested 25 months ago. The applicant argues the transponder isn't required for the practical test itself and that the examiner can just waive using it. How does 14 CFR 61.45 and the applicable transponder regulation address this situation?
questions.answer: The transponder argument doesn't hold up. Under 14 CFR 91.413, each transponder must be tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months before it can be used. Under 14 CFR 61.45(b), the aircraft must have the instruments and equipment required for the practical test in operative condition. For IFR flight — which is what an instrument checkride requires — a Mode C transponder is required in most controlled airspace per 14 CFR 91.215. The examiner cannot waive an airworthiness or equipment currency requirement under 61.45. If the transponder is out of its 24-month inspection, the aircraft is not legal for IFR use and the checkride cannot proceed.
questions.follow_up: Suppose the entire checkride will be conducted in Class G airspace, below 10,000 ft MSL, and the examiner is willing to accept that routing. Does the expired transponder inspection still ground the aircraft?
questions.follow_up_answer: This is a nuanced question. Under 14 CFR 91.215 and 91.413, transponder equipment requirements apply in specific airspace (Class A, B, C, above 10,000 ft MSL in Class E, etc.). In Class G airspace below those thresholds, a transponder is not legally required for VFR or IFR flight. However, for an instrument checkride, the examiner must still ensure the aircraft meets the requirements of 61.45, which requires instruments and equipment be operative as required for the operation. If the routing truly avoids all transponder-required airspace, the expired transponder inspection may not technically prevent the flight. In practice, however, the operational and safety risks — including loss of ATC radar service — make this a highly inadvisable approach, and most examiners would decline to proceed.

questions.question: What is automation management in the context of helicopter IFR operations, and why is it considered a core Single-Pilot Resource Management (SRM) skill?
questions.answer: Automation management is the ability to effectively monitor, control, and appropriately use installed automated systems — such as autopilots, avionics displays, and FMS — to reduce workload and improve situational awareness. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook identifies automation management as a core SRM component because the pilot must know when to engage automation, when to override it, and how to detect when it is not performing as expected. Mismanaging automation is a human factors error that contributes to the accident chain.

questions.question: Name three types of installed or airborne equipment that fall under automation management, and briefly describe what each does to assist the IFR helicopter pilot.
questions.answer: 1. Autopilot — maintains selected flight parameters (heading, altitude, airspeed, or coupled approach path) without continuous manual control input, reducing pilot workload during high-demand phases of flight. 2. Avionics and systems displays (e.g., EFIS, MFD, TAWS, TCAS, ADS-B) — present integrated flight, navigation, traffic, and terrain data to enhance situational awareness and reduce the need for the pilot to mentally compile information from multiple analog sources. 3. Flight Management System (FMS) — integrates navigation, fuel management, and performance data to provide precise lateral and vertical guidance; the pilot programs routes and the FMS automates position tracking and sequencing of waypoints.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'homing' and 'tracking' using ADF/NDB, and which one reflects poor automation or navigation management technique and why?
questions.answer: Homing means continuously adjusting heading to keep the ADF needle pointed at 0° relative bearing — the aircraft flies any heading necessary to point at the station. Tracking means identifying the wind correction angle and flying a specific magnetic course TO or FROM the station, resulting in a straight ground track. Homing reflects poor technique because in a crosswind it produces a curved, banana-shaped path to the station rather than a direct course. In an IFR context, relying on homing without applying wind correction is an example of failing to properly use available navigation information — a breakdown in automation and navigation management.

questions.question: You are flying an IFR helicopter approach coupled to your autopilot. At the final approach fix, you notice the autopilot is maintaining the correct heading but your vertical deviation indicator shows a full-scale fly-up deflection. What is your immediate automation management response, and what instrument cross-check helps confirm the situation?
questions.answer: The immediate response is to disengage the autopilot (if it is not correcting the deviation) and hand-fly while determining the cause. A full-scale fly-up on the vertical deviation means the aircraft is significantly below the desired glidepath, which is a critical safety concern — continued descent could lead to CFIT. The pilot should cross-check the altimeter (is the aircraft at or below the published step-down or glidepath altitude?), VSI (is the aircraft descending or level?), and the approach chart minimum altitudes. Automation management requires the pilot to recognize when automation is not performing correctly and immediately transition to manual control with proper instrument cross-check rather than trusting a single display.

questions.question: You are programming a direct-to waypoint into your FMS during cruise in IMC. At what point does managing the FMS become a threat to safety, and what SRM principle applies?
questions.answer: Managing the FMS becomes a threat when it diverts the pilot's attention from flying the aircraft and monitoring instruments for long enough to allow an undetected deviation or deterioration in situational awareness. This is called 'automation complacency' or 'head-down time.' The SRM principle that applies is workload management — the pilot must prioritize aircraft control first, then navigation, then communication. Best practice is to program the FMS during lower-workload phases, use automation to reduce workload rather than increase it, and always return to instrument cross-check immediately after inputting data. The Helicopter Flying Handbook also warns that a single poor decision (like fixating on a display in IMC) is often a link in the error chain leading to an accident.

questions.question: Your helicopter's pitot tube becomes blocked in IMC during climb but the drain hole remains open. How does this affect the airspeed indicator, and how should your automation management — specifically your use of avionics displays — compensate for the unreliable instrument?
questions.answer: With a blocked pitot tube and open drain hole, ram air pressure cannot build up while static pressure vents freely through the drain, causing the airspeed indicator to read zero and remain there. The pilot should recognize the unreliable ASI and immediately cross-reference other available avionics: the FMS or GPS groundspeed (which approximates true airspeed only in very low wind conditions; significant wind requires wind-correction adjustment), engine torque and collective position (which indicate approximate airspeed regime and performance envelope), and the vertical speed indicator (to confirm climb rate matches expected performance). If an autopilot with airspeed-hold mode is engaged, it should be evaluated for erroneous inputs or disengaged, as it may command incorrect control inputs based on failed data. Activate pitot heat if not already on. Automation management means using all available displays and cross-referencing them rather than fixating on a single failed instrument.

questions.question: A pilot flying an IFR helicopter with a coupled autopilot and FMS has programmed a T-route (low-altitude RNAV) into the FMS and engaged LNAV mode. During the flight, the pilot notices the aircraft is tracking the magenta line perfectly but is 500 feet below the MEA for that segment. How does this scenario illustrate the limits of automation management, and what is the pilot's responsibility?
questions.answer: This scenario illustrates 'automation complacency' — the pilot trusted the FMS lateral guidance (LNAV) and autopilot without independently verifying vertical compliance. T-routes are low-altitude RNAV routes requiring a specific MEA that guarantees both obstacle clearance and navigation signal reception. The FMS manages lateral track but does not automatically ensure the aircraft is at or above the MEA unless vertical navigation (VNAV) is also programmed and engaged. The pilot's responsibility is to independently cross-check altitude against the MEA published on the en route chart regardless of what the autopilot is doing. Automation management requires active monitoring — not passive observation. The pilot must intervene, climb to or above the MEA immediately, and verify that no obstacle clearance was compromised. This is also a violation of 14 CFR 91.177, which requires IFR flight at or above the minimum IFR altitude.
questions.follow_up: If the FMS database shows the same T-route waypoints but the MEA displayed in the FMS is different from what is published on the current en route chart, which source governs and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: The published en route chart governs. Per FAA guidance, the pilot is responsible for verifying that the avionics database is current (updated every 28 days per FAA-H-8083-15B) and that it matches current charted procedures. If a discrepancy exists between the FMS database and the published chart, the published chart takes precedence and the pilot must not use the FMS data that conflicts with the chart. The pilot should also report the discrepancy to the database provider. This underscores that automation is a tool to assist the pilot — regulatory and charted minimums always govern pilot action.

questions.question: During an IFR helicopter flight in IMC, your EFIS system fails, leaving you with only your backup analog instruments. Your autopilot, which relied on EFIS data inputs, also goes offline. Describe how you manage the transition away from automation and what instrument scan technique you would use to maintain control.
questions.answer: The immediate priority is to maintain aircraft control using the partial panel — the backup analog instruments. The pilot should identify which instruments are still functional (typically standby altimeter, standby ASI, magnetic compass, and possibly a backup attitude indicator or turn coordinator powered by a separate source) and immediately establish a cross-check using those instruments. The standard partial panel instrument scan uses the altimeter, airspeed indicator, and turn coordinator as the primary references since the attitude indicator is unavailable. The pilot should declare an emergency with ATC (14 CFR 91.3), request vectors or radar surveillance, and prioritize aviate-navigate-communicate. The loss of automation means the pilot must manually fly the aircraft with increased mental workload; workload management becomes critical — minimize non-essential tasks, brief ATC on the situation, and fly simple, shallow maneuvers. The transition from automation to manual flight in IMC must be immediate and deliberate to prevent spatial disorientation.
questions.follow_up: If the alternate static source is activated after the EFIS failure and the standby altimeter is now drawing from cabin static, what specific instrument errors must the pilot be aware of?
questions.follow_up_answer: When using alternate static source (cabin air), cabin pressure is slightly lower than ambient outside static pressure. This causes the standby altimeter to indicate slightly higher than actual altitude, the standby ASI to indicate slightly faster than actual airspeed, and the VSI to momentarily show a climb before stabilizing. The pilot must be aware of these errors and apply a mental correction — particularly important when determining proximity to minimum IFR altitudes or when configuring for an approach. The FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 explicitly describes these alternate static source errors.

questions.question: What is a portable Electronic Flight Bag (EFB), and what are the three classes of EFB defined by the FAA?
questions.answer: A portable EFB is an electronic device used by flight crew to perform flight operations functions traditionally accomplished with paper documents and tools. The FAA defines three classes: Class 1 EFBs are commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) portable devices not mounted to the aircraft structure, used only during cruise flight; Class 2 EFBs may be mounted on a mounting device but are still considered portable and may be used during all phases of flight; Class 3 EFBs are installed aircraft equipment subject to full avionics certification requirements (not considered portable and require an STC or equivalent). For Part 91 general aviation operations, Class 1 and 2 EFBs generally require no FAA authorization; however, the pilot remains responsible for validating data accuracy (e.g., chart currency, performance data) and ensuring the EFB does not create a distraction during flight. Class 3 EFBs are rare in general aviation helicopters.
questions.regulatory_ref: AC 120-76D (Guidelines for the Certification, Airworthiness, and Operational Use of Electronic Flight Bags)

questions.question: What types of functions or applications are commonly found on a portable EFB used in helicopter operations?
questions.answer: Common EFB functions include: electronic charts (approach plates, sectionals, helicopter route charts), aircraft performance calculations (weight and balance, takeoff/landing data), flight planning tools, weather data display, airport/heliport information, electronic checklists, logbook applications, and moving map/GPS navigation displays. The EFB can replace paper publications such as the AFM supplements, approach charts, and navigational charts, reducing pilot workload when used properly.
questions.regulatory_ref: AC 120-76D; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 1 (electronic flight bags mentioned as new technology)

questions.question: How often must the navigation database in a portable EFB be updated to ensure currency for IFR operations, and what is the consequence of using an out-of-date database?
questions.answer: Electronic navigation databases used for instrument approaches and en route navigation must be updated every 28 days (one AIRAC cycle) to remain current. Aeronautical chart publications (approach plates, sectionals) are revised on a 56-day cycle, but databases are updated on a 28-day cycle. Using an out-of-date database for IFR navigation is not authorized — the pilot may not use the EFB as a primary navigation source for approaches or routing if the database has expired. It can still be used for situational awareness, but the pilot must verify currency before relying on any data for instrument procedures.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter IFR approach into a remote helipad and your portable EFB locks up and becomes unresponsive mid-approach. What are your immediate actions, and what does this scenario reveal about EFB risk management?
questions.answer: Immediately revert to backup navigation sources — if a second device (another EFB, built-in avionics, or paper plates) is available, transition to it. If no backup is available, execute the published missed approach and do not continue to a potentially unsafe landing. This scenario highlights that portable EFBs are not certified avionics and can fail without warning. Proper EFB risk management requires: always carrying a backup (paper or second device), ensuring the device is fully charged preflight, and never relying on a single portable device as the sole source of approach data for IFR. The FAA recommends a 'no single point of failure' philosophy for EFB use.
questions.regulatory_ref: AC 120-76D Section 10 (risk management for EFB failure); 14 CFR 91.167 (fuel requirements); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM)

questions.question: A pilot tells you they use a moving map application on their tablet as their primary means of navigation during an IFR cross-country in the helicopter. What questions would you ask to determine if this use is appropriate and legal?
questions.answer: Key questions to ask: (1) Is the app's GPS receiver and software approved or only advisory? Most portable EFB GPS apps are not TSO-certified and cannot serve as a primary IFR navigation source unless the installed avionics provide the IFR GPS signal. (2) Is the navigation database current (within the 28-day AIRAC cycle)? (3) Is there a certified IFR GPS or VOR available as the primary navigation source? (4) Does the helicopter's avionics package or the operator's OpSpec authorize the EFB for navigation? (5) Is the EFB being used for situational awareness only, or as a primary navigation instrument? Under 14 CFR Part 91, a portable non-TSO'd EFB app cannot serve as the sole IFR navigation source; it must supplement certified avionics.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.205; AC 90-100A; AC 120-76D; TSO-C146 (RNAV equipment standards)

questions.question: During a night VFR helicopter flight you notice your EFB display is very bright and is degrading your night vision. What do you do, and what does this situation illustrate about EFB operational discipline?
questions.answer: Immediately reduce the screen brightness to the lowest usable level or switch the app to night mode/red-screen mode if available. If neither option sufficiently reduces glare, consider placing the device face-down or covering it until needed, relying on installed instruments. This situation illustrates that EFBs, while useful, can create new hazards if not managed — particularly for night vision degradation. Operational discipline includes: configuring the EFB for the expected lighting environment before flight, not making configuration adjustments while maneuvering, and understanding that the EFB is a workload management tool, not an additional distraction. The principle of managing automation (SRM) applies directly.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (SRM, workload management); AC 120-76D Section 8 (operational considerations); 14 CFR 91.9 (careless and reckless operation)

questions.question: A certificate holder under Part 135 wants to replace all paper approach plates with a Class 2 EFB in their helicopter fleet. What FAA authorization process must they follow, and what operational considerations are unique to helicopter IFR operations with an EFB?
questions.answer: Under Part 135, a certificate holder must obtain authorization from their FSDO/Flight Standards Office through appropriate OpSpec amendments (the specific OpSpec designation will vary by certificate holder). They must: (1) Conduct a risk assessment and submit an EFB implementation plan; (2) Demonstrate the device meets Class 2 criteria including an approved mounting solution; (3) Establish battery management and failure procedures in their GOM; (4) Ensure pilots receive documented training on EFB use, failure modes, and backup procedures; (5) Maintain a list of approved software and ensure database currency procedures are in the company manuals. Helicopter-specific considerations include the vibration environment (which can damage devices or cause display issues), limited cockpit space for mounting in small helicopters, single-pilot operations common in helicopters (increasing EFB workload risk), and the need for approaches to non-towered heliports not always well-represented in some EFB databases.
questions.follow_up: If the EFB is the only source of approach charts on board and the database is discovered to be expired after departure, what are the crew's options?
questions.follow_up_answer: The crew cannot use the expired EFB database as an authorized source for instrument approaches. Options include: (1) Return to departure airport if it has current chart information available through other means; (2) Contact ATC for radar vectors and request they provide minimums verbally if authorized; (3) Divert to an alternate where current chart data can be obtained or where they can land VFR; (4) Request an ATC 'no-gyro' or surveillance approach if available at the destination. The crew should not continue an IFR approach relying solely on an expired database — doing so could expose them to the wrong procedure, wrong minimums, or outdated obstacle data. Prevention is the key: a preflight currency check of the EFB database is a required item in a thorough Part 135 preflight.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 135; OpSpec A061; AC 120-76D Section 6 (Part 135 authorization); 14 CFR 135.83 (preparation of operations)

questions.question: During the oral exam, a candidate says: 'I always use my EFB's GPS moving map to fly GPS approaches — it shows me right on the approach course and I can see exactly where I am.' What misconceptions does this statement reveal, and how would you address them?
questions.answer: This statement reveals several critical misconceptions: (1) A portable EFB GPS is typically not TSO-certified (TSO-C146 or equivalent) and cannot legally serve as the sole navigation source for a GPS/RNAV instrument approach — the approach must be flown using a certified IFR-approved GPS receiver installed in the aircraft or meeting the IFR GPS equipment requirements; (2) The moving map provides situational awareness, not approach guidance — the CDI/deviation guidance for the approach must come from a certified navigator, not a tablet GPS app; (3) 'Showing me on the approach course' on a moving map is not equivalent to fly-to guidance meeting the accuracy and integrity standards required for instrument approaches (RAIM, WAAS, etc.); (4) Over-reliance on a single device creates the exact error chain described in ADM — the pilot may not be cross-checking certified instruments. The correct use of the EFB moving map is as a secondary situational awareness tool while primary approach guidance comes from certified avionics.
questions.follow_up: What is RAIM, why does it matter for GPS approaches, and does a portable EFB app typically provide valid RAIM alerts?
questions.follow_up_answer: RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) is a GPS receiver function that monitors the integrity of GPS satellite signals and alerts the pilot when the GPS signal is insufficient for navigation. For GPS instrument approaches, RAIM must be available at the destination and alternate — pilots should check RAIM availability during preflight using NOTAMs or the FAA RAIM prediction tool. Most portable EFB apps and consumer GPS chips do NOT provide valid RAIM alerts equivalent to certified avionics — they lack the algorithms and integrity monitoring required by TSO-C129 or TSO-C146. This is a fundamental reason why a portable EFB cannot serve as a primary IFR approach navigation source: it cannot guarantee the GPS integrity required for safe instrument approaches, especially in helicopter operations at low altitudes near terrain and obstacles.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.205; AC 90-100A (RNAV/GPS IFR requirements); TSO-C129, TSO-C145, TSO-C146; AIM 1-1-17 (GPS IFR operations); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: During an instrument helicopter checkride, who is responsible for providing the view limiting device — the examiner or the applicant?
questions.answer: The applicant is responsible for providing the view limiting device. Under 14 CFR 61.45(d)(2), when a practical test requires maneuvering solely by reference to instruments, the applicant must supply an appropriate view limiting device acceptable to the Administrator.

questions.question: What is the regulatory term used to describe the standard a view limiting device must meet for use on an instrument checkride?
questions.answer: The regulation states the device must be 'acceptable to the Administrator.' This means the FAA — typically represented by the examiner — must find the device appropriate for simulating instrument conditions. Common examples include foggles, Hooded devices, or a hood that effectively restricts the pilot's outside vision while still allowing the safety pilot or examiner to see outside the aircraft.

questions.question: Under what specific regulatory condition does the requirement to provide a view limiting device on a practical test get triggered?
questions.answer: The requirement is triggered when the practical test involves maneuvering the aircraft solely by reference to instruments. If any portion of the checkride requires the applicant to demonstrate flight solely by instrument reference — such as during an IFR helicopter rating test — the applicant must have an appropriate view limiting device available and acceptable to the examiner, per 14 CFR 61.45(d)(2).

questions.question: You show up to your instrument helicopter checkride with a pair of foggles that have a small crack in one lens. The examiner is not satisfied with them. What are your options at that point, and what regulation governs this decision?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.45(d)(2), the applicant bears the responsibility of providing a view limiting device acceptable to the Administrator (i.e., the examiner). If the examiner determines the device is unacceptable — for any safety or functional reason — the applicant must produce an acceptable alternative or the instrument portion of the checkride cannot proceed. Options include: producing a backup device if available, borrowing one acceptable to the examiner, or discontinuing/rescheduling that portion of the test. The examiner has the authority to reject any device deemed unsuitable, and the checkride cannot be completed without a compliant device for the instrument flight portions.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter instrument checkride and conditions are actual IMC for part of the flight. Does the requirement to bring a view limiting device under 14 CFR 61.45(d)(2) still apply, and why or why not?
questions.answer: Yes, the requirement still applies. The regulation requires the applicant to provide a view limiting device whenever the test involves maneuvering solely by reference to instruments — regardless of whether that occurs in actual or simulated IMC. In actual IMC, the view limiting device may not be actively worn, but the applicant is still expected to have one available because conditions could change, portions of the flight may occur in VMC requiring simulated instrument flight, or the examiner may require its use during certain maneuvers. Preparedness is the applicant's responsibility under 14 CFR 61.45(d)(2).

questions.question: A student tells you they plan to use a full instrument hood that restricts all forward and peripheral vision for their IFR helicopter checkride. From an examiner's perspective, what would make this device 'acceptable' versus 'unacceptable'?
questions.answer: An acceptable view limiting device must effectively prevent the applicant from using outside visual references while still allowing the safety pilot or examiner to maintain an unobstructed view outside the aircraft for collision avoidance. A hood that blocks all peripheral vision — including the examiner's view — would be unacceptable because it creates a safety hazard. An acceptable device limits only the applicant's vision to the instrument panel, does not physically interfere with flight controls, fits securely without falling off during maneuvering, and allows the required safety lookout function. The examiner holds final authority on acceptability under 14 CFR 61.45(d)(2).

questions.question: 14 CFR 61.45(d)(2) places the burden on the applicant to supply the view limiting device. If an applicant argues that the examiner's standards for 'acceptable' are arbitrary or unfair, what is the correct resolution process and what authority does the examiner have?
questions.answer: The examiner, acting as a designee of the Administrator, holds the authority to determine whether equipment meets regulatory standards during the practical test under 14 CFR 61.45(d). The examiner's acceptance decision is not arbitrary — it is grounded in whether the device achieves the regulatory purpose: allowing the applicant to maneuver solely by reference to instruments safely, while ensuring the examiner can maintain situational awareness for safety. If the applicant genuinely believes the rejection is improper, they may request that the examiner document the reason for rejection and may contact the FSDO that oversees the examiner. However, during the test itself, the examiner's determination is final. The applicant cannot compel the use of an unacceptable device, and the practical test cannot proceed for instrument portions without a compliant device.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant shows up without any view limiting device at all and it's a clear VMC day, can the examiner complete any part of the instrument helicopter checkride?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. If any task in the ACS requires the applicant to maneuver solely by reference to instruments, and the test is being conducted in VMC, a view limiting device is mandatory under 14 CFR 61.45(d)(2). Without one, those tasks cannot be evaluated. The examiner could potentially evaluate tasks that do not require instrument reference only, but the practical test would be incomplete and the rating could not be issued. The applicant would need to reschedule the instrument flight portions with a proper device.

questions.question: How does the requirement under 14 CFR 61.45(d)(2) to provide a view limiting device interact with the broader equipment requirements of 14 CFR 61.45 for a helicopter instrument rating practical test? Who bears responsibility for each category of required equipment?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.45, equipment responsibilities are divided. The applicant is generally responsible for providing the aircraft used on the practical test (61.45(a)), and the aircraft must meet airworthiness standards and be equipped for the tasks being tested — including all required IFR instruments per 14 CFR 91.205(d). The view limiting device under 61.45(d)(2) is a specific additional burden placed on the applicant, separate from the aircraft's avionics. This means the applicant must independently ensure a suitable device is present even if the aircraft owner or flight school does not provide one. The examiner is responsible for evaluating whether all equipment — aircraft and devices — meets the standard. No single party other than the applicant bears the 61.45(d)(2) responsibility; it cannot be delegated to the flight school or examiner.
questions.follow_up: If the helicopter used for the checkride has a functional autopilot — can that autopilot substitute for a view limiting device to demonstrate the applicant's ability to fly solely by reference to instruments?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. An autopilot cannot substitute for a view limiting device. The purpose of the view limiting device is to evaluate the applicant's personal ability to interpret and fly solely by reference to instruments, without outside visual cues. An autopilot manages the aircraft automatically and does not demonstrate pilot instrument proficiency. The ACS tasks require the applicant to actively manipulate the controls under simulated or actual instrument conditions. A view limiting device is still required per 14 CFR 61.45(d)(2) regardless of whether an autopilot is available or used on other portions of the test.

questions.question: Who is responsible for providing the helicopter used during autorotation tasks on a checkride, and what type of helicopter is required?
questions.answer: The applicant is responsible for providing the helicopter, and it must be a single-engine helicopter. Multi-engine helicopters are not acceptable for demonstrating autorotation tasks on the practical test.

questions.question: Why does the ACS specifically require a single-engine helicopter for autorotation tasks rather than allowing any certificated helicopter?
questions.answer: Autorotation is the procedure used to safely land a helicopter following engine failure. A single-engine helicopter has only one powerplant, so a complete power loss requires the pilot to execute a full autorotation. Multi-engine helicopters may be able to maintain flight on a remaining engine, making an authentic, complete autorotation demonstration impractical or unsafe in that configuration. The single-engine requirement ensures the task is operationally relevant and demonstrates the skill as it would occur in an actual emergency.

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 61.45, what are the general requirements for an aircraft provided by the applicant for a practical test?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.45, the aircraft provided by the applicant must be of U.S. registry unless authorized by the FAA; have a current airworthiness certificate; be in an airworthy condition; and be equipped for the tasks to be performed. The applicant must also have all required documents on board, including the airworthiness certificate, registration, operating limitations, and applicable weight and balance data. For autorotation tasks specifically, the ACS adds the requirement that it be a single-engine helicopter.

questions.question: An applicant shows up to their commercial helicopter checkride in a twin-engine helicopter. They plan to use it for all tasks, including autorotations. As the examiner, how do you handle this situation?
questions.answer: The checkride cannot proceed for the autorotation tasks in that aircraft. The ACS requires that the applicant provide a single-engine helicopter for autorotation tasks. The examiner should inform the applicant of this requirement before beginning or discontinuing the test. Depending on whether the autorotation tasks are required for the certificate or rating being sought, the applicant may need to reschedule with an appropriate single-engine helicopter. The examiner cannot waive this ACS requirement — it is a test standard, not a discretionary preference.

questions.question: You are preparing for your instrument helicopter checkride and plan to fly a turbine-powered single-engine helicopter. Does this aircraft satisfy the ACS requirement for autorotation tasks, and what documentation must you bring to the checkride?
questions.answer: Yes, a turbine-powered single-engine helicopter satisfies the ACS requirement — the standard specifies single-engine, not a particular engine type. For documentation, the applicant must bring: the airworthiness certificate, aircraft registration, applicable operating limitations (AFM/POH), weight and balance data, and any required maintenance records demonstrating airworthiness. Additionally, the pilot must have a current medical or valid BasicMed, a current flight review or equivalent, and the appropriate logbook endorsements. The aircraft must have all instruments and equipment required for the tasks on the practical test.

questions.question: A student argues that since their training facility only has twin-engine helicopters available, the examiner should waive the single-engine requirement for autorotation tasks. What is your response as an examiner, and what options does the applicant realistically have?
questions.answer: The single-engine requirement for autorotation tasks is an ACS standard — it cannot be waived by an examiner. The examiner's authority does not extend to modifying published test standards. The applicant's realistic options include: renting or borrowing a single-engine helicopter from another facility or owner; arranging a temporary approval through the FSDO if there are extraordinary circumstances (which would be highly unusual); or postponing the checkride until a compliant aircraft is available. The applicant should have identified this logistical requirement during checkride planning, well before the test date.

questions.question: If an applicant's single-engine helicopter becomes mechanically unairworthy during the checkride — discovered after completing ground tasks but before the autorotation flight maneuvers — what are the examiner's options, and how does this affect the overall test?
questions.answer: The examiner must discontinue the practical test at that point if the aircraft is unairworthy, as 14 CFR 61.45 requires the aircraft to be airworthy throughout the test. The examiner may issue a notice of disapproval if the applicant failed any task already evaluated, or may issue a letter of discontinuance if no tasks were failed — which allows the applicant to complete the remaining tasks at a later date with an airworthy aircraft without retesting the already-passed areas. The applicant must have the aircraft repaired and return with documentation confirming airworthiness. The examiner should document the discontinuance clearly, noting the reason as mechanical unairworthiness rather than applicant failure.
questions.follow_up: What is the difference between a notice of disapproval and a letter of discontinuance, and which one benefits the applicant more in this scenario?
questions.follow_up_answer: A notice of disapproval means the applicant failed the test and must retest all required tasks, paying all applicable fees again. A letter of discontinuance means the test was stopped for reasons other than applicant failure — the applicant retains credit for tasks already satisfactorily completed and only needs to complete the remaining tasks. In this scenario, if the applicant had not yet failed any task, a letter of discontinuance is significantly more favorable: the applicant keeps credit for completed oral and ground tasks and only needs to demonstrate the flight tasks, including autorotations, once a compliant airworthy aircraft is available.

questions.question: An applicant provides a single-engine helicopter that is equipped with a helicopter terrain awareness and warning system (HTAWS) and an autopilot, but the AFM states autorotations must be performed with the autopilot disengaged. During the checkride, the applicant begins an autorotation with the autopilot engaged. Does this affect the validity of the maneuver for ACS purposes?
questions.answer: Yes, this significantly affects the validity of the maneuver. Operating contrary to AFM limitations is a violation of 14 CFR 91.9, which requires compliance with operating limitations. If the AFM states autorotations must be performed with the autopilot disengaged, engaging it constitutes non-compliance with the aircraft's operating limitations. From an ACS perspective, this would be grounds for failure on that task — the applicant is not demonstrating the maneuver within the limitations of the aircraft. Additionally, it represents a safety risk because autopilot behavior during autorotation entry may mask or interfere with the pilot's control inputs, potentially obscuring the examiner's ability to evaluate actual pilot skill. The examiner should note the violation and evaluate the task as unsatisfactory.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant claims they didn't know the AFM prohibited autopilot use during autorotations, how does that affect your evaluation, and what does it tell you about their systems knowledge?
questions.follow_up_answer: Ignorance of the AFM limitation does not excuse the violation — the applicant is expected to know their aircraft's operating limitations as part of ACS knowledge requirements (CH.XIV area tasks). Not knowing this limitation reveals a gap in aircraft systems knowledge that is itself grounds for concern about overall test readiness. An examiner should probe further with oral questions about the AFM's limitations section, emergency procedures, and the applicant's preflight preparation process. If the applicant cannot demonstrate adequate knowledge of their own aircraft's operating limitations, the examiner has grounds to question whether the applicant is prepared to pass the knowledge standards, independent of the flight performance evaluation.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.9; 14 CFR 61.45; ACS CH.XIV.I; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: If you show up to your practical test in a multiengine helicopter, what additional requirement does the ACS place on you beyond the standard required Tasks?
questions.answer: You must demonstrate all Tasks specific to multiengine helicopters IN ADDITION to all other Tasks required for the certificate or rating. You cannot substitute multiengine-specific Tasks for standard Tasks — you must complete both sets.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Helicopter ACS, Area of Operation XIV, Task I (An); FAA-H-8083-21B

questions.question: Can a multiengine helicopter be used to satisfy all required Tasks on a practical test, or are there Tasks that remain specific to single-engine operations?
questions.answer: A multiengine helicopter can be used for all standard required Tasks, but it does not eliminate or replace the need to also demonstrate those Tasks specifically designated for multiengine helicopters. Both the standard Task list and the multiengine-specific Tasks must be completed.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Helicopter ACS, Area of Operation XIV, Task I (An)

questions.question: What is the purpose of designating certain Tasks as 'specific to a multiengine helicopter' in the ACS?
questions.answer: Multiengine helicopters have unique operational characteristics — such as engine failure procedures with a second engine running, engine-out performance, and OEI (One Engine Inoperative) operations — that do not exist in single-engine helicopters. The ACS designates these as separate Tasks to ensure the applicant demonstrates competency in scenarios that only arise in a multiengine environment.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Helicopter ACS, Area of Operation XIV, Task I (An); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: You are scheduled for a commercial helicopter checkride and plan to use a twin-engine helicopter. During the oral, the examiner asks you to walk through how your Task list differs from what it would be if you had brought a single-engine helicopter. What do you tell the examiner?
questions.answer: The core required Tasks remain the same regardless of which helicopter I bring — I must demonstrate all standard Tasks for the commercial certificate. However, because I brought a multiengine helicopter, I am also required to demonstrate the additional Tasks specifically designated for multiengine helicopters in the ACS, such as OEI operations and multiengine emergency procedures. My overall Task list is therefore longer than it would be for a single-engine helicopter.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Helicopter ACS, Area of Operation XIV, Task I (An); FAA-H-8083-21B

questions.question: An applicant brings a multiengine helicopter to the checkride but tells the examiner they are not comfortable performing the multiengine-specific Tasks and wants to skip them. How should the examiner handle this, and what are the implications for the applicant?
questions.answer: The examiner cannot waive the multiengine-specific Tasks. The ACS is the standard against which the applicant is evaluated, and those Tasks are required when a multiengine helicopter is presented. If the applicant is unwilling or unable to perform those Tasks, the examiner must discontinue the test. The applicant may reschedule — either with adequate preparation on the multiengine helicopter, or by using a single-engine helicopter (in which case the multiengine-specific Tasks would not apply).
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Helicopter ACS, Area of Operation XIV, Task I (An); 14 CFR 61.43

questions.question: A flight school has only twin-engine helicopters in its fleet, so all their students do their checkrides in multiengine aircraft. Does this mean those pilots receive any additional limitation on their certificates compared to students who tested in single-engine helicopters?
questions.answer: No — a helicopter certificate does not carry a single-engine or multiengine limitation the way fixed-wing certificates do. The certificate simply states 'helicopter.' However, by testing in a multiengine helicopter and completing the multiengine-specific Tasks, the applicant demonstrates broader competency. PIC currency and proficiency in specific aircraft types are still governed by 14 CFR 61.57, but the certificate itself is not limited by the type of helicopter used at the checkride.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Helicopter ACS, Area of Operation XIV, Task I (An); 14 CFR 61.57; 14 CFR 61.31

questions.question: During a checkride in a multiengine helicopter, the aircraft experiences an actual single-engine malfunction mid-flight. The examiner simulated an engine failure earlier in the flight and the applicant performed it acceptably. Now with a real emergency, the applicant declares an emergency and lands safely, but never completed one of the remaining multiengine-specific Tasks. Can the examiner issue the certificate?
questions.answer: No — if a required Task was not completed due to the early termination of the test, the examiner cannot issue the certificate for the incomplete Task list. Per 14 CFR 61.43, all required Tasks must be completed satisfactorily. The examiner should document the situation carefully. Under the discontinuation provision, the applicant retains credit for the Tasks already completed and, on a retest, would only need to complete the remaining Task(s) — but the certificate cannot be issued until all required Tasks, including all multiengine-specific ones, are satisfactorily demonstrated.
questions.follow_up: What if the examiner argues that the real engine failure itself constituted a demonstration of the remaining multiengine emergency Task?
questions.follow_up_answer: The examiner cannot unilaterally substitute an actual emergency for a required Task demonstration unless the emergency genuinely and fully met all the performance criteria and elements of that specific ACS Task as written. The ACS describes specific knowledge, risk management, and skill elements. A real emergency may partially satisfy some elements, but the examiner must evaluate each element against the standard. If the emergency fully met all criteria for the outstanding Task, the examiner could make that judgment call and document it thoroughly — but this is a high bar and the examiner's call must be defensible to the FAA.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Helicopter ACS, Area of Operation XIV, Task I (An); 14 CFR 61.43(e); FAA Order 8900.2

questions.question: An applicant holds a private pilot certificate earned in a single-engine helicopter and now wants to add an instrument rating using a multiengine helicopter. They argue they should not have to re-demonstrate any standard Tasks since they already hold a certificate. How do you address this as an examiner?
questions.answer: The applicant is incorrect. Each practical test is evaluated against the full applicable ACS for the certificate or rating being sought — in this case the instrument rating ACS. The applicant must complete all Tasks required by the instrument rating ACS for helicopters. Additionally, because they are presenting a multiengine helicopter, they must also demonstrate any multiengine-specific Tasks called out in the ACS. A previously held certificate establishes eligibility to test, not an exemption from required Tasks on the new test.
questions.follow_up: If this same applicant later wants to add a commercial certificate and again uses the same multiengine helicopter, will they need to re-demonstrate the multiengine-specific Tasks a second time?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes — each practical test is independently evaluated against the applicable ACS. The commercial helicopter ACS has its own set of required Tasks, and if the applicant again brings a multiengine helicopter, they must again satisfy all multiengine-specific Tasks called out in the commercial ACS. Credit from a previous test does not carry over to a new certificate or rating practical test, even if the same aircraft and same Task types were demonstrated before.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Helicopter ACS, Area of Operation XIV, Task I (An); 14 CFR 61.43; 14 CFR 61.65

questions.question: What does FSTD stand for, and what regulatory part governs the qualification of these devices?
questions.answer: FSTD stands for Flight Simulation Training Device. These devices are qualified under 14 CFR Part 60, which establishes the standards for flight simulators and flight training devices used in aviation training and testing.

questions.question: Can you show up to a checkride, use an FSTD for part of the practical test, and be evaluated by any DPE regardless of what training program you attended?
questions.answer: No. Use of an FSTD qualified under 14 CFR Part 60 for any portion of a practical test is only permitted when that testing is conducted within an FAA-approved training program. The applicant must be enrolled in and conducting the test through that approved program — it is not available to applicants training outside of an FAA-approved training program.

questions.question: You trained for your instrument rating at a Part 141 helicopter school that uses a Level D full flight simulator qualified under Part 60. On the day of your checkride, the simulator is down for maintenance. Can the examiner conduct the simulator portion of the test in a simulator at a nearby Part 142 training center that also has a Part 60-qualified device?
questions.answer: Not automatically. The use of an FSTD for a practical test must occur within the context of an FAA-approved training program. If the applicant is enrolled in a Part 141 program, the test must be conducted under that program's approval. Using a simulator at a separate Part 142 center would require that center's FAA-approved program to cover the applicant's testing — simply having a Part 60-qualified device is not sufficient without the applicant being within an approved program that authorizes use of that specific device for testing.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 60; 14 CFR Part 141; 14 CFR Part 142; ACS CH.XIV.I

questions.question: A student trained entirely under a Part 61 instructor — no Part 141 or Part 142 program involved. The student's instructor wants to use a Part 60-qualified helicopter simulator at a local training center for the IFR portion of the checkride. Is this permissible under the ACS?
questions.answer: No. The ACS is explicit that use of a Part 60 qualified FSTD for any portion of a practical test is only permitted when conducted within an FAA-approved training program. A Part 61 training pathway outside of an approved program does not meet this requirement. The practical test for this student must be conducted in an actual aircraft for those elements the FSTD would otherwise cover, unless the student transitions into and completes training under a qualifying approved program.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 61; 14 CFR Part 60; ACS CH.XIV.I

questions.question: What is the practical significance of the phrase 'all or part' in the ACS requirement that applicants may accomplish 'all or part of a practical test' in a Part 60 FSTD? How does this affect checkride planning?
questions.answer: The phrase 'all or part' acknowledges that an FSTD may be used to complete the entire practical test or only specific tasks, depending on the FSTD's qualification level, the FAA-approved training program's authorization, and the ACS requirements for the certificate or rating sought. In checkride planning, this means the examiner and applicant must confirm: (1) which tasks the program is approved to test in the FSTD, (2) which tasks require the actual aircraft, and (3) that the FSTD's qualification level supports each task being tested. Some maneuvers — particularly those requiring real-world environmental factors — may need to be demonstrated in the aircraft even when an FSTD is available.

questions.question: An examiner discovers mid-checkride that the Part 60 FSTD being used is qualified for the fixed-wing aircraft it was originally certified for, but the training center recently began using it for helicopter IFR training without updating the Part 60 qualification to include the helicopter model. The applicant is in the middle of their instrument helicopter checkride. What are the implications, and what should the examiner do?
questions.answer: This is a significant problem. Under 14 CFR Part 60, an FSTD must be qualified for the specific aircraft category and, where applicable, make and model it is simulating. A simulator qualified only for fixed-wing operations cannot legally be used to conduct a helicopter practical test — even if it is otherwise a Part 60 device. The examiner must discontinue the FSTD portion of the test immediately. Continuing would render those test results invalid and potentially expose the examiner, training center, and applicant to regulatory violations. The examiner should document the issue, notify the FSDO, and work with the applicant to reschedule using a properly qualified device or complete remaining tasks in the actual aircraft if permitted by the program approval.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 60, Subparts A–C; ACS CH.XIV.I
questions.follow_up: If the applicant already completed several tasks in the unqualified FSTD before the issue was discovered, can those completed tasks be credited toward the checkride, or must the entire test be restarted?
questions.follow_up_answer: Tasks completed in an unqualified FSTD cannot be credited toward the practical test because the device did not meet the Part 60 qualification requirement for helicopter operations — a foundational requirement for FSTD use in testing. The examiner has the authority to issue a Notice of Disapproval or simply discontinue and treat the event as incomplete. In either case, the entire practical test — or at minimum all tasks conducted in the non-compliant device — would need to be repeated in a properly qualified FSTD or the actual aircraft. The examiner should consult with the managing FSDO for guidance on how to officially document the event.

questions.question: A Part 142 training center has an FAA-approved training program for the helicopter ATP certificate and uses a Part 60-qualified Level C helicopter simulator. An applicant who completed ATP training there wants to use the same simulator for a subsequent add-on instrument rating practical test. The instrument rating is not specifically listed in the center's approved training program. Can the simulator be used for the instrument rating checkride?
questions.answer: No. The authorization to use a Part 60 FSTD for a practical test is tied specifically to an FAA-approved training program, and that program must cover the certificate or rating being tested. Even though the FSTD itself is Part 60 qualified and available at the center, using it for the instrument rating checkride requires that the center's approved program explicitly includes instrument rating training and testing. If the Part 142 program approval only covers the ATP certificate, the instrument rating practical test cannot be conducted in the FSTD under that program. The applicant would need to either train under a program that includes instrument rating authorization or conduct the test in an actual aircraft.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 60; 14 CFR Part 142; ACS CH.XIV.I
questions.follow_up: Can the Part 142 center amend its approved training program to add instrument rating testing, and how would that process work?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes. A Part 142 training center can submit a revision to its training specifications (TSpecs) to the FAA to add the instrument rating to its approved training program. This process involves submitting the proposed curriculum, training standards, and FSTD utilization plan to the responsible FSDO or CMO (Certificate Management Office) for review and approval. The FAA will evaluate whether the FSTD's Part 60 qualification level supports the tasks required for the instrument rating and whether the curriculum meets the applicable ACS standards. Until that amendment is approved, the center cannot use the simulator for instrument rating checkrides.

questions.question: Can an applicant use an Aviation Training Device (ATD) to complete a practical test for a pilot certificate or rating?
questions.answer: No. Applicants for a pilot certificate or rating are specifically prohibited from using an ATD to accomplish a practical test. ATDs may be used for certain training and currency purposes, but not for the actual practical test itself. The practical test must be conducted in an aircraft or, where authorized, a full flight simulator or flight training device of the appropriate level.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.4; 14 CFR Part 61 general ATD limitations

questions.question: What is the difference between an ATD and a Flight Training Device (FTD) when it comes to completing a 14 CFR 61.58 pilot-in-command proficiency check?
questions.answer: An ATD cannot be used to accomplish a 14 CFR 61.58 PIC proficiency check. An FTD, depending on its qualification level and the specific authorization in the applicable regulations, may be approved for certain proficiency checks. ATDs are the lowest level of FAA-approved training devices and carry the most restrictions on what tasks they can be used to satisfy.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.58; 14 CFR 61.1 (definitions of ATD, FTD, FFS)

questions.question: A pilot wants to use an ATD to complete the flight portion of a 14 CFR 61.57 flight review. Is this permitted?
questions.answer: No. The flight portion of a 14 CFR 61.57 flight review cannot be accomplished in an ATD. While an ATD may be used for the ground instruction portion or for certain instrument currency tasks under 61.57(c), the flight portion of the biennial flight review itself must be conducted in an aircraft or an appropriately qualified and authorized simulator or FTD — not an ATD.

questions.question: You are a helicopter student preparing for your instrument rating checkride. Your CFI-I says you've been logging ATD time toward your instrument experience requirements. On the day of the checkride, the helicopter is down for maintenance and your school only has an ATD available. Can you proceed with the checkride in the ATD?
questions.answer: No, you cannot proceed with the checkride in the ATD. Regardless of how much ATD time was legitimately logged toward instrument experience requirements, applicants for a pilot certificate or rating — including an instrument rating — are prohibited from using an ATD to accomplish a practical test. The checkride must be rescheduled until an aircraft, appropriately qualified FFS, or FTD is available.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.4; ACS helicopter instrument rating requirements

questions.question: A commercial helicopter pilot's 61.58 PIC proficiency check is due. The operator's only approved training device is an ATD. The pilot argues that since the ATD is FAA-approved and he has been training in it, it should count. How do you respond as the examiner?
questions.answer: FAA approval of an ATD for training purposes does not extend to its use for a 61.58 proficiency check. The regulations are explicit: an ATD cannot be used to accomplish a 14 CFR 61.58 proficiency check. The pilot must complete the check in an aircraft, a qualified Full Flight Simulator (FFS), or an appropriately qualified FTD as authorized under the applicable rules. FAA approval for training use and approval for check use are two distinct authorizations.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.58; 14 CFR 61.4; AC 61-136 (FAA approval of ATDs)

questions.question: Explain the practical reasoning behind why the FAA prohibits using an ATD for practical tests and flight reviews, given that ATDs are FAA-approved training devices.
questions.answer: ATDs are approved for training and building procedural proficiency in a low-cost, low-risk environment, but they do not replicate the full aerodynamic fidelity, motion cues, visual systems, or environmental conditions of actual flight. Practical tests and flight reviews are designed to evaluate real-world pilot competency and airmanship, which requires demonstration of skills in conditions that approximate actual flight. An ATD cannot adequately replicate the complexity and unpredictability of real flight conditions — such as actual turbulence, helicopter vibration and torque effects, or genuine emergency management — making it unsuitable as a sole means of evaluating pilot certification standards.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot holds an instrument rating and wants to use an ATD to maintain instrument currency under 14 CFR 61.57(c). He then argues that since ATD time counts for currency under 61.57(c), it should logically also count for the flight review under 61.57(a). As an examiner, how do you distinguish these two provisions and explain why one is permitted and the other is not?
questions.answer: These are two entirely separate provisions within 61.57. Under 14 CFR 61.57(c), the FAA explicitly authorizes the use of approved ATDs to accomplish specific instrument experience tasks for currency purposes — this is a targeted regulatory carve-out for currency maintenance. Under 14 CFR 61.57(a), the flight review requires a flight with a CFI that evaluates overall piloting proficiency, and the regulations do not extend ATD use to satisfy the flight portion of that review. The existence of an explicit authorization in 61.57(c) does not create an implicit authorization elsewhere in the regulation. Regulatory permissions are specific and cannot be extrapolated by analogy.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot completed the ground portion of the flight review with a CFI using the ATD, would that ground portion be valid, and what would still need to be accomplished?
questions.follow_up_answer: The ground training portion of a flight review has no specific regulatory restriction on the use of ATDs or ground-based training — it can be accomplished using any appropriate instructional means including an ATD, ground school, or oral review. What remains required is the flight portion: a minimum of one hour of flight training with a certificated flight instructor in an aircraft (or appropriately qualified simulator/FTD). The ATD cannot substitute for that flight portion. Once the CFI endorses the logbook, the review is complete only after both portions are satisfactorily accomplished.

questions.question: During an instrument helicopter checkride debrief, your applicant asks: 'If I fail one task today and need a retest, can I practice that specific maneuver in an ATD before my retest, and then do the retest in the ATD?' Address both parts of that question.
questions.answer: The applicant may absolutely use an ATD to practice and improve proficiency on the failed task before the retest — ATDs are well-suited for this kind of targeted remedial training, and there is no prohibition on using an ATD for training purposes. However, the retest (which is still a practical test for a pilot certificate or rating) cannot be conducted in an ATD under any circumstances. The retest must be conducted in an aircraft or a qualified FFS/FTD as appropriate. Using the ATD for remedial training is not only permitted but encouraged; using it for the actual retest is expressly prohibited.
questions.follow_up: What documentation should the applicant's CFI provide before the retest, and what must the examiner verify before proceeding?
questions.follow_up_answer: Before the retest, the CFI must provide a signed and dated logbook endorsement stating that the applicant has received additional training on the deficient area(s) and is now considered proficient. The examiner must verify this endorsement is present and current, confirm the applicant's identification and eligibility documents remain valid, and ensure the aircraft or qualified device being used for the retest is appropriate. The examiner is only required to retest the task(s) that were failed, not the entire practical test, though the examiner retains discretion to evaluate any task if safety concerns arise.

questions.question: What document authorizes an Aviation Training Device (ATD) for use in logging pilot training time, and how long is it valid?
questions.answer: An ATD is authorized by an FAA Letter of Authorization (LOA). The LOA is typically valid for 60 calendar months from the date of issue, after which it may be renewed if the ATD continues to meet FAA standards and the sponsor remains in compliance with all conditions of the authorization.

questions.question: What information is contained in an ATD's Letter of Authorization regarding pilot training?
questions.answer: The LOA specifies the pilot time credit allowances — meaning how many hours of ATD time may be credited toward specific certificates or ratings — along with the associated limitations on how that time may be logged and applied.

questions.question: Who issues the Letter of Authorization for an Aviation Training Device?
questions.answer: The FAA issues the Letter of Authorization for an ATD. The LOA is granted to the ATD manufacturer or sponsor following FAA evaluation and approval of the device.

questions.question: You are logging instrument time in an ATD for your instrument rating. How would you verify that the device is legally approved to credit that time toward your rating requirements?
questions.answer: You should physically review the ATD's FAA Letter of Authorization to confirm: (1) the LOA is current — still within its 60 calendar month validity period; (2) the device is approved for the specific type of time you intend to log (e.g., instrument experience, instrument training); and (3) there are no limitations in the LOA that would restrict your particular use. If the LOA has expired, the device cannot be used to credit training time toward FAA requirements.
